(RC Makati West) Editorial  Reginald T. Yu Editor-in-Chief As the Rotary Club of Manila prepares to open another year of inquiry, dialogue, and civic leadership, it does so with a tradition that has quietly become a barometer of national mood: inviting the Governor of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas as its first speaker of the year. This year’s engagement carries particular weight. The guest is Eli M. Remolona Jr., the 7th Governor of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, and the moment is unusually consequential. The year ahead — 2026 — will test not only economic fundamentals, but the country’s institutional maturity, policy discipline, and capacity to navigate a far more fragmented global order. This is no longer a post-pandemic recovery conversation. That chapter has closed. What lies ahead is a recalibration — harder, more structural, and more unforgiving of complacency. Globally, the narrative of “soft landings” and gentle normalization has begun to fray. Interest rates remain structurally higher than the decade-long norms many markets had grown accustomed to. Geopolitical tensions — whether in trade, energy, or security — are no longer episodic disruptions but persistent features of the landscape. Supply chains are being redesigned not for maximum efficiency, but for resilience and strategic alignment. For emerging economies like the Philippines, this environment presents both opportunity and risk. Capital is more discerning. Investors are no longer chasing yield blindly; they are pricing credibility, policy coherence, and institutional strength. In this context, central banks are not merely custodians of inflation targets—they are anchors of confidence. It is precisely here that Governor Remolona’s perspective becomes critical. Domestically, the Philippine economy enters 2026 with respectable momentum but unresolved tensions. Growth remains consumption-led, supported by remittances and a young demographic profile. Yet beneath the headline numbers lie structural questions that cannot be deferred indefinitely: • Can growth be sustained without reigniting inflationary pressures? • Will fiscal consolidation keep pace with ambitious infrastructure and social spending? • How resilient is the peso in an era of volatile capital flows and geopolitical shocks? • And perhaps most importantly: can policy coordination remain credible as political and economic cycles converge? Governor Remolona inherits a central bank that has earned international respect for its professionalism. But credibility, once earned, must be renewed continuously. The BSP’s challenge in 2026 will not simply be to manage inflation—it will be to manage expectations, especially in a society where economic optimism and economic anxiety often coexist. One of the underappreciated roles of a central bank is its function as a moral authority in economic life. Beyond interest rates and reserve requirements, it signals discipline in a world prone to excess, patience in an age of haste, and long-term thinking in political environments often governed by short horizons. Governor Remolona’s background — as an economist steeped in global finance and institutional reform — suggests a leadership style attuned to complexity rather than slogans. For business leaders, professionals, and civic stewards gathered at the Rotary Club of Manila, his message is expected to be less about reassurance and more about realism. And realism, in 2026, is itself a form of leadership. That the Rotary Club of Manila has long made it a point to hear from the BSP Governor at the start of the year is no accident. Rotary’s constituency — entrepreneurs, executives, professionals, and civic leaders — operates at the intersection of policy and practice. Decisions made in boardrooms, factories, clinics, and communities are shaped, directly or indirectly, by the signals sent from the central bank. In convening this conversation, the Club affirms its role not merely as a fellowship of service, but as a forum for informed citizenship. Rotary does not wait for certainty; it prepares its members to lead amid uncertainty. If there is one likely theme that will define the economic prospects of 2026, it is this: less comfort, more clarity. The era of cheap money is behind us. The tolerance for policy drift is narrowing. But for economies that can demonstrate discipline, adaptability, and institutional trust, the coming years may well reward seriousness over spectacle. As the Rotary Club of Manila listens to Governor Remolona, it does so not in search of predictions, but of bearings. In a world where noise is abundant, clarity is rare—and therefore invaluable. The question for 2026 is not whether challenges will arise. They will. The real question is whether the country’s institutions — and its leaders — are prepared to meet them with steadiness, credibility, and foresight. That is why this first speech matters. Guest of Honor and Speaker’s Profile  Dr. Eli Remolona Jr. is the Governor of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP). Before joining the BSP, he already had a long career in central banking. Governor Remolona worked at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York for 14 years and at the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) for 19 years. At the BIS in Basel, Switzerland, he was Head of Financial Markets and Editor of the BIS Quarterly Review. Afterwards, he served as Regional Head for Asia and the Pacific. He has taught at Williams College, Columbia University, New York University, the Asia School of Business and the University of the Philippines. He has published widely in scholarly journals, writing mainly on monetary policy, international finance and financial markets. He has a Ph.D. in economics from Stanford University. President’s Mid-Year Message  As we cross the midpoint of this Rotary Year, the Rotary Club of Manila must pause not merely to take stock of time elapsed, but to reflect with gratitude on the purpose fulfilled, the service rendered, and the collective spirit that has animated our work during the first half of this term. Indeed, the past six months have affirmed a truth long embedded in the DNA of this venerable Club: that service, when anchored on tradition yet responsive to contemporary needs, remains both relevant and transformative. Guided by Rotary’s enduring ideals and strengthened by the experience and commitment of our members, RC Manila has pursued its mission with quiet confidence, purposeful energy, and an unwavering sense of responsibility to the communities we serve. Across our various avenues of service, the Club has successfully implemented a wide range of initiatives and programs that reflect both breadth and depth -- programs that are not episodic gestures, but carefully designed interventions aimed at sustainable and measurable impact. Our flagship programs – LEAP Awards, ARAL Program, and Project RIVER – as well as our signature projects – TOWER Awards, Outstanding Ambassador Award, Journalism Award -- have continued to advance education, promote peace, recognize excellence in public service and labor, and uphold the vital role of a free and responsible press. Each initiative bears the imprint of thoughtful planning, strong partnerships, and the shared conviction that service must be meaningful, inclusive, and enduring. Equally significant has been the Club’s continued emphasis on fellowship and institutional strength. The first half of the year has seen active engagement among members, robust participation in meetings and projects, and a reaffirmation of the bonds that unite us as Rotarians and as friends. In a time when voluntary service competes with ever-growing personal and professional demands, the sustained commitment of our members stands as a testament to the enduring appeal of Rotary’s call to “Service Above Self.” This midpoint also offers an opportunity for introspection. Leadership in Rotary is not measured by individual visibility, but by the ability to harness collective wisdom, encourage collaboration, and ensure continuity. Any progress achieved thus far is the product of shared leadership – of the Directors and Officers who have discharged their duties with diligence, of Committee Chairs who have translated vision into action, and of each Manila Rotarian who quietly but consistently contributed time, talent, and treasure that give life to our programs. As we look toward the second half of the Rotary Year, we do so with both confidence and renewed urgency. There remains much to accomplish, milestones yet to be reached, and initiatives that invite further expansion and refinement. The challenge before us is not simply to sustain momentum, but to deepen impact, that is, to ensure that our projects continue to address real needs, inspire trust, and leave lasting benefits well beyond the confines of this Rotary Year. At this halfway point, it is worth remembering that while a presidency is finite, the legacy of service is not. Our task, therefore, is to build on the strong foundation already laid, to steward the Club’s resources wisely, and to honor the proud heritage of the Rotary Club of Manila by leaving it stronger, more united, and more responsive to the times. With gratitude for the journey thus far and optimism for the months ahead, we move forward -- celebrating our Club’s Destiny and Legacy -- steadfast in purpose, united in fellowship, and resolute in our commitment to service. A Midday of Meaning, Memory, and Mission: The 15th Weekly Membership Meeting of the Rotary Club of Manila PE Reginald T. Yu There Rotary meetings — and then there are gatherings that quietly affirm why institutions endure. On a December midday at the venerable Manila Polo Club, the Rotary Club of Manila convened its Fifteenth Weekly Membership Meeting for Rotary Year 2025–2026, the last regular meeting for the year 2025. It was not a meeting defined by clockwork precision or formal sequence alone, but by something deeper: continuity of purpose, fidelity to tradition, and the unmistakable sense that service — when done consistently and without spectacle — becomes history. As members and guests gathered over a shared meal, the atmosphere carried the familiar cadence of Rotary fellowship. Conversations crossed professions and generations; greetings were warm but unhurried. The room, steeped in decades of civic memory, seemed to understand that what was about to unfold was less a program and more a reaffirmation. Sacred Openings and Shared Ideals The formal program opened not with urgency, but with reverence. A solemn Doxology, rendered by Teatro Rizalia, gently centered the assembly, reminding everyone present that Rotary’s work — however practical — rests upon moral grounding. This was followed by an Invocation led by Director-elect Carlos G. “Caloy” Serapio, whose prayer framed the gathering as one not merely of minds, but of conscience. The national anthems of the United States and the Philippines, performed with dignity, underscored the international character of Rotary and the enduring bonds between peoples who share democratic ideals and a commitment to peace. The Rotary Club of Manila Hymn, sung by the RCM WF Music Chorale, followed — less a song than a collective memory set to music. When the Four-Way Test was recited, led by Past Director Issam Eldebs, it did not sound rehearsed. It sounded lived-in — principles tested and applied daily by men and women who understand that ethics are not slogans, but habits. Leadership in Quiet Motion The acknowledgment of guests, masterfully moderated by DSAA John M. Cutter, set the tone for a meeting that balanced protocol with warmth. A welcome song once again brought the Chorale to the fore, reinforcing the idea that Rotary gatherings are sustained not just by speeches, but by shared participation. President Raoul C. Creencia, during his President’s Time, spoke not as a figurehead but as a steward—offering reflections that tied recent accomplishments to Rotary’s broader mission. His remarks carried the confidence of leadership grounded in teamwork, a reminder that progress is seldom the work of one. Honoring Service Beyond Borders A defining moment of the meeting was the presentation of the Rotary Club of Manila Outstanding Ambassador of the Year Award. Introduced by Past District Governor Joaquin “Jackie” C. Rodriguez, Sr., Chairman of the Ambassador of the Year Committee, the award was conferred upon Her Excellency MaryKay L. Carlson, Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of the United States of America to the Philippines. Her Excellency MaryKay L. Carlson, Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of the United States to the Philippines, has been honored with the Rotary Club of Manila's Outstanding Ambassador of the Year Award. The recognition was not ceremonial flattery. It was acknowledgment of a diplomatic presence marked by consistency, respect, and a deep appreciation for people-to-people engagement. The serenade that followed — performed by Himig Rizalia — served as a cultural offering, affirming that gratitude, when sincere, is best expressed through shared heritage. The Ambassador was formally introduced by Rotarian Victor “Vic” G. Garcia III, after which she addressed the Club. Her speech, received with attentiveness and respect, stood as a testament to enduring alliances and mutual service — but its substance remains purposefully unrecorded here, allowing the moment itself to stand intact. Standing once more within the storied halls of the Manila Polo Club, Her Excellency MaryKay L. Carlson spoke not merely as a diplomat fulfilling protocol, but as a witness to a relationship shaped by time, trial, and trust. Her return to the Rotary Club of Manila—Asia’s first Rotary Club—was framed as both a privilege and a homecoming, underscoring the symbolic weight of place in the long arc of history. She began by acknowledging what Rotarians know instinctively but rarely articulate aloud: that service, when sustained and sincere, leaves an imprint. The Ambassador’s admiration for the Club’s recent accomplishments was not perfunctory praise. Her remark—that a single month’s report read like a year’s worth of work—was both astonishment and affirmation. It reflected an understanding that Rotary’s impact lies not in isolated events, but in relentless consistency, in showing up again and again for the common good. Receiving the Outstanding Ambassador Award, Ambassador Carlson responded not with personal triumph, but with collective humility. She accepted the recognition on behalf of the entire U.S. Embassy team, situating the honor within a broader narrative of partnership between nations. In doing so, she reinforced a central theme of her address: that diplomacy, like Rotary service, is never the work of one individual alone. It is sustained by teams, institutions, and shared purpose. People-to-People: The Quiet Architecture of Diplomacy At the heart of her reflections was a conviction that the strongest alliances are not forged solely through treaties or official statements, but through human connection. Ambassador Carlson emphasized that people-to-people ties form the living architecture of U.S.–Philippine relations. She highlighted the Philippine-American Educational Foundation (PAEF) — widely known as Fulbright — as a powerful symbol of this bond. Home to the world’s longest-running Fulbright Commission, the program stands as a quiet but enduring engine of mutual understanding. Through scholarships and exchanges, including in advanced fields such as space science and civil nuclear workforce development, generations of Filipinos and Americans have crossed borders not merely to study, but to return home transformed—carrying with them shared values, expertise, and lifelong connections. With more than 10,000 alumni, these exchanges have created a living bridge between societies, one that renews itself daily through classrooms, laboratories, public service, and innovation. The Ambassador made clear that such investments are not abstract ideals; they are deliberate commitments to a shared future. Service Rekindled: The Return of the Peace Corps Ambassador Carlson’s reflections turned next to the Peace Corps, another enduring symbol of grassroots partnership. During her tenure, 170 new volunteers were deployed to the Philippines — joining over 9,000 who have served Filipino communities since 1961. This achievement carried special resonance. In the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, when Peace Corps operations were halted worldwide, restarting the program required not only logistical coordination, but trust, resilience, and renewed commitment. Bringing Peace Corps back into service was, as the Ambassador noted, no small feat. It stood as proof that shared purpose can outlast even global disruption. Peace Corps volunteers, she emphasized, embody the very spirit that defines the U.S.–Philippine relationship: partnership rooted in humility, service grounded in respect, and a belief that real change begins at the community level. Partners in Prosperity: Building the Future Together Beyond people-to-people ties, Ambassador Carlson articulated a vision of the two nations as partners in prosperity. She pointed to collaborative initiatives such as the Luzon Economic Corridor, where the United States, the Philippines, Japan, and other like-minded partners are accelerating high-impact investments designed to spur growth from Subic Bay across key regions. She cited concrete examples to illustrate how diplomacy translates into livelihoods. The expansion of the Royal Cold Storage Facility in Bulacan by I Squared Capital, she explained, is not merely an infrastructure project — it is an investment in food security, job creation, and regional resilience. The firm’s commitment of over two billion U.S. dollars across logistics, energy, and digital infrastructure exemplifies how private-sector engagement can deliver tangible, lasting benefits. "… economic cooperation becomes an extension of service: a means of empowering communities, strengthening systems, and ensuring shared growth." In this framing, economic cooperation becomes an extension of service: a means of empowering communities, strengthening systems, and ensuring shared growth. Allies in Security, United in Crisis The Ambassador’s address then turned to the enduring strength of the U.S.–Philippine alliance as security partners. With the upcoming 75th anniversary of the Mutual Defense Treaty, she described the alliance as ironclad — not as rhetoric, but as lived reality. She referenced the United States’ recent announcement of 500 million U.S. dollars in supplemental foreign military financing to support the modernization of the Armed Forces of the Philippines and enhance maritime security. Yet, it was her discussion of disaster response that carried particular emotional weight. In recounting U.S. assistance following Super Typhoon Uwan, Ambassador Carlson emphasized that the 2.5 million dollars cited represented only the value of commodities delivered. It did not include the deployment of U.S. military airlift capabilities or personnel on the ground. This distinction mattered. It underscored a deeper truth: that in moments of crisis, alliances are measured not by statements, but by speed, presence, and solidarity. Rotary and the Spirit of Shared Purpose In closing, Ambassador Carlson drew a parallel between the alliance she represents and the institution before her. The Rotary Club of Manila, she observed, embodies the same spirit that animates strong international partnerships: leadership anchored in service, devotion to the common good, and a quiet refusal to be indifferent. As the world looks toward 2026 — the 80th anniversary of formal U.S.– Philippine diplomatic relations—her remarks resonated as both reflection and invitation. There is much to celebrate, yes, but also much to steward. The future, she implied, will belong to those who choose cooperation over isolation, service over self-interest, and shared destiny over short-term gain. In that sense, her address was not merely a speech — it was a reaffirmation of a covenant. One between nations. One between institutions. And one between people who believe that the truest measure of partnership is not power, but purpose. Ambassador Carlson and PP Chito Zaldarriaga during the Q&A Fellowship in Celebration As the program transitioned into celebration, the Rotary Club of Manila did what it has always done best: honor its own. Birthday celebrants — spanning seasoned past directors to current leaders and active members — were recognized not merely for another year lived, but for years of service given. In Rotary, birthdays are less about age and more about accumulated commitment. The list was long, the applause sincere. Each name carried with it stories of committee meetings, service projects, and quiet acts of generosity rarely seen but deeply felt. Welcoming New Stewards of Service Few moments in Rotary are as quietly powerful as an Induction of New Members. Introduced by President Creencia and presented by Past President Domingo S.B. “Boy” Guevara together with President-Elect Reginald T. “Reggie” Yu, the induction welcomed professionals from law, real estate, medicine, physical therapy, and commodities trading. Each new member stood not as an addition to a roster, but as a new custodian of Rotary’s ideals. Their Oath of Membership, administered by the President, was more than a formality — it was an entry into a lineage of service that predates them and will, in time, outlast them. Accountability and the Future in View Transparency and stewardship took center stage as Past District Governor Alexander P. “Alex” Cureg delivered the RCMFI Accomplishment and Financial Status Report. Numbers were presented not as abstractions, but as reflections of trust — resources entrusted by members to serve causes larger than themselves. This was followed by the NOMELEC Results, reported by President-Elect Reggie Yu, signaling continuity, order, and democratic process within the Club’s governance. Leadership, after all, is not only about vision, but about orderly succession. A Meeting That Echoes Forward When the meeting adjourned, there was no sense of finality — only momentum. Members lingered. Conversations resumed. Plans were quietly discussed. The Rotary Club of Manila, Asia’s first Rotary Club, once again demonstrated that longevity is not sustained by nostalgia, but by relevance; not by ceremony alone, but by service renewed week after week. In a world increasingly defined by noise and haste, this meeting offered something rarer: measured purpose, earned tradition, and a shared belief that service — when done faithfully — becomes legacy. 15th Weekly Membership Meeting Fellowship Club Administration  RCM Members’ Attendance Report
RY 2025-2026 List of Members Who Have Paid Their Annual Dues for RY 2025-2026 As of January 6, 2026 Governor’s Visit to the Rotary Club of Manila  The Governor’s Visit to the Rotary Club of Manila was held on December 15, 2025 at SMX MOA’s Meeting Room 7. Joining District Governor Mary Mei Rodrigo from the RIDistrict 3810 team were District Secretary General and DGND Hermie Esguerra, District Executive Secretary Eric Candidato, Chief of Staff George Ng, District Treasurer Cristy Esquiban, and District TRF Chair James Tan. With President Raoul Creencia were PE Reggie Yu (rendered the invocation), Assistant Internal Auditor /Director-elect Mike Roxas (led the recitation of The Rotarian Pledge), Director Warren So (led the recitation of the 4-Way Test), Director Edwin Hernandez (presented the RCM Board of Directors, Officers and Project Chair), Secretary Anton Mauricio (presented the Board of Directors and Officers), Assistant Secretary Paco Magsaysay, Vice Presidentelect/Assistant Treasurer Karlo Castro, Internal Auditor Nick Locsin, Director-elect/Board Legal Adviser Caloy Serapio, Director-elect/LEAP Chair Teddy Kalaw, Program Chair/Director-elect Del Lorenzana, and Oral Health Chair/ DSAA John Cutter. Rotary Club of Manila Brings Joy to SPED Students This Christmas  On December 10, 2025, the Ynares Event Center in Antipolo City came alive with laughter, joy, and the spirit of giving as the Rotary Club of Manila hosted its annual SPED Family Fun Day. This heartwarming event brought together special education (SPED) students and their families for a day filled with meaningful connections, holiday cheer, and acts of kindness. Guided by the Rotary motto, Service Above Self, the event celebrated the resilience and vibrant spirit of these remarkable young learners. Through thoughtful gift-giving, engaging activities, and shared moments of joy, the Rotary Club reaffirmed its commitment to fostering inclusion, dignity, and equal opportunities for all. OPLAN KALINGA: Surgical Outreach Mission at Our Lady of Grace Hospital  Our Lady of Grace Hospital in San Dionisio, Parañaque became a place of healing and compassion as the Rotary Club of Manila, RC Manila Foundation, Inc., and the World Surgical Foundation Philippines joined forces for OPLAN KALINGA. Held on December 11-12, 2025, this surgical outreach mission provided free, essential surgeries to patients who had long-awaited care they could not afford. Volunteer surgeons, nurses, and medical staff worked with precision and heart, ensuring that each patient left not only with improved health but also with renewed hope for the future. President Raoul Creencia attended the event, alongside Project Chair Dr. Paul Koh, Co-Chair Dr. Jun Aventura, and Secretary Anton Mauricio. The World Surgical Foundation Philippines team was led by its President, Dr. Suntay. For many, these procedures were life-changing, offering relief from pain and the chance to reclaim their daily lives. OPLAN KALINGA reflects the Rotary’s unwavering dedication to action-driven service. It’s about more than medical care—it’s about showing up for those who need it most and proving that compassion, when paired with action, can truly transform lives. Christmas Gift-Giving in Bulacan  The Rotary Club of Manila, in partnership with the Dangal ng Bulacan Foundation, Inc., brought much-needed relief and holiday cheer to four barangays across Bulacan. These communities, still recovering from severe flooding, were reminded that they are not alone this Christmas. The gift-giving activity held on December 20, 2025 was more than just distributing presents—it was about showing solidarity and offering a sense of hope during difficult times. Rotarians and volunteers worked hand in hand to deliver not only gifts but also a message of care and support. The event highlighted the power of partnerships and the importance of reaching out to those in need. For the families in Bulacan, it was a moment of joy amidst challenges, and for those who participated, it was a meaningful way to live out the true spirit of the season. The partnership between WASH-Ed and the Rotary Club of Manila focuses on: • WASH education outreach — delivering hygiene lessons and skill building to students and communities. • Community engagement projects — Rotary and Rotaract mobilizing volunteers and resources to support WASH learning and facilities. Country Above Self: The Officer and the Gentleman - The Life and Legacy of Rafael Moreno Alunan III PE Reginald T. Yu Editor’s Note: Writing about Rafael M. Alunan III is less the task of biography than of bearing witness. His story is not simply one of power attained or history shaped; it is a meditation on what it means to remain good in a world that rewards everything but goodness. He belongs to that rare generation who believed that public service is a sacred trust — who measured progress not by applause but by conscience. His moral clarity came not from privilege but from pilgrimage: from the crucible of duty, the classroom of faith, and the quiet courage of love. This piece closes not with finality but with continuity — because his mission, like the Republic’s, remains unfinished. Somewhere, perhaps even now, he is drafting another column, delivering another lecture, consoling another widow of a soldier, or advising a young mayor tempted by shortcuts. And when he speaks, the cadence is unchanged: calm, precise, resolute — a man who has mastered not only command, but compassion. In the end, Raffy Alunan’s life reminds us that greatness is not the absence of failure, but the refusal to surrender virtue in its aftermath. His journey affirms that faith and reason, leadership and humility, courage and tenderness — all can coexist in one heart devoted wholly to God and country. May this work stand not as monument but as mirror — reflecting the best of what we can still become if we, too, choose to serve above self. The gunfire began long before dawn. In the cold stillness of December 1989, as rebel forces rushed the financial heart of Makati and armed factions clashed across the nation’s capital, Raffy Alunan found himself standing once again in the uncertain space between order and collapse. Earlier that day, as part of a SAF company deployed to capture an NPA base camp, he had flown under the radar — literally — to make it home in time for his daughter’s birthday. But celebrations would soon be overtaken by the growing specter of political fracture. By nightfall, Manila was under siege. Rebel troops had overrun the business district. Civilians and foreign guests were trapped inside Makati’s hotels. The city’s lifeline was suspended between panic and paralysis. And into that crucible, Raffy Alunan — then serving as a key member of the Aquino administration — was tasked with a mission that would become emblematic of his entire public career: Negotiate the safe release of innocent lives in the middle of an armed rebellion. He moved quickly. He sought the cooperation of the Scout Rangers, appealed to their instincts as protectors, and asked for one thing: “Let us retrieve the civilians before the shooting consumes them.” In the face-to-face talks at the Manila Intercontinental Hotel, he worked with PMA Superintendent Major-General Arturo Enrile and coordinated the delicate exchanges that allowed government teams to extract trapped tourists and Filipinos from active conflict zones. It was a moment that distilled the essence of the path he had chosen — or perhaps, the path that had chosen him. Not power. Not politics. But stewardship. Crisis management. And the unyielding conviction that in moments of national fracture, one must stand where the lives are most at risk. By the time the coup attempt was quelled, dozens of civilians had been pulled to safety. The Republic had survived another tremor in its fragile democratic rebuilding. And Raffy Alunan had cemented a reputation he never sought but consistently proved worthy of — the steady hand in chaos, the quiet soldier-statesman whose duty was always to save, not to shine. This was but one episode in a long arc of service marked by danger, discipline, and moral resolve. But it captures, in a single frame, the truth of the man: When the Republic was threatened, he stepped forward. When lives hung in the balance, he negotiated for peace. When crisis erupted, he moved toward the fire — never away. This is the story of Rafael Moreno Alunan III. Not as myth. Not as crafted legend. But as he lived it — a life of stewardship, service, and fidelity to the moral values he believed could build a better Philippines. The Boy from Bacolod Long before Raffy would find himself negotiating with rebels in a besieged Manila hotel, or working beside presidents during some of the nation’s most precarious years, his story had already been set in motion by the weight — and quiet dignity — of a name he inherited. That name belonged first to Rafael Rivas Alunan Sr., a man born in 1885 in Talisay, Negros Occidental, who came of age in the uncertain dawn between Spanish rule and the burgeoning American administration. The elder Alunan was a scholar of the old mold — educated at the Colegio de Bacolod de los Recoletos, then at the Ateneo de Manila, graduating in business at seventeen and later reading law. He was not simply a participant in the nation-in-the-making; he was one of its architects. As a young legislator representing Negros Occidental’s 2nd District, he would serve three consecutive terms in the Philippine Assembly beginning in 1912, later becoming floor leader of the House. He would go on to hold posts that placed him at the crossroads of the country’s economic transformation — Secretary of Agriculture and Natural Resources, Secretary of Finance, Acting Secretary of Public Works, and, at the onset of the Pacific War, Secretary of the Interior. He was a prominent force in the sugar industry, heading the Bacolod-Murcia Milling Company and the Philippine Sugar Association at a time when sugar was one of the pillars of Philippine economic power. History, however, had harsher tests in store. When Japanese forces occupied the Philippines, Alunan Sr. held cabinet posts under duress. After the liberation, many officials of the wartime Philippine Republic faced accusations of treason. In February 1947, after a long legal ordeal, the charges against him were dismissed — there was no evidence that he had cooperated with the enemy beyond performing the duties required of him under occupation. He died that same year, his name cleared, leaving behind seven children and a legacy marked by service, controversy, vindication, and public purpose. It was into this lineage that Rafael de la Rama Alunan Jr. and Rosario Moreno welcomed their son on May 17, 1948. The boy would grow up hearing stories of his grandfather’s courage and trials, his devotion to duty, and the burden of public office in the hardest years of the nation. Though Raffy was too young to know him, he grew up under the shadow of what his grandfather represented — a reminder that service to one’s country was never abstract, never easy, and never without cost. But the greatest influence on the young Raffy was not the public servant etched into political history books. It was the quiet, everyday presence of the two people he would later describe as the most influential in his life: his parents. His father, Rafael Jr., carried his own brand of prudence and circumspection — values he passed on not through speeches, but through the example of how he carried himself through success, difficulty, and the long rhythms of family life. His mother, Rosario, shaped him with a firmness wrapped in gentleness. She introduced him to a spiritual and moral compass that would stay with him through decades of service, adversity, and public pressure. If the grandfather provided the name, it was the parents who gave the meaning. Raffy spent his childhood in Bacolod, surrounded by kin whose histories formed a tapestry of Philippine society through the decades: the Alunans, the Morenos, the Jalbuena, Lizares, Ramas, and other families whose ties stretched from Negros to Pampanga, from Baguio to Manila, and even — through the Puigs — to Catalonia in Spain. His was a lineage shaped by teachers, politicians, planters, and public servants. But within the family, the message was simple: heritage was never a medal; it was an obligation to live well and serve honorably. He studied at La Salle College–Bacolod until age sixteen. His youth was spent in the way many boys of his generation grew up: walking the streets with friends, watching movies, playing in the rain, and getting into harmless scrapes and fistfights that marked the rites of adolescence. They had little money but much camaraderie. Their bonds were forged in sports, long conversations, and shared adventures that filled the in-between hours of study and growing up. Vacations alternated between Bacolod, Manila, and Baguio — the latter a place Raffy would remember vividly for its cool air, pine-lined roads, and the fact that it was where his mother spent much of her youth. These were the years that shaped his sense of belonging to a family anchored in love and guided by strong values. His mother, Rosario, had a way of teaching that stayed with him long after childhood. She did not believe in boasting or drawing attention to achievements. She urged him to lead quietly, to act without fanfare, to be consistent and magnanimous. She emphasized thinking before speaking, choosing peace over conflict when possible, and standing firm when duty required it. These weren’t mere instructions — they became lifelong habits. By his teens, the world around him had grown larger, more complex. Manila — where he transferred at age sixteen — beckoned with its promise of opportunity and its storms of political change. But even then, Raffy already carried within him a compass his grandfather and parents had collectively forged: a belief in service, a respect for discipline, and a sense of duty that would one day define the man. But Raffy’s teenage years would also collide with the geopolitical currents of the 1960s. Southeast Asia was deep in the throes of the Cold War, and the Vietnam conflict was escalating. He found himself drawn to the discipline of the military early — from Boy Scouts in grade school to PMT in high school, then ROTC in college. The capture of the Philippine Military Academy’s imagination by U.S. Special Forces, the Green Berets, and PHILCAG’s missions abroad left a lasting impression. He seriously considered West Point or the PMA, even mulling over the idea as early as his high school years. Fate charted a different course, but the longing for structured service, for uniformed duty, remained quietly intact. Those youthful dreams did not fade but evolved, taking root in a deeper truth: that defending the country was not merely about the battlefield, but about moral courage — the courage to lead, to reform, to protect civilians, to uphold the law even when the law was unpopular. This moral framework — learned from Christian Brothers, reinforced by his parents, and inspired by the legacy of his grandfather — formed a conscience that would later guide him under fire, whether negotiating during a coup or dismantling private armies under Oplan Paglalansag. Even as a student, he gravitated toward ideas of stewardship. His degrees in Political Science, History, and Business Administration at De La Salle University were not accidents of convenience; they reflected a mind keenly attuned to understanding power, the human condition, and the forces that shape nations. It is from this crucible of childhood joys, parental wisdom, La Sallian discipline, and the looming silhouette of national vulnerability that Raffy Alunan III emerged — a young man ready to walk into decades of service he did not seek, but which the times would demand of him. Roots of Faith and Formation History has a way of calling certain people forward long before they realize they are being summoned. For Raffy, the calling did not arrive as a single dramatic moment, but through a series of quiet awakenings — small realizations accumulated across youth, education, and early adulthood that would prepare him for crises he had not yet imagined. He did not grow up dreaming of cabinet posts or political prominence. The life he envisioned was more private, grounded in the domestic hopes of a young man who wanted to marry early, build a family, and carve out a modest but meaningful path. Yet the world he inherited was not a quiet one, and the country he loved demanded more than private aspirations. The year was 1965, and the boy from Bacolod stepped off the ship in Manila with the wide-eyed certainty of youth and the silent discipline of his parents’ teaching. The capital smelled of gasoline, rain, and ambition. Jeepneys roared past vendors calling out the price of roasted corn; students in barong and mini-skirts swarmed the sidewalks of Taft Avenue. In this new rhythm, Raffy felt both small and boundless. He had come to De La Salle College, carrying a suitcase, a scholarship, and the invisible weight of a name already etched in public service. La Salle, then a bastion of Catholic rigor, believed that education was the art of forming conscience. Morning prayers blended with lectures on economics; Latin mottos on marble walls reminded the students that intellect without virtue was arrogance in uniform. Raffy thrived. He studied Political Science and Business Administration, believing that good governance demanded both morality and management. “They taught us to think in systems and to act in faith,” he would later write, “to balance heart and head, reason and compassion.” But the classroom was only half his teacher. Manila itself — uneasy under Marcos’s rising power, simmering with protest and poverty — became his moral proving ground. On weekends he visited slum areas with his classmates, bringing food and conversation rather than charity. The sight of barefoot children memorizing prayers beside open drains disturbed him far more than any textbook on social theory. “I began to understand that leadership was not about command,” he recalled. “It was about stewardship — about standing guard over the dignity of others.” Faith and the Forging of Conscience The Christian Brothers at La Salle hammered discipline into him: punctuality, precision, personal accountability. When he later pursued the MBA Senior Executive Program at the Ateneo Graduate School of Business, the Jesuits added something subtler — the art of discernment. They urged reflection before decision, conscience before convenience. “Faith and reason are not adversaries,” one professor told him. “They are the two wings of leadership.” Those dual influences fused into his personal creed. “Faith must translate into work; work must uplift others,” Raffy would summarize decades later. He learned that success unattached to service was spiritual bankruptcy. In college, Raffy stood at the crossroads of history and identity. The Cold War’s shadows had lengthened across Southeast Asia, and as the Vietnam conflict escalated, the question of national defense — how a small archipelagic nation could protect itself — weighed heavily on the minds of many young Filipinos. Raffy felt this weight personally. If he ever imagined a future in uniform, it was framed not by ambition but by the desire to help secure a country increasingly buffeted by external pressures and internal unrest. But another force was shaping him in equal measure — love. Love Enters the Frame One evening in 1967, a classmate invited him to a debut at the Vera-Perez mansion in Quezon City. The chandeliers glowed; the orchestra played Sinatra; and across the room stood a young woman whose poise quieted the noise around her. Elizabeth Jalbuena — Assumption College student, reserved yet radiant. “It was love at first sight,” Raffy said. “She had an elegance that disarmed me and a shyness that made me want to protect her.” He was eighteen; she was seventeen. He courted her the old-fashioned way: handwritten letters, long drives in a weather-beaten car that she treated like a Rolls-Royce, gentle humor to break her guarded silence. “When we first held hands,” she later told friends, “life was never the same again.” After two and a half years, he proposed — but only after securing employment. When he asked her father, the dignified Louie P. Jalbuena, for her hand, the older man studied him with the calm severity of a patriarch. “Do you have work?” he asked. Raffy answered yes. “Then take care of her,” Louie said, his tone half-blessing, half-command. They were married on May 16, 1970, at St. Andrew’s Church, a day before Raffy’s twenty-first birthday. The newlyweds laughed when Louie quipped, “The first fifty years are the hardest.” Time would prove him right. The Apprenticeship of Marriage Those early years were a laboratory of humility. Manila was expensive, salaries modest, dreams large. Elizabeth, whom he affectionately called Sweetheart or Mama, managed the household with precision. “She ran the house like a corporation — with kindness as capital and patience as profit,” Raffy liked to joke. He worked in executive positions for large corporations, absorbing the discipline of numbers and the politics of people. Boardrooms taught him about ambition; Elizabeth reminded him about compassion. “Each time I came home full of self-importance,” he admitted, “she’d hand me the baby and say, ‘Here’s your real work.’” They were blessed with five children — Katrina, Barni, Rafa, Christina, and Alexi — and later twelve grandchildren. Each name represented a chapter in his moral education. Dinner was sacred: everyone at the table, no gadgets, grace before meals. Stories flowed more than lectures. “Storytelling was my way of shaping conscience,” he said. “I’d tell them about courage under fire, about honesty when nobody’s watching, about helping a stranger without asking why.” The 1970s: Awakening The martial-law years darkened the nation but illuminated Raffy’s convictions. The decade that followed his graduation was tumultuous. The First Quarter Storm exploded, martial law followed, insurgencies grew, and political repression deepened. The Philippines had entered one of its most perilous eras. He watched classmates seek comfort in complicity while others disappeared into detention. “Fear is contagious,” he reflected, “but so is courage.” He kept his head down professionally yet lent quiet support to reformists and academics who spoke for justice. That moral tension — between safety and service — would define his choices later when the country regained its freedom. During these years, Raffy built a civilian career in the private sector. He worked for multinational companies, became exposed to management frameworks and corporate discipline, and learned the mechanics of organizational leadership — skills that would later serve him in unexpected, high-pressure roles in government. But while he was working in the private sphere, the country around him was unraveling. Rebellions simmered. Crime and corruption metastasized. Institutions weakened. The military strained under heavy expectations while the nation teetered between repression and upheaval. For someone like Raffy Alunan — whose conscience was molded by Christian Brothers, whose lineage carried the weight of public duty, and whose instincts leaned toward service — it was impossible not to feel the pull of a greater responsibility. At work, he began to see how institutions mirrored the people who ran them. Corruption in business, like in government, thrived on silence. He learned to speak up diplomatically, to correct without humiliating, to insist on transparency even when it slowed profit. “That period was my moral apprenticeship,” he said. “I was learning how to fight wrong without losing grace.” Faith at the Center Despite the political gloom, faith remained his compass. Sunday Mass was non-negotiable; so were nightly prayers with Elizabeth and the children. He joined community groups that bridged business with civic duty. One Jesuit retreat left an indelible mark: “If you want peace, work for justice.” Those words would echo when he later faced insurgents and terrorists as Interior Secretary. He also deepened his ties with the military reserve program, undergoing ROTC and later training with the PC-Special Action Force, finding in discipline a spiritual metaphor. “Drill and prayer are cousins,” he mused. “Both are about surrendering ego to a higher order.” Elizabeth, the Quiet General As the family grew, Elizabeth became his steadfast partner in leadership. She instilled manners, routine, and compassion in their children, ran earthquake drills, taught first aid, and managed household crises with calm authority. Raffy often said, half in jest, “I was the speaker of the house; she was the loudspeaker.” When disagreements flared, forgiveness became their diplomacy. “Forgiveness is essential,” he wrote. “Forgetting takes longer — but love is the memory that outlasts the quarrel.” Their marriage was more than companionship; it was his moral gymnasium. Through her, he learned patience in frustration, humor in exhaustion, tenderness in command. “Elizabeth reminded me that leadership begins at home,” he said. “If you cannot lead a family with empathy, you cannot lead a nation with justice.” The Birth of a Philosophy By the early 1980s, Raffy had become a seasoned executive with a growing unease about complacency. The Philippines, still under dictatorship, suffered brain drain, cronyism, and cynicism. He began writing essays and giving talks about ethical leadership, arguing that development without discipline was decay in disguise. He would later condense his worldview into a triad: God, Country, Family — in that order. “That hierarchy keeps me upright,” he explained. “It prevents idolatry of wealth or power. If I ever reverse it, I lose my soul.” Friends recall how he could shift from corporate language to moral reasoning effortlessly. Over lunch he might discuss market share; by dessert he’d quote Scripture on stewardship. He spoke softly, but his conviction carried weight. Those who dismissed him as idealistic learned that he was, in fact, relentless. The Unexpected Turn He did not seek government. Government sought him. His moral restlessness soon found purpose. In the mid-1980s, as the Marcos regime weakened and the opposition gained momentum, Raffy found himself increasingly connected with civic groups calling for democratic change. He became a trustee of Manindigan, an organization of professionals, entrepreneurs, and academics who openly opposed dictatorship and advocated for a return to democratic governance. At this time, Raffy stood at the crossroads between comfort and calling. He had already built a solid career in the corporate world — an executive in large firms, respected for his discipline and strategic mind. Yet something inside him felt unquiet. “I was earning well, but I wasn’t serving enough,” he would later admit. “The country was unraveling, and I could no longer stand watching from the sidelines.” The Marcos dictatorship was in its twilight. The air was thick with dissent, fear, and fatigue. Reformists, intellectuals, and professionals were beginning to converge under one banner: Manindigan — a movement whose name literally meant “to stand one’s ground.” It was a brotherhood of conscience, gathering lawyers, professors, entrepreneurs, priests, and journalists who believed that silence had become complicity. Raffy joined as a trustee. Inside candle-lit rooms in Quezon City, he and his peers debated freedom, ethics, and the price of integrity. Some were later jailed; others, exiled. For Raffy, the risk was personal. He had five young children and a wife whose steady faith never wavered. When the People Power Revolution unfolded in 1986, many of Manindigan’s members — and the broader middle-class movement it represented — transitioned into the rebuilding effort under President Corazon C. Aquino, the widow who became the nation’s moral compass. It was in this atmosphere of national renewal that Raffy Alunan was invited to join the government. For Raffy, it felt like destiny knocking. He did not see this as personal elevation. In his own account, public service — when done right — was nothing more than stewardship. In the face of crises, it meant stepping into spaces where one could help save lives, protect civilians, or restore order. It was never about power, and certainly not about fame. It was about responsibility. And so, after much discernment, Raffy accepted what he believed was a summons to serve the times. The Making of a Statesman In early 1991, President Aquino invited him to serve as Secretary of Tourism. The country was still healing from years of repression and chaos. Tourism had collapsed; infrastructure lay in ruins; and the nation’s image abroad was tainted by coups, kidnappings, and political instability. The role of Tourism Secretary was not one he imagined for himself. He inherited corruption in the ranks, decaying public assets, threats against tourists, and challenges that required firmness and moral clarity. Yet the moment he entered office, he realized how deeply its responsibilities were tied to safety, good governance, and national image. He brought with him a corporate manager’s precision and a public servant’s passion. His first order of business was to rebuild the industry’s credibility — both domestically and internationally. He met with airline executives, hotel owners, and travel associations, often working late into the night crafting policy that emphasized safety, sustainability, and service. He removed Pagsanjan Falls from the preferred destination list due to rampant moral decadence and crime against visitors — a bold move that sent a clear message: public safety and moral decency were non-negotiable. He oversaw Camp John Hay, helped preserve its natural state, and completed the reconstruction of Corregidor, transforming it into a national shrine of wartime heroism. But more critical were the emergencies. During the devastating 1989 earthquake, he organized search-and-rescue operations in Baguio. During the coup attempt that same year, rebel forces occupied Makati’s financial district, trapping civilians and foreign tourists in its hotels. Raffy was tasked to negotiate for their safe release — which he accomplished by working with Scout Rangers to protect lives and avoid further bloodshed. This coup-night episode — later recounted in vivid detail in his own writing — would become one of the defining moments of his early service. It was here, under overwhelming uncertainty, that Raffy Alunan began earning a reputation that followed him throughout his public life: A calm mind in chaos. A steward of lives. A servant of the Republic at its most fragile moments. He launched the “Rediscover the Philippines” campaign, not as a mere slogan but as a movement of national renewal. He believed that tourism could become a mirror of the nation’s soul. Under his leadership, the DOT began restoring heritage sites, training local guides, and promoting lesser-known regions to disperse economic growth beyond Metro Manila. But more than marketing, Raffy focused on ethics. He insisted that tourism projects uphold environmental responsibility and community inclusion — principles rare at the time. The Moral Machinery of Governance Inside Malacañang, he earned a reputation for integrity. Staffers noted his punctuality, his refusal to cut corners, and his ability to balance firmness with courtesy. “He didn’t raise his voice,” one aide said. “He raised standards.” President Aquino valued his independence of mind. During Cabinet meetings, when debates grew heated, she would sometimes turn to him and ask, “What do you think, Raffy?” He would answer with disarming calm: “Madam President, I think the right thing is rarely the easiest thing.” That line would become a quiet mantra of his governance style. He approached bureaucracy as both system and soul. He streamlined processes, championed decentralization, and mentored young civil servants to think beyond compliance. “Rules are useless if they don’t uplift lives,” he told them. “We are not paper-pushers — we are nation-builders.” Yet, reform always provokes resistance. Entrenched interests fought him subtly — through bureaucratic delay, whisper campaigns, and political sabotage. “I learned early that corruption doesn’t always wear a villain’s face,” he wrote. “Sometimes it smiles, shakes your hand, and invites you to lunch.” Through every trial, his moral compass pointed unwaveringly to service. “I entered government with clean hands and intended to leave the same way,” he told colleagues. “No title is worth my soul.” A New Chapter of Duty Raffy’s performance under the Aquino administration did not go unnoticed. When Fidel V. Ramos — a soldierstatesman and fellow believer in disciplined, values-driven governance — became president in 1992, he looked to Raffy Alunan to join his Cabinet. This would become the longest, most intense, and most consequential chapter of his public service. It was here that Raffy stepped not only into crisis after crisis, but into roles that demanded moral courage, strategic clarity, and an unshakeable commitment to what he later described as the essence of his service: “A life of stewardship and service characterized by crisis management, saving lives, and fidelity to our moral values for a better Philippines.” This was no longer the young man dreaming of West Point. Nor the corporate executive. Nor the newly married father hoping to build a quiet life. This was Raffy Alunan — called into the center of a nation in upheaval, becoming the man the times required. A Nation at the Brink Leadership, when stripped of ceremony and rhetoric, is measured not by speeches or symbols but by what one chooses to confront. When Raffy accepted President Ramos’ invitation to lead the Department of the Interior and Local Government, he was not stepping into an office — he was stepping into the Republic’s crucible. The early 1990s were dangerous years. The Cold War had just ended, leaving behind scattered insurgencies, banditry, radicalized factions, and heavily armed political clans. Ethnic tensions flared in the south. Kidnapping syndicates grew bold. The wounds left by Marcos-era authoritarianism had not yet healed, and institutions were fragile It was during this precarious period that Ramos called. “Raffy,” he said, “I need you at the Department of the Interior and Local Government.” The offer was not a promotion; it was a crucible. The DILG was a labyrinth of politics, policing, and local governance — a post where idealists often burned out or broke down. Raffy hesitated. His family had already endured years of his long absences and constant stress. Elizabet

As the Rotary Club of Manila prepares to open another year of inquiry, dialogue, and civic leadership, it does so with a tradition that has quietly become a barometer of national mood: inviting the Governor of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas as its first speaker of the year.

This year’s engagement carries particular weight. The guest is Eli M. Remolona Jr., the 7th Governor of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, and the moment is unusually consequential. The year ahead — 2026 — will test not only economic fundamentals, but the country’s institutional maturity, policy discipline, and capacity to navigate a far more fragmented global order.
This is no longer a post-pandemic recovery conversation. That chapter has closed. What lies ahead is a recalibration — harder, more structural, and more unforgiving of complacency.

Globally, the narrative of “soft landings” and gentle normalization has begun to fray. Interest rates remain structurally higher than the decade-long norms many markets had grown accustomed to. Geopolitical tensions — whether in trade, energy, or security — are no longer episodic disruptions but persistent features of the landscape. Supply chains are being redesigned not for maximum efficiency, but for resilience and strategic alignment.

For emerging economies like the Philippines, this environment presents both opportunity and risk. Capital is more discerning. Investors are no longer chasing yield blindly; they are pricing credibility, policy coherence, and institutional strength. In this context, central banks are not merely custodians of inflation targets—they are anchors of confidence.
It is precisely here that Governor Remolona’s perspective becomes critical.

Domestically, the Philippine economy enters 2026 with respectable momentum but unresolved tensions. Growth remains consumption-led, supported by remittances and a young demographic profile. Yet beneath the headline numbers lie structural questions that cannot be deferred indefinitely:
• Can growth be sustained without reigniting inflationary pressures?
• Will fiscal consolidation keep pace with ambitious infrastructure and social spending?
• How resilient is the peso in an era of volatile capital flows and geopolitical shocks?
• And perhaps most importantly: can policy coordination remain credible as political and economic cycles converge?

Governor Remolona inherits a central bank that has earned international respect for its professionalism. But credibility, once earned, must be renewed continuously. The BSP’s challenge in 2026 will not simply be to manage inflation—it will be to manage expectations, especially in a society where economic optimism and economic anxiety often coexist.

One of the underappreciated roles of a central bank is its function as a moral authority in economic life. Beyond interest rates and reserve requirements, it signals discipline in a world prone to excess, patience in an age of haste, and long-term thinking in political environments often governed by short horizons.

Governor Remolona’s background — as an economist steeped in global finance and institutional reform — suggests a leadership style attuned to complexity rather than slogans. For business leaders, professionals, and civic stewards gathered at the Rotary Club of Manila, his message is expected to be less about reassurance and more about realism.
And realism, in 2026, is itself a form of leadership.

That the Rotary Club of Manila has long made it a point to hear from the BSP Governor at the start of the year is no accident. Rotary’s constituency — entrepreneurs, executives, professionals, and civic leaders — operates at the intersection of policy and practice. Decisions made in boardrooms, factories, clinics, and communities are shaped, directly or indirectly, by the signals sent from the central bank.

In convening this conversation, the Club affirms its role not merely as a fellowship of service, but as a forum for informed citizenship. Rotary does not wait for certainty; it prepares its members to lead amid uncertainty.
If there is one likely theme that will define the economic prospects of 2026, it is this: less comfort, more clarity.

The era of cheap money is behind us. The tolerance for policy drift is narrowing. But for economies that can demonstrate discipline, adaptability, and institutional trust, the coming years may well reward seriousness over spectacle.
As the Rotary Club of Manila listens to Governor Remolona, it does so not in search of predictions, but of bearings. In a world where noise is abundant, clarity is rare—and therefore invaluable.

The question for 2026 is not whether challenges will arise. They will. The real question is whether the country’s institutions — and its leaders — are prepared to meet them with steadiness, credibility, and foresight.
That is why this first speech matters.

articles.title: Guest of Honor and Speaker’s Profile

body.text: Dr. Eli Remolona Jr. is the Governor of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP).

Before joining the BSP, he already had a long career in central banking. Governor Remolona worked at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York for 14 years and at the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) for 19 years. At the BIS in Basel, Switzerland, he was Head of Financial Markets and Editor of the BIS Quarterly Review.

Afterwards, he served as Regional Head for Asia and the Pacific. He has taught at Williams College, Columbia University, New York University, the Asia School of Business and the University of the Philippines. He has published widely in scholarly journals, writing mainly on monetary policy, international finance and financial markets. He has a Ph.D. in economics from Stanford University.

body.text: As we cross the midpoint of this Rotary Year, the Rotary Club of Manila must pause not merely to take stock of time elapsed, but to reflect with gratitude on the purpose fulfilled, the service rendered, and the collective spirit that has animated our work during the first half of this term.

Indeed, the past six months have affirmed a truth long embedded in the DNA of this venerable Club: that service, when anchored on tradition yet responsive to contemporary needs, remains both relevant and transformative. Guided by Rotary’s enduring ideals and strengthened by the experience and commitment of our members, RC Manila has pursued its mission with quiet confidence, purposeful energy, and an unwavering sense of responsibility to the communities we serve.

Across our various avenues of service, the Club has successfully implemented a wide range of initiatives and programs that reflect both breadth and depth -- programs that are not episodic gestures, but carefully designed interventions aimed at sustainable and measurable impact. Our flagship programs – LEAP Awards, ARAL Program, and Project RIVER – as well as our signature projects – TOWER Awards, Outstanding Ambassador Award, Journalism Award -- have continued to advance education, promote peace, recognize excellence in public service and labor, and uphold the vital role of a free and responsible press. Each initiative bears the imprint of thoughtful planning, strong partnerships, and the shared conviction that service must be meaningful, inclusive, and enduring.

Equally significant has been the Club’s continued emphasis on fellowship and institutional strength. The first half of the year has seen active engagement among members, robust participation in meetings and projects, and a reaffirmation of the bonds that unite us as Rotarians and as friends. In a time when voluntary service competes with ever-growing personal and professional demands, the sustained commitment of our members stands as a testament to the enduring appeal of Rotary’s call to “Service Above Self.”

This midpoint also offers an opportunity for introspection. Leadership in Rotary is not measured by individual visibility, but by the ability to harness collective wisdom, encourage collaboration, and ensure continuity. Any progress achieved thus far is the product of shared leadership – of the Directors and Officers who have discharged their duties with diligence, of Committee Chairs who have translated vision into action, and of each Manila Rotarian who quietly but consistently contributed time, talent, and treasure that give life to our programs.

As we look toward the second half of the Rotary Year, we do so with both confidence and renewed urgency. There remains much to accomplish, milestones yet to be reached, and initiatives that invite further expansion and refinement. The challenge before us is not simply to sustain momentum, but to deepen impact, that is, to ensure that our projects continue to address real needs, inspire trust, and leave lasting benefits well beyond the confines of this Rotary Year.

At this halfway point, it is worth remembering that while a presidency is finite, the legacy of service is not. Our task, therefore, is to build on the strong foundation already laid, to steward the Club’s resources wisely, and to honor the proud heritage of the Rotary Club of Manila by leaving it stronger, more united, and more responsive to the times.

With gratitude for the journey thus far and optimism for the months ahead, we move forward -- celebrating our Club’s Destiny and Legacy -- steadfast in purpose, united in fellowship, and resolute in our commitment to service.
