articles.title: A Midday of Meaning, Memory, and Mission: The 15th Weekly Membership Meeting of the Rotary Club of Manila

body.text: There Rotary meetings — and then there are gatherings that quietly affirm why institutions endure.

On a December midday at the venerable Manila Polo Club, the Rotary Club of Manila convened its Fifteenth Weekly Membership Meeting for Rotary Year 2025–2026, the last regular meeting for the year 2025. It was not a meeting defined by clockwork precision or formal sequence alone, but by something deeper: continuity of purpose, fidelity to tradition, and the unmistakable sense that service — when done consistently and without spectacle — becomes history.

As members and guests gathered over a shared meal, the atmosphere carried the familiar cadence of Rotary fellowship. Conversations crossed professions and generations; greetings were warm but unhurried. The room, steeped in decades of civic memory, seemed to understand that what was about to unfold was less a program and more a reaffirmation.
Sacred Openings and Shared Ideals
The formal program opened not with urgency, but with reverence.
A solemn Doxology, rendered by Teatro Rizalia, gently centered the assembly, reminding everyone present that Rotary’s work — however practical — rests upon moral grounding.
This was followed by an Invocation led by Director-elect Carlos G. “Caloy” Serapio, whose prayer framed the gathering as one not merely of minds, but of conscience.

The national anthems of the United States and the Philippines, performed with dignity, underscored the international character of Rotary and the enduring bonds between peoples who share democratic ideals and a commitment to peace. The Rotary Club of Manila Hymn, sung by the RCM WF Music Chorale, followed — less a song than a collective memory set to music.

When the Four-Way Test was recited, led by Past Director Issam Eldebs, it did not sound rehearsed. It sounded lived-in — principles tested and applied daily by men and women who understand that ethics are not slogans, but habits.
Leadership in Quiet Motion

The acknowledgment of guests, masterfully moderated by DSAA John M. Cutter, set the tone for a meeting that balanced protocol with warmth. A welcome song once again brought the Chorale to the fore, reinforcing the idea that Rotary gatherings are sustained not just by speeches, but by shared participation.

President Raoul C. Creencia, during his President’s Time, spoke not as a figurehead but as a steward—offering reflections that tied recent accomplishments to Rotary’s broader mission. His remarks carried the confidence of leadership grounded in teamwork, a reminder that progress is seldom the work of one.
Honoring Service Beyond Borders
A defining moment of the meeting was the presentation of the Rotary Club of Manila Outstanding Ambassador of the Year Award.

Introduced by Past District Governor Joaquin “Jackie” C. Rodriguez, Sr., Chairman of the Ambassador of the Year Committee, the award was conferred upon Her Excellency MaryKay L. Carlson, Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of the United States of America to the Philippines.

Her Excellency MaryKay L. Carlson, Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of the United States to the Philippines, has been honored with the Rotary Club of Manila's Outstanding Ambassador of the Year Award.

The recognition was not ceremonial flattery. It was acknowledgment of a diplomatic presence marked by consistency, respect, and a deep appreciation for people-to-people engagement. The serenade that followed — performed by Himig Rizalia — served as a cultural offering, affirming that gratitude, when sincere, is best expressed through shared heritage.

The Ambassador was formally introduced by Rotarian Victor “Vic” G. Garcia III, after which she addressed the Club. Her speech, received with attentiveness and respect, stood as a testament to enduring alliances and mutual service — but its substance remains purposefully unrecorded here, allowing the moment itself to stand intact.

Standing once more within the storied halls of the Manila Polo Club, Her Excellency MaryKay L. Carlson spoke not merely as a diplomat fulfilling protocol, but as a witness to a relationship shaped by time, trial, and trust. Her return to the Rotary Club of Manila—Asia’s first Rotary Club—was framed as both a privilege and a homecoming, underscoring the symbolic weight of place in the long arc of history.

She began by acknowledging what Rotarians know instinctively but rarely articulate aloud: that service, when sustained and sincere, leaves an imprint. The Ambassador’s admiration for the Club’s recent accomplishments was not perfunctory praise. Her remark—that a single month’s report read like a year’s worth of work—was both astonishment and affirmation. It reflected an understanding that Rotary’s impact lies not in isolated events, but in relentless consistency, in showing up again and again for the common good.
Receiving the Outstanding Ambassador Award, Ambassador Carlson responded not with personal triumph, but with collective humility.

She accepted the recognition on behalf of the entire U.S. Embassy team, situating the honor within a broader narrative of partnership between nations. In doing so, she reinforced a central theme of her address: that diplomacy, like Rotary service, is never the work of one individual alone. It is sustained by teams, institutions, and shared purpose.
People-to-People: The Quiet Architecture of Diplomacy

At the heart of her reflections was a conviction that the strongest alliances are not forged solely through treaties or official statements, but through human connection. Ambassador Carlson emphasized that people-to-people ties form the living architecture of U.S.–Philippine relations.

She highlighted the Philippine-American Educational Foundation (PAEF) — widely known as Fulbright — as a powerful symbol of this bond. Home to the world’s longest-running Fulbright Commission, the program stands as a quiet but enduring engine of mutual understanding. Through scholarships and exchanges, including in advanced fields such as space science and civil nuclear workforce development, generations of Filipinos and Americans have crossed borders not merely to study, but to return home transformed—carrying with them shared values, expertise, and lifelong connections.

With more than 10,000 alumni, these exchanges have created a living bridge between societies, one that renews itself daily through classrooms, laboratories, public service, and innovation. The Ambassador made clear that such investments are not abstract ideals; they are deliberate commitments to a shared future.
Service Rekindled: The Return of the Peace Corps

Ambassador Carlson’s reflections turned next to the Peace Corps, another enduring symbol of grassroots partnership. During her tenure, 170 new volunteers were deployed to the Philippines — joining over 9,000 who have served Filipino communities since 1961.

This achievement carried special resonance. In the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, when Peace Corps operations were halted worldwide, restarting the program required not only logistical coordination, but trust, resilience, and renewed commitment. Bringing Peace Corps back into service was, as the Ambassador noted, no small feat. It stood as proof that shared purpose can outlast even global disruption.

Peace Corps volunteers, she emphasized, embody the very spirit that defines the U.S.–Philippine relationship: partnership rooted in humility, service grounded in respect, and a belief that real change begins at the community level.
Partners in Prosperity: Building the Future Together

Beyond people-to-people ties, Ambassador Carlson articulated a vision of the two nations as partners in prosperity. She pointed to collaborative initiatives such as the Luzon Economic Corridor, where the United States, the Philippines, Japan, and other like-minded partners are accelerating high-impact investments designed to spur growth from Subic Bay across key regions.

She cited concrete examples to illustrate how diplomacy translates into livelihoods. The expansion of the Royal Cold Storage Facility in Bulacan by I Squared Capital, she explained, is not merely an infrastructure project — it is an investment in food security, job creation, and regional resilience. The firm’s commitment of over two billion U.S. dollars across logistics, energy, and digital infrastructure exemplifies how private-sector engagement can deliver tangible, lasting benefits.
"… economic cooperation becomes an extension of service: a means of empowering communities, strengthening systems, and ensuring shared growth."
In this framing, economic cooperation becomes an extension of service: a means of empowering communities, strengthening systems, and ensuring shared growth.
Allies in Security, United in Crisis

The Ambassador’s address then turned to the enduring strength of the U.S.–Philippine alliance as security partners. With the upcoming 75th anniversary of the Mutual Defense Treaty, she described the alliance as ironclad — not as rhetoric, but as lived reality.

She referenced the United States’ recent announcement of 500 million U.S. dollars in supplemental foreign military financing to support the modernization of the Armed Forces of the Philippines and enhance maritime security. Yet, it was her discussion of disaster response that carried particular emotional weight.

In recounting U.S. assistance following Super Typhoon Uwan, Ambassador Carlson emphasized that the 2.5 million dollars cited represented only the value of commodities delivered. It did not include the deployment of U.S. military airlift capabilities or personnel on the ground. This distinction mattered. It underscored a deeper truth: that in moments of crisis, alliances are measured not by statements, but by speed, presence, and solidarity.
Rotary and the Spirit of Shared Purpose

In closing, Ambassador Carlson drew a parallel between the alliance she represents and the institution before her. The Rotary Club of Manila, she observed, embodies the same spirit that animates strong international partnerships: leadership anchored in service, devotion to the common good, and a quiet refusal to be indifferent.

As the world looks toward 2026 — the 80th anniversary of formal U.S.– Philippine diplomatic relations—her remarks resonated as both reflection and invitation. There is much to celebrate, yes, but also much to steward. The future, she implied, will belong to those who choose cooperation over isolation, service over self-interest, and shared destiny over short-term gain.

In that sense, her address was not merely a speech — it was a reaffirmation of a covenant. One between nations. One between institutions. And one between people who believe that the truest measure of partnership is not power, but purpose.
Ambassador Carlson and PP Chito Zaldarriaga during the Q&A
Fellowship in Celebration
As the program transitioned into celebration, the Rotary Club of Manila did what it has always done best: honor its own.

Birthday celebrants — spanning seasoned past directors to current leaders and active members — were recognized not merely for another year lived, but for years of service given. In Rotary, birthdays are less about age and more about accumulated commitment.
The list was long, the applause sincere. Each name carried with it stories of committee meetings, service projects, and quiet acts of generosity rarely seen but deeply felt.
Welcoming New Stewards of Service
Few moments in Rotary are as quietly powerful as an Induction of New Members.

Introduced by President Creencia and presented by Past President Domingo S.B. “Boy” Guevara together with President-Elect Reginald T. “Reggie” Yu, the induction welcomed professionals from law, real estate, medicine, physical therapy, and commodities trading.

Each new member stood not as an addition to a roster, but as a new custodian of Rotary’s ideals. Their Oath of Membership, administered by the President, was more than a formality — it was an entry into a lineage of service that predates them and will, in time, outlast them.
Accountability and the Future in View

Transparency and stewardship took center stage as Past District Governor Alexander P. “Alex” Cureg delivered the RCMFI Accomplishment and Financial Status Report. Numbers were presented not as abstractions, but as reflections of trust — resources entrusted by members to serve causes larger than themselves.

This was followed by the NOMELEC Results, reported by President-Elect Reggie Yu, signaling continuity, order, and democratic process within the Club’s governance. Leadership, after all, is not only about vision, but about orderly succession.
A Meeting That Echoes Forward
When the meeting adjourned, there was no sense of finality — only momentum.

Members lingered. Conversations resumed. Plans were quietly discussed. The Rotary Club of Manila, Asia’s first Rotary Club, once again demonstrated that longevity is not sustained by nostalgia, but by relevance; not by ceremony alone, but by service renewed week after week.
In a world increasingly defined by noise and haste, this meeting offered something rarer: measured purpose, earned tradition, and a shared belief that service — when done faithfully — becomes legacy.
15th Weekly Membership Meeting Fellowship

articles.title: Rotary Club of Manila Brings Joy to SPED Students This Christmas

body.text: On December 10, 2025, the Ynares Event Center in Antipolo City came alive with laughter, joy, and the spirit of giving as the Rotary Club of Manila hosted its annual SPED Family Fun Day. This heartwarming event brought together special education (SPED) students and their families for a day filled with meaningful connections, holiday cheer, and acts of kindness.

Guided by the Rotary motto, Service Above Self, the event celebrated the resilience and vibrant spirit of these remarkable young learners. Through thoughtful gift-giving, engaging activities, and shared moments of joy, the Rotary Club reaffirmed its commitment to fostering inclusion, dignity, and equal opportunities for all.

articles.title: OPLAN KALINGA: Surgical Outreach Mission at Our Lady of Grace Hospital

body.text: Our Lady of Grace Hospital in San Dionisio, Parañaque became a place of healing and compassion as the Rotary Club of Manila, RC Manila Foundation, Inc., and the World Surgical Foundation Philippines joined forces for OPLAN KALINGA.
Held on December 11-12, 2025, this surgical outreach mission provided free, essential surgeries to patients who had long-awaited care they could not afford.
Volunteer surgeons, nurses, and medical staff worked with precision and heart, ensuring that each patient left not only with improved health but also with renewed hope for the future.

President Raoul Creencia attended the event, alongside Project Chair Dr. Paul Koh, Co-Chair Dr. Jun Aventura, and Secretary Anton Mauricio. The World Surgical Foundation Philippines team was led by its President, Dr. Suntay.
For many, these procedures were life-changing, offering relief from pain and the chance to reclaim their daily lives.

OPLAN KALINGA reflects the Rotary’s unwavering dedication to action-driven service. It’s about more than medical care—it’s about showing up for those who need it most and proving that compassion, when paired with action, can truly transform lives.
The Rotary Club of Manila, in partnership with the Dangal ng Bulacan Foundation, Inc., brought much-needed relief and holiday cheer to four barangays across Bulacan.

These communities, still recovering from severe flooding, were reminded that they are not alone this Christmas. The gift-giving activity held on December 20, 2025 was more than just distributing presents—it was about showing solidarity and offering a sense of hope during difficult times.

Rotarians and volunteers worked hand in hand to deliver not only gifts but also a message of care and support. The event highlighted the power of partnerships and the importance of reaching out to those in need.
For the families in Bulacan, it was a moment of joy amidst challenges, and for those who participated, it was a meaningful way to live out the true spirit of the season.

articles.title: Country Above Self: The Officer and the Gentleman - The Life and Legacy of Rafael Moreno Alunan III

body.text: Editor’s Note: Writing about Rafael M. Alunan III is less the task of biography than of bearing witness. His story is not simply one of power attained or history shaped; it is a meditation on what it means to remain good in a world that rewards everything but goodness. He belongs to that rare generation who believed that public service is a sacred trust — who measured progress not by applause but by conscience. His moral clarity came not from privilege but from pilgrimage: from the crucible of duty, the classroom of faith, and the quiet courage of love.

This piece closes not with finality but with continuity — because his mission, like the Republic’s, remains unfinished. Somewhere, perhaps even now, he is drafting another column, delivering another lecture, consoling another widow of a soldier, or advising a young mayor tempted by shortcuts. And when he speaks, the cadence is unchanged: calm, precise, resolute — a man who has mastered not only command, but compassion.

In the end, Raffy Alunan’s life reminds us that greatness is not the absence of failure, but the refusal to surrender virtue in its aftermath. His journey affirms that faith and reason, leadership and humility, courage and tenderness — all can coexist in one heart devoted wholly to God and country. May this work stand not as monument but as mirror — reflecting the best of what we can still become if we, too, choose to serve above self.

The gunfire began long before dawn. In the cold stillness of December 1989, as rebel forces rushed the financial heart of Makati and armed factions clashed across the nation’s capital, Raffy Alunan found himself standing once again in the uncertain space between order and collapse.

Earlier that day, as part of a SAF company deployed to capture an NPA base camp, he had flown under the radar — literally — to make it home in time for his daughter’s birthday. But celebrations would soon be overtaken by the growing specter of political fracture. By nightfall, Manila was under siege.

Rebel troops had overrun the business district. Civilians and foreign guests were trapped inside Makati’s hotels. The city’s lifeline was suspended between panic and paralysis. And into that crucible, Raffy Alunan — then serving as a key member of the Aquino administration — was tasked with a mission that would become emblematic of his entire public career: Negotiate the safe release of innocent lives in the middle of an armed rebellion.

He moved quickly. He sought the cooperation of the Scout Rangers, appealed to their instincts as protectors, and asked for one thing: “Let us retrieve the civilians before the shooting consumes them.” In the face-to-face talks at the Manila Intercontinental Hotel, he worked with PMA Superintendent Major-General Arturo Enrile and coordinated the delicate exchanges that allowed government teams to extract trapped tourists and Filipinos from active conflict zones.
It was a moment that distilled the essence of the path he had chosen — or perhaps, the path that had chosen him.
Not power.
Not politics.
But stewardship.
Crisis management.

And the unyielding conviction that in moments of national fracture, one must stand where the lives are most at risk. By the time the coup attempt was quelled, dozens of civilians had been pulled to safety. The Republic had survived another tremor in its fragile democratic rebuilding. And Raffy Alunan had cemented a reputation he never sought but consistently proved worthy of — the steady hand in chaos, the quiet soldier-statesman whose duty was always to save, not to shine.
This was but one episode in a long arc of service marked by danger, discipline, and moral resolve.
But it captures, in a single frame, the truth of the man:
When the Republic was threatened, he stepped forward.
When lives hung in the balance, he negotiated for peace. When crisis erupted, he moved toward the fire — never away.
This is the story of Rafael Moreno Alunan III.
Not as myth.
Not as crafted legend. But as he lived it — a life of stewardship, service, and fidelity to the moral values he believed could build a better Philippines.
The Boy from Bacolod

Long before Raffy would find himself negotiating with rebels in a besieged Manila hotel, or working beside presidents during some of the nation’s most precarious years, his story had already been set in motion by the weight — and quiet dignity — of a name he inherited.

That name belonged first to Rafael Rivas Alunan Sr., a man born in 1885 in Talisay, Negros Occidental, who came of age in the uncertain dawn between Spanish rule and the burgeoning American administration. The elder Alunan was a scholar of the old mold — educated at the Colegio de Bacolod de los Recoletos, then at the Ateneo de Manila, graduating in business at seventeen and later reading law. He was not simply a participant in the nation-in-the-making; he was one of its architects.

As a young legislator representing Negros Occidental’s 2nd District, he would serve three consecutive terms in the Philippine Assembly beginning in 1912, later becoming floor leader of the House. He would go on to hold posts that placed him at the crossroads of the country’s economic transformation — Secretary of Agriculture and Natural Resources, Secretary of Finance, Acting Secretary of Public Works, and, at the onset of the Pacific War, Secretary of the Interior. He was a prominent force in the sugar industry, heading the Bacolod-Murcia Milling Company and the Philippine Sugar Association at a time when sugar was one of the pillars of Philippine economic power.
History, however, had harsher tests in store.

When Japanese forces occupied the Philippines, Alunan Sr. held cabinet posts under duress. After the liberation, many officials of the wartime Philippine Republic faced accusations of treason. In February 1947, after a long legal ordeal, the charges against him were dismissed — there was no evidence that he had cooperated with the enemy beyond performing the duties required of him under occupation. He died that same year, his name cleared, leaving behind seven children and a legacy marked by service, controversy, vindication, and public purpose.

It was into this lineage that Rafael de la Rama Alunan Jr. and Rosario Moreno welcomed their son on May 17, 1948. The boy would grow up hearing stories of his grandfather’s courage and trials, his devotion to duty, and the burden of public office in the hardest years of the nation. Though Raffy was too young to know him, he grew up under the shadow of what his grandfather represented — a reminder that service to one’s country was never abstract, never easy, and never without cost.

But the greatest influence on the young Raffy was not the public servant etched into political history books. It was the quiet, everyday presence of the two people he would later describe as the most influential in his life: his parents.

His father, Rafael Jr., carried his own brand of prudence and circumspection — values he passed on not through speeches, but through the example of how he carried himself through success, difficulty, and the long rhythms of family life. His mother, Rosario, shaped him with a firmness wrapped in gentleness. She introduced him to a spiritual and moral compass that would stay with him through decades of service, adversity, and public pressure.
If the grandfather provided the name, it was the parents who gave the meaning.

Raffy spent his childhood in Bacolod, surrounded by kin whose histories formed a tapestry of Philippine society through the decades: the Alunans, the Morenos, the Jalbuena, Lizares, Ramas, and other families whose ties stretched from Negros to Pampanga, from Baguio to Manila, and even — through the Puigs — to Catalonia in Spain. His was a lineage shaped by teachers, politicians, planters, and public servants. But within the family, the message was simple: heritage was never a medal; it was an obligation to live well and serve honorably.

He studied at La Salle College–Bacolod until age sixteen. His youth was spent in the way many boys of his generation grew up: walking the streets with friends, watching movies, playing in the rain, and getting into harmless scrapes and fistfights that marked the rites of adolescence. They had little money but much camaraderie. Their bonds were forged in sports, long conversations, and shared adventures that filled the in-between hours of study and growing up.

Vacations alternated between Bacolod, Manila, and Baguio — the latter a place Raffy would remember vividly for its cool air, pine-lined roads, and the fact that it was where his mother spent much of her youth. These were the years that shaped his sense of belonging to a family anchored in love and guided by strong values.

His mother, Rosario, had a way of teaching that stayed with him long after childhood. She did not believe in boasting or drawing attention to achievements. She urged him to lead quietly, to act without fanfare, to be consistent and magnanimous. She emphasized thinking before speaking, choosing peace over conflict when possible, and standing firm when duty required it. These weren’t mere instructions — they became lifelong habits.

By his teens, the world around him had grown larger, more complex. Manila — where he transferred at age sixteen — beckoned with its promise of opportunity and its storms of political change. But even then, Raffy already carried within him a compass his grandfather and parents had collectively forged: a belief in service, a respect for discipline, and a sense of duty that would one day define the man.

But Raffy’s teenage years would also collide with the geopolitical currents of the 1960s. Southeast Asia was deep in the throes of the Cold War, and the Vietnam conflict was escalating. He found himself drawn to the discipline of the military early — from Boy Scouts in grade school to PMT in high school, then ROTC in college. The capture of the Philippine Military Academy’s imagination by U.S. Special Forces, the Green Berets, and PHILCAG’s missions abroad left a lasting impression. He seriously considered West Point or the PMA, even mulling over the idea as early as his high school years. Fate charted a different course, but the longing for structured service, for uniformed duty, remained quietly intact.

Those youthful dreams did not fade but evolved, taking root in a deeper truth: that defending the country was not merely about the battlefield, but about moral courage — the courage to lead, to reform, to protect civilians, to uphold the law even when the law was unpopular.

This moral framework — learned from Christian Brothers, reinforced by his parents, and inspired by the legacy of his grandfather — formed a conscience that would later guide him under fire, whether negotiating during a coup or dismantling private armies under Oplan Paglalansag.

Even as a student, he gravitated toward ideas of stewardship. His degrees in Political Science, History, and Business Administration at De La Salle University were not accidents of convenience; they reflected a mind keenly attuned to understanding power, the human condition, and the forces that shape nations.

It is from this crucible of childhood joys, parental wisdom, La Sallian discipline, and the looming silhouette of national vulnerability that Raffy Alunan III emerged — a young man ready to walk into decades of service he did not seek, but which the times would demand of him.
Roots of Faith and Formation

History has a way of calling certain people forward long before they realize they are being summoned. For Raffy, the calling did not arrive as a single dramatic moment, but through a series of quiet awakenings — small realizations accumulated across youth, education, and early adulthood that would prepare him for crises he had not yet imagined.

He did not grow up dreaming of cabinet posts or political prominence. The life he envisioned was more private, grounded in the domestic hopes of a young man who wanted to marry early, build a family, and carve out a modest but meaningful path. Yet the world he inherited was not a quiet one, and the country he loved demanded more than private aspirations.

The year was 1965, and the boy from Bacolod stepped off the ship in Manila with the wide-eyed certainty of youth and the silent discipline of his parents’ teaching. The capital smelled of gasoline, rain, and ambition. Jeepneys roared past vendors calling out the price of roasted corn; students in barong and mini-skirts swarmed the sidewalks of Taft Avenue. In this new rhythm, Raffy felt both small and boundless. He had come to De La Salle College, carrying a suitcase, a scholarship, and the invisible weight of a name already etched in public service.

La Salle, then a bastion of Catholic rigor, believed that education was the art of forming conscience. Morning prayers blended with lectures on economics; Latin mottos on marble walls reminded the students that intellect without virtue was arrogance in uniform. Raffy thrived. He studied Political Science and Business Administration, believing that good governance demanded both morality and management. “They taught us to think in systems and to act in faith,” he would later write, “to balance heart and head, reason and compassion.”

But the classroom was only half his teacher. Manila itself — uneasy under Marcos’s rising power, simmering with protest and poverty — became his moral proving ground. On weekends he visited slum areas with his classmates, bringing food and conversation rather than charity. The sight of barefoot children memorizing prayers beside open drains disturbed him far more than any textbook on social theory. “I began to understand that leadership was not about command,” he recalled. “It was about stewardship — about standing guard over the dignity of others.”
Faith and the Forging of Conscience

The Christian Brothers at La Salle hammered discipline into him: punctuality, precision, personal accountability. When he later pursued the MBA Senior Executive Program at the Ateneo Graduate School of Business, the Jesuits added something subtler — the art of discernment. They urged reflection before decision, conscience before convenience. “Faith and reason are not adversaries,” one professor told him. “They are the two wings of leadership.”

Those dual influences fused into his personal creed. “Faith must translate into work; work must uplift others,” Raffy would summarize decades later. He learned that success unattached to service was spiritual bankruptcy.

In college, Raffy stood at the crossroads of history and identity. The Cold War’s shadows had lengthened across Southeast Asia, and as the Vietnam conflict escalated, the question of national defense — how a small archipelagic nation could protect itself — weighed heavily on the minds of many young Filipinos. Raffy felt this weight personally.

If he ever imagined a future in uniform, it was framed not by ambition but by the desire to help secure a country increasingly buffeted by external pressures and internal unrest. But another force was shaping him in equal measure — love.
Love Enters the Frame

One evening in 1967, a classmate invited him to a debut at the Vera-Perez mansion in Quezon City. The chandeliers glowed; the orchestra played Sinatra; and across the room stood a young woman whose poise quieted the noise around her. Elizabeth Jalbuena — Assumption College student, reserved yet radiant. “It was love at first sight,” Raffy said. “She had an elegance that disarmed me and a shyness that made me want to protect her.”

He was eighteen; she was seventeen. He courted her the old-fashioned way: handwritten letters, long drives in a weather-beaten car that she treated like a Rolls-Royce, gentle humor to break her guarded silence. “When we first held hands,” she later told friends, “life was never the same again.”

After two and a half years, he proposed — but only after securing employment. When he asked her father, the dignified Louie P. Jalbuena, for her hand, the older man studied him with the calm severity of a patriarch. “Do you have work?” he asked. Raffy answered yes. “Then take care of her,” Louie said, his tone half-blessing, half-command.

They were married on May 16, 1970, at St. Andrew’s Church, a day before Raffy’s twenty-first birthday. The newlyweds laughed when Louie quipped, “The first fifty years are the hardest.” Time would prove him right.
The Apprenticeship of Marriage

Those early years were a laboratory of humility. Manila was expensive, salaries modest, dreams large. Elizabeth, whom he affectionately called Sweetheart or Mama, managed the household with precision. “She ran the house like a corporation — with kindness as capital and patience as profit,” Raffy liked to joke.

He worked in executive positions for large corporations, absorbing the discipline of numbers and the politics of people. Boardrooms taught him about ambition; Elizabeth reminded him about compassion. “Each time I came home full of self-importance,” he admitted, “she’d hand me the baby and say, ‘Here’s your real work.’”

They were blessed with five children — Katrina, Barni, Rafa, Christina, and Alexi — and later twelve grandchildren. Each name represented a chapter in his moral education. Dinner was sacred: everyone at the table, no gadgets, grace before meals. Stories flowed more than lectures. “Storytelling was my way of shaping conscience,” he said. “I’d tell them about courage under fire, about honesty when nobody’s watching, about helping a stranger without asking why.”
The 1970s: Awakening

The martial-law years darkened the nation but illuminated Raffy’s convictions. The decade that followed his graduation was tumultuous. The First Quarter Storm exploded, martial law followed, insurgencies grew, and political repression deepened. The Philippines had entered one of its most perilous eras. He watched classmates seek comfort in complicity while others disappeared into detention. “Fear is contagious,” he reflected, “but so is courage.” He kept his head down professionally yet lent quiet support to reformists and academics who spoke for justice. That moral tension — between safety and service — would define his choices later when the country regained its freedom.

During these years, Raffy built a civilian career in the private sector. He worked for multinational companies, became exposed to management frameworks and corporate discipline, and learned the mechanics of organizational leadership — skills that would later serve him in unexpected, high-pressure roles in government.
But while he was working in the private sphere, the country around him was unraveling.

Rebellions simmered. Crime and corruption metastasized. Institutions weakened. The military strained under heavy expectations while the nation teetered between repression and upheaval. For someone like Raffy Alunan — whose conscience was molded by Christian Brothers, whose lineage carried the weight of public duty, and whose instincts leaned toward service — it was impossible not to feel the pull of a greater responsibility.

At work, he began to see how institutions mirrored the people who ran them. Corruption in business, like in government, thrived on silence. He learned to speak up diplomatically, to correct without humiliating, to insist on transparency even when it slowed profit. “That period was my moral apprenticeship,” he said. “I was learning how to fight wrong without losing grace.”
Faith at the Center

Despite the political gloom, faith remained his compass. Sunday Mass was non-negotiable; so were nightly prayers with Elizabeth and the children. He joined community groups that bridged business with civic duty. One Jesuit retreat left an indelible mark: “If you want peace, work for justice.” Those words would echo when he later faced insurgents and terrorists as Interior Secretary.

He also deepened his ties with the military reserve program, undergoing ROTC and later training with the PC-Special Action Force, finding in discipline a spiritual metaphor. “Drill and prayer are cousins,” he mused. “Both are about surrendering ego to a higher order.”
Elizabeth, the Quiet General

As the family grew, Elizabeth became his steadfast partner in leadership. She instilled manners, routine, and compassion in their children, ran earthquake drills, taught first aid, and managed household crises with calm authority. Raffy often said, half in jest, “I was the speaker of the house; she was the loudspeaker.”
When disagreements flared, forgiveness became their diplomacy. “Forgiveness is essential,” he wrote. “Forgetting takes longer — but love is the memory that outlasts the quarrel.”

Their marriage was more than companionship; it was his moral gymnasium. Through her, he learned patience in frustration, humor in exhaustion, tenderness in command. “Elizabeth reminded me that leadership begins at home,” he said. “If you cannot lead a family with empathy, you cannot lead a nation with justice.”
The Birth of a Philosophy

By the early 1980s, Raffy had become a seasoned executive with a growing unease about complacency. The Philippines, still under dictatorship, suffered brain drain, cronyism, and cynicism. He began writing essays and giving talks about ethical leadership, arguing that development without discipline was decay in disguise.

He would later condense his worldview into a triad: God, Country, Family — in that order. “That hierarchy keeps me upright,” he explained. “It prevents idolatry of wealth or power. If I ever reverse it, I lose my soul.”

Friends recall how he could shift from corporate language to moral reasoning effortlessly. Over lunch he might discuss market share; by dessert he’d quote Scripture on stewardship. He spoke softly, but his conviction carried weight. Those who dismissed him as idealistic learned that he was, in fact, relentless.
The Unexpected Turn
He did not seek government. Government sought him.

His moral restlessness soon found purpose. In the mid-1980s, as the Marcos regime weakened and the opposition gained momentum, Raffy found himself increasingly connected with civic groups calling for democratic change. He became a trustee of Manindigan, an organization of professionals, entrepreneurs, and academics who openly opposed dictatorship and advocated for a return to democratic governance.

At this time, Raffy stood at the crossroads between comfort and calling. He had already built a solid career in the corporate world — an executive in large firms, respected for his discipline and strategic mind. Yet something inside him felt unquiet. “I was earning well, but I wasn’t serving enough,” he would later admit. “The country was unraveling, and I could no longer stand watching from the sidelines.”

The Marcos dictatorship was in its twilight. The air was thick with dissent, fear, and fatigue. Reformists, intellectuals, and professionals were beginning to converge under one banner: Manindigan — a movement whose name literally meant “to stand one’s ground.” It was a brotherhood of conscience, gathering lawyers, professors, entrepreneurs, priests, and journalists who believed that silence had become complicity. Raffy joined as a trustee. Inside candle-lit rooms in Quezon City, he and his peers debated freedom, ethics, and the price of integrity. Some were later jailed; others, exiled. For Raffy, the risk was personal. He had five young children and a wife whose steady faith never wavered.

When the People Power Revolution unfolded in 1986, many of Manindigan’s members — and the broader middle-class movement it represented — transitioned into the rebuilding effort under President Corazon C. Aquino, the widow who became the nation’s moral compass. It was in this atmosphere of national renewal that Raffy Alunan was invited to join the government. For Raffy, it felt like destiny knocking.

He did not see this as personal elevation. In his own account, public service — when done right — was nothing more than stewardship. In the face of crises, it meant stepping into spaces where one could help save lives, protect civilians, or restore order. It was never about power, and certainly not about fame. It was about responsibility.
And so, after much discernment, Raffy accepted what he believed was a summons to serve the times.
The Making of a Statesman

In early 1991, President Aquino invited him to serve as Secretary of Tourism. The country was still healing from years of repression and chaos. Tourism had collapsed; infrastructure lay in ruins; and the nation’s image abroad was tainted by coups, kidnappings, and political instability.

The role of Tourism Secretary was not one he imagined for himself. He inherited corruption in the ranks, decaying public assets, threats against tourists, and challenges that required firmness and moral clarity. Yet the moment he entered office, he realized how deeply its responsibilities were tied to safety, good governance, and national image. He brought with him a corporate manager’s precision and a public servant’s passion. His first order of business was to rebuild the industry’s credibility — both domestically and internationally. He met with airline executives, hotel owners, and travel associations, often working late into the night crafting policy that emphasized safety, sustainability, and service.

He removed Pagsanjan Falls from the preferred destination list due to rampant moral decadence and crime against visitors — a bold move that sent a clear message: public safety and moral decency were non-negotiable. He oversaw Camp John Hay, helped preserve its natural state, and completed the reconstruction of Corregidor, transforming it into a national shrine of wartime heroism.

But more critical were the emergencies. During the devastating 1989 earthquake, he organized search-and-rescue operations in Baguio. During the coup attempt that same year, rebel forces occupied Makati’s financial district, trapping civilians and foreign tourists in its hotels. Raffy was tasked to negotiate for their safe release — which he accomplished by working with Scout Rangers to protect lives and avoid further bloodshed.
This coup-night episode — later recounted in vivid detail in his own writing — would become one of the defining moments of his early service.
It was here, under overwhelming uncertainty, that Raffy Alunan began earning a reputation that followed him throughout his public life:
A calm mind in chaos.
A steward of lives.
A servant of the Republic at its most fragile moments.

He launched the “Rediscover the Philippines” campaign, not as a mere slogan but as a movement of national renewal. He believed that tourism could become a mirror of the nation’s soul. Under his leadership, the DOT began restoring heritage sites, training local guides, and promoting lesser-known regions to disperse economic growth beyond Metro Manila.
But more than marketing, Raffy focused on ethics. He insisted that tourism projects uphold environmental responsibility and community inclusion — principles rare at the time.
The Moral Machinery of Governance

Inside Malacañang, he earned a reputation for integrity. Staffers noted his punctuality, his refusal to cut corners, and his ability to balance firmness with courtesy. “He didn’t raise his voice,” one aide said. “He raised standards.”

President Aquino valued his independence of mind. During Cabinet meetings, when debates grew heated, she would sometimes turn to him and ask, “What do you think, Raffy?” He would answer with disarming calm: “Madam President, I think the right thing is rarely the easiest thing.” That line would become a quiet mantra of his governance style.

He approached bureaucracy as both system and soul. He streamlined processes, championed decentralization, and mentored young civil servants to think beyond compliance. “Rules are useless if they don’t uplift lives,” he told them. “We are not paper-pushers — we are nation-builders.”

Yet, reform always provokes resistance. Entrenched interests fought him subtly — through bureaucratic delay, whisper campaigns, and political sabotage. “I learned early that corruption doesn’t always wear a villain’s face,” he wrote. “Sometimes it smiles, shakes your hand, and invites you to lunch.” Through every trial, his moral compass pointed unwaveringly to service. “I entered government with clean hands and intended to leave the same way,” he told colleagues. “No title is worth my soul.”
A New Chapter of Duty
Raffy’s performance under the Aquino administration did not go unnoticed.
When Fidel V. Ramos — a soldierstatesman and fellow believer in disciplined, values-driven governance — became president in 1992, he looked to Raffy Alunan to join his Cabinet.
This would become the longest, most intense, and most consequential chapter of his public service.

It was here that Raffy stepped not only into crisis after crisis, but into roles that demanded moral courage, strategic clarity, and an unshakeable commitment to what he later described as the essence of his service: “A life of stewardship and service characterized by crisis management, saving lives, and fidelity to our moral values for a better Philippines.”
This was no longer the young man dreaming of West Point.
Nor the corporate executive.
Nor the newly married father hoping to build a quiet life.
This was Raffy Alunan — called into the center of a nation in upheaval, becoming the man the times required.
A Nation at the Brink

Leadership, when stripped of ceremony and rhetoric, is measured not by speeches or symbols but by what one chooses to confront. When Raffy accepted President Ramos’ invitation to lead the Department of the Interior and Local Government, he was not stepping into an office — he was stepping into the Republic’s crucible.
The early 1990s were dangerous years.

The Cold War had just ended, leaving behind scattered insurgencies, banditry, radicalized factions, and heavily armed political clans. Ethnic tensions flared in the south. Kidnapping syndicates grew bold. The wounds left by Marcos-era authoritarianism had not yet healed, and institutions were fragile It was during this precarious period that Ramos called. “Raffy,” he said, “I need you at the Department of the Interior and Local Government.” The offer was not a promotion; it was a crucible. The DILG was a labyrinth of politics, policing, and local governance — a post where idealists often burned out or broke down.
Raffy hesitated. His family had already endured years of his long absences and constant stress. Elizabeth worried quietly but never protested.
He brought no fanfare.
No political machinery.
No personal army of patronage.

Just the values learned from Christian Brothers, sharpened by corporate discipline, and anchored by a lifelong belief that public office is not a prize, but a stewardship. And stewardship during crisis meant confronting the darkest corners of power.
The Alunan Doctrine

When he assumed the DILG portfolio in July 1992, he brought with him not just credentials but conviction. His reputation as an incorruptible manager preceded him. Soldiers, mayors, and governors soon learned that he was both compassionate and uncompromising. He demanded efficiency, transparency, and loyalty — not to him, but to the Republic.

The first crisis confronting him was one the public had long feared but few had dared to address: the proliferation of warlordism and private armies across the country. These armed groups — funded by political clans, criminal networks, and extremist elements — were destabilizing communities, terrorizing civilians, and weakening the rule of law.
Alunan’s response was direct, disciplined, and historic.

He launched Oplan Paglalansag, a nationwide effort to dismantle private armed groups through coordinated police and military operations combined with clear legal parameters. It was the first major campaign in the post-dictatorship era to draw a firm line between legitimate security and political violence.

A key policy emerged from this campaign — one that would later bear his name: The Alunan Doctrine: Any elected official keeping more than two armed bodyguards would be presumed to maintain a private army — and the group could be disbanded under law.

It was a simple rule, but its message was thunderous: Political power must never be protected by private firepower. The Republic has only one legitimate armed force. And it must serve only the people.

Thousands of unauthorized weapons were seized. Private armies were dismantled. Local warlords were stripped of their monopoly on violence. It was a reform both bold and dangerous. The threats were real. Some were overt, others whispered. But for Raffy Alunan, stewardship required moral clarity — and moral courage.
Local Governance and National Stability

Beyond armed groups, the DILG is responsible for local government supervision — a complex ecosystem of governors, mayors, barangay officials, and local councils, each with distinct challenges and political dynamics. Under Alunan, this labyrinth was transformed through a combination of discipline, capacity building, and values-based leadership.

He championed programs that strengthened local autonomy while ensuring accountability. He helped professionalize LGUs and supported initiatives that encouraged transparency, disaster preparedness, coordinated law enforcement, and social development.
He believed deeply that peace was not merely the absence of conflict — it was the presence of functional, honest governance.

That sustainable development required order. That public safety was the ground zero of social progress. This framework — peace leading to development, development reinforcing peace — would guide his entire DILG tenure.
The Burden of Order
The early Ramos years were defined by crisis. And crisis did not arrive as isolated events; it came in waves.
Bombings.
Kidnappings.
Communist and separatist insurgencies.
Localized armed conflicts.
Warlord politics.

In every case, Raffy stepped into the fray not as a politician, but as a crisis manager whose primary mission was, as he would later summarize his entire career: “Saving lives and remaining faithful to our moral values for a better Philippines.”

He worked closely with the Philippine National Police, the military, and local government officials, often placing himself at the heart of volatile situations where a single misstep could cost lives. In those moments, he negotiated tense stand-offs, defused explosive confrontations, and held firm to the principle that protecting civilians was not merely a priority but a moral obligation. Task forces were formed under his direction, rescue operations were coordinated with precision, and every action taken was guided by the belief that human life must remain paramount.

His approach to crisis management was both disciplined and deliberate. He began by gathering intelligence to fully understand the situation on the ground. He ensured seamless coordination among agencies, believing that unity of effort was essential to effectiveness. He moved quickly but never recklessly, balancing urgency with careful judgment. Communication lines were kept open to avoid confusion and prevent escalation. And always, his goal was clear: to restore order without resorting to unnecessary force.

He never viewed a crisis as an arena for displaying authority. Instead, he saw it as a solemn responsibility to protect the public — to keep the peace, save lives, and uphold the values of a nation that depended on leaders who could stay steady in the face of danger.
A Soldier’s Heart, A Statesman’s Hand

Though a civilian by background, Raffy carried the spirit of a soldier — a calling that had first gripped him in childhood and matured through years in the Army Reserve. During his DILG years, this inclination deepened.
He trained with the Special Action Force, the First Scout Ranger Regiment, and the Special Forces Regiment (Airborne).
He would go on to earn the rank of Colonel in the AFP Reserve Command, eventually commanding entire Infantry Reserve Divisions.

In many ways, his dual identity — soldier and public administrator — allowed him to serve at DILG with a unique blend of courage and prudence. He understood the language of field commanders, the urgency of tactical decisions, and the delicate balance between force and negotiation.
President Ramos — himself a military man and democratic reformer — saw in Raffy a fellow steward, a leader who could uphold discipline without sacrificing conscience.
Together, they forged a period of relative stability during a time when the nation desperately needed anchors.
The Philosophy of Security

For Raffy, national security was not just about borders and bullets. It was about people — about human and ecological safety, social justice, and moral order. “Security,” he wrote, “is freedom from fear and want — and both require good governance.”

He visited conflict areas not as a spectator but as a messenger of peace: Basilan, Cotabato, Samar, the Cordilleras. Often, he went without cameras, speaking to rebels, priests, and farmers alike. He believed that listening was the first act of leadership.

He survived near-crashes in military aircraft, sea mishaps in Mindanao, and threats from groups that saw reform as ruin. “You don’t measure courage by the absence of fear,” he said. “You measure it by walking anyway.”

His military background deepened during this period. As a Colonel in the AFP Reserve, and an adopted member of the PMA Marangal Class of 1974, he commanded two infantry reserve divisions — the 131 and later the 9th. These experiences convinced him that citizen-soldiers and public officials share the same oath: to defend not power, but principle.
The President and the Public Servant
Those who witnessed the Ramos-Alunan partnership remember their chemistry. Ramos, ever the tactician, valued data and deadlines; Alunan valued discipline and decency.
Cabinet meetings often began with FVR’s brisk “Let’s do it!” and ended with Raffy’s measured reminders about ethics. They balanced each other — one the engineer, the other the conscience.

Ramos once told him privately, “You’re one of the few who tell me what I need to hear, not what I want to hear.” Raffy took that as the highest compliment. “FVR had moral courage,” he said. “He knew that loyalty is not silence; it’s honesty delivered with respect.”

Under their watch, the DILG became an incubator of reform. Local autonomy was strengthened; barangay justice systems were modernized; police professionalism was revived through merit-based promotions. Raffy’s motto was simple: “Unity, Sincerity, Cooperation, Collaboration.” He repeated it so often that subordinates called it “the four-fold creed.”
He explained it plainly: “Unity for purpose, sincerity in intention, cooperation in effort, and collaboration in execution — that’s how nations rise.”
The Man Within the Mission

Behind the authority, Raffy remained introspective. He still attended Mass whenever possible, sometimes in makeshift chapels inside army camps. He carried a small Bible in his briefcase — a habit he kept for decades.

At home, Elizabeth remained his emotional anchor. Their long phone calls became nightly rituals, her voice grounding him after days of policy battles. “When you’re surrounded by power,” she told him, “never forget who you are when you come home.” There were nights when exhaustion turned to doubt. “I asked God why public service demanded so much pain,” he later confessed. “The answer came softly: because love is proven by sacrifice.”

He lost friends to violence, witnessed betrayal within institutions he had trusted, and felt the loneliness of moral consistency in a field addicted to compromise. Yet he refused cynicism. “You cannot lead if you stop believing that people can change,” he wrote in his journal. “You must keep faith even when faith hurts.”
The Cost of Service

Behind the achievements, however, lay a cost the public rarely saw. Government service consumed him in ways that left little space for rest or family. The hours were unforgiving, the dangers constant, the scrutiny unrelenting. Weekends and holidays faded into a blur of briefings, field operations, emergency travel, and late-night decisions that could not wait for sunrise. His family saw him less and less as the demands of national security grew heavier.

Through all this, his wife Elizabeth — unwavering in loyalty and quiet strength — carried the burden of raising their children with grace and courage. While he confronted crises that often placed him in harm’s way, she kept their home intact, steadying the family he longed to protect but could seldom be present for.

He never glorified these sacrifices. In fact, he spoke of them with humility, even with a measure of regret, fully aware that public service, for all its nobility, can strain the very relationships one seeks to honor. It is here, in this tension between duty and home, that the most human side of his DILG years comes into sharpest relief.

He did not pursue recognition. He did not chase power. What he sought was far simpler and far more difficult: to do what was right, even when it came at personal cost. That fidelity to moral values — steady, uncompromising, and sincere — became the enduring trademark of his public life.
Leaving Office, Keeping the Mission
By 1996, after nearly four years in office, the cost of service had become visible. His hair had grayed; his children were growing up without him. He decided to step down, not in defeat but in peace.
He left the DILG poorer in possessions but richer in conviction. Upon his farewell, President Ramos said, “You served with integrity, and that’s the rarest currency in government.”
The press hailed him as “the Cabinet’s moral compass.” His colleagues called him “the Man who Walked the Talk.”

Back in private life, he returned to business and civic engagements, but the public still sought his voice on matters of governance and national security. He chaired the Philippine Council for Foreign Relations, lectured at universities, and wrote columns dissecting the moral anatomy of statecraft. Yet he never glamorized his years in power. “Government didn’t make me important,” he said. “It made me accountable.”
Harvard and the Renewal of Vision

For the first time in many years, Raffy Alunan awoke to a day without an urgent briefing to study, a crisis demanding his presence, or a convoy idling at the gate. The quiet was almost unsettling, a sharp contrast to the relentless cadence that had defined his life for so long. After years at the helm of the Department of the Interior and Local Government — years spent confronting private armies, insurgency, political violence, crime syndicates, and the slow erosion of institutions — he stepped into a setting that seemed impossibly distant from the intensity of Philippine public life: the serene, tree-lined avenues of Harvard University’s John F. Kennedy School of Government.
It was 1996.
He was fifty years old.
And though he could not yet see it, this single year — set between duty and rest, between service and self — would become the hinge on which his inner and outer worlds would turn.
Arrival in Cambridge

When he and his family arrived in Boston that autumn, the air carried the crisp scent of new beginnings. The redbrick buildings of Harvard Yard glowed in the afternoon light, their Georgian symmetry suggesting permanence, order, and legacy — things Raffy had tried to build back home. The Alunans rented a modest apartment near campus. For the first time in years, Raffy was a student again, not a Cabinet Secretary. He walked to class with a backpack instead of a briefcase, his notes in one hand, coffee in the other. “Harvard stripped me of titles,” he wrote in his journal. “Here I was not Secretary Alunan. I was simply Raffy from the Philippines, learning again how to listen.”

His classmates were a mosaic of global experience: young diplomats from Africa, NGO leaders from Latin America, civil servants from Eastern Europe. In seminars, he often found himself debating development policy with people half his age — but always with humility and humor. “Experience teaches you patterns,” he told one student who asked for advice. “But wisdom teaches you when to break them.”

Courses on governance, economics, and leadership challenged his assumptions. He absorbed new theories but weighed them against lived experience — against nights in Camp Crame, trips to conflict zones, the smell of gun oil and fear. “The classroom taught frameworks; the Philippines had taught reality,” he would later reflect. “Combining the two, I began to see governance not as command and control, but as community and conscience.”
A Year of Healing and Rediscovery

For Raffy, Harvard was more than an academic pilgrimage; it was a season of healing. The years in government had left scars — disappointments with politics, betrayals by allies, exhaustion from endless firefights both literal and bureaucratic. In Cambridge’s quiet libraries, he found space to think again, to pray again, to breathe.

He often attended Mass at St. Paul’s Parish in Harvard Square, sometimes bringing his children. “It was there I realized that peace is not the absence of conflict,” he wrote to a friend. “It’s the presence of purpose.”

The family flourished in that year abroad. They did housework and homework together, explored museums, and walked the cobblestone streets of Boston. On weekends, they shared clam chowder and laughter at Quincy Market. “We rediscovered ourselves as a family,” he said. “It was the happiest year of our lives.”

He also forged friendships with professors who would become lifelong mentors. One of them, a former diplomat, once told him, “You have the heart of a soldier and the mind of a statesman. But remember — every statesman must learn to rest, or he becomes a machine.” Raffy took the advice to heart. For the first time in decades, he learned to be still without feeling unproductive.

For nearly a year, the Alunan family lived in a modest apartment. Gone were the flashing police lights, the stream of meetings, the adrenaline of crisis. In their place: shared breakfasts, walks to the park, long discussions over homework, quiet nights, and the gentle rhythm of a family rediscovering one another.
He would later describe this year as “the most idyllic of our lives.”

They traveled together, learned together, laughed together. He washed dishes with his children, carried groceries, shoveled snow, did the housework that fame or office often steals from a man. In the simplicity of these routines, he found a joy that no title could equal.
The man who once negotiated with rebels and commanded security forces now learned to navigate Boston winters, work an American washing machine, and attend school events as simply “Dad.”
The Republic had its turn.
Now, his family did.
The Global Lens

At the Kennedy School, Raffy Alunan was hardly a novice. His years navigating crisis management, national security, governance, and institutional reform had given him a lived understanding of statecraft that no textbook could fully capture. Yet he arrived with characteristic humility, fully aware that learning is a lifelong discipline and that leadership must constantly evolve.

In Cambridge, he immersed himself in subjects that spoke directly to the challenges he had grappled with back home — governance and public administration, national security strategy, development policy, institutional reform, crisis leadership, and the ethics of public office. Each lecture, each case study, and every spirited exchange with classmates from across the world reinforced a truth he had long sensed on the ground: the problems confronting the Philippines were not unique, but the moral courage required to confront them was indispensable.

His professors quickly recognized the depth he brought to the classroom. His peers gravitated toward him, drawn not by title but by the authority of someone who had lived on the frontlines of governance, who had seen how institutions break and how societies heal.

And beneath the academic rigor, something more profound was taking place within him. The year became a season of reawakening — an opportunity to step back, to see his country from a wider lens, to measure what had been done and what remained unfinished. It reframed his life’s mission, deepened his understanding of the nation’s vulnerabilities, and strengthened his resolve to return home not to withdraw but to serve with renewed clarity and purpose.
Commencement and Homecoming

In June 1997, Raffy Alunan walked across the stage at Harvard Yard to receive his master’s degree. The setting was iconic, but what mattered more was the sight of Elizabeth and their children in the audience, waving proudly as his name was called. For a man who had spent so many years away from home in the service of the nation, this moment — simple, unadorned, familial — held a quiet, incomparable weight.

When he returned to the Philippines, it was without the trappings of public office, without the security escorts or the relentless pressure of a cabinet post. What he carried instead was far more enduring: a sharpened moral compass, a clarified worldview, and a renewed sense of purpose. Harvard had given him distance — not to detach from the Philippines, but to see it more clearly. And in that clarity, he rediscovered the depth of his commitment to the country he had long served.

From this point forward, his service would assume new forms. He would lend his voice to national security advocacy, guide institutions through corporate governance, lead in the military reserve force, engage more deeply in civic life, and eventually, find another arena of stewardship in Rotary. The cabinet title was gone, yet in its place emerged something rarer: the authority that comes from a life tested by crisis, tempered by discipline, and examined with honesty.
Harvard did not transform him into a different man.
It allowed him to become more fully the man he was meant to be.
A Citizen at Large

Most people leave government and close the chapter with finality, drawing a line between what came before and what will come after. For Raffy, leaving the Cabinet was not an ending but an inflection point. He returned to a Philippines still wrestling with the same forces he had confronted in office — political frailty, institutional gaps, national security concerns, and the persistent need for moral leadership. The tools he would use were different now. But the mission, in its essence, remained unchanged.

When he stepped back into private life after Harvard, he carried no official authority, yet the gravitas of his experience followed him. Years of crisis management, institution-building, and dangerous negotiations had given him an unusual vantage point from which to understand national fragility. The Harvard year had only sharpened that lens. He came home with a deeper appreciation for interdependence, for the global currents affecting Philippine stability, and for the ways strong institutions could lift or undermine a nation.

In the corporate world, he entered an environment that required a different kind of discipline. He served on the boards of major companies: At Pepsi-Cola Products Philippines, Inc., he served first as Independent Director, later as Chairman of the Audit Committee, insisting that transparency and consumer responsibility were not slogans but standards. He joined Sun Life of Canada (Philippines), where he helped modernize compliance and ethics systems. He advised the Sangley Airport Infrastructure Group, advocating local innovation and environmental responsibility long before “green logistics” became fashionable.

His roles spanned industries that were, in different ways, tied to national stability — consumer goods, insurance, defense manufacturing, energy, and infrastructure — industries ranging from beverage manufacturing to insurance, energy, defense production, and transport infrastructure. He moved through these boardrooms with the steady, reflective presence of someone who had seen institutions under stress and understood their long-term stakes. Decisions were never merely operational for him. They were tied to national resilience, workforce dignity, and ethical stewardship. His training in governance and his experience in government informed his approach. He favored long arcs over short-term wins, and institutional strengthening over expediency.

But his post-Cabinet life did not revolve solely around corporate responsibilities. His interest in national security — shaped by early aspirations of military service, tempered during his DILG years, and refined at Harvard — continued to grow. He became increasingly involved in foreign relations and strategic studies.

As chairman of the Philippine Council for Foreign Relations, he became an interlocutor between diplomats, military leaders, business executives, and academics. He assessed geopolitical developments with a steady hand, emphasizing credible deterrence, rule of law, and the need for cohesive national direction. His membership in institutions devoted to defense and maritime security expanded his understanding of how the Philippines fit into an increasingly contested regional order.

His military involvement deepened as well. Holding the rank of Colonel in the Reserve Forces, he commanded infantry divisions and was welcomed by elite units of both the AFP and the PNP. His bond with the uniformed services was not symbolic. It reflected a genuine alignment of values — discipline, moral courage, and preparedness. For him, national defense was not merely about weapons and formations; it was about character, leadership, and institutional integrity. Strength, he believed, was not performative. It was built quietly, consistently, and with purpose.

In the civic sphere, his service expanded further. He worked with organizations that promoted democratic values, institutional reform, youth development, athletic discipline, ethical leadership, and the spirit of EDSA. His influence in these circles was not anchored in charisma but in the steadiness of his moral compass. He became a mentor to emerging leaders and a resource person to policymakers navigating difficult terrain. Journalists often sought him for his sober assessments; his commentary never sensationalized issues but dissected them with clarity, experience, and an eye toward institutional upliftment.

His involvement in the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) and the Maritime League expanded his network and deepened his understanding of maritime security, critical technologies, and regional defense architecture.

He also found a voice as a public intellectual. Through essays and columns, he articulated a vision of the Philippines grounded in cohesion, discipline, and values-based governance. His coauthored book Silver Linings and his documentary “Tagaligtas” highlighted stories of service and resilience — narratives that reflected his belief that the nation’s strength lies not only in its institutions but in the character of its people. For him, the moral trajectory of a nation depended on its ability to cultivate virtues across sectors and generations.

Politics remained within his orbit, though he approached it differently now. Instead of seeking office, he founded a party list focused on good governance and national renewal. His political views were rooted less in partisanship than in his conviction that the country needed leaders grounded in integrity and accountability. He spoke not as a critic from the sidelines but as someone who had walked into crises and understood the price of fragility.

There was no retirement in the traditional sense. Instead, there was a widening of fields in which he could contribute. His schedule remained full: corporate meetings, national security forums, civic engagements, military activities, public lectures, and advisory roles. He carried no trappings of power, yet he moved within circles of influence by virtue of the reputation he had earned — measured, sober, disciplined, principled, and unafraid to speak the truth.

The most compelling figures navigate life with an internal gyroscope — a mechanism that stabilizes them regardless of external turbulence. In Raffy, that gyroscope was formed from a blend of family, faith, heritage, and experience. The boy from Bacolod, shaped by Christian Brothers, guided by his mother’s humility, and matured through the crucibles of governance and crisis, faced this new era with composure and clarity.
He also became President and Trustee of the Harvard Kennedy School Alumni Association of the Philippines, organizing forums that bridged technocrats and public servants.
His message was consistent: competence without conscience is chaos.

Raffy no longer held a Cabinet seat, but his relevance had grown broader. In the scattering of roles he took on — corporate steward, military colonel, educator, strategist, civic leader — one could trace a consistent through-line. Service, to him, was not confined to a position. It was a lifelong posture.

He had returned from Harvard not to rest but to resume the mission by other means. And in these years, his influence, though less public, became more enduring. Because the work was no longer tied to an office. It was tied to the man himself.

Indeed, great lives move in arcs rather than straight lines. The next arc of Raffy’s life would be less visible to the public, but no less significant. It was the period in which he transformed from a government official into a national resource — an adviser, strategist, thought leader, and custodian of institutional memory.
The Servant Among Soldiers

Though now a civilian, he remained active in the reserve forces of the Armed Forces of the Philippines. As Colonel of both the 131st and later 9th Infantry Division (Ready Reserve), he trained alongside younger officers who had grown up reading about him. He insisted on discipline, physical fitness, and moral example. “The uniform is borrowed authority,” he told them. “The moment you forget that, you become a bully instead of a protector.”

He was adopted by elite units — the PMA Marangal Class of 1974, the Special Action Force, the Special Forces Regiment (Airborne), and the First Scout Ranger Regiment — not for ceremonial reasons but because he lived their creed. His speeches before troops were simple yet stirring: “The fight for the Philippines is fought daily — in offices, in classrooms, in families. Keep your integrity clean; it’s the only armor that doesn’t rust.”
The Civic Visionary

Beyond the barracks and the boardroom, Raffy extended his reach into youth and sports development. As President of the Philippine Taekwondo Foundation, he championed martial discipline as moral formation. “Taekwondo teaches control — of body, of temper, of ego,” he said. “That’s the kind of defense every nation needs most.”

He served as Eminent Fellow of the Development Academy of the Philippines, Fellow of the Institute for Corporate Directors and Institute for Solidarity in Asia, organizations that trained thousands in ethical governance. To each new batch of executives, he delivered the same challenge: “Governance is character in operation. Systems will fail if the souls that run them are weak.”

In forums he could shift from economics to ethics with seamless logic. Asked once what single reform the Philippines most needed, he replied, “The reform of the Filipino conscience.” Silence followed — then applause.
Rotary, Faith, and the Final Mission

By 2023, Raffy had lived many lives: soldier, secretary, scholar, and citizen. Now, at seventy-five, he was called once more to serve — this time not by a President, but by the oldest Rotary club in Asia. The Rotary Club of Manila was entering its 105 year, and its members sought a leader of moral weight to steady its course. He had not campaigned for the office. In fact, he had tried to decline. But service has its own way of summoning those who have already served.
“I was content just to help quietly,” he would say later. “But Rotary is a family, and when family calls, you answer.”
The Unexpected Mandate

On July 6, 2023, beneath the chandeliers of the City of Dreams in Parañaque, Supreme Court Associate Justice Jose Midas Marquez administered his oath. The ballroom was filled with Rotarians in barong, their pins glinting like medals of faith. As he took the podium, Raffy Alunan looked out at the gathered faces and felt the old familiar mixture of duty and destiny.
“Service above self,” he said, “is not a slogan. It is an examination we take every day — and one we must keep passing even when no one is watching.”

He called for a culture anchored on unity, sincerity, cooperation, and collaboration — principles he had learned on battlefields and boardrooms alike. “Without them,” he warned, “any organization rots from within, no matter how grand its past.”
Storm Inside the Sanctuary

The year that followed would test those principles to the edge. Behind Rotary’s decorum lurked the same frailties he had encountered in government — ego, indifference, factionalism. He found himself presiding over disputes that seemed beneath men of their stature. “It pained me,” he admitted, “to see leaders forget that true elitism is measured by character, not comfort.”

He responded as he always had — with discipline tempered by empathy. He convened assemblies to air grievances openly, initiated a Health Check Survey to diagnose behavioral fault lines, and insisted that Rotary could not preach ethics without living them. When criticism came, he absorbed it silently. “Leadership,” he said, “is the art of keeping faith when others lose temper.”

Through the turbulence, he continued to celebrate what worked — the community projects, the mentorship of Rotaractors, the district awards that validated the club’s service. When District 3810 recognized RC Manila as Outstanding Club of the Year, he stood at the ceremony and smiled without bitterness. “The real elite,” he told his members, “are those who refuse to quit on each other.”
The Private Battle

Public figures are often remembered for their titles, decisions, and the crises they navigate. But the truest measure of a leader often resides not in how he performs under the lights, but in the life he builds when no one is watching. For Raffy, the most defining presence in that private realm was his wife, Elizabeth. Their marriage, built quietly and steadily over decades, formed the emotional ballast that allowed him to withstand the turbulence of public service.

Long before he became a Cabinet member, before the motorcades and crisis briefings and midnight calls, Raffy was a young man learning the contours of responsibility — not yet to a nation, but to a partner. Elizabeth entered his life not as a dramatic turning point but as a stabilizing force, someone whose gentleness softened the sharp edges of his discipline. She offered what few in public life ever find: an anchor that did not demand to be seen.

During his government years, the pressures were relentless. Crises do not adhere to office hours, nor do security briefings wait for family dinners to end.
