Raffy was often away — physically, mentally, emotionally — caught in the machinery of state, navigating threats that could not be deferred. While he served the Republic, Elizabeth served their home. She raised the children, managed the rhythms of daily life, and carried the unseen weight of worry that accompanies loving someone whose work inhabits danger.

It is easy to overlook this kind of labor because it is quiet. But the quietest influences are sometimes the most foundational. Behind the calm, steady posture Raffy showed the world was a partner who absorbed the anxieties he could not afford to display. She created the space where he could rest his defenses, where the world’s demands were momentarily suspended, where he was not a secretary or strategist or crisis manager, but simply a husband and father.

But life, in its unpredictable rhythm, would soon demand of him a courage different from the kind he had exercised in government. On March 13, 2024, Elizabeth passed away. Her loss marked a rupture in the narrative of his life — a point after which everything would be measured differently. For a man accustomed to confronting armed threats and political crises, grief was a battlefield without a map. There were no protocols for this kind of pain, no briefings to prepare him, no contingency plan to execute. The loss was intimate, irreversible, and profoundly human.

He returned to work because he had to, but he returned diminished, walking through familiar responsibilities with an unfamiliar hollowing in the chest. The country had taken much from him already — time, safety, peace of mind — but this was the price that cut deepest. Public service had always demanded sacrifice; what he did not foresee was that the cost would one day be measured in the currency of absence.

Yet Elizabeth’s influence did not end with her passing. Her memory became his compass. In the interviews and writings he would later share, a pattern emerged — not in statements of grief, but in the moral clarity he carried forward. The humility he showed, the discipline he practiced, the steadfastness he embodied were reflections of a man shaped not only by the crises he faced, but by the love that had steadied him. Her grace lived on in his restraint; her patience echoed in his deliberation; her quiet faith mirrored in the maturity of his convictions.

Their children, now grown, carried her warmth even as they inherited their father’s resolve. Family gatherings held a different timbre after 2005 — muted at times, but suffused with a tenderness that reflected their shared loss. Raffy learned to navigate a new landscape of fatherhood, one without the partner who had once held the center. But he did not retreat. He adapted, as he always had, drawing strength from faith, memory, and the knowledge that his wife’s legacy lived through the very family she had held together.

In the years that followed, he would take on roles across institutions — corporate, civic, military, diplomatic — yet those who knew him well could sense the quiet transformation. His service, always anchored in moral values, became even deeper, even more marked by a kind of inward stillness. It was as if grief had stripped away whatever remnants of vanity or ambition might have lingered, leaving only the essential: stewardship, duty, integrity, and the conviction that one’s life must mean something beyond self.
Elizabeth had been his sanctuary, and losing her forced him to build one within himself.
The public sees the statesman, the strategist, the soldier, the board director, the commentator.

But those who look closer — those who read the whole arc of his life — will see something more enduring: a man who learned to lead with discipline, but to live with grace; who confronted crises with courage, but faced love and loss with an even greater form of strength; who served his nation faithfully, while carrying within him the quiet legacy of the woman who helped build the man.
The Burden of Stewardship

In the months that followed, he threw himself into work with renewed purpose. He spoke often about unity, not as a slogan but as a discipline. He taught that sincerity is the bedrock of trust, that cooperation is the bridge between intent and impact, and that collaboration is how ordinary men achieve extraordinary things. His final addresses read like poems of faith:

“Uniting for a common purpose requires maturity and selflessness. It is in unity that we find the courage to face challenges, the compassion to support one another, and the wisdom to build a brighter future.”

He refused to be embittered by conflict. Instead, he used it as parable. “True leaders,” he said, “don’t win arguments; they win people back.” When his term as President of the Rotary Club of Manila ended on June 30, 2024, he stood before his members for the last time. The Manila Polo Club Turf Room was hushed as he spoke, his voice measured but clear. He thanked those who had labored faithfully, acknowledged the errors that had wounded unity, and closed with grace: “A club is only as good as its members want it to be. May we always want it to be good.”
Then he added softly, almost to himself, “I dedicate this year to God, who kept me whole, and to Elizabeth, who waited for me without complaint.”

After stepping down, he announced a temporary disengagement from official duties. “I need to pick up the pieces of my shattered life,” he told friends honestly. He spent quiet months settling family matters, writing, and reconnecting with his children and grandchildren. He also returned to the forums that had long been his ministry — speaking on national security, ethics, and faith as the country faced new geopolitical storms.

He remained convinced that the Philippines could still fulfill its promise if its citizens learned to place “country above self.” He spoke of it not as slogan but as sacrifice. “To love the nation,” he said, “is to surrender our comfort for its growth. We are all stewards of a dream too precious to abandon.”
Love as Legacy

When Mother’s Day arrived in 2024, he published a heart-rending tribute titled “What is Love Like for Fifty-Five Years.” It was both eulogy and love letter. He recounted their courtship at Assumption and La Salle, their family life filled with humor and humility, and the years of caregiving that tested and transfigured him. He ended with these words:
“I’ll miss our walks, our Holy Week retreats, our shared music. I’ll now only imagine her in others, in the places we’ve been, in every corner of our home. Until we meet again somewhere in time.”

Readers wept; Rotarians shared the piece across social media; friends saw in it the final proof that strength and tenderness can coexist. “Even in loss,” one colleague said, “he was teaching us how to love well.”
The Continuing Call

Today, Raffy Alunan sits on corporate and civic boards, mentoring leaders who call him simply “Sir Raffy.” His days are quieter now, but his purpose remains unyielding. He still writes, still lectures, still prays for a country he has spent a lifetime trying to heal.

He often quotes his favorite passage from St. Paul (2 Timothy 4:7): “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.” To friends who ask what keeps him going, he answers without hesitation: “Because the race is not done. My generation must pass the torch brighter than we received it.”

When he speaks to young leaders, his voice remains steady, his eyes alight with the same resolve that once lit Malacañang’s crisis rooms. “Serve freely,” he tells them. “Don’t count the hours. Walk your talk. Live your values.”
And when he pauses, as he often does, he looks heavenward before adding softly:
“If I’ve learned anything in this life, it’s that service is love made visible. And love — real love — never ends.”
Epilogue: The Quiet Strength that Remains
In the end, the story of Rafael Moreno Alunan III is not the story of a man who sought greatness. It is the story of a man who sought goodness — and in doing so, became great.

He did not chase the spotlight. It found him only because he stood where duty required him to stand: in disaster zones, in conflict areas, in policy rooms where the fate of the Republic hung in the balance, in communities long abandoned by the state, in the quiet hours of caregiving, in the moral crossroads of public life. Wherever he was needed, he appeared not with fanfare but with fidelity.
Across the long sweep of his life, one principle held him steady: A Filipino must stand for the Philippines.
Not as slogan, not as posture, but as a lived truth.

He lived this truth through crises survived, reforms enacted, dangers faced, and values upheld. He lived it through friendships forged in service, through brothers-inarms who claimed him as one of their own, through the communities that trusted him with their stories, their fears, their hopes. He lived it through years of quiet work — writing, teaching, advising, serving — long after the stage lights of government had dimmed.
Most of all, he lived it through love.

Elizabeth had been his first home, the steady heart of his youth, the companion through every season of his journey. Her strength became his mirror. Her dignity softened him. Her suffering refined him. Her loss reshaped him. And in the silence that followed her passing, he came to understand service in its most intimate form: the courage to begin again when half one’s world is gone.

It was then, in grief’s long shadow, that he discovered a clearer, deeper mission — to speak not only as a former cabinet secretary or soldier, but as an elder of the Republic. To warn without bitterness. To teach without condescension. To uplift without illusion. To remind his countrymen that patriotism is neither grand nor abstract; it is the sum of daily acts rooted in integrity.
He served because he believed the Philippines could be better.
He served because he believed Filipinos deserved more.

He served because the alternative — apathy, cynicism, surrender — was unacceptable to a man who had seen how fragile freedom is. His legacy, therefore, is not simply the reforms he championed or the institutions he strengthened, but the conscience he carried into every corner of the nation. A conscience shaped by memory, disciplined by danger, deepened by loss, and tempered by faith.

In the closing chapters of his life, he stands not as a hero carved from marble but as something far more human and therefore more enduring — a man who did his best, who kept his word, who stayed the course even whenit cost him, who loved his country without condition, and who walked steadily toward the horizon with hope still in his hands.
The Republic he defended will continue to face storms — political, moral, economic, geopolitical. Yet it is stronger because men like him carried its weight for as long as they could.
And so the story ends not with a farewell, but with continuity.

For as long as the Philippines produces stewards who place country above self, as long as its young draw wisdom from those who served before them, as long as truth remains alive in those who choose principle over convenience — the flame he carried will continue to burn.

Quietly. 
Steadily. 
Faithfully.
A life examined becomes a life shared. A life shared becomes a legacy.
And a legacy rooted in service becomes a nation’s inheritance.
This is the gift he leaves behind.
A Philippines he never stopped believing in.
A mission he never stopped pursuing.
A devotion that outlived every title and outlasted every storm. In the heart of the Republic, his footsteps remain.

photos.caption: At the Special Forces Regiment (Airborne) jump tower in Fort Magsaysay, Raffy Alunan is seen with two former Chiefs of Staff of the Armed Forces of the Philippines, General Lisandro Abadia and General Nick Enrile. The visit reflects Alunan’s long-standing engagement with the military and his deep respect for the elite airborne and special operations units whose courage and discipline he has consistently supported throughout his public service career.

A rare portrait of Rafael Rivas Alunan Sr., grandfather of Raffy Alunan. He served the nation with distinction as Congressman representing the 2nd District of Negros Occidental and later as Secretary of Agriculture during the administration of President Manuel L. Quezon. His leadership in both legislative and executive roles helped shape early agricultural policy and contributed to the strengthening of the Commonwealth government’s development agenda. This dignified portrait reflects a statesman whose dedication to public service left a legacy carried forward by future generations of the Alunan family.

Rafael Alunan Sr. serving as a member of President Manuel L. Quezon’s Cabinet during the Commonwealth era. As part of Quezon’s trusted circle of senior officials, he played a significant role in shaping early national policy and strengthening the administrative foundations of the soon-to-be independent Republic. His service during this formative period reflected both his competence and his deep commitment to public welfare — an ethos that would later influence his grandson, Raffy Alunan, in his own path of leadership and national service.

President Manuel L. Quezon inspecting and lifting a bundle of freshly harvested palay, symbolizing the nation’s commitment to agricultural progress during the Commonwealth era. Standing at his right is Raffy Alunan’s grandfather, who was serving as Secretary of Agriculture at the time. The photograph captures a historic moment that reflects both national pride in the country’s agrarian roots and the pivotal role played by Alunan’s grandfather in shaping early agricultural policy and rural development in the Philippines.

Raffy Alunan on the occasion of his First Communion, held on December 8, 1955, at La Salle College in Bacolod. The milestone marked an important moment in his early spiritual formation, reflecting the strong Catholic upbringing that would continue to guide his values and principles throughout his life.

Raffy Alunan is positioned at the center of the top row, directly behind the La Salle Brother seated in the first row. The photograph captures a moment from his early formation years, reflecting the disciplined environment and strong values imparted by the La Salle educational tradition — foundations that would later influence his leadership, service, and public life.

Basketball champions of the La Salle Grade School Typhoon League, the young team displays the discipline, teamwork, and competitive spirit nurtured during their formative years. Their victory reflects not only athletic skill, but the early development of character and camaraderie that La Salle continues to instill in its students.

A youthful portrait of Raffy Alunan from his La Salle yearbook, listed under his full name, Rafael Alunan y Moreno III. The entry reflects his early achievements as a well-rounded student: consistent Second Honors, active participation in Scouting and Dramatics, and membership in the Basketball Champion Team. Even in his formative years, the foundations of discipline, leadership, and versatility — traits that would later define his public service and national contributions — were already clearly evident.

A spirited gathering of La Salle High School classmates circa 1965, capturing the youthful camaraderie and lighthearted celebrations characteristic of their formative years. Amid the laughter, music, and shared stories, these moments strengthened bonds that would endure well beyond graduation. For Raffy Alunan and his peers, such gatherings were more than social occasions — they were the early threads of lifelong friendship woven in an era of innocence, optimism, and enduring school pride.

Raffy Alunan with his high school classmate Harry Rodriguez to his right, photographed at Paglaum Stadium in Bacolod City — fondly referred to in their youth as the “Tikalon Republic.” Joined by fellow La Salle classmates, the moment captures a slice of their formative years: carefree days of friendship, school spirit, and youthful exuberance in a place that shaped many of their earliest memories. The image reflects the enduring bonds forged in adolescence — connections that would accompany them well into adulthood.

Iñaki Ysasi, Nico Alonso, Harry Rodriguez, Eduardo Bonnin, Jong Revilla, Raffy Alunan, and Willy Racaza of La Salle Bacolod High School Class of 1965. The photograph reflects a formative era when the Christian Brothers played a pivotal role in shaping young boys into responsible, disciplined, and values-driven men. Their guidance left an enduring imprint on the class — instilling character, faith, and purpose that would influence their futures in public service, business, and community leadership.

Raffy Alunan at his high school graduation ball with Elizabeth, his steadfast companion and the only love of his life. Their enduring partnership — rooted in friendship, loyalty, and deep affection — began in youth and blossomed into a lifelong bond that shaped his personal journey. This photograph captures not only a milestone celebration, but also the early chapters of a love story that remained central to Alunan’s life, providing strength, grounding, and unwavering support through every season of his public and private endeavors.

A lively gathering of friends featuring Jerry Kilayko, Tina del Castillo, Elizabeth Jalbuena, Digoy Fernandez, and Rupert Suarez seated in front; with Candy Jalbuena, Carina Pelayo, Becka Favis, and Raffy Alunan standing behind them. The photograph captures the spirited camaraderie between La Sallites and Assumptionistas — two well-known academic communities whose alumni often found themselves together in the same social circles. The scene reflects an era of youthful fellowship, shared friendships, and memorable celebrations that helped shape enduring bonds across schools and generations.

Raffy Alunan (left), a La Sallite, and Ting Singson (right), an Atenean, share a light yet thoughtful exchange on courtship and music. During this period, Mr. Alunan was courting Elizabeth and sought Mr. Singson’s counsel, reflecting the camaraderie and mutual respect that marked their friendship.

Raffy Alunan during his formative years in the De La Salle College Naval Reserve Officers’ Training Corps (NROTC), circa 1966–1967. These early days in military training helped instill in him the values of discipline, leadership, and patriotism that would later define his service in national security and public life.

Raffy Alunan, then serving as Commanding Officer of the 9th Infantry Division Ready Reserve (9IDRR) of the Philippine Army, photographed at Camp Tecson during his induction into the elite First Scout Ranger Regiment. The moment marked a significant milestone in his long-standing commitment to national defense and reserve force development, underscoring his deep respect for the discipline, valor, and storied traditions of the Scout Rangers — one of the most formidable special operations units of the Armed Forces of the Philippines.

A vintage Boracay scene, captured during Elizabeth’s 60th birthday celebration at a charming al fresco Spanish restaurant along the island’s shoreline. Bathed in the warm glow of sunset and the island’s old-world serenity — before the rise of modern developments — the moment reflects a joyful milestone marked by family, love, and the timeless beauty of Boracay. For Raffy Alunan and Elizabeth, it remains one of their most cherished memories on the island they both held dear.

This photograph was taken in Shanghai while Raffy Alunan and wife Elizabeth were attending a wedding. Set against the vibrant backdrop of one of Asia’s most dynamic cities, the occasion brought together friends and families in celebration, offering a brief but memorable moment of joy and fellowship during his travels abroad.

Raffy Alunan with Special Action Force Commanding Officer, General Egay Aglipay, and PIO Chief, General Wykes Wycoco, during a field inspection of SAF units. The visit underscored the leadership’s commitment to ensuring that frontline troopers were fully supported — both operationally and logistically. Alunan personally helped oversee the distribution of essential equipment and supplies, reinforcing the administration’s focus on readiness, morale, and the welfare of elite police units tasked with the nation’s most demanding and high-risk operations.

“Walk for Peace” — A historic moment in September 1992, as Interior and Local Government Secretary Raffy Alunan leads a broad coalition of local officials, community leaders, military officers, and police commanders through the streets of Jolo, Sulu. The solidarity march, joined by Governor Tupay Loong, Representative Bin Sudi Tulawe, Asani Tammang, and all 18 municipal mayors of Sulu, signaled a united resolve to end armed conflict and advance development in the region. This public demonstration preceded a series of ‘Sulu Arms Limitation Talks,’ coordinated by Secretary Alunan and Senator Santanina Rasul, aimed at reducing the proliferation of weapons, strengthening peace efforts, and fostering stability in Muslim Mindanao. Supporting the initiative were Brig. Gen. Antonio Villamor of the 3rd Marine Brigade and PNP Provincial Director Rolando Hermosa — partners in a collective effort toward lasting peace and progress.”

DILG Secretary Raffy Alunan providing assistance to victims who had been held captive by Abu Sayyaf terrorists, the team works to ensure their safety, facilitate their recovery, and support their reintegration following a period of immense hardship.

At the Cotabato Airport, Secretary Raffy Alunan is welcomed by ARMM Governor Zac Candao, marking the start of an important engagement in the region. Accompanying him is Bong Lacson. The arrival underscores ongoing efforts to strengthen coordination and dialogue with local leaders in Mindanao.

At an MNLF camp just outside Jolo, Sulu, Secretary Raffy Alunan conducts an impromptu visit to initiate dialogue and explore avenues for peace. Seated to his right is Sulu Governor Sakur Tan, alongside the MNLF camp commander. Also present is Gen. Tam Manjoorsa of the MNLF Executive Committee, identifiable by his cap. The meeting reflects a critical effort to foster communication and build trust amid longstanding conflict in the region.

As Secretary of the Interior and Local Government, Raffy Alunan concurrently served as chair of the National Anti-Crime and Anti-Hijacking Task Force (NACAHT), the government’s principal inter-agency body for counterterrorism during the early 1990s. The role placed him at the forefront of emerging terror threats, including the activities of AlQaeda operatives already penetrating Southeast Asia at the time. Under his leadership, the task force undertook intensive coordination with military, police, intelligence, and international partners — laying early groundwork for the Philippines’ counterterrorism architecture long before global attention turned to transnational extremism.

Special Action Force Anniversary rites in 1993, attended by key national security leaders including Generals Timmy Imperial, Recaredo Sarmiento, Dictador Alqueza, and Avelino Razon, with Raffy Alunan joining the commemoration. The event honored the bravery, discipline, and sacrifice of the SAF troopers — elite lawenforcement professionals at the forefront of counterterrorism and high-risk operations. The gathering underscored the government’s commitment to strengthening the SAF’s capabilities during a period marked by complex internal security challenges, as well as Alunan’s steadfast support for the unit’s mission and its men and women in uniform.

Raffy Alunan receiving the Outstanding Achievement Medal (OAM) from President-elect Fidel V. Ramos — himself the first Commanding Officer of the Special Forces — and Brigadier General Leo Alvez, Commanding Officer of the Special Forces Regiment (Airborne), during the regiment’s anniversary celebration. The honor recognized Alunan’s exceptional contributions to national security, his steadfast support for the Armed Forces, and his deep engagement with the elite Special Forces community. The ceremony stands as a testament to his enduring commitment to country, service, and the men and women who safeguard the Republic with courage and distinction.

With Philippine National Police Chief, Director General Timmy Imperial, and members of the PNP General Staff at Camp Crame, circa January 1993. Raffy Alunan met with the police leadership during a pivotal period of institutional reform and intensified national security challenges. The gathering reflects the close coordination among top security officials as they worked to strengthen law enforcement capabilities, enhance public safety, and reinforce the PNP’s role in upholding peace and order throughout the country.

Col. Raffy Alunan, Commanding Officer of the 9th Infantry Division Disaster Response Regiment (PA), stands with Cabanatuan Mayor Julius Vergara, AFP Chief of Staff Gen. Dionisio Santiago, and Defense Secretary Angelo Reyes at the Commemorative Marker of the Battle of Cabu Bridge. The gathering pays tribute to the heroism and sacrifice of the soldiers who fought in this historic World War II engagement, honoring their legacy of courage and service to the nation.

Former DILG Secretary Raffy Alunan with President Fidel V. Ramos at the premiere of the documentary Tagaligtas, held on May 16, 2012. The film honored the valor and sacrifices of the Philippine Constabulary–Special Action Force (PC– SAF), whose legacy of courage both leaders deeply championed during their years of public service.

Maj. Gen. Alan Cabalquinto, Commander of the Army Special Forces (Airborne) Group, is positioned to the left of the principal subject. Standing fourth from the right is Capt. Sharon Reyes, while MSgt. Henry Hernia is seen kneeling fifth from the right. The photograph captures members of the elite Special Forces unit during a moment of camaraderie and professionalism.

Raffy Alunan in his capacity as a Colonel of the Reserve Forces of the Philippine Army. His rank reflects years of committed service to national defense, active engagement in readiness and mobilization programs, and his unwavering support for the Armed Forces of the Philippines. As a reservist officer, he contributed to strengthening civilian–military cooperation, disaster response capabilities, and homeland security efforts — demonstrating his belief that national service extends beyond government office and into the broader duty of safeguarding the Republic.

During the launch of the coffee-table book Silver Linings, former DILG Secretary Rafael “Raffy” Alunan III shares a moment with President Fidel V. Ramos. The event celebrated stories of resilience, leadership, and hope — values that both men embodied throughout their years of service to the nation.

Raffy Alunan is seen with officials and responders from the CAMANAVA Inter-Agency Rescue and Response unit and the 9th Infantry Division Disaster Response Regiment (9IDRR). The gathering highlights ongoing efforts to strengthen coordinated disaster preparedness and emergency operations in the CAMANAVA area.

At Nur Misuari’s camp in Sarangani, in the dead of night, Secretary Raffy Alunan participates in a sensitive back-channel mission to assess and advance emerging peace overtures. Seated to Misuari’s right is his former University of the Philippines classmate, Executive Secretary Ruben Torres. The encounter reflects a critical moment in the government’s quiet efforts to pursue dialogue amid conflict.

Photograph taken in January 1995 following the successful security operations that safeguarded Pope John Paul II during his visit to the Philippines — an event later revealed to have been targeted for assassination by Al-Qaeda operatives under the notorious Bojinka plot. Raffy Alunan stands at the center of the image, flanked on his right by Foreign Affairs Secretary Bobby Romulo and, partly obscured to his left, Defense Secretary Renato de Villa. The moment captures the gravity of a national security triumph achieved through swift coordination among government agencies, intelligence networks, and security forces, underscoring the high-stakes environment in which Alunan and the country’s top officials operated during one of the most consequential threats to Philippine and global security in the 1990s.

At the forward-most Philippine Marines outpost in Patikul, Sulu, Secretary Raffy Alunan stands with Vice President Joseph “Erap” Estrada and recently released Abu Sayyaf hostage Charles Walton, positioned between them. To Vice President Estrada’s left is Libyan Ambassador Rajab Azzarouq, whose diplomatic intervention was instrumental in securing Walton’s release. The moment captures a significant humanitarian milestone amid ongoing security challenges in the region.

In Phnom Penh, Cambodia, in 1993, Raffy Alunan meets with members of the Philippine United Nations peacekeeping contingent during one of the most pivotal moments in the country’s post-conflict reconstruction. The Philippine forces were deployed as part of the United Nations Transitional Authority in Cambodia (UNTAC), tasked with helping stabilize the nation after years of civil war.

Raffy Alunan with the Board of Trustees of the Philippine Council for Foreign Relations (PCFR), an organization composed of former diplomats, military officers, scholars, and seasoned practitioners in international affairs. The gathering reflects the council’s ongoing efforts to provide informed perspectives on foreign policy and national security, strengthen public understanding of global developments, and contribute to shaping the Philippines’ strategic direction in an increasingly complex international landscape. Alunan’s presence underscores his active engagement in dialogues that advance the country’s diplomatic and geopolitical interests.

Raffy Alunan and his Harvard classmates pose before the iconic statue of John Harvard at the university’s historic Yard. The famed bronze work, sculpted by Daniel Chester French — with Sherman Hoar serving as the model — remains one of the most recognizable symbols of Harvard University. The photograph captures a moment of camaraderie among classmates set against the storied backdrop of one of the world’s premier academic institutions.

Graduation day at the Harvard Kennedy School, where Raffy Alunan completed his Master in Public Administration in 1997. He studied at the John F. Kennedy School of Government during the 1996–1997 academic year under the guidance of distinguished faculty members, including John W. Thomas — Lecturer in Public Policy, Faculty Chair of the Singapore Program, and co-chair of the Leaders in Development Program — and Matt Andrews, the Edward S. Mason Senior Lecturer in International Development. This moment marked the culmination of Alunan’s intensive training in public leadership, governance, and international development, further equipping him for the highlevel responsibilities he would later undertake in government and public service.

Raffy Alunan at the historic Malkin Athletic Center in Cambridge, Massachusetts — the iconic Harvard gym where he often played basketball during his graduate school years. The court became a familiar gathering place for him, his son Rafa, his classmate Ato Salud, and other students and athletes who happened to be there. These informal games offered moments of camaraderie, father-and-son bonding, and welcome relief from the intensity of academic life at Harvard Kennedy School. In this setting, Alunan found a blend of discipline, fellowship, and simple joy that remains one of his fondest memories from his time in Cambridge.

Raffy Alunan with his Harvard classmates during an intensive group discussion at the Kennedy School. The session reflects the collaborative, globally diverse, and intellectually rigorous environment that defined his graduate studies. Surrounded by peers from various countries and professional backgrounds, Alunan engaged in debates, case analyses, and policy exercises that sharpened his strategic thinking and broadened his understanding of governance and international development. These moments of shared inquiry and critical dialogue became foundational to his later leadership in public service.

The inaugural Belle-lettrists’ Banquet & Awards, a joint endeavor of The Manila Times and the Harvard Kennedy Alumni Association of the Philippines, Inc., celebrating excellence in writing, commentary, and thought leadership. The event gathered distinguished authors, public intellectuals, and policy professionals in a night honoring the power of the written word to inform, inspire, and shape national discourse. It marked a meaningful collaboration between two institutions dedicated to elevating public conversation and recognizing literary contributions that strengthen democratic society.

A televised interview conducted by ANC’s Melissa Gecolea (in red) with the trustees of the Spirit of EDSA Foundation. Seated from left to right are Raffy Alunan, Joe Concepcion, Ramon Z. Carrion, Chris Carrion, and Rose Yenko. The discussion highlighted the Foundation’s continuing commitment to preserving the lessons, values, and democratic spirit of the 1986 EDSA People Power Revolution.

After successfully reaching the summit of Mt. Kinabalu, Raffy Alunan begins the arduous descent by rope amid freezing rain. As the heavens opened, sudden torrents cascaded down the mountain’s granite slopes, turning narrow paths into perilous waterfalls. The scene captures both the danger and the determination of a climber navigating nature’s raw power at one of Southeast Asia’s most formidable peaks.

Pandemic-weary alumni of the Harvard Kennedy School gathered at The Peninsula Manila for the 2022 Bureaucrats’ Ball, marking one of the first major in-person reunions after years of global disruption. The occasion brought together public servants, policy professionals, and development leaders eager to reconnect, exchange insights, and reaffirm a shared commitment to governance and nation-building. The event served as a symbolic return to fellowship and civic purpose, reflecting the resilience and enduring camaraderie of the HKS community in the Philippines.

At the “Tapatan” public affairs forum hosted by Melo Acuña, Secretary Raffy Alunan engages in a substantive discussion alongside Rex Robles and Atty. Anna Basman. The panel examined the final draft of the Bangsamoro Basic Law, which was then under detailed scrutiny in Congress. The dialogue offered critical insights into the law’s implications for governance, peace, and regional autonomy in Mindanao.

Forum on the South China Sea issue held at the Asian Institute of Management (AIM), where Raffy Alunan joined a distinguished panel that included former Philippine Ambassador to China Chito Sta. Romana, Senator Letty Ramos-Shahani, international trade law expert Tony Abad, DFA Assistant Secretary Henry Bensurto, and education advocate Mike Luz. The discussion brought together leading voices in diplomacy, governance, and national strategy to examine geopolitical developments, maritime rights, and the policy challenges facing the Philippines in the region.

Raffy Alunan with the world-renowned Kukkiwon Taekwondo Demonstration Team, celebrated globally for their exceptional athleticism, discipline, and artistry in martial arts performance. The encounter reflects Alunan’s support for cultural exchange, youth development, and the promotion of sports as a bridge between nations. The team’s visit showcased the spirit of Korean martial tradition while highlighting shared values of perseverance, respect, and excellence — principles that resonate strongly with Alunan’s own advocacy for character-building and national pride.

Golden anniversary dinner of the Philippine Military Academy Class of 1974 held at Camp John Hay in February 2024. Raffy Alunan joined the distinguished alumni as they marked fifty years since graduation — a milestone for a class that served during one of the most turbulent and defining chapters in modern Philippine history. Their collective experiences, forged in an era of political transition and national challenge, continue to resonate in the country’s security and governance landscape.

Raffy Alunan speaking at the Bacolod City Plaza during his Senate campaign in 2016, addressing the crowd with clarity and conviction on issues central to governance, national security, and responsible citizenship. Returning to his home province, he spoke before Negrenses not only as a public servant but as a proud son of Bacolod, reaffirming his long-standing commitment to the welfare, dignity, and progress of the Filipino people. The event reflected both his deep roots and his continuing dedication to public service on the national stage.

A campaign sortie during Raffy Alunan’s senatorial bid in 2016, capturing his engagement with communities across the country as he presented his platform of good governance, national security, and public service. The scene reflects the energy, resolve, and grassroots connection that characterized his efforts to bring his message directly to the Filipino people.

A campaign poster from Raffy Alunan’s 2016 senatorial bid, capturing the themes of leadership, security, and public service that defined his platform. The imagery and messaging reflect his decades-long record in government, national security, and civic engagement, presenting him as a steady and principled voice advocating for reform, strong institutions, and the protection of Filipino communities. The poster stands as a visual testament to his continued commitment to national service and his aspiration to contribute further to the country’s progress through legislative work.

The incoming Directors and Officers of the Rotary Club of Manila for Rotary Year 2023–2024, with Raffy Alunan serving as President. The photograph marks the beginning of a new term of leadership for Asia’s first and oldest Rotary club — an organization renowned for its enduring legacy of service, fellowship, and civic engagement. Under Alunan’s stewardship, the board embraced a renewed commitment to advancing humanitarian initiatives, strengthening community partnerships, and upholding the Rotary ideals of integrity, compassion, and service above self.

The Rotary Club of Manila had the honor of hosting Chief of Staff of the Armed Forces of the Philippines, General Carlito Galvez Jr., who delivered an insightful address to the membership. Speaking with clarity and conviction, Gen. Galvez offered a comprehensive overview of the AFP’s strategic vision for 2018 — encompassing modernization efforts, enhanced territorial defense, internal security reforms, and the strengthening of partnerships with civilian institutions. His presentation provided Rotarians with a deeper understanding of the military’s evolving role in safeguarding national sovereignty and promoting lasting peace and development across the country.

Raffy Alunan and his wife, Elizabeth, were inseparable companions throughout their marriage, sharing countless journeys across the globe. Whether traveling for official engagements, personal milestones, or moments of quiet respite, they approached every trip as partners — united in curiosity, purpose, and affection. Their travels abroad became a tapestry of shared memories, reflecting a bond strengthened by adventure, mutual support, and a deep, enduring love that accompanied them wherever they went.

The family of Raffy Alunan gathered at the wake of Elizabeth Jalbuena Alunan in March 2024. Surrounded by children, grandchildren, and loved ones, the moment reflects the profound bonds of family, shared grief, and enduring remembrance for a wife, mother, and matriarch whose life left a lasting imprint on all who knew her.

Raffy Alunan serving as guest speaker at the ASIS International Philippine Chapter Convention in December 2012. Addressing an audience of security professionals, risk managers, and industry leaders, he delivered insights on national security, public safety, and the evolving challenges in both domestic and global threat environments. His presence underscored his longstanding advocacy for strategic security planning, inter-agency cooperation, and the professionalization of the country’s security sector.

Raffy Alunan renders a final salute to former President Fidel V. Ramos as the nation bids him farewell, honoring a leader who dedicated his life to country, service, and the strengthening of democratic institutions. In this solemn moment, Alunan stands among those paying tribute as FVR is ceremonially welcomed into eternity — “arrival honors” befitting a soldier-statesman whose legacy continues to inspire generations of Filipinos.

Raffy Alunan presents a commemorative memento to Vice President Leni Robredo on behalf of President Tony Abad and the assembled members of the Board of Directors during the inaugural Harvard Kennedy School Bureaucrats’ Ball. The event gathered public servants and policy professionals in a celebration of leadership, service, and good governance. Alunan’s gesture symbolized the collective appreciation of the organization for the Vice President’s commitment to transparency, accountability, and the welfare of the Filipino people.

Raffy Alunan joins members of the Reform the Armed Forces Movement (RAM), the Volunteers Against Crime and Corruption (VACC), anti-drug advocates, netizens, and citizen-soldiers in a peaceful march along Buendia Avenue toward the Chinese Consulate. The demonstration called attention to China’s unlawful incursions and continued occupation of areas within the West Philippine Sea. The unified presence of civic groups, security reform advocates, and concerned citizens underscored a collective demand for respect for Philippine sovereignty, adherence to international law, and the defense of the nation’s maritime rights.

Raffy Alunan delivering the overview at the 3rd Forum on the West Philippine Sea, titled “Understanding 21st Century China: All Under Heaven,” held at the Asian Institute of Management on April 2, 2014. In his remarks, Alunan framed the geopolitical, historical, and strategic dimensions of China’s rise, setting the tone for a substantive discourse on regional security, maritime rights, and the shifting balance of power in the Asia-Pacific.

Raffy Alunan takes his oath of office as President of the Harvard Club of the Philippines in 2014, with former President Fidel V. Ramos serving as the inducting officer. The ceremony marked a significant moment of leadership within the Harvard alumni community, reflecting Alunan’s commitment to fostering dialogue, scholarship, and public service among graduates of the university. With FVR — himself a renowned statesman and Harvard alumnus — administering the oath, the occasion symbolized the continuity of leadership, mentorship, and civic engagement across generations.

Raffy Alunan serving as a member of the Board of Governors of the Management Association of the Philippines (MAP), one of the country’s most influential business and management organizations. In this capacity, he collaborated with industry leaders, policymakers, and senior executives to advance good governance, professional excellence, and responsible corporate citizenship. His involvement in MAP underscores his longstanding commitment to nation-building through ethical leadership, strategic thinking, and the strengthening of institutions that shape the country’s economic and managerial landscape.

Former DILG Secretary Raffy enjoys a round of golf with friends at the Escombro Golf Club. The gathering offered a welcome moment of camaraderie and relaxation, reflecting the enduring friendships and shared leisure pursuits that balance the demands of public service and civic leadership.

Barangay Alunan — Raffy Alunan and his wife Elizabeth are pictured with their children and grandchildren, reflecting the close-knit family bonds and multigenerational unity that remain at the heart of their lives. The photograph captures not only a family gathering, but the enduring values of love, continuity, and shared legacy that define the Alunan household.
