VICE PRES. RICARDO S.B. “Ricky” GUEVARA Editorial  Reginald T. Yu Editor-in-Chief HE Rotary Club of Manila is deeply honored to welcome as our Guest Speaker Mr. Manjit T. Singh Reandi, President and Chief Executive Officer of the John Hay Management Corporation (JHMC), for what promises to be a rich, timely, and thought-provoking dialogue on leadership, development, and the enduring craft of management in an age of constant transformation. Mr. Reandi stands at the helm of one of the country’s most strategic and symbolically significant institutions. Camp John Hay is not merely an economic zone or a prime real estate development; it is a living convergence of history, environmental stewardship, global enterprise, and public trust. To lead such an institution requires more than technical competence. It calls for vision tempered by prudence, innovation guided by values, and a deep respect for the delicate balance between progress and preservation. In today’s environment, leaders are confronted by unprecedented challenges. Rapid technological change, shifting economic landscapes, heightened public scrutiny, and the growing demand for sustainability and ethical governance have redefined what effective leadership looks like. The old models of command and control are giving way to more nuanced forms of stewardship — where leaders must inspire rather than impose, listen as much as they direct, and build institutions that can endure beyond personalities and terms of office. It is within this context that Mr. Reandi’s insights become particularly compelling. His experience at John Hay offers a front-row view of how complex organizations are guided through competing demands: economic growth and environmental care, global competitiveness and local community interests, operational efficiency and long-term legacy. His perspective on development is not confined to physical infrastructure or financial performance, but extends to the cultivation of human capital, the strengthening of institutional culture, and the creation of systems that uphold transparency, accountability, and excellence. For Rotarians, whose calling is leadership in service, this conversation resonates at a deeper level. Rotary has always believed that true leadership is not measured by authority, but by the positive and lasting impact one leaves on people and communities. The principles that guide our movement — integrity, service above self, and the pursuit of the common good — find natural parallels in the demands placed upon leaders in both the public and private sectors today. Mr. Reandi’s journey invites us to reflect on our own roles as leaders in our respective fields. How do we make decisions that are both bold and responsible? How do we nurture organizations that are resilient in the face of uncertainty? How do we ensure that growth does not come at the expense of values, and that success is shared rather than hoarded? As the Rotary Club of Manila gathers to listen and engage, we look forward not only to learning from Mr. Reandi’s experiences, but also to being challenged by them. His story is an invitation to examine leadership not as a position, but as a lifelong discipline — one that demands clarity of purpose, courage of conviction, and an unwavering commitment to serve something greater than oneself. In welcoming Mr. Manjit T. Singh Reandi, we anticipate an exchange that will enlighten, inspire, and reaffirm the timeless truth that when leadership is anchored on integrity and vision, development becomes not just growth, but progress with meaning and legacy. Guest of Honor and Speaker  Manjit T. Singh Reandi was appointed as a Director of the Board of the John Hay Management Corporation (JHMC) on 08 April 2024. He was subsequently elected by the JHMC Board as President and Chief Executive Officer on 07 April 2025. A dynamic entrepreneur and executive leader, Mr. Singh Reandi brings to the JHMC Board extensive experience in finance, public administration, corporate operations, and social impact initiatives. He holds a Bachelor of Science in Commerce from Lacson Colleges, and earned his Master’s in Professional Studies, major in Public Administration, from Cavite State University in 2020. He also completed the Leadership and Management Development Program at the Ateneo Graduate School of Business, as well as professional courses in marketing strategy, digital transformation, and family business management. An accomplished entrepreneur, Mr. Singh Reandi is the Founder and CEO of ReCash Prime Finance Corp., Pluma Builders Co., and Reandi Realms Realty. He also served as CEO of Reandi OPC, Chief Finance Officer of Papa Sarwan Lending Corp., and held key leadership positions in Peacock Direct Loans Inc. and Peacock Financing Corp. His work spans industries including finance, housing, real estate, and construction, and has been marked by a strong emphasis on strategic growth and ethical operations. In addition to his professional engagements, Mr. Singh Reandi is actively involved in civic and humanitarian causes. He currently serves as a Board Director of the Philippine Red Cross – Makati Chapter and of the North Luzon School for the Visually Impaired, Inc., and is a Past President of the Rotary Club of Forbes Park, through which he has championed education, community development, and inclusive service. With a broad skill set covering entrepreneurship, operations management, public service, and financial leadership, Mr. Singh Reandi is well-positioned to contribute to the mission and strategic direction of JHMC, particularly in driving sustainable development and economic resilience within Camp John Hay. President’s Message  Mid-Year Review in Da Nang, Vietnam In a significant milestone for our District 3810, District Governor Mary Mei V. Rodrigo is set to lead the Mid-Year Review in Da Nang, Vietnam on 22-26 January 2026, bringing together the Presidents of the various Rotary Clubs in the District along with key District Officers. The Rotary Club of Manila will be participating in this event, and a report will be made during the 3-day activity. The annual Mid-Year Review serves as a strategic checkpoint for club leaders and district officers to assess progress on goals, share best practices, and deepen collaboration halfway through the Rotary year. Under Governor Rodrigo’s leadership, the gathering aims to strengthen alignment on the District’s theme of service, fellowship, and impact, ensuring that clubs across Manila, Pasay, Cavite, and Occidental Mindoro remain united in advancing Rotary’s mission of “Service Above Self.” The event will give all the Club Presidents the opportunity to formally report on the club’s performance and direction. Its importance may be understood in several key aspects: • Accountability and Transparency

The mid-year review allows the Club President to account to the members —and to the district, when applicable—on how plans, commitments, and resources have been utilized during the first half of the Rotary year. It reinforces transparency in leadership and strengthens trust within the club. It will be recalled that I gave my mid-year report to the membership during last week’s membership meeting. • Assessment of Goals and Performance

By reporting on service projects, membership growth, attendance, Rotary Foundation giving, and public image initiatives, the Club President can objectively measure whether the club is on track to meet its annual goals. It highlights both achievements and areas that need attention or improvement. • Opportunity for Course Correction

Challenges inevitably arise midstream. The review provides a timely opportunity to recalibrate strategies, reallocate resources, or revise timelines, ensuring that the club finishes the Rotary year strong rather than merely continuing on an ineffective path. • Alignment with District and Rotary International Priorities

Through the President's report, the club can assess whether its activities remain aligned with district thrusts and Rotary International priorities, including The Rotary Foundation goals and the Action Plan. This alignment is crucial for relevance and impact. • Engagement and Motivation of Members 

A well-delivered mid-year report recognizes the efforts of officers and members, celebrates milestones, and renews enthusiasm. It reminds members that their contributions matter and that there is still time to make meaningful progress before year-end. • Continuity and Leadership Transition 

The mid-year review also serves as a bridge between the current and incoming leadership. Clear reporting and documentation help ensure continuity, smoother transition, and institutional memory within the club. In sum, the Rotary Mid-Year Review is not merely a reporting exercise. It is a strategic leadership moment where the Club President reflects, realigns, and re- energizes the club toward fulfilling its commitments to service above self. Leaders by Vocation, Rotarians by Heart PE Reginald T. Yu The Rotary Club of Manila gathered in the gracious halls of the Manila Polo Club for its 17th Weekly Membership Meeting of Rotary Year 2025–2026, a luncheon assembly marked by fellowship, institutional updates, and, most notably, two compelling Classification Talks delivered by Star Rotarians Rowel Janson S. Ong and Jason Romeo C. Valderrama. The meeting opened formally with the Call to Order by President Raoul C. Creencia and concluded with his Adjournment, framing an afternoon that blended Rotary tradition with professional inspiration. Moderating the program with steady warmth and precision was Rotarian Ingill Ra, who guided the flow of proceedings and ensured that each segment of the meeting unfolded with dignity and purpose. The invocation was led by Rotarian Juanito A. “John” Simon, followed by the singing of the Philippine National Anthem and the Rotary Club of Manila Hymn by the RCM World-Famous Music Chorale, and the solemn recitation of the Four-Way Test led by Star Rotarian Chris C. Tamesis. Rotarian Ingill Ra also formally acknowledged the guests in attendance and welcomed everyone on behalf of the Club, after which the RCM World-Famous Music Chorale rendered a Welcome Song that set a gracious and celebratory tone. Birthday celebrants for the period, Rotarian Jherry Zheng (January 9) and Rotarian Paul Kho (January 10), were honored with the traditional “Maligayang Bati / Happy Birthday” song, once again led by the Chorale. The meeting then turned to matters of governance and stewardship. Assistant Internal Auditor Michael D. “Mike” Roxas, Treasurer of the Rotary Club of Manila Foundation, Inc. (RCMFI), delivered a clear and transparent Report on the Financial Status of RCMFI, underscoring the Club’s commitment to accountability. This was followed by the Announcement of the RCMFI Election of the Board of Trustees for Rotary Year 2026–2027, presented by PE Reginald T. “Reggie” Yu, Chairman of the RCMFI NOMELEC, who outlined the electoral process and reminded members of the importance of active participation in the life of the Foundation. During President’s Time, President Raoul C. Creencia shared updates and reflections, reaffirming the Club’s direction for the year and paving the way for the intellectual and professional highlight of the afternoon: the Classification Talks of two of the Club’s Star Rotarians. Star Rotarian Rowel Janson S. Ong Classification: Real Estate Professional Services – Agency / Development Consultancy Star Rotarian Rowel Janson S. Ong began his talk with characteristic humility and efficiency, noting that he had intentionally trimmed his presentation to focus on substance rather than length. He introduced himself as the founder and principal of Hard Assets Express, Inc., a real estate brokerage and development consultancy firm that, in his words, “connects the right property to the right purpose.” He explained that Hard Assets Express, established in 2014, was built on a multidisciplinary foundation that brings together the expertise of a licensed civil engineer and broker, a senior real estate professional with deep experience in major land and property transactions, and a partner lawyer who ensures that every deal is legally sound and fully compliant. This structure, he emphasized, allows the firm to go beyond simple buying and selling and instead provide strategic, end-to-end advisory services for individuals, developers, and corporate clients. Drawing from over a decade of practice, Ong shared how the company’s capabilities span corporate and commercial site sourcing, residential and investment brokerage, and full real estate consultancy, including site selection, valuation, highest-and-best-use analysis, and development feasibility. Accredited with the country’s top developers and supported by a nationwide broker network, Hard Assets Express has helped major corporations such as Wilcon Depot identify and secure strategic expansion sites across the Philippines, completing dozens of locations out of more than a hundred evaluated. He illustrated the firm’s reach through a roster of projects and partners: hotel and resort developments in Boracay and La Union, high-rise and mixed-use projects in Binondo and Mandaluyong, industrial and logistics facilities, township and residential subdivisions, and prime commercial properties in Metro Manila and beyond. With more than 360 hectares of land sold for development, numerous highrise parcels transacted, and a strong portfolio of residential and commercial deals, Ong presented a picture of a company built on technical rigor, speed of execution, and, above all, integrity. What resonated deeply with the Rotarians in attendance was his emphasis on trust and long-term partnership. “We do not just close deals,” he said in essence, “we help our clients make good real estate decisions.” In the Rotary context, this philosophy mirrored the Four-Way Test and the ideal of Service Above Self: professional excellence anchored on ethics, prudence, and relationships that endure. Star Rotarian Jason Romeo C. Valderrama Classification: Construction Project Management Taking the podium next, Star Rotarian Jason Romeo C. Valderrama offered a narrative that seamlessly wove personal journey, professional discipline, and social responsibility. A relatively new member of the Rotary Club of Manila, having joined only in November, he nonetheless spoke with the quiet confidence of a seasoned leader. A civil engineer by training and a graduate of the University of the Philippines Diliman, with an MBA from the Ateneo Graduate School of Business, Valderrama founded JCV & Associates Project Management and Development, Inc. (JCVA) in 2014. He clarified at the outset that his firm is not a contractor, but a professional consultancy that represents the interests of project owners, standing at the critical intersection of client, designer, and builder to ensure that cost, schedule, quality, safety, and reputation are all protected. With nearly two decades of experience, Valderrama shared that JCVA has served over 170 clients and completed more than 250 projects, with a combined capital expenditure exceeding three billion US dollars and a built area of over two million square meters. Today, the firm is among the top five construction consultancy companies in the Philippines by market share, is fully Filipino-owned, and holds dual ISO certifications, with a third — on environmental management — soon to be added. Beyond impressive statistics, however, his talk gained moral depth when he spoke of the role of honest and competent project management in safeguarding public trust. He alluded to national controversies in infrastructure and flood control, stressing that many such failures could have been avoided through professional, ethical, and transparent management — principles that resonate strongly with Rotary’s advocacy for integrity in all vocations. Valderrama also highlighted JCVA’s commitment to corporate social responsibility. As an alumnus of the University of the Philippines, he has led initiatives to build and refurbish student facilities, sponsor engineering scholars, and operate a structured internship program that nurtures the next generation of Filipino professionals. His firm’s guiding belief, he concluded, is that “successful engineering projects do not happen by accident; they are engineered” — a statement that encapsulates both technical mastery and deliberate leadership. STAR Rotarians Rowel Janson S. Ong and Jason Romeo C. Valderrama engaged in a Q&A session with PD Issam Eldebs, Sec. Anton Mauricio, PDG Alex Cureg, PSAA Gunter Matschuck, and Rtn. Philip Recto. A Meeting of Vocation and Values The Classification Talks of Star Rotarians Ong and Valderrama transformed the 17th Weekly Membership Meeting into more than a routine luncheon. They became a living testament to Rotary’s ideal that every profession, when practiced with competence, conscience, and compassion, becomes a channel of service. From real estate advisory grounded in integrity to construction management anchored in accountability and nation-building, both speakers demonstrated how excellence in one’s calling can uplift communities and strengthen institutions. The afternoon concluded with the Presentation of Certificates of Appreciation by President Raoul C. Creencia, a gesture that formally recognized the contributions of the speakers and participants, before he finally declared the meeting adjourned. In the elegant setting of the Manila Polo Club, amid fellowship and shared purpose, the Rotary Club of Manila once again affirmed that its strength lies not only in its history and traditions, but in the caliber of men and women who live out Rotary values in their daily professional lives. LIBERTY AND PROSPERITY | The Making of Chief Justice Artemio Villaseñor Panganiban Jr.  From a barefoot newsboy sleeping on the pavements of Sampaloc to a jurist whose judgment helped steady the Republic at its most perilous hour, the life of Artemio Villaseñor Panganiban Jr. unfolds as a dramatic study in endurance, conscience, and faith. Forged by poverty, sharpened by discipline, delayed by rejection, and ultimately entrusted with the nation’s highest judicial office, his journey is neither linear nor comfortable — but relentlessly purposeful. This is the story of a man who believed that law must do more than restrain power; it must protect liberty, nurture prosperity, and remain worthy of the people it serves — even when history demands decisions before dawn. PROLOGUE: The Republic at Dawn At dawn on January 20, 2001, the Philippines was no longer governed by certainty. The night had ended, but the morning refused to arrive cleanly. Manila stirred under a low sky, its streets restless with rumor and anger. Barricades stood at Mendiola. Protesters clustered like unsettled weather. Somewhere between the palace and the people, authority had fractured. Government, that great machinery of order, had stalled. Inside this moment — before the oath, before the headlines, before history hardened into verdict — Artemio Villaseñor Panganiban Jr. prayed. He was not a man drawn to drama. He did not court crisis or relish the spotlight of emergency. He had spent his life inside institutions, not outside them — believing, stubbornly, that constitutions mattered even when crowds did not. But now the Constitution itself trembled. Joseph Estrada was still, technically, President. Gloria Macapagal Arroyo was Vice President — unable to act while legality remained unresolved. The military watched. The streets waited. A coup was imaginable. Bloodshed was possible. Silence was dangerous. In the quiet hours before noon, Art reached a conclusion that would follow him for the rest of his life. If the law waited, chaos would arrive first. And so, at approximately 5:30 in the morning, he made a call — not as a politician, not as a strategist, but as a jurist confronting the edge of collapse. He called the Chief Justice and proposed something radical in its simplicity: swear her in. Do it now. 
Do it lawfully. 
Do it before the Republic fractures beyond repair. That call — invisible to the crowd, absent from photographs — would become one of the most consequential acts of judgment in modern Philippine history. To understand how a man could make such a decision, one must return not to the Supreme Court, but to a sidewalk in Sampaloc — where a boy once learned that survival itself requires discipline, and that order, when absent, must be built by hand. The Boy Who Slept on Pavement Sampaloc did not produce future Chief Justices. It produced workers. Survivors. Children who learned early that hunger was not an event but a condition. In a cramped rented apartment on Cataluña Street, the youngest of four children grew up listening to adult conversations about money that never stretched far enough. His father, Artemio Sr., had left school early to support seven younger siblings after the death of his own father. His mother, Patricia Villaseñor, had little formal education but possessed the quiet endurance common to women who carry families through scarcity. For the youngest son, childhood ended early. He sold newspapers before dawn. He sold cigarettes during the day. He learned which streets produced buyers and which produced trouble. Some nights, it made no sense to go home. He slept on sidewalks — not from neglect, but from calculation. The papers arrived early. He needed to be there first. Years later, he would recall those nights without sentimentality. He remembered the cold stone beneath his back. The envy he refused to indulge when he imagined classmates sleeping in beds. He remembered telling himself, again and again, that this was temporary — that discipline would outlast deprivation. It was here, long before law books or Latin maxims, that Art learned his first philosophy: endure first, explain later. School became refuge. He studied not because teachers praised him, but because excellence was the only escape route he could see. He graduated with honors from public schools — Juan Luna Elementary, Victorino Mapa High — rising in crowded classrooms where obscurity was the default fate. When he was accepted to the University of the Philippines on scholarship, it seemed that fate had finally cracked open. Then came the bus fare. Fifteen centavos. That was the distance between Sampaloc and Diliman — between promise and possibility. He never complained. He simply walked to Far Eastern University instead. FEU and the Construction of Ambition Far Eastern University was not his second choice. It became his proving ground. He walked into FEU carrying more than notebooks. He carried urgency. He studied as if time itself were rationed. He graduated summa cum laude in pre-law, cum laude in law, and in 1959 was named the Most Outstanding Student of the entire university. Yet the transformation was not merely academic. He entered FEU with almost no understanding of faith. Catholic by baptism, secular by upbringing, he once failed a scholarship interview because he could not name the persons of the Trinity. It would later become one of his favorite stories — told not for humor, but as testimony. At FEU, faith arrived quietly. A chaplain noticed the disciplined student. A priest invited him to Student Catholic Action. Another insisted that integrity was not enough — leadership required moral responsibility for others. Slowly, a boy raised without catechism began to read Scripture not as doctrine, but as instruction. Leadership followed. He became president of the FEU Central Student Organization — the youngest ever elected. He co-founded the National Union of Students of the Philippines, discovering that influence required listening as much as command. In student assemblies, he learned how ideals fracture under pressure — and how institutions survive compromise without surrender. It was also here that he met Elenita Carpio. She was thoughtful, precise, intellectually formidable. Where he was urgency, she was balance. Where he pushed, she measured. Their partnership would anchor him through decades of ambition and uncertainty. But before life offered stability, it would test resolve. The Bar Exam and the Discipline of Pain In 1960, as bar candidates across the country arranged their schedules, sharpened their pencils, and rehearsed doctrines late into the night, Art lay flat on a hospital bed. The timing could not have been worse. The Philippine Bar Examination was not merely an academic hurdle; it was a rite of passage that determined whether years of sacrifice would harden into profession or dissolve into regret. For many, it was the most demanding intellectual trial of their young lives. For Art, it arrived when his body had begun to fail him. Fever drained his strength. His head throbbed. His limbs felt heavy, unresponsive. Doctors advised rest. Friends urged caution. The sensible choice — the rational choice — was withdrawal. There would be other years, they said. Better to recover fully than to risk collapse. But withdrawal carried its own cost. It meant postponement without guarantee. It meant prolonging dependency. It meant risking the erosion of momentum he had fought so hard to build. And, perhaps most painfully, it meant conceding that circumstance — not discipline — would dictate his limits. Then his dean arrived. Jovito R. Salonga, himself already a figure of moral and intellectual authority, looked at the weakened young man and said words that would lodge permanently in Art’s memory: “Do not quit.” There was no lecture. No pep talk. Just conviction. Salonga understood something essential about the student before him: that quitting now would wound him more deeply than any physical strain. That endurance, once surrendered, is difficult to reclaim. So, Art rose from the hospital bed and entered the examination hall. For four relentless weeks, he endured the bar examinations while ill. Each day demanded sustained concentration — hours of legal reasoning, careful writing, precision under pressure. The questions were unforgiving. The days were long. The nights offered little relief. His body weakened even as his mind was forced into sustained clarity. It was an ordeal of balance: pushing hard enough to perform, but not so hard as to collapse. He finished not with exhilaration, but with exhaustion. When the results were released, his name appeared among the top ten — sixth overall, with a rating of 89.55 percent. There was satisfaction, yes — but not celebration. What marked the moment most deeply was not triumph, but confirmation. Proof that pressure did not fracture him. Proof that adversity, when met with discipline, could be absorbed rather than feared. Proof that he could endure without compromise. It would become a defining trait — one that would surface again and again in courtrooms, committees, crises, and moments when retreat would have been easier than resolve. Yet even as congratulations arrived and professional doors seemed poised to open, opportunity once again revealed its conditional nature. A scholarship awaited him at Yale — a chance to pursue graduate legal studies at one of the world’s most storied institu-tions. It was the culmination of academic excellence, the validation of promise. But validation did not pay for passage. He applied for financial assistance. He sought a travel grant. He waited. The answer came back: denied. Without funds for airfare, the scholarship became an abstraction. The door closed — not dramatically, not cruelly, but decisively. Years later, Art would say this was the moment when the world seemed to collapse around him. He had done everything right. He had endured illness, excelled under pressure, earned distinction. And still, the horizon withdrew just as he approached it. The disappointment was profound. But it was not terminal. In time, he would come to see this denial not as an ending, but as a redirection — one that forced him Rotary Club of Manila inward, toward mentorship instead of credentials; toward institution-building instead of personal advancement; toward a path that would ultimately carry him farther than Yale ever could. The world had not closed. It had simply asked him to enter through a different door. The Mentor and the Moral Spine The Yale scholarship that never materialized became, in retrospect, one of the most formative disappointments of Art’s life. He had wanted it badly. Not for prestige — but for completion. He sensed, even then, that law was not merely a profession but a calling that demanded the sharpest tools available. Yale represented the pinnacle. But money intervened, as it had before. When the travel grant was denied, frustration gave way to something darker: the feeling that no matter how hard he worked, the ceiling might always descend just before he reached it. It was at this juncture that Jovito R. Salonga stepped fully into his life — not merely as a former dean, but as a moral architect. Salonga had walked the path Art dreamed of. He had studied at UP, Harvard, and Yale. He had absorbed not only legal technique but the ethical traditions of Western jurisprudence. When Yale became unreachable for his young protégé, Salonga made a quiet offer that would change everything: If you cannot go to Yale, Yale will come to you. At Salonga, Ordoñez and Associates, where Art apprenticed from 1961 to 1963, law was not practiced as transaction. It was practiced as responsibility. Cases were dissected for principle as much as outcome. Victory without integrity was considered failure. Political expediency was distrusted. Conscience mattered. Here, Art learned something more valuable than advanced degrees: judgment. Salonga introduced him to a lineage of Filipino legal giants — Jose W. Diokno, whose human rights advocacy would become legend; Claudio O. Teehankee, whose judicial courage would later define an era. These were not men who merely interpreted law. They embodied it. Art absorbed their example with reverence. He learned that law divorced from morality becomes tyranny by another name. That judges must sometimes stand alone — and accept isolation as the cost of fidelity. This apprenticeship forged his moral spine. When he left to establish his own firm in 1963 — PABLAW — he carried with him not only legal competence, but a philosophy: success must never outpace conscience. Independence by Design Art did not rush into government service. Offers came early — invitations to become a judge, to join Malacañang as a technical assistant. He declined them all. The reasons were not ideological. They were practical, even parental. Public service did not pay enough to shield his family from the kind of insecurity he had known as a child. He was determined that his children would never sleep on pavements — metaphorical or otherwise. So, he built independence first. PABLAW grew steadily. He became a respected practicing lawyer, then a senior partner. Teaching followed — at Far Eastern University, Assumption Convent, San Sebastian College. His classrooms were demanding. He insisted on clarity, precision, and ethical reasoning. Law, he told students, was not about cleverness. It was about trust. Beyond the courtroom and classroom, he ventured into business — not for opulence, but for autonomy. He founded Baron Travel Corporation in 1967, then Arpan Tourism Industries Corporation in 1974. What began as pragmatic entrepreneurship evolved into leadership at scale. He would eventually lead the Philippine Society of Travel Agents, the Tourism Organization of the Philippines, and even the global American Society of Travel Agents, becoming the first Asian to chair it internationally. This mattered. By the time he reached his forties, Art had achieved something rare: freedom from political dependency. He owed no patron his livelihood. He could say no — and often did. He also achieved something quieter but more enduring: the restoration of a childhood dream. The boy who once slept on sidewalks waiting for newspapers now ran travel companies that took him — and later his children — across the world. The Yale degree he never earned would, in time, be eclipsed by something more personal: five children who would graduate from Harvard, Stanford, Chicago, Michigan, and Berkeley. Scarcity had been defeated — not by luck, but by architecture. Faith Finds Its Voice For many men of ambition, faith is an accessory — useful in ceremony, silent in decision. For Art, faith arrived late — and then refused to stay quiet. His early encounters at FEU had planted questions. Years of reading, listening, and reflection followed. But it was only in the mid-1980s, when he and his wife Elenita joined Bukas Loob sa Diyos (BLD), that faith ceased to be theoretical. BLD demanded vulnerability. It asked professionals to pray aloud, to confess uncertainty, to submit ambition to discernment. It was not comfortable — which is precisely why it reshaped him. He became a servant leader. A marriage encounter facilitator. A speaker in Life in the Spirit seminars. He read Scripture not as metaphor but as instruction. Leadership, he began to believe, was not granted by election alone — it was discerned. Faith soon pulled him into national service. He became secretary of the Council of the Laity of the Philippines, a delegate to the Second Plenary Council of the Philippines, and later — improbably — the only Filipino appointed by Pope John Paul II to the Pontifical Council for the Laity. The irony was not lost on him. The boy who once could not name the Trinity now advised the Vatican on the life of the faithful. Faith had not replaced law in his life. It had disciplined it. Rotary, Earthquake, and the Test of Leadership In 1990, Art found himself standing at the threshold of an institution older than the Republic he would one day help steady. The Rotary Club of Manila — the first Rotary club in Asia and among the most influential civic organizations in the Philippines — was not merely a luncheon forum or a professional network. It was a proving ground for leadership, a gathering of Cabinet secretaries and jurists, captains of industry and ambassadors, physicians, educators, and public servants whose conversations often spilled beyond the ballroom and into the national bloodstream. Its presidency was not sought. It was conferred. Rotary tradition in Manila did not reward ambition. It elevated those who topped the open election for the Board of Directors, an arrangement that made the presidency both inevitable and inescapable. When Art emerged with the highest number of votes, the path ahead was clear — even if he did not wish to walk it. His first instinct was refusal. The presidency demanded near-total commitment. Former presidents had taken leaves of absence from their professions to serve properly. Art, at the time, was deeply embedded in multiple worlds: a flourishing law practice, expanding business interests, a growing family, and an intense commitment to Bukas Loob sa Diyos (BLD), where he and his wife were entrusted with leadership roles that required spiritual, emotional, and logistical labor. This was not a role that could be added casually to an already full life. And so, he did what had become his reflex in moments of consequence: he prayed. Not briefly. Not performatively. He entered a sustained process of discernment, gathering trusted companions, particularly within BLD, to pray with him — not for success, but for clarity. He asked not whether he could lead Rotary, but whether he should. The answer that emerged shocked even him. When the time came to articulate his presidential vision, he announced a credo that stunned the Club: LOVE GOD. SERVE MAN. The reaction was immediate — and fierce. Rotarians were aghast. Religion, they warned, had no place in a civic institution built on pluralism and neutrality. The credo was divisive. Unprecedented. Risky. Some feared it would alienate non-Christian members. Others worried it would reduce Rotary’s work to moral exhibitionism. No one could recall a Rotary president anywhere who had framed his term so explicitly in theological language. Art listened patiently. He explained calmly. He did not retreat. He argued that Rotary’s foundational maxims — Service Above Self, He Profits Most Who Serves Best — were not merely civic slogans but moral truths, deeply consonant with the commandment to love one’s neighbor. His credo, he insisted, was not an imposition of belief but a clarification of purpose. Faith, for him, was not sectarian. It was catalytic. On July 12, 1990, he was inaugurated. He distributed a 76-page Program of Action, unprecedented in the Club’s history — detailing 178 projects, a calendar of execution, and a proposed budget of ₱90 million, an amount that dwarfed anything the Club had attempted before. Skepticism followed him into the ballroom. Then, four days later, the earth itself intervened. On July 16, 1990, a 7.7-magnitude earthquake tore through Luzon, flattening communities, burying buildings, and killing more than two thousand people. Baguio lay in ruins. Panic spread faster than information. Suffering arrived before response. At the next Rotary meeting, there was no prepared speech. Art stood and made an appeal — not for ceremony, not for recognition, but for immediate action. He asked the Club to help the poor, the injured, the displaced — the least visible victims of a catastrophe too vast for any one institution to manage. What followed stunned even him. Within thirty minutes, pledges reached ₱5.5 million. By the next day, contributions exceeded expectations many times over. Doctors volunteered their services. Businessmen redirected resources. Rotary Anns mobilized clothing and food. A tent city rose in Burnham Park, sheltering hundreds of families. Rotary clubs abroad responded as well. The Rotary Club of Waikiki organized a massive airlift — over 3,300 kilograms of relief goods flown in from Hawaii. This was not charity as gesture. It was compassion as mobilization. Standing amid the whirlwind of response, Art understood something fundamental about leadership. Conviction, when aligned with compassion, could move institutions faster than policy, more decisively than procedure, and more enduringly than rhetoric. His credo had been tested — not in theory, but in catastrophe. And it had held. For the first time, he allowed himself to believe that faith, when married to action, was not divisive at all. It was transformative. The Reckoning of a Year — and the Quiet Accumulation of Trust When June 1991 arrived, Art did not speak of legacy. He spoke of accounting. True to his nature, he refused to let the Rotary presidency dissolve into memory without measurement. At his valedictory meeting, he distributed a 94-page Final Report — a document unprecedented in the history of the Rotary Club of Manila. It was exhaustive, almost severe in its precision. Numbers were tallied. Projects itemized. Outcomes measured against promises. Of the 178 projects pledged at the start of his term, 185 had been implemented. Of the ₱90 million budget once deemed unrealistic, nearly all had been responsibly deployed. Committees had multiplied. Attendance had deepened. Service had expanded beyond rhetoric into reach. But what mattered most was not arithmetic. It was credibility. For the first time in years, Manila Rotary was being spoken of not merely as influential, but as effective. Not merely prestigious, but purposeful. The Club had rediscovered its moral center without sacrificing its civic breadth. Art did not claim credit. Instead, he offered confession. In his closing address, he described himself not as a successful leader, but as an unworthy servant, sustained not by talent alone but by grace. It was an unsettling posture for an audience accustomed to triumphal retrospectives. Yet it resonated. His humility did not diminish his authority — it clarified it. Something had shifted. Men who had once regarded him as a capable lawyer now saw him as a trusted steward. Business leaders observed how he balanced vision with discipline. Clergy took note of a layman who understood that faith, to be credible, must translate into service. Public officials — watchful, pragmatic — recognized in him a rare combination: decisiveness without arrogance, conviction without cruelty. He had passed a test few recognized at the time. Not of popularity, but of governance. From Civic Leadership to National Visibility In the years that followed, Art did not announce ambition. He returned quietly to his law practice, his businesses, his writing, his work in Catholic lay movements. Yet invitations began arriving — first sporadically, then persistently. He was asked to chair awards committees, to mediate disputes, to speak on governance, ethics, and the rule of law. He became Chief Legal Counsel of the Parish Pastoral Council for Responsible Voting (PPCRV) — a role that placed him near the moral fault lines of Philippine democracy. He advised without theatrics. He guarded credibility as fiercely as outcomes. During elections, when passions flared and accusations multiplied, he insisted on process. When activists demanded instant righteousness, he cautioned patience. When institutions faltered, he argued not for replacement — but for reform. This was not the language of partisanship. It was the language of institutional preservation. Presidents noticed. The Call from Malacañang — and the First Refusal By 1992, the country stood again at a turning point. A new administration was taking shape. The wounds of authoritarianism had not fully healed; democratic institutions remained fragile, distrusted, incomplete. President-elect Fidel V. Ramos summoned Art for a private meeting. The offer was direct: Secretary of Justice. It was the kind of appointment that would have thrilled many. For Art, it triggered caution. He had not campaigned. He had not sought office. More importantly, he sensed that politics — even in reformist guise — would exact a cost his family and conscience might not be prepared to pay. He declined. Ramos pressed him. Not with flattery, but with reasoning. He spoke of trust. Of observed competence. Of Rotary. Of PPCRV. Of a country that needed steady hands more than loud voices. Still, Art hesitated. Then came the alternative. “If not the Cabinet,” Ramos said, “then the Supreme Court.” It was not a consolation prize. It was a summons. Seven Rejections By the early 1990s, Art had done everything one was supposed to do before entering public service. He had built professional independence. He had raised his children into academic excellence. He had led civic institutions without scandal. He had deepened his faith into discipline. When the call to serve finally came, it did not come gently. It came with rejection. From 1992 to 1995, vacancies opened repeatedly in the Supreme Court. Each time, Art’s name was submitted to the Judicial and Bar Council. Each time, it was scrutinized. Each time, it was questioned. And each time, it was passed over. Seven times. Objections arose from the past — some vague, some petty, some resurrected from decades-old client dissatisfaction. A former case was reexamined. An old grievance was amplified. Others were deemed “more qualified,” usually because they had climbed the judicial hierarchy instead of practicing law. Each rejection landed heavily. Art was not naïve. He understood institutional caution. But the cumulative effect was corrosive. Each screening became a public exposure. Each delay, a whisper of doubt. Each rejection, a silent question: Was this calling real—or self-invented? At night, he prayed with increasing urgency. “How long, O Lord?” 
“Why humiliation if the path is Yours?” 
“Why surrender ambition only to be tested again?” The law had taught him patience. Faith demanded more. In January 1995, after the seventh rejection, something broke — and something else was born. He surrendered completely. He prayed not for appointment, but for removal of desire. “Take all that I am,” he offered. 
“My career. My ambition. My will.” 
“Do what You want.” For the first time in years, he stopped hoping. Ask. Seek. Knock. In July 1995, when Art had finally convinced himself that the chapter was closed, the past returned quietly—almost apologetically. A friend from the Supreme Court approached him without ceremony, without persuasion, without the urgency that usually accompanies opportunity. It was said almost in passing, as if testing the air. “Why don’t you try again?” the justice asked. “There won’t be another vacancy for years.” The words were simple. The effect was not. Art dismissed the suggestion almost immediately. He had already surrendered. Months earlier, after seven humiliating rejections by the Judicial and Bar Council, he had made peace with what he believed was God’s answer. He had prayed not for appointment, but for detachment. He had offered up the ambition itself, believing that obedience meant letting go. To hope again felt like disobedience. To apply again felt like pride disguised as perseverance. And yet — the words lingered. They followed him home. They surfaced in the quiet between conversations. They returned in moments of stillness, unwelcome and unresolved. He could not tell whether they were temptation or invitation. On the night of July 29, 1995, sleep refused him. Past midnight, he lay awake, staring into the darkness, rehearsing the same question over and over—not aloud, but with the intensity of a cross-examination. Was he clinging to ambition? Or resisting obedience? He rose and prayed. Not briefly. Not casually. For hours. He did not ask to be appointed. He did not ask to be vindicated. He asked only for clarity—for the grace to know whether persistence would be faithfulness or defiance. He told God that he had already surrendered the dream. Why, then, would it not leave him alone? Near dawn, exhausted, unanswered, he slept. The following morning, Sunday, he served as a Special Minister of Holy Communion, as he had done many times before. The ritual was familiar. The church was quiet. His role was routine. Then the Gospel was read. From Luke: Ask and you shall receive. 
Seek and you shall find. 
Knock and the door shall be opened to you. The effect was immediate and physical. His skin prickled. Cold sweat gathered at his temples. Gooseflesh rose along his arms. The words did not sound ancient; they sounded personal—uncomfortably so. He whispered inwardly, almost in protest: “My Lord, is this meant for me?” But discipline had taught him caution. He had spent too many years in law to trust first impressions, even spiritual ones. He feared mistaking desire for discernment. That day, he prayed again. “If this is truly Your will,” he asked quietly, “give me another sign. One more. I do not want to be deceived by my own longing.” One week later, in the same church, with the same priest, the Gospel was read again—this time the account of the Transfiguration. A cloud came and overshadowed them… and a voice said: This is my Son, my Chosen One. Listen to Him. Listen. The word struck him harder than the first reading. Not ask. 
Not seek. 
Not knock. Listen. In that single command, the conflict resolved itself. Listening did not mean ambition. It meant obedience. It meant acting not because he wanted to rise, but because he was being called to respond. That was enough. He submitted his name to the Judicial and Bar Council once more. The resistance returned immediately. At one meeting, there was a concerted effort to strike his name from the list. Old objections resurfaced. Familiar skepticism hardened. The vote came dangerously close. Only one member intervened. “Let us defer this,” the member said. “We are meeting again next week.” It was a procedural delay. Nothing more. Two days later, the same member spoke to him privately. “Unless something extraordinary happens,” he said plainly, “you will be removed next week.” Unless a miracle happens. Art did not panic. He prayed — not defensively, not anxiously, but defiantly in faith. He had reached a strange calm. He no longer argued his merits. He no longer rehearsed rebuttals. He rested entirely on a conviction that had crystallized within him: Human forces, however exalted, could not override divine will. At the next meeting, something inexplicable occurred. No one objected. 
The accusations did not resurface. 
The arguments did not return. 
The opposition did not speak. 
Silence filled the room. For the first time in three years, his name survived the screening. There was no applause. No announcement. No sense of triumph. Only a quiet, unmistakable knowing. The miracle had arrived — not with thunder, but with stillness. And the door, at last, had opened. The Bench In October 1995, President Fidel V. Ramos appointed Artemio Panganiban Jr. as Associate Justice of the Supreme Court. When Ramos later asked him how he had finally passed the Judicial and Bar Council, Art answered without irony: “I did not do it. The Lord did.” The bench changed him — and revealed him. He wrote relentlessly. Opinions poured from his chambers. Decisions were not merely rendered; they were reasoned. Colleagues soon noticed the pattern: clarity without arrogance, firmness without cruelty. Justice Antonio Carpio would later call him “the most prolific writer of the Court.” More than a thousand decisions bore his name. He chaired divisions. Led reform committees. Wrote books — one each year — as if compelled to account for his stewardship. His judicial philosophy crystallized into a simple, audacious premise: The judiciary must protect liberty and nurture prosperity. Law, he argued, was not merely restraint. It was enablement. Predictable justice encouraged economic growth. Fair courts strengthened democracy. Liberty without order was chaos; order without liberty was tyranny. Then history intruded. EDSA, Judgment at Dawn January 2001 was not a legal puzzle to be solved by precedent or procedure. It was a moral emergency, unfolding faster than doctrine could keep pace. The streets had already rendered their verdict. President Joseph Estrada had lost the confidence of the people—his authority eroded not by court ruling, but by public withdrawal. Protesters massed at EDSA. Barricades hardened around Mendiola. The chants grew louder, angrier, less patient. Yet in the cold language of law, he remained President. On the other side stood Vice President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo — endowed with moral authority, buoyed by popular support, but still tethered by constitutional constraint. She could not act without risking illegitimacy. The Constitution, designed to ensure order, now threatened paralysis. The military hesitated. Each hour of delay increased the danger of miscalculation. A coup — open or disguised — was no longer unthinkable. Government machinery faltered. Authority fractured. The Republic stood exposed, suspended between legality and collapse. From within the Supreme Court, Art watched the situation darken. He saw the abyss clearly—not as abstraction, but as consequence. He imagined what hesitation could unleash: violence at the barricades, bloodshed justified by confusion, the Constitution rendered irrelevant by force. He understood that once order dissolved, no court ruling could restore it intact. He feared violence more than controversy. He feared constitutional collapse more than personal criticism. And so, he did what he had trained himself to do his entire life: he withdrew from noise and turned inward — to reflection, to prayer, to judgment. In the quiet hours before dawn on January 20, he reached a conclusion that would mark him permanently. The Constitution, he believed, had to be saved from annihilation by inaction. If the law could not move forward decisively, it would be overtaken by events beyond its control. There was only one path left. He placed the call to Chief Justice Hilario Davide Jr. His words were direct. Unembellished. Grave. Swear her in. Davide listened. The proposal was extraordinary — not because it was illegal, but because it was unprecedented. It carried risk. It invited criticism. It would be misunderstood. But it offered one essential thing: continuity of constitutional order without resort to force. By noon, before uncertainty could metastasize into violence, Gloria Macapagal Arroyo took the oath of office. The immediate crisis passed. The Republic held. But the argument did not. The decision would divide opinion for decades. Scholars would debate it. Politicians would weaponize it. Critics would accuse the Court of intervention; defenders would call it constitutional rescue. History would refuse easy consensus. When the legality of Arroyo’s presidency later reached the Supreme Court, Art did what his conscience and integrity required: he recused himself. So did Davide. The Court deliberated without them. The result was unequivocal. Thirteen justices voted unanimously to uphold Arroyo’s ascension to the presidency, and later to deny with finality Estrada’s motion for reconsideration. The Court spoke. 
History continued to argue. 
Art did not. 
He had not acted to seize power. 
He had not acted to choose a president. 
He had acted, as he understood it, to preserve order when order was about to fail. In moments like that, he believed, a jurist is not judged by popularity or applause — but by whether, when the Constitution trembles, he chooses courage over comfort and responsibility over silence. Chief Justice On December 20, 2005, Artemio Villaseñor Panganiban Jr. ascended to the highest judicial office in the land as Chief Justice of the Philippines. There was no campaign trail behind him. No whispered lobbying. No calculated pilgrimage to political powerbrokers. He had not even sought an audi

HE Rotary Club of Manila is deeply honored to welcome as our Guest Speaker Mr. Manjit T. Singh Reandi, President and Chief Executive Officer of the John Hay Management Corporation (JHMC), for what promises to be a rich, timely, and thought-provoking dialogue on leadership, development, and the enduring craft of management in an age of constant transformation.

Mr. Reandi stands at the helm of one of the country’s most strategic and symbolically significant institutions. Camp John Hay is not merely an economic zone or a prime real estate development; it is a living convergence of history, environmental stewardship, global enterprise, and public trust. To lead such an institution requires more than technical competence. It calls for vision tempered by prudence, innovation guided by values, and a deep respect for the delicate balance between progress and preservation.

In today’s environment, leaders are confronted by unprecedented challenges. Rapid technological change, shifting economic landscapes, heightened public scrutiny, and the growing demand for sustainability and ethical governance have redefined what effective leadership looks like. The old models of command and control are giving way to more nuanced forms of stewardship — where leaders must inspire rather than impose, listen as much as they direct, and build institutions that can endure beyond personalities and terms of office.

It is within this context that Mr. Reandi’s insights become particularly compelling. His experience at John Hay offers a front-row view of how complex organizations are guided through competing demands: economic growth and environmental care, global competitiveness and local community interests, operational efficiency and long-term legacy. His perspective on development is not confined to physical infrastructure or financial performance, but extends to the cultivation of human capital, the strengthening of institutional culture, and the creation of systems that uphold transparency, accountability, and excellence.

For Rotarians, whose calling is leadership in service, this conversation resonates at a deeper level. Rotary has always believed that true leadership is not measured by authority, but by the positive and lasting impact one leaves on people and communities. The principles that guide our movement — integrity, service above self, and the pursuit of the common good — find natural parallels in the demands placed upon leaders in both the public and private sectors today.

Mr. Reandi’s journey invites us to reflect on our own roles as leaders in our respective fields. How do we make decisions that are both bold and responsible? How do we nurture organizations that are resilient in the face of uncertainty? How do we ensure that growth does not come at the expense of values, and that success is shared rather than hoarded?

As the Rotary Club of Manila gathers to listen and engage, we look forward not only to learning from Mr. Reandi’s experiences, but also to being challenged by them. His story is an invitation to examine leadership not as a position, but as a lifelong discipline — one that demands clarity of purpose, courage of conviction, and an unwavering commitment to serve something greater than oneself.

In welcoming Mr. Manjit T. Singh Reandi, we anticipate an exchange that will enlighten, inspire, and reaffirm the timeless truth that when leadership is anchored on integrity and vision, development becomes not just growth, but progress with meaning and legacy.

Manjit T. Singh Reandi was appointed as a Director of the Board of the John Hay Management Corporation (JHMC) on 08 April 2024. He was subsequently elected by the JHMC Board as President and Chief Executive Officer on 07 April 2025.
A dynamic entrepreneur and executive leader, Mr. Singh Reandi brings to the JHMC Board extensive experience in finance, public administration, corporate operations, and social impact initiatives.

He holds a Bachelor of Science in Commerce from Lacson Colleges, and earned his Master’s in Professional Studies, major in Public Administration, from Cavite State University in 2020. He also completed the Leadership and Management Development Program at the Ateneo Graduate School of Business, as well as professional courses in marketing strategy, digital transformation, and family business management.

An accomplished entrepreneur, Mr. Singh Reandi is the Founder and CEO of ReCash Prime Finance Corp., Pluma Builders Co., and Reandi Realms Realty. He also served as CEO of Reandi OPC, Chief Finance Officer of Papa Sarwan Lending Corp., and held key leadership positions in Peacock Direct Loans Inc. and Peacock Financing Corp. His work spans industries including finance, housing, real estate, and construction, and has been marked by a strong emphasis on strategic growth and ethical operations.

In addition to his professional engagements, Mr. Singh Reandi is actively involved in civic and humanitarian causes. He currently serves as a Board Director of the Philippine Red Cross – Makati Chapter and of the North Luzon School for the Visually Impaired, Inc., and is a Past President of the Rotary Club of Forbes Park, through which he has championed education, community development, and inclusive service.

With a broad skill set covering entrepreneurship, operations management, public service, and financial leadership, Mr. Singh Reandi is well-positioned to contribute to the mission and strategic direction of JHMC, particularly in driving sustainable development and economic resilience within Camp John Hay.

body.text: Mid-Year Review in Da Nang, Vietnam

In a significant milestone for our District 3810, District Governor Mary Mei V. Rodrigo is set to lead the Mid-Year Review in Da Nang, Vietnam on 22-26 January 2026, bringing together the Presidents of the various Rotary Clubs in the District along with key District Officers. The Rotary Club of Manila will be participating in this event, and a report will be made during the 3-day activity.

The annual Mid-Year Review serves as a strategic checkpoint for club leaders and district officers to assess progress on goals, share best practices, and deepen collaboration halfway through the Rotary year. Under Governor Rodrigo’s leadership, the gathering aims to strengthen alignment on the District’s theme of service, fellowship, and impact, ensuring that clubs across Manila, Pasay, Cavite, and Occidental Mindoro remain united in advancing Rotary’s mission of “Service Above Self.”
The event will give all the Club Presidents the opportunity to formally report on the club’s performance and direction. Its importance may be understood in several key aspects:

• Accountability and Transparency

The mid-year review allows the Club President to account to the members —and to the district, when applicable—on how plans, commitments, and resources have been utilized during the first half of the Rotary year. It reinforces transparency in leadership and strengthens trust within the club. It will be recalled that I gave my mid-year report to the membership during last week’s membership meeting.

• Assessment of Goals and Performance

By reporting on service projects, membership growth, attendance, Rotary Foundation giving, and public image initiatives, the Club President can objectively measure whether the club is on track to meet its annual goals. It highlights both achievements and areas that need attention or improvement.

• Opportunity for Course Correction

Challenges inevitably arise midstream. The review provides a timely opportunity to recalibrate strategies, reallocate resources, or revise timelines, ensuring that the club finishes the Rotary year strong rather than merely continuing on an ineffective path.

• Alignment with District and Rotary International Priorities

Through the President's report, the club can assess whether its activities remain aligned with district thrusts and Rotary International priorities, including The Rotary Foundation goals and the Action Plan. This alignment is crucial for relevance and impact.

• Engagement and Motivation of Members 

A well-delivered mid-year report recognizes the efforts of officers and members, celebrates milestones, and renews enthusiasm. It reminds members that their contributions matter and that there is still time to make meaningful progress before year-end.

• Continuity and Leadership Transition 

The mid-year review also serves as a bridge between the current and incoming leadership. Clear reporting and documentation help ensure continuity, smoother transition, and institutional memory within the club.

In sum, the Rotary Mid-Year Review is not merely a reporting exercise. It is a strategic leadership moment where the Club President reflects, realigns, and re- energizes the club toward fulfilling its commitments to service above self.

articles.title: Leaders by Vocation, Rotarians by Heart

body.text: The Rotary Club of Manila gathered in the gracious halls of the Manila Polo Club for its 17th Weekly Membership Meeting of Rotary Year 2025–2026, a luncheon assembly marked by fellowship, institutional updates, and, most notably, two compelling Classification Talks delivered by Star Rotarians Rowel Janson S. Ong and Jason Romeo C. Valderrama.
The meeting opened formally with the Call to Order by President Raoul C. Creencia and concluded with his Adjournment, framing an afternoon that blended Rotary tradition with professional inspiration.

Moderating the program with steady warmth and precision was Rotarian Ingill Ra, who guided the flow of proceedings and ensured that each segment of the meeting unfolded with dignity and purpose. The invocation was led by Rotarian Juanito A. “John” Simon, followed by the singing of the Philippine National Anthem and the Rotary Club of Manila Hymn by the RCM World-Famous Music Chorale, and the solemn recitation of the Four-Way Test led by Star Rotarian Chris C. Tamesis.

Rotarian Ingill Ra also formally acknowledged the guests in attendance and welcomed everyone on behalf of the Club, after which the RCM World-Famous Music Chorale rendered a Welcome Song that set a gracious and celebratory tone. Birthday celebrants for the period, Rotarian Jherry Zheng (January 9) and Rotarian Paul Kho (January 10), were honored with the traditional “Maligayang Bati / Happy Birthday” song, once again led by the Chorale.

The meeting then turned to matters of governance and stewardship. Assistant Internal Auditor Michael D. “Mike” Roxas, Treasurer of the Rotary Club of Manila Foundation, Inc. (RCMFI), delivered a clear and transparent Report on the Financial Status of RCMFI, underscoring the Club’s commitment to accountability. This was followed by the Announcement of the RCMFI Election of the Board of Trustees for Rotary Year 2026–2027, presented by PE Reginald T. “Reggie” Yu, Chairman of the RCMFI NOMELEC, who outlined the electoral process and reminded members of the importance of active participation in the life of the Foundation.

During President’s Time, President Raoul C. Creencia shared updates and reflections, reaffirming the Club’s direction for the year and paving the way for the intellectual and professional highlight of the afternoon: the Classification Talks of two of the Club’s Star Rotarians.
Star Rotarian Rowel Janson S. Ong Classification: Real Estate Professional Services – Agency / Development Consultancy

Star Rotarian Rowel Janson S. Ong began his talk with characteristic humility and efficiency, noting that he had intentionally trimmed his presentation to focus on substance rather than length. He introduced himself as the founder and principal of Hard Assets Express, Inc., a real estate brokerage and development consultancy firm that, in his words, “connects the right property to the right purpose.”

He explained that Hard Assets Express, established in 2014, was built on a multidisciplinary foundation that brings together the expertise of a licensed civil engineer and broker, a senior real estate professional with deep experience in major land and property transactions, and a partner lawyer who ensures that every deal is legally sound and fully compliant. This structure, he emphasized, allows the firm to go beyond simple buying and selling and instead provide strategic, end-to-end advisory services for individuals, developers, and corporate clients.

Drawing from over a decade of practice, Ong shared how the company’s capabilities span corporate and commercial site sourcing, residential and investment brokerage, and full real estate consultancy, including site selection, valuation, highest-and-best-use analysis, and development feasibility. Accredited with the country’s top developers and supported by a nationwide broker network, Hard Assets Express has helped major corporations such as Wilcon Depot identify and secure strategic expansion sites across the Philippines, completing dozens of locations out of more than a hundred evaluated.

He illustrated the firm’s reach through a roster of projects and partners: hotel and resort developments in Boracay and La Union, high-rise and mixed-use projects in Binondo and Mandaluyong, industrial and logistics facilities, township and residential subdivisions, and prime commercial properties in Metro Manila and beyond.

With more than 360 hectares of land sold for development, numerous highrise parcels transacted, and a strong portfolio of residential and commercial deals, Ong presented a picture of a company built on technical rigor, speed of execution, and, above all, integrity.
What resonated deeply with the Rotarians in attendance was his emphasis on trust and long-term partnership.
“We do not just close deals,” he said in essence, “we help our clients make good real estate decisions.”
In the Rotary context, this philosophy mirrored the Four-Way Test and the ideal of Service Above Self: professional excellence anchored on ethics, prudence, and relationships that endure.
Star Rotarian Jason Romeo C. Valderrama Classification: Construction Project Management

Taking the podium next, Star Rotarian Jason Romeo C. Valderrama offered a narrative that seamlessly wove personal journey, professional discipline, and social responsibility. A relatively new member of the Rotary Club of Manila, having joined only in November, he nonetheless spoke with the quiet confidence of a seasoned leader.

A civil engineer by training and a graduate of the University of the Philippines Diliman, with an MBA from the Ateneo Graduate School of Business, Valderrama founded JCV & Associates Project Management and Development, Inc. (JCVA) in 2014. He clarified at the outset that his firm is not a contractor, but a professional consultancy that represents the interests of project owners, standing at the critical intersection of client, designer, and builder to ensure that cost, schedule, quality, safety, and reputation are all protected.

With nearly two decades of experience, Valderrama shared that JCVA has served over 170 clients and completed more than 250 projects, with a combined capital expenditure exceeding three billion US dollars and a built area of over two million square meters. Today, the firm is among the top five construction consultancy companies in the Philippines by market share, is fully Filipino-owned, and holds dual ISO certifications, with a third — on environmental management — soon to be added.

Beyond impressive statistics, however, his talk gained moral depth when he spoke of the role of honest and competent project management in safeguarding public trust. He alluded to national controversies in infrastructure and flood control, stressing that many such failures could have been avoided through professional, ethical, and transparent management — principles that resonate strongly with Rotary’s advocacy for integrity in all vocations.

Valderrama also highlighted JCVA’s commitment to corporate social responsibility. As an alumnus of the University of the Philippines, he has led initiatives to build and refurbish student facilities, sponsor engineering scholars, and operate a structured internship program that nurtures the next generation of Filipino professionals. His firm’s guiding belief, he concluded, is that “successful engineering projects do not happen by accident; they are engineered” — a statement that encapsulates both technical mastery and deliberate leadership.
STAR Rotarians Rowel Janson S. Ong and Jason Romeo C. Valderrama engaged in a Q&A session with PD Issam Eldebs, Sec. Anton Mauricio, PDG Alex Cureg, PSAA Gunter Matschuck, and Rtn. Philip Recto.
A Meeting of Vocation and Values

The Classification Talks of Star Rotarians Ong and Valderrama transformed the 17th Weekly Membership Meeting into more than a routine luncheon. They became a living testament to Rotary’s ideal that every profession, when practiced with competence, conscience, and compassion, becomes a channel of service. From real estate advisory grounded in integrity to construction management anchored in accountability and nation-building, both speakers demonstrated how excellence in one’s calling can uplift communities and strengthen institutions.

The afternoon concluded with the Presentation of Certificates of Appreciation by President Raoul C. Creencia, a gesture that formally recognized the contributions of the speakers and participants, before he finally declared the meeting adjourned.

In the elegant setting of the Manila Polo Club, amid fellowship and shared purpose, the Rotary Club of Manila once again affirmed that its strength lies not only in its history and traditions, but in the caliber of men and women who live out Rotary values in their daily professional lives.

articles.title: Rotary Club of Manila President-Elect Meets Cardinal Tagle, Extends Invitation for 107th Induction Ceremonies

body.text: Rotary Club of Manila President-Elect Reggie Yu was granted a brief but meaningful audience with His Eminence Luis Antonio Cardinal Tagle, Pro-Prefect of the Section for the First Evangelization and New Particular Churches of the Dicastery for Evangelization, Grand Chancellor of the Pontifical Urban University, and Metropolitan Archbishop emeritus of Manila, during a short meeting at the airport as the Cardinal awaited his onward flight to Hong Kong.

During the encounter, Yu personally handed Cardinal Tagle a formal invitation to serve as Guest of Honor and Speaker at the Rotary Club of Manila’s 107th Induction and Handover Ceremonies, scheduled in July, marking another milestone for Asia’s first and largest Rotary club.

The meeting took place in the early hours of the morning, reflecting the Cardinal’s tightly packed international schedule and the limited window available for a personal audience. Despite this, Cardinal Tagle received the invitation with warmth and attentiveness, and expressed his willingness to look into his calendar to explore the possibility of flying from Rome to Manila to participate in the historic event.

The invitation comes at a time when the Rotary Club of Manila has been emphasizing the importance of moral and values-based leadership amid growing public concern over governance issues, including widespread frustration over the country’s flood-control crisis and calls for greater accountability. In this context, the Club has turned to spiritual leaders whose influence and credibility continue to resonate deeply with Filipino communities.

Cardinal Tagle, regarded as the highest-ranking Filipino in the Catholic Church today, is widely respected for his pastoral leadership, humility, and strong engagement with grassroots communities. His global role in the Vatican and enduring connection with the Philippine Church have made him a moral and spiritual reference point for many Filipinos.

Yu expressed hope that, should the Cardinal’s schedule permit, his presence at the Rotary induction would be both an honor for the organization and an inspiration to its members as they begin a new Rotary year of service.
The Rotary Club of Manila, founded in 1919, is preparing for its 107th Induction and Handover Ceremonies as part of its continuing commitment to leadership, service, and nationbuilding.
