OF LEDGERS AND LANDSCAPES | The Life, Learning,  and Cultural Stewardship of Jaime del Carmen Laya PE Reginald T. Yu There are men who leave their mark through force of personality, and there are those whose influence is quieter, almost architectural. They do not dominate rooms. They design them. They do not seek to be remembered. They ensure that what follows them does not collapse. Jaime “Jimmy” del Carmen Laya belongs unmistakably to the second kind. He never believed that leadership was about being right in public. He believed it was about building systems sturdy enough to withstand error, ambition, and time. The Day the Radio Spoke Jimmy remembers the radio more clearly than the room. Memory, over time, is selective. It releases faces, loosens edges, dims the color of walls and furniture. But sound — especially the sound that arrives uninvited — has a way of staying intact. Even now, what remains most vivid to Jimmy Laya is not where he was standing, nor how the light fell that morning, but the voice that came through the radio: calm, factual, almost indifferent to the weight of what it carried. He did not learn that his time in government had ended through a sealed envelope, a discreet phone call, or the courtesy of advance notice. There was no formal goodbye, no moment staged for transition. He learned it the way nations often learn the truth about themselves — suddenly, impersonally, through broadcast. It was February 1986. Just moments earlier, he had come from a courtesy call on President Corazon Aquino, part of the Marcos Cabinet led by Cesar E. A. Virata — his former professor, mentor, and longtime collaborator in both academe and government. The meeting itself bore the unmistakable tone of an ending, though no one named it as such. It was polite, restrained, almost ritualistic. History, for a brief moment, observed manners. There were no raised voices, no proclamations of rupture. Only the quiet understanding that the country was moving, that the ground beneath institutions was shifting, and that the structures of authority were being rearranged in real time. Then the radio spoke. The announcement was spare. The Cabinet had been replaced. No embellishment followed. No commentary on service rendered, no enumeration of years spent, no acknowledgment of personal cost or professional sacrifice. The words were delivered plainly, as if describing a change in traffic flow or a shift in weather. And in that very plainness lay their finality. Jimmy absorbed the news without visible reaction. What struck him was not the abruptness of the announcement, but its inevitability. Governments, he had long believed, must move forward decisively. They could not pause for sentiment, nor wait for individuals to gather their thoughts. Institutions, if they were to function at all, could not be hostage to personal closure. Power, once withdrawn, had to be relinquished cleanly. He would later reflect that the moment felt less like an expulsion than a conclusion — one reached not by argument or protest, but by circumstance. Public office, in his understanding, was never an extension of the self. It was not identity. It was a role — necessary for a time, demanding in its season, and finite by design. In that sense, there was no bitterness to process, no sense of loss to mourn. What mattered was not how the departure unfolded, but whether the work done within the institution would endure after the individual had stepped away. That distinction — between position and purpose — had guided him long before that day. It had shaped how he taught, how he governed, how he managed, and how he collected and preserved. Titles were temporary. Systems were what remained. As he moved forward from that moment, there was no dramatic recalibration of self, no existential unraveling. The radio announcement did not unsettle his sense of direction. If anything, it clarified it. It reaffirmed a belief he had practiced quietly throughout his life: that authority must never be confused with permanence, and that influence is most meaningful when it survives one’s absence. The day the radio spoke did not end Jimmy Laya’s public life. It simply returned him to what he had always trusted most — work that required no applause, institutions that could stand without him, and a life defined not by how loudly one exits a room, but by whether the room still holds its shape long after one has gone. A House Built of Books Jaime del Carmen Laya was born on January 8, 1939, into a household where learning was not celebrated as achievement, but practiced as habit. Knowledge in that home was not ornamental. It was not something displayed, cited, or used to establish superiority. It was lived. Books were present not as trophies, but as tools — handled, returned to shelves, taken down again. Conversation did not revolve around accolades or ambition, but around ideas, stories, and the steady obligations of daily life. Learning was not framed as a path upward, but as a way of staying oriented in the world. His father, Juan Cabreros Laya, was a novelist, playwright, and cultural worker of quiet distinction. He moved easily between literature and public engagement, between the discipline of writing and the demands of civic life. At a time when Filipino letters were still shaping a national voice, Juan Laya wrote with moral seriousness and historical consciousness. His novel Lahing Kayumanggi would later become required reading for teachers of Pilipino in the 1950s. Another work, His Native Soil, earned the Commonwealth Literary Award for the Novel in 1940 — an honor bestowed at the Metropolitan Theater by President Manuel L. Quezon. During the Japanese Occupation, he was active in Dramatic Philippines, a theater group that persisted under conditions of scarcity and risk. Art, in that sense, was not an abstraction. It was something done in real time, under pressure, with consequence. His mother, Silvina del Carmen, was a teacher whose influence was felt less through instruction than through example. She continued in public education and would later become a superintendent in the public school system, raising her children with steadiness rather than spectacle. She demonstrated what it meant to prepare carefully, to speak plainly, to finish what one had started. From her, Jimmy absorbed the idea that authority did not require volume, and that competence, once established, did not need to be announced. Between them, an unspoken ethic governed the household: do not take advantage of others; do your work well; let your actions speak. These were not rules recited aloud. They were expectations embedded in routine. Ethics were transmitted through repetition — through watching adults do what they said they would do, day after day. This quiet continuity shaped him more deeply than any single admonition could have.
The only boy in a household of sisters, Jimmy grew accustomed early to solitude. Left largely to his own devices, he learned to occupy himself quietly — watching plays alone, wandering through Filipiniana libraries, reading without supervision. The war intruded early into his consciousness, not as narrative, but as atmosphere. He was still very young when Manila burned. Yet the memory stayed — not as fear, but as light. The unnatural glow in the night sky. The sense that something familiar was being undone. He remembered Japanese patrols moving through the streets, their presence both routine and menacing, and then, just as vividly, the sudden release of joy when American troops marched down Rizal Avenue in 1945, greeted by crowds that seemed to materialize out of nowhere. For a brief time, an American soldier — a Texan named Joseph Slay — was billeted in their Sampaloc home. The detail lingered not because it was extraordinary, but because it was intimate. The soldier slept without a mosquito net after spraying the room with DDT. It was an ordinary human accommodation amid extraordinary circumstances. The war, he learned early, was not only fought in headlines and battles. It unfolded in living rooms, in borrowed beds, in gestures of temporary coexistence. These memories endured not because they were dramatic, but because they revealed how fragile normalcy could be, and how easily it could be disrupted by forces beyond one’s control. Then came the loss that altered the architecture of his thinking. When his father died suddenly in a car accident, Jimmy was still young — barely into adolescence. The death was abrupt and irrevocable. There was no long illness to prepare for it, no gradual loosening of ties. One day his father was there; the next, he was not. The loss left a permanent mark. It introduced him early to finitude, not as abstraction, but as lived fact. Life no longer appeared open-ended, but bounded. Time, he understood, was not guaranteed. The question that followed was not dramatic, but practical: if time were limited, what should be done with it? What obligations mattered most? What work was worth sustained effort? This awareness did not make him reckless. It made him careful. He learned to value preparation over impulse, structure over improvisation. Even as a boy, he gravitated toward order — not rigid order, but coherence. He wanted things to make sense. He was drawn to systems that explained themselves, to arrangements where parts related logically to one another. Books became companions in this search. Reading was not escape, but orientation. He read widely and without hierarchy — history, economics, literature, architecture, numbers, art — absorbing not only content, but form: how arguments were built, how narratives held together, how balance was achieved without excess. Through reading, he learned to recognize proportion, clarity, and restraint — qualities that would later shape his approach to finance, education, governance, and visual culture. Long before he encountered balance sheets or museum collections, he was already training his eye to see how parts related to wholes, how excess weakened structure, and how meaning often resided not in what was added, but in what was deliberately left out. By the time he entered adulthood, the foundations were already laid — not in ambition, but in discipline; not in spectacle, but in attention. The habits formed in that early household would follow him everywhere, quietly informing the life he would go on to build. Formal schooling did not interrupt this domestic education; it extended it. Jimmy’s early years in elementary school revealed nothing flamboyant. He was not remembered as a prodigy in the theatrical sense, nor as a student who sought attention. What distinguished him even then was steadiness. Teachers noted his seriousness — not severity, but attentiveness. He listened carefully, followed instructions precisely, and completed work without dramatics. Excellence, for him, was not a performance. It was a habit. By the time he reached Arellano High School, from which he graduated in 1953, these habits had hardened into instinct. The school was demanding, and the postwar years offered little indulgence for distraction. Jimmy adapted easily to structure. Timetables appealed to him. Rules clarified expectations. Within those boundaries, he found freedom rather than constraint. He gravitated toward subjects that required internal order — mathematics, logic, structured argument — yet he never abandoned his love for reading. Literature remained present not as escapism, but as moral calibration. Stories trained his sense of proportion: how actions led to consequences, how choices accumulated over time. His classmates would later recall him as diligent rather than dazzling. He was not the loudest voice in the room, nor the quickest to volunteer opinion. But when he spoke, his comments were precise. There was an economy to his thinking that suggested early restraint — an instinct to say only what advanced understanding. School, for Jimmy, was never merely preparation for a career. It was rehearsal for responsibility. By the time he left Arellano High School, the trajectory was already visible, even if unnamed. The boy who had grown up surrounded by books had learned to move comfortably between discipline and curiosity, between rule-following and independent judgment. He carried with him not a hunger for distinction, but a respect for structure — an understanding that institutions, like people, functioned best when built deliberately and maintained carefully. The University of the Philippines would refine these instincts. But they had been formed long before he ever set foot in Diliman. The Discipline of Excellence At the University of the Philippines At the University of the Philippines Diliman, Jimmy Laya’s gifts became unmistakable — not because they announced themselves loudly, but because they held under scrutiny. At the core of this long arc stood an academic formation that never loosened its grip on his thinking. Jimmy was trained rigorously in accounting and finance. He moved through the campus with an ease that came from preparation rather than confidence. The work did not overwhelm him; it organized him. When he graduated magna cum laude in 1957 with a degree in business administration and placed eighth in the Certified Public Accountant examinations at the age of eighteen, the achievements were remarkable even by the university’s exacting standards. Yet they did not intoxicate him. If anything, they sharpened his curiosity. He was far less interested in the applause that followed than in the mechanics beneath it. Numbers, for Jimmy Laya, were never abstractions. They were expressions of order — ways of describing how effort translated into outcome, how resources moved, how institutions either held together or quietly failed. While others saw accounting as terminal expertise, he saw it as a language that pointed toward deeper questions. Why did certain organizations remain coherent under stress while others fragmented? What invisible assumptions held systems together? Where did discipline end and judgment begin? These questions could not be answered locally, or quickly. He left for the United States not in pursuit of prestige, but of perspective. At Georgia Institute of Technology, where he earned a master’s degree in industrial management in 1960, he encountered an environment that emphasized process over personality, optimization over intuition. Systems were dissected, tested, improved. Efficiency was treated not as speed, but as alignment. From there, he went on to Stanford University, earning a doctorate in financial management in 1965. Stanford exposed him to a culture of analytical rigor that was both demanding and unsentimental. Ideas were not admired for elegance alone. They were stresstested. Models were dismantled. Assumptions were challenged not to provoke debate, but to reveal limits. The experience resonated deeply with him. Yet he did not return home armed with ideological certainty or missionary zeal. He returned with tools — and with a sharpened skepticism toward easy answers. The more he learned, the more he understood how partial most explanations were. Complexity, he realized, was not an obstacle to be conquered, but a condition to be respected. As a Ford Foundation grantee, he became the first Ph.D. in business produced by the U.P. College of Business Administration — an institutional milestone that symbolized his lifelong role as bridge-builder between global rigor and local responsibility. His classrooms were marked by clarity rather than charisma. He did not seek to persuade students into agreement. He sought to train them in discernment. Arguments had to be coherent. Assumptions had to be named. Conclusions had to survive scrutiny. He believed education was not about producing consensus, but competence. Not about shaping opinion, but cultivating judgment. Ideas, he insisted, only mattered if they could function under pressure. Students sensed this immediately. He was demanding without being theatrical, exacting without humiliation. He corrected errors not to assert authority, but to protect standards. Over time, it became clear that his seriousness was not severity. It was respect — for the discipline, for the institution, and for the students who had entrusted him with their formation. Leadership, when it arrived, did so without declaration. Jimmy did not seek prominence. He worked within systems, respected hierarchy, and followed institutional processes with care. Yet his reliability set him apart. He noticed structural problems others had learned to work around. He asked why inefficiencies persisted. He proposed solutions quietly, implemented them patiently, and stayed to see whether they worked. Trust accumulated around him almost incidentally. By the time he succeeded Cesar E. A. Virata as Dean of the College of Business Administration in 1967, the transition felt natural rather than ambitious. He was still young, but he had already demonstrated a rare capacity to hold complexity without losing coherence. As dean, his gaze extended beyond the classroom. He began thinking about how education itself was structured — about curricula that responded to real conditions, about graduate programs that prepared leaders rather than technicians, about research institutions that supported inquiry rather than prestige. He was no longer concerned only with producing graduates. He was thinking about building an ecosystem — one that could generate professionals who understood not just how to succeed, but how to sustain. The work was meticulous, demanding, and unfinished. And it was only beginning. Rebuilding Business Education When Jimmy Laya assumed the deanship of the University of the Philippines College of Business Administration in 1967, he did not experience the moment as a promotion. He experienced it as a problem that had been waiting to be named. The College, as he encountered it, was competent but incomplete. It produced graduates who knew how to compute, how to analyze figures, how to perform within established frameworks. Yet too often, they struggled to see how those frameworks related to one another. Knowledge existed in compartments. Accounting, economics, management, agriculture, policy — each was taught as if it occupied a separate universe, intersecting only by accident. To Jimmy Laya, this fragmentation was not merely academic. It reflected an economy that no longer existed. The Philippines he saw emerging was a system of interdependencies — agriculture feeding industry, industry shaping services, services influencing policy, policy restructuring incentives that rippled back through the entire economy. Business education that treated these domains as discrete disciplines was, in effect, training students for a world already in retreat. If education did not evolve, it would become technically proficient yet strategically blind. He did not announce this diagnosis with fanfare. Jimmy Laya did not begin with speeches or sweeping declarations. He began with structure. Administration, as he understood it, was not about persuasion alone. It was about alignment — of curricula with reality, of faculty expertise with institutional goals, of student formation with the responsibilities they would eventually carry. He believed that reform should be quiet, methodical, and defensible. Each proposal had to withstand a simple but unforgiving question: What problem does this solve that the existing structure cannot? If the answer was unclear, the proposal did not proceed. From this logic emerged the Doctoral Program in Business Administration. It was not conceived as an abstract exercise in theory, nor as a credential to be accumulated. It was designed to cultivate scholars capable of grappling seriously with Philippine conditions — men and women who could bring rigorous analytical tools to local realities rather than importing models uncritically. The aim was intellectual sovereignty, not imitation. The Master of Agribusiness Management followed naturally. Jimmy Laya had long been troubled by the way development discourse treated agriculture as a residual category — important in rhetoric, marginal in strategy. He rejected the notion that agriculture was pre-modern or peripheral. It was central, structurally and morally, to the Philippine economy. To ignore it was not only analytically flawed, but socially irresponsible. The program sought to reconnect business education to the land, to production cycles, to the lives and labor of those who sustained the economy long before balance sheets recorded their value. The five-year Bachelor of Science in Business Administration and Accountancy proved more controversial. Critics argued that it would delay students’ entry into the workforce, that it imposed unnecessary rigor in an economy hungry for credentialed labor. Jimmy Laya was unmoved. Time, he believed, was not wasted if it was used to integrate learning. Accountancy, in his view, was not simply technical proficiency. It was ethical responsibility. Those entrusted with certifying truth in numbers carried a burden that could not be rushed. Students needed time — not only to master technique, but to mature into judgment. Compression, he felt, risked producing efficiency without conscience. He also insisted on a full-time MBA program, resisting pressures to accommodate part-time formats that prioritized convenience over immersion. Serious management education, he believed, required sustained engagement — space to think, to argue, to fail safely, and to reconsider assumptions. Then came the joint degree programs — with Agriculture, Economics, and Home Economics. These were not experiments designed to impress. They were correctives. Business students, Jimmy Laya believed, needed to understand production systems, labor realities, consumer behavior, and the economics of hospitality and service. Management divorced from context was management in name only. Faculty reaction was mixed. Some welcomed the changes; others worried about disruption, dilution, or loss of disciplinary purity. Jimmy Laya listened carefully, but he did not govern by consensus alone. Institutions, he understood, often resist reform not because ideas are wrong, but because they unsettle routines that have grown comfortable. His responsibility was not to eliminate discomfort, but to ensure that it led somewhere constructive. In 1971, this philosophy took institutional form with the establishment of the U.P. Business Research Foundation. The Foundation created a formal bridge between scholarship and practice. Faculty were encouraged to conduct research that mattered, to engage in consultancy without abandoning academic rigor, and to hold professorial chairs that recognized sustained contribution rather than episodic achievement. It institutionalized something Jimmy Laya had long practiced intuitively: that theory gains strength when tested against reality, and that practice deepens when subjected to disciplined inquiry. That same year, his attention turned to the College’s physical environment. The existing facilities no longer matched the seriousness of its ambitions. Classrooms were functional but inadequate. Research space was limited. Informal intellectual exchange — the kind that happens between lectures, in hallways and shared rooms — was constrained. Ideas, Jimmy Laya believed, needed space — literal space — to develop fully. Plans were quietly drawn for a new building. Not a grand monument, but a structure that conveyed permanence rather than improvisation. One that suggested the College expected to be there for the long term, and intended to do its work with gravity. Construction would begin in 1976, after his term had ended, but the impulse was unmistakable: institutions should look as serious as they intend to be. Recognition arrived, predictably and awkwardly. In 1967, the same year he became dean, Jimmy Laya was named one of The Outstanding Young Men of the Philippines (T.O.Y.M.) by the Philippine Jaycees, cited for Business Education. He accepted the honor with gratitude, but without attachment. Awards, he believed, were secondary indicators at best. They mattered only insofar as they affirmed that an institution was moving in the right direction. They were never the point. By the time he stepped down as dean in 1975, the College of Business Administration had been quietly transformed. It was no longer merely training professionals. It was shaping institutional thinkers — men and women prepared to navigate complexity without resorting to simplification. Jimmy Laya had not imposed a personality on the College. He had given it something far more durable: a structure capable of evolving without him. Rotary: The Weekly Rehearsal of Public Virtue Jimmy Laya joined the Rotary Club of Manila in 1975, at a point in his life when professional responsibility had begun to accumulate and public visibility had become unavoidable. By then, he had already moved through academe into government, and his days were increasingly shaped by institutions that demanded judgment under pressure. To an outsider, Rotary might have appeared redundant — another organization competing for time, another set of meetings layered onto an already full schedule. To Jimmy Laya, it was something else entirely. It was practice. He entered Rotary not seeking expansion, but consolidation. Sponsored by its Past Vice President Jose Roberto “Robbie” Delgado, co-founder, CEO, and chairman of the Transnational Diversified Group, Jimmy approached the Club without expectation of prominence or influence. What attracted him was not Rotary’s prestige, but its structure — its stubborn refusal to reinvent itself simply to remain interesting. In a professional world increasingly enamored with novelty, disruption, and rhetorical urgency, Rotary’s insistence on repetition struck him as quietly radical. The same meetings. The same order of business. The same questions asked again and again, even when the answers appeared obvious. Especially when they appeared obvious. His classification, Government–Education, was descriptive rather than aspirational. Rotary did not ask him to transform, to rebrand, or to perform a version of himself for approval. It required something far more demanding: presence. Attendance. Participation. Return. It insisted that one show up not when inspired, but when routine threatened to dull attention. Its genius lay precisely in that risk. Truth, fairness, goodwill, mutual benefit — these were not principles meant to dazzle. They were standards meant to be rehearsed. Their power came not from eloquence, but from persistence. Recited weekly, they worked their way quietly into reflex. Jimmy Laya understood this immediately. He had spent his life inside systems where ethical lapses rarely arrived dramatically. They crept in through exception, through haste, through the small accommodations made when no one seemed to be watching. Rotary’s discipline lay in preventing that creep. It was about reliability. His contribution was steady rather than spectacular, cumulative rather than episodic. It merely acknowledged what had already been consistent. Later designated Senior Active, he became part of the Club’s institutional memory, even as other professional obligations intermittently drew him away. The work involved scrutiny rather than celebration — reviewing records, examining controls, asking whether procedures were followed not in spirit alone, but in fact. For many, it would have seemed a burdensome assignment. For Jimmy Laya, it was familiar ground. He had long believed that institutions failed not because of bad intentions, but because of neglected systems. Transparency, accountability, and internal control were not bureaucratic irritants; they were moral safeguards. When systems weakened, even the most idealistic organizations became vulnerable — to error, to complacency, to quiet drift. As Internal Auditor, he approached Rotary the same way he approached banks, universities, and public offices — not with suspicion, but with care. The goal was not to catch wrongdoing, but to ensure that trust was deserved. Integrity, he believed, had to be verifiable. Rotary, for Jimmy Laya, was never separate from the rest of his life. It was not an extracurricular commitment. It was rehearsal — a place where the habits required of public service could be practiced without the distortions of power or urgency. Patience. Restraint. Consistency. The willingness to submit oneself to rules even when one had outgrown the need for supervision. In a world increasingly impatient with continuity, Rotary offered something rare: the discipline of staying the course. Of returning, week after week, to principles that did not change simply because the world around them did. For Jimmy Laya, that discipline was not nostalgic. It was essential. When Theory Meets Gravity Jimmy Laya did not enter government believing that good ideas automatically prevailed. When Gerardo P. Sicat — his former cohort and young career co-instructors at the University of the Philippines — assumed leadership of the National Economic and Development Authority in 1974, he invited Jimmy Laya to serve as his deputy — not as an act of patronage, but of confidence. Jimmy’s work quickly earned him respect within the technocratic core of government. So indispensable did he become that Central Bank Governor Gregorio S. Licaros requested to share his services, leading to his concurrent role as Deputy Governor. By the time he accepted senior roles in national administration, he had spent enough years inside complex institutions to understand a hard truth: policy rarely failed because people did not know better. It failed because systems did not align. Intent drifted away from execution. Authority outpaced accountability. Political urgency collided with administrative reality. Between what was imagined and what could actually be implemented, gaps formed — and it was in those gaps that even well-meaning reforms quietly unraveled. He arrived in government without illusions of mastery. What he brought instead was a habit of observation. He paid attention to how decisions moved — or stalled — as they passed through layers of bureaucracy. He noticed where discretion hardened into privilege, where exceptions accumulated until rules no longer held, where processes designed for clarity had become rituals of accommodation. It was this reputation — for precision, restraint, and institutional loyalty — that led President Ferdinand E. Marcos to elevate him to Minister of the Budget, where Jimmy introduced reforms aimed not at expansion, but at restoring coherence to public expenditure. During this time, the country was already straining under the weight of its own complexity. Programs had multiplied rapidly, often in response to political imperatives rather than long-term coherence. New initiatives were layered on top of old ones, rarely retired, frequently overlapping. Budgeting, in practice, had become reactive — less a strategic instrument than an annual exercise in negotiation, bargaining, and deferral. The budget no longer described a plan. It described a truce. Jimmy Laya did not respond with rhetoric. He did not cast himself as a reformer battling entrenched interests. He framed his task in a quieter, more demanding way. What the system required, he believed, was not reinvention, but repair. Repair meant restoring the relationship between planning and budgeting — ensuring that expenditures reflected articulated priorities rather than inherited entitlements. It meant clarifying lines of responsibility so that programs could be evaluated not only for intent, but for outcome. It meant insisting on procedures that could be defended not just in political forums, but within the logic of the institution itself. He treated the budget not as a statement of desire, but as an expression of constraint. Every peso allocated carried a cost beyond its immediate use. It foreclosed alternatives. It signaled preference. To deny this was to invite imbalance. Governments, he understood, did not collapse only from corruption or crisis. They collapsed when promises outran capacity. Multi-year perspectives were introduced to counter the short-termism that distorted annual cycles. Regional rationalization sought to align national priorities with local realities, reducing duplication and unevenness that had crept into implementation. None of these measures were revolutionary. That was precisely their point. They were attempts to make government legible to itself — to allow decision-makers to see, clearly and honestly, what the state was actually doing. Jimmy Laya believed that opacity bred irresponsibility, while clarity, even when uncomfortable, created the conditions for discipline. What frustrated him most was not resistance from politicians. He understood their pressures, their constituencies, their need to respond visibly. What troubled him was the quiet erosion of rules through exception. Each exemption appeared reasonable in isolation. Taken together, they hollowed out the system. Flexibility, unbounded, became arbitrariness. His response was not confrontation, but structure. If discretion could not be eliminated — and he knew it could not — it had to be bounded. Choices had to be traceable. Deviations had to be justified. Systems had to be strong enough to absorb pressure without deforming beyond recognition. The work was slow. It required patience rather than flair, persistence rather than proclamation. It did not lend itself to dramatic narratives of victory or defeat. It also did not make headlines. What it did was more difficult, and more enduring. It reduced the likelihood of sudden failure. It lowered the risk of collapse disguised as momentum. It strengthened the institutional fabric in ways that would only become visible when tested by strain. For Jimmy Laya, that was the measure of success. Not applause, but endurance. Not recognition, but resilience. Central Banking Under Constraint In 1981, when the position became vacant, Jimmy Laya was appointed Governor of the Central Bank of the Philippines, becoming the youngest person ever to hold the post. The appointment was widely noted for its symbolism — youth elevated to one of the most consequential economic offices in the country — but symbolism was the least of his concerns. The timing could not have been more unforgiving. The global environment was tightening its grip. Interest rates abroad were rising sharply, driven by policy shifts far beyond Philippine control. International capital was becoming cautious, selective, impatient. At home, confidence was already brittle, sustained more by habit than conviction. Political uncertainty hovered over every major decision, shaping expectations in ways that monetary instruments alone could not correct. Jimmy Laya entered the office with no illusion that authority equaled sovereignty. Central banks, he understood, operated within constraint. Their tools were powerful, but finite. Their decisions reverberated through markets, but they could not command trust by decree. He rejected the romantic image of the central banker as a figure operating in a realm of technical purity, insulated from politics and human behavior. Monetary decisions, he knew, were entangled — woven through expectations, fears, international pressures, and domestic narratives. The challenge was not to pretend these forces did not exist, but to navigate them without surrendering coherence. Then came August 1983. The assassination of Senator Benigno Aquino Jr. ruptured what little confidence remained. The shock was not only political; it was psychological. Markets respond not just to numbers, but to meaning, and the event signaled instability that could not be priced easily. Capital flows thinned almost immediately. Investors hesitated. Credit tightened. Rumors traveled faster than data. By 1984, the Philippines faced a full-blown financial crisis. Foreign financing dried up. Debt obligations loomed larger than available reserves. The margin for maneuver narrowed until there was almost none left. Eventually, a debt standstill became unavoidable — a decision as sobering as it was consequential. It marked the point at which external confidence could no longer be sustained by internal assurances alone. These were the moments when technocratic training met its limits. Models faltered under conditions they had not been designed to accommodate. Historical precedent offered guidance, but no blueprint. Every decision carried consequences that extended far beyond balance sheets — into employment, prices, livelihoods, and national credibility. Jimmy Laya did not later describe this period with defensiveness or self-exculpation. He acknowledged missteps where they occurred. He recognized constraints where they prevailed. He accepted the reality that some outcomes were shaped by forces beyond domestic control. Powerful countries pursued their own interests. International institutions had their own thresholds of tolerance. The global financial system was not neutral terrain. Yet even within these constraints, he insisted on discipline. Decisions, he believed, had to be reasoned, documented, and defensible. Not because they would always succeed, but because coherence itself was stabilizing. Panic was contagious. So was disorder. A central bank that appeared uncertain amplified fear. One that acted methodically — even under strain — signaled resolve. Clarity, even when painful, was preferable to reassurance built on illusion. It was during these years — almost paradoxically — that Jimmy Laya made one of his most enduring and least expected contributions. Amid financial crisis, when reserves were scarce and attention consumed by survival, he expanded the Central Bank’s acquisition of Philippine artworks and pre-Hispanic artifacts. Institutions, he believed, derived authority not only from function, but from meaning. A central bank was not merely a vault or a regulator. It was a symbol of continuity. In moments when confidence was fragile, when faith in systems wavered, cultural memory served as reassurance that the nation was more than its crisis. Art, in this sense, was not decoration. It was assertion. The acquisition of works by Félix Resurrección Hidalgo, Simón Flores, and others — alongside ancestral gold and pre-Hispanic artifacts — was an act of institutional self-definition. It declared that even under strain, the country would not abandon its story. That while numbers fluctuated and capital retreated, identity endured. These collections would later form the nucleus of what became the Museo ng Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, a permanent repository of cultural memory housed within a financial institution. The juxtaposition was deliberate. Finance and heritage were not opposites. They were parallel forms of stewardship — one concerned with resources, the other with meaning. The decision reflected a belief that crises, while destabilizing, also clarified priorities. And that even in moments of contraction, a nation must remember who it is — or risk losing more than solvency. For Jimmy Laya, central banking was never only about managing currency. It was about preserving coherence — economic, institutional, and cultural — when the forces arrayed against it were strongest. That, he believed, was the quiet responsibility of power exercised without illusion. The Custodian of Memory Jimmy Laya’s sensitivity to memory found earlier expression in another role — one that spoke directly to his understanding of visual culture, space, and the obligations of stewardship. In 1979, he was appointed the first Action Officer of the Intramuros Administration, at a time when the historic walled city stood at a crossroads. Decades after the war, Intramuros remained scarred not only by physical destruction, but by uncertainty. Parts of it had been reconstructed hastily. Other sections had been left to decay. The danger was not simply neglect, but misinterpretation. Intramuros was not merely a site. It was a palimpsest — a record of layered histories written over one another: colonial ambition etched into stone, religious devotion embedded in orientation and form, wartime destruction visible in absences as much as in ruins, and postwar neglect evident in improvisations that confused survival with restoration. To intervene without understanding these layers was to risk turning memory into caricature. Jimmy Laya understood this immediately. He approached the task not as a developer seeking activation, nor as a curator arranging spectacle, but as a scholar trained to read form. He believed that buildings were texts, and that restoration required literacy. Walls were not neutral surfaces. Their thickness, alignment, and articulation responded to climate, defense, and ritual. Gates were oriented deliberately — toward procession, toward surveillance, toward threshold. Ornamentation was not excess. It was language. To erase these features in the name of modernization was not progress. It was amnesia. Under his stewardship, attention shifted from isolated attractions to coherence. Fortifications were studied as systems rather than backdrops. Gates were treated as sequences rather than landmarks. Ecclesiastical structures were understood not simply as devotional spaces, but as spatial narratives — arrangements of light, proportion, and movement designed to shape experience over time. Objects were collected, catalogued, and documented with care. Publications followed — not glossy promotional material, but records meant to endure. The aim was not to impress visitors, but to orient them. Intramuros, Jimmy Laya believed, should be encountered as an archive one could walk through, where understanding deepened with attention rather than speed. He resisted the temptation to dramatize restoration. There were no grand unveilings meant to announce transformation. The work was incremental, deliberate, and often invisible to casual observers. Success was measured not by crowds, but by fidelity — to original form, to documented history, to the quiet intelligence embedded in the built environment. The structure, dating back nearly three centuries, bore the marks of multiple adaptations. Some were sympathetic. Others were distortions accumulated over time. Once again, Jimmy Laya insisted that restoration was not reinvention. It was responsibility. The task was not to leave a personal imprint, nor to update the building to contemporary taste. It was to remove the accretions that obscured its logic and allow the original form — its proportions, materials, and intent — to speak again. Modern intervention, where necessary, had to be legible and restrained, never pretending to be what it was not. This approach required humility. It demanded acceptance that the restorer was a temporary steward, not an author. The same sensibility that guided his work in budgeting and central banking — respect for structure, suspicion of excess, insistence on coherence — found its natural counterpart in visual culture. In both realms, Jimmy Laya believed that systems endured not because they dazzled, but because they were intelligible. Flourish without structure collapsed under scrutiny. Restraint, properly exercised, became a form of care. For Jimmy Laya, preservation was not nostalgia. It was continuity. And continuity, he understood, was the quiet labor that allowed memory to survive without becoming spectacle. Culture as National Infrastructure When Jimmy Laya assumed the role of Minister of Education, Culture and Sports in 1984, he inherited a portfolio that many regarded as ancillary to what were then called the “serious” concerns of governance. Economic stabilization, political negotiation, and security dominated public discourse. Education and culture, by contrast, were often framed as downstream considerations — important, perhaps, but postponable. He did not share that view. To Jimmy, education and culture were not supplemental. They were structural. They shaped not only what a society knew, but how it behaved under strain. Economic systems could be repaired. Political arrangements could be renegotiated. But when a nation lost coherence — when it ceased to recognize shared standards of responsibility, memory, and meaning — recovery became far more elusive. He believed that nations did not fail only through fiscal mismanagement or external shock. They failed through erosion. Education systems that trained for skill without responsibility produced competence without conscience. Cultural institutions treated as luxuries fostered a public life disconnected from memory. The result, he feared, was a society that functioned efficiently but hollowly — capable of output, but uncertain of purpose. His tenure in the ministry was brief and politically turbulent, unfolding amid intensifying national uncertainty. Yet his approach did not waver. He resisted spectacle and avoided grand proclamations. Instead, he focused on alignment — between policy and preservation, between educational outcomes and civic responsibility, between cultural investment and long-term continuity. Education, in his view, was not merely about throughput — how many students passed through classrooms, how quickly credentials were issued. It was about formation. What habits were being cultivated? What standards were being normalized? What responsibilities were being quietly deferred? Culture, likewise, was not an adornment. It was infrastructure of a different kind. It shaped how societies remembered themselves, how they oriented future generations toward the past without becoming captive to it. After 1986, released from the immediacy of formal office, Jimmy Laya returned to this work with greater clarity and patience. Freed from the constraints of ministerial timeframes, he could focus on institutional architecture rather than policy firefighting. As Chairman of the National Commission for Culture and the Arts, beginning in 1996, he presided over a period of critical consolidation. The Philippine cultural landscape had long been fragmented — multiple agencies operating with overlapping mandates, uneven resources, and unclear lines of authority. Good intentions abounded, but coherence was lacking. Jimmy approached the problem as he always had: not through reinvention, but through structure. In 1998, the National Museum System was enacted, providing long-overdue clarity to the stewardship of the nation’s material heritage. Roles were defined. Responsibilities were aligned. Resources were stabilized. It was, in essence, a budgetary act applied to culture — an exercise in institutional design that treated heritage not as sentiment, but as obligation. The effect was subtle but profound. Cultural work could now proceed with continuity rather than improvisation. Preservation ceased to depend solely on personalities or short-term advocacy. It became embedded in the system itself. Years later, when Jimmy Laya assumed the chairmanship of the Cultural Center of the Philippines, he encountered a different but related challenge. The CCP’s iconic structure — already heavy with symbolic and architectural significance — required attention. Time had taken its toll. Systems aged. Standards evolved. The temptation, in such moments, was cosmetic transformation. Jimmy Laya rejected that temptation outright. He was precise in his language. This was not renovation. It was rehabilitation. The distinction mattered. Renovation implied replacement, reinvention, the imposition of contemporary taste. Rehabilitation implied care — investigation, repair, strengthening. The goal was not to modernize appearance, but to restore function. The building, he insisted, would look the same. Its form already carried meaning. Its proportions, materials, and spatial logic were part of its identity. The task was to ensure that it could continue to serve — technically, acoustically, structurally — for generations yet to come. To intervene without erasing. To strengthen without altering character. Once again, the pattern was unmistakable. In finance, in education, in culture, Jimmy Laya’s instinct was identical: build systems that could endure without explanation. body.text: Dr. Andreas Michael Pfaffernoschke, Ambassador of the German Embassy in Manila, has a distinguished diplomatic career. Born in Berlin on June 19, 1962, he has dedicated his career to advancing international relations and representing Germany worldwide.
Ambassador Pfaffernoschke completed his secondary school qualification in Berlin in 1980. He earned a master’s degree in economics in 1985 and a Doctor of Economics degree in 1990, both in Berlin.

Dr. Pfaffernoschke began his diplomatic career in 1990 with training for the higher foreign service at the Federal Foreign Office in Berlin. He has held key positions at the Federal Foreign Office in Bonn and at German embassies in Dakar and Moscow. He also served at the Permanent Mission of Germany to the United Nations in Geneva and New York, demonstrating expertise in multilateral diplomacy. From 2006 to 2010, Dr. Pfaffernoschke served as Deputy Head of Division at the Federal Foreign Office in Berlin. He was Head of Division from 2016 to 2020, further establishing his leadership in international affairs.

Before his current role in Manila, Dr. Pfaffernoschke was the German Ambassador to Ouagadougou from 2020 to 2023. His broad experience and understanding of global issues support Germany's diplomatic efforts in thePhilippines. Dr. Pfaffernoschke is married with four children. Both professionally and personally, he is committed to promoting international connections and mutual understanding.

articles.title: A City in the Pines, A Vision in Motion: Rotary Club of Manila’s 18th Weekly Membership Meeting with JHMC President & CEO Manjit T. Singh Reandi

body.text: The stately halls of the Manila Polo Club once again became a meeting ground of minds and missions as the Rotary Club of Manila convened its 18th Weekly Membership Meeting for Rotary Year 2025–2026. Presided over by Vice President Ricardo S.B. “Ricky” Guevara and deftly moderated by Past District Governor Alexander P. “Alex” Cureg, the gathering unfolded not merely as a luncheon meeting, but as a journey — through history, ecology, community development, and a bold vision of inclusive, sustainable tourism — led by the day’s distinguished guest speaker, Mr. Manjit T. Singh Reandi, President and Chief Executive Officer of the John Hay Management Corporation (JHMC).

From the outset, there was a palpable sense that this would be more than a routine address. As Rotarians and guests settled in, the familiar rhythms of fellowship, song, and shared purpose set the tone, but it was the anticipation of hearing from the steward of one of the country’s most storied and environmentally significant landscapes — Camp John Hay in Baguio City — that lent the afternoon its particular gravity.
From History to Living Heritage

Mr. Reandi began by situating Camp John Hay within the long arc of Philippine and global history. Once a rest-and-recreation haven for American servicemen, the camp bears the name of John Milton Hay, U.S. Secretary of State under Presidents William McKinley and Theodore Roosevelt. It was, he noted with solemn poignancy, at the gates of Camp John Hay that the first bomb of World War II in the Philippines fell in December 1941. And within its grounds still stands the table on which General Tomoyuki Yamashita formally surrendered in 1945 — now preserved at the U.S. Ambassador’s Residence in the John Hay Reservation Area.

Yet Camp John Hay is not a relic frozen in time. Spread across 625 hectares, divided between a 30-hectare Special Economic Zone and a 325-hectare Reservation Area encompassing 14 barangays, it is today a living, breathing ecosystem and economic hub. “We are,” Mr. Reandi quipped with a smile, “the only city in the Philippines with fully air-conditioned outdoors,” referring to Baguio’s pine-cooled climate — made even cooler, by scientific measurement, within the forested core of the camp itself.
Stewardship of the Environment

Central to his message was a profound respect for nature. Camp John Hay, he shared, contains 53.6 percent of Baguio City’s remaining forest reserve and the majority of its pine trees. This is not merely scenic capital; it is ecological responsibility.

JHMC, he proudly noted, is the only government-owned and controlled corporation in the country with ISO certification in environmental management. Their initiatives range from biodiversity conservation — such as the partnership with the Department of Environment and Natural Resources’ research arm and the protection of a 30-hectare experimental forest — to the revival of an 11-hectare bambusetum, one of the largest in Northern Luzon, home to rare and even China-endemic bamboo species.

Equally innovative is their wildfire mitigation strategy: the use of agave plants, rich in water content, as natural firebreaks — an indigenous solution now validated through research partnerships with local universities.
Community at the Heart of Development

Beyond forests and facilities, Mr. Reandi emphasized that the true soul of Camp John Hay lies in its people. Eighty percent of JHMC’s workforce comes from the Cordilleras, and under his leadership, the camp’s development has taken on a distinctly inclusive, community-centered character.

From partnering with local artisans for Christmas markets and cultural bazaars, to welcoming the famed “Pony Boys” of Wright Park and Loakan into the camp as part of its tourism experience, JHMC has sought to ensure that growth is shared. Through collaborations with TESDA, DSWD, and DTI, the John Hay Training Center now offers free skills development and entrepreneurship programs to residents of the reservation barangays — equipping them not only to find employment within the zone, but to build sustainable livelihoods of their own. The Philippine Experience Program, launched with the Department of Tourism, positions Camp John Hay as the northern gateway to the country’s cultural tapestry, beginning at the historic Bell House.
Here, heritage courts, amphitheaters, secret gardens, and soon a market-place for local produce converge to create an immersive narrative of Cordilleran and Filipino identity.
A Vision of Inclusive, Future-Ready Tourism

Innovation, however, does not stop at community markets and heritage trails. Mr. Reandi outlined an ambitious roadmap: the development of golf tourism linked to international markets, explored through engagements in Japan and plans to connect Baguio seamlessly via Clark International Airport; and most strikingly, a proposed cable car system stretching from Tuba, Benguet, into Camp John Hay and looping through key points in the city — envisioning a car-free, congestion-free Baguio that marries mobility with minimal environmental impact. Complementing this are plans for a major Cordillera museum, skywalks, forest boardwalks, and expanded hospitality facilities — all designed under green architecture principles, ensuring that progress never comes at the cost of the environment.

Economically, the numbers underscore the camp’s significance: 7 to 8 million visitors annually, gross sales reaching approximately ₱1.45 billion, and more than 3,200 direct jobs, with many more indirectly supported. Tourism and hospitality remain the anchor, but a growing ecosystem of eco-friendly, innovation-driven enterprises signals a diversified and resilient future.
Rotary and the Spirit of Service

Throughout his presentation, what resonated most with the Rotarian audience was not merely the scale of projects, but the philosophy behind them: stewardship, inclusivity, transparency, and service — values that mirror Rotary’s own ideals. Mr. Reandi spoke of quarterly dialogues with locators, of governance reforms, of gender and development excellence, and of anti-red tape initiatives that have placed JHMC among the top-performing GOCCs in the country.
In him, the Club saw not only a corporate leader, but a custodian of heritage and a partner in nation-building.

As Vice President Ricky Guevara later presented the Certificate of Appreciation, the applause that filled the hall was not perfunctory. It was the collective recognition that Camp John Hay, under its present stewardship, stands as a model of how history, environment, community, and economic vitality can be woven into a single, coherent vision of sustainable progress.

The 18th Weekly Membership Meeting thus concluded not merely with the formalities of adjournment, but with a renewed sense of inspiration. In the cool pine air of Baguio evoked through words and images, Rotarians were reminded that service, when guided by foresight and compassion, can indeed transform landscapes — and lives.
