The forthcoming address of His Excellency Dr. Andreas Michael Pfaffernoschke, Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of the Federal Republic of Germany to the Philippines, comes at a moment when the value of principled diplomacy and genuine International partnership has never been more urgent.

His presence as Guest of Honor and Speaker is not merely ceremonial. It is a timely opportunity to reflect on the depth, maturity, and promise of Philippines-Germany relations — two nations separated by geography but united by a shared commitment to democratic values, multilateral cooperation, and sustainable development.

In a world increasingly shaped by geopolitical tension, economic uncertainty, climate vulnerability, and rapid technological change, Germany stands as a global leader in advocating rules-based order, innovation-driven growth, and climate responsibility. The Philippines, for its part, is an emerging regional partner - resilient, youthful, and strategically positioned in Southeast Asia, with a growing role in shaping the future of the Indo-Pacific.
Ambassador Pfaffernoschke represents a diplomatic tradition that views cooperation not as charity, but as partnership; not as short-term transaction, but as long-term investment in people,

institutions, and shared progress. Germany's engagement with the Philippines - across development cooperation, renewable energy, climate adaptation, vocational training, technology transfer, governance, and private sector collaboration - has consistently reflected this philosophy.
As we anticipate his address, we do so with the expectation of insights grounded in both global perspective and local relevance:
• How nations can work together amid shifting geopolitical alignments
• How economic cooperation can be aligned with sustainability and inclusivity
• How technological and human capital development can be leveraged for long-term resilience
• And how trust, dialogue, and shared values remain the bedrock of meaningful international relations

For the Rotary community and for readers of The Balita, this moment is especially significant. Rotary's ideals of international understanding, peace through service, and leadership beyond borders find a natural resonance in the mission of diplomacy. The work of building bridges — between cultures, institutions, and generations — is the common ground where civic leadership and statecraft meet.

The visit of Ambassador Pfaffernoschke invites us to look beyond immediate concerns and toward a broader horizon: a Philippines that is an active, confident partner in global cooperation; and a Germany that continues to engage not only with governments, but with civil society, business, and community leaders in shaping a shared future.

Before he takes the podium, we welcome him with deep respect and high expectation. His forthcoming message promises not only to illuminate the state of Philippines-Germany relations, but to challenge us to think more expansively about our role in a world where progress is no longer the task of any one nation, but the shared responsibility of all.
Reflections on the Mid-Year Review and Receiving the “People’s Choice” Award

The recently concluded Mid-Year Review of Rotary International District 3810, held in the vibrant coastal city of Da Nang, Vietnam, was a meaningful convergence of leadership, reflection, and shared commitment to Service Above Self. Convened under the guidance of District Governor Mary Mei Rodrigo, the gathering brought together Rotary Club Presidents and District Officers from across the district to assess progress, share best practices, and renew collective resolve for the remainder of the Rotary year.
As President of the Rotary Club of Manila, I was honored to represent Asia’s First Club in this much-awaited activity.

Set against Da Nang’s dynamic blend of tradition and modernity, the Mid-Year Review served as both a checkpoint and a catalyst. Club Presidents presented their accomplishments, challenges, and innovations, fostering an atmosphere of transparency, collaboration, and mutual learning. The exchange of ideas and the sharing of unique experiences by each Club President underscored the strength of Rotary’s network — diverse in experience, yet united in purpose.

A highlight of the event was the presentation of first-semester accomplishments by the Presidents of the Rotary Clubs in the District, delivered either personally or through their designated representatives.

Summarizing and presenting our Club’s mid-year accomplishments within a five-minute window was no small challenge. Yet, I believe our presentation succeeded in clearly conveying the depth of our work and the values that guide our service. At the conclusion of the sessions, I was deeply honored to be chosen by my fellow Rotary Club Presidents as the “People’s Choice” Awardee — an affirmation made especially meaningful as it came from peers who fully understand the demands, responsibilities, and realities of club leadership.

Receiving the award was, for me, a deeply humbling and affirming experience. While it was presented in recognition of the presentation and its content, I view it as something far greater than a personal distinction. It was, in truth, a reflection of the shared values, collective efforts, and quiet dedication of the entire Rotary Club of Manila — of officers and members who give generously of their time, talent, and heart in service to others.

Our Club’s Mid-Year Review report was intentionally honest. It celebrated milestones reached and programs delivered, but it also acknowledged the work that still lies ahead — the goals yet to be met, the mission yet to be fully realized, and the continuous “levelling up” that we, as Rotarians, must always strive for. In Rotary, progress is never static; it is a journey of constant learning, refinement, and recommitment to service.

In that context, receiving the “People’s Choice” award felt less like an endpoint and more like a quiet but meaningful confirmation. It affirmed that the Rotary Club of Manila is moving in the right direction, that our efforts are aligned with the values we espouse, and that our projects are resonating beyond our own Club. More importantly, it reinforced a belief I hold deeply -- that leadership in Rotary is not measured by accolades or applause, but by our capacity to inspire others, to build genuine connections, and to create impact where it truly matters.

I share this recognition with every member of the Rotary Club of Manila. It belongs to the hands that serve, the minds that plan, and the hearts that remain steadfast in our commitment to serve. If the award signifies anything at all, it is that our collective work is touching lives, strengthening communities, and contributing, in our own way, to the broader Rotary mission. For that affirmation, I am profoundly grateful — and even more motivated to continue the work ahead.

Our Club’s Mid-Year Review report was intentionally honest. It celebrated milestones reached and programs delivered, but it also acknowledged the work that still lies ahead — the goals yet to be met, the mission yet to be fully realized, and the continuous “levelling up” that we, as Rotarians, must always strive for.

The Da Nang Mid-Year Review has reaffirmed for me the value of coming together at the midpoint of the Rotary year — not just to assess our metrics and milestones, but to deepen fellowship and reignite our shared purpose. I return from this gathering with fresh insights, renewed energy, and an even greater appreciation for the transformative power of peer-driven encouragement.

In true Rotary spirit, the event was a testament to the idea that when leaders learn from one another and celebrate shared successes, the entire district moves forward — stronger, more aligned, and ever more committed to service.

Rotarian Rafael “Raf” S. Dionisio Named 2025 TOYM Awardee for Regenerative Tourism and Circular Economy Entrepreneurship

Rotarian Rafael “Raf” S. Dionisio has been named one of the 2025 honorees of The Outstanding Young Men (TOYM) Awards, one of the country’s most prestigious recognitions for exemplary leadership and service. Raf was selected for the category of Regenerative Tourism and Circular Economy Entrepreneurship, emerging as one of only four awardees chosen nationwide from a competitive field of 150 nominees.

The TOYM Awards, jointly conferred by Junior Chamber International (JCI) Philippines and the TOYM Foundation, honor young Filipinos whose professional excellence and civic commitment contribute significantly to nation-building. The 2025 edition carries the theme “Excellence in Action: Building a Better Tomorrow,” underscoring the role of visionary leadership in addressing the country’s most pressing social, environmental, and economic challenges.

A committed member of the Rotary Club of Manila (RCM), Dionisio has been a consistent and passionate advocate for sustainable development, particularly in advancing initiatives that integrate environmental stewardship with inclusive economic growth. Within Rotary, he has actively championed projects aligned with sustainability, climate action, and community resilience, helping advance the organization’s mission of “Service Above Self” in the context of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals.

Professionally, Raf is a social entrepreneur whose work spans multiple sectors, including forestry, agriculture, food, education, travel, construction, and sustainability. His enterprises and advocacy focus on regenerative development models that go beyond minimizing harm, instead restoring ecosystems, empowering local communities, and building circular systems that reduce waste and maximize resource efficiency.

Through his leadership in regenerative tourism, Raf has promoted approaches that protect natural landscapes while creating livelihood opportunities for host communities. His work in the circular economy emphasizes responsible production, sustainable supply chains, and innovative business models that transform environmental challenges into engines for inclusive growth.

Being named a TOYM 2025 awardee places Raf among an elite group of young Filipino leaders recognized for their outstanding contributions to society. His selection as one of only four honorees nationwide highlights the growing importance of sustainability-driven entrepreneurship and the pivotal role of the private sector in advancing climate action and long-term national development.

The Rotary Club of Manila joins the broader Rotary and JCI communities in congratulating Rotarian Raf Dionisio for this well-deserved honor, celebrating his vision, integrity, and unwavering commitment to building a more sustainable and resilient Philippines.

articles.title: Inside the Flood Control Scandal: Singson Speaks to Aleco

body.text: In the quiet, amber-lit setting of an intimate breakfast gathering, a small circle of members from the Rotary Club of Manila’s Aleco Group listened closely to a rare and unvarnished account from former Department of Public Works and Highways Secretary and former Independent Commission for Infrastructure Commissioner Rogelio “Babes” Singson.

It was not a ceremonial talk nor a retrospective filled with pleasantries. It was a sober, firsthand exposition by a man who once stood at the front lines of one of the country’s most corruption-prone sectors, offering a clinical and deeply unsettling dissection of what he described as the ongoing crisis in flood control governance.

Secretary Singson spoke with the precision of an engineer and the moral clarity of a reform advocate as he laid bare the anatomy of what has come to be known as the “Flood Control Corruption Exposed” scandal—a multibillion-peso web of alleged irregularities that, since 2024, has not only submerged communities but steadily eroded public trust and institutional integrity.

Peeling back the layers of the General Appropriations Act, he described a sophisticated system of budgetary manipulation carried out not with force, but with paperwork, signatures, and strategic legislative insertions. According to his analysis, an estimated ₱500 billion has flowed through more than 5,500 flood control projects, with a significant portion coursing through the ₱214-billion Unprogrammed Appropriations. This pool of funds, he warned, has become fertile ground for ghost projects, bloated costs, and the alleged concentration of contracts among a small circle of favored firms, reportedly insulated by political patrons who themselves benefit from the system.

Beyond exposing fiscal irregularities, Singson lamented the abandonment of a science-based vision he had championed during the administration of President Benigno "Noynoy" Aquino III: Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM). This holistic framework treats rivers, watersheds, forests, agriculture, solid waste systems, drainage, and coastal zones as one interconnected ecological system. Its neglect, he explained, is now evident in denuded uplands that dump silt into rivers, plastic waste that clogs urban waterways, eroded farmlands and landfill runoff that poison estuaries, and flood control structures rendered ineffective by upstream degradation and downstream mismanagement. The nation, he said, has been addressing symptoms while ignoring the disease.

He also expressed grave concern over the distortion of the Convergence Fund, originally designed to enable DPWH to collaborate with agencies such as the Departments of Education, Tourism, and Health to produce infrastructure with multiplied social impact. In some cases, he noted, the mechanism has reportedly evolved into a channel for procedural circumvention, where success is measured less by public safety or functionality and more by the speed of fund obligation and disbursement.

Citing reports from Bulacan, he pointed to claims that as much as ₱2 billion a month had been spent through in-house construction arrangements and borrowed contractor licenses, all shielded by the presumption of regularity, even as questions lingered over quality, necessity, and genuine public value.

Yet Singson's message was not one of despair. As the discussion drew to a close, he offered a framework for reform distilled into what he called the "Five Rs of Good Governance": the Right Project, at the Right Cost, implemented by the Right People, with the Right Quality, and delivered Right on Time. Simple in formulation, the principles demand a level of discipline that would fundamentally challenge entrenched practices.

He then issued a call that resonated strongly with his Rotary audience: the creation of a Citizens’ Mandated Audit. This proposed coalition would bring together civil society organizations, professional associations, faith-based groups, and volunteer institutions to conduct independent reviews of public works—scrutinizing budgets, validating physical accomplishments, and demanding transparency and accountability. Complementing this, he advocated for an Integrity Pledge for contractors, modeled on the uncompromising standards of Hong Kong’s Independent Commission Against Corruption, binding participation in public projects not only to technical competence but to enforceable ethical commitments.

For the Rotary Club of Manila, the discussion pointed to a clear civic role. With members drawn from engineering, architecture, accounting, law, environmental science, information technology, urban planning, education, and community leadership, the organization possesses a depth of professional expertise uniquely suited to support such a citizen-led audit initiative. It can convene multi-sector coalitions, partner with universities and watchdog groups, train citizen-auditors, deploy technical review teams, and provide a trusted, non-partisan platform for the responsible and factual presentation of findings.

Beyond auditing, Rotary's service tradition also positions it to help revive the principles of Integrated Water Resources Management through watershed rehabilitation, solid-waste programs, river and estero clean-ups, coastal protection, and public education that links environmental stewardship with anti-corruption advocacy. In this way, flood control is reframed not as a cycle of concrete pouring and ribbon-cutting, but as a long-term commitment to systems thinking, sustainability, and integrity.

Secretary Singson's testimony that morning served both as a warning and a roadmap. Flooding, he underscored, is not solely an act of nature. It is, too often, the product of distorted priorities, corrupted processes, and weakened institutions. But precisely because it is man-made, it can also be undone—if informed citizens, principled professionals, and values-driven institutions choose to stand not on the sidelines of polite concern, but on the front lines of truth, accountability, and nation-building.

A Convergence of Values, Vision, and Global Responsibility: The Rotary Club of Manila’s 19 Weekly Membership Meeting PE Reginald T. Yu At precisely 12:30 p.m. on January 29, 2026, the gavel fell and the 19th Weekly Membership Meeting of the Rotary Club of Manila for Rotary Year 2025–2026 was formally called to order by President Raoul C. Creencia, setting the tone for an afternoon marked by diplomacy, fellowship, reflection, and global perspective. The historic Manila Polo Club, long a witness to pivotal conversations in Philippine civic life, once again became a venue where local leadership met international thought. What unfolded was not merely a luncheon meeting, but a carefully choreographed gathering that reflected Rotary’s enduring role as a bridge — between nations, cultures, and ideas. Opening Rites: Ceremony Anchored in Meaning The meeting opened with an invocation led by former Ambassador and Rotarian Victor G. “Vic” Garcia III, grounding the assembly in gratitude and purpose. In a gesture both symbolic and resonant with the day’s international theme, the National Anthem of Germany was rendered, followed by the Philippine National Anthem, affirming mutual respect between host and guest nations. The Rotary Club of Manila Hymn, sung by the RCM World Famous Music Chorale, reaffirmed the Club’s shared identity, while the solemn recitation of The Four-Way Test, led by Past Director Issam Eldebs, reminded members that ethical clarity remains Rotary’s moral compass in an increasingly complex world. Fellowship and Recognition: The Human Core of Rotary Past Sergeant-at-Arms Güenter Gerhard G. “Günter” Matschuck, serving as Moderator, formally acknowledged the distinguished guests present — diplomatic, civic, and Rotarian — before the hall was filled with music once more as the Chorale led the Welcome Song, an audible expression of Rotary’s culture of warmth and inclusivity. The celebration of January birthday celebrants followed, honoring Rotarians Butch Campos, Past Director Abe Pascual, Toti Cortez, and Danny Go. The familiar strains of Maligayang Bati / Happy Birthday Birthday reminded everyone present that Rotary, even at its most formal, remains a fellowship rooted in personal connection. President’s Time: Leadership in Continuity In his President’s Time, Raoul C. Creencia addressed the membership with the steady cadence of a leader mindful of both tradition and trajectory. His remarks reinforced the Club’s commitment to relevance — locally grounded yet globally aware — and prepared the audience for a discourse that would stretch far beyond Manila, into Europe, the Indo-Pacific, and the shifting architecture of international relations. Introducing the Guest-of-Honor Moderator PSAA Güenter Matschuck then delivered a thoughtful, warm, and unmistakably personal introduction of the Guest of Honor and Speaker — an introduction so comprehensive it unfolded over a good twenty minutes — before finally presenting His Excellency Andreas Michael Pfaffernoschke, Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of the Federal Republic of Germany to the Philippines. The introduction was both professional and affectionate, reflecting a relationship built not merely on protocol but on shared values, mutual respect, and longstanding engagement between German and Filipino communities. A World in Flux, Anchored by Shared Principles Ambassador Pfaffernoschke began not with geopolitics, but with gratitude — thanking the Rotary Club of Manila for the invitation, acknowledging President Creencia, Ambassador Garcia, PD Issam Eldebs, and extending special recognition to Günter Matschuck, whom he credited for personally encouraging his appearance before the Club. Speaking with warmth and candor, the Ambassador struck a tone that was at once conversational and consequential. He reflected briefly on his tenure in the Philippines with his wife Marina, sharing their travels across the archipelago — from Iloilo’s Dinagyang Festival to more than twenty islands visited so far — emphasizing that to truly understand the Philippines, one must go beyond Manila and encounter its people where they live and celebrate. The Ambassador anchored his address in history by quoting Dr. José Rizal, recalling the national hero’s admiration for German discipline, science, and culture during his stay in Germany in the late 19th century. Rizal’s completion of Noli Me Tangere in Berlin and the novel’s first publication there were cited as enduring symbols of the deep intellectual and cultural ties between the two nations — a relationship formally established diplomatically in 1954, and now matured into what the Ambassador described as a strategic, high-stakes partnership. The heart of Ambassador Pfaffernoschke’s address lay in a sober assessment of the global geopolitical environment, highlighting a world where long-held assumptions are eroding, international law is increasingly challenged by power politics, and the use of force to alter borders has re-entered global discourse — once unthinkable to a generation shaped by post-war Europe. Drawing parallels between Europe and Asia, he underscored how security in Ukraine and stability in the Indo-Pacific are inextricably linked, asserting that Germany and the Philippines share a moral obligation to defend the rules-based international order, whether in Eastern Europe or the West Philippine Sea. In unequivocal terms, Ambassador Pfaffernoschke reaffirmed Germany’s support for the Philippines in upholding UNCLOS and the 2016 Arbitral Award, stressing that freedom of navigation and respect for sovereignty are not abstract ideals but economic necessities for a trading nation like Germany, whose livelihoods depend on secure sea lanes in Southeast Asia. He also expressed strong support for the Philippines’ 2026 ASEAN Chairmanship, highlighting it as an opportunity for Filipino leadership to guide the region under the theme “Navigating Our Future Together,” and noting the symbolic importance of the upcoming 50th anniversary of the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation. On economic relations, the Ambassador spoke with notable frankness. Germany remains the Philippines’ largest trading partner within the EU, with trade volumes approaching €7 billion, and a substantial surplus favoring the Philippines. Yet he emphasized that trust, predictability, and ease of doing business are indispensable currencies. While acknowledging reforms already undertaken by the Philippine government, he candidly cited persistent challenges — bureaucracy, corruption, and regulatory unpredictability—illustrating these concerns with concrete examples familiar to the business community, including issues affecting major German investors. The Ambassador outlined expanding defense cooperation, referencing high-level visits, joint training, cybersecurity collaboration, and Germany’s growing presence in the Indo-Pacific. He also highlighted Germany’s €35-million climate resilience investment in the Philippines, implemented through GIZ, as evidence of long-term commitment. Equally compelling was his emphasis on people-to-people relations: tens of thousands of Filipinos living and working in Germany, ongoing efforts to facilitate skilled labor mobility, and cultural exchanges such as the Philippines’ role as Guest of Honor at the 2025 Frankfurt Book Fair. The Ambassador concluded on a deeply personal note, praising Filipino hospitality and the enduring spirit of Bayanihan, which he described not as a slogan but a lived value that makes partnership possible even joyful. His closing words expressed optimism, gratitude, and a sincere affection for the Philippines, punctuated by a heartfelt “Maraming maraming salamat po.” Dialogue, Appreciation, and Closure An Open Forum followed, allowing members to engage the Ambassador directly — an exchange emblematic of Rotary’s tradition of thoughtful, respectful dialogue. President Creencia then presented the Certificate of Appreciation, formally thanking Ambassador Pfaffernoschke for an address that was at once intellectually rigorous and profoundly relevant. At 2:00 p.m., President Creencia adjourned the meeting, closing a gathering that reaffirmed the Rotary Club of Manila’s role as a convener of ideas that matter — not only to Rotarians, but to the nation and the wider world. In an era of uncertainty, the 19th Weekly Membership Meeting stood as a reminder that principled dialogue, anchored in shared values, remains one of Rotary’s greatest contributions to a world in flux. PRES. RAOUL C. CREENCIA Editorial  Reginald T. Yu Editor-in-Chief The presence of Commissioner Charlito Martin Rada Mendoza as Guest of Honor and Speaker at this Weekly Membership Meeting could not be more timely. After months of public anxiety, institutional introspection, and reform work behind the scenes, the Bureau of Internal Revenue has formally lifted the suspension on tax audits — effective January 27, 2026 — not as a return to old habits, but as a decisive pivot toward a more disciplined, transparent, and accountable system of tax administration. The resumption of audits under newly issued circulars and orders marks a clear acknowledgment of past vulnerabilities and a firm commitment to correct them. The reforms are not cosmetic. They strike at the very points where public trust was most eroded. The introduction of a single-instance audit per taxpayer per taxable year, enforced through an electronic Letter of Authority, decisively ends the specter of repetitive, overlapping, and sometimes harassing examinations. The automatic consolidation of existing audits beginning March 4, 2026 further signals the Bureau’s resolve to simplify processes and reduce discretion that invites abuse. Just as critically, the explicit prohibition of audits in public venues restores professional boundaries long blurred, reinforcing both taxpayer dignity and institutional integrity. Perhaps most consequential is the renewed emphasis on personal accountability. Under the new rules, violations of audit procedures now carry administrative, civil, and even criminal consequences for erring officials. This is not merely regulatory tightening — it is a cultural reset. It reframes enforcement not as power exercised over taxpayers, but as responsibility exercised on behalf of the Republic. These reforms reflect the governing philosophy Commissioner Mendoza brings to the Bureau: reform that is structural, data-driven, and grounded in due process. His professional journey — from private legal practice to senior revenue operations oversight and frontline customs leadership — has shaped an administrator keenly aware that credibility, once lost, can only be rebuilt through consistency, restraint, and institutional discipline. Beyond audits, the Bureau’s recent issuances reveal a broader responsiveness to economic realities and technological change. The increase in tax-exempt de minimis benefits, effective January 6, 2026, quietly but meaningfully acknowledges the pressures of inflation on Filipino workers. By raising ceilings on items such as rice subsidies and clothing allowances, the Bureau signals that revenue collection need not come at the expense of basic employee welfare. Likewise, the extension of VAT filing deadlines for non-resident digital service providers reflects regulatory pragmatism. As the tax net expands into the digital economy, the Bureau has shown a willingness to adjust timelines when systems encounter real-world constraints — an important signal to global service providers navigating Philippine compliance for the first time. The rollout of an enhanced electronic documentary stamp tax system and the clarified, extended deadlines for online registration of books of accounts further underscore the Bureau’s digital direction. Compliance is being nudged away from paper, ambiguity, and physical presence toward traceable, system-based processes that protect both the taxpayer and the State. Taken together, these measures tell a coherent story. This is not a Bureau retreating from enforcement, nor one blindly asserting authority. It is an institution attempting — deliberately and publicly — to recalibrate its role: firm but fair, modern but mindful, exacting yet accountable. For taxpayers, professionals, and civic leaders alike, the message is clear. The pause in audits was not an abdication of duty; it was an opportunity to rebuild the rules of engagement. The resumption, under reformed procedures, challenges both sides of the tax relationship to meet higher standards of conduct. In that sense, today’s conversation is not merely about tax policy. It is about trust — how it is broken, how it is rebuilt, and how institutions earn the moral authority to collect what is due. Under the current reform agenda, the Bureau of Internal Revenue appears determined to prove that reform is not an announcement, but a discipline — one that must be practiced daily, in full view of the public it serves. Guest of Honor and Speaker  President Ferdinand Marcos, Jr. appointed Charlito Martin Rada Mendoza as Commissioner of the Bureau of Internal Revenue on November 12, 2025, entrusting him with the leadership of the country’s primary revenue agency at a critical moment for reform and modernization. He brings to the role a rare combination of legal expertise, frontline operational experience, and broad fiscal policy perspective. Before leading the Bureau, Commissioner Charlie served as DOF Undersecretary for the Revenue Operations Group from April 2024 to November 2025, overseeing the country’s complex tax collection operations across both the Bureau of Internal Revenue and the Bureau of Customs to ensure that both agencies meet annual revenue collection targets. He initiated the DOF’s BRAVE—Border Security Enhancement, Revenue Collection and Revenue-Base Protection, Adaptive Regulations, Vigilant Enforcement, and Effective Engagement with Stakeholders—a campaign against smuggling and illicit trade, with digitalization at its core. With BRAVE and complementary fiscal reforms, the DOF exceeded its 2024 revenue target, posting PHP 4.42 trillion, or 16.7% of GDP, the country’s highest revenue effort in 27 years. Earlier in his public service career, Commissioner Charlie served as District Collector of the Bureau of Customs, Port of Cebu, from July 2019 to October 2022. During his tenure, the Port achieved notable gains in revenue performance and border protection. One of his enduring contributions was the institutionalization of quality management reforms, which made Cebu the first BOC revenue district to secure ISO 9001:2012 certification for its main Port and all sub-ports. Before entering government service, Commissioner Charlie built a distinguished career in private legal practice. He began as an Associate Lawyer at Angara Abello Concepcion Regala and Cruz Law Offices (ACCRALAW), later joining Suarez and Narvasa Law Firm. In 2014, he co-founded the Palafox Patriarca Romero and Mendoza Law Firm and served as its first Managing Partner. Alongside his legal practice, he devoted time to legal education, teaching at San Beda University College of Law, New Era University College of Law, and San Sebastian Recoletos Institute of Law. He also lectured at the Manila Law Center of the New Era University for the Mandatory Continuing Legal Education Program. He placed third in the 2004 Philippine Bar Exams after earning his Bachelor of Laws degree from San Beda University. He is also a licensed Geodetic Engineer, having earned a degree in Geodetic Engineering from the University of the Philippines. Grounded in integrity and professionalism, Commissioner Charlie leads the Bureau of Internal Revenue with a clear reform agenda anchored on DARES—Digital and Data Transformation, Audit Reform and Accountability, Revenue Collection and Base Protection, Employee Empowerment and Welfare Promotion, and Service Excellence and Stakeholder Engagement. Through this framework, he is steering the BIR toward a more responsive, technology-enabled, and predictable tax administration—one that strengthens public trust, supports voluntary compliance, empowers its workforce, and delivers fair and efficient service to taxpayers as partners in nation-building. President’s Message  CHIEF TAXMAN IS OUR GUEST SPEAKER In today’s Weekly Membership Meeting, the Rotary Club of Manila will be greatly honored by the presence of Commissioner Charlito Martin Mendoza of the Bureau of Internal Revenue as our Guest of Honor and Speaker. His participation in this event underscores the Bureau’s pivotal role in ensuring fiscal stability, promoting good governance, and supporting the government’s broader development agenda. It is a privilege for us to welcome the Commissioner and to benefit from the insights of the country’s chief tax administrator. Today’s gathering presents a timely and valuable opportunity to gain a deeper understanding of the comprehensive reforms and innovative solutions that the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) is currently undertaking to modernize tax administration and enhance revenue collection. These initiatives — particularly in the areas of digitalization, process streamlining, data-driven enforcement, and taxpayer education — reflect the Bureau’s strong commitment to efficiency, transparency, and service excellence. In an increasingly complex economic environment, the need for a responsive and forward-looking tax system cannot be overstated. The reforms being pursued by the BIR are essential not only in improving collection performance, but also in creating a fair and predictable tax regime that encourages compliance, supports business growth, and strengthens public confidence in government institutions. By embracing innovation and reform, the Bureau continues to adapt to emerging challenges while upholding its mandate to serve the Filipino people. We also recognize that sustainable revenue generation is a shared responsibility. The continued engagement of the BIR with the private sector, professional organizations, and other stakeholders plays a crucial role in fostering collaboration, mutual understanding, and voluntary compliance. Dialogues such as this allow stakeholders to better appreciate the direction of tax policy and administration, and to align their own practices with national priorities. Graciously accepting our invitation and for sharing his leadership, vision, and expertise with us. We are confident that the perspectives to be shared today will be both enlightening and inspiring, and will further strengthen cooperation between the Bureau of Internal Revenue and its stakeholders as we collectively work toward a more efficient, equitable, and sustainable tax system for the nation. Next week, we are honored to welcome Philippine Sports Commission Chairman John Patrick Gregorio as our Guest Speaker. As the primary government agency mandated by law to formulate national sports policies, set strategic directions, and coordinate amateur sports development programs across the country, the Commission plays a vital role in nation-building. This engagement presents a timely opportunity to gain insights into the Commission’s current priorities and initiatives in promoting a healthy, disciplined citizenry, as well as its ongoing efforts to support and develop elite athletes for international competitions. BORN INTO THE REPUBLIC: The Making of Victor de Guzman Garcia III PE Reginald T. Yu In the great chambers where the destinies of nations are debated — where the language of law tempers the impulses of power, and where the hopes of small states must stand with dignity before the ambitions of great ones — there are diplomats whose names are etched quietly into the architecture of history. They are not conquerors, nor demagogues, nor men of spectacle. They are builders: of consensus, of institutions, of bridges across cultures and centuries. Victor de Guzman Garcia III belongs to that lineage. He would one day sit in the Security Council of the United Nations as a young adviser while the Cold War still divided the world into rival camps. He would later help craft the very “constitution of the oceans” that now anchors the Philippines’ sovereign rights in the West Philippine Sea. He would represent his country in the nuclear councils of Vienna, in the strategic corridors of Moscow, in the humanitarian crises of Kobe and Los Angeles, and in the ceremonial heart of Malacañang, where protocol becomes the language of respect among states. Yet long before he affixed his signature to global treaties, before he addressed assemblies and negotiated conventions, he was a child of a young republic — born into a family where diplomacy was not merely a profession but a calling, and where the service of country was woven into daily life. His story is, in many ways, the story of Philippine diplomacy itself:
from post-war emergence to Cold War alignment,
from archipelagic assertion to multilateral leadership,
from bilateral courtesies to the forging of international law. It is the story of how a nation of islands learned to speak with one voice in the world — and how one man, trained by history, law, and conscience, helped that voice be heard. This is not a tale of glamour, though embassies and ceremonies would mark its chapters. It is a chronicle of patience, discipline, sacrifice, and quiet courage. It is the life of a man who believed that the true measure of diplomacy lies not in headlines, but in the slow, steadfast work of building order where chaos threatens, and understanding where mistrust prevails. Before he became an architect of treaties, a defender of overseas Filipinos, a guardian of protocol, and a mentor to a new generation of diplomats, Vic Garcia was first a son — listening to his father recount a moment when the Philippines, newly independent, stood proudly among the nations of the world. It is there, in that intimate moment of inheritance and aspiration, that his story truly begins. Heirs to a Calling On a quiet evening in Manila in the early 1950s, a young boy listened intently as his father recounted a scene that seemed drawn from the pages of a history book. The setting was Westminster Abbey, its ancient stone walls resonant with the weight of centuries. The occasion was June 2, 1953 — the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II. But what made the story unforgettable was not the splendor of crowns and pageantry. It was the pride in his father’s voice. Ambassador Enrique Melocoton Garcia had stood there not as a subject of the British Crown, but as the diplomatic representative of a newly independent republic. For the Philippines, barely seven years free from colonial rule, it was a moment of symbolic arrival on the world stage. For his son, Victor de Guzman Garcia III, it was a moment of quiet awakening. As he listened, wide-eyed, he felt — without yet fully understanding — that the life of a diplomat was a life lived at the intersection of history and hope, where personal destiny could merge with the destiny of a nation. Vic was born into diplomacy. His father was among the pioneers of the Philippine Foreign Service, entering the Department of Foreign Affairs at its founding in 1946, when the young republic was just beginning to define its place in a fractured postwar world. His mother, Roberta Laperal de Guzman, brought to this peripatetic life a deep sense of faith, grace, and emotional anchoring. Together, they raised their children in embassies and official residences across continents, where conversations at the dinner table often revolved around world events, state visits, and the delicate art of representing the Philippines with dignity. From an early age, Vic learned that diplomacy was not merely about protocol and ceremony. It was about service. A diplomat, his father taught him, carries the voice of his people and the honor of his country wherever he goes. That sense of representation — of standing for something larger than oneself — would become the moral core of his career. His formal education mirrored the breadth of his upbringing. He studied at De La Salle in Manila, then at Universidad Central in Madrid, later at University College London, and finally at Ateneo Law School. Business, political science, international affairs, and law formed a multidisciplinary foundation that equipped him to understand power, economics, culture, and legal order as interconnected forces. Europe exposed him to the long memory of nations and the institutional frameworks that governed their relations. Law trained him in precision, argument, and respect for rules — the very grammar of international relations. Returning to Manila, he entered Ateneo Law School at a time when the Philippines itself was navigating political and social transformation. He graduated in 1977, already determined to follow the path that had quietly beckoned since childhood. Three years earlier, in 1974, he had taken and passed the highly competitive Career Foreign Service Officer Examination, a defining threshold for those who aspired to serve the country abroad. For him, it was not simply a professional milestone; it was a personal calling fulfilled. By the time he and his contemporaries formally completed their studies in 1977, Vic was already a young Vice-Consul at the Department of Foreign Affairs in Padre Faura. His immediate superior was Ambassador Armando D. Manalo, a brilliant diplomat and gifted writer who was then one of the closest advisers of the Secretary of Foreign Affairs, General Carlos P. Romulo. Romulo — statesman, soldier, Pulitzer Prize-winning author, and former President of the United Nations General Assembly — was affectionately and reverently called “The General,” a moniker he himself enjoyed. It was Romulo who discerned the promise of the young officer. Recognizing both his legal training and his instinct for international affairs, Romulo sent Garcia to his first overseas assignment: the Permanent Mission of the Philippines to the United Nations in New York. For a young diplomat, it was both an honor and a baptism by fire. At the United Nations, Vic was thrust into the demanding world of multilateral diplomacy at a moment when the Cold War still defined the global order. The General Assembly was a forum of ideological contestation, decolonizing nations asserting their voices, and great powers maneuvering for influence. In committee rooms and plenary halls, he learned that diplomacy was rarely about simple victories. It was about building coalitions, crafting language that could command consensus, and reconciling national interest with global responsibility. He witnessed firsthand the workings of the Security Council, on which the Philippines would later serve from 1980 to 1981. He observed how international peace and security were debated under the shadow of superpower rivalry, and how smaller states, through preparation and moral clarity, could still make their voices heard. He worked closely with seasoned diplomats, including Ambassador Alejandro Yango, whose mastery of UN procedure and negotiation became an informal school for the young officer. These early years in New York were formative in the deepest sense. They exposed Vic to the complexity of multilateralism, where one negotiated not with a single counterpart but with the entire community of nations. They also taught him patience, discipline, and the importance of law as a stabilizing force in international affairs. From the vantage point of later decades, he would look back on this period as the crucible of his professional identity. The foundations laid at the United Nations — under the mentorship of Romulo and Manalo, amid the ideological crosscurrents of the Cold War — would serve him well as he rose through the ranks of the Foreign Service. Through sheer hard work, perseverance, and sacrifice, he would eventually be appointed Ambassador in 1989, at the age of fortytwo — one of the youngest in the annals of Philippine diplomatic history. The boy who had once listened to stories of coronations and chancelleries had now entered the world where history was made not in spectacle alone, but in the painstaking work of dialogue, negotiation, and law. Born into the republic, shaped by family, education, and early exposure to the highest councils of nations, Victor Garcia III had begun a journey that would carry him from the halls of the United Nations to the front lines of treaty-making, crisis management, and statecraft — always guided by the quiet conviction that to serve one’s country abroad was both a privilege and a solemn trust. Architect of the Oceans, Envoy of the Filipino People By the late 1970s and early 1980s, Vic had moved beyond the apprenticeship of diplomacy into its most demanding arena: the crafting of international law itself. The United Nations was no longer merely a forum he observed; it was a laboratory in which he helped forge the rules that would govern relations among states for generations. Among the most consequential chapters in the diplomatic life of Victor de Guzman Garcia III was his participation in the negotiations of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) — a treaty often described as the “constitution of the oceans.” For the Philippines, an archipelagic nation whose history, security, and economic future are inseparable from the sea, the stakes could not have been higher. Garcia, however, has always been careful to place his own role in its proper historical context. At the time of the negotiations, he was still a young officer of the Foreign Service, serving as an adviser and member of the Philippine delegation. He does not, and has never, claimed personal credit for the intellectual leadership or authorship of the Philippine position. That distinction rightly belongs to the brilliant Senator Arturo M. Tolentino, the principal architect and indefatigable champion of the Philippine archipelagic doctrine, together with the country’s foremost legal luminaries who formed the core of the delegation — former Solicitor General Estelito P. Mendoza, former Secretary of Justice Vicente Abad Santos, Ambassador Pablo Suarez, and other senior diplomats and jurists whose scholarship and statesmanship secured one of the most important victories of Philippine diplomacy in the twentieth century. The negotiations themselves were arduous and historic. Maritime powers, concerned with freedom of navigation, and developing and archipelagic states, determined to safeguard their security and resources, had to reconcile competing interests in order to establish a comprehensive legal regime for the world’s oceans. For the Philippines, the recognition of the archipelagic concept — treating the waters enclosed by the outermost islands as an integral part of national territory — was a matter of sovereignty and survival. Garcia witnessed at close range how law, diplomacy, and national vision converged in the painstaking search for consensus. UNCLOS was opened for signature at Montego Bay, Jamaica, on December 10, 1982. The Philippine delegation to this historic event was led by Senator Tolentino, with Ambassador Pablo Suarez, Ambassador Reynaldo Arcilla, and First Secretary of the Philippine Mission to the United Nations in New York, Victor G. Garcia III, as members. After affixing his own signature to the Convention, Senator Tolentino asked the three other members of the delegation to sign individually as well, as each had been granted full powers by the President of the Philippines to do so. Thus, four Filipinos formally signed UNCLOS on behalf of the Republic. Of the four, it is Garcia who remains today the sole surviving signatory. He has always regarded this not as a personal accolade, but as a solemn historical trust: to be a living witness to the moment when the Philippines, through the vision of its statesmen and the rigor of its legal minds, helped shape the rules that now govern the seas. Decades later, when the 2016 Arbitral Award would affirm the country’s sovereign rights in the West Philippine Sea under UNCLOS, Garcia would look back on Montego Bay not with claims of authorship, but with quiet gratitude that he had been present at the creation of a legal framework that continues to safeguard the nation’s maritime destiny. For him, the experience was formative in a deeper sense. It revealed how a small and developing country, armed with principled arguments and guided by exceptional leadership, could leave an enduring imprint on international law. It also reinforced the lesson that would define his career: that in diplomacy, true legacy is not measured by personal prominence, but by faithful participation in causes that outlive one’s own name. Rome and the Human Face of Diplomacy After the high drama of global negotiations, Vic’s career took him into the equally demanding world of consular and bilateral diplomacy. As Minister and Consul-General in Rome, he confronted the realities faced by thousands of Filipinos working abroad, many of whom lacked proper documentation and lived in precarious conditions. Europe, he learned, was not only a theater of grand politics but also a landscape of human stories — of caregivers, domestic workers, and professionals whose welfare depended on the vigilance of their embassy. Rome was also the seat of the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), where Vic represented the Philippines in discussions that linked diplomacy to development. Through persistent engagement, the Philippines secured loans and technical assistance for agricultural programs, translating multilateral dialogue into concrete benefits for farmers back home. It was diplomacy measured not in communiqués, but in livelihoods His exposure to European integration deepened his understanding of sovereignty in a regional context. The European Union, he observed, balanced shared regulations with enduring national identities — a tension that resonated with his own country’s efforts to assert independence while participating in regional and global institutions. Kobe, Earthquakes, and Resilience In Japan, as Consul-General in Kobe and Osaka, Vic encountered diplomacy under the shadow of natural disaster. The Great Hanshin Earthquake of 1995 devastated Kobe, leaving thousands dead and entire neighborhoods in ruins. The Philippine community was not spared, and the consulate became both a refuge and a coordination center. Crisis management, he discovered, demanded the same qualities as highlevel negotiation: calm under pressure, clarity of communication, and empathy. The experience reinforced his conviction that the essence of diplomacy lay not only in representing the state, but in protecting its citizens wherever they might be. Los Angeles and the Power of a Global Community If Kobe tested his crisis response, Los Angeles tested his capacity for largescale community mobilization. As Consul-General in the early 1990s, he oversaw one of the largest Filipino populations abroad, concentrated in Southern California and extending to parts of Texas, Arizona, and Nevada. The consulate’s workload was relentless, ranging from labor disputes to immigration concerns, from cultural promotion to emergency assistance. Then, in 1991, Mount Pinatubo erupted in the Philippines, unleashing one of the largest volcanic events of the 20th century. From Los Angeles, Vic spearheaded fundraising efforts among Filipino-American organizations, coordinating with the Philippine Red Cross and the Commission on Overseas Filipinos. The campaign raised approximately one million US dollars for the victims — a testament to the solidarity of a diaspora and the leadership that could harness it. For Vic, this episode illustrated a central truth: that the nation extended far beyond its geographic borders. The Filipino community abroad was not merely a constituency to be served, but a strategic and moral asset, capable of mobilizing resources and advocacy in times of need. Vienna: At the Crossroads of Global Governance Professionally and personally, Vienna would become the most fulfilling chapter of his diplomatic life. Appointed Ambassador to Austria and concurrently Permanent Representative to the United Nations Office in Vienna, he found himself at the nexus of some of the world’s most critical institutions: the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), the United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO), and the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organization (CTBTO). In this setting, his legal acumen and multilateral experience converged. He played an active role in negotiations that led to the adoption of the UN Convention against Transnational Organized Crime and the UN Convention against Corruption — landmark instruments aimed at combating human trafficking, terrorism, cybercrime, and systemic graft. These treaties reflected a growing global consensus that security in the modern world depended as much on the rule of law as on military strength. At the IAEA, he engaged in discussions on the peaceful uses of nuclear energy, advocating for technical assistance to developing countries. It was a delicate balance: promoting access to nuclear technology for medicine, agriculture, and power generation, while supporting strict safeguards to prevent proliferation. The role required both scientific literacy and political sensitivity — qualities he had cultivated through years of interdisciplinary study and practice. Vienna was also where his family’s own diplomatic legacy took a generational turn. His son, Hendrik, pursued advanced studies in international affairs at the Vienna Diplomatic Academy and later joined the Philippine Foreign Service, eventually rising to become Chief of Mission and a future Ambassador and Deputy Permanent Representative to the UN in New York. . His daughter, Roxanne, built a career at the IAEA, overseeing technical assistance programs for developing countries. For Vic, there was quiet pride in seeing the values of service and international engagement take root in the next generation. The Diplomat as Treaty-Maker Across these varied assignments — Rome, Kobe, Los Angeles, Vienna — Vic’s role evolved from representative to architect, from advocate to negotiator of global norms. Whether crafting provisions on maritime sovereignty, mobilizing aid for disaster victims, or shaping conventions against crime and corruption, he demonstrated a consistent philosophy: that diplomacy must be anchored in law, animated by compassion, and guided by a clear sense of national interest. He believed that firmness and courtesy were not opposites but complements. One could defend a country’s position with resolve while remaining open to dialogue and compromise. This approach, honed in committee rooms and crisis centers alike, would later prove invaluable when he took on one of the most challenging postings of his career — representing the Philippines in the heart of a resurgent great power. That next chapter would take him to Moscow, into the strategic calculations of a nation described by Winston Churchill as “a riddle wrapped in a mystery inside an enigma,” and into a world where history, power, and national interest intersected with renewed intensity. Moscow, Malacañang, and the Meaning of a Life in Diplomacy On a cold winter morning in 2008, Vic arrived in Moscow to assume one of the most demanding posts of his career: Ambassador of the Philippines to the Russian Federation, with concurrent accreditation to Armenia, Belarus, and Ukraine. The city was wrapped in snow and history, its grand avenues and onion-domed cathedrals bearing the weight of empire, revolution, and renewed great-power ambition. In his mind echoed the words of Winston Churchill, who had once described Russia as “a riddle, wrapped in a mystery, inside an enigma,” adding that the key to understanding it lay in its national interest. Vic would soon find that this insight was as relevant in the twenty-first century as it had been in the twentieth. Russia, a permanent member of the UN Security Council and heir to the strategic legacy of the Soviet Union, was asserting its place in a changing global order. It viewed its near abroad, particularly Ukraine, as part of its historical and security sphere. While the Philippines, anchored in international law and a treaty alliance with the United States, would later vote against Russia’s actions in Ukraine, Vic’s tenure was marked by professionalism and mutual respect. There were no outstanding bilateral disputes, and he was received with the full courtesies due an ambassador, including audiences at official functions with President Vladimir Putin and exchanges with Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov and senior Kremlin advisers. Beyond geopolitics, he encountered a Russia of immense cultural depth: the music of Tchaikovsky, the ballets of the Bolshoi, the literary heritage of Tolstoy and Dostoevsky. Even language became a bridge. Though Russian was notoriously difficult, he and his wife, Connie, took the effort to learn enough to navigate daily life, discovering along the way that Tagalog was being taught at Moscow State University by Russian scholars who had studied in the Philippines. It was a reminder that cultural diplomacy often runs quietly beneath the currents of power politics. From Moscow, Vic reflected on the evolving landscape of international relations. The Cold War certainties of his early career had given way to a multipolar world in which the Philippines sought a calibrated balance — friend to all, foe to none — while steadfastly defending its sovereignty and rights under international law. It was the same philosophy that underpinned the country’s reliance on UNCLOS and the 2016 Arbitral Award in the West Philippine Sea, a legal framework he himself had helped craft decades earlier. The Art of Protocol and the Theater of the State If Moscow represented the geopolitics of power, his earlier service as Chief of Protocol of the Department of Foreign Affairs had immersed him in the theater of state. In Malacañang Palace, where the rituals of the republic unfold, Vic was responsible for ensuring that the courtesies of diplomacy were observed with precision and respect. From arranging state visits to organizing the President’s vin d’honneur for the diplomatic corps, he learned that symbolism, when properly understood, could convey messages of amity, equality, and national dignity more eloquently than words. The role demanded an encyclopedic knowledge of ambassadors, precedence, and protocol, and a temperament that combined firmness with tact. A single misstep could cause embarrassment; a well-executed ceremony could strengthen relationships. For Vic, protocol was not mere formality. It was a language of respect, a way of acknowledging the sovereignty and culture of others while affirming one’s own. In negotiations, he carried the same balance. Courtesy opened doors; firmness protected interests. He believed in first understanding the other side’s perspective, then seeking a middle ground without surrendering principle. It was a method he had refined from the Security Council to treaty committees, from consular crises to bilateral talks. Family: The Quiet Pillar of a Public Life Behind the public roles stood a family that bore the weight of constant relocation and adjustment. His wife, Connie, was, in his words, “the perfect ambassador’s wife,” an indispensable partner who managed residences, hosted counterparts, and created an atmosphere of warmth that complemented official engagements. In diplomacy, social functions are not peripheral; they are extensions of policy, spaces where trust is built over conversation and shared meals. Connie’s grace and organizational skill made their homes abroad true extensions of the Philippine mission. Their children, Hendrik and Roxanne, grew up across cultures, experiencing both the privilege and the disruption that come with a diplomat’s life. They learned early that friendships might be temporary and that schools would change, sometimes abruptly. Yet these very disruptions nurtured resilience and a global outlook. In Vienna, the family’s story came full circle. Hendrik earned a master’s degree at the Vienna Diplomatic Academy and later joined the Philippine Foreign Service, eventually rising to become Chief of Mission II and on the cusp of appointment as Ambassador and Deputy Permanent Representative to the United Nations in New York. He would also obtain a second master’s degree from Harvard’s Kennedy School of Government, continuing the tradition of intellectual rigor and public service. Roxanne, for her part, joined the International Atomic Energy Agency, overseeing technical assistance programs that brought peaceful nuclear applications to developing countries. For their father, these paths were a source of deep pride — not as personal achievements, but as evidence that the values of service and global engagement had taken root in the next generation. Faith, Purpose, and Service Beyond Retirement Throughout his career, Vic drew strength from faith and a sense of purpose. He believed that ethical leadership meant leading by example, telling the truth, treating colleagues with respect, and inspiring them to reach their full potential. These principles sustained him through crises, difficult negotiations, and the inevitable disappointments that accompany public life. After retiring from active diplomatic service, he did not withdraw from engagement. He assisted in family enterprises and devoted time to the Lourdes Grotto Shrine Foundation in San Jose del Monte, Bulacan, which serves pilgrims and supports charitable activities. He also became involved in the Philippine Council for Foreign Relations, contributing to policy discussions and promoting international understanding. For him, retirement was not an end, but a transition from official duty to civic and spiritual service. Rotary: Fellowship and Service Above Self Parallel to his diplomatic life ran another thread of service: his membership in the Rotary Club of Manila. Inducted in 1997, with Past District Governor Vince Carlos as his sponsor, he found in Rotary a community that resonated with his own ideals of public service and ethical conduct. The club’s Four-Way Test — truth, fairness, goodwill, and benefit to all — mirrored the values he sought to uphold in diplomacy. Rotary provided a platform for fellowship that transcended borders. Wherever he was posted, his membership opened doors to clubs abroad, reinforcing the idea that service and goodwill form a universal language. He took particular pride in the heritage of the Rotary Club of Manila as the oldest and largest in Asia, and in its role in fostering people-to-people connections, including through the recognition of foreign ambassadors who had contributed to Philippine relations. A Life Framed by Law, Service, and History As Vic looked back on a career spanning four decades, he found it difficult to single out one defining moment. The signing of UNCLOS in Montego Bay stood out, as did the negotiation of conventions against transnational crime and corruption, the management of crises from earthquakes to volcanic eruptions, and the representation of the Philippines in capitals and international organizations across the globe. Each assignment, he believed, had demanded its own form of courage and creativity. He often reflected on the figures who had inspired him: his father, Ambassador Enrique Garcia, who rose from the province of Aklan to become a pioneer of Philippine diplomacy; national heroes such as José Rizal and Apolinario Mabini; statesmen like Manuel Quezon; and global leaders from Abraham Lincoln to Winston Churchill. From them, and from his own mentors in the Department of Foreign Affairs, he drew lessons on leadership, sacrifice, and the enduring power of ideas. If he were to title his memoir, he said, it would be “Why Be an Ambassador?” The answer, implicit in the story of his life, lay in the opportunity to serve something larger than oneself — to give voice to a nation, to protect its people, and to contribute, however modestly, to the architecture of peace and order. To young Filipinos considering the Foreign Service, his counsel was both inspiring and candid. Diplomacy, he would say, offers the privilege of representing the country, of exploring cultures, and of participating in the making of history. But it is not a path to wealth or glamour. It is a vocation of sacrifice, sustained by patriotism and a commitment to the common good. In the end, Vic measured success not by rank or decoration, but by fidelity to purpose. He had sought to uphold the interests of the Philippines, to defend its citizens in distress, to strengthen the rule of law, and to build bridges of understanding in a world often divided by fear and ambition. From the boy who once listened to tales of coronations to the statesman who helped shape the law of the seas and the conventions of global justice, his journey embodied the quiet heroism of public service. It was a life lived, in the fullest sense, in the service of the Republic. Epilogue: Why Be an Ambassador? In the autumn of his life, when official titles had been set aside and the diplomatic passport had finally been returned, Vic often reflected on a question he once posed to himself and later to generations of young Filipinos: “Why be an ambassador?” The answer, he knew, could never be reduced to rank, ceremony, or privilege. It lay instead in the long arc of service that began with a boy listening to stories of Westminster Abbey and ended with a statesman who had helped write the law of the seas, defend migrant workers, negotiate global treaties, and represent the Philippines in the councils of great powers. To be an ambassador, in his understanding, was to become the living bridge between history and hope. He had stood in the negotiating halls of Montego Bay as the Philippines secured its maritime soul. He had spoken in Vienna for the peaceful uses of nuclear science and for the global war against crime and corruption. He had walked the snow-covered streets of Moscow while balancing principle and pragmatism amid great-power rivalry. He had comforted distressed Filipinos after earthquakes and volcanic eruptions, mobilized diaspora compassion across oceans, and safeguarded dignity through the quiet precision of protocol. Yet perhaps his most enduring legacy was not written in treaties or communiqués, but in people. In his son, Hendrik, now himself a rising diplomat of the Republic. In his daughter, Roxanne, advancing development through international institutions. In the countless young foreign service officers he examined, mentored, and inspired. In Rotarians who saw in him the living embodiment of Service Above Self. And in a nation whose maritime rights and diplomatic stature rest in part on foundations he helped lay. He had lived through eras — the Cold War, the birth of multilateral law, the reemergence of great-power rivalry — and in each, he chose the same compass: national interest anchored in international law, pursued with courtesy, courage, and conscience. For him, diplomacy was never transactional. It was moral. It was the disciplined pursuit of peace. It was the art of defending one’s country without losing one’s humanity. It was, at its core, an expression of love for country. And so, when asked how he wished to be remembered, he did not speak of honors or decorations, though they came. He spoke instead of having lived a purposeful life — as a lawyer, as a husband, as a father, as a Rotarian, and above all, as a servant of the Republic. A life that proved that a boy from Manila, raised in chancelleries and classrooms, guided by faith and family, could one day help shape the law of oceans, the fight against global crime, and the dignity of a nation among nations. A life that answered, in full: “Why be an ambassador?” Because in a world of conflict and uncertainty, someone must carry the flag not in battle,
but in dialogue;
not in conquest,
but in conscience;
not in silence,
but in the steady, principled voice of a people. In The News  RCM Past President/Former Supreme Court Chief Justice Artemio Panganiban’s Col

articles.title: A Convergence of Values, Vision, and Global Responsibility: The Rotary Club of Manila’s 19 Weekly Membership Meeting

body.text: At precisely 12:30 p.m. on January 29, 2026, the gavel fell and the 19th Weekly Membership Meeting of the Rotary Club of Manila for Rotary Year 2025–2026 was formally called to order by President Raoul C. Creencia, setting the tone for an afternoon marked by diplomacy, fellowship, reflection, and global perspective. The historic Manila Polo Club, long a witness to pivotal conversations in Philippine civic life, once again became a venue where local leadership met international thought.
What unfolded was not merely a luncheon meeting, but a carefully choreographed gathering that reflected Rotary’s enduring role as a bridge — between nations, cultures, and ideas.
Opening Rites: Ceremony Anchored in Meaning

The meeting opened with an invocation led by former Ambassador and Rotarian Victor G. “Vic” Garcia III, grounding the assembly in gratitude and purpose. In a gesture both symbolic and resonant with the day’s international theme, the National Anthem of Germany was rendered, followed by the Philippine National Anthem, affirming mutual respect between host and guest nations.

The Rotary Club of Manila Hymn, sung by the RCM World Famous Music Chorale, reaffirmed the Club’s shared identity, while the solemn recitation of The Four-Way Test, led by Past Director Issam Eldebs, reminded members that ethical clarity remains Rotary’s moral compass in an increasingly complex world.
Fellowship and Recognition: The Human Core of Rotary

Past Sergeant-at-Arms Güenter Gerhard G. “Günter” Matschuck, serving as Moderator, formally acknowledged the distinguished guests present — diplomatic, civic, and Rotarian — before the hall was filled with music once more as the Chorale led the Welcome Song, an audible expression of Rotary’s culture of warmth and inclusivity.

The celebration of January birthday celebrants followed, honoring Rotarians Butch Campos, Past Director Abe Pascual, Toti Cortez, and Danny Go. The familiar strains of Maligayang Bati / Happy Birthday Birthday reminded everyone present that Rotary, even at its most formal, remains a fellowship rooted in personal connection.
President’s Time: Leadership in Continuity

In his President’s Time, Raoul C. Creencia addressed the membership with the steady cadence of a leader mindful of both tradition and trajectory. His remarks reinforced the Club’s commitment to relevance — locally grounded yet globally aware — and prepared the audience for a discourse that would stretch far beyond Manila, into Europe, the Indo-Pacific, and the shifting architecture of international relations.
Introducing the Guest-of-Honor

Moderator PSAA Güenter Matschuck then delivered a thoughtful, warm, and unmistakably personal introduction of the Guest of Honor and Speaker — an introduction so comprehensive it unfolded over a good twenty minutes — before finally presenting His Excellency Andreas Michael Pfaffernoschke, Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of the Federal Republic of Germany to the Philippines.

The introduction was both professional and affectionate, reflecting a relationship built not merely on protocol but on shared values, mutual respect, and longstanding engagement between German and Filipino communities.
A World in Flux, Anchored by Shared Principles

Ambassador Pfaffernoschke began not with geopolitics, but with gratitude — thanking the Rotary Club of Manila for the invitation, acknowledging President Creencia, Ambassador Garcia, PD Issam Eldebs, and extending special recognition to Günter Matschuck, whom he credited for personally encouraging his appearance before the Club.

Speaking with warmth and candor, the Ambassador struck a tone that was at once conversational and consequential. He reflected briefly on his tenure in the Philippines with his wife Marina, sharing their travels across the archipelago — from Iloilo’s Dinagyang Festival to more than twenty islands visited so far — emphasizing that to truly understand the Philippines, one must go beyond Manila and encounter its people where they live and celebrate.

The Ambassador anchored his address in history by quoting Dr. José Rizal, recalling the national hero’s admiration for German discipline, science, and culture during his stay in Germany in the late 19th century. Rizal’s completion of Noli Me Tangere in Berlin and the novel’s first publication there were cited as enduring symbols of the deep intellectual and cultural ties between the two nations — a relationship formally established diplomatically in 1954, and now matured into what the Ambassador described as a strategic, high-stakes partnership.

The heart of Ambassador Pfaffernoschke’s address lay in a sober assessment of the global geopolitical environment, highlighting a world where long-held assumptions are eroding, international law is increasingly challenged by power politics, and the use of force to alter borders has re-entered global discourse — once unthinkable to a generation shaped by post-war Europe.

Drawing parallels between Europe and Asia, he underscored how security in Ukraine and stability in the Indo-Pacific are inextricably linked, asserting that Germany and the Philippines share a moral obligation to defend the rules-based international order, whether in Eastern Europe or the West Philippine Sea.

In unequivocal terms, Ambassador Pfaffernoschke reaffirmed Germany’s support for the Philippines in upholding UNCLOS and the 2016 Arbitral Award, stressing that freedom of navigation and respect for sovereignty are not abstract ideals but economic necessities for a trading nation like Germany, whose livelihoods depend on secure sea lanes in Southeast Asia.

He also expressed strong support for the Philippines’ 2026 ASEAN Chairmanship, highlighting it as an opportunity for Filipino leadership to guide the region under the theme “Navigating Our Future Together,” and noting the symbolic importance of the upcoming 50th anniversary of the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation.

On economic relations, the Ambassador spoke with notable frankness. Germany remains the Philippines’ largest trading partner within the EU, with trade volumes approaching €7 billion, and a substantial surplus favoring the Philippines. Yet he emphasized that trust, predictability, and ease of doing business are indispensable currencies.

While acknowledging reforms already undertaken by the Philippine government, he candidly cited persistent challenges — bureaucracy, corruption, and regulatory unpredictability—illustrating these concerns with concrete examples familiar to the business community, including issues affecting major German investors.

The Ambassador outlined expanding defense cooperation, referencing high-level visits, joint training, cybersecurity collaboration, and Germany’s growing presence in the Indo-Pacific. He also highlighted Germany’s €35-million climate resilience investment in the Philippines, implemented through GIZ, as evidence of long-term commitment.

Equally compelling was his emphasis on people-to-people relations: tens of thousands of Filipinos living and working in Germany, ongoing efforts to facilitate skilled labor mobility, and cultural exchanges such as the Philippines’ role as Guest of Honor at the 2025 Frankfurt Book Fair.

The Ambassador concluded on a deeply personal note, praising Filipino hospitality and the enduring spirit of Bayanihan, which he described not as a slogan but a lived value that makes partnership possible even joyful. His closing words expressed optimism, gratitude, and a sincere affection for the Philippines, punctuated by a heartfelt “Maraming maraming salamat po.”
Dialogue, Appreciation, and Closure
An Open Forum followed, allowing members to engage the Ambassador directly — an exchange emblematic of Rotary’s tradition of thoughtful, respectful dialogue.
President Creencia then presented the Certificate of Appreciation, formally thanking Ambassador Pfaffernoschke for an address that was at once intellectually rigorous and profoundly relevant.

At 2:00 p.m., President Creencia adjourned the meeting, closing a gathering that reaffirmed the Rotary Club of Manila’s role as a convener of ideas that matter — not only to Rotarians, but to the nation and the wider world.

In an era of uncertainty, the 19th Weekly Membership Meeting stood as a reminder that principled dialogue, anchored in shared values, remains one of Rotary’s greatest contributions to a world in flux.
