Bridging Islands, Building Futures: The 22nd Weekly Membership Meeting of the Rotary Club of Manila  The chandeliers of the Manila Polo Club shimmered softly as Rotarians, partners, and distinguished guests gathered for the 22nd Weekly Membership Meeting of the Rotary Club of Manila. There was an anticipatory hum in the air — not merely for fellowship, which the Club does so well — but for substance. The afternoon promised both. At exactly 12:30 PM, Director Edwin Hernandez gaveled the meeting to order, drawing the room into a shared moment of purpose. Club Secretary Antonilo DC. “Anton” Mauricio led the invocation, a solemn prayer that anchored the gathering in gratitude and service. The Philippine National Anthem followed, voices rising in unison, before the RCM World-Famous Music Chorale lent its harmonies to the Rotary Club of Manila Hymn and the Four-Way Test — words that have guided generations of Rotarians in their public and private dealings. Club Treasurer Paul Joseph M. “PJ” Garcia acknowledged the guests, ensuring that each visiting Rotarian and dignitary felt not merely welcomed, but embraced. Deputy Sergeant-at-Arms John Michael “John” Cutter, who moderated the program, shepherded the flow of the afternoon with calm precision. The Chorale’s welcome song warmed the hall, and the Club paused to honor its February celebrants: Rotarian Nico Hallare, Past Internal Auditor Jordan Pizarras, and Rotarian Dr. Jun Aventura, whose birthdays were marked with music and applause. It was a meeting suffused with fellowship—but also with gravity. For the Club was about to hear from one of the most consequential development institutions headquartered in its own city. The President’s Time Director Edwin Hernandez, presiding in the President’s stead as President Raoul Creencia was en route to Baguio to represent RCM at the Rotary Club of Baguio's 88th Anniversary, took the podium during President’s Time. He reflected on Rotary’s enduring relevance in a world of accelerating change, reminding members that leadership today requires both imagination and institutional partnership. Development, he noted, is not a spectator sport. It is a shared responsibility — one that demands collaboration between civil society, government, and multilateral institutions. That sentiment proved an apt prelude to the main address. Introducing the Voice of Development Past Vice-President Joel C. Valdes introduced the Guest of Honor and Speaker, Mr. Andrew Jeffries, Country Director for the Philippines of the Asian Development Bank. The title of his address — “Asian Development Bank: Overview – Key Priorities and Initiatives” — belied the sweep and immediacy of the issues he would cover. A Bank Founded in Manila, Shaping a Region Mr. Jeffries began with perspective. The Asian Development Bank (ADB), founded in 1966, now counts 69 member countries, 50 of them within the Asia-Pacific region, and 41 borrowing members. Headquartered in Manila, ADB has grown into one of the world’s preeminent multilateral development institutions. He described its core business in three succinct words: Finance. Knowledge. Partnerships. • Finance, through sovereign and non-sovereign lending. • Knowledge, drawn from crosscountry experience and practical lessons. • Partnerships, which mobilize additional capital and expertise far beyond ADB’s own balance sheet. In 2024 alone, ADB committed $24.3 billion in loans, grants, and investments, and mobilized an additional $14.9 billion in cofinancing. These are not abstract figures; they are arteries of development, carrying opportunity into economies that need long-term, patient capital. The Philippines, as a founding member and host country, occupies a special place. It holds 2.377% of ADB’s shares and remains one of its largest clients. In fact, the country is ADB’s second-largest portfolio in the Asia-Pacific region — second only to India — with an active portfolio of $12.5 billion as of December 2025. Mr. Jeffries structured his remarks around ADB’s partnership strategy with the Philippines—aligned with the Philippine Development Plan and anchored on three pillars: • Intensifying Social and Human Capital Development • Boosting Economic Competitiveness and Quality Infrastructure • Nature-Based Development and Disaster Resilience Pillar I: Investing in Human Capital Here, ADB supports the Pantawid Pamilyang Pilipino Program (4Ps), the Walang Gutom (Zero Hunger) initiative, universal health care, and JobStart Philippines. Mr. Jeffries underscored that poverty reduction and productivity enhancement are inseparable. Social protection is not charity — it is economic strategy. When vulnerable households receive electronic food vouchers or access to healthcare, they do not merely survive; they stabilize communities and sustain domestic demand. Pillar II: Transformative Infrastructure The second pillar drew audible interest from the room. ADB is financing portions of the North–South Commuter Railway, the largest ADB project in the AsiaPacific region at $7 billion. The project will link Clark to Calamba, reshaping mobility across Luzon. He also highlighted the Davao Public Transport Modernization, the first citywide modernization program of its kind in the Philippines, and the ambitious Bataan–Cavite Interlink Bridge, envisioned as one of the world’s longest bridges of its type. Infrastructure, he reminded the audience, is not merely concrete and steel. It is connectivity—economic, geographic, and social. In an archipelagic nation, it determines whether farmers reach markets, whether labor reaches opportunity, and whether regions prosper together. Pillar III: Climate and Disaster Resilience The Philippines, battered by over 20 typhoons annually, stands at the frontlines of climate risk. ADB’s programs include flood resilience and adaptation projects, climate change action programs, marine ecosystem initiatives, and renewable energy ventures such as rooftop solar and electric mobility ecosystems. Under Strategy 2030, ADB aims for climate finance to reach half of its total committed financing by 2030, with cumulative climate financing exceeding $100 billion. The message was unmistakable: climate action is no longer peripheral — it is central to development. ASEAN 2026: The Philippines at the Helm With the Philippines chairing ASEAN in 2026, Mr. Jeffries detailed ADB’s integrated support package to help deliver key policy outcomes and flagship events across finance, green economy, energy connectivity, tourism, social protection, digital transformation, and cross-cutting regional resilience. Regional cooperation, he emphasized, is embedded in ADB’s charter. It is not optional. It is foundational. The Economic Outlook: Fundamentals and Fragility Turning to the macroeconomic outlook, Mr. Jeffries spoke candidlyabout the Philippines’ recent growth performance and expectations of a rebound. Domestic consumption — about 70% of GDP — remains a stabilizing force, bolstered by remittances. Yet infrastructure investment momentum and global trade fragmentation remain variables to watch. The fundamentals, he assured the audience, are sound: affirmed credit ratings, a liquid banking sector, easing inflation, and policy space for interest rate adjustments. But growth, he cautioned, is not automatic. It requires execution — particularly in infrastructure and MSME support. On that note, he offered a compelling example: an upcoming supply-chain finance facility designed to channel affordable working capital to micro, small, and medium enterprises by sharing credit risk with local banks. In a country where MSMEs comprise 99% of enterprises yet receive less than 10% of formal financing, such mechanisms could be transformative. A Dialogue of Institutions The Open Forum that followed was animated. Rotarians posed questions on infrastructure decongestion, the future of NAIA modernization, the role of private capital, and the geopolitical implications of regional fragmentation. Mr. Jeffries responded with clarity and candor, weaving data with institutional insight. Mr. Jeffries engaged in a Q&A session with PP Archit Bartolome, Treas. PJ Garcia, Sec. Anton Mauricio, PDG Alex Cureg, and PDG Obet Pagdanganan. At the conclusion, Director Edwin Hernandez presented Mr. Jeffries with a Certificate of Appreciation — a symbol not merely of gratitude, but of alignment. Rotary’s commitment to “Service Above Self” found resonance in ADB’s mandate to foster inclusive, resilient growth. At 2:00 PM, Director Hernandez adjourned the meeting. The Larger Meaning The 22nd Weekly Membership Meeting was not simply another date on the Club calendar. It was a reminder that the Rotary Club of Manila, founded in 1919, continues to convene voices that shape the destiny of nations. In welcoming the Country Director of the Asian Development Bank, the Club affirmed its place at the intersection of civic leadership and economic transformation. Bridges were discussed — literal and metaphorical. Railways, bridges, and flood barriers. But also bridges between institutions, between public and private sectors, between local needs and regional vision. In a hall filled with Rotarians — men and women committed to ethical leadership—the message was clear: development is collective work. And in Manila, where ADB was born and Rotary took root over a century ago, the partnership between service and strategy continues to build futures worthy of the next generation. Meeting Fellowship Editorial  Reginald T. Yu Editor-in-Chief On Thursday, February 26, 2026, at 11:00 a.m., beneath open skies and across the sweeping fairways of The Manila Southwoods Golf and Country Club, the Rotary Club of Manila gathers for what may appear to be a day of sport — but is, in truth, something far deeper. This is not merely a golf event. 
This is One Fellowship. In a club as storied and historic as the Rotary Club of Manila — the first Rotary club in Asia and the largest in the Philippines — fellowship is not an accessory to service. It is its foundation. Before we deliberate on policy, before we chart ambitious projects, before we raise millions in funds and steward institutions older than most organizations in this nation, we must first remain connected as men and women bound by trust. And trust is not built in boardrooms alone. It is built walking side by side down a fairway. 
It is built in friendly banter before a tee shot. 
It is built in shared silence while reading the green. 
It is built in laughter over a missed putt and quiet respect after a well-struck drive. Golf, in many ways, mirrors leadership. It is a game of integrity — you call your own penalties. It is a game of patience — you cannot rush the rhythm. It is a game of focus — distractions cost you strokes. It is a game of humility — even the best players are reminded that perfection is elusive. Rotary leadership demands the same virtues. As we approach a new Rotary year — one that calls for greater unity, greater collaboration, and greater resolve — this gathering becomes more than recreation. It becomes strategic alignment. A reminder that the culture we build today will determine the impact we leave tomorrow. The theme says it clearly: One Fellowship. Not “my” fellowship. 
Not “your” circle. 
Not “kanya-kanya.” But one. In a club with members of diverse generations, industries, and tenures — from seasoned statesmen to young idealists — cohesion does not happen automatically. It must be nurtured intentionally. Events like this are how culture is strengthened. They allow newer members to feel seen, and long-standing members to feel valued. They soften hierarchies. They dissolve assumptions. They remind us that beyond titles and committees, we are simply Rotarians who share a calling to serve. And then, as the sun lowers and the day transitions from the course to the clubhouse, fellowship continues — cocktails the Rotary way. It is in these unguarded moments that ideas surface organically. A youth project may be conceived between sips. A partnership may begin in a casual exchange. A mentorship relationship may quietly form at the bar. Many of Rotary’s most enduring initiatives did not begin with a formal motion. They began with conversation. We often speak about moving Rotary International forward. About strengthening institutions. About preserving legacy. But none of that is sustainable if we neglect the very fabric that holds us together — camaraderie. This February 26, let every swing carry intention. Let every handshake carry warmth. Let every conversation carry respect. Because when fellowship is genuine, service becomes natural. 
When unity is real, leadership becomes powerful. 
When trust is strong, a 107- year-old institution does not merely survive — it thrives. The scorecard will record birdies and bogeys. But the true measure of the day will not be strokes taken. It will be bonds strengthened. 
It will be unity reinforced. 
It will be One Fellowship — lived, not just declared. And in Rotary, that is always the ultimate victory. President’s Message  RC Baguio’s 88th Anniversary Last Thursday, February 19, I had the distinct honor of serving as Guest of Honor and Speaker at the 88th Anniversary Gala Night of our daughter club, the Rotary Club of Baguio. Accompanied by IPP Jujut Enriquez and PE Reggie Yu, we journeyed to the City of Pines to celebrate this remarkable milestone. In my remarks, I could not resist a bit of lighthearted humor. I observed that at 88 years, RC Baguio has already outlived the traditional anniversary gemstone list—which, as we know, ceremoniously concludes at 75 years with the diamond. Beyond that, there appears to be no official guidance. It is almost as if the list gently tells those fortunate enough to surpass 75: “Good luck—kayo na ang bahala.” But perhaps that is precisely the point. To go beyond the diamond is to transcend convention. It is to move past prescribed milestones and into a legacy defined not by gemstones, but by grit, grace, and generations of service. And in that respect, RC Baguio shines in a category entirely its own. 75 has diamond as its gemstone. And perhaps this is fitting. A diamond is treasured not only for its brilliance, but for the structure that gives rise to that brilliance. Each carbon atom is closely connected to the next. Carbon atoms are beautifully bound together, forming a lattice that can withstand tremendous pressure. Its strength, therefore, does not come from its size — it comes from its connections. And that is what 88 years truly represent. 
Not merely age. 
Not merely tradition. 
But bonds — tempered by trial, strengthened by service, and unbroken by time itself. In my speech, I underscored that not having a gemstone actually makes 88 years extraordinary; because when the world runs out of gemstones to describe RC Baguio, it means that the Club itself has become THE gemstone. As such, its worth is now beyond measure, beyond category, beyond comparison. At 88 years, RCB is no longer defined by the brilliance of a stone… but by the brilliance of its service. Besides, I said, the Rotary Club of Baguio has never needed a gemstone or any traditional symbol to define its worth. This is because from its earliest days, it already held something far more valuable: a legacy shaped by genuine service and anchored in a founding story that ties it directly to the roots of Rotary in the Philippines. And this is where the Rotary Club of Manila plays an important role – with its leaders planting the seeds of Rotary in Baguio. This is why, I said, we were celebrating more than history. We were celebrating character. We were celebrating consistency. We were celebrating a club that has remained relevant because it has remained principled. In Rotary, anniversaries are not just about age. If age alone defined us, then the Rotary Club of Manila — the oldest in Asia — would have been retired, given a plaque, and told to relax decades ago. But here we are: still moving and still serving. Perhaps the greatest beauty of the RCB milestone is this: Eighty-eight years may sound long — yet for Rotary, this is only the beginning. I ended my speech with this -- There are two questions every great anniversary dares to ask: “How far have we come?” and “How fiercely will we continue?” In regard to the second question, I expressed my belief that the Rotary Club of Baguio will not merely move forward — it will surge, unstoppable and unmistakable, leaving footprints of service wherever it passes. The anniversary celebration is not RC Baguio’s past shining; but its future roaring. The foregoing is the summary of my message to our daughter club. In retrospect, I had to make the difficult decision to miss our own weekly meeting in order to accept a speaking engagement—an invitation from our daughter club. It was not a choice made lightly. Yet I am deeply grateful that I did. That evening became more than a formal engagement; it was a moment of fellowship and affirmation. It also allowed me to share meaningful time with PE Reggie and IPP Jujut, strengthening not only our camaraderie but our shared sense of purpose. More importantly, it was an opportunity to make something visible and tangible: that the Rotary Club of Manila—the mother club their members look up to with such awe and respect -- stands not at a distance, but side by side with them. In their milestone celebration, our presence was a quiet but powerful message: that heritage is not merely remembered; it is lived, shared, and extended through fellowship and support. Sometimes leadership calls us to be present where our presence speaks louder than our schedule. And in that moment, standing with our daughter club – the Rotary Club of Baguio -- it truly did. CHOSEN EVERY DAY | Raoul Chicano Creencia and Mylene Tupas Marcia: A Life Built on Faith, Partnership, and Purpose  Editor’s Note: As we continue to celebrate Love Month this February, we turn our pages not toward fleeting romance, but toward something rarer and far more enduring — the quiet, deliberate love that is chosen every single day. In this special feature, we share the story of Raoul Creencia and Myls Marcia — two accomplished lawyers, respected leaders, and devoted parents whose partnership has withstood ambition, public responsibility, national controversy, and the evolving seasons of family life. Theirs is not a love story defined by spectacle, but by steadiness. Not by grand declarations, but by daily discipline. Not by perfection, but by perseverance. From college rivals who sharpened each other’s minds, to courtroom professionals who once stood on opposing sides of history, to parents now watching their daughter begin her own journey — Raoul and Myls remind us that lasting love is not stumbled upon. It is built. It is protected. It is practiced. In an age that often celebrates beginnings, their story honors endurance. May this feature inspire us all to reflect not only on how love begins — but on how it is sustained, deepened, and chosen again and again through the years. The Morning Before the Vows The house was quiet in a way it had not been for years. Myls woke before dawn, not from restlessness but from awareness. There are mornings that carry weight long before the sun rises, and this was one of them. She lay still for a moment, listening — to the soft hum of the airconditioning, to the faint stirring of the city beyond their windows, to the unfamiliar absence of hurried footsteps in the hallway. In the next room, a garment bag hung carefully from the closet door. Ivory silk. Hand-stitched lace. A dress chosen not by her, but by the young woman who had once needed help tying her shoes. Her daughter was getting married. The thought did not arrive with tears. It arrived with steadiness. This is what we prepared her for. Across the room, Raoul was already awake. He stood by the window with a cup of coffee in hand, watching the horizon shift from charcoal to muted gold. The skyline of Manila stretched before him — familiar towers, familiar roads, a city that had witnessed their careers, their cases, their public service. He had stood before tribunals without hesitation. He had navigated national controversies. He had led rooms filled with strong voices. Yet this morning required a different kind of composure. “She’s ready,” he said quietly, without turning. Myls rose and joined him. “I know.” They did not elaborate. They rarely needed to. They had spent decades refining the art of understanding without explanation. For a long moment, they simply stood there — side by side, as they had stood through law school examinations, through opposing arguments in the impeachment of a president, through sleepless nights with a newborn, through leadership roles that demanded more than comfort ever allowed. Their story had not been dramatic. It had been deliberate. Built on schedules carefully aligned. On disagreements resolved before sleep. On faith practiced more often than proclaimed. On the daily choice to remain — even when ambition pulled in different directions. Outside, light expanded slowly across the sky. Myls reached for his hand. He clasped it without looking. There was comfort in the familiarity of that gesture. They had once been young leaders competing for a student election. Once, he had approached her at a college gate with a folded sheet of paper and a question that was not really about the paper at all. Once, she had promised herself that love would wait. It had not waited. It had grown. And now it stood before them in the form of a daughter ready to begin her own life. “We did our part,” Myls said softly. Raoul nodded. “We continue to.” Not as central figures. Not as decisionmakers. But as foundation. Foundations do not demand attention. They hold. As the sun finally broke across the skyline, the house stirred — a door opening, quiet footsteps, the beginning of a day that would mark a new chapter. They released each other’s hands only when they had to. Not out of reluctance. 
But out of readiness. 
And together, they stepped forward into the morning. The Paper at the Gate The gates were still closed when Myls arrived. She wasn’t late. She simply liked being early — early enough to observe without being observed, early enough to settle her thoughts before the day began demanding them. A small cluster of students milled around the entrance, shifting backpacks, trading sleepy jokes, checking watches like time might obey impatience. Myls stood slightly apart, not aloof — just composed. The posture of someone used to keeping her own counsel. She had come from an all-girls school. Years of polished discipline. A world where confidence didn’t need to announce itself to be real. She was reading notes when a shadow fell across the page. “Can you read this?” She looked up. Raoul Creecia stood there with a folded sheet in his hand, his expression casual enough to seem effortless — except there was a glint in his eyes that said he had already rehearsed this moment and was pretending he hadn’t. It was, she would later realize, his particular kind of charm: competence dressed as spontaneity. Myls took the paper. “What is it?” “A write-up,” he said. “Just… tell me if it makes sense.” She scanned it — then read it properly. Not skimming. Not browsing. Reading the way she’d learned to read commitments even before she had the language for them: carefully, with respect for detail, with an instinct for what mattered. Raoul watched her eyes move. He liked the way she didn’t rush. He liked the seriousness behind her silence. When she finished, she handed it back. “You argue well,” she said, voice even. “But your conclusion jumps too quickly. You need to support it. You can’t expect people to follow you just because you’re sure.” It wasn’t flirtation. It was critique. Raoul blinked once, surprised — and then, against his will, smiled. Most people didn’t correct him that directly. He found he didn’t mind. 
He found he wanted more of it. That was how it began: not with romance, not with fireworks, but with a sentence that challenged him. A correction offered without cruelty. A girl who wasn’t impressed. And a boy who had never come in second suddenly realizing he could. The Girl Who Won the Election Raoul had been elected Class President since Grade Four. It had become a rhythm: the campaigning, the speeches, the inevitable result. His classmates trusted him the way people trust sunrise. Leadership wasn’t an effort. It was expectation. So, when the results of their freshman election were posted, he expected his name at the top without thinking. He stood in front of the bulletin board and read the list once. Then again. President: Myls Marcia 
Vice-President: Raoul Creecia He stared longer than necessary. Not anger. Not jealousy. Curiosity. Because the name was unfamiliar, but the victory wasn’t. To beat him, she had to be — what? Smarter? More disciplined? More liked? Or just… different? Later, in the classroom, he watched her without making it obvious. She wasn’t loud. She didn’t collect attention like trophies. She led by the quiet authority of competence. When she spoke, she didn’t fill the air — she placed words precisely, as if she respected language too much to waste it. She managed meetings the way some people managed storms: by staying calm in the center of them. Raoul thought, with a grudging admiration that quickly became something warmer: Who is this girl who just ended my winning streak? He didn’t yet know her history. He didn’t know about the bake shop, the supplier negotiations, the promise she’d made to her parents. He only knew that she had disrupted something he’d always assumed would remain unbroken. And, unexpectedly, he felt… grateful. Because winning all the time had never taught him how to grow. But she might. Flour on Her Hands, Fire in Her Mind If you asked Myls why she moved through the world the way she did — measured, deliberate, unshaken — she might not have given you a grand answer. She would have said something simple. Work had to be done. Responsibilities had to be met. Promises had to be kept. She grew up inside the warm, fragrant reality of her parents’ small bake shop in Quezon City. It wasn’t romantic. It was practical: early mornings, heavy sacks, customers who were kind and customers who weren’t, suppliers who needed payment, employees who needed salaries, and a family that learned to stretch a peso without letting it stretch their dignity. Her father sometimes took her with him to meet suppliers. When funds were tight, he would talk quietly, respectfully — and when the negotiations reached a point where politeness needed clarity, Myls would step in. “Give us until next week,” she’d say. “You know we settle. We always do.” She wasn’t pleading. She was promising. The adults would blink, then nod, because there was something about her — young as she was — that sounded like a person who meant what she said. That was where her certainty began: not in dreams, but in necessity. In high school, one day, a teacher explained Martial Law and the suspension of civil liberties. Myls listened, and something inside her shifted. Laws weren’t just rules. They were levers. They could protect people or crush them. They could uphold dignity or suspend it. She went home and told her parents she wanted to be a lawyer. Her mother smiled first. Her father went quiet, not from disapproval, but from the weight of what it meant. “You’ll be the first,” he said. Myls nodded like she understood fully. She didn’t, not yet. But she would. And when she entered college, she carried that dream like a private oath. She also carried another promise: she would not enter a relationship until she finished college. Education first. Discipline first. Love could wait. She didn’t know that love was already walking toward her at the department gates with a paper in his hand. Allies in Leadership By sophomore year, leadership no longer felt like a classroom exercise. It had weight. Raoul was elected Vice-President of the AB Student Council, a role that stretched beyond familiar faces and into the larger machinery of campus life. Meetings multiplied. Proposals required approval. Student concerns arrived unfiltered and urgent. It was the first time leadership felt less like recognition and more like responsibility. Myls served as Secretary of the AB Student Council. The title did not carry the same visibility, but it carried consequence. She recorded proceedings with precision. She clarified motions when debate blurred them. She organized resolutions so that momentum did not dissolve into noise. When discussions grew heated, she would lean forward slightly, pen poised, waiting for language to sharpen itself. If Raoul energized a room, Myls steadied it. 
He could speak with conviction and gather attention. 
She could listen with discipline and gather coherence. At first, their collaboration was practical. He would outline an initiative. She would ask, “How will we implement it?” He would propose a timeline. She would refine it into structure. 
He would rally enthusiasm. She would ensure sustainability. But slowly, something subtler began forming beneath the mechanics. Raoul noticed that Myls did not seek recognition. When meetings concluded successfully, she rarely claimed credit. She preferred that things simply work. He began consulting her before major discussions — not out of courtesy, but because her judgment sharpened his. “What am I missing?” he would ask. She would not answer immediately. She would think. And when she spoke, it was rarely to oppose him. It was to strengthen the idea. “Consider the second-year students,” she might say. “They’ll experience this differently.” Or, “If we phrase it that way, it sounds unilateral. Try framing it as collaboration.” She was not diminishing him. She was refining him. For someone accustomed to leading from the front, this was new. And valuable. Meanwhile, Myls observed something in Raoul she had not expected. He carried responsibility without theatricality. When criticism came — and it did — he absorbed it without deflection. He did not retreat from pressure. He leaned into it. She saw that leadership for him was not about applause. It was about forward motion. And slowly, respect deepened into trust. There were late afternoons when council meetings stretched past sunset. The campus would empty gradually, leaving corridors quiet and echoing. They would walk toward the gates together, still discussing unfinished matters. “You’re too cautious,” he would tease lightly. 
“And you’re too confident,” she would reply. But neither accusation was sharp. They were calibrations. By the time law school arrived, their instinct to lead had matured. In his junior year, Raoul was elected President of the Law Student Government. The atmosphere in law school was different — more intense, more exacting, less forgiving of error. Representation carried sharper edges. Faculty negotiations required tact. Student concerns were no longer theoretical — they affected futures. The role demanded composure under scrutiny. Myls stood firmly behind him. Not as an afterthought. 
Not as silent support. 
But as a partner in preparation. She reviewed drafts of his speeches late into the night. She adjusted phrasing to ensure clarity. She reminded him when passion needed tempering, when firmness needed gentleness. On election night, when results were announced and applause rose in the hall, Raoul’s instinctive glance was not toward the crowd. It was toward her. 
She did not beam. 
She nodded. That nod meant more than celebration. It meant, You’re ready. Raoul began to understand that strength did not diminish when supported — it expanded. Myls understood that supporting did not lessen her power — it expressed it. They were no longer simply classmates in positions. 
They were learning how to stand beside one another. 
And neither yet knew that this was rehearsal. For courtrooms. 
For public controversy. 
For marriage. 
For parenthood. 
For the decades ahead when leadership would no longer be about campus councils, but about navigating life side by side. What began as collaboration had become alignment. Not rivalry. 
Not dependency. 
But partnership. And partnership, once formed in youth through respect and shared responsibility, has a way of enduring. Law School: Standing Beside Law school did not tolerate vanity. It stripped away comfort and exposed capacity. By the time Raoul reached his junior year, he had already felt the tightening pressure that law school applied to every student. Recitations were surgical. Professors dismantled arguments without apology. Reputation could be built in a semester — and undone in a single unprepared moment. When nominations opened for President of the Law Student Government, Raoul did not rush forward. He understood the weight of the position. This was no longer undergraduate enthusiasm. The Law Student Government carried real responsibility — liaison with faculty, representation of student concerns, negotiation during academic disputes, organizing initiatives that shaped professional futures. Leadership here was less about visibility and more about composure. It required steadiness. 
It required credibility. 
And perhaps most of all, it required trust. When he finally agreed to run, it was not with bravado. It was with deliberation. Myls was among the first to know. “You’re considering it,” she said one evening as they reviewed case digests in the library. He nodded. “I won’t do it lightly.” She closed her book and studied him — not as a girlfriend, not merely as a friend — but as someone who understood what leadership cost. “You’re ready,” she said. 
It was not flattery. 
It was assessment. And for Raoul, her assessment mattered more than the opinions of a hundred classmates. Campaigning in law school was quieter than in college, but more exacting. There were no loud rallies, no banners hung across walkways. There were conversations in corridors, discussions after class, questions about priorities, expectations about integrity. Raoul answered thoughtfully. He did not promise sweeping reform. He spoke about representation, about clarity in communication between faculty and students, about fairness in procedure. Myls did not campaign theatrically. She did not hover or persuade on his behalf. Instead, she did something far more powerful. She listened. She absorbed the concerns of classmates who trusted her judgment. She clarified misunderstandings. When asked privately what she thought, she answered honestly: “He will take it seriously.” That was enough. Election results were announced in a classroom filled with tension disguised as indifference. When Raoul’s name was read as President of the Law Student Government, applause rose — respectful, measured. He acknowledged the room. But instinctively, his eyes searched for one face. Myls did not rush forward. 
She did not claim proximity. 
She simply met his gaze and nodded once. You earned this. The moment was not triumphant. It was grounding. The months that followed were demanding. As President, Raoul faced concerns that were often complicated and sometimes contentious. Faculty policies were questioned. Student grievances required careful navigation. Schedules conflicted. Expectations multiplied. There were evenings when fatigue showed in the way he loosened his tie and leaned back in his chair. “Too many voices,” he would say quietly. “Then prioritize,” Myls would reply. “Which ones carry consequence?” She reviewed drafts of his speeches — not to soften them, but to sharpen them. “You’re too forceful here,” she would point out. “If you want collaboration, don’t frame it as confrontation.” Or, “You’re underselling the issue. Say it clearly. They’ll respect clarity.” She never tried to control the direction. She refined the articulation. He began to notice something he had not fully understood before. Leadership, when shared in private, became steadier in public. There were nights when he questioned whether he had responded too firmly, or not firmly enough. She would listen first. “You acted in good faith,” she would say. “Stand by that.” Her confidence did not inflate him. It stabilized him. And in return, he saw the weight she carried in her own academic pursuits. Law school demanded excellence from her just as relentlessly. When she doubted herself — rare, but real — he did not offer hollow reassurance. "You’re prepared,” he would say. “You “don’t need to prove what you already are.” They were not rescuing each other. They were fortifying each other. What defined that season was not public success. It was alignment. Raoul learned that standing at the front of a room felt different when someone stood behind him not as an admirer, but as an equal. Myls learned that supporting did not diminish her own strength — it amplified shared purpose. They were no longer two ambitious students moving in parallel. They were beginning to move in concert. And though neither articulated it then, this was rehearsal. Rehearsal for seasons when one would need to lead publicly and the other would need to steady privately. Rehearsal for moments when disagreement would test maturity. Rehearsal for marriage. Because what they practiced in law school was not dominance. It was partnership. And partnership — once formed in youth through respect, humility, and shared responsibility — does not fade easily. It deepens. The Three Months It did not happen in one dramatic moment. There was no betrayal. No explosive argument. 
Just accumulation. Law school consumed them. 
Responsibilities multiplied. 
Expectations tightened. And somewhere between ambition and exhaustion, they stopped choosing each other as deliberately as before. Calls became shorter. Meetings became transactional. Affection became assumed rather than expressed. And one day, without formally declaring it, they stepped back. Three months. It was supposed to give them space. It gave them clarity. For Raoul, the days felt functional but incomplete. He threw himself into work. Into preparation. Into proving — to himself perhaps — that he did not need distraction. But distraction wasn’t what he had lost. He had lost conversation that mattered. He had lost the one person who challenged him without diminishing him. He had lost the steadiness of knowing someone understood the unspoken parts of him. For Myls, the silence was louder. She had been the one to suggest space. Practical. Rational. If they were to build serious careers, perhaps they needed to remove emotional complication. But in the quiet, she discovered something uncomfortable. Love was not a complication. It was an anchor. She missed his certainty. Missed the way he approached problems head-on. Missed the simple familiarity of studying beside someone who knew her strengths and her doubts. Three months is not long in calendar time. It is long in the heart. When they saw each other again — unexpectedly, at a gathering of mutual friends — there was no drama. Just recognition. “You look tired,” he said softly. “So do you,” she replied. Silence lingered, but it wasn’t hostile. It was heavy with what had been understood separately. “I don’t want distance,” he said finally. “Neither do I.” And in that moment, love stopped being a possibility. It became a decision. The Steakhouse By the time they completed law school and began carving their paths in separate law offices, the foundation between them had shifted from youth to intention. They were no longer experimenting with what might be. They were building what would endure. Eight years had passed since the morning at the gates. Eight years of growth, strain, reconciliation, shared ambition. Raoul chose a steakhouse in Quezon City — not flashy, not ostentatious. Just solid. Reliable. A place that mirrored what he hoped to offer. He had already spoken to her mother. 
He had already secured the ring. But when the moment arrived, his confidence felt different — less about winning, more about vulnerability. “We’ve grown,” he said, reaching across the table. “We’ve fought for this. I don’t want a life that doesn’t include you.” She studied him — not the boy who had never come in second, but the man who had learned that partnership was stronger than victory. Marriage, for Myls, was not romance. It was commitment. It was waking up every day and choosing again. She didn’t hesitate. “Yes.” No theatrics. 
No spectacle. 
Just certainty. Manila Cathedral The Manila Cathedral stood vast and solemn the day they married. Stone arches. Sunlight filtering through stained glass. The weight of history surrounding a promise that felt both ancient and entirely their own. Myls felt nervous as she walked down the aisle. Not because she doubted him. But because she understood the gravity of what they were entering. Raoul reached for her hand. Her breath steadied. In that clasp was everything they had already survived — law school, separation, ambition, expectation. They had saved for this wedding themselves. Planned it together. Built it without excess, but with intention. When they spoke their vows, they were not promising ease. They were promising presence. They did not know then that one day they would stand on opposite sides during the impeachment of a president and still return home united. They did not know the public responsibilities that awaited them. They only knew this: 
They had chosen. 
And they would continue choosing. When History Brushed Their Doorstep Some seasons do not ask permission before entering your life. They arrive in headlines. In public conversations. In tension that hums beneath ordinary days. The impeachment of President Estrada was one of those seasons. By then, Raoul and Myls were practicing lawyers, building their reputations steadily, focused on their respective professional paths. Neither sought the spotlight. Neither sought drama. Yet history has a way of brushing against even those who do not stand at its center. Raoul was among the convenors of a group of lawyers calling for accountability and the impeachment of the President. It was not about prominence; it was about principle. When the moment demanded clarity of position, he stood where his convictions led him. Like many others, he went to EDSA during EDSA Dos — not for spectacle, but because he believed participation was part of citizenship. Myls, meanwhile, was part of the Firm that handled the impeachment case. Her role was professional, structured within the responsibilities of her office. She did not seek personal recognition. She carried out her duties as a lawyer — precise, disciplined, faithful to her mandate. It was only gradually that they both recognized the quiet irony: They were on opposing sides of a national moment. Not adversaries. Not combatants. Simply aligned differently in a complex chapter of the country’s story. One evening at home, documents spread across the dining table, they paused. “So,” Myls said lightly, though her eyes were thoughtful, “we find ourselves across the aisle.” Raoul smiled. “It appears so.” There was no tension in the room. No raised voices. Only acknowledgment. They respected each other’s positions the way they always had — by examining reasoning, not attacking character. They debated in measured tones. They listened. They disagreed where necessary. But they never questioned each other’s integrity. History was loud outside. Inside, they were steady. That season did not test their loyalty to each other. It revealed it. Because they had long ago agreed on something deeper than alignment on every issue: They would attack ideas, not each other. 
They would stand firm in principle. And they would always return to the same side of the table at the end of the day. The Rules of Their Marriage Marriage, they learned early, was not sustained by grand gestures. It was sustained by systems. They had their rules. Some spoken. Some instinctive. Rule One: The wife is always right. 
Rule Two: If there is doubt, refer to Rule One. The joke endured because it carried truth — not about superiority, but about humility. When arguments arose — and they did — they refused escalation. They attacked the issue. 
Never the person. 
No kitchen-sinking. No resurrecting old grievances for leverage. If emotions ran high, they paused. Not to withdraw. To breathe. Raoul, more often than not, was the first to approach reconciliation. He understood that pride could win arguments but lose peace. Myls understood that silence, if prolonged, could build walls. So, they never slept without resolution. Sometimes the resolution was full agreement. Sometimes it was simply understanding. But it was always intentional. Because love, they both knew, does not erode from catastrophe. It erodes from neglect. And neglect was the one adversary they refused to allow. The Child Who Re-centered the World When Mikee was born, the world did not stop. It shifted. Success was no longer measured solely in courtroom victories or leadership roles. It was measured in presence. School programs attended. Bedtime stories read. Conversations not rushed. For Myls, motherhood unfolded like a quiet expansion. There was fierceness in it — protective, instinctive — but also tenderness that surprised even her. She had always been disciplined. Now she was deeply attuned. Ambition did not disappear. It rearranged itself. Career decisions were filtered through a new question: Will this cost presence? They protected family time the way they protected court deadlines. Dinner was sacred. 
Vacations were deliberate. Even in seasons of intense professional demand, one thing remained constant: 
If it mattered to Mikee, it mattered to them. What They Modeled Without Saying Children learn not from instruction alone, but from observation. Mikee grew up watching two lawyers who disagreed without cruelty. Two leaders who apologized when wrong. Two professionals who treated staff, colleagues, and strangers with equal respect. She saw faith not as ritual, but as practice — prayer before decisions, gratitude spoken aloud, service rendered quietly. She saw forgiveness enacted in real time. She saw humor rescue tension. She saw her parents choose each other daily. They did not lecture her on integrity. She saw it in the way contracts were honored. They did not define discipline. She saw it in the hours they prepared for hearings. They did not romanticize marriage. She saw it in the way arguments ended before sleep. And slowly, without spectacle, values settled into her bones. When Love Becomes Legacy As Mikee grew older, independence surfaced naturally. Her decision to live abroad did not fracture them. It revealed what they had built. There were moments of nostalgia — photographs held longer than necessary, stories retold with softer laughter. There was pride. And, beneath it, the quiet ache every parent understands. But more than fear, there was trust. Because they had not raised a daughter to cling. They had raised her to stand. And now, as she prepared for marriage, the cycle widened. They saw in her the patience they had practiced. The discernment they had modeled. The steadiness they had chosen. Love, they realized, was no longer only theirs. It had multiplied. The Moment They Knew There was no single announcement. No cinematic revelation. Just a gradual recognition. They saw it in the way Mikee spoke about her future — not impulsively, not romantically, but thoughtfully. She asked questions. She weighed decisions. She listened more than she spoke. She was no longer seeking permission. 
She was seeking perspective. One evening, after dinner, she lingered at the table longer than usual. “There’s something I want to talk to you about,” she said. Myls felt it before she heard it. 
Raoul remained still, steady as ever. When Mikee finished speaking — about commitment, about partnership, about building a life intentionally — there was no panic in the room. No protective tightening. Just silence filled with pride. After she left the table, Myls exhaled slowly. “She’s ready.” Raoul nodded. “She is.” It wasn’t confidence in the world. It was confidence in her. Joy and Ache When they imagined her building a life of her own, emotions did not arrive neatly. They arrived layered. Joy — bright and undeniable. Watching her step into adulthood with clarity felt like watching a sunrise they had prayed for. Pride — deep and steady. She had grown into a woman who could stand on her own reasoning. Nostalgia — softer, more dangerous. The memory of small hands in theirs. First steps. First day of school. And fear — not of her choice, but of the world that would test her. It is the paradox of parenthood. You raise a child to be strong enough to leave. And then you must be strong enough to let her. What They Told Her About Love They did not romanticize marriage when they spoke to her. They respected it too much for that. “Choose someone who respects your mind,” Myls told her. “Not just your heart.” “Choose someone whose values are not negotiable,” Raoul added. “Because when everything else shifts, values remain.” They spoke of partnership as active, not passive. Of commitment as daily. Of conflict as inevitable — but never destructive if approached with humility. “Attack the issue,” Raoul said with a faint smile, “not each other.” They spoke of forgiveness. Of apologizing first. Of not keeping score. They spoke of faith — not as obligation, but as foundation. Love, they told her, is not sustained by emotion alone. It is sustained by discipline. 
By respect. 
By the willingness to grow. Returning to the Morning The house stirred softly. A door opened. Footsteps crossed the hallway. The day had arrived. In the quiet before everything began — before guests, before photographs, before vows — Raoul and Myls stood together once more by the window. The city moved forward as it always had. So had they. Once, they had been young leaders competing for student office. Once, he had approached her with a folded paper. Once, she had promised herself love would wait. Instead, love had grown — through exams, through separation, through courtrooms and controversies, through sleepless nights and sacred routines. It had grown quietly. 
Deliberately. 
Chosen. Myls reached for his hand again. There were no tears now. Only fullness. “We did what we were meant to do,” she said. Raoul nodded. “And we continue.” Because love does not end when a child marries. It evolves. 
It widens. 
It steadies. Outside, the sky brightened completely. Inside, something gentler settled — not loss, but release. They had once stood at an altar in the Manila Cathedral promising to choose each other for life. They had kept that promise. Now they would watch their daughter make her own. Raoul turned to her. “Still choosing?” he asked quietly. Myls smiled. “Every day.” And together, they stepped away from the window and toward the sound of their daughter’s laughter — toward lace, toward vows, toward the next generation of love. Not at the center. 
But as foundation. And foundations, when built on faith, discipline, and deliberate devotion, do not crack with time. They endure. Epilogue: The Quiet Truth Years from now, when photographs fade slightly and memories soften at the edges, what will remain is not the grandeur of the wedding day. It will be the choices. The nights they resolved arguments before sleep. The mornings they prayed before decisions. The moments they stood on opposite sides of history and still came home united. The day they let go without breaking. Their love story was never about spectacle. It was about steadiness. It was about two disciplined hearts learning that victory is not winning alone — it is building together. And if their story teaches anything, it is this: Love endures not because it is easy. It endures because it is chosen. Again. And again. And again. Rotary Club of Baguio’s 88th Charter Anniversary  Before the event... articles.title: Bridging Islands, Building Futures: The 22nd Weekly Membership Meeting of the Rotary Club of Manila

body.text: The chandeliers of the Manila Polo Club shimmered softly as Rotarians, partners, and distinguished guests gathered for the 22nd Weekly Membership Meeting of the Rotary Club of Manila. There was an anticipatory hum in the air — not merely for fellowship, which the Club does so well — but for substance. The afternoon promised both.

At exactly 12:30 PM, Director Edwin Hernandez gaveled the meeting to order, drawing the room into a shared moment of purpose. Club Secretary Antonilo DC. “Anton” Mauricio led the invocation, a solemn prayer that anchored the gathering in gratitude and service. The Philippine National Anthem followed, voices rising in unison, before the RCM World-Famous Music Chorale lent its harmonies to the Rotary Club of Manila Hymn and the Four-Way Test — words that have guided generations of Rotarians in their public and private dealings. Club Treasurer Paul Joseph M. “PJ” Garcia acknowledged the guests, ensuring that each visiting Rotarian and dignitary felt not merely welcomed, but embraced. Deputy Sergeant-at-Arms John Michael “John” Cutter, who moderated the program, shepherded the flow of the afternoon with calm precision. The Chorale’s welcome song warmed the hall, and the Club paused to honor its February celebrants: Rotarian Nico Hallare, Past Internal Auditor Jordan Pizarras, and Rotarian Dr. Jun Aventura, whose birthdays were marked with music and applause.
It was a meeting suffused with fellowship—but also with gravity. For the Club was about to hear from one of the most consequential development institutions headquartered in its own city.
The President’s Time

Director Edwin Hernandez, presiding in the President’s stead as President Raoul Creencia was en route to Baguio to represent RCM at the Rotary Club of Baguio's 88th Anniversary, took the podium during President’s Time. He reflected on Rotary’s enduring relevance in a world of accelerating change, reminding members that leadership today requires both imagination and institutional partnership. Development, he noted, is not a spectator sport. It is a shared responsibility — one that demands collaboration between civil society, government, and multilateral institutions.
That sentiment proved an apt prelude to the main address.
Introducing the Voice of Development

Past Vice-President Joel C. Valdes introduced the Guest of Honor and Speaker, Mr. Andrew Jeffries, Country Director for the Philippines of the Asian Development Bank. The title of his address — “Asian Development Bank: Overview – Key Priorities and Initiatives” — belied the sweep and immediacy of the issues he would cover.
A Bank Founded in Manila, Shaping a Region

Mr. Jeffries began with perspective. The Asian Development Bank (ADB), founded in 1966, now counts 69 member countries, 50 of them within the Asia-Pacific region, and 41 borrowing members. Headquartered in Manila, ADB has grown into one of the world’s preeminent multilateral development institutions.
He described its core business in three succinct words: Finance. Knowledge. Partnerships.
• Finance, through sovereign and non-sovereign lending.
• Knowledge, drawn from crosscountry experience and practical lessons.
• Partnerships, which mobilize additional capital and expertise far beyond ADB’s own balance sheet.

In 2024 alone, ADB committed $24.3 billion in loans, grants, and investments, and mobilized an additional $14.9 billion in cofinancing. These are not abstract figures; they are arteries of development, carrying opportunity into economies that need long-term, patient capital. The Philippines, as a founding member and host country, occupies a special place. It holds 2.377% of ADB’s shares and remains one of its largest clients. In fact, the country is ADB’s second-largest portfolio in the Asia-Pacific region — second only to India — with an active portfolio of $12.5 billion as of December 2025.
Mr. Jeffries structured his remarks around ADB’s partnership strategy with the Philippines—aligned with the Philippine Development Plan and anchored on three pillars:
• Intensifying Social and Human Capital Development
• Boosting Economic Competitiveness and Quality Infrastructure
• Nature-Based Development and Disaster Resilience
Pillar I: Investing in Human Capital
Here, ADB supports the Pantawid Pamilyang Pilipino Program (4Ps), the Walang Gutom (Zero Hunger) initiative, universal health care, and JobStart Philippines.

Mr. Jeffries underscored that poverty reduction and productivity enhancement are inseparable. Social protection is not charity — it is economic strategy. When vulnerable households receive electronic food vouchers or access to healthcare, they do not merely survive; they stabilize communities and sustain domestic demand.
Pillar II: Transformative Infrastructure

The second pillar drew audible interest from the room. ADB is financing portions of the North–South Commuter Railway, the largest ADB project in the AsiaPacific region at $7 billion. The project will link Clark to Calamba, reshaping mobility across Luzon.

He also highlighted the Davao Public Transport Modernization, the first citywide modernization program of its kind in the Philippines, and the ambitious Bataan–Cavite Interlink Bridge, envisioned as one of the world’s longest bridges of its type.

Infrastructure, he reminded the audience, is not merely concrete and steel. It is connectivity—economic, geographic, and social. In an archipelagic nation, it determines whether farmers reach markets, whether labor reaches opportunity, and whether regions prosper together.
Pillar III: Climate and Disaster Resilience

The Philippines, battered by over 20 typhoons annually, stands at the frontlines of climate risk. ADB’s programs include flood resilience and adaptation projects, climate change action programs, marine ecosystem initiatives, and renewable energy ventures such as rooftop solar and electric mobility ecosystems.

Under Strategy 2030, ADB aims for climate finance to reach half of its total committed financing by 2030, with cumulative climate financing exceeding $100 billion. The message was unmistakable: climate action is no longer peripheral — it is central to development.
ASEAN 2026: The Philippines at the Helm

With the Philippines chairing ASEAN in 2026, Mr. Jeffries detailed ADB’s integrated support package to help deliver key policy outcomes and flagship events across finance, green economy, energy connectivity, tourism, social protection, digital transformation, and cross-cutting regional resilience.
Regional cooperation, he emphasized, is embedded in ADB’s charter. It is not optional. It is foundational.
The Economic Outlook: Fundamentals and Fragility

Turning to the macroeconomic outlook, Mr. Jeffries spoke candidlyabout the Philippines’ recent growth performance and expectations of a rebound. Domestic consumption — about 70% of GDP — remains a stabilizing force, bolstered by remittances. Yet infrastructure investment momentum and global trade fragmentation remain variables to watch.

The fundamentals, he assured the audience, are sound: affirmed credit ratings, a liquid banking sector, easing inflation, and policy space for interest rate adjustments. But growth, he cautioned, is not automatic. It requires execution — particularly in infrastructure and MSME support.

On that note, he offered a compelling example: an upcoming supply-chain finance facility designed to channel affordable working capital to micro, small, and medium enterprises by sharing credit risk with local banks. In a country where MSMEs comprise 99% of enterprises yet receive less than 10% of formal financing, such mechanisms could be transformative.
A Dialogue of Institutions

The Open Forum that followed was animated. Rotarians posed questions on infrastructure decongestion, the future of NAIA modernization, the role of private capital, and the geopolitical implications of regional fragmentation. Mr. Jeffries responded with clarity and candor, weaving data with institutional insight.
Mr. Jeffries engaged in a Q&A session with PP Archit Bartolome, Treas. PJ Garcia, Sec. Anton Mauricio, PDG Alex Cureg, and PDG Obet Pagdanganan.

At the conclusion, Director Edwin Hernandez presented Mr. Jeffries with a Certificate of Appreciation — a symbol not merely of gratitude, but of alignment. Rotary’s commitment to “Service Above Self” found resonance in ADB’s mandate to foster inclusive, resilient growth.
At 2:00 PM, Director Hernandez adjourned the meeting.
The Larger Meaning

The 22nd Weekly Membership Meeting was not simply another date on the Club calendar. It was a reminder that the Rotary Club of Manila, founded in 1919, continues to convene voices that shape the destiny of nations. In welcoming the Country Director of the Asian Development Bank, the Club affirmed its place at the intersection of civic leadership and economic transformation.

Bridges were discussed — literal and metaphorical. Railways, bridges, and flood barriers. But also bridges between institutions, between public and private sectors, between local needs and regional vision.

In a hall filled with Rotarians — men and women committed to ethical leadership—the message was clear: development is collective work. And in Manila, where ADB was born and Rotary took root over a century ago, the partnership between service and strategy continues to build futures worthy of the next generation.
Meeting Fellowship

body.text: Reginald T. Yu
Editor-in-Chief

On Thursday, February 26, 2026, at 11:00 a.m., beneath open skies and across the sweeping fairways of The Manila Southwoods Golf and Country Club, the Rotary Club of Manila gathers for what may appear to be a day of sport — but is, in truth, something far deeper.

This is not merely a golf event. 
This is One Fellowship.

In a club as storied and historic as the Rotary Club of Manila — the first Rotary club in Asia and the largest in the Philippines — fellowship is not an accessory to service. It is its foundation. Before we deliberate on policy, before we chart ambitious projects, before we raise millions in funds and steward institutions older than most organizations in this nation, we must first remain connected as men and women bound by trust.
And trust is not built in boardrooms alone.

It is built walking side by side down a fairway. 
It is built in friendly banter before a tee shot. 
It is built in shared silence while reading the green. 
It is built in laughter over a missed putt and quiet respect after a well-struck drive.

Golf, in many ways, mirrors leadership. It is a game of integrity — you call your own penalties. It is a game of patience — you cannot rush the rhythm. It is a game of focus — distractions cost you strokes. It is a game of humility — even the best players are reminded that perfection is elusive.
Rotary leadership demands the same virtues.

As we approach a new Rotary year — one that calls for greater unity, greater collaboration, and greater resolve — this gathering becomes more than recreation. It becomes strategic alignment. A reminder that the culture we build today will determine the impact we leave tomorrow.
The theme says it clearly: One Fellowship.

Not “my” fellowship. 
Not “your” circle. 
Not “kanya-kanya.”
But one.

In a club with members of diverse generations, industries, and tenures — from seasoned statesmen to young idealists — cohesion does not happen automatically. It must be nurtured intentionally. Events like this are how culture is strengthened. They allow newer members to feel seen, and long-standing members to feel valued. They soften hierarchies.
They dissolve assumptions. They remind us that beyond titles and committees, we are simply Rotarians who share a calling to serve.

And then, as the sun lowers and the day transitions from the course to the clubhouse, fellowship continues — cocktails the Rotary way. It is in these unguarded moments that ideas surface organically. A youth project may be conceived between sips. A partnership may begin in a casual exchange. A mentorship relationship may quietly form at the bar.
Many of Rotary’s most enduring initiatives did not begin with a formal motion. They began with conversation.

We often speak about moving Rotary International forward. About strengthening institutions. About preserving legacy. But none of that is sustainable if we neglect the very fabric that holds us together — camaraderie.
This February 26, let every swing carry intention. Let every handshake carry warmth. Let every conversation carry respect.

Because when fellowship is genuine, service becomes natural. 
When unity is real, leadership becomes powerful. 
When trust is strong, a 107- year-old institution does not merely survive — it thrives.
The scorecard will record birdies and bogeys. But the true measure of the day will not be strokes taken.

It will be bonds strengthened. 
It will be unity reinforced. 
It will be One Fellowship — lived, not just declared.
And in Rotary, that is always the ultimate victory.
RC Baguio’s 88th Anniversary

Last Thursday, February 19, I had the distinct honor of serving as Guest of Honor and Speaker at the 88th Anniversary Gala Night of our daughter club, the Rotary Club of Baguio. Accompanied by IPP Jujut Enriquez and PE Reggie Yu, we journeyed to the City of Pines to celebrate this remarkable milestone.

In my remarks, I could not resist a bit of lighthearted humor. I observed that at 88 years, RC Baguio has already outlived the traditional anniversary gemstone list—which, as we know, ceremoniously concludes at 75 years with the diamond. Beyond that, there appears to be no official guidance.
It is almost as if the list gently tells those fortunate enough to surpass 75: “Good luck—kayo na ang bahala.”

But perhaps that is precisely the point. To go beyond the diamond is to transcend convention. It is to move past prescribed milestones and into a legacy defined not by gemstones, but by grit, grace, and generations of service. And in that respect, RC Baguio shines in a category entirely its own.
75 has diamond as its gemstone. And perhaps this is fitting.

A diamond is treasured not only for its brilliance, but for the structure that gives rise to that brilliance. Each carbon atom is closely connected to the next. Carbon atoms are beautifully bound together, forming a lattice that can withstand tremendous pressure. Its strength, therefore, does not come from its size — it comes from its connections.

And that is what 88 years truly represent. 
Not merely age. 
Not merely tradition. 
But bonds — tempered by trial, strengthened by service, and unbroken by time itself.

In my speech, I underscored that not having a gemstone actually makes 88 years extraordinary; because when the world runs out of gemstones to describe RC Baguio, it means that the Club itself has become THE gemstone. As such, its worth is now beyond measure, beyond category, beyond comparison. At 88 years, RCB is no longer defined by the brilliance of a stone… but by the brilliance of its service.

Besides, I said, the Rotary Club of Baguio has never needed a gemstone or any traditional symbol to define its worth. This is because from its earliest days, it already held something far more valuable: a legacy shaped by genuine service and anchored in a founding story that ties it directly to the roots of Rotary in the Philippines. And this is where the Rotary Club of Manila plays an important role – with its leaders planting the seeds of Rotary in Baguio.

This is why, I said, we were celebrating more than history. We were celebrating character. We were celebrating consistency. We were celebrating a club that has remained relevant because it has remained principled. In Rotary, anniversaries are not just about age. If age alone defined us, then the Rotary Club of Manila — the oldest in Asia — would have been retired, given a plaque, and told to relax decades ago.
But here we are: still moving and still serving.
Perhaps the greatest beauty of the RCB milestone is this:
Eighty-eight years may sound long — yet for Rotary, this is only the beginning.
I ended my speech with this -- There are two questions every great anniversary dares to ask: “How far have we come?” and “How fiercely will we continue?”

In regard to the second question, I expressed my belief that the Rotary Club of Baguio will not merely move forward — it will surge, unstoppable and unmistakable, leaving footprints of service wherever it passes. The anniversary celebration is not RC Baguio’s past shining; but its future roaring.
The foregoing is the summary of my message to our daughter club.

In retrospect, I had to make the difficult decision to miss our own weekly meeting in order to accept a speaking engagement—an invitation from our daughter club. It was not a choice made lightly. Yet I am deeply grateful that I did.

That evening became more than a formal engagement; it was a moment of fellowship and affirmation. It also allowed me to share meaningful time with PE Reggie and IPP Jujut, strengthening not only our camaraderie but our shared sense of purpose.

More importantly, it was an opportunity to make something visible and tangible: that the Rotary Club of Manila—the mother club their members look up to with such awe and respect -- stands not at a distance, but side by side with them. In their milestone celebration, our presence was a quiet but powerful message: that heritage is not merely remembered; it is lived, shared, and extended through fellowship and support.
Sometimes leadership calls us to be present where our presence speaks louder than our schedule. And in that moment, standing with our daughter club – the Rotary Club of Baguio -- it truly did.

articles.title: Aleco Donates 25 Books of Philippine Almanac to Bataan School in Honor of Tong Payumo

body.text: In a heartfelt tribute to the late Rotarian and and active Aleconian Tong Payumo, Aleconian PT Chito Tagaysay has donated 25 copies of the Philippine Almanac to the University of Nueva Caceres, Bataan on February 23, 2026. The donation honors Payumo, a formerly active Aleconian, for his contributions to the community.
