When she and Ingill began to discern their life together, he sensed something he had rarely felt before: not excitement alone, but a quiet certainty. In a life shaped by discipline and responsibility, this was a new language of grace.
Their early married years were anything but easy.

After completing seminary, Ingill began ministry in a small pioneering church near a university. The work was demanding, the resources scarce, the future uncertain. They lived in cramped quarters, navigating the insecurities of young adulthood with little financial stability. The rhythms of pastoral life — late-night counseling, endless meetings, the emotional burdens of congregants — quickly consumed his time and energy.
Unconsciously, he placed his calling above everything else. The church came first. Ministry came first. Vision came first. Love, he assumed, would simply endure.

In this, he was repeating a pattern he had witnessed in childhood. His father had devoted himself wholly to the church, while his mother carried the weight of family survival. Sacrifice had been normalized. Emotional absence had been quietly accepted as the price of faithfulness.

But Angie had not grown up in hardship. She had not been formed by scarcity, nor by the assumption that endurance must always be silent. She was strong, but she was also sensitive. And what pained her most was not the lack of comfort, but the feeling of being unseen — of standing beside a man who spoke of love and service to the world, yet struggled to offer the same attentiveness at home.
The birth of their child intensified both the joy and the tension. Fatherhood brought Ingill a new awareness of responsibility, but it also exposed his immaturity.
He loved his family deeply, yet he had not yet learned how to balance vision with presence, mission with tenderness.

It was a season of quiet conflict, not of dramatic arguments, but of unspoken loneliness. Angie remained faithful, supportive, and prayerful, yet the cost of that faithfulness was heavy. Only later would he fully recognize how much she had carried, and how patient her love had been.
In time, the mirror of her endurance forced him to confront himself.

He began to see that peacebuilding, reconciliation, and moral leadership could not be abstract ideals lived only in public arenas. They had to be practiced in the smallest, most intimate spaces. The family, he realized, was the first classroom of peace, the first society in which justice, sacrifice, and empathy were tested.

Repentance, in this context, was not theatrical. It was slow and humbling. It meant learning to listen, to apologize, to make space, to reorient priorities. It meant recognizing that a life lived “for the sake of the world” loses its moral authority if it neglects the one person to whom one has vowed lifelong care.

Angie’s role in his life was not merely supportive; it was formative. Her art, which often explored themes of journey, fragility, and hope, became a silent dialogue with his own search for meaning. Through her eyes, he learned to see the human soul not as a problem to be solved, but as a mystery to be cherished.

Marriage, for him, became a school of reconciliation more demanding than any diplomatic negotiation, and more sacred than any institutional mission. It taught him that love is not proven by intention but by consistency; not by words but by presence.

Later, when he would speak to young leaders about moral and innovative leadership, he would do so not as a theoretician, but as one who had learned — through failure and forgiveness — that the credibility of public service is forged in private faithfulness.

In Angie, he found not only a companion, but a quiet theologian of life, one who taught him that peace is not first built between nations, but between two hearts learning to walk together in patience, humility, and trust.
Scholar of Reconciliation

By the time Ingill Ra completed his formal studies, he no longer thought of education as a ladder of degrees. He understood it as a convergence — a long, inward process by which experience, faith, and disciplined inquiry fused into a single moral vision. What emerged from that convergence was not simply expertise, but a philosophy of reconciliation.

Theology had taught him how civilizations interpret suffering and hope, how sacred narratives shape the way people endure loss and imagine redemption. Family therapy had shown him how wounds travel across generations, how silence can be as destructive as open conflict, and how healing begins only when pain is acknowledged and dignity restored. Interfaith education had revealed that truth does not fear dialogue, and that faith matures when it learns to listen with humility. Public administration, finally, exposed the architecture of power — how institutions preserve memory, how policies shape behavior, and how civil society, more than governments alone, determines the moral direction of a nation.

Gradually, he came to see a profound parallel. Nations, like families, fracture not primarily because of ideology, but because of unhealed fear. And reunification, like reconciliation in a household, cannot be imposed by authority. It must be prepared in the heart.

This insight became the core of his thinking. Korea’s division, he concluded, was not merely geopolitical. It was psychological and spiritual. Two systems had hardened into two identities. Each had learned to survive by defining itself against the other. Over decades, this survival instinct had become a narrative of destiny, reinforced by education, propaganda, and collective memory. No treaty alone could undo that.

What was required was a transformation of moral imagination — a way for Koreans, North and South, to see one another again not as enemies shaped by ideology, but as members of a single historical family shaped by suffering and endurance.

Here, his understanding of Hongik Ingan deepened. It ceased to be only an ancient founding ideal and became a framework for public life. A nation, he came to believe, is not fully mature when it is merely strong or prosperous. It is mature when it is generous. Not when it dominates, but when it serves. Not when it is unified by fear, but when it is unified by shared responsibility for the human family.

This led him to a conviction that would shape all his later work: reunification is not the end of the Korean journey, but the beginning of its true civilizational mission. A reunited Korea, in his vision, would not exist for itself alone.
It would exist to embody a moral lesson for a divided world — that historical wounds can be healed without erasing identity, and that power can be reconciled with compassion

In his comparative study of divided and democratizing societies, he observed that lasting transformation never came from elite negotiation alone. It emerged when ordinary citizens began to see themselves as moral stakeholders in the nation’s future. Taiwan’s democratic transition, South Africa’s truth and reconciliation process, and post-war Europe’s integration all revealed the same pattern: peace endured only when it was carried by conscience, not merely by constitutions.

From this synthesis arose what he would later describe as Moral and Innovative Leadership. Leadership, in this sense, had to be moral because it must be rooted in conscience before it is expressed in policy. It had to be innovative because historical wounds cannot be healed with inherited formulas. They require new languages of trust, new structures of cooperation, and new stories of shared destiny.

Reconciliation, in his framework, was never sentimental. It was architectural. It involved the slow rebuilding of trust, the reshaping of collective memory, and the formation of citizens who could imagine unity not as surrender, but as responsibility. It required patient education, cultural empathy, and institutions that rewarded cooperation rather than fear. Above all, it required time, because neither families nor nations are healed in a single conversation or a single summit.

This is why Ingill Ra never reduced peace to diplomacy alone. He invested instead in youth, educators, faith leaders, artists, athletes, and civic organizers — the quiet shapers of a future moral consciousness. He believed that before borders can change, hearts must change; before systems can be unified, memory must be reconciled.

In this sense, he was not merely a scholar who studied reconciliation. He became a thinker of healing as civilization-building. Where others spoke of security, he spoke of trust. Where others spoke of ideology, he spoke of identity. Where others spoke of victory, he spoke of belonging.

And where history had taught Koreans to endure division, he sought to teach them something more demanding: to imagine reunion — not as the triumph of one system over another, but as the restoration of a family long separated, finally learning to recognize itself again.
From Village to World Stage

By the time Ingill Ra entered the arena of international institutions, he no longer saw the world as a collection of disconnected problems. He saw it as a web of relationships — some broken, some fragile, some waiting to be restored. His years of study had prepared his mind; his years of service had prepared his heart. What remained was the testing ground where ideals meet reality.
One of the first global platforms where this synthesis took form was the world of sport.

At the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), where he served as Director of Social Responsibility, he encountered a realm that spoke a language understood across borders, cultures, and creeds. Football fields, he realized, could become classrooms of character and laboratories of peace. The roar of a crowd, the discipline of training, the shared joy of victory and the shared pain of loss — these were universal experiences, capable of uniting young people long before they learned the vocabularies of politics or religion.

It was in this context that he conceived and launched “Midnight Football,” a program designed for youth in vulnerable urban communities. In many cities, the hours after dark were the most dangerous — when crime, drugs, and violence lured the restless and the forgotten. Rather than responding with punishment alone, he and his colleagues asked a different question: What if the night could be reclaimed as a space of belonging rather than fear?

They worked with police, schools, and neighborhood leaders. On game nights, residents parked their motorcycles around makeshift fields, turning on their headlights to illuminate the pitch. Under those beams of light, boys who might otherwise have drifted into gangs or detention centers learned teamwork, discipline, and trust. Parents and officers stood side by side, not as adversaries but as guardians of a shared future.

One message he received from a young participant, newly released from juvenile detention, stayed with him: a simple note saying he was coming home and wanted to return to the team. It was not eloquent. It did not need to be. It carried the quiet miracle of hope — the sense that someone still believed he belonged.

Around the same period, Ingill helped organize the first regional football tournament for persons with disabilities, bringing athletes from more than fifty Asian nations to Abu Dhabi. What began as an event became a movement. Barriers that had long kept people with disabilities at the margins of sport began to fall. National federations revised policies, opened facilities, and invested in inclusive programs.

To see ambassadors, government officials, families, and athletes celebrate together was to witness a living parable: that dignity does not depend on physical perfection, and that society is healed when the most vulnerable are welcomed into its center.
From the stadium, his path led to the United Nations system.

At the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), where he served as Director of Resource Mobilization and External Cooperation, he encountered a different, yet equally fundamental, truth: that peace begins with bread. “Food is love,” his colleagues often said, and he came to understand the depth of that phrase. Hunger is not merely a biological condition; it is a moral emergency.
A child who goes to sleep hungry does not have the luxury of contemplating ideals of democracy or reconciliation.

Yet he also learned that compassion, if not coupled with empowerment, can become dependency. Sustainable peace, he believed, required capacity-building — training farmers, strengthening fisheries, restoring forests, and enabling communities to provide for themselves with dignity. Aid, in this vision, was not charity alone; it was partnership.

His travels with the UN and other organizations took him to remote regions, conflict zones, and communities rebuilding after disaster. In Mongolia, after a long and exhausting assignment, he experienced an act of hospitality that crystallized his faith in the goodness of ordinary people. A stranger at the airport insisted on taking him not to a hotel, but to his own modest home. There, the man’s wife prepared meals, offered their bed, and treated him as family.
Only later did they explain why. Years earlier, they had worked in Korea, where an employer had welcomed them with the same warmth. This, they said, was their chance to repay that kindness.
To Ingill, it was a living illustration of moral reciprocity across borders — a reminder that one act of love can travel silently through time and space, returning when least expected.

In conflict-affected areas, including parts of the Middle East and the Korean Peninsula, he worked with partners to build sports facilities, schools, and community centers. These were not mere structures; they were statements of hope, spaces where children from opposing sides could meet not as enemies, but as teammates.

Gradually, his leadership style evolved. If in his early years he had been driven by vision and urgency, now he learned the deeper power of listening. Every culture, he discovered, carries its own wisdom, its own rhythm of trust. Solutions imposed from outside rarely endure. Transformation, to be authentic, must be owned from within.

Language barriers humbled him. Even in English, the global lingua franca, accents and idioms demanded patience and attentiveness. Communication, he learned, is an act of respect before it is an exchange of information.

Through these experiences, a pattern became clear. Whether in a Mongolian home, a Palestinian playground, an African village, or an Asian metropolis, the same human longings surfaced: to be seen, to be valued, to belong, to hope. And everywhere, he found that when people were approached not as problems to be fixed but as partners to be honored, something remarkable happened. Trust grew. Creativity emerged. Communities found their own paths toward healing.

The boy from Beomnaetgol, who had once looked out at the distant sea and wondered about the wider world, now moved across continents with a single conviction: that humanity, in all its diversity and division, was still one family — capable of extraordinary cruelty, yes, but also of extraordinary compassion.
The Korean Dream and the Wound of Division
For all his travels and global engagements, the deepest question of Ingill Ra’s life remained rooted in the soil of his own divided homeland.

Korea’s partition was not, for him, an abstract geopolitical arrangement. It was a wound carried in memory, culture, and family history. He had grown up hearing stories of flight and loss, of relatives separated by an invisible line, of a war that never truly ended but merely hardened into an armistice. The Demilitarized Zone, silent yet heavily armed, stood as both a physical barrier and a moral symbol — a reminder that ideology, once absolutized, could fracture a people for generations.

In 2002, when he visited Pyongyang and Jeongju, the division ceased to be theoretical. He met teachers, farmers, and families whose faces, language, and manner were unmistakably his own. In them he saw not enemies, but kin — brothers and sisters shaped by the same history, separated by forces far larger than themselves. In that encounter, reunification became not a political aspiration but a human imperative, like the longing to be reunited with a longlost member of one’s own family.

It was around this period that he encountered the vision of the “Korean Dream” as articulated by Dr. Hyun Jin Preston Moon, founder of the Global Peace Foundation. This vision reimagined Korea’s future not in terms of economic ascent alone — remarkable as that ascent had been — but as a moral and civic calling. It spoke of reconciliation after division, dignity after suffering, and a national destiny rooted in service to the global community.

For Ingill Ra, the Korean Dream was not a personal concept to originate or promote, but a shared vision to steward. It gave language and structure to what his own life had already been teaching him: that Korea’s story was not meant to culminate merely in prosperity or power, but in healing; not merely in invaded so many times in its history had rarely, if ever, become an aggressor itself. It was a civilization shaped less by conquest than by endurance, less by domination than by moral resilience.
security, but in a renewed vocation to serve humanity.

This vision resonated deeply with the ancient Korean ideal of Hongik Ingan — “to benefit all humanity.” Rooted in the founding narrative of the Korean people, this principle had long defined Korea’s moral DNA. It explained, in part, why a nation that had been
invaded so many times in its history had rarely, if ever, become an aggressor itself. It was a civilization shaped less by conquest than by endurance, less by domination than by moral resilience

Through the lens of the Korean Dream, Hongik Ingan ceased to be only an ancient maxim and became a framework for Korea’s future. A unified Korea, in this understanding, would not exist merely to resolve a security problem or to complete a national project. It would exist to fulfill a civilizational responsibility: to stand as a bridge between ideologies, cultures, and civilizations, and to demonstrate that historical wounds can be healed without erasing identity, and that power can be reconciled with compassion.

This was why, in his work, Ingill Ra consistently emphasized that reunification could not be reduced to diplomacy or economics. Like reconciliation in a family, it required healing of memory, transformation of narratives, and the rebuilding of trust. Decades of separation had created two systems, but more deeply, two psychological worlds. Each had learned to define itself against the other. No agreement alone could dissolve that. What was needed was a change of moral imagination — a rediscovery of shared identity beneath imposed division.

In this sense, reunification was not, for him, the final goal, but the threshold of a larger mission. A Korea restored to unity would be called not inward, but outward — to offer the world the fruits of its suffering: a mature commitment to peace, a deepened sense of human dignity, and a renewed devotion to the idea that nations, like individuals, find their highest purpose not in self-assertion, but in living for the sake of others.

Thus, the Korean Dream as he embraced it was never a nationalist slogan. It was a civilizational hope, grounded in history, faith, and moral responsibility — a vision entrusted to him and to his generation not to own, but to carry forward, for Korea and for the human family it was called to serve.
The Philippines: A Brother Nation
If Korea was the wound that shaped Ingill Ra’s life, the Philippines became the mirror in which that wound found unexpected healing.

If Korea was the wound that shaped Ingill Ra’s life, the PhFrom his earliest visits, he felt a familiarity that went beyond hospitality. It was not only the warmth of Filipino smiles or the ease of conversation, but a deeper resonance — a sense that the two nations shared a history written not merely in treaties, but in sacrifice.ilippines became the mirror in which that wound found unexpected healing.

Whenever he spoke of the Korean War, he did so with reverence. Sixteen nations had answered the call to defend a small peninsula at the edge of Asia, but among them, the Philippines held a singular place in his heart. Exactly 7,420 young Filipino soldiers crossed the sea in 1950, leaving behind families, farms, and classrooms to fight for a people they had never met. Around 299 wounded were wounded and 112 did not return. Those who did carried memories of frozen mountains, sudden battles, and the quiet heroism of comradeship.

To Ingill, their presence in Korea was not an episode of military history; it was an act of moral kinship. “Without them,” he often said, “my life, and the life of my nation, might not have been possible.
Two figures embodied this shared destiny for him

One was a seventeen-year-old war correspondent, Benigno “Ninoy” Aquino Jr., who arrived in Korea armed not with a rifle, but with a pen and a camera. Too young to fight, he chose instead to bear witness — to tell the story of Filipino courage and Korean suffering. Decades later, his image
would appear on the Philippine 500- peso bill, a quiet reminder that truth and sacrifice are forms of service as noble as combat.

The other was a young officer named Fidel V. Ramos, a graduate of West Point who would later become President of the Philippines. In Korea, Ramos commanded troops against overwhelming odds, demonstrating a leadership forged in discipline and resolve. For Ingill, the arc of Ramos’s life — from the battlefield to the presidency — symbolized how courage in defense of others could mature into statesmanship in service of one’s own people.

These stories were not, for him, nostalgic tributes. They were moral touchstones. They illustrated what he believed to be the highest form of patriotism: love of one’s own nation expressed through responsibility toward another.

In the Philippines, he also encountered a living tradition of faith that resonated deeply with his own. Churches stood at the heart of communities. Prayer was woven into public life. Even amid poverty and political turmoil, a profound trust in God animated daily existence. It reminded him of his own childhood in Busan, where faith had been both refuge and compass.

What moved him most, however, was the Filipino understanding of family and community. The concept of kapwa — the other as another self — echoed the Korean sense of jeong, the deep emotional bond that arises from shared life and shared struggle. In both cultures, relationship preceded contract, and loyalty was measured not by convenience, but by presence.

This cultural consonance found institutional expression in his growing relationship with Rotary in the Philippines, particularly with the Rotary Club of Manila. From his first visit to a weekly meeting, he sensed that Rotary was more than a service organization; it was a fellowship bound by ethical commitment. The Four-Way Test, with its simple yet demanding questions — Is it the truth? Is it fair to all concerned? Will it build goodwill and better friendships? Will it be beneficial to all concerned? — struck him as a secular articulation of the very values he had been preaching across cultures.
Through Rotary, he and his wife engaged in projects that brought service from abstraction into intimacy. One of the most formative was their involvement with a hospice for children.

Angie, with her background in fine arts, taught painting to the young patients and later participated in charity exhibitions to support the center. Together, they witnessed not only the vulnerability of life, but the quiet heroism of caregivers and volunteers who returned week after week, year after year, offering presence where cure was no longer possible.

In those rooms, filled with fragile bodies and luminous spirits, Ingill felt again the convergence of all the themes that had shaped his life: suffering and dignity, faith and action, the global and the personal. The children were not beneficiaries of charity; they were teachers of courage. Their parents were not objects of pity; they were models of love refined by pain.

As his work with the Global Peace Foundation deepened in the Philippines, he began to see the nation’s potential role in the broader architecture of peace. Mindanao’s long journey from conflict toward dialogue, marked by the collaboration of Christian, Muslim, and indigenous leaders, appeared to him as a microcosm of what the world itself needed to learn. Peace there had not been achieved by decree alone, but by the patient weaving of trust among communities, by the recognition of shared suffering, and by the courage to imagine a common future.

He often spoke of the Philippines as a “teacher nation” — one that, through its history and values, could offer the world a model of coexistence rooted in faith, hospitality, and resilience. Its educational ideals — Maka-Diyos, Maka-Tao, Maka-Kalikasan, MakaBansa — seemed to him not merely national mottos, but universal principles: reverence for God, respect for humanity, care for creation, and love of country understood as moral responsibility rather than narrow nationalism.

In this light, the relationship between Korea and the Philippines assumed a new, almost providential dimension. One nation carried the wound of division and the longing for reunification. The other carried a tradition of spiritual depth and communal solidarity. Together, he believed, they could form a bridge — between North and South, between past and future, between faith and policy.

When he invited Filipino friends and colleagues to stand with Korea in its dream of peaceful reunification, he did so not as a diplomat seeking support, but as a brother appealing to shared values. The same hands that had once held rifles in defense of Korean freedom, he now asked to hold a vision of reconciliation grounded in faith and human dignity.

In this partnership, Ingill Ra saw not strategy, but destiny: two peoples, bound by history and hope, called to remind a fractured world that sacrifice can give birth to solidarity, and that nations, like families, can choose to live not for themselves alone, but for the sake of others.
Moral and Innovative Leadership

By the time Ingill Ra assumed broader responsibilities within the Global Peace Foundation as Regional President for the Asia–Pacific, his understanding of leadership had been refined by decades of experience across cultures, institutions, and generations. He no longer thought of leadership primarily as authority or position. He understood it as moral influence — an ability to awaken vision, to cultivate responsibility, and to draw out the best from others in service of a shared future.

He often described himself, half in jest, as a “pathfinder rather than a commander.” In meetings with government officials, educators, religious leaders, youth organizers, and business executives, he rarely imposed conclusions. Instead, he asked questions, listened carefully, and sought to surface the deeper values that already
lived in the room. Only when people recognized their own moral stake in an issue, he believed, could genuine and lasting change begin.
This philosophy found its most vivid expression in his work with young people.

Across the Asia–Pacific — particularly in the Philippines, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, and Thailand — he devoted immense energy to leadership formation. One of the flagship initiatives under his guidance was the Global Youth Summit (GYS), which by 2024 had reached more than 12,000 young leaders across seventeen cities in the Philippines alone

What distinguished these gatherings from conventional conferences was not their scale, but their spirit. Instead of asking students and young professionals to come to a single capital city, his team went to them — into provincial universities, community centers, faith institutions, and even informal settlements. Each summit was anchored on a concrete social challenge, often aligned with a specific Sustainable Development Goal: education, poverty alleviation, environmental stewardship, interfaith harmony, mental health, or community resilience.

There, in classrooms and town halls, Muslim and Christian students sat side by side. Indigenous youth spoke of ancestral wisdom and modern aspirations. Young women stepped forward as leaders in spaces where tradition had once confined them to silence. Dialogue was not an academic exercise; it was an encounter of stories, hopes, and responsibilities

Ingill insisted that the youth not be treated as future leaders, but as leaders now. They were encouraged to design and implement community projects, supported by small seed grants and mentorship. The message was clear: leadership is not defined by age or title, but by the courage to act for the common good.
From these experiences emerged what he articulated as Moral and Innovative Leadership
“Moral,” because it begins with the recognition of human dignity, the courage to stand for truth, and the willingness to serve something larger than oneself.

“Innovative,” because it refuses to be trapped by inherited patterns of conflict or apathy, and instead seeks new ways of collaboration, communication, and problem-solving rooted in local culture and creativity.
For him, innovation without morality risked becoming cleverness without conscience. Morality without innovation risked becoming nostalgia without relevance. The future, he believed, demanded both.
One moment in India crystallized this synthesis.

Invited to speak before a gathering of scholars and national leaders on the future of peace in the Indo-Pacific, he prepared a carefully structured lecture. Yet as he stood before the audience, he felt compelled to set his notes aside. Instead, he spoke from the heart about Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam — the ancient Indian principle that “the world is one family.” He drew parallels to Korea’s Hongik Ingan and to the Global Peace Foundation’s vision of One Family Under God. He spoke of civilizations not as rivals, but as complementary moral traditions, each bearing wisdom for a wounded world.

The response was profound. Among those present was the granddaughter of Mahatma Gandhi, who later remarked that the address had been delivered “from the heart, not from notes.” The following day, the President of the National Federation of Indian

Universities approached him with an unexpected proposal: that he be honored with the 2025 Best Speaker Award — not as a personal accolade, but as a symbol of the academic community’s alignment with a valuesbased movement for peace.
Such moments did not inflate his sense of self; they deepened his sense of responsibility. Recognition, he believed, is never an endpoint. It is a summons to greater fidelity to one’s calling.

Across the region, his leadership was marked by a distinctive blend of urgency and patience. Urgency, because he believed the challenges facing humanity — polarization, ecological crisis, violent extremism, and the erosion of trust — could not wait. Patience, because he knew that moral transformation cannot be rushed. It must be cultivated, like character in a child or trust in a community.

In countless conversations with young people, he returned to the same themes: purpose, dignity, and service. He urged them to see themselves not merely as citizens of a nation, but as stewards of a civilization. He reminded them that history is shaped not only by those who hold power, but by those who hold conscience.

Often, after his talks, students would linger. Some shared their struggles — family pressures, doubts about the future, disillusionment with politics. Others spoke of awakening, of a renewed desire to live for something larger than personal success. A few, with a mixture of awe and determination, would say, “We want to live a life like yours.”

These encounters moved him deeply, not because they affirmed his achievements, but because they revealed the hunger of a generation for meaning. He understood that what they were truly seeking was not a model to imitate, but a vision to inhabit — a sense that their lives, too, could become bridges between peoples, healers of wounds, builders of peace.

For Ingill Ra, this was the true measure of leadership: not the number of programs launched or positions held, but the number of hearts awakened to responsibility, and the number of minds liberated to imagine a world reconciled.
One Family Under God — Legacy and Benediction

As Ingill Ra reflects on a life that has carried him from a one-room home on a Busan hillside to the halls of international institutions, from refugee memories to global peace platforms, he
does not speak first of accomplishments. He speaks of gratitude.
Gratitude for a father who taught him to stand with conviction, even when standing meant standing alone.
Gratitude for a mother who embodied quiet sacrifice and whose tenderness revealed that love is often expressed in small, faithful acts.
Gratitude for a wife whose patience and artistry taught him that peace begins not in treaties but in relationships, not in speeches but in presence.
Gratitude for a nation that rose from ruins with discipline and hope, and for another nation — the Philippines — that once crossed the sea to defend Korea’s very right to exist.

He often says that his deepest strength, even now, comes not from institutions or titles, but from the constancy of prayer and the companionship of Angie, who has walked with him through every season, every transition, every doubt. Each morning begins in the same way: a moment of stillness, an offering of the day to God, a prayer for leaders and young people across the countries he
loves. It is a simple ritual, but it anchors a life lived across time zones and cultures.

For all his global engagements, his most demanding discipline has remained the practice of kindness in ordinary encounters. Taxi drivers, hotel staff, young volunteers, government officials, students — he believes the moral quality of leadership is revealed not on stages, but in these unscripted moments. Vision, he has learned, collapses if it is not sustained by humility. Grand ideals lose their credibility if they are not lived in small gestures of respect.
When asked what he is most grateful for, he often answers in an unexpected way: for questions.

For the questions that unsettled him as a child in a divided land. For the questions that drove him across continents as a young volunteer. For the questions that pushed him into disciplines beyond theology, into social work, education, and public policy. For the questions young people now ask him about purpose, justice, and the future.
To be questioned, he believes, is to be invited into meaning. It is to be reminded that one’s life is part of a larger conversation that stretches across generations.

And when he speaks of legacy, he does not speak of monuments or programs bearing his name. He returns instead to an image that has accompanied him through the years, shaped in part by his wife’s art and poetry: the image of a small fish swimming within a vast current, or a wildflower carried by the wind.

Each human life, he reflects, is fragile and brief, yet not insignificant. We move within a great river of history, often unaware of how our small acts of faithfulness, courage, or compassion contribute to a larger movement of healing.
This vision found lyrical expression in a poem written by Angie, shared during one of her exhibitions — lines that have become, for them, a kind of benediction:
Across the rough wilderness, you came like a flower in flight. Even the shadow of a single petal shines with light, whispers the gentle wind.
From the first moment of your journey, with a small body and all your strength, you swam forward.
Even in sharp, crashing waves, your path became a soft current, says the kind wind.

In these words, Ingill sees his own story, and the story of every person who chooses to live not for self alone, but for the sake of others. A small body, moving forward with all its strength. A fragile life, carried by a purpose larger than itself. A current of goodness, barely visible perhaps, yet real.

From Beomnaetgol to New York, from Africa to the United Nations, from football fields to peace summits, from a divided peninsula to the dream of reunification, his life has traced one continuous arc: the conviction that humanity is not destined for perpetual fracture, that history need not end in hostility, and that faith — when joined to courage, discipline, and love — can become a force for reconciliation.

“Hongik Ingan,” the ancient Korean ideal of living for the benefit of all humanity, and “Maka-Diyos, MakaTao, Maka-Kalikasan, Maka-Bansa,” the Filipino vision of a people rooted in God, dignity, creation, and nationhood, converge in a single phrase that has come to define his life’s work:
One Family Under God.
It is not a slogan. It is a hope shaped by war and healed by service.

It is a theology tested by history and refined by relationships. It is a dream that sees in every culture, every faith, every nation, not a rival to be defeated, but a brother or sister to be embraced.
And so, the boy who once stood in a public square holding a petition board, uncertain and afraid, now stands before the world with a different message — spoken not with placards, but with a life:

That peace is possible. That reconciliation is worth the cost. That small lives, lived with faithfulness, can become part of a great current of renewal. Like a wildflower carried by the wind. Like a small fish swimming steadily toward the open sea

photos.caption: Past District Governor and 2020 Rotary Club of Manila President Jackie Rodriguez— Ingill’s Rotary sponsor and mentor—has been a decisive and steady guide in his journey of service. Through wise counsel, personal example, and unwavering encouragement, PDG Jackie helped shape not only his understanding of Rotary’s ideals, but also his deeper commitment to servant leadership, integrity, and fellowship. More than a sponsor in name, he has been a mentor in the truest sense, walking with him, opening doors of learning and responsibility, and inspiring him to serve with humility, purpose, and a heart for the greater good.

Ingill previously served as Senior Officer for Resource Development and External Cooperation at the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) for the Asia– Pacific region, where he worked closely with governments, international agencies, and development partners to mobilize resources and strengthen cooperation in addressing food security, sustainable agriculture, and rural development. Today, he carries this depth of multilateral experience into his role as Asia–Pacific President of the Global Peace Foundation (GPF), representing the organization in its continuing collaboration with the United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (UNESCAP). In this capacity, and under GPF’s Special Consultative Status with the United Nations, he helps advance dialogue and partnership between civil society and the UN system in support of peace, sustainable development, and regional cooperation.

At a Global Peace Foundation gathering, Ingill stands in quiet reflection alongside his mentor, Dr. Hyun-jin Preston Moon, and Dr. Nona Ricarfort, sharing a moment of dialogue, wisdom, and collective vision. Surrounded by fellow advocates of peace and values-based leadership, the scene captures the intergenerational transmission of purpose—where experience, scholarship, and moral conviction converge to reaffirm a common mission of unity, service, and the pursuit of a more harmonious world.

Above photo: Manila Con 22 — In 2017, the Global Peace Foundation (GPF) mounted what would become one of the most ambitious K-pop gatherings ever staged in the Philippines: the “One K Concert” in Manila. More than forty Korean pop groups were brought together on one stage, transforming the city into a vibrant crossroads of music, youth culture, and international goodwill. Beyond the spectacle, the concert carried a deeper purpose — to use the universal language of music to promote unity, peace, and shared humanity, drawing thousands of young people into a celebration that transcended borders and reminded all that harmony can be built not only through diplomacy, but through art, energy, and collective joy.

In Indonesia, Ingill meets with Nasaruddin Umar, a distinguished Muslim scholar, Grand Imam, and the 25th Minister of Religious Affairs, in a moment that powerfully underscores the importance of interfaith dialogue and cooperation. Their encounter reflects a shared commitment to peace, mutual respect, and the belief that religious leaders, working across traditions, can help bridge divides, nurture understanding, and guide communities toward harmony and the common good.

With Professor Jin-Wook Choi and his wife — one of the most respected figures in Ingill’s academic life and a formative mentor from his alma mater. Professor Choi served for many years as a distinguished professor at Dankook University, later becoming its Vice President, and went on to found and lead the Action for Korea United Professors Association, a movement dedicated to national unity, civic responsibility, and values-based scholarship. Their presence together reflects a lifelong bond between teacher and student, and the enduring influence of education in shaping leaders committed not only to professional excellence, but to service, conscience, and the greater good of society.

In Belfast — once scarred by decades of conflict and now widely regarded as a living symbol of reconciliation — Ingill stands with a delegation from the Dubai Peace Award Institution, alongside former Zanzibar President Karume and Global Peace Foundation International President Jim Flynn, in the company of peacebuilders from around the world. The gathering reflects how places once defined by division can become beacons of dialogue and healing, and how leaders from different nations and traditions can come together to affirm a shared commitment to understanding, unity, and the hard but hopeful work of building lasting peace.

The Tuesday Club — a weekly gathering of senior leaders from media, business, government, and civil society who come together in a spirit of collegiality and reflection. More than a meeting, it is a forum for the exchange of wisdom, experience, and candid insight, where seasoned minds engage in thoughtful dialogue on the challenges and possibilities facing the nation, and where ideas are shaped with a shared hope of contributing, in their own quiet but influential ways, to the country’s future.

Strengthening leadership across Asia through the building of strategic partnerships and trusted government networks, Ingill works alongside key figures and institutions shaping the region’s future. These include collaboration with the Youth Ministers of Malaysia and Mongolia, the President of the U.S. Peace Corps Thailand, ASEAN Ambassadors based in Washington, D.C., and the Executive Director of the United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (UNESCAP). Together, these engagements reflect a shared commitment to youth development, regional cooperation, and values-based leadership, forging bridges between governments, international organizations, and civil society to advance peace, understanding, and sustainable progress across the Asia-Pacific.

Above photo: The Global Peace Festival 2022 brought together visionaries and leaders from government, business, faith, civil society, youth, and the arts in a powerful convergence of minds and hearts, united by a shared longing for peace and human dignity. More than a celebration, it was a platform for dialogue and inspiration — where diverse sectors affirmed common values, renewed their commitment to service, and explored how values-based leadership can shape a more compassionate, just, and harmonious world for the next generation.

Ingill delivers an energetic and deeply engaging special lecture to the students of the Technological University of the Philippines (TUP), challenging and inspiring them to see beyond the classroom and toward lives of purpose, service, and leadership. Drawing from his own journey and global experience, he speaks of values, responsibility, and the power of young people to become agents of positive change, igniting in the audience a renewed sense of possibility and a call to use their talents not only for personal success, but for the betterment of their communities and nation

In the United Arab Emirates, athletes with disabilities took center stage in a pioneering regional football festival that marked a significant milestone for inclusive sports in Asia. More than a tournament, the gathering celebrated courage, ability, and equal opportunity, demonstrating how football can break barriers, challenge perceptions, and create spaces where every individual — regardless of physical condition — can belong, compete, and shine. The event broadened the vision of Asian football, affirming that the game’s true power lies not only in excellence on the pitch, but in its capacity to foster dignity, confidence, and unity for all.

In 2009, Ingill made history by becoming the first to envision and champion social development through football as a core program of the Asian Football Confederation (AFC). Recognizing the game’s unique power to transcend language, culture, and social divides, he transformed football from a mere sport into a platform for education, inclusion, and hope. Under his leadership, the AFC embraced the ball as an instrument of change—reaching marginalized communities, empowering youth, promoting values of teamwork and discipline, and demonstrating that the world’s most beloved game could also be one of its most effective tools for building character, fostering peace, and uplifting lives across Asia.

Members of the AFC Social Responsibility Committee convene at a regional meeting alongside key leaders, including His Royal Highness Prince Ali bin Al Hussein of Jordan, to chart the course for football’s growing role as a force for social good. United by a shared vision, they deliberate on programs that harness the game’s immense influence to promote youth development, inclusion, peace-building, and community empowerment across Asia, reaffirming that beyond competition and trophies, football carries the responsibility — and the potential — to inspire positive change in the lives of millions.

At the 2023 Global Peace Convention, the Global Peace Leadership Corps is formally launched as a bold new platform to mobilize and nurture a generation of young leaders dedicated to service, ethical leadership, and nation-building. Envisioned as a network of values-driven changemakers, the Corps brings together youth from diverse backgrounds who share a commitment to peace, dialogue, and the common good, empowering them to translate idealism into concrete action for their communities, their countries, and the world.

Pia Wurtzbach, Miss Universe 2015, takes part in the Global Youth Summit as a goodwill ambassador, lending her voice, presence, and influence to the cause of peace, service, and youth empowerment. Beyond the crown and the spotlight, she embodies a commitment to compassion and social responsibility, inspiring young leaders and reaching out to communities in need with messages of hope, dignity, and the belief that service, when driven by values, can uplift lives and help build a more caring and united society

At an AFC gathering, Ingill, together with his wife, engages in thoughtful dialogue with senior leaders of the football community, building partnerships and shared commitments to advance social responsibility through sport. Beyond protocol and formalities, their presence reflects a deeper mission — to help shape programs that use football as a platform for education, inclusion, youth empowerment, and peace, and to affirm that the beautiful game, in the hands of principled leaders, can become a powerful instrument for uplifting communities and strengthening the social fabric across Asia.

At the 2025 Indo-Pacific Peace Forum in New Delhi, India, leaders from across governments, civil society, the academe, and the private sector gathered in a powerful show of solidarity to advance regional cooperation and affirm shared values. The forum served as a platform for dialogue on peace, security, and sustainable development, underscoring the conviction that the challenges of the Indo-Pacific can only be met through partnership, mutual respect, and a common commitment to the dignity and well-being of all. In this convergence of nations and perspectives, the spirit of unity for peace and collaboration across the Indo-Pacific was both symbolized and renewed.

A visit to the Philippine Embassy in Japan with Filipino women leaders, symbolizing the strengthening of civic solidarity and shared purpose across the Asia-Pacific. The gathering reflects the vital role of women in diplomacy, community building, and peopleto-people ties, as they come together to affirm their commitment to leadership, service, and the nurturing of enduring connections between nations and cultures in the region.

Together with leaders and implementors of the National Service Training Program (NSTP), Ingill takes part in a series of workshops dedicated to equipping and inspiring young people to become the next generation of peacebuilders. Through dialogue, training, and the sharing of best practices, the sessions focus on nurturing values-based leadership, civic responsibility, and a spirit of service, empowering the youth to translate idealism into concrete action and to play an active role in building more just, compassionate, and harmonious communities.

Having his wife, Angjee, joyfully walk beside him in Rotary service has made Ingill’s journey of giving even deeper, warmer, and more meaningful. Her presence brings not only companionship, but shared purpose—transforming service into a partnership of hearts, where commitment is strengthened by love, and where every act of generosity is enriched by the quiet joy of serving together for the good of others.

Ingill’s wife, Angjee Ra — herself a renowned Korean painter whose work reflects depth, sensitivity, and cultural soul — stands beside him as a constant source of strength, support, and inspiration. In her quiet presence and creative spirit, she embodies the partnership that undergirds his public mission, reminding all that behind every life of service and leadership is a wellspring of love, understanding, and shared purpose that sustains the journey

Ingill proudly champions the vision and legacy of his mentor, Dr. Hyun-jin Preston Moon, as he holds a special edition of BizNewsAsia published by fellow Manila Rotarian Tony Lopez. The moment reflects the passing on of ideals across generations — of leadership grounded in values, of peace-building rooted in service, and of a commitment to articulate a bold and hopeful vision for Asia and the world through both action and the written word

A joyful family moment in Manila as Ingill warmly welcomes his son’s family and his beloved grandson, Nam-guk. The child’s name, meaning “southern country,” carries special resonance, for it echoes the land Ingill has come to cherish as his own — Nam-guk, the warm and beautiful Philippines. In this tender gathering across generations, personal affection and adopted homeland converge, reflecting a life that has bridged cultures and nations, and a grandfather’s quiet hope that love for family and love for country may one day grow together in the heart of a young boy.

At the All Nations Women’s Group (ANWG) of the YWCA Manila, Ingill signs on behalf of Dr. Hyun-jin Preston Moon, author of The Korean Dream, in a symbolic moment of continuity and shared purpose. The occasion reflects how a vision articulated in one generation is received, affirmed, and carried forward by the next, as women leaders from diverse cultures and backgrounds gather to embrace common aspirations for peace, unity, and the flourishing of future generations.

At the 2023 Global Peace Convention in Manila, retired Philippine Air Force General Edward Libago stands alongside active PAF officers in a strong show of solidarity for a peace initiative spearheaded by the Global Peace Foundation. Their presence reflects the armed forces’ enduring commitment not only to national security, but also to peacebuilding, dialogue, and the nurturing of a culture of unity. Together, they affirm that lasting peace is built through cooperation among military leaders, civil society, and the international community, working hand in hand to uphold stability, mutual understanding, and the shared aspiration for a more harmonious world.

At the highly successful Global Youth Summit 2026, held in partnership with SM and the Bea Mendoza Foundation (BMF), Angjee, Leonard Faustino (Executive Director of GPF Philippines), and Bea Mendoza (CEO of BMF) stand united in a shared commitment to the next generation of leaders. Together, they champion the youth who are boldly taking the lead in advancing the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, affirming that through collaboration across the private sector, civil society, and values-driven organizations, young people can be empowered to become innovators, advocates, and builders of a more inclusive, sustainable, and hopeful future.

Ingill is invited to the Philippine House of Representatives as a special speaker in commemoration of the 80th anniversary of the United Nations, a fitting recognition of his lifelong work in diplomacy, peacebuilding, and international cooperation. The occasion includes a courtesy visit to House Speaker Martin Romualdez (Speaker Bojie Dy), underscoring the convergence of global ideals and national leadership, and reaffirming the Philippines’ enduring commitment to the UN’s founding vision of unity, dialogue, and shared responsibility for a more just and peaceful world.

The early days at the Asian Football Confederation, when Ingill first took on the mantle of advancing social responsibility through sport, coincided with a deeply personal chapter of his life — when his daughter was just three years old. It was a season marked by beginnings on many fronts: the launching of programs that would harness football for education, inclusion, and peace, and the quiet, formative years of fatherhood, when he was shaping not only initiatives across the region but also the values and dreams of a young child at home. The image speaks of a man balancing global 使命 and family, building a legacy in both the public arena and the intimate world of parenthood.

In 2025, alongside long-standing partner SM, and in collaboration with Bless Microfinance and the Global Peace Foundation, Ingill addresses a new generation of young leaders with a message of hope, purpose, and responsibility. Drawing from years of experience in peace-building, social development, and values-based leadership, he challenges the youth to see themselves not merely as beneficiaries of opportunity, but as future builders of communities and stewards of change — empowered to lead with integrity, compassion, and a commitment to shaping a more just and sustainable society.

GPF volunteers and staff stand as living witnesses to the belief that lasting national transformation begins with the renewal of the individual heart and character. United by the vision of One Family Under God, they work side by side across cultures, faiths, and backgrounds, driven by a shared conviction that when people grow in values, compassion, and responsibility, societies are strengthened and nations are uplifted. Through their service, they affirm that peace is not merely a lofty ideal, but a daily practice — built through countless acts of understanding, solidarity, and love for the common good

Ingill stands with members of the Global Peace Foundation’s Asia–Pacific leadership team, a diverse group of visionaries and practitioners united by a shared commitment to peace-building, values-based leadership, and regional cooperation. Together, they represent a growing movement across cultures and nations, working collaboratively to translate the vision of unity, service, and human dignity into concrete programs that uplift communities and strengthen the foundations of lasting peace throughout the Asia–Pacific region.

A regional gathering that vividly illustrates
how the social power of football is steadily
expanding across the Middle East —
bringing together communities, leaders,
and young people around a shared passion
for the game, and harnessing its ability to
transcend borders, bridge cultures, inspire
hope, and serve as a unifying force for
education, inclusion, and peace.

The Commission on Higher Education of the Philippines (CHED) has been a steadfast and active partner of the Global Peace Foundation in advancing peace education and transformative learning across the country and the region. Through collaborative programs, policy support, and academic exchanges, CHED has helped integrate values-based leadership, intercultural understanding, and social responsibility into higher education, thereby strengthening regional cooperation and nurturing a generation of students equipped not only with professional competence, but with the moral vision and civic commitment needed to become builders of peace and positive change in Asia and beyond.

Building a network grounded in shared vision and mutual trust, forged through a lasting partnership with the Villa family. Their collaboration reflects the strength that emerges when relationships are anchored in common values, long-term commitment, and a collective desire to serve, creating a foundation upon which meaningful initiatives and enduring impact can be built.

Rotary has given Ingill a wellspring of enduring motivation and a clear sense of mission in life, anchoring his desire to serve in values that transcend personal success. To be part of the Rotary Club of Manila — a fellowship of true gentlemen bound by integrity, compassion, and a commitment to the common good — has been, for him, a special gift from God. Within this brotherhood, he has found not only opportunities to serve, but also lifelong friendships, wise mentors, and a community that continually calls him to live out his faith and ideals through action, generosity, and humble leadership.

Leaders of leading universities across Asia come together in a spirit of collaboration to advance shared values, a common vision, and deeper cooperation throughout the region. United by the belief that education is a cornerstone of peace and progress, they exchange ideas and forge partnerships that strengthen academic excellence, promote cross-cultural understanding, and prepare future generations to lead with integrity, compassion, and a sense of responsibility to the wider Asian and global community

With Architect Felino “Jun” Palafox — one of the country’s most respected urban planners and a visionary leader whose work has shaped cities and communities across the Philippines and the region. Serving together on the Board of the Global Peace Foundation Philippines, they share a commitment to values-based leadership and nationbuilding, bringing together expertise in development, policy, and social responsibility to help advance initiatives that promote sustainable growth, human dignity, and lasting peace.

Ingill is conferred the Best Speaker Award for 2025 by the President of the Confederation of Indian Universities and the Chairman of the Indian Institute of Ecology and Environment, in recognition of his exceptional ability to articulate ideas that inspire, enlighten, and move audiences toward action. The honor affirms the depth of his thought, the clarity of his vision, and the moral force of his message — one that bridges education, environmental stewardship, and global responsibility — resonating strongly with academic leaders and students alike across the region.

Allight Village, the Global Peace Foundation’s signature community development program, stands as a beacon of hope for off-grid and underserved communities. By bringing sustainable energy, basic services, and livelihood opportunities, it has transformed darkness into light —both literally and figuratively. Today, these once-isolated villages are no longer defined by scarcity but by resilience, as local residents, working hand in hand with committed partners, now sustain and grow the initiative themselves, proving that when communities are empowered, they become stewards of their own progress and architects of a brighter future.

More than any measure of success or personal achievement, Ingill hopes to leave behind a legacy of meaning — one defined not by titles or accolades, but by lives touched, values passed on, and seeds of hope planted in the hearts of others. A legacy that speaks of service over self, compassion over indifference, and a quiet yet enduring contribution to a world made a little more just, more humane, and more united because he chose to live with purpose

Gorriceta is the Managing Partner and Head of the Corporate, Banking and Finance, and Technology, Media, and Telecommunications (TMT) Groups of Gorriceta Africa Cauton & Saavedra. – a multi- awarded and full-service Philippine law firm established in 2015 with offices in Singapore, Malaysia, and Thailand.
