At the Crossroads of Sovereignty and Truth: The Rotary Club of Manila’s 23rd Weekly Membership Meeting  At 12:30 PM, beneath the stately chandeliers and quiet elegance of the Manila Polo Club, President Raoul C. Creencia called the 23rd Weekly Membership Meeting of the Rotary Club of Manila to order. It was a gathering that felt both familiar and consequential — a convergence of fellowship and public discourse that has long defined the traditions of Asia’s first Rotary club. Outside, the late February sun filtered gently through the polo grounds. Inside, the room was filled with the steady hum of conversation among Rotarians, guests, and visiting dignitaries. The Rotary Club of Manila has always been more than a venue for luncheon meetings; it has served for more than a century as a forum where ideas, policy, and conscience meet. This particular Thursday would prove to be no exception. Moderating the program was STAR Rotarian Chris C. Tamesis, whose composed presence guided the meeting with both warmth and efficiency. Fellowship, Reflection, and the Rotary Spirit The meeting began with the familiar rituals that anchor Rotary gatherings across the world. The invocation was delivered by STAR Rotarian Francisco Roberto D. C. Mauricio, whose prayer invited reflection on gratitude, stewardship, and the responsibility of leadership. His words carried the quiet reminder that service, in Rotary, begins with humility before it becomes action. Members rose for the Philippine National Anthem, followed by the stirring strains of the Rotary Club of Manila Hymn, performed by the RCM World-Famous Music Chorale. Their voices echoed through the hall with a tone of pride and camaraderie, reinforcing the shared identity that binds generations of Rotarians. The recitation of The Four-Way Test was led by Vice President Karlo Eugene Josef M. Castro, whose clear cadence reminded those present of Rotary’s enduring ethical compass: Of the things we think, say, or do: Is it the truth? Is it fair to all concerned? Will it build goodwill and better friendships? Will it be beneficial to all concerned? These words — simple yet profound —continue to guide Rotarians across continents and cultures. Guests were warmly acknowledged by Moderator Chris Tamesis, reflecting Rotary’s longstanding tradition of hospitality. The RCM World-Famous Music Chorale returned with a spirited Welcome Song, setting a tone of celebration for the afternoon. The meeting also honored several birthday celebrants, including STAR Rotarian Coco Mauricio, Rotarian Raji Mendoza, Past Vice President Fausto Preysler, and Rotarian Jonas Gonzales. The traditional rendition of Maligayang Bati / Happy Birthday added a lighthearted moment to the proceedings. President’s Time: Stewardship of a Living Institution During President’s Time, President Raoul Creencia addressed the membership with a tone that balanced optimism and vigilance. Rotary clubs, he noted, must continually adapt to a rapidly shifting world — one defined by geopolitical tensions, technological disruption, and evolving civic responsibilities. The Rotary Club of Manila, founded in 1919, has witnessed nearly every chapter of modern Philippine history: colonial transition, independence, war, reconstruction, and democratic renewal. Through each era, the club has sought to remain both a moral compass and a convening force for dialogue. This meeting would soon remind everyone present why such dialogue matters. Introducing the Voice of the Afternoon The afternoon’s guest speaker was introduced by Director-Elect Carlos G. Serapio, whose introduction captured both the professional stature and intellectual courage of the guest. The speaker, Mr. David Nye, is a former Foreign News Editor of The Global Times in Beijing, China, a journalist whose career has placed him at the crossroads of international politics, media narratives, and the evolving power dynamics of the 21st century. His address carried a title that immediately signaled the gravity of the discussion ahead: “Narratives and National Interest: The Philippines in an Era of Global Influence.” What followed was not merely a speech. It was a sobering reflection on the complex battlefield where geopolitics, propaganda, and national identity now intersect. Narratives, Sovereignty, and the Invisible Battlefield Mr. Nye began with a vivid image that set the tone for the entire address: the Philippines standing at a crossroads where the salt spray of the West Philippine Sea meets the silent digital currents of psychological warfare. In his telling, the conflict surrounding the West Philippine Sea is not simply a territorial dispute. It is a layered struggle unfolding simultaneously across physical, informational, and psychological domains. He described two parallel fronts confronting the Philippines. The first is visible: maritime confrontations, gray-zone tactics, and acts of intimidation in contested waters. The second is invisible: a war of narratives unfolding in media platforms, social networks, and public discourse. The danger, he argued, is that nations can lose the second war long before the first one is fought. Gray Zone Tactics and the Strategy of Pressure According to Nye, the maritime actions of the People’s Republic of China in the West Philippine Sea illustrate what strategic scholars call “gray zone tactics.” These are actions carefully calibrated to remain below the threshold of open warfare, yet sufficiently aggressive to achieve strategic goals. Among the examples he cited were: • harassment of Filipino fishermen • environmental destruction of coral reefs • water cannon attacks on Philippine resupply missions • maritime intimidation by large coast guard vessels These acts, he emphasized, are not isolated incidents. They are components of a strategy designed to normalize encroachment and slowly reshape international perception of ownership. The ultimate objective is not necessarily to win a dramatic confrontation — but to create a new status quo. The Psychological Objective Yet Nye stressed that the physical confrontations at sea serve a deeper purpose. Their real function is psychological. Repeated intimidation is designed to produce a sense of helplessness — a narrative that a smaller nation cannot stand against a superpower. This is where the second front of the conflict emerges: information warfare. He described how propaganda networks attempt to frame the issue as a stark choice: “Submission or War.” In this false narrative, any defense of Philippine sovereignty is portrayed as reckless warmongering, while surrender is rebranded as “pragmatic peace.” Such framing, he explained, is a classic psychological tactic intended to divide public opinion and paralyze policy decisions. The Role of Disinformation Nye warned that the battlefield of influence has expanded dramatically in the digital age. Through networks of online trolls, coordinated messaging campaigns, and sympathetic influencers, narratives can be amplified with astonishing speed. These campaigns often promote defeatist rhetoric, question the legitimacy of Philippine defense policies, and portray foreign dominance as inevitable. By repeating such messages frequently enough, the objective is to reshape public perception. But the antidote, Nye argued, lies in transparency. He praised the Philippine government’s strategy of inviting journalists to accompany maritime patrols and document confrontations at sea. When the world sees video footage of water cannons or aggressive maneuvers, propaganda loses its power. “Light,” he said, “is the most effective disinfectant against disinformation.” The Challenge of Internal Vulnerability Perhaps the most uncomfortable part of Nye’s speech addressed the issue of internal complicity. He spoke candidly about what intelligence experts call a “Fifth Column”—individuals or institutions within a country that inadvertently or deliberately advance the interests of a foreign power. Such influence can manifest through political lobbying, economic incentives, and strategic investments designed to shape decision-making at multiple levels of government. Nye warned that influence operations often target local political structures, where financial incentives can create pockets of support that undermine national policy. He also referenced the complex role of Philippine Offshore Gaming Operators (POGOs), which in some cases facilitated flows of unregulated capital and the presence of foreign actors operating outside Philippine regulatory oversight. These developments, he suggested, highlight the need for vigilance in protecting strategic sectors such as telecommunications, infrastructure, and energy. Economic Independence as National Defense Nye argued that sovereignty in the modern era cannot rely solely on military strength. Economic resilience, he said, is equally critical. The Philippines must continue expanding trade partnerships with countries that respect international law and territorial sovereignty — including Japan, Australia, the European Union, and fellow ASEAN members. When a nation’s economy depends excessively on a single partner, that dependency can become a geopolitical lever. True independence requires diversified partnerships. Asymmetric Defense From a strategic standpoint, Nye emphasized the importance of asymmetric defense capabilities. Rather than attempting to match the naval strength of a much larger power, smaller states can develop systems designed to raise the cost of aggression. These include: • coastal defense systems • drone surveillance • cyber-security infrastructure • intelligence coordination with allies In such an approach, deterrence is achieved not by size but by strategic complexity. Educating the Next Generation A particularly compelling part of Nye’s message focused on civic education. He described the 2016 Arbitral Ruling under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea as a legal milestone that affirms Philippine rights in the West Philippine Sea. For Nye, the ruling is not simply a legal document — it is a symbol of national dignity and international law. He urged that future generations of Filipinos must understand its significance. A nation aware of its rights, he said, is far harder to manipulate. A Call for National Unity Nye concluded with a message that transcended politics. The struggle over the West Philippine Sea, he argued, should not be viewed through partisan lenses. It is not about being “pro-American” or “pro-Chinese.” It is about being pro-Filipino. The ocean, he observed, does not recognize political parties. When sovereignty erodes, it erodes for every citizen. He ended with a stirring reminder: The Philippines endured centuries of colonial rule. 
Its people fought hard for independence. To surrender sovereignty now — whether through intimidation or persuasion — would betray that long struggle. The Filipino spirit, he declared, cannot be bought. Dialogue and Reflection Following the address, the meeting opened into a lively Open Forum, where Rotarians engaged the speaker with thoughtful questions about geopolitics, media narratives, and the responsibilities of democratic societies in the age of digital information warfare. The exchange reflected the Rotary Club of Manila’s enduring role as a forum for serious civic conversation. Mr. David Nye engaged in a Q&A session with Sec. Anton Mauricio, PD Abe Pascual, DE Caloy Serapio, PIA Jordan Pizarras, STAR Rtn. Coco Mauricio, and PVP Joel Valdes. President Raoul Creencia later presented a Certificate of Appreciation to Mr. Nye in recognition of his insightful and thought-provoking address. A Meeting that Echoes Beyond the Hall At 2:00 PM, President Raoul formally adjourned the meeting. Yet the ideas shared that afternoon lingered long after the final applause. For over a century, the Rotary Club of Manila has brought together leaders not only to exchange pleasantries but to confront the questions that shape the nation’s future. On that Thursday in March, the conversation turned toward one of the defining challenges of our time: How a nation protects not only its territory — but its truth, its sovereignty, and its sense of self in a world where power increasingly moves through narratives. And as Rotarians departed the Manila Polo Club that afternoon, many carried with them a renewed awareness that defending the Philippines today requires more than ships and diplomacy. It requires clarity of mind, courage of conviction, and unity of purpose. Meeting Fellowship STEWARD OF CONTINUITY | Alberto Gatmaitan Romulo and the Discipline of Public Service  Steward of Continuity Alberto Gatmaitan Romulo and the Discipline of Public Service By PE Reginald T. Yu ALBERTO Gatmaitan Romulo entered public life late and left it quietly. In between, he occupied some of the highest offices of the Philippine state — not as a performer of authority, but as its steward. Trained by institutions long before he led them, shaped by restraint rather than ambition, Romulo’s life offers a rare study in how power can be exercised without noise, how service can endure without ownership, and how leadership, at its best, leaves things stronger than it found them. Character is revealed not in moments of triumph, but in moments when power could be used — and is not. There are people who enter a room and immediately announce themselves. Their presence fills the space, their authority made visible through volume, posture, or command. Alberto “Bert” Gatmaitan Romulo was not one of them. Those who met him for the first time often found themselves recalibrating their expectations. The authority came later — sometimes only after conversation had already begun. Bert spoke carefully. He listened longer than most. He rarely interrupted. When he disagreed, he did so without edge or spectacle, as though disagreement itself were not an act of combat but an invitation to think more precisely. This was not hesitation. It was discipline. Restraint, for Bert, was not a personality trait. It was a habit. Late one night, years ago, a stranger entered his home uninvited. The situation was inherently volatile: a private space breached, children sleeping upstairs, the ever-present possibility of fear escalating into violence. Yet when Bert encountered the intruder, there was no eruption. No assertion of dominance. No performance of authority. There was only composure. He greeted the man. Asked him to leave. Walked him out. Then returned upstairs to check on his children before resuming sleep. The incident ended not with confrontation, but with quiet closure. The story spread not because of danger averted, but because of the manner in which it was done. It unsettled people. It challenged assumptions. Was this courage? Was it confidence? Or was it something rarer — a temperament trained to refuse escalation even when escalation was justified? Bert never offered an explanation. He never told the story himself. That, too, was characteristic. Those who worked with Bert over the years observed the same pattern in less dramatic settings. Meetings that could have turned adversarial did not. Conflicts that invited theatrical posturing were met instead with questions. Decisions were framed not as victories to be claimed, but as consequences to be weighed. He seemed instinctively resistant to the intoxication of authority. Where others experienced power as permission — to speak louder, to dominate, to impose — Bert experienced it as constraint. The higher the office, the narrower the margin for error. The greater the responsibility, the greater the need for self-control. This inversion puzzled some. In political environments that reward assertion, Bert’s refusal to dramatize himself could be mistaken for passivity. It never was. Those who tested him learned quickly that restraint did not mean softness. It meant that when he finally spoke, he had already done the work others rushed past. Bert believed that power, once displayed, diminished. Authority, once flaunted, weakened. Influence, to endure, had to be exercised sparingly. He distrusted impulse. He distrusted moral grandstanding. He distrusted certainty that arrived too quickly. Instead, he cultivated preparation — intellectual, emotional, and ethical. Decisions, he believed, should feel inevitable only after they had been thoroughly questioned. This discipline made him reliable in moments when institutions faltered. When tempers flared, he cooled the room. When consensus fractured, he rebuilt process. When others sought cover, he sought clarity. It was not that he avoided conflict. It was that he refused to let conflict define him. In an age increasingly shaped by noise, Bert’s manner can seem almost anomalous. Yet it was precisely this quality — this refusal to weaponize power — that would place him, again and again, at the center of events where steadiness mattered more than spectacle. Before the titles, before the offices, before the public record, there was already a governing principle at work: power exists not to be displayed, but to be held. The chapters that follow trace how that principle was formed, tested, and applied across a lifetime of public service. But at its core, the story begins here — not with position, but with temperament. Not with ambition, but with restraint. Formation: The Making of Discipline Alberto Gatmaitan Romulo was born on August 7, 1933, in the town of Camiling, Tarlac, when the Philippines itself was still learning the discipline of independence. The nation was young, its institutions newly formed, its ambitions tempered by uncertainty. In the provinces, life moved at a deliberate pace. Seasons mattered more than slogans. Reputation was something earned slowly, and once lost, rarely recovered. Camiling offered no appetite for excess. It was a place that rewarded steadiness and distrusted display. In such towns, one learned early that attention was not something to seek, but something to deserve. Bert grew up in a household that reflected those values. His father, Gilberto Peña Romulo, and his mother, María Asuncion Buendia Gatmaitan, came from Pangasinan and Pampanga — regions shaped by work ethic, thrift, and a quiet sense of obligation. Authority in the Romulo home did not announce itself. It was assumed. Expectations were conveyed without flourish. Words were used sparingly, and precisely. Don Gregorio Romulo (1865–1921), the grandfather of Alberto Gatmaitan Romulo, belonged to a generation of Filipino leaders who helped shape local governance during the formative years of the American period. He served as Mayor of Camiling, Tarlac, in 1901, and later as Governor of Tarlac from 1910 to 1914, earning a reputation for steady leadership and public trust at a time of profound political transition. Born in Dagupan, Pangasinan, to Don Alberto Romulo and Doña Juana Besacruz, Don Gregorio received his formal education at Colegio de San Juan de Letran, one of the country’s most venerable institutions of learning. His life reflected the values of education, public service, and civic responsibility — values that would echo across generations. Alberto Gatmaitan Romulo, affectionately known as “Bert,” was later named in honor of his great-grandfather, a quiet testament to this enduring family legacy. His wife, Doña Maria Peña de Romulo (1869–1948) — Bert’s grandmother— was born to Angelo Peña and Ines Cabrera. The couple were married on July 15, 1894, forming a union that anchored the Romulo family through decades of social and political change. Together, Don Gregorio and Doña Maria laid the foundations of a lineage distinguished by public service, intellectual pursuit, and national contribution. In that environment, self-control was not framed as discipline imposed from above, but as respect extended outward — to parents, to elders, to the order of things. Restraint was learned not through reprimand, but through example. Even as a child, Bert displayed a preference for order. He was observant rather than demonstrative, attentive rather than impulsive. Teachers noticed that he listened intently, often longer than others, and spoke only after forming his thoughts. When he did speak, it was rarely to impress. More often, it was to clarify. preference for order. He was observant rather than demonstrative, attentive rather than impulsive. Teachers noticed that he listened intently, often longer than others, and spoke only after forming his thoughts. When he did speak, it was rarely to impress. More often, it was to clarify. By the late 1940s, Bert was a student at Ateneo de Manila, entering adolescence at a school that demanded not only intellect, but conscience. The Jesuit formation emphasized reflection before action, judgment before assertion. Excellence carried responsibility; brilliance without ethics was incomplete. Bert thrived in this environment not because he sought distinction, but because it aligned with habits already forming. He questioned assumptions. He resisted easy conclusions. He learned to pause — not as hesitation, but as method. At Ateneo, authority was earned through preparation. That lesson stayed with him. Upon graduating with First Honors in 1950, Bert made a choice that surprised some of his peers. He did not turn immediately toward law, philosophy, or public life. Instead, he chose numbers. At De La Salle University, he pursued commerce, majoring in accounting. The discipline offered no refuge for rhetoric. Balances had to reconcile. Every figure demanded explanation. Optimism unsupported by evidence was not inspirational — it was wrong. He graduated as Salutatorian, cum laude, in 1954, not through flourish, but through consistency. Accounting taught Bert something enduring: that every decision carries a cost, and that costs deferred do not disappear — they accumulate. Long before he would encounter national budgets or public finance, he had already absorbed its first rule: discipline is not the enemy of compassion; it is its prerequisite. Only after mastering limits did Bert turn to law. In his early twenties, at Manuel L. Quezon University, he encountered legal reasoning not as combat, but as structure. Law, he came to understand, was not primarily about winning arguments. It was about designing frameworks strong enough to withstand disagreement without collapse. Rules mattered because they were shared. Authority mattered because it was restrained. Properly understood, law did not impose order through fear; it sustained it through consent. Bert absorbed this quietly. He did not approach law as a stage for performance, but as a discipline of design — an architecture within which human conflict could be contained, managed, and resolved. He received his law degree in 1959. By the early sixties, his intellectual formation carried him farther still. In Madrid, at the Universidad de Madrid, Bert pursued advanced legal studies and earned his Doctor of Laws degree in 1962, with the distinction sobresaliente, the university’s highest honor. Madrid offered more than academic achievement. It offered distance. From Europe, Bert learned to see the Philippines not only as a place of immediate concern, but as part of a longer historical arc. European legal traditions emphasized continuity over rupture, precedent over impulse. Institutions endured precisely because they resisted haste. For a young Filipino scholar, the lesson was clarifying: progress did not require constant disruption. Often, it required patience. Living abroad sharpened his sense of proportion. He learned that legitimacy accumulates slowly and dissolves quickly. That authority, once abused, is difficult to restore. That institutions, not personalities, carry societies forward. By early adulthood, Bert had achieved something unusual but revealing. He was both a Certified Public Accountant and a member of the Philippine Bar — trained in precision and structure, in limits and systems. The pairing was not accidental. Accounting taught him restraint. Law taught him design. Together, they shaped a mind wary of shortcuts and deeply suspicious of solutions that promised speed without durability. Those close to him noticed his temperament even then. He did not rush decisions. He did not escalate disagreements. When challenged, he paused, gathered facts, and weighed consequences. Silence, when used deliberately, became persuasive. This was not indecision. It was preparation. By 1956, Bert had not yet entered organized civic leadership, much less public office. But the essentials were already in place. The discipline of restraint — intellectual, emotional, ethical — had been forged quietly over more than two decades. The world had not yet tested him. That would come next. Civic Awakening: Learning Leadership Among Equals By the early 1960s, Bert had returned to the Philippines intellectually complete but civically untested. He was in his late twenties — credentialed, trained, and deeply formed — yet still standing just outside the arena where character meets consequence. He had learned how systems worked. What he had not yet learned was how people did. That lesson would come not from government, but from civic life. The invitation arrived casually, almost unceremoniously. A friend — Albert del Rosario — asked Bert to join the Manila Jaycees. It was the sort of organization that rarely makes headlines but often makes leaders: young professionals committed to service, debate, and action, bound not by ideology but by shared responsibility. Bert accepted without fanfare. He did not see it as a step toward anything larger. At the time, it was simply a place where men of similar age and ability gathered to do useful work. What he encountered instead was his first rehearsal for public life. The Jaycees operated on a principle unfamiliar to many who would later hold office: authority was temporary, accountability immediate, and ego quickly exposed. There were no permanent titles, no inherited prestige. Leadership rotated. Decisions were debated openly. Influence had to be earned anew each year. For Bert, this environment proved instructive. He was not the most forceful voice in the room. He did not dominate discussions. Instead, he listened — often longer than others — and spoke with care. When disagreements arose, he showed an instinctive resistance to escalation. He asked clarifying questions. He sought consensus not through compromise of principle, but through precision of argument. It did not go unnoticed. Within his first year, Bert was invited onto a leadership slate. In an election led by Albert del Rosario, he was chosen as one of the directors alongside Sonny Belmonte, Ting Bengzon, and Ronnie Buencamino. Del Rosario himself was elected president by acclamation in 1969. For Bert, the election mattered less than the process. This was leadership without entitlement. Authority conferred not by age or pedigree, but by trust. It would shape how he understood power from that point forward. It would shape how he understood power from that point forward.The Jaycees were not a rehearsal for politics in the narrow sense. They were something more demanding: a test of temperament. Meetings were long. Opinions varied. Consensus was difficult. There were no staff to shield leaders from criticism, no protocol to mask disagreement. Bert discovered that his instinct for restraint — honed in classrooms and libraries — translated unexpectedly well into civic life. Where others grew impatient, he slowed the discussion. Where tempers flared, he softened tone without diluting substance. He did not seek to win arguments. He sought to make decisions durable. This made him dependable. This made him dependable.Colleagues began turning to him not in moments of celebration, but in moments of uncertainty. When discussions stalled, he was asked to clarify options. When disagreements hardened, he was asked to reframe the question. He became, quietly, a stabilizing presence. It was here — among peers, not superiors — that Bert first learned the subtle difference between authority and trust. Looking back years later, Bert would describe this period with characteristic understatement. He did not present it as destiny unfolding, nor as ambition awakening. But he acknowledged its significance. The Jaycees introduced him to something he had not yet encountered: the mechanics of collective decision-making. The reality that leadership was not about personal conviction alone, but about persuading others to share responsibility for an outcome. It was also his first exposure to public scrutiny — not from voters or media, but from equals who were unafraid to challenge him. That experience proved formative. Twenty-three years later, during a celebration marking Albert del Rosario’s sixtieth birthday, Bert would recall how that early invitation into civic life altered his trajectory. It was during that gathering that he thanked del Rosario not only for friendship, but for opening a door he had not known he was approaching. Twenty-three years later, during a celebration mWhen Bert later won his first electoral contest, del Rosario was the first to congratulate him. But that moment lay far in the future. By 1964, Bert’s participation in civic life had done something subtle but irreversible. It had shifted his understanding of responsibility. Public service was no longer abstract. It was personal. It involved disagreement, compromise, persistence, and restraint practiced under pressure. He did not yet seek office. He did not yet speak of governance. But the habits required for both were quietly taking root. The Jaycees did not give Bert ambition. They gave him rehearsal. Work Without Applause By this time, Bert had already acquired something rare for a man barely past thirty: a reputation for reliability without spectacle. He was not yet visible to the electorate, but he was known in institutions that valued discretion — corporate boards, policy circles, professional associations, and civic networks where competence mattered more than visibility. This was not accidental. Bert’s life after Spain unfolded not as a straight ascent, but as a deliberate accumulation of responsibility. He worked first where precision was unforgiving. In the late 1950s and early 1960s, as a cost accountant for the Container Corporation of America in Los Angeles, Bert learned how decisions reverberated across balance sheets. Numbers allowed no rhetoric. They revealed truth without emotion. The discipline stayed with him. Back in the Philippines, he entered legal and corporate service quietly. In 1959, he began working closely with Justice César Bengzon, then Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, serving as his assistant secretary. Bengzon was not merely a jurist; he was a moral benchmark — so austere in integrity that even proximity demanded discipline. Bert absorbed this ethic without commentary or imitation. It became internal. From there, his career progressed not through ambition but through trust. In the early 1960s, he served as Executive Committee Secretary at Elizalde & Company, then as Comptroller of Samar Mining, Inc. These were not headline positions. They were stabilizing ones. Colleagues noted that Bert did not dominate meetings. He clarified them. When others argued, he reconciled. When decisions stalled, he structured a way forward. Yet it was public health — not law or finance — that quietly expanded his understanding of service. In the mid-1960s, Don Paquito Ortigas invited Bert to become Executive Director of the Philippine Tuberculosis Society, an institution founded in 1910 and long committed to prevention, treatment, and research. Tuberculosis was increasingly under control, but its management required coordination across barangays, clinics, volunteers, and local governments — long before “community based healthcare” became policy language. Bert thrived in this environment. Throughout the late 1960s and early 1970s, he worked closely with barangays across Greater Manila, helping to strengthen referral systems, volunteer networks, and logistical coordination. It was here — almost unknowingly — that he learned grassroots governance: how credibility is earned face to face, how trust travels person to person, how institutions only function when communities believe in them. These were not political lessons yet. But they would become political instincts By 1970, Bert’s professional life had expanded beyond national borders once more. He was appointed Director of Finance and Administration of Jaycees International, headquartered in Coral Gables, Florida. The role required relocating his family to the United States for two years, overseeing financial systems for a global organization operating across dozens of countries. The assignment was daunting. He was selected from a large field of candidates, entrusted with ensuring that the organization not only functioned but remained solvent. Those who worked with him later recalled how quickly doubts faded. Bert brought order without intimidation, discipline without rigidity. Leadership, he believed, was a form of stewardship. By the time he returned to Manila in the early 1970s, his worldview had widened — but his temperament remained unchanged. He was more convinced than ever that institutions mattered, and that service required systems strong enough to survive their leaders. It was during this period — 1975, to be precise — that Alberto Romulo entered the Rotary Club of Manila. He did not arrive as an aspirant. He arrived as a student. Rotary was not impressed by résumés. It was sustained by memory. Its rituals, committees, and expectations formed a parallel education — one rooted in service but governed by procedure. Bert plunged into it with characteristic seriousness. Under the mentorship of Father Francisco “Frank” G. Reyes, OFM of the Santuario de San Antonio, he was appointed board secretary almost immediately. It was an apprenticeship by immersion. The Rotary Club of Manila operated through more than fifty committees, each with its own rhythms and histories. Bert attended multiple meetings a day, listened carefully, took meticulous notes, and learned how consensus was built rather than imposed. A Presidency That Revealed a Governing Style Rotary suited him. It rewarded preparation, discouraged ego, and placed service within structure. By 1977, just two years after joining, Bert was elected president of the Rotary Club of Manila — by one of the largest margins in the club’s history. His presidency was methodical and expansive. The day after his election in 1977, Bert visited every elected director individually — not ceremonially, but deliberately — to discuss mission, responsibility, and expectations. Mentorship, for him, was not inspiration. It was architecture. During his presidency, he appointed Francisco “Paqui” Ortigas III as board secretary, quietly preparing another generation for leadership. Those who served under him recall Those who served under him recallsomething consistent: clarity without coercion. Bert did not command. He aligned. That year, he hosted the Diamond Joint District Conference of Districts 380, 382, 385, and 386 in celebration of sixty years of service, publishing a commemorative Diamond Book and producing medallions, car stickers, and plates to mark the milestone — not as souvenirs, but as a record. Past District Governor Marianito Lichauco’s History of Rotary in the Philippines was supported and disseminated to all Philippine Rotarians, allowing the organization to “reach out to the past” in order to ground the present. He launched Operation Paglilinis ng Palengke, emphasizing public hygiene at the grassroots. He sponsored the Waiters Placement Seminar, bridging livelihood with dignity. Through RCM’s Medico-Surgical “Reach Out” Mission, medical assistance was extended to indigent communities in Northeastern Mindanao. The club participated in the First Metro Manila Restaurant and Small Eateries Cleanliness Contest. A Christmas Drive distributed ₱20,000 worth of goods. A ₱5,000 check was extended to the Rotary Club of Gumaca for fire victims. The Tulungan Center in Malate was completed at a cost exceeding ₱32,000. RCM Foundation, Inc. was established. Six Paul Harris Fellows were produced during his term. None of this was loud. All of it endured. By the late 1970s, his life had reached a rare equilibrium. He was professionally accomplished, deeply embedded in civic institutions, and intellectually grounded. At home, with his wife Rosie Lovely Tecson-Romulo, he was raising their children — Lupe, Mons, Roman, Berna, and Erwin — in a household where duty was modeled rather than preached. Politics had not yet called him. But the habits required for it — restraint, patience, institutional loyalty, and moral clarity — had already been rehearsed for nearly two decades. When history finally disrupted that equilibrium, Alberto Romulo would not need to reinvent himself. He would simply step forward. The moment invited grandeur. Bert declined excess. Bert articulated the logic with characteristic restraint: history was not nostalgia; it was instruction. One of the quiet triumphs of Bert’s Rotary presidency was achieved not through ceremony, but through credibility. Through sustained institutional engagement, Rotary secured Presidential Proclamation No. 1809, declaring January 29 to February 4 of every year as Rotary International Week in the Philippines. It was not a political act. It was a civic acknowledgment — recognition that voluntary service, when organized and sustained, merited national regard. Bert never claimed the achievement. He treated it as evidence that institutions, when patient, could be heard without shouting. The TOWER Awards: Recognition Without Privilege Among Bert’s most enduring contributions was the strengthening and institutionalization of the TOWER Awards, conceived in 1976 to honor Filipino workers whose excellence rarely attracted public notice. The philosophy was deliberate. The awards were not for prominence, but for contribution. They affirmed dignity without conferring rank. Bert ensured that the program was structurally embedded within Rotary Manila — not attached to his presidency, not branded by personality. Committees were formed. Criteria were clarified. Continuity was protected. Decades later, the TOWER Awards would remain Rotary Manila’s longest running and most nationally recognized program — a quiet confirmation of Bert’s belief that the best institutions survive their founders by design. Youth, Work, and the Shape of the Future The TOWER Awards: Recognition Without Privilege Bert’s Rotary presidency gave particular attention to the future — not as abstraction, but as preparation. Career information convocations were organized for graduating students. Job training and placement seminars were conducted for out-of-school youth and wards of Boys’ Town. Rotaract and Interact clubs were not merely sponsored but integrated into the club’s rhythm. Students were invited into Rotary meetings as participants, not symbols. During Youth Activities Week, Bert invited Diwata Reyes, then Editor-inChief of The Philippine Collegian, as Guest of Honor and Speaker — a subtle but unmistakable signal that critical thinking and civic engagement belonged in the same room. Bert was not unsettled by dissent. He believed institutions weakened when they excluded questioning voices. Perhaps the most revealing moments of Bert’s Rotary presidency occurred away from ballrooms and proclamations. During a visit to the children’s pavilion of the National Orthopedic Hospital, Bert and fellow Rotarians encountered a suffering that resisted language. Children lay crowded into cribs, many immobilized by casts, others suspended by slings. The club had come to deliver ten new cribs and to see what modest interventions — paint, cleanliness, order — could accomplish. Bert later wrote of the children’s eyes, of small hands waving, of a boy forcing a smile through pain. There was no rhetoric in the account. Only observation. From this encounter flowed Rotary’s intensified commitment to the 3-H Program — Health, Hunger, and Humanity. Under Bert’s watch, more than 70,000 doses of tetanus toxoid vaccine were airlifted from Canada to the Philippines for Rotary’s first fullscale immunization effort. For Bert, compassion was not sentimental. It was logistical. Bert’s presidency also deepened Rotary Manila’s international engagement. The club hosted the First Asian Rotary Fellowship Golf Tournament, attended Rotary International Conventions in Tokyo (1978) and Rome (1979), and expanded friendships across Asia. These exchanges mattered to Bert not for ceremony, but for habit. He believed that contact preceded trust, and trust preceded cooperation. Long before he would represent the Philippines abroad, he was already practicing diplomacy in its quietest form. Leaving Without Residue As his presidency concluded in June 1979 at the Manila Hilton, Bert did not speak of legacy. In his valedictory message, he spoke instead of obligation. His valedictory message at the close of his Rotary presidency was revealing — not for what it claimed, but for what it emphasized. There was no triumphalism. Instead, there was gratitude, continuity, and a call to carry the torch forward. He spoke of children in hospital wards, of modest interventions that produced dignity rather than dependency. He invoked not power, but responsibility — the idea that progress was built from countless small acts of discipline and care. Even then, one could glimpse the statesman he would later become. Rotary taught him something no classroom could: how ideals survived when translated into budgets, committees, and minutes of meetings. It taught him that leadership was less about command than about trust, and that institutions endured only when leaders resisted the temptation to personalize them. By 1979, when Bert stepped down as Rotary president, he had not yet entered politics. But the transition was already underway — not outwardly, but inwardly. He had learned how to carry authority lightly. He invoked the Roman citizen who carried a soldier’s pack beyond the required mile — not out of duty, but choice. Leadership, he believed, always demanded more than mandate. He passed the torch deliberately to President-Elect Francisco “Paqui” M. Ortigas III, thanked his board, acknowledged the Rotary Anns, and expressed gratitude to his wife, Lovely Romulo, whose presence he described simply and without flourish. There was no attempt to linger. By the end of the 1970s, Bert had not yet sought elective office. But he had already mastered a rarer discipline: how to lead without owning, how to influence without imposing, and how to leave without diminishing those who followed. When national politics finally called, it would not find a novice. It would find a man trained by institutions — ready to enter power having first learned its limits. The Threshold of Power: Entering Politics Without Losing Restraint Bert did not enter politics out of impatience. For most of his adult life, he had believed that institutions — when properly tended — could correct themselves. He trusted process. He trusted continuity. He trusted that reform, however slow, was preferable to rupture. By the early 1980s, he was already in his late forties — an age when many politicians were planning their second or third ascent. Bert had resisted that timetable. He had watched politics from close range, advised quietly, and served institutions whose influence depended on credibility rather than coercion. What he had not done — deliberately — was seek office. That restraint would make his eventual entry consequential. Then came August 1983. The assassination of Benigno “Ninoy” Aquino Jr. did not immediately turn Bert into a politician. It did something quieter and more unsettling: it collapsed his belief that silence was still a form of responsibility. Like many Filipinos of his generation — especially those who had spent decades building institutions from within — he waited at first, watching, listening, measuring. The streets, however, were no longer waiting. What followed in the months after Ninoy’s death was not merely outrage, but moral disorientation. Institutions that were supposed to protect order had become instruments of fear. The careful balance Bert had spent years mastering — between authority and restraint, power and accountability — had tipped. By 1984, the question confronting him was no longer whether he was prepared for politics. It was whether his refusal to enter it had become a form of evasion. Those closest to him noticed the change. He spoke less, but thought more intensely. Conversations that once revolved around policy design began circling back to first principles: legitimacy, consent, responsibility. The habits of discipline that had defined his life now pushed him toward a conclusion he had long resisted. Enough was enough. When Bert decided to run for the Regular Batasang Pambansa representing Quezon City, it was not framed as ambition. It was framed as duty. He joined a slate that included figures of unquestioned moral standing — Justice Cecilia Muñoz Palma and Orly Mercado — individuals whose presence signaled seriousness rather than opportunism. The decision was neither impulsive nor ideological theater. It was practical. By then, the Marcos regime had begun to fray — economically weakened, morally exhausted, and increasingly disconnected from public trust. Institutions were brittle. Voices inside government were few, and many of them compromised. Bert believed that withdrawal no longer preserved integrity. He entered the race without the vocabulary of defiance. His campaign was quiet, disciplined, and grounded in competence rather than outrage. He spoke of budgets, accountability, and the dangers of governing without limits — language that rarely electrified crowds but resonated with voters weary of excess. The campaign was austere by design. Bert did not posture. He did not promise transformation. He spoke instead about competence, restraint, and institutional repair. Voters responded not to charisma, but to credibility. He won. The Batasang Pambansa was not designed to be adversarial. It was a legislature operating within constraints, its independence circumscribed, its debates often performative. Many who entered it chose either accommodation or theatrics. Bert chose neither From 1984 to 1986, Bert served as assemblyman during one of the most volatile periods in Philippine political history. The Batasan itself was an uneasy institution — functioning, but strained; deliberative, but constrained. Bert approached it the only way he knew how: by mastering its rules, respecting its procedures, and using its limited space to insist on accountability. He was not a firebrand. He did not posture. He studied bills, asked procedural questions, and pressed for clarity in appropriations. His interventions were precise. When he spoke, it was usually late in the discussion — after listening, after weighing, after identifying where language failed logic. Colleagues noticed that he did not personalize disagreement. He challenged proposals without challenging people. In a political culture shaped by loyalty tests and retaliation, this unsettled both allies and opponents. Bert did not seek confrontation. But neither did he retreat. He was not incendiary. He was meticulous. February 1986: The Collapse of Certainty Then, in February 1986, the system finally collapsed. The snap elections of February 1986 ended whatever illusion of permanence the regime still possessed. The weeks that followed — marked by contested results, public outrage, and quiet defections — pushed the country toward rupture. The EDSA People Power Revolution did not merely depose a regime; it dissolved the political order that had governed Bert’s brief legislative career. The Batasang Pambansa was abolished. The question facing the country — and Bert himself — was what would replace it. When the EDSA People Power Revolution unfolded, Bert was not on the barricades. He was not on television. He was inside government, watching the institutional scaffolding give way. What distinguished him during those days was not visibility, but steadiness. He understood that revolutions succeeded or failed not only on the streets, but in the days after — when decisions had to be made without scripts, when power changed hands faster than rules could be rewritten. President Corazon Aquino, assembling a government amid uncertainty, looked not for loyalists but for stabilizers. She chose Bert as interim Minister of the Budget during the transition period. It was an inspired, if understated, choice. It was not a glamorous assignment. It was, in fact, among the most perilous. The new government inherited empty coffers, fractured agencies, and a public hungry for immediate transformation. Expectations were vast. Resources were not. Bert accepted the role without public celebration. Budgets reveal values. In times of upheaval, they also reveal discipline — or its absence. Bert brought to the task what he had always brought to institutions under strain: structure without rigidity, principle without drama. He believed that reform without fiscal responsibility was merely rhetoric postponed. His tenure was brief but consequential. He helped restore coherence to public finance at a moment when coherence itself was fragile. There were no grandstanding speeches, no self congratulation. There was simply work. Governing Without Noise When elections were called in 1987, Bert faced another decision. He could have remained safely within the executive branch, insulated from electoral risk. Instead, he resigned and ran for the twenty-four-seat Senate. He won — placing among the top candidates. The Constitution shortened what would have been a six-year term to five. Bert used every year. The Senate he joined was newly restored but deeply unsettled. Democracy had returned, but habits had not yet caught up. The chamber was crowded with ambition, memory, grievance, and expectation. Many senators spoke as if history itself were listening. Bert listened as if history would ask questions later. He was quickly recognized not for eloquence, but for dependability In the early years of the restored Congress, legislation arrived unevenly — some bold, some hasty, many symbolic. Bert gravitated instinctively toward the less visible work: shaping committee outputs, reconciling conflicting drafts, ensuring that laws were implementable rather than merely expressive. He believed that a bill unfinished in its details was a promise deferred to failure. By the early 1990s, his colleagues had come to rely on him as a stabilizing force. When debates grew heated, Bert would often intervene not with argument but with structure — summarizing positions, identifying points of convergence, and proposing a procedural path forward. It was leadership by calibration. This made him an unlikely but effective Majority Leader, a role he would hold for five years. Working closely with Senate President Neptali Gonzales Sr., Bert helped guide the legislative agenda with a rhythm that emphasized preparation over performance. The Senate functioned not because voices were raised, but because schedules were respected, committees were disciplined, and negotiations were conducted quietly. A former Senate President, Paterno, would later describe Bert’s stewardship as “indefatigable,” praising his ability to balance competing egos while maintaining legislative momentum. The compliment was telling: it spoke not of dominance, but of endurance. Bert’s legislative record reflected this temperament. Over the course of his Senate career, he served as principal author of 48 laws and co-author of 127 others — figures impressive not for their quantity alone, but for their coherence. His interests gravitated toward fiscal responsibility, governance reform, and institutional clarity. He was wary of laws that promised benefits without identifying funding, or authority without accountability. That wariness extended to his own conduct. In the mid-1990s, as pork barrel politics increasingly blurred the lines between legislation and patronage, Bert made a decision that surprised even his allies. For the final three years of his term, he refused to use his allocated discretionary funds. He argued publicly — and repeatedly — that legislators were not implementers, that appropriations belonged to the executive branch, and that the temptation to conflate lawmaking with spending eroded institutional integrity. It was not a popular position. It was not meant to be. Bert never framed the decision as moral superiority. He framed it as constitutional fidelity. “Legislators should legislate,” he said. “Project implementation is an executive function.” The clarity of the statement left little room for misinterpretation. Throughout these years, Bert remained remarkably consistent in another way: he resisted permanence. When his second term concluded in 1998, he declined to seek a third, despite encouragement from supporters who believed his experience was needed. Term limits, he insisted, were not inconveniences to be navigated but principles to be honored. This belief was not theoretical. It governed his choices even when it constrained them. By the end of his Senate career, Bert had become something increasingly rare in Philippine politics: a figure respected across factions, trusted across administrations, and untouched by scandal. body.text: Mark S. Gorriceta is the Managing Partner and Head of the Corporate, Banking and Finance, and Technology, Media, and Telecommunications (TMT) Groups of Gorriceta Africa Cauton & Saavedra. – a multi- awarded and full-service Philippine law firm established in 2015 with offices in Singapore, Malaysia, and Thailand.

He represents domestic conglomerates in their digitization efforts as well as the Philippines’ top technology companies – both local and global entities – and further renders his expertise in corporate structuring, tax, banking & finance, capital markets, equity financing, and in navigating complex cross-border commercial transactions. With over 20 years of experience in private practice, Mark has developed an extensive expertise in complex corporate transactions, commercial contracts, and regulatory matters in a range of areas that impact businesses – whether for start-ups or for Top 1000 companies in the Philippines. He is a leading lawyer in the Philippines in the fields of Capital Markets, Mergers & Acquisitions, and Securities Law. Mark has been recognized as one of the Philippines’ Top 100 Lawyers for four consecutive years (2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, and 2024) by the Asia Business Law Journal. With pioneering expertise on the law on digital assets, fintech, blockchain, virtual currencies, e-commerce, data privacy, and artificial intelligence, he is legal counsel to the biggest and most impactful technology and online companies in the Philippines and has been recognized as one of the Top Technology Media & Telco Lawyers in Asia and Ranked # 1 in the Philippines in the Tech/Fintech space.

A member of the Philippine Bar, Mark graduated law with honors and holds a Bachelor of Arts – Political Science degree from the Ateneo de Manila University. He completed certificate courses in Finance at the Asian Institute of Management. He attended certificates courses in Corporate Finance at Harvard University. He also completed several Masterclasses on Blockchain, Distributed Ledger & Smart Contracts in Singapore and Hong Kong. Mark is currently a faculty member of the Ateneo de Manila University’s Graduate School of Business and teaches Mergers & Acquisitions for the Advanced Module Diploma Course in Corporate Finance. Mark also serves as lecturer at the Fintech and Regulatory Innovation Program of the Mapua University in collaboration with the University of Cambridge of England.

Dr. Donald Patrick Lim stands as one of the Philippines’ most accomplished and forwardlooking leaders in the fields of digital transformation, business innovation, and nationbuilding. He currently serves as President of DITO CME Holdings Corporation, a publicly listed investment holding company with interests in telecommunications, media, and technology, including DITO Telecommunity. He is also the President of the Management Association of the Philippines for 2026.

Over the past two decades, Dr. Lim has held key leadership roles across multiple industries — media, advertising, telecommunications, and digital — making him one of the few executives with deep, cross-sector expertise. He previously served as Country CEO of Dentsu Aegis Philippines, Chief Digital Officer of ABS-CBN Corporation, Managing Director of MRM Manila, and CEO of Yehey Corporation and Media Contacts Manila. Across these positions, he helped shape the evolution of the Philippine digital economy and mentored a new generation of marketing and technology professionals.

Recognizing the need for national collaboration in emerging technologies, Dr. Lim founded the Blockchain Council of the Philippines and the Cybersecurity Council of the Philippines, and he is the Trustee and Board Chair of the Global AI Council Philippines. These organizations unite government, industry, and academe to build digital trust, advance innovation, and prepare the Philippines for the challenges of an AI-driven and blockchain-enabled future. His leadership has made him a central figure in the country’s efforts to establish governance frameworks and ethical standards in the digital age.

Beyond his corporate and advocacy work, Dr. Lim is a respected educator, researcher, and thought leader. He has taught in leading universities, including the University of Asia and the Pacific, De La Salle University, San Beda University, and Enderun Colleges, where he currently teaches courses on Blockchain and Artificial Intelligence. He has also been an adjunct professor at the Asian Institute of Management and Bradford University in the United Kingdom.

Catherine Denise “Catz” GACPh Jalandoni is a leading voice in ethical AI, digital governance, and inclusive innovation— shaping conversations that bridge technology, policy, and social impact across borders.

As President of the Global AI Council Philippines, she advances responsible AI adoption while positioning the Philippines within global dialogues on artificial intelligence, fintech, and emerging technologies.

Catz also serves as the President of the Global AI Council Philippines and the Institute of Corporate Directors Philippines, where she champions leadership excellence, corporate responsibility, and future-ready governance. Through CSJ Events Management, she leads advocacy-driven initiatives that convene government, industry, and civil society around transformative ideas and policy-aligned innovation.

A passionate advocate for women’s leadership in technology, Catz consistently amplifies the role of women in shaping ethical, inclusive, and people-centered digital futures. Her work emphasizes the importance of governance frameworks that ensure AI and fintech innovations expand opportunity, protect trust, and deliver real social value.

Beyond her professional leadership, Catz brings a deeply human lens to innovation. As a mother of five and a recognized thought leader in AI and digital transformation, she inspires others—especially women— to take space, own their expertise, and lead with conviction. Her leadership reflects a powerful blend of policy insight, entrepreneurial drive, and values-based advocacy, ensuring that technology serves not just markets, but people and communities worldwide.

articles.title: At the Crossroads of Sovereignty and Truth: The Rotary Club of Manila’s 23rd Weekly Membership Meeting

body.text: At 12:30 PM, beneath the stately chandeliers and quiet elegance of the Manila Polo Club, President Raoul C. Creencia called the 23rd Weekly Membership Meeting of the Rotary Club of Manila to order. It was a gathering that felt both familiar and consequential — a convergence of fellowship and public discourse that has long defined the traditions of Asia’s first Rotary club.

Outside, the late February sun filtered gently through the polo grounds. Inside, the room was filled with the steady hum of conversation among Rotarians, guests, and visiting dignitaries. The Rotary Club of Manila has always been more than a venue for luncheon meetings; it has served for more than a century as a forum where ideas, policy, and conscience meet. This particular Thursday would prove to be no exception.
Moderating the program was STAR Rotarian Chris C. Tamesis, whose composed presence guided the meeting with both warmth and efficiency.
Fellowship, Reflection, and the Rotary Spirit
The meeting began with the familiar rituals that anchor Rotary gatherings across the world.

The invocation was delivered by STAR Rotarian Francisco Roberto D. C. Mauricio, whose prayer invited reflection on gratitude, stewardship, and the responsibility of leadership. His words carried the quiet reminder that service, in Rotary, begins with humility before it becomes action.

Members rose for the Philippine National Anthem, followed by the stirring strains of the Rotary Club of Manila Hymn, performed by the RCM World-Famous Music Chorale. Their voices echoed through the hall with a tone of pride and camaraderie, reinforcing the shared identity that binds generations of Rotarians.
The recitation of The Four-Way Test was led by Vice President Karlo Eugene Josef M. Castro, whose clear cadence reminded those present of Rotary’s enduring ethical compass:
Of the things we think, say, or do:
Is it the truth?
Is it fair to all concerned?
Will it build goodwill and better friendships?
Will it be beneficial to all concerned?
These words — simple yet profound —continue to guide Rotarians across continents and cultures.

Guests were warmly acknowledged by Moderator Chris Tamesis, reflecting Rotary’s longstanding tradition of hospitality. The RCM World-Famous Music Chorale returned with a spirited Welcome Song, setting a tone of celebration for the afternoon.

The meeting also honored several birthday celebrants, including STAR Rotarian Coco Mauricio, Rotarian Raji Mendoza, Past Vice President Fausto Preysler, and Rotarian Jonas Gonzales. The traditional rendition of Maligayang Bati / Happy Birthday added a lighthearted moment to the proceedings.
President’s Time: Stewardship of a Living Institution
During President’s Time, President Raoul Creencia addressed the membership with a tone that balanced optimism and vigilance.
Rotary clubs, he noted, must continually adapt to a rapidly shifting world — one defined by geopolitical tensions, technological disruption, and evolving civic responsibilities.

The Rotary Club of Manila, founded in 1919, has witnessed nearly every chapter of modern Philippine history: colonial transition, independence, war, reconstruction, and democratic renewal. Through each era, the club has sought to remain both a moral compass and a convening force for dialogue.
This meeting would soon remind everyone present why such dialogue matters.
Introducing the Voice of the Afternoon
The afternoon’s guest speaker was introduced by Director-Elect Carlos G. Serapio, whose introduction captured both the professional stature and intellectual courage of the guest.

The speaker, Mr. David Nye, is a former Foreign News Editor of The Global Times in Beijing, China, a journalist whose career has placed him at the crossroads of international politics, media narratives, and the evolving power dynamics of the 21st century.
His address carried a title that immediately signaled the gravity of the discussion ahead:
“Narratives and National Interest: The Philippines in an Era of Global Influence.”
What followed was not merely a speech. It was a sobering reflection on the complex battlefield where geopolitics, propaganda, and national identity now intersect.
Narratives, Sovereignty, and the Invisible Battlefield

Mr. Nye began with a vivid image that set the tone for the entire address: the Philippines standing at a crossroads where the salt spray of the West Philippine Sea meets the silent digital currents of psychological warfare.

In his telling, the conflict surrounding the West Philippine Sea is not simply a territorial dispute. It is a layered struggle unfolding simultaneously across physical, informational, and psychological domains.
He described two parallel fronts confronting the Philippines.
The first is visible: maritime confrontations, gray-zone tactics, and acts of intimidation in contested waters.
The second is invisible: a war of narratives unfolding in media platforms, social networks, and public discourse.
The danger, he argued, is that nations can lose the second war long before the first one is fought.
Gray Zone Tactics and the Strategy of Pressure
According to Nye, the maritime actions of the People’s Republic of China in the West Philippine Sea illustrate what strategic scholars call “gray zone tactics.”
These are actions carefully calibrated to remain below the threshold of open warfare, yet sufficiently aggressive to achieve strategic goals.
Among the examples he cited were:
• harassment of Filipino fishermen
• environmental destruction of coral reefs
• water cannon attacks on Philippine resupply missions
• maritime intimidation by large coast guard vessels
These acts, he emphasized, are not isolated incidents.
They are components of a strategy designed to normalize encroachment and slowly reshape international perception of ownership.
The ultimate objective is not necessarily to win a dramatic confrontation — but to create a new status quo.
The Psychological Objective
Yet Nye stressed that the physical confrontations at sea serve a deeper purpose.
Their real function is psychological.
Repeated intimidation is designed to produce a sense of helplessness — a narrative that a smaller nation cannot stand against a superpower.
This is where the second front of the conflict emerges: information warfare.
He described how propaganda networks attempt to frame the issue as a stark choice:
“Submission or War.”
In this false narrative, any defense of Philippine sovereignty is portrayed as reckless warmongering, while surrender is rebranded as “pragmatic peace.”
Such framing, he explained, is a classic psychological tactic intended to divide public opinion and paralyze policy decisions.
The Role of Disinformation

Nye warned that the battlefield of influence has expanded dramatically in the digital age. Through networks of online trolls, coordinated messaging campaigns, and sympathetic influencers, narratives can be amplified with astonishing speed.
These campaigns often promote defeatist rhetoric, question the legitimacy of Philippine defense policies, and portray foreign dominance as inevitable.
By repeating such messages frequently enough, the objective is to reshape public perception.
But the antidote, Nye argued, lies in transparency.
He praised the Philippine government’s strategy of inviting journalists to accompany maritime patrols and document confrontations at sea.
When the world sees video footage of water cannons or aggressive maneuvers, propaganda loses its power.
“Light,” he said, “is the most effective disinfectant against disinformation.”
The Challenge of Internal Vulnerability

Perhaps the most uncomfortable part of Nye’s speech addressed the issue of internal complicity. He spoke candidly about what intelligence experts call a “Fifth Column”—individuals or institutions within a country that inadvertently or deliberately advance the interests of a foreign power.
Such influence can manifest through political lobbying, economic incentives, and strategic investments designed to shape decision-making at multiple levels of government.
Nye warned that influence operations often target local political structures, where financial incentives can create pockets of support that undermine national policy.

He also referenced the complex role of Philippine Offshore Gaming Operators (POGOs), which in some cases facilitated flows of unregulated capital and the presence of foreign actors operating outside Philippine regulatory oversight.
These developments, he suggested, highlight the need for vigilance in protecting strategic sectors such as telecommunications, infrastructure, and energy.
Economic Independence as National Defense
Nye argued that sovereignty in the modern era cannot rely solely on military strength.
Economic resilience, he said, is equally critical.

The Philippines must continue expanding trade partnerships with countries that respect international law and territorial sovereignty — including Japan, Australia, the European Union, and fellow ASEAN members.
When a nation’s economy depends excessively on a single partner, that dependency can become a geopolitical lever.
True independence requires diversified partnerships.
Asymmetric Defense
From a strategic standpoint, Nye emphasized the importance of asymmetric defense capabilities.
Rather than attempting to match the naval strength of a much larger power, smaller states can develop systems designed to raise the cost of aggression.
These include:
• coastal defense systems
• drone surveillance
• cyber-security infrastructure
• intelligence coordination with allies
In such an approach, deterrence is achieved not by size but by strategic complexity.
Educating the Next Generation
A particularly compelling part of Nye’s message focused on civic education.
He described the 2016 Arbitral Ruling under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea as a legal milestone that affirms Philippine rights in the West Philippine Sea.
For Nye, the ruling is not simply a legal document — it is a symbol of national dignity and international law.
He urged that future generations of Filipinos must understand its significance.
A nation aware of its rights, he said, is far harder to manipulate.
A Call for National Unity
Nye concluded with a message that transcended politics.
The struggle over the West Philippine Sea, he argued, should not be viewed through partisan lenses.
It is not about being “pro-American” or “pro-Chinese.”
It is about being pro-Filipino.
The ocean, he observed, does not recognize political parties. When sovereignty erodes, it erodes for every citizen.
He ended with a stirring reminder:

The Philippines endured centuries of colonial rule. 
Its people fought hard for independence.
To surrender sovereignty now — whether through intimidation or persuasion — would betray that long struggle.
The Filipino spirit, he declared, cannot be bought.
Dialogue and Reflection

Following the address, the meeting opened into a lively Open Forum, where Rotarians engaged the speaker with thoughtful questions about geopolitics, media narratives, and the responsibilities of democratic societies in the age of digital information warfare.
The exchange reflected the Rotary Club of Manila’s enduring role as a forum for serious civic conversation.
Mr. David Nye engaged in a Q&A session with Sec. Anton Mauricio, PD Abe Pascual, DE Caloy Serapio, PIA Jordan Pizarras, STAR Rtn. Coco Mauricio, and PVP Joel Valdes.
President Raoul Creencia later presented a Certificate of Appreciation to Mr. Nye in recognition of his insightful and thought-provoking address.
A Meeting that Echoes Beyond the Hall
At 2:00 PM, President Raoul formally adjourned the meeting.
Yet the ideas shared that afternoon lingered long after the final applause.
For over a century, the Rotary Club of Manila has brought together leaders not only to exchange pleasantries but to confront the questions that shape the nation’s future.
On that Thursday in March, the conversation turned toward one of the defining challenges of our time:
How a nation protects not only its territory — but its truth, its sovereignty, and its sense of self in a world where power increasingly moves through narratives.
And as Rotarians departed the Manila Polo Club that afternoon, many carried with them a renewed awareness that defending the Philippines today requires more than ships and diplomacy.
It requires clarity of mind, courage of conviction, and unity of purpose.
Meeting Fellowship
