Reginald T. Yu
Editor-in-Chief

There are moments in history when the world quietly crosses an invisible threshold — when a new force begins to shape economies, societies, and even the way human beings understand themselves. Today, that force is Artificial Intelligence. It is transforming industries, redefining productivity, and altering the contours of global competition with a speed that few could have imagined only a decade ago.

For a nation like the Philippines, standing at the intersection of opportunity and uncertainty in the digital age, the question is no longer whether artificial intelligence will influence our future, but how prepared we are to shape that future responsibly.

It is therefore both timely and consequential that the Rotary Club of Manila, through its 24th Weekly Membership Meeting, brings attention to the theme “The State of the Nation in AI.” This gathering invites Rotarians to engage with one of the most important conversations of our era — the emergence of artificial intelligence and related technologies such as blockchain as transformative forces that will influence nearly every sector of Philippine society. As the country continues its transition toward a knowledge-driven economy, the discussion on AI has moved beyond the laboratories of technologists and into the broader arenas of public policy, governance, business, and civic leadership.

Artificial intelligence has already begun reshaping the world in ways both visible and subtle. Algorithms increasingly guide financial decisions, enhance medical diagnostics, optimize logistics networks, and personalize digital experiences. Across the globe, governments are grappling with how to harness these capabilities while safeguarding ethical principles and public trust. For emerging economies like the Philippines, the stakes are particularly high. AI represents both an extraordinary opportunity for national advancement and a challenge that requires foresight, discipline, and collaboration.

For decades, the Philippines has built its reputation as a global center for talent in information technology and business process management. The country’s workforce, young, dynamic, and highly adaptable, has been a critical driver of the digital services industry. Yet the rise of artificial intelligence is redefining the landscape in which that talent operates. Automation, machine learning, and intelligent systems are changing the nature of work itself. Jobs that once depended on repetitive processes are evolving toward roles that demand creativity, strategic thinking, and advanced technical skills. The nation must therefore ensure that its workforce is not displaced by the new technological wave but empowered by it.

This transformation demands a holistic approach that integrates education, industry, and government policy. Universities must adapt their curricula to prepare students for the realities of a digital and AI-driven economy. Businesses must invest in innovation and research rather than merely adopting technologies developed elsewhere. Policymakers must craft frameworks that encourage progress while protecting the public interest. In this sense, artificial intelligence is not simply a technological issue — it is a national development issue.

Equally important is the ethical dimension of artificial intelligence. As machines become capable of making decisions that influence human lives, society must ask profound questions about accountability, fairness, and transparency. Algorithms trained on biased data can inadvertently reproduce inequality. Automated systems, if poorly governed, may undermine privacy and erode trust in institutions. These concerns remind us that technology itself is neutral; it is the values guiding its use that determine whether it becomes a force for progress or a source of unintended harm.

Here lies the enduring relevance of Rotary. For more than a century, the Rotary Club of Manila has stood as a forum where leaders from different fields gather to discuss ideas that shape the nation. Rotary’s guiding principle of Service Above Self compels its members to view technological innovation not merely as a tool for profit but as a means of advancing the common good. When conversations about artificial intelligence take place within such a setting, they acquire a deeper dimension. They become discussions not only about innovation but about responsibility.

The Philippines is entering a critical moment in its digital evolution. Around the world, nations are racing to establish leadership in artificial intelligence. Investments in research laboratories, startup ecosystems, and technology infrastructure are accelerating. Countries that succeed in cultivating AI capabilities will not only strengthen their economies but also shape the global standards governing this technology. Those that fail to adapt risk falling behind in a world increasingly driven by data and intelligent systems.

Yet the Philippines possesses advantages that should not be underestimated. The country’s vibrant technology community, its entrepreneurial spirit, and its growing culture of innovation provide fertile ground for progress. Filipino ingenuity has repeatedly demonstrated an ability to transform constraints into opportunities. If these strengths are aligned with thoughtful policy and sustained investment in education and research, the nation can carve out a meaningful role in the global AI ecosystem.

Still, progress will require more than ambition. It will demand collaboration across sectors and a shared commitment to preparing society for the changes that lie ahead. Artificial intelligence cannot be viewed solely as a technological phenomenon; it must be understood as a societal transformation. It will influence employment, governance, national security, and even the ways communities interact with information and truth. The responsibility of leaders is therefore not only to embrace innovation but to guide it with wisdom.

This is why conversations such as the one convened at the Rotary Club of Manila are so vital. They create a space where civic leaders, professionals, entrepreneurs, and policymakers can reflect on the direction of the nation and the forces shaping its future. They remind us that technological change is not an abstract concept unfolding somewhere else in the world; it is happening here, within our own institutions, industries, and communities.

Artificial intelligence will undoubtedly transform the Philippines in the years ahead. The question is whether that transformation will be guided by deliberate strategy and ethical leadership or by the uncontrolled momentum of technological disruption. Forums like this gathering encourage the former. They invite thoughtful dialogue and inspire the kind of leadership that ensures innovation remains aligned with the broader aspirations of society.

Ultimately, the rise of artificial intelligence is not just about machines learning to think. It is about human beings learning to lead in a world where technology moves faster than ever before. It is about recognizing that the future of innovation must remain anchored in the timeless values of responsibility, integrity, and service.

In convening this timely discussion on “The State of the Nation in AI,” the Rotary Club of Manila once again affirms its role as a platform for meaningful national dialogue. The conversation it hosts today is not merely about technology. It is about the direction of the Philippines itself. And as Rotarians gather to explore this evolving frontier, they do so with the understanding that the true measure of progress lies not in the power of our machines, but in the wisdom with which we choose to use them.
My Kuya Edgard

In Rotary, we often speak of fellowship as one of the quiet yet enduring gifts of membership. We may first come together as colleagues and professionals, but over time those associations deepen into something far more meaningful -- friendships forged through shared ideals, companionship in service, and a sense of brotherhood grounded in a common calling. It is in that spirit of fellowship that we remember today our fellow Manila Rotarian, Edgard Cabangon.

Edgard and I called each other “Kuya,” a simple yet warm term of endearment that reflected the easy familiarity between us. While we were not particularly close, there was a quiet friendship that existed between us. I had known his late father—the good Ambassador—and would occasionally attend his birthday celebrations and other gatherings where I would see Kuya Edgard.
Through Rotary, I would later have the opportunity to know my Kuya better.

Kuya Edgard lived a life that spoke eloquently of perseverance and resolve. Through determination and hard work, he continued to build and expand the various family businesses entrusted to him. Yet those who encountered him within the fellowship of the Rotary Club of Manila knew that his accomplishments in business were only one dimension of who he was. What distinguished him most was not merely the success he achieved, but the character with which he carried it.

There was something unmistakably authentic about Kuya Edgard. He was proud of his journey and of the values that had guided him along the way. But that pride was never accompanied by arrogance. Rather, it was the quiet confidence of a man who had worked hard, overcome challenges, and earned the right to stand where he stood.

Within our Rotary meetings and gatherings, Kuya Edgard was a familiar and reassuring presence. During the times when he was able to personally attend, he did not simply show up -- he participated with sincerity and warmth. Whether during a luncheon or a simple conversation among friends, one could sense that he genuinely valued the fellowship that Rotary nurtures.
The Rotary Club of Manila, after all, is a rare space in our world -- where accomplished men gather not to compete with one another, but to serve together.

Kuya Edgard understood that deeply. He recognized that the true measure of success is not found in wealth or recognition alone, but in the difference one makes in the lives of others. In that sense, his life reflected one of the enduring ideals we hold dear in Rotary: Service Above Self.

On a more personal note, I will always remember Kuya Edgard’s kindness and generosity in our own interactions. Even while he was already undergoing treatment, he continued to respond to my requests for media coverage of the various activities of the Club and of the District. That quiet willingness to support Rotary -- even while facing personal challenges -- spoke volumes about his commitment to the fellowship we share. I also remember the welcoming smile he carried whenever our paths crossed. It was a simple gesture, yet one that conveyed warmth and goodwill -- qualities that often say more about a person than any formal achievement.

Kuya Edgard’s generosity likewise extended in ways that I personally experienced. He graciously sponsored a newspaper spread featuring my induction as RCM President, a gesture that I deeply appreciated and will always remember. Despite his failing health, he also made sure that his news crew continued covering the Club’s activities and that these were featured in the press.

Regrettably, I must also admit a personal sadness -- that I never had the opportunity to visit him in the hospital. It is one of those small regrets that reminds us how quickly time passes, and how important it is to cherish the presence of our friends while we still have the chance.

Indeed, the Rotary ideal is often expressed not in grand pronouncements, but in the quiet consistency with which a person lives. Kuya Edgard embodied that quiet consistency. He worked hard, built much, and in his own way contributed to the greater good. Through it all, he remained connected to the fellowship that binds us together as Rotarians.

For those of us privileged to share that fellowship with him, our memories will not simply be of a businessman or a civic leader. We will remember the man who sat beside us at the same tables, who shared in the same laughter, and who joined us in the same mission of service.

In the Rotary Club of Manila -- the oldest Rotary club in Asia -- our legacy is not defined solely by the projects we undertake or the milestones we celebrate. It is also shaped by the lives of the men who pass through our fellowship, each leaving behind a part of their story, their character, and their example.
Kuya Edgard’s story is now part of that legacy.

As we remember him today, we do so with gratitude -- for his friendship, for his presence among us, and for the inspiration of a life lived with determination and purpose. Though he may no longer sit beside us in fellowship, the memory of our brother Rotarian remains woven into the shared history of this Club and into the hearts of those who knew him.
May we honor that memory by continuing the work that Rotary calls us to do: to serve with integrity, to lead with humility, and to nurture the fellowship that gives meaning to our journey.

And so today we say not only farewell, but also thank you -- to our brother in Rotary, Edgard Cabangon. His life reminds us that success finds its deepest meaning when it is accompanied by generosity, humility, and service to others.
May he rest in peace, and may his legacy continue to inspire us all.

Guest of Honor and Speaker  His Excellency Jing Quan was born in July 1975 in Shaanxi Province, China. Ambassador Jing earned a bachelor's degree in English from Xian Foreign Studies University, a master’s degree, and subsequently a PhD in international relations. He entered the foreign service in 1997 as a Staff Member at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and remained in that role until 1998. In 1998-2002, he was Attaché and Third Secretary, Embassy of the People's Republic of China in the Kingdom of Thailand. 2002-2009, he was Third Secretary and Deputy Director, Department of North American and Oceanian Affairs, Ministry of Foreign Affairs. 2009-2011, he was Second Secretary and later First Secretary, Embassy of the People's Republic of China in the United States of America. 2011-2018, he went back home to be First Secretary, Director and Counsellor, Department of North American and Oceanian Affairs. 2018-2021, Deputy Director-General, Department of North American and Oceanian Affairs, MFA. 2021-2025, as Minister and subsequently the Deputy Chief of Mission, Embassy of the People's Republic of China in the United States of America. On December 11, 2025, he officially became the People’s Republic of China’s Ambassador to the Republic of the Philippines. Ambassador Quan is married with one daughter. The Intelligence Age Begins: Rotary Club of Manila Hosts a Landmark Dialogue on Artificial Intelligence PE Reginald T. Yu The 24th Weekly Membership Meeting of the Rotary Club of Manila gathered Rotarians, guests, and distinguished thought leaders at the historic Manila Polo Club for a timely and farreaching conversation on one of the most transformative forces of our time — Artificial Intelligence. Presided over by Rotary Club of Manila President Raoul C. Creencia, the meeting underscored Rotary’s enduring tradition of convening leaders to examine issues that will shape the future of society. With Club Secretary Antonilo D.C. “Anton” Mauricio serving as moderator, the program seamlessly blended Rotary’s cherished traditions of fellowship and ceremony with a compelling discussion about the opportunities and challenges presented by the rapidly emerging Intelligence Age. Opening Ceremonies and Fellowship The meeting began with registration and fellowship over lunch, a moment that allowed Rotarians and guests to reconnect and strengthen the friendships that form the bedrock of the organization’s service mission. President Raoul C. Creencia formally called the meeting to order and welcomed the assembly to an afternoon that promised both intellectual stimulation and meaningful dialogue. The invocation was delivered by Director-Elect Delfin N. “Del” Lorenzana, whose prayer invited reflection on wisdom, humility, and responsibility in leadership— qualities that are increasingly vital in a world being reshaped by technological change. Members then rose for the Philippine National Anthem, reaffirming Rotary’s deep commitment to the nation and its future. The RCM World-Famous Music Chorale followed with a stirring rendition of the Rotary Club of Manila Hymn, reminding those present of the Club’s proud legacy as the oldest Rotary club in Asia. Rotarian Steve “Momo” Mommaerts then led the members in the recitation of The Four-Way Test, Rotary’s timeless ethical guide that calls upon every Rotarian to measure actions and decisions against the highest standards of truth, fairness, goodwill, and benefit to all concerned. Secretary Antonilo D.C. “Anton” Mauricio then offered the Acknowledgement of Guests, warmly recognizing visiting Rotarians, distinguished speakers, and friends of the Club. The RCM World-Famous Music Chorale returned to the stage to perform the Welcome Song, further reinforcing the sense of camaraderie and fellowship that has long characterized Rotary gatherings. Celebrating Rotary Fellowship The meeting also paused to celebrate several Rotarians marking birthdays during the week. Those recognized included DGND Hermie Esguerra, Rotarians Brendan Egan, JB Pallasigue, Ben Ibuyan, and STAR Rotarian Winston Ginez. The RCM World-Famous Chorale led the traditional “Maligayang Bati / Happy Birthday” tribute, a cheerful interlude that reminded everyone present that Rotary is not only an organization of service and leadership but also a fellowship of enduring friendship. President’s Time During President’s Time, President Raoul C. Creencia reflected on the responsibility of leaders to remain attentive to the forces shaping society’s future. In a rapidly evolving world, he noted, civic organizations must continually expand their understanding of emerging developments — particularly those that promise to transform economies, institutions, and everyday life. Artificial Intelligence, he observed, represents one of the defining issues of our era. The technology’s ability to reshape industries, education, governance, and communication means that conversations about AI can no longer remain confined to technical circles. They must involve leaders from every sector of society. This perspective set the stage for the afternoon’s centerpiece discussion. Introducing the Panel “The State of the Nation in AI” The panel discussion, introduced by Club Secretary Anton Mauricio, focused on the theme “The State of the Nation in AI.” The speakers represented the Global AI Council Philippines, a multidisciplinary initiative that brings together experts from technology, law, business, and public policy to help shape the country’s approach to artificial intelligence. The distinguished panelists included: Dr. Donald Patrick Lim, Chairman and Co-Founder of the Global AI Council Philippines. Atty. Mark S. Gorriceta, Corporate Secretary and Co-Founder of the Global AI Council Philippines. Ms. Catherine S. Jalandoni, Founder and President of the Global AI Council Philippines. Together, the panelists offered a broad and insightful perspective on how the Philippines must prepare for the profound transformations brought about by AI. Entering the Intelligence Age 
Dr. Donald Patrick Lim’s Strategic Perspective Dr. Donald Patrick Lim began the discussion with a thoughtful preamble that framed artificial intelligence as a defining force of the present rather than a distant possibility. AI, he emphasized, is already transforming how businesses operate, how governments serve citizens, how students learn, and how societies make decisions. For that reason, the real question facing the world today is no longer whether AI will change the world. The more urgent question is how societies will shape AI so that it improves the world rather than harms it. For the Philippines, artificial intelligence presents both tremendous opportunity and serious challenge. The country possesses important advantages, including a young and digitally savvy population, a globally competitive workforce, and a vibrant ecosystem of technology entrepreneurs. For many years these strengths helped establish the Philippines as a global leader in outsourcing, customer support, and digital services. Yet the very technologies that created these industries are now disrupting them. Lim explained that AI systems capable of translating languages instantly and performing sophisticated knowledge work are gradually eroding the traditional advantages of English proficiency and service specialization. In this new environment, countries can no longer rely solely on their workforce’s communication skills. They must instead develop the capacity to create, design, and deploy AI-enabled technologies themselves. In other words, the Philippines must move beyond being merely a user of AI tools and instead aspire to become a builder of AI-driven industries. Education and the Foundations of Intelligence One of the most important themes of Lim’s presentation concerned education and workforce preparation. Although many governments have begun discussing the inclusion of artificial intelligence in school curricula, Lim argued that the most urgent priority is actually far more fundamental. Before students can master AI, they must develop the ability to think clearly, reason logically, and solve problems independently. He explained that even highly capable university students often struggle with basic mental calculations or analytical reasoning because of an overreliance on digital tools. Without strong foundational skills in mathematics and logical thinking, students may find themselves ill-equipped to design or guide AI systems effectively. Thus, rather than rushing prematurely into specialized technical instruction, the country must strengthen the basic intellectual foundations that enable students to process information, identify problems, and formulate solutions. Artificial intelligence, Lim emphasized, is ultimately shaped not by machines but by the questions humans ask and the decisions humans make. Three Principles for Responsible AI Development According to Lim, responsible AI development must be anchored on three essential principles. First, technology must place humans first. Artificial intelligence should enhance human potential and creativity rather than undermine human dignity or displace meaningful work without consideration of social consequences. Second, AI must be used responsibly and ethically. Systems must operate transparently, and their outputs must be accountable to the public. Third, artificial intelligence must contribute to national competitiveness. Nations that harness AI effectively will lead the next era of economic growth, while those that fail to adapt risk falling behind. For Lim, these principles underscore the importance of collaboration across sectors. Governments, businesses, universities, and civil society must work together to ensure that the benefits of AI are distributed widely and responsibly. Technology, Law, and Governance 
Atty. Mark S. Gorriceta’s Perspective The second speaker, Atty. Mark S. Gorriceta, brought a legal and policy perspective to the discussion. A pioneer in technology law in the Philippines, Gorriceta has been deeply involved in shaping the country’s regulatory framework for emerging technologies. His work spans areas such as blockchain, cryptocurrency, e-commerce, digital banking, and cybersecurity. He explained that artificial intelligence has quickly become a major legislative concern, with numerous bills currently being discussed in Congress. Many of these proposals, Gorriceta noted, approach AI primarily from a defensive standpoint, focusing on the possibility that automation could displace jobs. While such concerns are understandable, he cautioned that regulation must not focus exclusively on job protection. Artificial intelligence also raises important questions about governance, trust, literacy, transparency, and the spread of misinformation. Deepfakes and automated social media manipulation, for example, present serious challenges for democratic societies. Gorriceta emphasized that legislation must balance two equally important goals. On one hand, governments must protect citizens from potential harm and ensure that AI systems are used responsibly. On the other hand, policymakers must avoid stifling innovation by regulating technologies that are still rapidly evolving. Crafting effective AI policy therefore requires careful judgment and continuous dialogue between lawmakers, industry experts, and civil society. The Philippines and ASEAN AI Leadership Gorriceta also discussed the Philippines’ opportunity to play a significant role in shaping the future of artificial intelligence within Southeast Asia. With the country serving as ASEAN Chair, the Philippines has a unique platform from which to contribute to regional discussions on technology governance and innovation. Developing a coherent ASEAN framework for AI will be essential in promoting collaboration, sharing best practices, and ensuring that the region remains competitive in the global digital economy. If approached strategically, Gorriceta suggested, artificial intelligence could become not only a technological tool but also a diplomatic and economic bridge connecting ASEAN nations in shared development. A Mother’s Motivation 
Catherine S. Jalandoni on Building the Future The final speaker, Ms. Catherine S. Jalandoni, offered a deeply personal perspective that brought emotional resonance to the discussion. As Founder and President of the Global AI Council Philippines, she explained that her involvement in AI advocacy began not from technological curiosity but from a very human concern: the future of her children. As a mother of five, she realized that the technologies being developed today will define the world in which the next generation will live and work. That realization prompted her to ask a simple but urgent question: what can be done today to ensure that the Philippines is prepared for that future? When the Global AI Council Philippines was formed, the group quickly discovered that even experts from different industries lacked clear answers to many of the questions surrounding artificial intelligence. Instead of waiting for solutions from elsewhere, the organization decided to begin a national conversation. Its mission was to break down silos, connect stakeholders, and encourage collaboration among government agencies, private industry, academic institutions, and civic organizations. Jalandoni emphasized that the work has been largely voluntary and driven by a shared sense of responsibility. The initiative has received no guarantees of reward, yet many leaders have stepped forward to contribute their time and expertise because they recognize the stakes involved. Artificial intelligence, she observed, was introduced into the world without clear guardrails. Now the challenge is to establish those guardrails while the technology continues to evolve. This task requires leadership, cooperation, and courage. A Nation Beginning to Move Despite the complexity of the challenge, Jalandoni expressed optimism about the progress already made. Within a year, the Global AI Council Philippines has helped bring together national government leaders, local government units, members of Congress, and private sector organizations to begin addressing the opportunities and risks of artificial intelligence. The goal is not perfection but momentum. As AI continues to advance, the Philippines must move quickly to develop its own strategies for innovation, workforce development, and responsible governance. The country’s greatest asset, she concluded, remains its people — their creativity, resilience, and willingness to collaborate in pursuit of a better future. Open Forum and Dialogue The panel discussion concluded with an Open Forum, during which Rotarians engaged the speakers with thoughtful questions and reflections. The conversation ranged widely across topics such as workforce transformation, education reform, technological ethics, and the potential role of AI in strengthening economic competitiveness. Participants recognized that artificial intelligence will inevitably reshape industries and institutions. Yet they also affirmed that the direction of this transformation will depend on human choices, values, and leadership. Recognition and Appreciation Following the discussion, President Raoul C. Creencia presented Certificates of Appreciation to the three panelists in recognition of their valuable insights and contributions to the Club’s continuing educational mission. Their participation reflected Rotary’s commitment to fostering dialogue that bridges professional expertise with civic responsibility. Rotary and the Future The 24th Weekly Membership Meeting of the Rotary Club of Manila demonstrated once again the organization’s enduring role as a forum for thoughtful engagement with the issues shaping the modern world. Artificial intelligence may be driven by complex algorithms and advanced computing power, but its ultimate impact will be determined by human judgment. By bringing together leaders from technology, law, business, and civil society, the Rotary Club of Manila reaffirmed its belief that progress must be guided by ethics, collaboration, and a commitment to the common good. As the world stands at the threshold of the Intelligence Age, Rotary’s timeless principle of Service Above Self remains as relevant as ever — reminding us that technological advancement must always serve humanity’s highest aspirations. OXYGEN AND FIRE | Joaquin Capen Rodriguez’s Life of Ambition, Integrity, and Stewardship  The first warning did not come through politics or finance. It came at dusk. There was a time when Philippine rivers flickered at twilight — when humid air carried the faint hum of insects and small lights pulsed above the water. Children chased them. Farmers paused. Night descended not as darkness, but as glow. Then one evening, Joaquin “Jackie” Capen Rodriguez noticed they were gone. No announcement marked their departure. Nature does not accuse aloud. It simply withdraws. Fireflies survive only where balance endures — where air is clean, where rivers breathe, where ecosystems hold. When they vanish, something has already shifted. Jackie had lived through louder disruptions. He was born into war, carried as an infant into the mountains while his mother was imprisoned. He built companies, lost hundreds of millions in collapse, argued across ideological divides, presided over civic institutions, endured public opposition, buried the woman who shared sixty-three years of his life. He had survived fire. But the absence of fireflies unsettled him differently. Because it was not event-driven. It was generational. His generation had measured forests in board feet and rivers in megawatts. Expansion had meant progress. Speed had meant success. The earth had seemed inexhaustible. Now the air felt subtly thinner. He began to think in terms of oxygen. Oxygen had sustained him as a hidden infant in the Cordillera mountains. It had filled his lungs on varsity courts where he tried to prove he belonged. It steadied him after financial collapse. It animated the forests he later tried to replant. It was what cities needed more of — literally and figuratively. Oxygen is invisible yet essential. So are integrity, humility, and legacy. To understand Joaquin Capen Rodriguez is to trace a life shaped by fire and oxygen — by war and ambition, loss and recalibration, enterprise and service. He would come to measure success not by scale or title, but by atmosphere. Not by what he accumulated, but by what remains breathable after he is gone. His story begins in war — an infant carried into the mountains so he might live. And it ends decades later by a river, an old man standing at dusk, searching the dark for lights that once flickered freely. A Child of War and Mountains Joaquin “Jackie” Capen Rodriguez was born on April 27, 1941, at 1:45 in the morning, in Ugac Norte, Tuguegarao, Cagayan — a province that, within months, would become part of the front line of a global war. He entered the world into a family shaped by layered histories. His grandmother, Florence Noel Capen, traced her lineage to Alsace-Lorraine, a region long contested between France and Germany — itself a symbol of shifting borders and divided sovereignties. His paternal line carried Spanish roots from Galicia and Catalonia, including Jewish and Hispanic ancestry. His father bore the bearing of a frontier builder; his mother the discipline of American-influenced education. It was a household where Europe, America, and the Philippine frontier converged. But history was accelerating. On December 8, 1941 — hours after the attack on Pearl Harbor — Japanese forces began bombing key installations across the Philippines. Within days, Northern Luzon was engulfed in military movement. Tuguegarao and nearby regions became strategically exposed due to their proximity to airfields and transport routes. Civilian life unraveled quickly. Roads filled with evacuees. Communication lines faltered. Rumors traveled faster than verified reports. Families hid valuables, burned documents, prepared for displacement. Jackie’s mother was arrested and later imprisoned in Camp Holmes in Baguio, a detention site that held both Filipino civilians and foreign nationals. The imprisonment was not ideological; it was part of the machinery of occupation. In wartime, vulnerability is often arbitrary. For the infant Jackie — barely eight months old — the risk was existential. The decision was made swiftly. He would be removed from the lowlands and taken into the Cordillera mountains, to Pasil, Kalinga. It was not a dramatic evacuation. There were no convoys or escorts. It was quiet, deliberate concealment — the kind that saves lives without fanfare. The journey into the mountains marked his first experience of displacement. Pasil was geographically removed from the main military routes. Japanese forces focused on cities, transport corridors, and coastal access points. The highlands offered natural insulation. The terrain itself was protection. While urban centers experienced surveillance, shortages, and uncertainty, life in Kalinga retained its rhythm. Agriculture continued. Tribal governance functioned. Ritual and kinship maintained order. For a child whose birth year coincided with invasion, this environment became formative. He did not grow up surrounded by constant gunfire or military patrols. Instead, his earliest memories were shaped by mountain air, river currents, and communal life. The Cordillera landscape imposed patience. Rice was cultivated by season, not by urgency. Rivers moved steadily regardless of political upheaval. He absorbed, almost unconsciously, a different model of authority. In tribal communities, leadership was earned through respect and responsibility rather than imposed through hierarchy alone. Courage was not performative; it was demonstrated in daily conduct. His parents, despite separation and uncertainty, maintained discipline in his upbringing. His mother, shaped by American schooling, emphasized structure and moral clarity. His father embodied resilience and adaptability. Though wartime constrained communication, the household narrative reinforced continuity — that this period of disruption would not define the family’s future. Language became a quiet instrument of stability. With his grandfather, he spoke Spanish — a bridge to lineage and memory. With his mother, English — the language of education and emerging governance. With neighbors and peers, he spoke Ibanag, Itawis, Ilocano, and Kalinga. He moved between linguistic worlds with ease. Each language carried a different cadence of thought. He learned that identity could shift without dissolving. One could inhabit multiple cultural frameworks without fragmentation. This early cultural fluency would later prove invaluable in business negotiations, civic leadership, and diplomacy. But at the time, it was simply normal life. War remained present but indirect. He was aware of absence — of a mother imprisoned, of conversations hushed when adults gathered. He sensed vulnerability without fully understanding its scale. What the war taught him, even before comprehension, was fragility. War taught him this early: order can vanish quickly, institutions can falter, and security is never guaranteed. The mountains, however, taught him perspective. Nature endured. Seasons returned. Life continued beyond human conflict. This dual exposure — instability and continuity — shaped his temperament. He would later respond to financial collapse, institutional conflict, and political tension not with panic, but with recalibration. He had already learned, as an infant, that survival sometimes requires relocation rather than resistance. That protection can be quiet. That stability must be maintained, not assumed. When he eventually descended from the mountains into a nation rebuilding after occupation, he carried with him an internal compass formed by displacement and refuge. War did not define him as trauma. It defined him as adaptable. Stability, he would later conclude, is never permanent. But perspective can be. The Grandfather and The Castle If Kalinga gave Jackie breadth of perspective, his grandfather gave him structure. Judge Joaquin Rodriguez Serra was born in Tarragona, Spain — a Mediterranean city shaped by Roman ruins and centuries of political transition. His father came from Galicia in northern Spain, a region known for its maritime resilience and deep Catholic tradition. His mother was Catalan, of Jewish and Hispanic descent, raised in a culture long accustomed to balancing local identity with broader national authority. He arrived in the Philippines during a period of transition. Spanish colonial rule had ended. American administration had begun reshaping institutions — courts, schools, civil governance. The country was redefining itself in real time. The judge would become appointed governor of Mindanao during the American era — specifically overseeing what were then referred to as the Provincias Moras, regions where Muslim communities had historically maintained autonomy and resistance to outside control. Mindanao at that time was not yet the commercial hub it would later become. It was frontier territory — culturally diverse, politically sensitive, economically underdeveloped. Governance required more than legal authority. It required negotiation between religious communities, indigenous traditions, and colonial administrative systems. Rodriguez Serra operated within this complexity. He was not merely an official; he was a bridge. Davao: Building More Than Property In Davao, he established Hacienda Carmen — not simply as agricultural enterprise, but as a long-term stake in land that was still being structured economically and socially. Ownership in frontier regions often signaled power. But what distinguished him was what followed. He later donated land to local natives — land that still carries the name Carmen today. The gesture reflected not charity alone, but philosophy: stewardship over extraction. He also founded Echo de Davao, the region’s first newspaper. Establishing a press in an emerging city is a declaration that public discourse matters — that information, transparency, and civic dialogue are foundations of growth. His Bolton Street residence in Davao was more than home. It housed his office and printing operations. Decades later, that property would become the site of the University of Mindanao — a transition from private estate to educational institution. In these decisions, a pattern emerges: what begins as personal enterprise often becomes public infrastructure. That pattern would not be lost on his grandson. Manila and the Commonwealth Circle In 1920, at the urging of President Manuel Quezon, Rodriguez Serra relocated to Manila. The capital during the Commonwealth period was a crucible of political thought. Independence from the United States was being negotiated. Constitutional frameworks were being refined. Intellectual leaders debated the shape of Filipino identity. He moved within circles that included Jose Laurel, Sergio Osmeña, Claro Recto, Quentin Paredes, and other architects of early republican leadership. Yet he did not pursue office aggressively. He practiced law. He maintained his bearing. He embodied continuity between Spanish-era jurisprudence and American-modeled legal reform. When he died in 1956 at eighty-seven years old, three presidents and eleven senators attended his wake. It was a public affirmation of stature. But for young Jackie, the lessons were not delivered in ceremony. They were delivered in conversation. The Refusal to Shift As English steadily replaced Spanish in the courts and commercial houses of Manila, many professionals adjusted quickly. English opened doors. It meant access to American administrators, broader clientele, smoother integration into the new power structure shaping the country. The transition was practical, even inevitable. Judge Joaquin Rodriguez Serra understood this as well as anyone. Yet he did not fully make the shift. He continued to practice largely in Spanish, drafting arguments and delivering reasoning in the language that had formed his legal mind. Clients diminished. Opportunities narrowed. Younger lawyers adapted faster, moved more fluidly in English proceedings, aligned themselves with the emerging order. To outside observers, the judge’s insistence seemed impractical — perhaps even stubborn. Why cling to a fading language when adaptation promised expansion? But to him, the matter was not about nostalgia. It was about coherence. He did not reject modernity. He resisted erasure. Language, for him, carried more than vocabulary; it carried memory, lineage, intellectual formation. To abandon it entirely for convenience felt like surrendering continuity. Adaptation, yes. But not self-abandonment. His grandson watched quietly. The lesson was not delivered as a lecture. It was absorbed through pattern. The judge did not complain about lost clients. He did not dramatize sacrifice. He simply continued. From that quiet persistence, Jackie internalized a distinction that would guide him decades later: influence may diminish; dignity must not. The judge often spoke of family as a castle — not a monument of stone, but a structure of reputation built generation after generation. Each decision was a block. Education added strength. Discipline reinforced walls. Generosity fortified foundations. Recklessness, dishonor, or negligence weakened them. Wealth, he would explain, is movable. It can be gained, multiplied, lost. Reputation is structural. Once cracked, it requires generations to repair. “In family,” he would say to his grandson, “the respect for one is the respect for all.” It was not sentimental advice. It was intergenerational discipline. To carry a surname was to carry cumulative weight. Young Jackie grew up aware that his name was not merely personal — it was inherited architecture. He observed the judge in small details: the way he entered a room without haste, the way he held silence when others argued, the way he refused to raise his voice even when challenged. Authority did not require volume. Composure was its own form of strength. Children absorb posture before they understand principle. Jackie learned that steadiness outlasts spectacle. Years later, when ₱950 million evaporated in the Oranbo collapse, the metaphor returned with force: you can lose land, but not the blocks. Integrity, discipline, and family cohesion remained. The spine formed in childhood held. Competition and The Education of Belonging When Jackie returned fully to Manila for formal schooling, he entered a world very different from the Cordillera mountains of his early years. Post-war Manila was rebuilding with energy and ambition. American influence shaped curriculum and civic life. English dominated elite education. Schools like American School and later De La Salle were incubators for the country’s future professionals — lawyers, executives, public officials. In that environment, Jackie sensed something subtle but persistent: he stood slightly apart. He carried Spanish lineage in a society redefining itself after colonial transition. Spanish surnames still suggested prestige in certain circles, but they also signaled a fading chapter of history. He had grown up among mountain communities speaking dialects that many Manila classmates did not know. His childhood had included tribal rhythms unfamiliar to urban elites. He was neither fully provincial nor fully metropolitan. Neither wholly of the old order nor entirely of the new. It was not exclusion he felt. It was difference. 
Difference presents a quiet fork in the road.
It can produce withdrawal — a gradual retreat into caution. Or it can produce effort. He chose effort. “I always tried a little harder,” he would later say. The sentence sounds modest, almost casual. In truth, it captures a defining habit. Sports became his proving ground. On the basketball court and tennis court, lineage dissolved. Performance was visible, immediate, undeniable. If you could run faster, defend harder, shoot accurately, endure conditioning — standing followed naturally. The clarity appealed to him. In social spaces, belonging could feel implicit and layered with nuance. On the court, belonging was earned through contribution. Varsity athletics demanded discipline. Practices were repetitive. Conditioning was relentless. Coaches emphasized teamwork over ego. Preparation often determined the outcome long before the whistle blew. He learned that defeat, while public, was instructive. A missed shot required adjustment. A lost match required analysis. Loss did not define identity; it provided information. Adolescence sharpened awareness of difference — accent, posture, subtle social codes. But instead of breeding resentment, it intensified drive. Insecurity, he discovered, can be converted into fuel if directed toward preparation rather than comparison. The pattern formed almost unconsciously: 
Compete harder. 
Prepare longer. 
Recover faster. He did not resent classmates who seemed naturally at ease in elite circles. He studied them. He matched them. Often, he surpassed them — not by entitlement, but by effort. That discipline would follow him into boardrooms and negotiations. The executive who studied mining geology before assuming leadership, the investor who structured deals carefully, the Rotary officer who prepared thoroughly before proposing initiatives — each traced back to a young athlete who refused retreat. Belonging, he learned early, is not granted. It is built. And once built, it steadies. Structure and Leadership Athletics taught him more than endurance and accuracy. It introduced him to structure. On a team, talent alone is insufficient. Five players move, but only if they move together does the game open. A captain is not appointed by proclamation; he is recognized by performance. Teammates follow the player who delivers when it matters, who runs drills without complaint, who absorbs pressure without collapse. Jackie began to notice something subtle: authority on the court is fragile. A captain who fails to perform loses influence quickly. A player who lectures but cannot defend loses credibility. Respect cannot be demanded; it must be demonstrated repeatedly. He watched older teammates rise and fall in standing based on consistency. He saw how quickly admiration shifted when performance declined. Leadership, he realized, was not a static title. It was a daily test. That insight stayed with him. Years later, in boardrooms and civic organizations, he would instinctively distrust authority detached from competence. Titles meant little without delivery. Influence, he would come to believe, must be renewed continually through credibility. Sports also introduced him to public vulnerability. When a game is lost, there is no private interpretation. The scoreboard is visible. Teammates feel it. Spectators register it. There is no hiding behind explanation. He learned to walk off the court after defeat without excuse. To shake hands. To return to practice. Loss became part of rhythm, not rupture. That quiet conditioning prepared him, though he did not know it then, for larger arenas where setbacks would carry heavier consequences. Financial collapse, institutional opposition, political tension — none of these would feel entirely unfamiliar. He had already experienced the discipline of recovery under watchful eyes. Post-War Manila and Ambition The Manila he inhabited during his De La Salle years amplified this instinct toward striving. Post-war optimism still animated the city. Infrastructure projects were expanding. New commercial districts were rising. Families who had rebuilt after occupation were now thinking in terms of growth. The Philippines, confident in its education system and regional position, encouraged ambition. Young men were expected not merely to inherit, but to build. In classrooms and corridors, conversations were rarely small. They revolved around enterprise, law, engineering, public service. The assumption was forward movement. Jackie’s competitive instinct fit naturally into that environment. He did not need to be convinced that effort would matter; he had already tested that premise on the court. But there was a difference in tone. For some classmates, ambition felt like extension of entitlement. They carried inherited advantage comfortably, as if success were expected outcome. For Jackie, ambition was not assumed. It was pursued. The mountain-raised boy who had grown up speaking multiple dialects did not presume he belonged automatically among Manila’s future elite. He worked to belong. 
He studied harder. 
Trained longer. 
Prepared more carefully. 
He did not see advantage as birthright. 
He saw it as target. And that difference — subtle but decisive — would define the manner in which he later built enterprises, navigated setbacks, and carried responsibility. He did not assume scale. He earned it. Carrying the Habit Forward When Jackie eventually stepped into mining and real estate, the habits he had formed in adolescence did not announce themselves dramatically. They simply reappeared. Before entering an industry, he immersed himself in it. In mining, he did not rely on summaries from engineers; he studied geological reports. He learned how extraction sites functioned, how commodity pricing moved with global demand, how regulatory approvals could stall progress. In real estate, he walked properties personally, examined infrastructure plans, questioned projections. Preparation had become reflex. He did not assume competence would transfer automatically from one field to another. He treated each venture the way he once approached a new season in athletics: understand the terrain, train deliberately, earn your place. He could have leaned more heavily on surname and association. His lineage carried history. His connections were substantial. But instinct resisted complacency. On a court, reputation does not win games. In business, it does not secure sustainable returns. Work does. The discipline that once governed conditioning drills now governed boardroom preparation. Meetings were not improvised; they were structured. Risks were assessed before capital was deployed. Decisions were revisited and recalibrated when necessary. When the Asian Financial Crisis struck in 1997 and Oranbo collapsed under the weight of systemic shock, the same internal rhythm activated. He did not indulge paralysis. He reviewed exposure. He gathered family. He restructured strategy. The competitor who had once analyzed missed shots now analyzed leverage ratios. Defeat required response. The team instinct also surfaced. In athletics, individual brilliance means little without coordinated execution. In enterprise, success depended on sons, partners, managers, financiers. Shared objective mattered more than personal ego. Later, in Rotary leadership, that understanding deepened. Volunteer institutions cannot be commanded; they must be aligned. He approached civic leadership not as proprietor but as teammate — listening, persuading, adjusting. The young man who once said he “always tried a little harder” did not outgrow that impulse. He refined it. The effort became more strategic. The competitiveness became quieter. The drive remained constant. Difference had never weakened him. It had trained him. Being slightly apart in school had sharpened discipline. Being raised in multiple cultural environments had expanded adaptability. Feeling the need to prove himself had cultivated resilience. Over time, these traits ceased to feel compensatory. They became structural. And that work ethic — steady, unadvertised, persistent — would become one of the most consistent threads running through his life, from mining pits to diplomatic halls to family gatherings on Sunday afternoons. Rise and Scale By his late thirties, Jackie had moved decisively into large-scale enterprise. The Philippines during the 1980s and early 1990s was a country in transition. Political upheaval had reshaped leadership. Economic reforms were uneven but ambitious. Infrastructure development accelerated. Frontier industries — mining, property development, agribusiness — attracted entrepreneurs willing to operate at scale. Jackie did not gravitate toward small ventures. He entered sectors where decisions affected terrain, capital flows, and long-term regional growth. At thirty-nine, he became president of Benguet Exploration Mining Corporation — a position that placed him at the center of an industry both economically critical and politically sensitive. Mining in the Philippines has always been complicated. It requires regulatory negotiation, environmental compliance, community engagement, and large capital investment. Commodity prices fluctuate with global markets. Infrastructure costs are significant. Returns are rarely immediate. Mining demands patience and risk tolerance. It also demands conviction. Jackie approached it methodically. He immersed himself in operational details — geology, extraction logistics, regulatory frameworks. He negotiated with engineers and financiers alike. The role required both strategic overview and granular understanding. The scale of mining changed his perception of enterprise. Decisions were no longer about individual properties or transactions; they were about multiyear projections and international commodity cycles. Success followed. Early wins reinforced confidence. Strategic decisions proved effective. Leadership authority solidified. He developed a reputation for decisiveness and preparedness. Diversification followed naturally. Agriculture expanded. Real estate acquisitions increased. Asset management structures became more formalized. In 1990, he established Guidance Management Corporation — not simply as holding vehicle, but as mechanism to consolidate and protect family assets for future generations. The move reflected foresight. He was thinking in decades, not quarters. Momentum built steadily. Confidence, however, can subtly shift into assumption. When success compounds, it creates the impression that disciplined preparation can neutralize most variables. Markets appear navigable. Risk appears manageable. Scale appears controllable. The line between competence and overconfidence is rarely visible in real time. The Oranbo Opportunity Then came Oranbo. Three and a half hectares in Pasig — strategically located at a time when Metro Manila’s urban expansion was accelerating. The site presented development potential aligned with regional growth trends. Infrastructure projects were underway. Commercial real estate demand was rising. The purchase price was ₱950 million. Jackie put down ₱500 million. The remaining ₱450 million was financed through bank loans. A Singapore-based development partner entered into agreement, bringing international expertise and projected capital leverage. It was not speculative recklessness. It was structured. It was calculated. It was consistent with prevailing optimism in Southeast Asian markets during the mid-1990s. Across the region, growth was strong. Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, and the Philippines were experiencing rising investment flows. Credit was accessible. Currency values appeared stable. Few anticipated systemic collapse. The Shock of 1997 In July 1997, Thailand devalued the baht. What began as localized currency adjustment spread rapidly. Investor confidence evaporated across Southeast Asia. The Philippine peso weakened sharply. Interest rates spiked. Credit tightened abruptly. Foreign capital withdrew. The Asian Financial Crisis was not gradual. It was sudden. Projects dependent on leveraged financing were exposed immediately. Debt servicing costs rose. Asset values fell. Development timelines stalled. Oranbo, built on carefully structured assumptions, became vulnerable to forces beyond managerial control. Within months, the financial architecture underpinning the project destabilized. The property was lost. Nearly a billion pesos in value disappeared. The Psychological Break Financial loss at that scale is not merely a number on paper. It alters internal equilibrium. Jackie had believed in preparation, negotiation, and disciplined risk assessment. Those principles had served him well for decades. The crisis revealed limits. Systemic collapse does not discriminate between reckless and careful operators. The loss punctured a quiet assumption: that disciplined leadership could always outmaneuver volatility. He has described that period not as despair, but as clarity. Ambition had been tested. The illusion of control had been exposed. Regrouping The critical response came not in panic, but in regrouping. Family gathered. Sons were already involved in enterprise. The decision was made collectively: withdraw emotionally or rebuild strategically. They rebuilt. The loss did not fracture the family structure. It reinforced it. The metaphor inherited from his grandfather resurfaced with renewed force. The castle held — not because land was secure, but because character and cohesion remained. What endured after Oranbo was not asset base, but cohesion. The family enterprise adjusted. Risk assessment became more conservative. Leverage was approached with greater caution. Expansion remained possible, but tempered by experience. The collapse did not end ambition. It refined it. From Scale to Stewardship The Oranbo episode marked a turning point. Before the crisis, expansion had been central. After it, stewardship became more pronounced. He began to think more consciously about sustainability — not only environmental sustainability, but financial and generational sustainability. Growth without structural resilience is fragile. The experience deepened his later environmental advocacy. Mining had already exposed him to the tension between extraction and preservation. The financial crisis exposed the tension between leverage and durability. Both taught the same lesson: Scale without balance is unstable. The competitive athlete had matured into executive leader. The executive leader had been tested by systemic collapse. And from that testing emerged something quieter, but stronger — perspective. Love, Partnership, and the Architecture of Continuity Long before Oranbo collapsed. Long before mining presidencies and Rotary debates. There was Sonja. Jackie met Sonja Habana in the early 1960s, when his life was still gathering direction but not yet momentum. The Philippines was optimistic then — rebuilding from war, industrializing cautiously, believing in upward movement. Young men with ambition felt the horizon widening. Sonja came from Davao, from a family whose own history mirrored the frontier ethic that had shaped parts of his lineage. The Habana clan traced its roots to Iloilo but had moved south in search of opportunity, building quietly and steadily. There was nothing ostentatious about her background. It was disciplined, rooted, hardworking. They met through shared circles — family connections, gatherings, conversations that began politely and extended longer than expected. There was no cinematic drama, no instant proclamation. What unfolded was something steadier. What caught his attention was not glamour. It was composure. She carried herself with an ease that did not seek approval. She listened more than she spoke. Her faith was not performative; it was integrated into daily conduct. There was a steadiness in her — the kind that does not draw the room’s attention immediately but, once noticed, becomes quietly indispensable. He, by contrast, was forward-moving. Competitive. Already thinking about enterprise, expansion, possibility. His mind leaned toward the next venture, the next horizon. They were different in tempo: he accelerated; she anchored — and the difference created balance. And that difference created balance rather than friction. Courtship in that era was not casual. Families observed. Intentions were clarified. Conversations extended beyond affection to questions of direction. What kind of life would they build? Where would they live? What principles would guide them? Jackie knew, even then, that his future would not be static. Mining, agriculture, real estate — these were not professions rooted in one place. They required travel, risk, relocation. Stability would not come from predictability. Sonja understood the life he was building would never be predictable. She chose him anyway. They married in 1962. He was young, ambitious, convinced that the future would reward effort. What he did not yet fully grasp was that expansion without anchor becomes drift. She became that anchor. Their marriage developed around a deliberate, almost intuitive division of strength. He managed the outer world — negotiations, acquisitions, risk exposure, capital allocation. She managed the inner world — the daily architecture of family life, the tone of discipline, the formation of character. It was not a hierarchy. It was complementarity. While he traveled to Spain, Thailand, and the United States pursuing enterprise, she ensured that home remained consistent. Their four sons — Joaquin Jr. (Jack), Sean, Armando Carlos (Archie), and Antonio — were raised not with entitlement, but with expectation. Church attendance was habitual. Education was nonnegotiable. Respect was required. Conversations were direct. Sunday lunches became ritual. Not elaborate affairs — simply consistent ones. Everyone present. Stories shared. Disagreements aired without theatrics. It was through these repeated, almost ordinary moments that cohesion formed. Families that build multigenerational enterprises often fracture not because of financial stress, but because of relational neglect. Sonja understood this instinctively. She cultivated unity deliberately. When Oranbo collapsed in 1997 and nearly ₱950 million evaporated, the crisis entered their home not as accusation but as recalibration. External perception shifted. Leverage tightened. Years of disciplined growth appeared suddenly vulnerable. Moments like that test more than balance sheets. They test marriages. There were no dramatic confrontations. No visible recriminations. Instead, there was reassessment. Sons gathered. Strategy was reexamined. Expenses were reviewed. Expansion paused. She reinforced calm. He absorbed the blow. The castle held. Parenting had always been part of their long view. Their sons were not raised merely to inherit assets; they were raised to understand responsibility. They learned business mechanics, yes — but also restraint. They were taught that power, unchecked by conscience, corrodes families. They were reminded that a surname carries obligation. Succession was gradual. Leadership was transferred deliberately. By the time Jackie began devoting more time to Rotary and civic service, the next generation was prepared to assume operational control. This was possible because home had been structured with foresight. Their life together unfolded across geographies — Davao, Manila, Madrid, Malaga, Bangkok, Los Angeles, Orlando. Each move required adaptation. Each adjustment required negotiation. Through it all, partnership endured. Sixty-three years. Longevity in marriage is rarely the product of uninterrupted harmony. It is the result of continuous adjustment. They argued. They recalibrated. They forgave. They resumed. He built externally. She preserved internally. And in that interplay, continuity solidified. Three months and three weeks before he would publicly reflect on his life, Sonja passed away. Grief in later years is less explosive than in youth. It arrives as subtraction. The house feels altered. The air feels thinner. Routine becomes echo. He speaks of it without dramatization. Happiness once meant full schedules and three meals a day; now it means one simple meal. Once it meant playing basketball or tennis; now it means watching a game quietly. Once it meant travel to Paris or Madrid; now it means sitting with grandchildren. Loss recalibrates scale; ambition softens, and presence enlarges. When asked how he wishes to be remembered, he does not cite mining leadership, diplomatic service, or Rotary initiatives. He does not mention assets or titles. He answers simply: Ulirang Ama — Most Outstanding Father. It is not modesty; it is order. Enterprises rise and fall. Public positions rotate. Recognition fades. But if children stand steady — if grandchildren inherit coherence — then the architecture endures. Marriage was not a chapter in his life. It was the foundation beneath all others. He may have built companies. But together, they built continuity. With the household steady and the next generation stepping forward, he began turning outward — to service and institution-building beyond his own enterprises. Rotary: From Profit to Service Jackie entered the Rotary Club of Manila in 2016. By then, he was an established businessman. Mining had expanded his scale. Family enterprise was stable. His sons were assuming operational leadership. The urgency of daily management had begun to ease. A different question surfaced: 
If enterprise builds wealth, what builds balance? Rotary offered an answer. In business, success had always been measurable — margins, assets, return on capital. Authority carried weight; decisions translated directly into outcome. Rotary spoke a different language. There were no dividends. No contracts compelling compliance. Projects advanced only through persuasion. Leadership conferred responsibility, not control. In mining, approval meant execution. In Rotary, approval required conviction. The adjustment refined him. When he was elected President of the Rotary Club of Manila in 2019 — with the shortest span between induction and presidency in the Club’s recent memory — he treated the office not as culmination, but as discipline. He embraced servant-leadership not as slogan, but as practice: authority without ownership, influence without compensation, responsibility without entitlement. In volunteer institutions, capital carries little weight; credibility carries everything — and must be earned repeatedly. His presidency emphasized structure and measurable service. Environmental programs were sharpened. Educational initiatives strengthened. Governance was documented carefully. He believed Rotary’s moral authority depended on procedural clarity. Through the TREES initiative, he pushed for sustainability over symbolism. Early reforestation efforts had prioritized visibility; survival rates lagged. He insisted on monitoring, community engagement, and higher survival rather than higher headlines. Bamboo became strategic — fastgrowing, soil-stabilizing, economically viable. Environmentalism detached from livelihood fails in developing contexts. Bamboo aligned ecology with income. His thinking broadened: cities generate carbon; they must also generate oxygen He began advocating for municipal ecological parks — five to ten hectares dedicated not merely to recreation but to oxygen production and environmental education. It was not anti-development; it was ecological accounting. Extraction must be balanced by restoration. Programs like Alay Lakad reinforced another conviction: peace is built through opportunity. Inequality fuels grievance; education reduces it. Scholarships and youth development were not charity, but preventative investment. His diplomatic experience in Serbia had shown him how disparities harden into fracture. Rotary allowed him to work upstream — strengthening cohesion before division. After completing his club presidency, fellow Rotarians urged him to run at the district level. Leadership beyond a single club required election by weighted vote across District 3810. He entered the race for District Governor Nominee for Rotary Year 2024–2025. Two candidates stood: Joaquin Capen Rodriguez of the Rotary Club of Manila, and Vilma Castillo Vinluan of the Rotary Club of Sampaloc. On November 9, 2021, District Governor Robert G. Koa announced the results of the election conducted through the Rotarycontracted SimplyVoting platform. Of 129 weighted votes cast, Jackie received 56.6 percent. His closest opponent received 43.4 percent. There were no abstentions. The margin was clear, though not overwhelming. It signaled both confidence and the presence of differing expectations within the district. He was declared District Governor Nominee for Rotary Year 2024–2025. District 3810 spans Manila, Pasay, Cavite, and Occidental Mindoro — a wide geographic and socio-economic range. Governance at that scale requires diplomacy as much as direction. Jackie approached the role with the same discipline that had defined his presidency. Documentation mattered. Compliance mattered. Integrity mattered. He believed strong institutions protect both leaders and members; structure prevents favoritism; procedure prevents arbitrariness. But structure, when applied firmly, can unsettle those accustomed to flexibility. The tensions that would later surface did not begin in hostility. They began in philosophy. For Jackie, Rotary’s values — integrity, fairness, transparency — were operational standards, not ceremonial words. As District Governor, he acted accordingly. And that commitment would soon test him more severely than any business setback ever had. Ideology and Peace Jackie’s friendship with self-exiled Communist Party of the Philippines founder and leader Jose Maria Sison endured not because they agreed, but because neither man feared disagreement. One evening, long after insurgency had reshaped the country’s political landscape, they sat across a modest dining table. No press. No audience. Just two men aware that history had placed them on different sides of the same national wound. “You build enterprises,” Sison said evenly. “But who owns the land beneath them?” Jackie paused. Silence, he believed, clarifies thought. “The question is not ownership alone,” he replied. “It is opportunity. If people participate in growth, they defend stability.” “Stability for whom?” Sison asked. The exchange did not escalate; it deepened. Sison argued that the system preserved elite advantage and that reform without rupture merely prolongs injustice. Jackie did not deny inequality. He had seen rural poverty firsthand. But he rejected the idea that destruction guarantees justice. “If you burn institutions,” he said, “you still have to build new ones. Power does not disappear. It transfers.” They moved between theory and lived experience — revolutionary models and economic realities. What lingered for Jackie was not the rhetoric, but the shared premise: both wanted a better Philippines. They differed on method, not on diagnosis. At one point, the tone softened. “If education had been equitable decades ago,” Jackie said quietly, “perhaps fewer young men would carry rifles.” “Education within a broken system teaches obedience,” Sison replied. The argument never resolved It was not meant to. Jackie never romanticized armed struggle. He knew its cost. But he also refused to reduce insurgency to criminality alone. Inequality creates vacuum; where opportunity is absent, resentment organizes itself. The conversation clarified his conviction: reform must be structural — but lawful. Justice must be pursued — but without violence Later, in peace consultations, he carried that perspective w

body.text: His Excellency Jing Quan was born in July 1975 in Shaanxi Province, China.
Ambassador Jing earned a bachelor's degree in English from Xian Foreign Studies University, a master’s degree, and subsequently a PhD in international relations.
He entered the foreign service in 1997 as a Staff Member at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and remained in that role until 1998.
In 1998-2002, he was Attaché and Third Secretary, Embassy of the People's Republic of China in the Kingdom of Thailand.
2002-2009, he was Third Secretary and Deputy Director, Department of North American and Oceanian Affairs, Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
2009-2011, he was Second Secretary and later First Secretary, Embassy of the People's Republic of China in the United States of America.
2011-2018, he went back home to be First Secretary, Director and Counsellor, Department of North American and Oceanian Affairs.
2018-2021, Deputy Director-General, Department of North American and Oceanian Affairs, MFA.
2021-2025, as Minister and subsequently the Deputy Chief of Mission, Embassy of the People's Republic of China in the United States of America.
On December 11, 2025, he officially became the People’s Republic of China’s Ambassador to the Republic of the Philippines.
Ambassador Quan is married with one daughter.
