articles.title: Between Enterprise and Nation | The Life, Leadership, and Public Service of Abdulgani Matua Macatoman

body.text: On a humid morning in July 2017, Abdulgani “Gani” Matua Macatoman stood quietly in his office, looking out over the Manila skyline.

The city was already alive with motion. Traffic crept along the avenues below, office towers reflected the early sunlight, and the restless energy of the capital hummed through the streets. In a few hours, he would formally assume a new role.
The appointment letter lay on the desk beside him.
“Undersecretary of the Department of Trade and Industry.”
For many professionals, such a title would represent the culmination of ambition — a position of national influence within one of the government’s most important economic institutions.
Yet Gani’s thoughts were not focused on the prestige of the office.
They were focused on responsibility.

Accepting the appointment meant stepping away from the private enterprise he had spent years helping build. It meant leaving behind the daily decisions of corporate leadership and entering the far more complex world of national policy.
And it meant trusting that the company he helped create would continue forward under new leadership.
Across the room sat his wife, Mufaida Unda Alonto Macatoman.

Together they had built Global Empire International Group of Companies, navigating the uncertainties of entrepreneurship and the demands of developing projects in industries as challenging as renewable energy and infrastructure.
Now the moment had come for a transition.
As Gani prepared to enter government service, Mufaida would assume full leadership of the enterprise as President and Chief Executive Officer, guiding the company into its next chapter.
Neither of them spoke for a moment.
They both understood the weight of what was about to happen.
Public service has a way of changing the trajectory of a life. It shifts the center of responsibility from organization to nation, from boardroom decisions to policies that affect millions.
Gani picked up the appointment letter again.

For a brief instant, the memories of a much earlier time came rushing back — memories of the community in Mindanao where he had grown up, of parents who taught him that leadership meant keeping one’s commitments, of teachers who insisted that education carried with it a duty to serve others.
Those lessons had shaped every step of the journey that brought him to this moment.
Now they would shape what came next.
He placed the letter back on the desk and turned toward the door.
Outside, a new chapter of responsibility awaited.
But the story of how he arrived there — how a boy raised in the communities of Mindanao came to stand at the intersection of enterprise and national leadership — began many years earlier.
Roots in Mindanao

Long before Gani would sit across negotiating tables with international investors, long before he would help shape policies affecting Philippine enterprise and trade, his life unfolded in a place where leadership was understood in its most basic form — within the rhythms of family and community.

Mindanao, the island where he was raised, is a land of remarkable diversity. Its landscapes range from fertile plains and coastal waters to mountainous regions and bustling towns shaped by centuries of cultural exchange. Generations of communities — Muslim, Christian, and indigenous — have lived side by side, each contributing traditions that form the region’s rich social fabric.
For the young Gani, Mindanao was not simply a geographic location. It was the environment that shaped his earliest understanding of responsibility.
The communities where he grew up valued relationships deeply. Families maintained close ties with neighbors, relatives, and elders whose wisdom carried quiet authority.

Respect for age and experience was ingrained from childhood. Children were taught to listen carefully when elders spoke, for their stories were not merely anecdotes but lessons drawn from lives shaped by struggle and perseverance.
Within the Macatoman household, these values were reinforced every day.
His parents believed strongly that character formed the foundation of success. Material circumstances, they reminded their children, might rise or fall with time, but integrity remained constant.

His father, Abdulrahman Macatoman, embodied discipline and responsibility. A man of firm convictions, he believed that leadership began with personal accountability. If a promise was made, it must be kept. If a task was undertaken, it must be completed with diligence.
From him, the young Abdulgani learned that credibility is earned slowly and lost quickly.

His mother, Rasmia Matua Macatoman, by contrast, represented the quiet strength that sustains families through life’s uncertainties. Patient and deeply rooted in faith, she emphasized compassion, humility, and the importance of treating others with dignity.
From her, he absorbed the belief that leadership must be tempered with empathy.
Together, his parents created a home environment where expectations were clear. Education was not optional. Discipline was not negotiable. And faith was not merely professed — it was practiced.

The family’s circumstances were modest, but the atmosphere within the household was rich in encouragement. Books were valued. Curiosity was welcomed. Questions were met with thoughtful conversation rather than dismissal.
Family gatherings often became informal classrooms.

Relatives and elders would share stories about the past — stories of communities navigating economic hardship, of individuals who overcame adversity through determination, and of leaders who placed service above personal comfort.
The young Gani listened attentively.
In those moments, he began to understand something fundamental about leadership: that it often grows quietly within communities long before it becomes visible in public life.
Life in Mindanao also instilled resilience.

The region’s history has been shaped by both opportunity and challenge. Communities learned to adapt to shifting economic conditions, political changes, and the complexities of a multicultural society.
For young people growing up in such an environment, adaptability was not merely useful — it was essential.
Gani’s childhood unfolded within this atmosphere of both stability and uncertainty. The lessons he absorbed during those years would later become central to his leadership philosophy.
Hard work was necessary. Integrity was non-negotiable. And service to others was a responsibility that accompanied success.
Yet childhood was not defined solely by lessons and discipline.

Like many young boys, he was curious about the wider world beyond his immediate surroundings. Books opened windows into places and ideas far beyond the boundaries of his community. Through reading, he discovered stories about leaders, innovators, and thinkers whose influence extended across nations.
Education soon became the pathway through which those possibilities might be explored.

When he entered Camp Keithley Elementary School in Marawi City, teachers quickly noticed his seriousness toward learning. He approached assignments with quiet determination, rarely seeking attention but consistently demonstrating diligence.
His teachers encouraged that curiosity.
They understood that education could serve as a bridge between the realities of rural life and the opportunities that lay beyond.

Later, at the Mindanao State University Training Center, his intellectual horizons expanded further. Surrounded by students from different backgrounds across Mindanao, he encountered new perspectives on politics, economics, and social development.
These experiences introduced him to a broader national conversation.

For many young Filipinos of his generation, the question of how one might contribute to the country’s progress was deeply personal. The Philippines was navigating economic transitions and social challenges that demanded both innovation and leadership.
Gani began to imagine a future where he might play a role in that process.

Teachers and mentors recognized his potential and encouraged him to pursue higher education beyond Mindanao. Their advice planted a seed that would eventually lead him to Manila — a journey that would expand his horizons and prepare him for the responsibilities that awaited him.
Yet even as his ambitions grew, the lessons of Mindanao remained firmly anchored within him.
The values learned in childhood — respect, discipline, humility, and faith — would accompany him through every stage of his life.
In later years, when he found himself working in government institutions, advising businesses, or advocating for economic development, he would often reflect on those early influences.
They were the compass that guided his decisions. And they reminded him that leadership, in its truest form, begins not in public office but in the communities that first shape a person’s character.
The Discipline of Education
The classroom at Camp Keithley Elementary School in Marawi City was quiet except for the soft scratching of pencils against paper.
Rows of wooden desks faced the chalkboard where numbers had been carefully written in neat columns. The exercise seemed simple enough: solve the arithmetic problems and show the process step by step.
For most of the students, the task required concentration.
For the young Abdulgani Macatoman, it required something more — precision.

He leaned forward slightly as he worked through the equations, methodically checking each calculation before moving to the next line. Numbers, he had begun to realize, followed a logic that rewarded patience and careful thought.
His teacher watched the room attentively as students worked. When she reached Gani’s desk, she paused briefly.
His answers were correct.
More than that, the work showed an unusual attention to detail for a student his age.
Moments like these were small and easily overlooked, yet they often revealed something about the future direction of a young mind.

For Gani, the discipline required in those early classroom exercises mirrored the values he had learned at home. His parents had instilled in him a respect for effort and preparation. School, therefore, was not merely an obligation — it was an opportunity.
From the beginning, he approached his studies with seriousness.

Camp Keithley provided more than academic instruction. Located in Marawi City, the school operated within an environment shaped by both community life and the presence of nearby institutions that valued order and discipline.
Students were expected to arrive prepared. Teachers emphasized not only academic performance but also responsibility, respect, and cooperation.
Gani responded well to that structure.

He developed an early interest in subjects that demanded logical thinking and careful analysis. Mathematics and accounting concepts — though still simple at the elementary level — captured his attention.

Numbers made sense. 
They followed rules. 
And when those rules were understood, problems could be solved.
Yet education was never confined to the classroom alone.

Outside school hours, conversations at home continued to reinforce the lessons of discipline and perseverance. His parents reminded their children that learning was a privilege — one that many families struggled to obtain.
As he progressed through his elementary years, teachers began encouraging him to aim higher. They recognized not only his academic ability but also his quiet determination.
Such encouragement can shape a young student’s sense of possibility.
For Gani, it planted the idea that education might eventually carry him beyond the boundaries of his hometown.
The Training Center Years
When Gani later entered the Mindanao State University Training Center for his secondary education, his world expanded significantly.

The Training Center brought together students from different communities across Mindanao. In the hallways and classrooms, conversations reflected a wide range of backgrounds, cultures, and perspectives.
For many students, the school served as a gateway to opportunities beyond their local communities.
Gani quickly immersed himself in the environment.
High school introduced new academic challenges and intellectual debates. Subjects became more complex, and expectations for independent thinking grew.
At the same time, the Training Center offered opportunities for students to participate in organizations and activities beyond academic coursework.
Gani began to explore these opportunities.
Through student activities and school initiatives, he gained his first experiences working collaboratively with peers to organize events and manage responsibilities.
These early leadership experiences were modest in scale but meaningful in impact.
They taught him an important lesson: leadership often begins with small responsibilities carried out faithfully.
Teachers again played a pivotal role during these years.
Several mentors recognized his discipline and intellectual curiosity.
They encouraged him to pursue higher education and to consider fields where analytical thinking and leadership could be applied.
Their advice broadened his ambitions.
By the time he approached graduation, Gani had begun considering a future that extended beyond Mindanao.
Manila, with its universities and national institutions, represented the next stage of that journey. Leaving home would not be easy.
But it was necessary.
The lessons learned in Marawi and at the Training Center had prepared him for that step.

And soon, the young student from Mindanao would find himself entering a much larger world — one where the ideas he had cultivated in the classroom would begin to intersect with the realities of business, governance, and national development.
A New World in Manila
When Abdulgani Macatoman arrived in Manila to pursue higher education, the experience felt like stepping into an entirely different universe.

The capital moved with a rhythm that was both exhilarating and intimidating. Streets were crowded with students, workers, and entrepreneurs chasing their own ambitions. Conversations in classrooms often extended late into the evening, fueled by debates about politics, economics, and the future of the country.
For a young man from Mindanao, Manila was both a challenge and an opportunity.

He enrolled at the University of the East, one of the country’s most respected institutions for business and legal education. There he pursued a Bachelor of Science in Commerce, majoring in Accounting — a discipline that appealed to his methodical nature and his affinity for structured reasoning.
Accounting demanded precision. Numbers left little room for ambiguity. Each calculation required discipline, patience, and clarity of thought.

For Gani, the field became more than a technical specialization. It was a way of understanding how organizations functioned — how financial systems shaped decisions and how accountability could be measured.
Yet even as he immersed himself in accounting studies, he recognized that leadership required a broader intellectual framework.
The world of enterprise did not operate solely on financial logic. It was also shaped by laws, institutions, and governance systems.

Determined to deepen his understanding, he pursued legal studies while continuing his academic journey. Law offered insight into how societies organize themselves, how regulations shape markets, and how institutions maintain order.

Eventually he expanded his education further through a Master’s Degree in Business Administration, completing a trio of disciplines — accounting, law, and management — that would later define his professional versatility.
Each field offered a different perspective. Accounting sharpened analytical discipline.
Law illuminated the structures of governance. Business administration provided the strategic lens through which organizations could grow and innovate.
Together they formed an intellectual toolkit that would guide Gani throughout his career.
Business, he believed, was not merely about profit.
It was about creating value — value for workers, for investors, and for society.
This belief eventually led him to participate in ventures that sought to combine entrepreneurship with long-term development goals.
Among the most significant of these was the creation of Global Empire International Group of Companies Inc.

The company emerged during a period when renewable energy and infrastructure development were becoming increasingly important to the Philippines’ economic future. As the country grappled with rising energy demands and the need for sustainable power solutions, businesses operating in these sectors faced both enormous challenges and extraordinary opportunities.
Within Global Empire International Group, Gani became deeply involved in strategic planning and corporate leadership.
Yet from the very beginning, the enterprise was not solely his undertaking.
It was the product of a partnership.
A Partnership in Leadership
Behind many leadership journeys stand individuals whose contributions remain less visible but equally vital.
For Abdulgani Macatoman, that presence has been his wife, Mufaida.

Long before she became a business executive, Mufaida had built a career in journalism. She served as an executive broadcast journalist for TV3 Malaysia, where she developed a reputation for professionalism and insight.

Broadcast journalism demanded the ability to interpret complex events quickly and communicate them clearly to a wide audience. It required discipline, composure under pressure, and a deep awareness of the social forces shaping public life.

Those experiences would later prove invaluable when she entered the world of enterprise. Over time, Mufaida transitioned from journalism into business leadership. Together with her husband, she helped establish Global Empire International Group of Companies Inc.

Within the organization she initially served as Chief Operating Officer, overseeing the operational structure that allowed the company to function efficiently. Her work required navigating regulatory frameworks, coordinating projects, and managing teams working within the emerging field of renewable energy.
The company gradually developed expertise in solar and power solution industries, sectors that were gaining importance as the Philippines explored sustainable energy alternatives.
For more than a decade Mufaida accumulated extensive executive management experience, becoming a central figure in the company’s development.

Then in July 2017, the trajectory of the Macatoman family’s professional life took a decisive turn. Abdulgani Macatoman accepted an appointment as Undersecretary of the Department of Trade and Industry.
Public service required his complete focus. Government ethics demanded that he step away from direct corporate leadership.
At that moment, the responsibility for guiding Global Empire International Group passed fully to Mufaida.
She assumed the role of President and Chief Executive Officer, leading the company through the next stage of its development.
The transition reflected not only professional capability but also trust.

Under her leadership, the company continued its work in renewable energy and development-oriented ventures, sustaining the enterprise even as her husband entered the demanding world of national policy.
Yet her interests extended beyond corporate leadership.

In the 2022 national elections, Mufaida Macatoman served as the first nominee of the Ang Kabuhayang Kayang Kaya (AKKK) Party-List, a movement advocating entrepreneurship development, livelihood opportunities, and economic empowerment.
Her advocacy mirrored many of the values that had guided the couple’s shared journey: the belief that enterprise could become a powerful tool for uplifting communities.
The Call to Government Service

The path that eventually led Gani national government did not begin with a single appointment or political ambition. Rather, it unfolded gradually — through a series of engagements that exposed him to the inner workings of public institutions and the complex responsibilities of governance.

By the time he entered formal government service, Gani had already spent years working at the intersection of enterprise, policy, and civic engagement. His experience in business had allowed him to see firsthand how economic decisions made in government offices reverberated across industries and communities. Regulations could determine whether entrepreneurs thrived or struggled; policies could open markets or close doors.
These observations slowly drew him closer to public service.

His earliest roles in government came through advisory work. He served as a Consultant in the Office of the President of the Republic of the Philippines, where he gained insight into the processes through which national priorities were shaped and coordinated.
The experience offered a rare vantage point into the machinery of governance, where decisions often required balancing competing interests and long-term national goals.

At around the same time, he also served as Executive Officer in the Department of Education, Culture and Sports (DECS). The role exposed him to another dimension of public policy — education, a sector he believed formed the foundation of national development. If entrepreneurship and economic growth created opportunity, education ensured that citizens could seize it.

His work later expanded into areas connected with national security and law enforcement. Gani served as a Consultant to the Philippine Center on Transnational Crime (PCTC) as well as to the Office of the Chief of the Philippine National Police (PNP). These engagements required coordination across agencies addressing complex challenges that extended beyond national borders.
Alongside these responsibilities, he also served as a Lieutenant Colonel in the Philippine Army, reflecting his broader commitment to national service.

Through these varied roles, Gani gained a deeper understanding of how public institutions operate. Governance required patience and discipline. It demanded the ability to work within systems that moved deliberately and often required consensus among multiple stakeholders.
These early experiences prepared him for a turning point that would significantly expand his responsibilities.

In July 2017, President Rodrigo Roa Duterte appointed Abdulgani Macatoman as Assistant Secretary of the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI). The appointment placed him within the agency responsible for shaping the country’s economic competitiveness, promoting trade and investment, and supporting the development of Filipino enterprises.

Gani entered the department with a perspective shaped by years in business and advisory roles in government. He understood the concerns of entrepreneurs as well as the institutional realities of public administration.
His diligence and work ethic soon earned the confidence of leadership within the department.
Barely a year after his appointment, in July 2018, he was promoted to Undersecretary for Special Concerns, a role that required coordination across key programs and strategic initiatives.
The scope of his responsibilities continued to grow.

In February 2019, he was given an additional appointment as Undersecretary of the Trade Promotions Group, placing him in a position where his experience in enterprise and international engagement would become particularly valuable.
By that point, Gani had moved fully into the center of the country’s economic policy framework.

The responsibilities awaiting him would involve not only government administration but also engagement with industries, entrepreneurs, and international partners seeking to understand the opportunities within the Philippine economy.
It was a role that demanded both technical expertise and diplomatic skill.
And it marked the beginning of one of the most significant chapters of his public life.
Inside the Department of Trade and Industry
When Abdulgani Macatoman assumed leadership responsibilities within the Department of Trade and Industry, he stepped into one of the most complex arenas of Philippine economic policy.

The agency carried a broad mandate: strengthening domestic industries, promoting exports, attracting foreign investment, and supporting the millions of micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) that form the backbone of the country’s economy.

These enterprises represent the entrepreneurial spirit of the Philippines. From family-owned workshops and neighborhood retailers to emerging technology ventures, MSMEs provide employment for a vast segment of the population.
Yet they also face formidable challenges — limited access to financing, difficulties in reaching international markets, and the pressures of competing in a globalized economy.

Gani understood these realities well. Having spent much of his career in business, he was familiar with the obstacles entrepreneurs encounter when navigating regulatory systems and competitive markets.
Within the Department of Trade and Industry, he sought to help bridge the gap between policy and practice.

His responsibilities placed him at the intersection of government strategy and private sector development. Programs aimed at strengthening export competitiveness and improving the country’s investment climate became central to the department’s work.

International engagement also played an important role. Trade promotion required constant dialogue with foreign investors, business chambers, and economic partners interested in exploring opportunities in the Philippines.

Gani’s experience in enterprise and international business circles proved valuable in these discussions. He understood the questions investors often asked: How stable are regulatory systems? What opportunities exist in emerging sectors? How can partnerships between local industries and foreign companies be structured to benefit both sides?

Such conversations were rarely limited to economic statistics. They involved building confidence — demonstrating that the Philippines possessed both the resources and the institutional capacity to support long-term investment.

The department’s work also intersected with regional development initiatives, particularly those connected to Mindanao. Expanding economic opportunities in historically underserved regions formed an important part of the country’s broader development strategy.

For Gani, this aspect of the work carried personal meaning. The island where he had grown up possessed enormous economic potential, and initiatives that encouraged entrepreneurship and investment there represented opportunities to strengthen communities as well as industries.
The role demanded constant movement between policy discussions, consultations with business leaders, and international engagements.

Yet throughout these responsibilities, Gani remained guided by a principle that had shaped his career from the beginning. Economic development should not exist solely in policy documents or corporate balance sheets.
It should translate into opportunity — into jobs created, enterprises strengthened, and communities empowered.
Within the Department of Trade and Industry, he sought to advance that vision.
The Global Arena
As the Philippine economy became increasingly integrated into global markets, Gani’s responsibilities also took on an international dimension.

Trade diplomacy had become an essential component of economic policy. Nations competed not only through domestic reforms but also through their ability to attract investment, expand export markets, and position themselves strategically within regional alliances.
Gani’s experience in the private sector proved invaluable in these discussions.

Having spent years interacting with international investors and business organizations, he understood the concerns that often shaped investment decisions — regulatory stability, infrastructure capacity, and the predictability of economic policy.

His work frequently intersected with organizations such as the Foreign Chamber Council of the Philippines, where representatives from foreign business chambers discussed the evolving conditions for investment and trade.
These dialogues were not merely technical. They were conversations about trust.

Investors sought assurance that the Philippines could provide a stable environment for long-term development. Government leaders, in turn, sought partnerships that could generate employment, stimulate innovation, and strengthen domestic industries.
Gani often found himself at the intersection of these interests, helping bridge perspectives between global investors and national policy priorities.
In doing so, he contributed to a broader effort to position the Philippines as a competitive participant in the global economy.
Mindanao and the Promise of Development
While his responsibilities increasingly involved national and international initiatives, Gani never lost sight of the region that had shaped his earliest experiences.
Mindanao remained central to his vision for inclusive development.

For decades, the island had faced challenges that extended beyond economics — political tensions, uneven infrastructure development, and the lingering effects of conflict. Yet it also possessed enormous potential.
Rich natural resources, strategic geographic location, and vibrant communities offered opportunities for economic transformation.
Gani believed that entrepreneurship and investment could become powerful instruments for stability.

Through initiatives connected to organizations such as the Bangsamoro Business Council, he advocated for programs designed to attract investors, support local enterprises, and create employment opportunities in the region.
Economic development, he believed, could complement broader peacebuilding efforts by giving communities a stake in stability and progress.
Mindanao, in this sense, represented more than a policy priority.
It was the place where his own journey had begun.
The Public Voice
Leadership sometimes requires more than policy work.
It also requires communication.
Gani’s commitment to entrepreneurship advocacy eventually extended into media through the program “Kabuhayan at Negosyo,” broadcast nationally on Channel 23 and DWIZ 882.

The show offered practical discussions about business development and livelihood opportunities. Entrepreneurs shared their experiences, experts discussed strategies for small businesses, and viewers across the country gained access to information that might otherwise remain confined to policy circles.
For Gani, the program served an important purpose.
Economic knowledge should not belong exclusively to specialists.
Entrepreneurs across the Philippines — whether operating in urban centers or rural communities — deserved access to insights that could help them succeed.
By bringing discussions about enterprise into the public sphere, the program sought to encourage a culture of innovation and initiative.
Ideas and Advocacy
Beyond his work in government and media, Gani also contributed to discussions about emerging economic sectors.
Among these was the global halal economy, a rapidly expanding market encompassing food production, finance, tourism, and consumer goods designed to meet the needs of Muslim populations worldwide.

Recognizing the Philippines’ potential role in this sector, Gani authored “Global Halal Economy,” a work exploring how the country could position itself strategically within this international market.

The book examined not only commercial opportunities but also the broader implications of halal industries for inclusive development — particularly in regions such as Mindanao with significant Muslim populations.
For Gani, the subject represented more than economic analysis.
It reflected a broader belief that development strategies must recognize cultural diversity and regional strengths.
Recognition and Responsibility
Over the course of his career, Gani’s work has been acknowledged through numerous awards and recognitions.

Among them were distinctions such as Management Man of the Year from the Philippine Council of Management, recognition as one of the Ten Most Influential Filipinos by the Philippine Cancer Society, the Lambert Award, and honors from the University of the East as one of its most outstanding alumni.
He has also served as a Reserve Lieutenant Colonel in the Armed Forces of the Philippines, reflecting another dimension of his commitment to national service.
Yet those who know him personally often remark that Gani rarely dwells on recognition.
For him, awards serve less as milestones than as reminders of responsibility.
Leadership, he believes, is measured not by accolades but by the lives affected through one’s work.
Service Above Self
Public service does not always take place within the formal structures of government.

For Abdulgani Macatoman, another dimension of service emerged through an institution whose influence has quietly shaped leaders across generations — the Rotary Club of Manila, the oldest Rotary club in Asia and one of the most respected civic organizations in the Philippines.
His introduction to Rotary came through an invitation from Past Director Amado “Amading” Valdez, who recognized in Gani a set of values deeply aligned with the organization’s mission.
In 2016, Gani joined the Rotary Club of Manila.

Rotary’s guiding principle — “Service Above Self” — resonated immediately with him. The philosophy mirrored the lessons he had carried since childhood in Mindanao: that leadership must be measured not by personal advancement but by the willingness to serve others.
Within Rotary, Gani found a community of professionals, entrepreneurs, and public servants united by a shared commitment to humanitarian service and ethical leadership.

The club’s projects ranged widely — from education and health initiatives to disaster relief and community development programs. Through these efforts, Rotary provided an avenue where professional expertise could be transformed into practical service.
Gani approached Rotary in the same way he approached every responsibility in his life: with quiet diligence and a sense of stewardship.

He participated actively in the club’s activities, contributing not only his professional experience but also his perspective on economic development, entrepreneurship, and community empowerment. Over time, his colleagues recognized both his integrity and his commitment to the institution.
After more than nine years as a member of the Rotary Club of Manila, Gani was appointed Club Auditor for Rotary Year 2026–2027.

The role carries significant responsibility within the organization. The Club Auditor helps safeguard financial transparency and institutional accountability — principles that are essential to sustaining trust within a century-old institution.
For Gani, the position reflected a natural alignment between his professional training in accounting and governance and Rotary’s emphasis on ethical stewardship.
Yet the significance of Rotary in his life extends beyond titles or roles.
The organization represents a community where leadership is expressed through service — through projects that uplift communities, support education, and respond to humanitarian needs.
In Rotary, Gani found a continuation of the same ideals that had guided his journey from the beginning.

Integrity. 
Responsibility.
And the belief that service, when practiced consistently and humbly, can strengthen the fabric of society.
Family and the Meaning of Legacy

In the public imagination, leadership is often measured through titles held, policies shaped, or institutions guided. Yet for Gani, the deeper measure of a life’s work has always been far more personal.
It lies in family.

Despite the wide scope of his professional journey — spanning enterprise, government service, civic leadership, and public advocacy — Gani has remained deeply conscious that the foundations of character are built not in public office but within the quiet spaces of home.

Throughout the many transitions of his career, one constant presence has been his wife, Mufaida. Their partnership has extended far beyond shared professional endeavors. It has been rooted in a mutual understanding that leadership, whether in business or public service, requires both sacrifice and support. The responsibilities that accompany such roles often demand long hours, difficult decisions, and a willingness to place the needs of institutions and communities ahead of personal convenience.
In such moments, the strength of a family becomes essential.

For Gani, the encouragement and steadfast presence of his wife have been a source of stability throughout the demands of public life. Together they have navigated the shifting landscapes of enterprise and national service while maintaining a home environment centered on faith, humility, and mutual respect.
Their family life has been shaped by the same principles that guided Gani’s upbringing in Mindanao — values passed down from parents who believed that character mattered more than circumstance.
Those values now form the foundation of the household he and Mufaida have built together.
The couple has been blessed with three children: Abdul Hakeem, Amirah Jareeza, and Kamilah Amber.

For Gani, fatherhood represents one of the most meaningful responsibilities of his life. While public leadership carries its own obligations, raising children offers a different kind of legacy — the opportunity to shape the next generation’s understanding of integrity, discipline, and compassion.
In conversations with his children, he often returns to the lessons he learned as a young boy growing up in Mindanao.
Respect for others. Commitment to education. The importance of humility even in moments of success.
And above all, the understanding that leadership is not defined by recognition but by service.
These are the principles he hopes will guide them as they pursue their own paths in life.
Balancing family life with the demands of professional responsibility has never been simple.

Public service often requires travel, extended meetings, and responsibilities that stretch far beyond normal working hours. Yet Gani has remained mindful of the importance of preserving time for the moments that define family life — shared meals, celebrations of milestones, and the quiet conversations that strengthen relationships.
Such moments provide perspective.
They remind him that the ultimate purpose of leadership is not merely institutional achievement but the well-being of people and communities.
As the years have passed, Gani has come to view legacy not as something measured through individual accomplishments but as something reflected in the lives touched along the way.

Legacy can be found in the entrepreneurs who gain opportunities through economic development initiatives. It can be seen in the communities strengthened through cooperation and investment. It can be felt in the institutions that continue to serve long after individual leaders have stepped aside.
But perhaps most enduringly, legacy lives within family.
It lives in the values passed from one generation to the next, in the quiet example of integrity, and in the lessons children carry forward into their own lives.
For Gani, this understanding brings his life’s journey full circle.
The boy who once listened attentively to the wisdom of elders in Mindanao now finds himself sharing those same lessons with his own children.
The principles remain unchanged.

Faith. 
Humility. 
Responsibility. 
Service.
These values shaped his beginnings, guided his career, and now define the legacy he hopes to leave behind.
Epilogue: The Measure of Leadership
The life of Abdulgani Macatoman illustrates a quiet but powerful truth about leadership.
Influence does not always emerge from dramatic moments or public attention.
More often, it grows steadily through years of disciplined work, ethical decisions, and the willingness to serve beyond personal interest.
Gani’s journey — from the communities of Mindanao to the halls of national government — reflects that philosophy.
He has moved between sectors that often appear distinct: enterprise and policy, local communities and international markets, private initiative and public service.
Yet throughout these transitions, one principle has remained constant.
Leadership must serve others.

The Philippines today continues to navigate the challenges of economic development, globalization, and social transformation. Within that evolving landscape, leaders who can bridge perspectives between sectors remain essential.
Gani’s career stands as an example of that bridge.
A life lived between enterprise and nation.
And a reminder that the true legacy of leadership is measured not only by achievements, but by the opportunities created for others to succeed.

articles.title: A Convergence of Purpose: The March 24 Joint Meeting of Three Rotary Clubs

body.text: In a rare and meaningful convergence of Rotary fellowship and purpose, the Rotary Club of Manila, the Rotary Club of Makati, and the Rotary Club of Makati West gathered on March 24 for a Joint Meeting that was as much a reaffirmation of shared ideals as it was a call to collective action.

It was a gathering that transcended routine. Three of the country’s most storied Rotary institutions came together not merely to exchange courtesies, but to engage in dialogue on issues that cut across sectors, industries, and communities. The room carried a palpable sense of anticipation — one shaped by the presence of leaders who understood that service, at its highest form, demands both reflection and resolve.
Opening Ceremonies
The meeting formally commenced with the Call to Order, setting the tone for an afternoon anchored on Rotary’s enduring values — service above self, fellowship, and ethical leadership.

At the helm of the gathering were the presidents of the three clubs: Raoul Creencia of the Rotary Club of Manila, Eddie Galvez of the Rotary Club of Makati, and Gino Dumatol of the Rotary Club of Makati West. Their presence symbolized not only leadership, but unity — three institutions moving in concert toward a shared vision.

Among those recognized during the program were Jed Balayan, Treasurer of Rotary Club of Makati West; Louie Asioche, District Secretary and incoming District Governor; and Aaron Virata-Mempil of Rotary Club of Makati, who served as moderator for the afternoon’s program.

The invocation and national anthem grounded the assembly in both spiritual reflection and patriotic duty, reminding all present that Rotary’s mission is inseparable from the larger narrative of nation-building.
Fellowship and Shared Purpose

What distinguished the March 24 gathering was not merely its scale, but its spirit. Conversations unfolded naturally across tables — between seasoned Rotarians and new members, between leaders of different clubs, between individuals united by a common calling.

This was Rotary in its most authentic form — not confined within the identity of a single club, but expressed through collaboration. The joint meeting became a living testament to the power of collective action, where relationships were strengthened and new possibilities quietly began to take shape.
The Address of the Guest of Honor and Speaker
The highlight of the afternoon was the address of the Guest of Honor and Speaker, The Honorable Senator Francis Pancratius "Kiko" Pangilinan.

Speaking with candor and conviction, Senator Pangilinan opened with an apology for his delayed arrival, having come directly from a Senate hearing addressing the escalating crisis in the Middle East. Yet, rather than dwell on uncertainty, he framed the moment as an opportunity — a call to transform crisis into catalyst.
He addressed the audience not merely as Rotarians, but as leaders in the private sector, capable of shaping outcomes far beyond the confines of their respective professions.

At the heart of his speech was a powerful and deeply human narrative: the condition of the Filipino farmer. He spoke of a reality that has long persisted but remains insufficiently addressed — that those who feed the nation often cannot feed themselves.

He painted vivid portraits of elderly farmers who had spent decades tilling the land, their combined years of service reaching nearly two centuries, yet who remained trapped in cycles of poverty and indebtedness.

This, he emphasized, is not simply a matter of food supply — it is a matter of justice. Food security, in his framing, must be understood alongside food justice. A nation cannot claim stability when its primary food producers remain among its most vulnerable.

He highlighted the structural weaknesses in the agricultural sector, particularly the lack of support systems for farmers and fisherfolk. Investments in infrastructure and technology, while important, will fall short if the human foundation of agriculture remains neglected.

To address this, he outlined key reforms aimed at strengthening the sector from within. Among these were the revival of the Bureau of Agricultural Cooperatives and the renationalization of extension services — measures designed to empower farmers, improve productivity, and create sustainable support networks.

He contrasted the Philippine experience with that of more developed agricultural systems, where close coordination between extension workers and farmers ensures both efficiency and resilience. The disparity, he noted, underscores the urgency of reform.
President Raoul C. Creencia, Pres. Eddie Galvez (RC Makati), and Pres. Dino Dumatol (RC Makati West) presented a Plaque of Appreciation to Senator Francis "Kiko" Pangilinan.

The discussion then widened to include energy security, particularly in light of the ongoing geopolitical tensions affecting global oil supply. The Philippines’ heavy dependence on imported oil exposes it to external shocks — an exposure that calls for a decisive shift toward renewable energy.
But beyond policy, Pangilinan’s message was fundamentally about partnership.

He underscored the indispensable role of the private sector — and organizations like Rotary — in bridging gaps that government alone cannot address. He cited initiatives that allow direct procurement from farmers, eliminating exploitative intermediaries and ensuring fairer incomes.

More importantly, he extended an invitation: for Rotarians to actively participate in nation-building by investing in agricultural systems, supporting cooperatives, and using their networks to create sustainable impact.
His speech was not merely informative — it was a challenge. A challenge to rethink priorities, to act with urgency, and to recognize that meaningful change requires collective effort.
Reflections and Closing
As the program transitioned toward its conclusion, the atmosphere shifted from attentive listening to thoughtful reflection.

The conversations that followed bore the imprint of the afternoon’s message — serious, purposeful, and forward-looking. There was a shared understanding that the issues discussed were not distant concerns, but immediate realities requiring action.

The Joint Meeting, in its entirety, became more than a scheduled gathering. It became a moment of alignment — of three Rotary clubs recognizing the strength of unity and the responsibility that comes with it.
The Adjournment marked the formal close of the program, but not the end of its impact.
Epilogue: Toward a Unified Rotary Action

If there was a single thread that ran through the March 24 Joint Meeting, it was this: the recognition that leadership, especially in times of uncertainty, demands more than position — it demands purpose.
In bringing together the Rotary Club of Manila, the Rotary Club of Makati, and the Rotary Club of Makati West, the meeting affirmed a simple but profound truth:

That the future is best shaped not in isolation, but in unity.

And in that shared space — through dialogue, reflection, and a renewed commitment to service — the foundations of that unity were strengthened, one meaningful conversation at a time.
Meeting Fellowship

Editor-in-Chief

In a country long burdened by questions of transparency, efficiency, and institutional trust, the emergence of a 23- year-old entrepreneur helping to place government records on-chain is not merely noteworthy. It is quietly disruptive.
Brandon "Gelo" Wong represents a generation that does not wait for systems to evolve. It builds new ones.

At an age when most are still finding their footing, Wong has already positioned himself at the intersection of technology, governance, and national infrastructure. As co-founder and Chief Growth Officer of BYC Ventures, he is part of a team that has helped bring over $90 billion worth of government records onto blockchain. This is not simply a milestone in scale. It is a statement of direction.
This is not innovation for its own sake. It is innovation aimed at a problem that has defined the Philippine public sector for decades. Trust.
The Real Currency: Credibility
For all the debates surrounding blockchain, its most enduring promise remains immutability.
In governance, that translates to credibility.
When records cannot be altered, when transactions leave permanent and verifiable trails, and when systems are designed around transparency, the nature of public accountability begins to change.
Through its flagship platform, Lumen, BYC Ventures is building what it calls a Truth Operating System. It is a digital backbone where data integrity is not assumed but engineered.

The implications are significant. In agencies such as the Department of Budget and Management, Department of Public Works and Highways, Department of Information and Communications Technology, and even within the Congress of the Philippines, the adoption of such systems points to a shift toward proactive accountability.
A Different Kind of Builder
Wong’s story begins early, with entrepreneurship at 14. But what distinguishes him is not just timing. It is focus.
Many founders build for convenience or scale. Wong builds within institutions that are complex, slow-moving, and resistant to change.
Operating in that space requires more than technical skill. It demands the ability to engage policymakers, navigate bureaucracy, and translate innovation into something government can adopt.
That he has represented the Philippine blockchain sector in policy discussions suggests a rare dual fluency. He understands both the language of systems and the language of governance.
A Regional Signal
BYC Ventures’ work carries implications beyond the Philippines.

Across Southeast Asia, governments are searching for ways to modernize without compromising security. The Philippines’ deployment of blockchain at scale signals that emerging economies can build their own solutions.
It also suggests that public sector innovation can be collaborative. It need not be confined within government. It can be shaped alongside entrepreneurs who are willing to challenge legacy systems.
The Necessary Caution
Technology does not eliminate human failure. It changes its form.

Blockchain can secure records, but it cannot guarantee the accuracy of what is entered. It can promote transparency, but only if access is properly managed. It can strengthen trust, but only if institutions remain accountable.
There is also the question of resilience. As systems become digital, they must withstand cyber threats, technological shifts, and future disruptions.
The reference to post-quantum readiness reflects this awareness. But awareness must be matched by vigilance from both builders and regulators.
Beyond One Individual
It is tempting to frame this as a story of youthful success. A 23-year-old building systems of national importance.
But the larger story is about who is shaping the future.
For decades, governance systems were built within institutions. Today, they are increasingly influenced by entrepreneurs.
This shift is inevitable. The question is whether it will be guided by purpose.
Closing Reflection
In University of Asia and the Pacific, where Wong studied Entrepreneurial Management, there is a tradition of linking enterprise with responsibility. His work reflects that idea.
The challenge now is not only to scale infrastructure, but to deepen impact.
Can systems like Lumen influence not just records, but decisions? Can they improve not just efficiency, but fairness? Can they help create a government that is not only transparent, but trusted?
These questions remain open.
There is a quiet symbolism in placing government records on blockchain. It is an act of permanence.
But permanence is not the goal.
Trust is.
The Last Quarter

The month of April signals the Rotary year’s entering its final quarter. As we welcome this final phase of our service year, a quiet but unmistakable shift begins to take place. The calendar itself seems to quicken, and what once felt like a long horizon of plans and aspirations now comes into sharper focus -- measured not in months, but in the tangible impact of what has been done, and what still remains within reach.
For a Club President, this period is both reflective and resolute.

It is a time to look back with honest clarity. The past months have been filled with intention -- flagship projects launched, new initiatives introduced, and long-standing signature programs faithfully carried out. Each meeting, each outreach, each partnership represents not just activity, but commitment: to service, to fellowship, and to the ideals that bind Rotarians together. Some efforts exceeded expectations; others may have encountered challenges. Yet all of them contribute to the living story of the Club -- one written not in perfection, but in perseverance.
At the same time, the last quarter is not merely about looking back -- it is about finishing well.

There is a renewed sense of purpose in ensuring that what was started is brought to meaningful completion. Projects must not only be implemented, but sustained. Commitments must not only be fulfilled, but strengthened. The energy of the Club often finds a second wind during this period, as members recognize that there is still time to make a difference -- to deepen impact, to expand reach, and to leave something enduring.

Equally important is the recognition that leadership, especially in Rotary, is never a solitary endeavor. Whatever has been accomplished in the past months is the result of collective effort -- of members who gave their time, ideas, and resources; of partners who shared in the vision; and of a community that allowed the Club to serve. Gratitude becomes more pronounced during this time, not as a formality, but as a sincere acknowledgment that leadership is ultimately an act of stewardship.

There is also a forward-looking dimension to this final stretch. As the current Rotary year begins to wind down, the groundwork for continuity must be laid. The next set of leaders top billed by PE Reggie will soon take the helm, and it is essential that they inherit not only completed projects, but a strong foundation -- clear systems, sustained relationships, and an inspired membership ready to carry the mission forward.

In many ways, the last quarter defines the tone of the entire year. It is where intentions are validated by outcomes, where vision is translated into legacy. It reminds us that leadership is not measured solely by what is initiated, but by what is sustained and entrusted to others.

As President, one comes to appreciate that the true value of the year lies not only in milestones achieved, but in the lives touched and the spirit of service strengthened within the Club. And as the Rotary year approaches its close, there is both fulfillment and humility in knowing that while one’s term may be finite, the work of Rotary -- and the opportunity to serve -- continues far beyond it.

articles.title: Project Report: RCM-RCMFI Reading Literacy Teacher Training Project with Reading Specialists

body.text: READING SPECIALISTS x ILUGIN ELEMENTARY SCHOOL
Snapshot of Training

The recent national conversation revealed the learning challenges of our country where 88% of students entering Grade 7 struggle to read at their level. The Reading Specialists, in partnership with Rotary Club of Manila, Rotary Club of Manila Foundation, Kabisig ng Kalahi Foundation, and Ilugin Elementary School, spent Feb 7 and Feb 23, 2026 in a two-day interactive workshop on the Science of Reading. 60 teachers from Kindergarten to Grade 7 level attended 16 hours of training aimed at equipping them with the tools and knowledge to develop skills in reading and comprehension. This report highlights how partnerships are empowering our teachers to make a real difference in ensuring that all Filipino children are able to read.
Feedback from Participants
❝ The two day training is very informative to us, as a teacher in Kindergarten it gives me more ideas or strategies on how I handle teaching my learners how to read in a fun way.❞
❝ I would like to express my heartfelt appreciation to all speakers for sharing your expertise in reading. You have given it all. All I need to do is to choose which strategies fit my learners.❞
Survey Results

For each day of the training, teachers were asked to fill in a survey. The results revealed that 100% of teachers either agreed or strongly agreed that the training content was relevant to their needs as a teacher and was presented in an engaging and effective way.

Looking even further at the survey results, it revealed that the most gain was in the Day 1 topic on the Science of Reading and theoretical models of reading, and the Day 2 topic of using the Frayer Model for teaching vocabulary. This suggests that awareness of the models and concepts of the Science of Reading were training topics that connected the most with the teachers who participated in the training sessions.

In addition, 92% of teachers said “Yes” when asked whether they were able to apply the strategies demonstrated on Day 1. The graph shows the breakdown of the strategies they applied, which shows that strategies on Phonological Awareness (PA) were applied by 73%, followed by spelling, sound cards, and decoding. With these results, follow-up training to strengthen decoding practices can be conducted to further encourage the adoption of a variety of strategies for teaching decoding and comprehension in the classroom.

The two days of interactive training, as supported by the survey results and comments from the participants, helped the teachers of Ilugin Elementary School gain an improved understanding of the Science of Reading, have confidence to apply new strategies in teaching reading in their practice. With the positive results, teachers can be further supported to keep using what they learned in their classrooms every day.
From the teachers of Ilugin Elementary School, Pasig City
❝ I already used the sound cards in my class and also the spelling activities. They enjoyed it. They also enjoyed the rhyming game, phoneme segmentation and blending activities.❞
❝ I will try the magnetic letters/words because I know that it really works for my learners; they can use their fine motor skills, as well as enjoy and have fun while learning.❞
To our friends at the Rotary Club Manila and the Rotary Club Manila Foundation, Inc.,

They say it takes a village, and we are so grateful you are part of ours! Your sponsorship allowed us to bring our teachers together for two Saturdays last February of interactive training, where they are guided to try out different materials and apply the Science of Reading. They learned new strategies that will change the way young Filipino students engage with learning to read and reading to learn. Thank you for recognizing the value of a well-trained teacher and for being a true champion for literacy in our country.
Warmly, The Reading Specialists

Avenues of Service:
• Community Service
• Vocational Service
• Youth Service
Areas of Focus:
• Community Economic Development
• Maternal and Child Health
• Disease Prevention and Treatment
Report:
RI District 3810, in partnership with PAFJO TMJ OFP Inc., successfully conducted the “Handog Makeover District Dental Mission”.

This project, conceptualized together with PDG Joyce Ambray, was designed to support individuals aged 16 to 35 who often struggle to secure employment because appearance and presentation requirements can stand in their way — knowing that a confident smile can open doors.

In this project, fifty (50) young jobseeker beneficiaries received wellfitted dentures, completing a journey that began weeks earlier in the private clinics of volunteer dentists from PAFJO TMJ OFP Inc. and the Rotary Club of Manila Phenomenal Dentists, a daughter club of the Rotary Club of Manila. There, they underwent oral rehabilitation procedures such as prophylaxis, fillings, and extractions. The final denture installation during the mission marked the culmination of their dental transformation — restoring both function and self-esteem.

Far beyond oral health, the program included grooming sessions for men and makeup tutorials for women, followed by styling assistance to ensure they dressed appropriately for the workplace. Each beneficiary received a professional ID photo for job applications. In a heartfelt display of Rotary service, volunteers also donated pre-loved corporate attire, shoes, and belts, helping beneficiaries feel confident and ready for professional environments.

Rotary Club of Manila members prepared beneficiaries for employment by conducting simulated job interviews. These sessions equipped participants with the confidence and communication skills to take on real-world opportunities. Some qualified beneficiaries were even hired on the spot, achieving their dreams of gainful employment.
Manila Rotarians who participated and donated included:
• DGND Hermie Esguerra - assorted shirts, blazers, pants, long sleeves, and belts
• IPP Jujut Enriquez - 1 tuxedo, 1 blazer, 3 full suits, 3 long sleeve office polo shirts, 2 female tops and 2 dresses from his wife
• PE Reggie Yu - 1 suit
• Dir. Mike Albaña - 30 neckties, 10 suits, and 20 long-sleeve office shirts
• PD/IS Albert Alday - 4 office bags
• Sec. Anton Mauricio - shirts and belts
• Rtn. Teddy Tee - 2 suits and 2 white long sleeves

The project was attended by respected Rotary leaders, including Past District Governors Ernie Choa, Josie Ang, Robert Koa, DGN Jun Pasion, Members of the Executive Committee, District Officers, and United Chosen Presidents, showing unified district commitment under District Governor Mary Mei Rodrigo.
This project reflects Rotary’s spirit— transforming lives through service and opening brighter futures for those in need.

Yours in Rotary Service,
 
PP Herminio S. Esguerra

body.text: Incoming Board of Trustees RY 2026-2027 Organizational Meeting led by Chair-Elect/RCM President Raoul Creencia, held last March 19, 2026, 2:15 PM at the Turf Room, Manila Polo Club.

Present were Chair-Elect/RCM Pres. Raoul Creencia, Incumbent Chair/Trustee-Elect Alex Cureg, Incumbent Treas./President-Elect Mike Roxas, Incumbent Sec./Elect Anton Mauricio, Incumbent BLA/Elect Caloy Serapio, Trustee-elect Ner Lonzaga, Trustee-elect Mike Albaña, Trustee-elect Noy Benedicto, Trustee-elect Del Lorenzana, and RCM President-Elect Reggie Yu.
Present via Zoom was Trustee-elect Karlo Castro.
RC Manila, RC Makati, and RC Makati West Joint Meeting

The Rotary Club of Manila’s Joint Meeting with the Rotary Club of Makati and the Rotary Club of Makati West, held on March 24, 2026 at Shangri-La Makati, was featured on RC Makati’s publication. The guest of honor and speaker was Senator Francis Pancratius “Kiko” Nepomuceno Pangilinan.

The Rotaract Club of Philippine Christian University - Manila participated in the Philippine Rotaract Conference (PROCON) Iloilo 2026, sponsored by the Rotary Club of Manila. The conference was held in Grand Xing Imperial Hotel, Iloilo City on February 20-22, 2026.

The Rotary Youth Leadership Awards (RYLA) 2026, with the Rotary Club of Manila as Major Co-Host, successfully sponsored five delegates from the Rotaract Club of De La Salle, Rotaract Club of Manila, and Rotaract Club of Philippine Christian University.
The two-day leadership camp was held on March 28–29, 2026 (Saturday and Sunday) at the Kim Siong Community in Silang, Cavite.

RYLA is a dynamic leadership development program designed for individuals aged 14–30, primarily college students and young professionals who exhibit strong leadership potential. Participants are nominated and sponsored by Rotary clubs, and the program is open to both Rotaractors and non-Rotaractors.
45th Charter Anniversary of RC Intramuros Manila (Daughter Club of RC Manila)

DGND Hermie Esguerra, Special Assistant to the Governor-Manila SDG Albert S. Alday and PS Aries Balanay attended the 45th Charter Anniversary of the Rotary Club of Intramuros Manila, daughter club of the Rotary Club of Manila, last March 20, 2026 at the Ilustrado Restaurant in Intramuros, Manila.

DGND Hermie Esguerra is an Honorary Member of the Rotary Club of Intramuros Manila. Special Assistant to the Governor, Manila SDG Albert S. Alday was likewise an Honorary Member of said club in RY 2017-2018. PS Aries Balanay was a President of the Rotary Club of Intramuros Manila in RY 2017-2018 before transferring to the Rotary Club of Manila during RY 2022-2023.

Present were Committee Chairman DGND Herminio S. Esguerra; Committee members SDG Reginald T. Yu, SDG Aries B. Balanay, SDG Michael Jaey C. Albaña, SDG Albert S. Alday, and Rtn. Rhea Vitto Tabora.
