photos.caption: A moment suspended in sunlight and laughter in 1960 — Bollie at eight, already protective and steady, beside Cecile at three, radiant with childhood ease. On the warm sands of Durban’s South Coast, this simple scene captures more than a day at the beach; it reflects the quiet beginnings of a lifelong bond shaped by family, place, and memory.

A moment frozen in time — Bollie, standing leftmost, shares the frame with friends on Durban Beach in South Africa after completing their final year of high school in 1970. With the city skyline rising behind them and the shoreline alive with energy, the photograph captures more than youthful camaraderie; it reflects a turning point, where friendship, freedom, and the promise of what lies ahead meet under the warmth of the coastal sun.

A tender Christmas moment between Bollie and his late mother, Eva Vorster —captured in a warm exchange of love and laughter. Dressed in festive spirit, Bollie presents a gift as they lean in with affection, a simple yet profound gesture that speaks of gratitude, closeness, and the enduring bond between mother and son.

A glimpse into Bollie's formative years at Harrismith High School in South Africa, where discipline, teamwork, and school spirit took early root. Set against the backdrop of a marching band in formation, the scene reflects a time of structure and camaraderie — foundations that would later shape his leadership style and enduring commitment to excellence.

Inside a canvas training tent in Pretoria, Bollie stands among fellow recruits in disciplined formation beside their neatly arranged camp beds and mess kits, embodying the order and rigor of basic military training. Under the steady gaze of their instructor, every detail — from posture to preparation — reflects the early shaping of soldiers, where routine, resilience, and respect are forged long before they step onto the field.

Bollie in uniform, off duty yet ever disciplined — taking a quiet moment to tend to his gear with steady focus. Even in rest, there is purpose: each stitch checked, each detail attended to, reflecting the quiet professionalism, self-reliance, and readiness that define a soldier’s life beyond the field.

Bollie stands in full combat uniform during the final phase of the South African Border War in 1989, a conflict intertwined with the Namibian War of Independence and the Angolan Bush War. Dressed in a nutria-brown bush hat, first-pattern shirt, and secondpattern trousers, he carries a Vektor R4 (5.56mm) assault rifle and wears Pattern 70/73 webbing complete with essential field gear. Behind him, a helicopter lifts through the dust, capturing the harsh, arid terrain where discipline, training, and resilience defined every mission.

Out in the open fields, Bollie shares a quiet moment with a companion beside their truck, the day’s hunt in hand — a pheasant marking the reward of patience and skill. Against the wide, earthy landscape and overcast sky, the scene captures more than sport; it reflects camaraderie, tradition, and the unspoken bond formed in the stillness of the hunt.

Bollie Bolton shares a moment with a Russian friend in Tallinn in 2017, captured during a night out in the countryside. Set against the quiet of the outdoors, the scene reflects a shared experience rooted in travel, friendship, and the stories that unfold when cultures meet far from home.

A glimpse into Bollie's life in South Africa 43 years ago — set against a vast, untamed landscape where nature stretches endlessly beyond the horizon. In this moment of focus and solitude, the image reflects a younger Bollie immersed in the outdoors, capturing a chapter defined by independence, adventure, and the formative experiences that helped shape the man he would become.

Bollie, in blue, sits at the table in a moment of quiet ease, surrounded by friends and the simple comforts of shared company. With a thoughtful, almost reflective expression, he anchors the scene — where conversation lingers, glasses rest half-filled, and time seems to slow in the warmth of familiar company and unspoken understanding.

At 27, Bollie Bolton is captured in a moment of ease and quiet confidence, gathered with friends around a table filled with conversation and laughter. In a setting that feels both intimate and lived-in, the image reflects a young man already carrying a strong presence — grounded, observant, and at home in the company he keeps, as life unfolds in the simple richness of shared moments.

A portrait of Bollie in his early years as General Manager of Holiday Inn in South Africa — confident, composed, and already embodying the professionalism that would define his career. With a warm, assured smile and a presence that blends approachability with authority, the image captures a young leader in his prime, shaping his path in the world of hospitality with vision and quiet excellence.

Bollie arrives on Sila Island, stepping onto its striking pink-tinged sands — naturally colored by crushed coral —marking the beginning of a vision brought to life. Beside the helicopter and the open sea, this moment captures more than a landing; it reflects the culmination of design, determination, and dream, as Bollie goes on to shape the island’s future with the creation of eight exclusive luxury villas set against one of nature’s most beautiful canvases.

Bollie shares a warm and cheerful moment with Mrs. Takako Okada, Owner and Vice Chairperson of Okada Manila, captured in an evening of elegance and connection. Their lighthearted gesture reflects not only mutual respect, but also the camaraderie found among leaders in the world of hospitality — where relationships are built as much on warmth as they are on excellence.

A taste of tradition and craftsmanship — Bollie shares a proud moment alongside a friend as they prepare boerewors, the beloved South African sausage made from ground beef, pork fat, and a distinctive blend of spices. Laid out in generous coils, the boerewors reflects more than culinary skill; it carries heritage, camaraderie, and the joy of creating something meant to be shared around the table.

Bollie, during his tenure as Business Development Director of Lyceum of the Philippines University in 2013, stands alongside some of the country’s top master chefs — a meeting of minds dedicated to elevating culinary and hospitality excellence. The moment reflects his active role in bridging industry and academia, fostering collaboration, and helping shape the next generation of professionals in the field.

Bollie stands alongside Governor Jose Enrique “Joet” Garcia III of Bataan, both raising a single finger in a shared gesture of unity and purpose. Captured in a moment of ease and camaraderie, the image reflects a meeting of minds — where experience, leadership, and a common vision come together, grounded in service and a commitment to progress.

Bollie shares a fun and spirited moment with La Jolla’s cheerful mascot, Pawi — short for "pawikan" (sea turtle) — capturing the playful side of hospitality. With smiles, thumbs up, and a sense of lighthearted energy, the scene reflects the welcoming atmosphere and family-friendly charm that La Jolla embodies — where every guest experience is meant to be warm, memorable, and full of joy

Bollie shares a playful and endearing moment with his “best friend” during his time as General Manager at Huma Island Resort and Spa in Palawan. Set against a lush tropical backdrop, the scene captures a lighter side of leadership — where even in the midst of responsibility, there is room for curiosity, connection, and the simple joy of unexpected companionship.

Bollie shares a proud and lighthearted moment with his La Jolla Hotel and Beach Resort team, united in spirit and purpose before a vibrant showcase of their premier destination. With smiles all around and fingers raised in a gesture of number one, the scene reflects not only the warmth of hospitality but the shared pride of a team committed to excellence, service, and the promise of memorable experiences by the sea.

A defining moment of shared purpose and vision — Bollie, alongside his long-time friend Jackie Rodriguez, marks the founding of the South African Friendship Society on November 3, 1996. Gathered among peers in an atmosphere of dialogue and engagement, the occasion reflects their commitment to fostering education, cultural exchange, and meaningful connection — laying the groundwork for a community built on learning, friendship, and mutual growth.

Bollie shares a moment of fellowship with Rotary Club of Manila Past President Jackie Rodriguez and former Ilocos Sur Governor and Congressman Chavit Singson during an RCM meeting. Captured in an atmosphere of camaraderie and shared purpose, the image reflects the convergence of leadership, experience, and enduring commitment to service that defines the Rotary spirit.

Bollie shares a relaxed moment with fellow Rotary Club of Manila colleague and tourism professional Mike Albaña over coffee at The Peninsula Manila. Set against the hotel’s grand and tranquil interiors, the scene captures a pause between engagements — where conversation flows easily, and shared experience in hospitality and service deepens a long-standing professional camaraderie.

Bollie shares an elegant evening with Ms. Cory Quirino and distinguished friends, captured in a setting of refined hospitality and warm camaraderie. Surrounded by timeless interiors and gracious company, the moment reflects the relationships and shared circles that have long been part of Bollie’s journey — where connection, conversation, and mutual respect come naturally.

The Bolton Family — Bollie, Macy, and Maia — captured in a warm and intimate moment that reflects the heart behind every achievement. Standing together with ease and affection, the image speaks of a shared journey grounded in love, support, and quiet strength — where family remains the constant source of inspiration through every chapter

Maia and Macy share a joyful moment during a memorable visit to South Africa, proudly wearing their colors for the Rugby World Cup. With flags painted on their cheeks and excitement in the air, the scene captures the spirit of the game — where family, national pride, and shared celebration come together in a moment of pure happiness.

Maia Bolton, a proud member of the Miriam College Varsity Team and daughter of Bollie, beams with accomplishment after winning the gold medal at the Philippine Taekwondo Association Grand Tournament in 2026. Captured in a moment of triumph, the image reflects not only her discipline and dedication to the sport, but also the strength of character and perseverance that define a true champion.

Bollie stands proudly on stage at Best Western Plus Metro Clark in Angeles City, honored with the Mabuhay Award for Excellence in Hospitality during the 2025 Tres Awards in March 2026. Holding his citation with quiet pride, the moment reflects a lifetime of dedication to the craft of hospitality — where vision, service, and an unwavering commitment to guest experience come together in well-earned recognition.

Bollie is honored as Asian Leader in Hospitality Management Excellence at the 2025 Asia’s Golden Icon Awards, a recognition that underscores his enduring impact on the industry. This distinction reflects decades of visionary leadership, operational excellence, and an unwavering commitment to elevating hospitality standards — cementing his legacy as a respected figure not only in the Philippines, but across the region.

A testament to his respected standing in the industry, Bollie served as a judge for the Front of House category at the 18th Mabuhay Awards in 2013. This role reflects the trust placed in his expertise and discerning eye — recognizing not only his deep understanding of hospitality operations, but also his commitment to upholding excellence in guest service and professional standards.

A recognition of both expertise and influence, Bollie was awarded a Plaque of Appreciation as a Distinguished Speaker at the 10th EdukCircle International Convention on Business, Tourism and Hospitality in 2017. Held at the University of the Philippines Diliman, the honor reflects his ability to inspire, educate, and share real-world insights — bridging industry experience with the next generation of hospitality professionals.

Bollie receives the Asia’s Influential Leader Award, presented by Undersecretary Vidal Villanueva and Congresswoman Marissa Del Mar Magsino, in a moment that celebrates both achievement and influence. Framed by a grand stage and a distinguished audience, the recognition honors his leadership in hospitality — marked by vision, innovation, and a lasting impact on the industry and the communities he serves.

A joyful portrait of Bollie’s family in South Africa — spanning generations and bound by warmth, laughter, and shared roots. Gathered in the embrace of nature, the image reflects the heart behind the man: a legacy not only of leadership and achievement, but of family, love, and the enduring connections that ground it all.

articles.title: Where Intelligence Meets Purpose: The 28th Weekly Membership Meeting of the Rotary Club of Manila

body.text: At precisely 12:30 PM, the gavel fell. With quiet authority, President Raoul C. Creencia called to order the 28th Weekly Membership Meeting of the Rotary Club of Manila, convened within the stately halls of the Manila Polo Club. What unfolded that afternoon was not merely a gathering of Rotarians, but an encounter between tradition and transformation, where the enduring values of Rotary were set against the rapidly evolving landscape of artificial intelligence.
Guided by Moderator STAR Rotarian Ingill Ra, the program moved with the elegance and precision that has long defined the Club’s culture.

The invocation, solemnly delivered by Rotarian Ramon Alberto B. “Ramby” Nolido, centered the assembly in reflection and gratitude. This was followed by an audio-visual presentation of the Philippine National Anthem, stirring in every attendee a renewed sense of national pride and shared responsibility.

The room resonated with the Rotary Club of Manila Hymn, performed by the RCM WF Music Chorale, a familiar melody that continues to bind generations of Rotarians. Soon after, STAR Rotarian Oliver L. Pantaleon led the recitation of the Four-Way Test, reaffirming the ethical framework that remains the bedrock of Rotary’s identity.

As host, STAR Rotarian Ingill Ra extended a gracious acknowledgment of guests and members, setting a tone of warmth and inclusivity. The Chorale returned with a welcome song that lifted the atmosphere, seamlessly transitioning the program into a moment of celebration as the Club honored its birthday celebrants. Names were called, greetings were exchanged, and laughter filled the room as the Maligayang Bati was rendered with heartfelt enthusiasm.
President’s Time: A Steady Hand on the Helm

During President’s Time, President Raoul addressed the membership with clarity and purpose, articulating both the responsibilities of the present and the possibilities of the future. His message carried the quiet strength of a leader who understands that stewardship is not only about continuity, but about preparing the institution for what lies ahead. It was a reminder that Rotary’s relevance is sustained not by tradition alone, but by its ability to adapt while remaining anchored in its core values.
Ms. Delby Bragais, President of the Inner Wheel Club of Manila, and Ms. Jeanne Harn, Ms. Philippines Earth 2007, extended a warm invitation to their upcoming fundraising event, "Dinner Dance!"
The Introduction: Framing the Future
The afternoon took on a more anticipatory tone as Club Secretary Antonilo D.C. “Anton” Mauricio stepped forward to introduce the Guest of Honor and Speaker, Dr. Erika Fille T. Legara.

His introduction was both precise and compelling, presenting not only her distinguished credentials as Managing Director and Chief AI & Data Officer of the Education Center for AI Research and Associate Professor at the Asian Institute of Management, but also underscoring the importance of the subject she was about to address. Artificial intelligence, he suggested, is no longer a distant concept reserved for technologists; it is an undeniable force shaping industries, institutions, and the very way society functions.
Artificial Intelligence — Responsible Use and Aid to Productivity

Dr. Legara began with an ease and authenticity that immediately connected with her audience. There was no attempt to overwhelm with jargon or abstraction. Instead, she invited the room into a conversation — one that sought to make artificial intelligence both understandable and relevant.

She opened with a thought that lingered throughout her talk: the future is already here, but it is not evenly distributed. In that single line, she captured the paradox of modern innovation — where extraordinary technological advancements coexist with uneven access and understanding.

From there, she gently dismantled the mystique surrounding artificial intelligence. She explained that what many perceive as a singular, almost mythical entity is in reality the convergence of three forces: vast amounts of data, increasingly powerful computing systems, and the evolution of algorithms capable of identifying patterns and making predictions. These elements, when brought together, form the foundation upon which modern AI systems are built.
Yet, she was careful to temper expectations. The intelligence we see today, she explained, is not the all-encompassing, human-like intelligence often portrayed in films.

What exists now is something far more specific — systems that excel in narrowly defined tasks. They can process language, recommend products, detect fraud, or analyze behavior with remarkable precision, but they remain confined to the boundaries of their design.

What made her presentation particularly compelling was her ability to ground these ideas in real-world applications, many of them developed within the Philippine context. She spoke of systems capable of assessing the value of repossessed motorcycles by analyzing images, sounds, and technical specifications — reducing hours of expert work into minutes. She described how financial institutions have used AI to better understand borrowers, allowing them to extend credit more responsibly while significantly reducing default rates. These were not abstract possibilities; they were tangible examples of how technology can drive both efficiency and inclusivity.

Her discussion then shifted to the public sector, where the impact of artificial intelligence becomes even more profound. She spoke of initiatives that use AI to detect malnutrition among children, enabling faster intervention and potentially changing the trajectory of young lives. She described systems designed to identify learning disabilities at an early stage, allowing for timely support in communities that may otherwise lack access to specialists. She shared how AI is being used to map disaster risks across the country, providing decision-makers with hyperlocalized data that can guide critical actions during times of crisis.
Each example reinforced a central theme: technology, when guided by purpose, can become a powerful instrument for social good.

As the presentation progressed, Dr. Legara introduced the concept of generative artificial intelligence — a more recent development that allows machines not just to analyze data, but to create new content. She demonstrated how these systems can write, interpret, simulate conversations, and even assist in complex decision-making processes. Yet, even as she showcased these capabilities, she maintained a measured perspective. These tools, she emphasized, are meant to augment human intelligence, not replace it. Judgment, ethics, and accountability remain firmly within the domain of people.

In her closing, she turned her focus to leadership. Artificial intelligence, she asserted, is neither inherently good nor bad. Its impact depends entirely on how it is used. For organizations like the Rotary Club of Manila — institutions built on service, integrity, and community — the responsibility is clear. The challenge is not simply to adopt new technologies, but to ensure that they are harnessed in ways that uplift, include, and empower.
A Dialogue of Minds

The open forum that followed was marked by thoughtful engagement. Members posed questions that reflected both curiosity and discernment, exploring not only the opportunities presented by artificial intelligence, but also its ethical implications and practical applications within their respective fields.
It was evident that the conversation had moved beyond passive listening. The room had become a space for dialogue, where ideas were tested, perspectives were shared, and understanding deepened.
A Gesture of Gratitude
PDG Jackie Rodriguez presented President Raoul Creencia with a bannerette from the Rotary Club of Madrid.

In recognition of her insightful and thought-provoking presentation, President Raoul presented Dr. Legara with a Certificate of Appreciation. It was a simple gesture, yet one that carried the weight of collective gratitude for a message that had both informed and inspired.
Closing the Afternoon
At 2:00 PM, the meeting was formally adjourned.

And yet, as members slowly dispersed, there remained an unmistakable sense that something more enduring had taken place. The afternoon had not merely added to the Club’s calendar of meetings; it had expanded its horizon.

For in that space — where tradition stood firmly rooted and the future quietly unfolded — the Rotary Club of Manila once again affirmed its place not only as a steward of legacy, but as a participant in shaping what comes next.
Meeting Fellowship

PRES. RAOUL C. CREENCIA
Reginald T. Yu
Editor-in-Chief

In a time when nations are increasingly defined by lines — on maps, in policies, and across ideologies — it is both timely and necessary that the Rotary Club of Manila welcomes as Guest of Honor and Speaker Hon. Voltaire D. Mauricio, a man whose life’s work has been devoted to navigating precisely these lines.

A former consul general in Osaka and London, he has stood at the intersection of diplomacy, culture, and national interest. His career reminds us that the work of building bridges between nations is neither abstract nor ceremonial. It is deliberate, often difficult, and always consequential.

This week’s Weekly Membership Meeting is more than a gathering. It is an opportunity to reflect on a fundamental question: What does it mean to lead in a world that is increasingly interconnected, yet persistently divided?

Diplomacy, at its core, is not merely the art of negotiation. It is the discipline of understanding. It requires the ability to listen beyond language, to recognize interests beneath positions, and to find common ground where none appears to exist. These are not skills reserved for ambassadors alone. They are competencies that Rotary, at its best, cultivates in each of its members.

For over a century, the Rotary Club of Manila has operated not just as a civic organization, but as a quiet force of continuity. Through wars, political transitions, economic upheavals, and global crises, it has remained steadfast in its commitment to service above self. Yet today’s challenges call for something more.
They call for relevance.

In an age where influence is measured not only by authority but by credibility, Rotary must continually ask itself: Are we merely preserving tradition, or are we actively shaping the future? Are we content with being witnesses to change, or are we prepared to be agents of it?

The presence of Hon. Mauricio offers a subtle but powerful reminder. Leadership today is no longer confined to boardrooms or government offices. It is exercised in conversations, in collaborations, and in the everyday decisions that either divide or unite.
The theme “Unite for Good” is not a slogan. It is a mandate.

To unite is not to agree on everything. It is to commit to a shared purpose despite differences. It is to recognize that progress is rarely the product of uniformity, but often the result of respectful engagement among diverse perspectives.

As Rotarians, we are uniquely positioned to model this kind of leadership. Our network spans professions, sectors, and generations. Our projects touch lives in ways that statistics alone cannot capture. But the true measure of our impact lies not only in what we do, but in how we do it.

Do we listen with intent? 
Do we lead with integrity? 
Do we act with a sense of responsibility that extends beyond ourselves?
These are the quiet questions that define enduring leadership.

As we gather this Thursday at the Manila Polo Club, we do so not merely to hear a distinguished speaker, but to engage in a deeper reflection on our role in a rapidly evolving world. The flags that form the backdrop of this meeting are more than symbols of nations. They are reminders of the diversity we are called to embrace — and the unity we are challenged to build.
In the end, Rotary’s strength has never been in its history alone, but in its ability to adapt that history to the demands of the present.
And perhaps that is the enduring lesson of diplomacy, and of leadership itself:
That even in a world of many flags, there must always be a common cause.
And it is ours to carry forward.
The Last Two Months

There's a particular clarity that arrives when a term of office begins to wind down. Entering the final two months of service as President of Asia’s First Rotary Club, I find myself in that space between reflection and resolve -- where the past year comes into sharper focus, and the responsibility to finish strong feels more urgent than ever.

When I began my term in July last year, everything was defined by possibility. Plans were laid out with optimism, calendars were filled with intent, and each project carried the promise of impact. Now, with only a short stretch of time remaining, those plans have either taken shape, evolved, or, in some cases, taught us difficult but valuable lessons. Leadership, I have come to realize, is not about the flawless execution of every idea, but about the ability to adapt, persevere, and keep moving the club forward.

These final weeks are not a time to slow down -- they are a call to sharpen focus. There is still much to be done: projects to complete, commitments to honor, and opportunities to seize. In fact, the coming weeks will be quite busy, as we roll out three of our signature initiatives: the Ambassador Awards, the Tower Awards, and the Journalism Awards. Each of these programs represents not only the culmination of months of preparation, but also the very essence of what our club stands for -- recognizing excellence, celebrating service, and uplifting voices that contribute meaningfully to society.

The Ambassador Awards will serve as a powerful reminder of the enduring value of representation and goodwill, honoring individuals who have exemplified the art of bridging communities and fostering deeper understanding. The Tower Awards, meanwhile, stand as a meaningful tribute to our bluecollar workers -- those whose quiet, steadfast contributions form the backbone of our economy and whose efforts deserve far greater recognition. The Journalism Awards, for their part, reaffirm the indispensable role of truth and responsible storytelling, especially in an era when clarity, integrity, and discernment in public discourse are more vital than ever.
Taken together, these are not merely events on a calendar—they are living expressions of our values, brought to life through purposeful action and collective resolve.

Alongside these, we look forward to the Club Awards, which will be held during our final weekly meeting on June 25. This gathering will serve as both a celebration and a moment of closure -- a time to recognize the collective efforts of our members and officers who have made the year meaningful and impactful. It is in this culminating event that we bring together the threads of the entire term, acknowledging both individual and shared accomplishments.

The temptation, perhaps, is to begin easing into transition mode, to mentally step aside in anticipation of new leadership. But stewardship demands otherwise. The trust given by the members of the club was not for most of the year -- it was for the entire term. And so, the responsibility remains as real today as it was on the first day.

Indeed, these final months invite a deeper sense of gratitude. The presidency is often described in terms of responsibility, but it is equally a privilege. The opportunity to work alongside dedicated members, to witness acts of service, and to be part of a collective striving toward a greater good -- these are experiences that leave a lasting imprint. It is in this period of looking back that one fully appreciates the people who made the journey meaningful: the officers who carried heavy loads without hesitation, the members who showed up time and again, and the partners who believed in the club’s mission.

There is also value in acknowledging imperfections. Not every goal may have been achieved, not every initiative fully realized. Yet even in these gaps lie lessons -- about planning, collaboration, and the realities of balancing ambition with capacity. These insights are not marks of failure; they are contributions to the club’s institutional memory, guiding future leaders toward even better outcomes.

As the term approaches its conclusion, I am reminded that leadership is measured not only by what is started, but by what is sustained and completed. The final stretch is an opportunity to reaffirm commitments, to bring closure where it is needed, and to celebrate progress where it has been made. It is a chance to demonstrate that consistency and dedication endure until the very end.

In many ways, these last two months define the legacy of a presidency. They reflect whether the energy that marked the beginning was carried through to the finish, and whether the club emerges not just intact, but strengthened. We will endeavor to finish strong as it means honoring the trust that was given, the work that was undertaken, and the purpose that brought everyone together in the first place.
And so, with gratitude for the journey and determination for what remains, the focus is clear: to lead, to serve, and to finish well.
