Celebrating his 80th birthday with elegance, warmth, and unmistakable vitality, Günter Matschuck stands as a living testament to resilience, reinvention, and enduring purpose. From surviving the devastation of wartime Germany to building a meaningful life across continents, his journey reflects not only professional achievement, but also the triumph of character over adversity. Surrounded by family, friends, and generations shaped by his example, this milestone celebration honored far more than longevity — it celebrated a life lived with courage, discipline, curiosity, and gratitude.

Captured during Günter Matschuck’s 80th birthday celebration, this family portrait reflects
the enduring legacy of a life shaped by resilience, reinvention, and love across generations
and continents. From the ruins of wartime Germany to a new life built in the Philippines, the
journey that began in hardship ultimately blossomed into a thriving multigenerational
family bound together by gratitude, strength, and shared history. Surrounded by children
and grandchildren, Günter stands not only as an engineer and international businessman,
but as the patriarch of a family whose greatest inheritance was never material success alone,
but the values of perseverance, discipline, and unity passed on through generations.

Even after building a life across continents, Cologne always remained home in Günter Matschuck’s heart. During his annual visits to the city where he grew up, memories of wartime survival, postwar reconstruction, and youthful dreams inevitably returned along the banks of the Rhine. Standing before the iconic Cologne Cathedral, he reflected not only on the city’s remarkable rebirth from the devastation of the Second World War, but also on his own journey of resilience, reinvention, and gratitude. For Günter, returning to Cologne was never merely a visit — it was a quiet homecoming to the place where his story began.

articles.title: Diplomacy, Duty, and the Moral Compass of Nations: Rotary Club of Manila Welcomes Former Consul General Atty. Voltaire D. Mauricio at the 29th Weekly Membership Meeting

body.text: There are some gatherings in the life of the Rotary Club of Manila that become more than mere weekly assemblies. They evolve into moments of reflection — occasions where history, public service, statesmanship, and moral responsibility converge in one room, among men and women bound by a shared belief that leadership is ultimately an act of stewardship.

The 29th Weekly Membership Meeting of the Rotary Club of Manila, held on May 7, 2026 at the historic Manila Polo Club, unfolded precisely in that spirit. Moderated by Past Director Issam Eldebs, the afternoon gathering carried the familiar warmth and dignity characteristic of Asia's first Rotary club, yet it also possessed a rare intellectual gravitas, owing largely to the presence of the Guest of Honor and Speaker, former Philippine Consul General to Osaka and London, Atty. Voltaire D. Mauricio.

The meeting formally commenced with the Call to Order led by President Raoul C. Creencia, whose steady stewardship throughout Rotary Year 2025-2026 has consistently emphasized fellowship anchored on substance and relevance.

An invocation was delivered by Vice President Ricardo S.B. "Ricky" Guevara, followed by the singing of the Philippine National Anthem through an audio-visual presentation and the Rotary Club of Manila Hymn rendered by the RCM WF Music Chorale. The Four-Way Test was solemnly recited under the leadership of DSAA David J. "Dave" Reynolds, reminding everyone present that beyond business, politics, or diplomacy, Rotary’s enduring relevance lies in its insistence on truth, fairness, goodwill, and mutual benefit.

Past Director Issam Eldebs acknowledged the distinguished guests in attendance before the atmosphere shifted into one of warmth and celebration with musical performances by the RCM WF Music Chorale. Birthday celebrants included Past Director Amading Valdez, Rotarian Jerry Agnes, and Rotarian J. Alfonso L. Katigbak, all of whom were greeted with the traditional “Maligayang Bati” by the chorale.
Yet beneath the conviviality of fellowship and song lingered a sense that the afternoon’s true centerpiece was still to come.
Presentation of The Rotary Foundation's Recognition Gift
From left: VP Ricky Guevara, Multiple Paul Harris Fellow; VPE Karlo Castro, Major Donor; STAR Rtn. Coco Mauricio, New Paul Harris Fellow; and STAR Rtn. Oliver Pantaleon, New Paul Harris Fellow

During President’s Time, President Raoul C. Creencia led a special recognition for IT Arik Carranceja, acknowledging his invaluable support and contributions to the club. The recognition reflected the Rotary Club of Manila’s continuing appreciation for individuals whose quiet dedication often sustains the unseen machinery behind meaningful organizational work.

The introduction of the Guest of Honor and Speaker was delivered by Rotarian Shigeru Shimoda, who welcomed Atty. Mauricio not merely as a veteran diplomat, but as a public servant whose career had traversed some of the most important arenas of Philippine foreign service.
What followed was not the conventional diplomatic lecture many may have anticipated.

Instead, Atty. Mauricio offered something far more compelling: a sweeping historical meditation on the origins of diplomacy itself—one that transformed centuries of geopolitical evolution into a vivid and remarkably accessible human story.
The Origins of Diplomacy: From Kingdoms to Nations

Speaking with the cadence of a storyteller rather than the stiffness of a bureaucrat, Atty. Mauricio began not with treaties or international law, but with the timeless opening line of childhood fairy tales: “Once upon a time, in a kingdom far, far away, there lived a king.”

What initially sounded whimsical soon unfolded into an insightful framework for understanding the origins of diplomacy. Long before modern nation-states emerged, he explained, the world was divided into kingdoms ruled by kings, queens, princes, and princesses. These kingdoms were often in conflict, frequently over borders, territory, and power.
War, however, eventually exhausted even the mightiest rulers.
And so kingdoms sought peace.

To negotiate peace, one kingdom would send a trusted emissary—often a sibling, son, uncle, or other close relative — to another kingdom. The message carried by such an envoy was deeply symbolic: “Treat this person as if you were treating me, the king.”

In one of the afternoon’s most memorable lines, Atty. Mauricio described these early emissaries as “glamorized hostages.” If peace failed, the envoy’s life could be endangered. But if goodwill prevailed, these emissaries became living embodiments of trust between rival powers.
Thus, diplomacy was born not from abstractions, but from vulnerability, reciprocity, and mutual dependence.

As kingdoms evolved into empires and eventually into modern nation-states, the tradition remained. Relatives were replaced by professional diplomats, but the underlying principle endured: when one country sends an ambassador to another, it sends a representative who symbolically embodies the head of state itself.
Understanding the Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary

Atty. Mauricio then guided the audience deeper into the architecture of modern diplomacy, particularly the meaning behind one of the most misunderstood diplomatic titles: Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary.

The term “Extraordinary,” he explained, signifies that the ambassador is to be treated as though he were the very president or prime minister of the sending nation. In many countries, only two individuals are accorded the title “His Excellency”: the nation’s head of state and the ambassador representing another sovereign state.
The second word — “Plenipotentiary” — derives from the Latin roots plenum and potens, meaning “full power.”
Such ambassadors possess the authority to bind their governments in diplomatic engagements and agreements within their jurisdictions.
For many in attendance, the lecture became an education not merely in terminology, but in the immense trust and responsibility carried by those tasked with representing nations abroad.

Equally fascinating was Atty. Mauricio’s clarification that only ambassadors assigned to capital cities truly carry the rank and privileges associated with ambassadors extraordinary and plenipotentiary. Consuls General, despite their importance, are not ambassadors in the technical sense.
He cited Israel as a unique exception in diplomatic history, where embassies had historically been located in Tel Aviv instead of Jerusalem due to geopolitical pressures from neighboring states.
The audience listened intently—not merely because the lecture was informative, but because Atty. Mauricio possessed the rare gift of making international relations feel deeply human.
Diplomacy as the First Line of Defense

As his discourse progressed, the former Consul General shifted from history to contemporary relevance. Diplomacy, he stressed, becomes most crucial precisely during moments of conflict. Before nations deploy armies or engage in war, diplomatic channels must first be exhausted. Diplomacy remains humanity’s first line of defense against violence.
The statement carried unmistakable weight in an era increasingly defined by geopolitical tensions, territorial disputes, economic rivalries, and ideological fragmentation.
For the Rotarians gathered inside the Manila Polo Club that afternoon, the message resonated beyond statecraft. It was also a lesson in leadership, communication, restraint, and moral courage.

Atty. Mauricio further distinguished between political ambassadors and career ambassadors within the Philippine foreign service. Political ambassadors, he explained, serve largely at the pleasure of the President who appoints them, while career ambassadors may continue beyond a presidential term due to their professional standing within the foreign service corps.
But perhaps the most powerful part of his address emerged toward the conclusion, when he pivoted away from technical diplomacy and returned instead to Rotary itself.
Rotary as a Moral Compass

In a room filled with businessmen, professionals, civic leaders, and public servants, Atty. Mauricio reminded everyone that Rotary’s Four-Way Test is not merely ceremonial rhetoric. It is, in many ways, a moral framework for diplomacy, governance, and human relationships themselves.
“Is it the truth? Is it fair to all concerned? Will it build goodwill and better friendships? Will it be beneficial to all concerned?”
These questions, recited countless times in Rotary meetings across the world, suddenly acquired renewed depth under the lens of international relations.
Diplomacy, he implied, is ultimately not only about treaties and negotiations. It is about trust. About fairness. About the pursuit of peace without surrendering dignity.
And in that sense, Rotary and diplomacy share a common soul.
The Rotarian, much like the diplomat, serves as a bridge-builder.
The diplomat negotiates between nations. The Rotarian builds understanding among communities. Both seek peace, goodwill, and mutual progress.

By the time Atty. Mauricio concluded his address, the room was no longer merely listening to a lecture on foreign affairs. It had become immersed in a reflection on civilization itself — how societies evolved from kingdoms to nations, from warfare to dialogue, and from suspicion to cooperation.

An open forum followed, where members had the opportunity to engage directly with the distinguished speaker, further enriching the afternoon’s exchange of ideas. President Raoul C. Creencia later presented Atty. Mauricio with a Certificate of Appreciation in recognition of his insightful and thought-provoking address.
The meeting formally adjourned under the leadership of President Creencia.
Yet long after the gathering concluded, the resonance of the afternoon lingered.

For in a world increasingly fractured by division, misinformation, and conflict, Atty. Voltaire D. Mauricio reminded the Rotary Club of Manila that diplomacy — at its finest — is not merely a profession.
It is an act of civilization.

And perhaps, at its deepest level, Rotary itself is an expression of the same enduring hope: that human beings, despite differences in nation, ideology, religion, or background, can still choose dialogue over hostility, goodwill over suspicion, and understanding over conflict.
In the end, kingdoms may rise and fall, governments may change, and geopolitical alignments may shift.
But truth, fairness, goodwill, and service remain timeless.

And that, perhaps, was the afternoon’s most enduring lesson. President Raoul Creencia presented former Philippine Consul General to Osaka and London, Atty. Voltaire D. Mauricio with a Certificate of Appreciation.

Re:
2025 Census Final Report for Rotary Club of Manila
I. Executive Summary

This final report presents the 2025 patient census of the Manila Cleft Care Center under Operation Smile Philippines, implemented in partnership with the Rotary Club of Manila. The census documents patients served, cleft conditions addressed, procedures performed, surgery dates, and donor support recorded throughout the year. This partnership reflects a shared commitment to providing safe, timely, and comprehensive care for children and adults with cleft conditions.
Funding Source:
• Rotary District Designated Fund Contribution of RID 3810 and 5150: US$ 18,278
• Cash Contributions of Rotary Club of Manila/RCManila Fondation, Inc.: US$ 5,720.00
• NON ROTARIAN MATCH: US$ 9,400
• The Rotary Foundation World Fund: US$ 14,622.00
TOTAL PROJECT FUNDING: US$ 48,020.00
II. Partnership Overview

The partnership between Operation Smile Philippines and the Rotary Club of Manila plays a vital role in expanding access to life-changing cleft surgeries. Through financial support, advocacy, and community engagement, the Rotary Club of Manila has helped ensure that patients receive quality surgical care regardless of their ability to pay.
This collaboration aligns with Rotary’s commitment to health, service, and humanitarian action, and Operation Smile’s mission that a smile is a fundamental human right.
III. Facility and Program Overview
• Facility: Manila Cleft Care Center (RMC)
• Address: 2629 New Panaderos St., Sta. Ana, Manila
• Implementing Organization: Operation Smile Philippines
• Key Partner: Rotary Club of Manila
• Program Focus: Comprehensive cleft care for surgical intervention and multidisciplinary support
• Reporting Period: Calendar Year 2025
IV. Patient Profile Overview
Based on the 2025 census records:
• Patients served were predominantly infants and young children, with ages ranging from a few months old to early childhood, highlighting the importance of early surgical intervention.
• Both male and female patients benefited from the program, ensuring inclusive and equitable access to care.

• The most frequently recorded diagnoses include:

Unilateral Cleft Lip
• Other cleft-related conditions requiring surgical correction
V. Medical and Surgical Services Provided
The following services were documented in the census:
• Dental Examination: Conducted as part of the comprehensive cleft care protocol.

• Surgical Procedures: 

Cheiloplasty was the most performed procedure during the reporting period.
All surgeries were performed following Operation Smile’s global medical standards, ensuring patient safety, ethical practice, and quality outcomes.
VI. Role and Contribution of the Rotary Club of Manila
The Rotary Club of Manila provided critical support that directly contributed to the successful delivery of cleft lip and palate surgeries in 2025. This included:
• Financial sponsorship of surgical procedures
• Support for operating costs and patient care
• Strengthening awareness and advocacy for cleft care in the community
Through this partnership, Rotary members helped restore smiles, improve health outcomes, and give patients renewed confidence and opportunity.
VII. Key Observations
• Early-age surgical intervention remains a priority and was consistently achieved throughout the year.
• The partnership with the Rotary Club of Manila strengthened program sustainability and reach.
• The Manila Cleft Care Center continues to serve as a critical access point for cleft care in Metro Manila and nearby provinces.
VIII. Conclusion

The 2025 Manila Cleft Care Center Census Report, implemented in partnership with the Rotary Club of Manila, demonstrates the powerful impact of collaboration in delivering life-changing medical care to 97 beneficiaries. Together, Operation Smile Philippines and the Rotary Club of Manila have helped ensure that more children and families can look forward to healthier lives and brighter futures.
This report stands as both an official record of patients served and a testament to the shared commitment to service above self.

Editor-in-Chief

There was a time when sustainability was viewed as a peripheral concern — a matter delegated to annual reports, public relations departments, or regulatory checklists designed merely to satisfy minimum standards. Today, that illusion no longer survives contact with reality.

Across the world, climate disruption is no longer a distant scientific projection. It has become an economic force, a geopolitical risk, a supply chain disruptor, a public health challenge, and increasingly, a defining test of leadership itself. Typhoons grow more destructive.

Heat waves become more unforgiving. Floods cripple infrastructure and commerce with alarming regularity. Entire industries now confront a future where resilience is no longer optional, but existential.

In this new era, the question confronting the private sector is no longer whether sustainability matters. The question is whether businesses possess the courage to move beyond mere compliance and embrace genuine transformational leadership.

For far too long, many corporations have approached sustainability reporting and environmental regulations as burdens to be managed rather than opportunities to lead. Compliance became the goal instead of the baseline. Carbon disclosures became exercises in optics rather than catalysts for operational change. Net zero pledges were announced with fanfare, yet often detached from meaningful structural reforms within organizations themselves.
But the world has changed — and stakeholders have changed with it.

Investors today increasingly examine environmental, social, and governance performance not as secondary considerations, but as indicators of long-term institutional viability. Consumers have become more discerning about the values embodied by the companies they support. Employees, especially younger generations, increasingly seek organizations whose missions align with broader societal purpose. Regulators continue to tighten disclosure expectations. And communities, particularly those most vulnerable to climate impacts, now expect corporations to participate meaningfully in building resilience rather than merely extracting profit.

Against this backdrop, sustainability reporting must no longer be viewed as a compliance exercise imposed by the Securities and Exchange Commission or by evolving global standards. It must instead be understood for what it truly represents: a mechanism for transparency, accountability, and trust.
Trust has become one of the rarest and most valuable currencies in modern society. And transparency is the foundation upon which that trust is built.

Corporations willing to honestly measure, disclose, and address their environmental footprint signal something profoundly important to the public: that they are prepared to confront reality rather than obscure it. Such transparency may expose vulnerabilities in the short term, but in the long run, it strengthens credibility, sharpens operational discipline, and reinforces stakeholder confidence.
The most forward-looking organizations now recognize that sustainability and profitability are no longer opposing forces. In fact, resilience itself has become a strategic economic advantage.

Companies that invest in energy efficiency reduce long-term operating costs. Businesses that strengthen climate resilience within their supply chains reduce disruption risks. Enterprises that innovate around sustainable technologies position themselves ahead of inevitable market transitions. Financial institutions increasingly favor firms with robust ESG performance. Even insurance markets now price climate exposure with growing sophistication.
Simply put, sustainability is no longer charity. It is strategy.
Yet beyond economics lies an even deeper moral imperative.

Every generation inherits obligations it did not choose but cannot ignore. Ours happens to confront one of the greatest collective challenges in modern history: whether economic progress can continue without compromising the ecological stability upon which civilization itself depends.

The private sector cannot solve this challenge alone. Governments, civil society, academe, and communities all possess vital roles to play. But neither can business remain a passive observer. The scale of corporate influence — over capital, technology, labor, infrastructure, manufacturing, and innovation — places upon the private sector a unique responsibility to lead with vision and urgency.

Leadership in sustainability therefore requires more than polished declarations. It demands integration. Climate resilience must move beyond annual reports and become embedded within corporate governance, investment decisions, operational planning, procurement systems, risk management frameworks, and organizational culture itself.
The organizations that will define the future are not merely those that comply with regulations, but those that understand that resilience is now inseparable from leadership.

This is especially true in countries like the Philippines, where vulnerability to climate-related disasters remains among the highest in the world. Here, sustainability is not an abstract global conversation. It is deeply personal. It affects livelihoods, agriculture, energy security, public health, infrastructure, and the survival of communities themselves.
For Philippine corporations, the challenge is therefore not simply to participate in sustainability conversations, but to help shape them with courage, innovation, and accountability.
The path forward will not always be easy. Genuine transformation rarely is. But history consistently favors institutions willing to adapt before circumstances force adaptation upon them.

Ultimately, the companies that endure will not be remembered solely for the profits they generated, but for the resilience they helped build, the integrity with which they operated, and the future they chose to protect.
For sustainability is no longer merely about compliance.

It is about stewardship. 
It is about leadership.
And above all, it is about whether today’s institutions possess the wisdom to think beyond the next quarter — and the courage to act for generations yet to come.
The Quiet Architecture of Impact: The Beauty of Club Flagship and Signature Projects

In every Rotary club, there are projects that respond to immediate needs, and there are those that ultimately come to define the club’s very identity. Beyond its distinguished standing as Asia’s First Club, the Rotary Club of Manila has likewise earned recognition, among many others, as a club whose awards carry genuine institutional weight, gravitas, and credibility — distinctions that are regarded not merely as ceremonial honors, but as meaningful affirmations of excellence, service, and public trust. Hence, RCM’s Outstanding Ambassador Awards, the TOWER Awards, and the Journalism Awards.
These are the signature projects — initiatives that transcend routine service activity and become enduring expressions of vision, purpose, and institutional character.

While the terms “signature” and “flagship” projects are often used interchangeably, there is a subtle distinction between them. A flagship project is usually the Club’s initiated project for a particular year, which is aimed to be carried on in the succeeding years. A signature project, on the other hand, reflects the unique personality and values of the club — the type of service initiative that people immediately associate with it. One emphasizes prominence; the other, identity. Yet both occupy a special place in the life of a Rotary club.

This Rotary year, three flagship projects were implemented by our esteemed Club – the LEAP (Leaders Excelling in ADR and Peacebuilding) Awards, ARAL (Advancing Resources for Accelerated Learning) Program, and Project RIVER (Rotary Initiative for Vulnerability Elimination and Resilience).

The journey toward implementing these projects has made this Rotary year memorable for me and all those involved in its conceptualization and planning. Flagship and signature initiatives often require long periods of consultation, fundraising, and execution. They demand not only financial resources, but also patience, persistence, and organizational discipline. Unlike one-time activities that may be completed within a single Rotary year, these projects frequently require continuity across multiple leadership cycles and the sustained commitment of many Rotarians.
And yet, precisely because of these demands, they become deeply fulfilling.

One source of fulfillment comes from the process of conceptualization itself. Every meaningful flagship project begins as an idea — sometimes modest, sometimes ambitious, but always rooted in a desire to create lasting value. Rotarians experience a distinct sense of purpose when they identify a community need and begin transforming abstract aspirations into a concrete service model.
The planning phase brings a different kind of fulfillment. Here, ideals are tested against practical realities. Budgets must be prepared. Partnerships must be formed.
Volunteers must be organized. Timelines must be established. Obstacles inevitably emerge.

This stage requires discipline and humility. We are fully aware that impactful service is not sustained by enthusiasm alone. It depends on structure, accountability, teamwork, and continuity. The challenge of transforming a vision into an executable program often strengthens club cohesion because members begin working not merely as volunteers, but as stewards of a shared mission.

Planning also teaches an important Rotary lesson: meaningful service is collaborative. No flagship or signature project succeeds because of a single leader. It succeeds because many individuals contribute different strengths — strategic thinkers, organizers, communicators, fundraisers, technical experts, and quiet workers who simply ensure that every detail is attended to. In this sense, the project becomes more than a community initiative; it becomes an exercise in collective leadership.
But perhaps the deepest fulfillment comes during implementation itself.

There is a profound emotional reward in witnessing a project move from paper into reality. These moments validate the countless hours spent in meetings, planning sessions, and fundraising activities. They remind Rotarians that service, when sustained with seriousness and compassion, can create tangible and enduring change.
Flagship and signature projects also provide another form of fulfillment that is often overlooked: institutional legacy.

Many Rotary activities are necessarily temporary, responding to immediate concerns or annual opportunities. But signature initiatives have the capacity to outlive individual presidents and officers. Over time, they become woven into the identity of the club itself.

This continuity creates a powerful sense of meaning because Rotarians realize they are participating in something larger than a single Rotary year. They become custodians of an institutional tradition of service.

There is also fulfillment in seeing younger or newer members eventually assume ownership of projects once initiated by earlier leaders. This transfer of stewardship reflects one of Rotary’s most important principles: continuity of service beyond individual leadership terms. A truly successful flagship project is one that no longer depends on its original proponents because the club itself has embraced and sustained the mission.

Importantly, not all fulfillment comes from scale or public recognition. Some of the most meaningful signature projects may remain relatively modest in size but deeply transformative in impact. The value of a Rotary project should never be measured solely by publicity, cost, or visibility. Often, the most enduring projects are those that consistently address genuine needs with sincerity and reliability.

Moreover, flagship and signature projects strengthen the moral identity of a club. They answer an essential question: What does this club stand for? Over time, these initiatives become visible manifestations of the club’s priorities, compassion, and values. They shape how communities perceive Rotary and how Rotarians perceive themselves.

Ultimately, the fulfillment derived from implementing flagship and signature projects lies not only in outcomes, but in the process itself. The experience demands vision, discipline, teamwork, resilience, and continuity. It transforms service from occasional activity into sustained institutional purpose.

And perhaps that is why these projects occupy such a special place in Rotary life. They are not merely programs. They are enduring expressions of commitment — reminders that when service is pursued with imagination, structure, and perseverance, it can leave a legacy far greater than any single year of leadership.

Beyond Compliance, Beyond Convenience: The Rotary Club of Manila Confronts the Climate Imperative PE Reginald T. Yu THE Rotary Club of Manila gathered beneath the familiar elegance of the Manila Polo Club for its 30th Weekly Membership Meeting of Rotary Year 2025–2026, an afternoon that began in fellowship yet gradually unfolded into a deeply meaningful discussion on leadership, sustainability, and national responsibility. Moderated by President-Elect Reggie Yu, the meeting carried an atmosphere that was at once warm and reflective. While the traditions of Rotary remained firmly present through music, fellowship, and camaraderie, there was also a growing awareness among attendees that leadership in today’s world can no longer remain confined to ceremonial distinction or institutional prestige. Increasingly, it must confront the pressing realities of climate change, resilience, and sustainable development. Held on Thursday, May 14, 2026, the gathering centered on the timely and intellectually compelling theme, “Beyond Compliance: Private Sector Leadership in Resiliency and Sustainability.” The very title suggested that the afternoon would move beyond environmental rhetoric and regulatory obligation toward a more transformative conversation about the role of institutions, industries, and communities in shaping the future. At exactly 12:30 in the afternoon, President Raoul C. Creencia formally called the meeting to order, setting into motion another chapter in the enduring tradition of fellowship and discourse that has long defined the Rotary Club of Manila. Ceremonial Traditions and Fellowship The solemnity of the gathering was first established through the Invocation delivered by Director-Elect John Nico P. “Nico” Valencia, followed by the Audio-Visual Presentation of the Philippine National Anthem. The Rotary Club of Manila Hymn was then rendered by the RCM World-Famous Music Chorale with the stirring familiarity that has become inseparable from the club’s institutional identity. Rotarian Raymond N. “Ray” Davis led the recitation of The FourWay Test, whose principles of truth, fairness, goodwill, and benefit to all seemed especially relevant in a world increasingly shaped by environmental uncertainty and social vulnerability. President-Elect Reggie Yu acknowledged the guests in attendance with warmth and familiarity, recognizing not merely their presence but their shared participation in a larger national conversation about responsible leadership. The RCM World-Famous Music Chorale followed with a welcome song that softened the formality of the proceedings and reminded everyone present that Rotary gatherings are sustained not only by institutional continuity but by friendship, music, and fellowship. The afternoon likewise paused to celebrate life’s joyful milestones as the club recognized its birthday celebrants. Rotarians Jun Coyuito, Mac Macapagal, Jun Bella, Jack Rodriguez, Jun Follosco, and J Alfonso L. Katigbak, together with Past Director Ner Lonzaga, were warmly greeted before the chorale rendered “Maligayang Bati” and “Happy Birthday” with cheerful enthusiasm. The moment provided a welcome reminder that even amid discussions of global challenges, Rotary remains anchored in human relationships and shared celebration. President’s Time and Institutional Reflection During President’s Time, President Raoul C. Creencia reflected on the importance of institutions remaining responsive to changing realities. There was a subtle but unmistakable recognition that Rotary itself — an organization founded upon service, ethical leadership, and civic engagement — must continuously redefine what meaningful service entails in an era increasingly shaped by climate volatility and socio-economic uncertainty. The meeting’s intellectual centerpiece would soon reinforce precisely that point. Introduction of the Guest of Honor and Speaker Director Michael Jaey C. “Mike” Albaña introduced the Guest of Honor and Speaker with evident pride, presenting an impressive portrait of a Filipino whose work now spans the global intersection of science, diplomacy, environmental policy, and climate resilience. The guest speaker, Dr. Glenn S. Banaguas, carried credentials reflecting not merely academic accomplishment but international relevance and influence. A UN Sasakawa Laureate, Chairman and President of ASEAN Science Diplomats, Chairman of the U.S.ASEAN Fellows for Science and Technology, Executive Fellow of the Geneva Centre for Security Policy, Distinguished Fellow of the Royal Society of Arts in the United Kingdom, and Climate Diplomat for the European Union-Asia Expert Panel for Climate Diplomacy, Dr. Banaguas represented a rare fusion of scientific rigor and policy advocacy. From the outset, his presentation challenged the audience to reconsider climate change not as a distant environmental concern but as an immediate operational, economic, social, and moral reality. The Climate Smart Philippines Framework Dr. Banaguas framed his presentation around the concept of a “Climate Smart Philippines,” emphasizing that resilience and sustainability are no longer optional aspirations but strategic necessities for survival and long-term prosperity. He described the Philippines as a geographically and administratively complex nation composed of 81 provinces, 146 cities, 1,488 municipalities, and more than 42,000 barangays — a reality that makes climate governance both extraordinarily difficult and critically important. At the heart of his discussion was the concept of “Climate Smart” governance, built upon the dual imperatives of climate change mitigation and climate change adaptation. These, he explained, form what he called “A TRIP to Resiliency and Sustainability.” The acronym TRIP stood for Track, Risk, Impact, and Policy, a fourdimensional framework designed to help governments, institutions, and corporations systematically understand and respond to climate realities. Tracking Climate Realities The “Track” component focused on analyzing human resources, demographics, historical climate data, and long-term climate projections involving rainfall and temperature changes. What followed was among the most sobering portions of the presentation. Using internationally recognized climate projections, Dr. Banaguas demonstrated how average temperatures in both Metro Manila and Cebu are expected to rise significantly over the coming decades. For the National Capital Region, projected average temperatures could increase by more than two degrees Celsius before the end of the century. Cebu exhibited a similarly alarming trajectory. These were not speculative fears intended merely to provoke concern. They were evidence-based projections grounded in climate science. Equally concerning were projections involving precipitation patterns. Metro Manila is expected to experience increasing rainfall intensity over successive decades, while Cebu similarly reflects increasingly unstable climate conditions. The implications, he emphasized, extend far beyond weather inconvenience. Climate change reshapes economies, labor systems, agriculture, transportation, health outcomes, infrastructure, and social stability itself. Risk, Vulnerability, and the Geography of Disaster The presentation then shifted toward risk analysis using the United Nations disaster risk framework, which identifies disaster risk as a function of hazard, exposure, and vulnerability. Through a series of geographic risk maps, Dr. Banaguas illustrated the increasing vulnerability of various Philippine regions to rain-induced landslides, flooding, drought, tropical cyclones, and sea-level rise. The visual impact of the maps transformed climate discourse from abstraction into immediacy. The Philippines was no longer merely “vulnerable” in a general sense. Entire provinces and cities could now be assessed according to their relative exposure to environmental hazards. Particularly striking was his discussion on the changing nature of Philippine seasons. The rainy season, once relatively predictable, has now become increasingly erratic. Climate unpredictability has become so severe that defining clear seasonal boundaries has become difficult. Likewise, droughts — once relatively infrequent — are now occurring with greater regularity, accompanied by rising heat indices and episodes of extreme heat. Climate Change and Business Operations For the business community present at the Manila Polo Club, the implications of the presentation became increasingly personal and operational. Dr. Banaguas carefully connected climate science to the realities of business continuity and economic survival. Changing wind patterns, severe storms, flooding, and infrastructure vulnerability all carry direct economic consequences. Businesses today face disruptions in logistics, communications, productivity, transportation, energy reliability, and supply chains. He emphasized that climate change can no longer be relegated to corporate social responsibility departments alone. It has become a central business risk. Storms delay communications and operations. Flooding halts productivity. Sea-level rise threatens infrastructure. Extreme weather creates cascading economic repercussions across industries. The message was clear: sustainability is no longer simply about compliance. It is about institutional survival. Psychological and Human Dimensions of Climate Change Perhaps the most unexpected and deeply human portion of the presentation involved psychological resilience. Dr. Banaguas spoke about the emotional consequences experienced by communities repeatedly exposed to disasters — trauma, fear, anxiety, apprehension, and emotional fatigue. Yet he also introduced a remarkable phrase: “post-traumatic growers.” Rather than viewing vulnerable populations merely as victims, he emphasized the capacity of communities to emerge stronger, wiser, and more resilient through adversity. In a country where faith and spirituality remain deeply woven into social life, Dr. Banaguas also explored the role of religiosity as a climatedisaster resiliency measure. Various religious traditions, he explained, often provide emotional stability, moral coherence, and collective solidarity during periods of crisis. Faith, in many vulnerable communities, becomes not merely a spiritual refuge but a mechanism of resilience. Policy, Governance, and Sustainability Priorities The discussion then transitioned into policy analysis, emphasizing that resilience requires institutional integration rather than isolated initiatives. Policies, Republic Acts, climate action plans, and local government frameworks must work cohesively if sustainability efforts are to succeed. Dr. Banaguas outlined several priority areas essential to national climate resilience, including food security, water sufficiency, sustainable energy, human security, ecological and environmental stability, climatesmart industries and infrastructure, as well as knowledge management and capacity development. These priorities, he argued, demand participation not only from government but from the private sector itself. This became the philosophical core of the afternoon.
The phrase “Beyond Compliance” was not rhetorical flourish. It was a challenge.
Businesses must move beyond minimal regulatory obedience toward active climate leadership. Net Zero Emissions and ESG Leadership Dr. Banaguas discussed the growing importance of net-zero emissions strategies and decarbonization initiatives involving infrastructure, energy consumption, transportation systems, waste management, food systems, human activity, and agriculture. He connected these efforts to the globally recognized ESG framework — Environmental, Social, and Governance — and demonstrated how the TRIP framework could serve as a practical pathway toward meaningful ESG integration. For many in attendance, the discussion reinforced the growing realization that sustainability reporting, carbon accounting, and environmental stewardship are no longer merely public relations exercises. They are increasingly tied to investor confidence, institutional credibility, and long-term competitiveness. Climate Smart Mindanao and Localized Action The latter portion of the presentation highlighted actual climate-smart initiatives implemented across Mindanao through partnerships involving MINDA, DILG, CHED, NEDA, DOST, and various local stakeholders. Dr. Banaguas showcased collaborative efforts and sustainability initiatives in Davao City, Sarangani Province, Sultan Kudarat Province, South Cotabato Province, Tacurong City, General Santos City, and Cagayan de Oro City. These examples grounded the discussion in practical reality. Climate resilience was no longer theoretical. It was already being attempted, negotiated, and implemented across Philippine communities. What emerged from these examples was a vision of sustainability not as centralized bureaucracy but as collaborative governance involving local governments, institutions, scientists, businesses, educators, and communities. Open Forum and Institutional Reflection By the time the open forum began, the mood inside the Manila Polo Club had noticeably shifted. What began as a traditional weekly membership meeting had evolved into a searching conversation about leadership itself. Questions from members reflected a growing recognition that the private sector can no longer afford passive observation. Sustainability reporting, SEC compliance, carbon management, and ESG frameworks were increasingly viewed not as burdens but as strategic necessities tied directly to institutional survival and stakeholder trust. The Rotary Club of Manila — itself an institution more than a century old — appeared uniquely positioned to host such a conversation. For over one hundred years, the club has witnessed wars, economic upheavals, political transitions, natural disasters, and national transformation. Yet this gathering suggested that perhaps one of the defining challenges of the present generation will not merely be governance or economics, but stewardship itself. The stewardship of institutions.
The stewardship of industries.
The stewardship of future generations. Closing Ceremonies and Final Reflections As President Raoul C. Creencia later presented Dr. Glenn Banaguas with a Certificate of Appreciation, the gesture represented more than ceremonial gratitude. It acknowledged the importance of difficult conversations — the kind that compel institutions to think beyond convenience, beyond compliance, and beyond tradition. At exactly 2:00 in the afternoon, President Creencia formally adjourned the meeting. Yet long after the luncheon tables had emptied and the familiar rhythms of Manila resumed outside the Polo Club gates, the central question of the afternoon continued to linger: In a climate-challenged century, what does responsible leadership truly demand? For the Rotary Club of Manila, the 30th Weekly Membership Meeting may well have offered an answer. Leadership today is no longer measured solely by influence, achievement, or longevity. Increasingly, it will be measured by whether institutions possessed the courage to act before resilience became impossible. 9th Regular Board Meeting  The Rotary Club of Manila held its 9th Regular Board Meeting on May 13, 2026 at the Manila Room of the Elks Club, Makati City. Present were President Raoul Creencia; Directors Edwin Hernandez, Warren So, Hans Palacios, Rami Chahwan, and Mike Albaña; Treasurer PJ Garcia; Internal Auditor Nick Locsin; Director-elect/Board Legal Adviser Caloy Serapio; Secretary Paco Magsaysay; Assistant Treasurer/Vice President-elect Karlo Castro; Secretary Anton Mauricio; Director-elect/Assistant Internal Auditor Mike Roxas; and Deputy Sergeant-at-Arms Dave Reynolds. 31st Weekly Membership Meeting Program  ROTARY CLUB OF MANILA 31st Weekly Membership Meeting

PRES. RAOUL C. CREENCIA 31st Weekly Membership Meeting Editorial  Reginald T. Yu Editor-in-Chief THE forthcoming 31st Weekly Membership Meeting of the Rotary Club of Manila arrives at a moment when the Philippines, like many democracies around the world, finds itself confronting profound questions about governance, institutional trust, and the future direction of the Republic itself. For too long, conversations about constitutional reform in the Philippines have oscillated between political opportunism and public skepticism. Many citizens have become weary of hearing proposals for change that appear designed less to strengthen democratic institutions and more to extend political advantage. Yet history also teaches us that nations unwilling to periodically reexamine their foundations risk becoming prisoners of outdated structures ill-equipped to confront modern realities. It is within this context that the address of Mr. Manuel SD. Lopez, Lead Convenor of the People’s Constitutional Reform Initiative (PCRI), becomes especially significant. The proposed “2026 People’s Constitution” is not merely another academic exercise or political slogan. At its core lies a deeper and more urgent question: How do we build a Republic that is genuinely responsive to the aspirations, frustrations, and evolving needs of its people? The challenges confronting the Philippines today are no longer the same as those that shaped the 1987 Constitution nearly four decades ago. The world has changed dramatically. Economic competition has intensified. Technology has transformed governance and communication. Geopolitical tensions increasingly influence domestic stability. Public demand for accountability has become sharper and more immediate. Citizens expect institutions not only to preserve democracy, but to deliver competence, efficiency, and results. Constitutional reform, therefore, should never be treated as a forbidden conversation. Democracies mature not by avoiding difficult questions, but by engaging them courageously and intelligently. At the same time, any effort to amend or rewrite the Constitution must be approached with extraordinary vigilance, wisdom, and public participation. Constitutional reform cannot belong exclusively to politicians, legal scholars, or ideological blocs. It must belong to the people themselves. The legitimacy of any proposed constitutional framework ultimately rests not on the elegance of its legal language, but on the trust and confidence it earns from ordinary citizens. This is why forums such as the Rotary Club of Manila’s Weekly Membership Meeting matter. For 107 years, the Rotary Club of Manila has served not merely as a fellowship organization, but as a civic platform where ideas of national consequence can be discussed thoughtfully, responsibly, and with intellectual rigor. At a time when public discourse is often reduced to outrage, noise, and polarization, spaces that encourage principled dialogue become increasingly indispensable. Equally meaningful is the Club’s decision to confer the RCM Ambassador Award for 2026 upon His Excellency Miguel Utray Delgado. Diplomacy remains one of the quiet but essential pillars of peace, development, and international cooperation. The enduring relationship between the Philippines and Spain continues to evolve beyond the complexities of history into a partnership grounded in mutual respect, cultural exchange, economic collaboration, and shared democratic values. In honoring Ambassador Delgado, the Rotary Club of Manila affirms an important truth: that nation-building is not accomplished solely through domestic reform, but also through constructive engagement with the international community. The convergence of these two themes during the 31st WMM — constitutional reform and diplomatic partnership — is both timely and symbolic. One speaks to the strengthening of our internal foundations as a Republic. The other reminds us of the importance of building bridges beyond our shores. Both require vision.
Both require courage.
And both ultimately depend on leadership rooted not in personal ambition, but in service to something greater than oneself. As Rotarians, civic leaders, and citizens gather for this important session, the hope is not necessarily that everyone will agree. Democracies do not demand uniformity of opinion. What they require is the willingness to listen seriously, think critically, and engage respectfully in pursuit of the common good. The future of the Republic deserves nothing less. Hosted by Director Edwin Hernandez, the meeting was also attended by President Raoul Creencia, Secretary Anton Mauricio, Consultant Anna Kun-Toledo, and Executive Secretary Lhea Lozano. As a non-political, non-partisan civic organization, RCM confers awards free from governmental or partisan influence. This independence gives its recognitions a purity of intent: awards are given solely on merit, character, and contribution to the public good.
5. Strong International Linkages

Being part of Rotary International’s global network of professionals and leaders gives RCM global visibility and credibility. Awards such as the Outstanding Ambassador Award are strengthened by RCM’s reputation within diplomatic circles and its long relationships with the international community.
6. A Legacy of Honoring Excellence

RCM has a proud tradition of acknowledging outstanding public servants, diplomats, workers, and institutions. This continuity of honoring excellence -- done consistently, thoughtfully, and with discernment -- builds long-term credibility. Recipients know they are joining a distinguished roster, and nominators know the award’s prestige is well-earned.
7. Gravitas Comes From Who We Are

The club’s stature comes from its membership: respected leaders, community builders, and professionals who have themselves earned trust, honor, and integrity. When RCM recognizes someone, that recognition carries the collective prestige of its members.
In essence, RCM’s authority to confer meaningful awards arises from its age, its legacy, its service, its independence, its global connections, and the reputation of its members.
That combination is rare -- and that is why an award from the Rotary Club of Manila truly means something.

articles.title: Beyond Compliance, Beyond Convenience: The Rotary Club of Manila Confronts the Climate Imperative

body.text: THE Rotary Club of Manila gathered beneath the familiar elegance of the Manila Polo Club for its 30th Weekly Membership Meeting of Rotary Year 2025–2026, an afternoon that began in fellowship yet gradually unfolded into a deeply meaningful discussion on leadership, sustainability, and national responsibility.

Moderated by President-Elect Reggie Yu, the meeting carried an atmosphere that was at once warm and reflective. While the traditions of Rotary remained firmly present through music, fellowship, and camaraderie, there was also a growing awareness among attendees that leadership in today’s world can no longer remain confined to ceremonial distinction or institutional prestige. Increasingly, it must confront the pressing realities of climate change, resilience, and sustainable development.

Held on Thursday, May 14, 2026, the gathering centered on the timely and intellectually compelling theme, “Beyond Compliance: Private Sector Leadership in Resiliency and Sustainability.” The very title suggested that the afternoon would move beyond environmental rhetoric and regulatory obligation toward a more transformative conversation about the role of institutions, industries, and communities in shaping the future.

At exactly 12:30 in the afternoon, President Raoul C. Creencia formally called the meeting to order, setting into motion another chapter in the enduring tradition of fellowship and discourse that has long defined the Rotary Club of Manila.
Ceremonial Traditions and Fellowship

The solemnity of the gathering was first established through the Invocation delivered by Director-Elect John Nico P. “Nico” Valencia, followed by the Audio-Visual Presentation of the Philippine National Anthem. The Rotary Club of Manila Hymn was then rendered by the RCM World-Famous Music Chorale with the stirring familiarity that has become inseparable from the club’s institutional identity.

Rotarian Raymond N. “Ray” Davis led the recitation of The FourWay Test, whose principles of truth, fairness, goodwill, and benefit to all seemed especially relevant in a world increasingly shaped by environmental uncertainty and social vulnerability.

President-Elect Reggie Yu acknowledged the guests in attendance with warmth and familiarity, recognizing not merely their presence but their shared participation in a larger national conversation about responsible leadership.

The RCM World-Famous Music Chorale followed with a welcome song that softened the formality of the proceedings and reminded everyone present that Rotary gatherings are sustained not only by institutional continuity but by friendship, music, and fellowship.

The afternoon likewise paused to celebrate life’s joyful milestones as the club recognized its birthday celebrants. Rotarians Jun Coyuito, Mac Macapagal, Jun Bella, Jack Rodriguez, Jun Follosco, and J Alfonso L. Katigbak, together with Past Director Ner Lonzaga, were warmly greeted before the chorale rendered “Maligayang Bati” and “Happy Birthday” with cheerful enthusiasm. The moment provided a welcome reminder that even amid discussions of global challenges, Rotary remains anchored in human relationships and shared celebration.
President’s Time and Institutional Reflection

During President’s Time, President Raoul C. Creencia reflected on the importance of institutions remaining responsive to changing realities. There was a subtle but unmistakable recognition that Rotary itself — an organization founded upon service, ethical leadership, and civic engagement — must continuously redefine what meaningful service entails in an era increasingly shaped by climate volatility and socio-economic uncertainty.
The meeting’s intellectual centerpiece would soon reinforce precisely that point.
Introduction of the Guest of Honor and Speaker

Director Michael Jaey C. “Mike” Albaña introduced the Guest of Honor and Speaker with evident pride, presenting an impressive portrait of a Filipino whose work now spans the global intersection of science, diplomacy, environmental policy, and climate resilience.

The guest speaker, Dr. Glenn S. Banaguas, carried credentials reflecting not merely academic accomplishment but international relevance and influence. A UN Sasakawa Laureate, Chairman and President of ASEAN Science Diplomats, Chairman of the U.S.ASEAN Fellows for Science and Technology, Executive Fellow of the Geneva Centre for Security Policy, Distinguished Fellow of the Royal Society of Arts in the United Kingdom, and Climate Diplomat for the European Union-Asia Expert Panel for Climate Diplomacy, Dr. Banaguas represented a rare fusion of scientific rigor and policy advocacy.
From the outset, his presentation challenged the audience to reconsider climate change not as a distant environmental concern but as an immediate operational, economic, social, and moral reality.
The Climate Smart Philippines Framework

Dr. Banaguas framed his presentation around the concept of a “Climate Smart Philippines,” emphasizing that resilience and sustainability are no longer optional aspirations but strategic necessities for survival and long-term prosperity.

He described the Philippines as a geographically and administratively complex nation composed of 81 provinces, 146 cities, 1,488 municipalities, and more than 42,000 barangays — a reality that makes climate governance both extraordinarily difficult and critically important.

At the heart of his discussion was the concept of “Climate Smart” governance, built upon the dual imperatives of climate change mitigation and climate change adaptation. These, he explained, form what he called “A TRIP to Resiliency and Sustainability.”

The acronym TRIP stood for Track, Risk, Impact, and Policy, a fourdimensional framework designed to help governments, institutions, and corporations systematically understand and respond to climate realities.
Tracking Climate Realities
The “Track” component focused on analyzing human resources, demographics, historical climate data, and long-term climate projections involving rainfall and temperature changes.
What followed was among the most sobering portions of the presentation.

Using internationally recognized climate projections, Dr. Banaguas demonstrated how average temperatures in both Metro Manila and Cebu are expected to rise significantly over the coming decades. For the National Capital Region, projected average temperatures could increase by more than two degrees Celsius before the end of the century. Cebu exhibited a similarly alarming trajectory.
These were not speculative fears intended merely to provoke concern. They were evidence-based projections grounded in climate science.

Equally concerning were projections involving precipitation patterns. Metro Manila is expected to experience increasing rainfall intensity over successive decades, while Cebu similarly reflects increasingly unstable climate conditions.
The implications, he emphasized, extend far beyond weather inconvenience.
Climate change reshapes economies, labor systems, agriculture, transportation, health outcomes, infrastructure, and social stability itself.
Risk, Vulnerability, and the Geography of Disaster
The presentation then shifted toward risk analysis using the United Nations disaster risk framework, which identifies disaster risk as a function of hazard, exposure, and vulnerability.

Through a series of geographic risk maps, Dr. Banaguas illustrated the increasing vulnerability of various Philippine regions to rain-induced landslides, flooding, drought, tropical cyclones, and sea-level rise.

The visual impact of the maps transformed climate discourse from abstraction into immediacy. The Philippines was no longer merely “vulnerable” in a general sense. Entire provinces and cities could now be assessed according to their relative exposure to environmental hazards.

Particularly striking was his discussion on the changing nature of Philippine seasons. The rainy season, once relatively predictable, has now become increasingly erratic. Climate unpredictability has become so severe that defining clear seasonal boundaries has become difficult.
Likewise, droughts — once relatively infrequent — are now occurring with greater regularity, accompanied by rising heat indices and episodes of extreme heat.
Climate Change and Business Operations
For the business community present at the Manila Polo Club, the implications of the presentation became increasingly personal and operational.

Dr. Banaguas carefully connected climate science to the realities of business continuity and economic survival. Changing wind patterns, severe storms, flooding, and infrastructure vulnerability all carry direct economic consequences.

Businesses today face disruptions in logistics, communications, productivity, transportation, energy reliability, and supply chains. He emphasized that climate change can no longer be relegated to corporate social responsibility departments alone. It has become a central business risk.
Storms delay communications and operations. Flooding halts productivity. Sea-level rise threatens infrastructure. Extreme weather creates cascading economic repercussions across industries.
The message was clear: sustainability is no longer simply about compliance. It is about institutional survival.
Psychological and Human Dimensions of Climate Change
Perhaps the most unexpected and deeply human portion of the presentation involved psychological resilience.
Dr. Banaguas spoke about the emotional consequences experienced by communities repeatedly exposed to disasters — trauma, fear, anxiety, apprehension, and emotional fatigue.
Yet he also introduced a remarkable phrase: “post-traumatic growers.”
Rather than viewing vulnerable populations merely as victims, he emphasized the capacity of communities to emerge stronger, wiser, and more resilient through adversity.

In a country where faith and spirituality remain deeply woven into social life, Dr. Banaguas also explored the role of religiosity as a climatedisaster resiliency measure. Various religious traditions, he explained, often provide emotional stability, moral coherence, and collective solidarity during periods of crisis.
Faith, in many vulnerable communities, becomes not merely a spiritual refuge but a mechanism of resilience.
Policy, Governance, and Sustainability Priorities
The discussion then transitioned into policy analysis, emphasizing that resilience requires institutional integration rather than isolated initiatives.
Policies, Republic Acts, climate action plans, and local government frameworks must work cohesively if sustainability efforts are to succeed.

Dr. Banaguas outlined several priority areas essential to national climate resilience, including food security, water sufficiency, sustainable energy, human security, ecological and environmental stability, climatesmart industries and infrastructure, as well as knowledge management and capacity development.
These priorities, he argued, demand participation not only from government but from the private sector itself.

This became the philosophical core of the afternoon.
The phrase “Beyond Compliance” was not rhetorical flourish. It was a challenge.
Businesses must move beyond minimal regulatory obedience toward active climate leadership.
Net Zero Emissions and ESG Leadership

Dr. Banaguas discussed the growing importance of net-zero emissions strategies and decarbonization initiatives involving infrastructure, energy consumption, transportation systems, waste management, food systems, human activity, and agriculture.

He connected these efforts to the globally recognized ESG framework — Environmental, Social, and Governance — and demonstrated how the TRIP framework could serve as a practical pathway toward meaningful ESG integration.

For many in attendance, the discussion reinforced the growing realization that sustainability reporting, carbon accounting, and environmental stewardship are no longer merely public relations exercises. They are increasingly tied to investor confidence, institutional credibility, and long-term competitiveness.
Climate Smart Mindanao and Localized Action

The latter portion of the presentation highlighted actual climate-smart initiatives implemented across Mindanao through partnerships involving MINDA, DILG, CHED, NEDA, DOST, and various local stakeholders.

Dr. Banaguas showcased collaborative efforts and sustainability initiatives in Davao City, Sarangani Province, Sultan Kudarat Province, South Cotabato Province, Tacurong City, General Santos City, and Cagayan de Oro City.
These examples grounded the discussion in practical reality.
Climate resilience was no longer theoretical.
It was already being attempted, negotiated, and implemented across Philippine communities.

What emerged from these examples was a vision of sustainability not as centralized bureaucracy but as collaborative governance involving local governments, institutions, scientists, businesses, educators, and communities.
Open Forum and Institutional Reflection
By the time the open forum began, the mood inside the Manila Polo Club had noticeably shifted.
What began as a traditional weekly membership meeting had evolved into a searching conversation about leadership itself.

Questions from members reflected a growing recognition that the private sector can no longer afford passive observation. Sustainability reporting, SEC compliance, carbon management, and ESG frameworks were increasingly viewed not as burdens but as strategic necessities tied directly to institutional survival and stakeholder trust.
The Rotary Club of Manila — itself an institution more than a century old — appeared uniquely positioned to host such a conversation.

For over one hundred years, the club has witnessed wars, economic upheavals, political transitions, natural disasters, and national transformation. Yet this gathering suggested that perhaps one of the defining challenges of the present generation will not merely be governance or economics, but stewardship itself.

The stewardship of institutions.
The stewardship of industries.
The stewardship of future generations.
Closing Ceremonies and Final Reflections

As President Raoul C. Creencia later presented Dr. Glenn Banaguas with a Certificate of Appreciation, the gesture represented more than ceremonial gratitude. It acknowledged the importance of difficult conversations — the kind that compel institutions to think beyond convenience, beyond compliance, and beyond tradition.
At exactly 2:00 in the afternoon, President Creencia formally adjourned the meeting.
Yet long after the luncheon tables had emptied and the familiar rhythms of Manila resumed outside the Polo Club gates, the central question of the afternoon continued to linger:
In a climate-challenged century, what does responsible leadership truly demand?
For the Rotary Club of Manila, the 30th Weekly Membership Meeting may well have offered an answer. Leadership today is no longer measured solely by influence, achievement, or longevity.
Increasingly, it will be measured by whether institutions possessed the courage to act before resilience became impossible.
The Rotary Club of Manila held its 9th Regular Board Meeting on May 13, 2026 at the Manila Room of the Elks Club, Makati City.

Present were President Raoul Creencia; Directors Edwin Hernandez, Warren So, Hans Palacios, Rami Chahwan, and Mike Albaña; Treasurer PJ Garcia; Internal Auditor Nick Locsin; Director-elect/Board Legal Adviser Caloy Serapio; Secretary Paco Magsaysay; Assistant Treasurer/Vice President-elect Karlo Castro; Secretary Anton Mauricio; Director-elect/Assistant Internal Auditor Mike Roxas; and Deputy Sergeant-at-Arms Dave Reynolds.

THE forthcoming 31st Weekly Membership Meeting of the Rotary Club of Manila arrives at a moment when the Philippines, like many democracies around the world, finds itself confronting profound questions about governance, institutional trust, and the future direction of the Republic itself.

For too long, conversations about constitutional reform in the Philippines have oscillated between political opportunism and public skepticism. Many citizens have become weary of hearing proposals for change that appear designed less to strengthen democratic institutions and more to extend political advantage. Yet history also teaches us that nations unwilling to periodically reexamine their foundations risk becoming prisoners of outdated structures ill-equipped to confront modern realities.
It is within this context that the address of Mr. Manuel SD. Lopez, Lead Convenor of the People’s Constitutional Reform Initiative (PCRI), becomes especially significant.

The proposed “2026 People’s Constitution” is not merely another academic exercise or political slogan. At its core lies a deeper and more urgent question: How do we build a Republic that is genuinely responsive to the aspirations, frustrations, and evolving needs of its people?

The challenges confronting the Philippines today are no longer the same as those that shaped the 1987 Constitution nearly four decades ago. The world has changed dramatically. Economic competition has intensified. Technology has transformed governance and communication. Geopolitical tensions increasingly influence domestic stability. Public demand for accountability has become sharper and more immediate. Citizens expect institutions not only to preserve democracy, but to deliver competence, efficiency, and results.
Constitutional reform, therefore, should never be treated as a forbidden conversation. Democracies mature not by avoiding difficult questions, but by engaging them courageously and intelligently.

At the same time, any effort to amend or rewrite the Constitution must be approached with extraordinary vigilance, wisdom, and public participation. Constitutional reform cannot belong exclusively to politicians, legal scholars, or ideological blocs. It must belong to the people themselves. The legitimacy of any proposed constitutional framework ultimately rests not on the elegance of its legal language, but on the trust and confidence it earns from ordinary citizens. This is why forums such as the Rotary Club of Manila’s Weekly Membership Meeting matter.

For 107 years, the Rotary Club of Manila has served not merely as a fellowship organization, but as a civic platform where ideas of national consequence can be discussed thoughtfully, responsibly, and with intellectual rigor. At a time when public discourse is often reduced to outrage, noise, and polarization, spaces that encourage principled dialogue become increasingly indispensable.

Equally meaningful is the Club’s decision to confer the RCM Ambassador Award for 2026 upon His Excellency Miguel Utray Delgado. Diplomacy remains one of the quiet but essential pillars of peace, development, and international cooperation. The enduring relationship between the Philippines and Spain continues to evolve beyond the complexities of history into a partnership grounded in mutual respect, cultural exchange, economic collaboration, and shared democratic values.

In honoring Ambassador Delgado, the Rotary Club of Manila affirms an important truth: that nation-building is not accomplished solely through domestic reform, but also through constructive engagement with the international community.

The convergence of these two themes during the 31st WMM — constitutional reform and diplomatic partnership — is both timely and symbolic. One speaks to the strengthening of our internal foundations as a Republic. The other reminds us of the importance of building bridges beyond our shores.

Both require vision.
Both require courage.
And both ultimately depend on leadership rooted not in personal ambition, but in service to something greater than oneself.

As Rotarians, civic leaders, and citizens gather for this important session, the hope is not necessarily that everyone will agree. Democracies do not demand uniformity of opinion. What they require is the willingness to listen seriously, think critically, and engage respectfully in pursuit of the common good.
The future of the Republic deserves nothing less.

body.text: The RCM ProPatria Journalism Awards Committee met on May 14, 2016, to vote on nominations for the print, TV, radio, and online categories for institution and individual awards.

Present were President Raoul Creencia, DE/BLA Caloy Serapio, Chair Dean Amading Valdez, Secretary Anton Mauricio, STAR Rotarians Chris Tamesis, Oliver Pantaleon, and Winston Ginez, Director Edwin Hernanddz, Past District Governor Jackie Rodriguez, and President-elect Reggie Yu.
The Club Awards Committee met last Friday, May 15, 2026, at the Sandtrap of Manila Golf and Country Club.
Hosted by Director Edwin Hernandez, the meeting was also attended by President Raoul Creencia, Secretary Anton Mauricio, Consultant Anna Kun-Toledo, and Executive Secretary Lhea Lozano.
The Outstanding Workers of the Republic (TOWER) Awards 2026 Board of Judges and Screening Committee met on May 19, 2026 at the Board Room, 10th floor, PEZA Office, West Tower, Pasay City.
Present were PEZA Deputy Director General Emmanuel Cortero, PEZA Group Manager Rowena Naguit, President Raoul Creencia, Past President Romy Nones, and STAR Rotarian Jason Valderrama.
The ALECO meeting, hosted by IA Nick Locsin on May 18, 2026, focused on discussing preparations for the RCM Golf President's Cup.
