articles.title: TRUST THE PROCESS | A Life of Scholarship, Leadership, Service, and Purpose of Dr. Albert Singson Alday

body.text: FEW lives follow the path originally imagined for them. Albert Singson Alday's certainly did not. Raised in a family of physicians, scholars, and educators, he seemed destined for a conventional story of professional success. Instead, his life became a series of unexpected turns — academic triumphs and painful disappointments, abandoned dreams and new beginnings, failures that became foundations for future achievements. Spanning the worlds of philosophy, medicine, law, education, entrepreneurship, Rotary, and JCI, his journey reveals a man who discovered that life's greatest lessons are often found not in the goals we attain, but in the setbacks that teach us who we are.
The room was silent except for the rustle of paper and the occasional turning of a page.
Around him sat hundreds of examinees, each hoping that years of study, sacrifice, and ambition would finally culminate in a single word: Passed.
For Albert Singson Alday, this was not the first time he had sat for the Philippine Bar Examination.
Nor would it be the last.

By then, he had already accumulated credentials most people would consider more than enough for a successful life. He was a Cum Laude graduate of the University of the Philippines. He held a degree in Philosophy, a Bachelor of Laws, a doctorate in Metaphysics, and would later earn a Master of Laws from Boston University. He had taught generations of students, helped build academic institutions, led civic organizations, and accumulated a list of accomplishments that would satisfy many ambitions.
Yet on that day, seated among aspiring lawyers, none of those achievements seemed to matter.
What mattered was a dream that had stubbornly refused to die.

As he waited for the signal to begin, Albert found himself reflecting on a question that had followed him for much of his life: Why do some goals come easily while others remain maddeningly beyond reach?
It was a question he knew well.

As a child, he had competed relentlessly for academic honors and discovered that excellence often attracted controversy as much as recognition. As a university student, he had entered medicine only to realize that the profession he admired was not necessarily the profession he was meant to pursue. As a law graduate, he had come painfully close to admission to the Bar on multiple occasions, only to see success slip away by the narrowest of margins.
Again and again, life had challenged his assumptions about merit, effort, and destiny.
Yet each disappointment carried an unexpected gift.

The failed physician became a philosopher.
The unsuccessful lawyer became an educator.
The student who once measured success through medals and rankings gradually became a builder of institutions, a mentor of future leaders, and a servant of causes greater than himself.
Looking back, it is tempting to view those detours as interruptions.
Albert eventually came to see them differently.
They were the journey.

For the story of Albert Singson Alday is not ultimately about degrees earned, offices held, or honors received. It is the story of a man shaped by generations of educators and scholars, tested repeatedly by adversity, and sustained by a belief that life's setbacks often conceal its most important lessons.
It is the story of a lifelong student who never stopped learning, a leader who discovered that service matters more than status, and a challenger who, despite every disappointment, refused to quit.
Above all, it is the story of a philosophy that emerged not from books or classrooms but from experience itself:
Trust the process.
An Inheritance of Learning, Duty, and Sacrifice
Long before Albert Singson Alday entered a classroom, he inherited a story.

It was not a story of wealth or privilege in the conventional sense, but one shaped by education, public service, perseverance, and sacrifice. Across both sides of his family, achievement was rarely separated from responsibility. Success was respected, but it was expected to be earned; learning was prized, but it was expected to be shared.
These values formed the invisible inheritance that awaited him at birth.

On his father's side, the story began in the schools and battlefields of a generation tested by war. His grandfather, Pedro Quizon Alday, was an educator who rose to become a school superintendent and later served as an officer in the United States Armed Forces in the Far East during the Second World War. Like many Filipinos of his generation, he paid a heavy price for duty. Killed during the liberation, he never returned home. His remains were never recovered; only his bloodstained uniform was returned to his family.
The loss altered the course of those he left behind.

His children grew up without a father, and their ambitions were shaped as much by necessity as by aspiration. Dreams were often adjusted to accommodate circumstances. Yet rather than breaking the family, hardship seemed to deepen its commitment to education. The next generation produced physicians, pharmacists, educators, and professionals whose accomplishments reflected both talent and perseverance.
Among them was Albert's father, Adalberto Alday.

Originally drawn to engineering, he eventually pursued medicine at the University of the Philippines after practical realities redirected his plans. What followed was a distinguished career in microbiology, public health, and medical education, culminating in leadership roles at the U.P. College of Public Health and other institutions. To Albert, however, his father's significance extended beyond academic credentials. He represented a model of quiet discipline, humility, and intellectual rigor.
A similar story unfolded on his mother's side.

The Singsons and Parels of Northern Luzon had long produced educators, scholars, physicians, and public servants whose influence extended beyond their immediate communities. Their legacy included political leaders, university deans, researchers, and pioneers in their respective fields. Yet what impressed Albert most was not their prominence but their shared belief that education was life's most enduring asset.
No one embodied that belief more completely than his mother, Dr. Aretas Singson Alday.

A physician, professor, and eventually founding dean of a medical school, she approached education with an almost missionary zeal. Academic excellence was not merely encouraged; it was cultivated through discipline, preparation, and persistence. She believed deeply that talent without effort was wasted potential and that achievement required deliberate work.
Her influence on Albert would be profound.

From her he learned diligence, perseverance, and the habit of aiming higher than circumstances seemed to permit. From his father he learned humility, respect for others, and the importance of treating every person with dignity regardless of status. Together, they created a household where intellectual achievement and moral character were regarded not as competing virtues but as complementary obligations.

Surrounding them were relatives who reinforced the same lessons. Distinguished educators such as Dean Erlinda Singson Echanis and Dr. Cristina Parel demonstrated what could be achieved through scholarship and public service. Their accomplishments expanded Albert's sense of what was possible while reminding him that education's ultimate purpose extended beyond personal advancement.
Looking back, it becomes clear that the most important inheritance Albert received was not material.
It was cultural.
He inherited a reverence for learning. A respect for institutions. A belief in service.
And an understanding that adversity, however painful, could be transformed into opportunity through perseverance and discipline.

These values would accompany him through every stage of his life. They would sustain him through academic rivalries, professional disappointments, failed examinations, and personal setbacks. They would influence his decisions as a student, educator, administrator, entrepreneur, Rotarian, and civic leader.
Long before Albert began building a life of his own, generations before him had already laid its foundations.
Their stories became part of his story. Their sacrifices became part of his inheritance.

And from that inheritance emerged a conviction that would guide him for the rest of his life: that education is life's greatest investment, integrity its firmest foundation, and service its highest purpose.
The Household That Formed Him
Albert was born into a family where education was not merely valued — it was expected.

Long before he entered a classroom, learning already occupied a place of honor within the household. Academic achievement, professional excellence, and public service were recurring themes in family conversations, not because they were imposed as obligations, but because they were deeply embedded in the stories of the generations that came before him.
On both sides of the family, achievement carried a common thread: sacrifice.

His paternal grandfather, Pedro Quizon Alday, was an educator and school superintendent whose life reflected both the promise and tragedy of his generation. A graduate of the Philippine Normal School and an officer in the United States Armed Forces in the Far East, he never returned from the Second World War. Killed during the liberation and identified only through a bloodstained uniform, he left behind a young family whose future would be shaped by loss as much as by opportunity.

The consequences of that loss reverberated through the next generation. Albert's father, Adalberto Alday, grew up in circumstances that demanded resilience. Dreams of becoming an engineer gave way to medicine, not because it was an easier path but because it was the path available. Working while studying, he eventually graduated from the University of the Philippines College of Medicine and built a distinguished career in microbiology, public health, and medical education. Along the way, he developed a reputation not only for academic rigor but also for humility and accessibility — qualities that would leave a lasting impression on his son.
The story on Albert's mother's side carried a similar reverence for learning.

The Singsons and Parels of Northern Luzon produced educators, physicians, public servants, and scholars whose influence extended well beyond their communities. Among them was Cristina Parel, the pioneering statistician who established the U.P. Statistics Center, and Erlinda Singson Echanis, who would later serve as Dean of the U.P. College of Business Administration. Their accomplishments reinforced a lesson that Albert encountered repeatedly throughout his youth: education was the most enduring form of inheritance.
No one embodied that lesson more completely than his mother, Dr. Aretas Singson Alday.

A physician, professor, and eventually founding dean of a medical school, she approached education with a seriousness that bordered on mission. Her expectations were demanding, but they were grounded in the conviction that discipline creates opportunity. She believed that talent mattered less than preparation, and that achievement was rarely accidental.
Albert would later credit much of his academic discipline to her influence.
If his mother taught perseverance, his father taught perspective.

Dr. Bert Alday often reminded his son that success meant little if it created distance from other people. He encouraged him to respect individuals regardless of their social standing and to treat janitors, clerks, professors, and executives with equal courtesy. The lesson was subtle but powerful. In a family filled with accomplished professionals, humility remained a prized virtue.

The household itself reflected these values. Conversations moved easily from medicine to education, from public affairs to current events. Academic accomplishment was admired, but integrity was expected. Titles carried weight, yet character carried more.

Growing up in such an environment offered advantages, but it also created expectations. Albert was constantly surrounded by examples of excellence. Distinguished physicians, educators, researchers, and administrators were not distant public figures; they were relatives, mentors, and family friends. Their achievements inspired him, but they also established standards that could be difficult to ignore.
Yet what Albert remembers most is not the prestige attached to their names. It is the atmosphere they created.

The adults who surrounded him shared a common belief that knowledge carried responsibility. Education was not pursued solely for personal advancement but as a means of contributing to society. Learning was expected to lead to service. Achievement was expected to lead to stewardship.

Years later, Albert would follow a path very different from the one many anticipated. He would move through philosophy, medicine, law, education, entrepreneurship, Rotary, and JCI, accumulating experiences that few could have predicted. Yet beneath those varied pursuits lay values that had been instilled long before he chose a profession.

The discipline to persevere through setbacks.
The belief that education remains life's greatest investment.
The conviction that integrity matters more than recognition.

And the understanding that one's success acquires meaning only when it benefits others.
Those lessons did not come from textbooks or lectures.
They came from a household where learning was a way of life and where the examples set by previous generations quietly shaped the aspirations of the next.

Before Albert ever entered the wider world, the foundations had already been laid. The competitor, the scholar, the educator, and the leader he would eventually become were all, in some measure, products of the household that formed him.
A Childhood in Las Piñas
When Albert was growing up, Las Piñas was still a town in transition.

The sprawling commercial landscape that would later define the southern corridor of Metro Manila did not yet exist. Alabang-Zapote Road remained a modest thoroughfare, bordered by open spaces, salt beds, and emerging subdivisions that hinted at the area's future growth. Shopping options were limited, traffic was manageable, and much of daily life retained the character of a developing suburb rather than a bustling city.
For a young boy, however, Las Piñas was less a place than a world.

It was where childhood unfolded through a series of routines and rituals that, decades later, remained vivid in memory. Mornings often began with a bowl of Quaker Oats and an episode of Sesame Street. Evenings revolved around the television schedule, particularly the Japanese robot cartoons that captivated an entire generation of Filipino children.

Mondays belonged to Mekanda Robot, Tuesdays to Daimos, Wednesdays to Mazinger Z, Thursdays to UFO Grendizer, and Fridays to Voltes V. Like many boys of his era, Albert followed them with near-religious devotion.
Yet his childhood was shaped as much by collecting as by watching.

He accumulated die-cast robots, Star Wars action figures, Matchbox cars, Super Trump cards, comic books, and Lego sets with the enthusiasm of someone who saw joy in assembling worlds piece by piece. Weekend excursions often revolved around these pursuits. Greenhills, Rustan's, Philcite, and the emerging shopping centers of Metro Manila became destinations not merely for purchases but for discovery. Every toy carried the promise of a new adventure; every collection felt like a project waiting to be completed.
Looking back, Albert readily admits that he was a fortunate child.

As the youngest member of the family, he occupied a special place in the affections of parents, relatives, and older siblings. The household provided comforts that many Filipino families could only aspire to, yet it was not a home where privilege translated into complacency. Beneath the toys, outings, and childhood indulgences existed an unmistakable expectation that education mattered.
That expectation came primarily from his parents.

Both physicians and educators, they viewed learning not simply as a means of professional advancement but as a responsibility. Academic excellence was encouraged early and reinforced consistently. Even before Albert fully understood its significance, he absorbed the message that achievement required effort and that opportunities carried obligations.
The contrast between comfort and discipline would become one of the defining characteristics of his upbringing.

He enjoyed the pleasures of childhood — a growing toy collection, favorite restaurants, family outings, basketball games, and weekends spent exploring Metro Manila. Yet he was also raised in a household where achievement was expected rather than celebrated as exceptional. Success was never treated as an entitlement. It was treated as the product of preparation.

Sports provided another window into the world around him. Through his father, Albert developed an early fascination with basketball during the golden age of the Crispa-Toyota rivalry. He memorized player names and jersey numbers, followed games obsessively, and dreamed, at least briefly, of becoming an athlete himself. The dream would eventually yield to reality, but the competitive spirit that sports awakened remained.

More enduring, perhaps, was his growing curiosity about how things worked. While other children saw only the surface of events, Albert increasingly found himself asking questions. Why did communities develop the way they did? How were institutions organized? Why did people behave differently under similar circumstances? Such interests remained largely dormant during childhood, but they foreshadowed the intellectual pursuits that would later draw him toward philosophy, law, and public affairs.

If there was a defining feature of Albert's early years, it was the sense of security that surrounded them. Family gatherings were frequent. Meals were shared. Parents remained active participants in his education and development. The household provided not only material comfort but also stability, a foundation from which ambition could safely grow.

Years later, when asked what he missed most about childhood, Albert rarely mentioned the toys, the cartoons, or the restaurants that populated his memories. What he missed most were the ordinary moments spent with his parents and sister — the conversations, the meals, and the quiet certainty that everyone he loved would be gathered around the same table.
The nostalgia is telling.
For all the achievements that would later define his life, Albert's fondest memories remained rooted in something simpler: family.

It was within that environment — part privilege, part discipline, and entirely shaped by love — that the foundations of his character were quietly being laid. The competitive student, the philosopher, the educator, the civic leader, and the lifelong learner all had their beginnings in that suburban corner of Las Piñas, where a young boy spent his days collecting toys, watching robot cartoons, and gradually absorbing the values that would guide him for the rest of his life.
The Making of a Competitor
Long before Albert encountered philosophy, law, or leadership, he learned a lesson that would shape much of his life: excellence has a price.

The lesson emerged gradually during his years at De La Salle-Santiago Zobel School, where achievement was not merely encouraged but measured, ranked, and publicly recognized. For Albert, whose elementary years were governed by a disciplined routine of study supervised closely by his mother, academic success became both a habit and an expectation. Homework was completed before play. Reviewers were prepared in advance. Examinations were approached with seriousness. While other children enjoyed long afternoons outdoors, much of Albert's time was devoted to preparation.
The sacrifices often went unnoticed. What others saw were the results.

By fourth grade, he had begun receiving academic honors. The medals continued in the years that followed, culminating in a string of top distinctions that established him as one of the school's strongest students. Success brought satisfaction, but it also introduced him to a reality that few children anticipate: achievement changes relationships.

Classmates who once seemed indifferent now viewed him as a rival. Academic rankings transformed friendships into competitions and ordinary examinations into contests of prestige. Albert gradually discovered that standing at the top of a class could be surprisingly isolating. The better he performed, the more he found himself defined by his accomplishments rather than by his personality.
It was an experience that would leave a lasting impression.

Years later, he would often remark that life at the top can be lonely. The observation was not born of arrogance but of experience. Excellence attracts admiration, yet it can also create distance. People see the outcome without always understanding the effort that produced it.
That tension surfaced dramatically during one of the defining controversies of his elementary years.

In fifth grade, an error in recording grades caused Albert to be announced publicly as a bronze medalist despite having earned the highest academic standing in his class. The mistake was eventually corrected after a review by school administrators, but the incident revealed something he had never previously considered. Institutions, no matter how well intentioned, are imperfect. Fairness cannot always be assumed. Sometimes one must advocate for oneself even when the facts seem obvious.
The lesson became even more pronounced two years later.

Upon graduating from grade school, Albert found himself at the center of a dispute involving valedictory honors. Because he had briefly attended Manila Science High School before returning to Zobel, some questioned whether he satisfied the school's eligibility requirements despite having earned the necessary academic standing. What began as a school matter eventually escalated beyond the campus, drawing the attention of educational authorities and senior administrators.

For a young student, the experience was bewildering. He had done what he believed was expected of him — worked hard, studied diligently, and earned the grades required. Yet achievement alone proved insufficient to shield him from controversy.

A compromise was eventually reached, recognizing two valedictorians. Albert accepted the decision, partly out of practicality and partly because he still intended to spend his high school years at the institution. More important than the outcome, however, was the lesson it left behind. Competition, he discovered, is rarely confined to performance alone.
It often involves perceptions, rules, personalities, and circumstances beyond one's control.

The realization marked an important stage in his development. Until then, he had largely viewed success as a straightforward equation between effort and results. His experiences taught him that life is considerably more complicated. Merit matters, but so do institutions, interpretations, and human nature.
Yet rather than discouraging him, the experience deepened his competitive instincts.

Albert was not motivated merely by the desire to win. He was driven by the challenge of testing his limits. Each setback became an invitation to work harder. Each disappointment became a reason to improve. The controversies that surrounded some of his achievements strengthened his resolve rather than weakening it.

Looking back, it is tempting to view these episodes simply as childhood rivalries. In reality, they represented something more significant. They were Albert's first encounters with themes that would recur throughout his life: perseverance in the face of adversity, the imperfect nature of institutions, and the necessity of defending one's convictions without sacrificing integrity.
By the time he entered high school, he had become more than an excellent student.
He had become a competitor.

Not the kind who measured success solely by victory, but the kind who understood that achievement often requires persistence through disappointment, criticism, and uncertainty. It was a lesson he would revisit repeatedly in the years ahead, whether in medicine, law, academia, business, or civic leadership.
For now, however, he remained a young student standing at the threshold of adolescence, unaware that the greatest challenges — and the most important transformations — still lay ahead.
The Zobel Years: Scholarship, Rivalry, and Awakening
By the time Albert entered high school at De La Salle-Santiago Zobel School, he had already become accustomed to academic success.

For years, achievement had been the organizing principle of his young life. Homework followed a strict routine. Examinations were approached with military discipline. Medals had become familiar companions. Much of this discipline came from his mother, whose unwavering commitment to academic excellence transformed study into a daily ritual rather than an occasional obligation.
Yet high school would challenge him in ways that grades never could.

The competition was fiercer than anything he had previously encountered. Many of the students who had once trailed behind him academically were now discovering their own strengths, and the field became increasingly crowded with talented rivals. For the first time, Albert found himself surrounded by peers who could match his intellect, challenge his assumptions, and compete for the same distinctions he had long considered attainable.
The experience was both exhilarating and unsettling.

Success no longer depended solely on effort. It required resilience, adaptability, and the ability to perform under constant scrutiny. Academic rankings became matters of intense interest, and rivalries sometimes extended beyond the classroom. Questions about honors and recognition occasionally evolved into disputes that tested not only achievement but character.

One such controversy emerged when Albert graduated from grade school. Because he had briefly attended Manila Science High School before returning to Zobel, some questioned his eligibility for valedictorian honors despite his academic standing. The matter eventually reached educational authorities and the office of Bro. Andrew Gonzalez, FSC. A compromise recognizing two valedictorians resolved the dispute, but the experience left a lasting impression.
It was his first meaningful encounter with a truth that would reveal itself repeatedly throughout adult life: excellence does not insulate one from controversy. In fact, it often invites it.

High school presented a similar lesson. Despite graduating as salutatorian and receiving the prestigious St. Brother Miguel Leadership Award, Albert could not entirely suppress the feeling that he had fallen short of his own expectations. Years later, he would summarize the sentiment with a line that remained lodged in his memory: "You never win the silver. You only lose the gold." The remark was less an expression of disappointment than a reflection of the standards he imposed upon himself.
Yet while competition occupied much of his attention, another transformation was quietly taking place.

For much of his childhood, Albert had been something of a loner. Academic success had often created distance between him and his classmates, many of whom regarded him more as a rival than a friend. High school forced him out of that isolation. Student organizations, extracurricular activities, and shared experiences gradually taught him lessons no textbook could provide.

Through the Math Club, he confronted one of his weaker subjects. Through the Student Council, he encountered the realities of leadership and politics. The Interact Club introduced him to service and offered his first glimpse into the ideals that would later draw him to Rotary. Even the Student Judicial Board exposed him to ethical dilemmas and organizational dynamics that foreshadowed challenges he would later encounter in professional life.
These experiences broadened his understanding of success.
Achievement, he began to realize, was not solely an individual pursuit.
Organizations depended on cooperation. Leadership required persuasion. Influence demanded relationships. Intelligence alone was not enough.

The lesson was reinforced through scientific research, an area where Albert's curiosity found practical expression. Drawing inspiration from environmental concerns in Las Piñas, he conducted studies on water salinity and fluoride content that earned championship honors at Science Congress competitions. The projects reflected more than technical competence. They revealed an emerging habit of mind: the belief that problems exist to be investigated and understood before they can be solved.
Research taught him patience. Leadership taught him perspective. Friendship taught him humility.
Together, they began reshaping a young man who had long defined himself primarily through academic performance.

Writing also emerged as an important outlet during these years. Through essays, poetry, and reflection, Albert found a means of expressing thoughts that often remained unspoken in everyday conversation. His success in the National Rizal Essay Writing Contest hinted at abilities that extended beyond the classroom and foreshadowed the intellectual interests that would later draw him toward philosophy and law.

By the time he graduated from Zobel in 1990, Albert was no longer simply the highly competitive student who had entered its gates years earlier. He remained ambitious, certainly, but his understanding of achievement had become more nuanced. The rivalries, controversies, friendships, and leadership experiences of adolescence had expanded his horizons beyond grades and medals.
Most importantly, they had begun teaching him a lesson that would shape the rest of his life: that accomplishment may open doors, but character determines what one does after walking through them.
The realization would prove invaluable when he entered the University of the Philippines, where many of the assumptions that had guided him thus far would be challenged once again.
The University of the Philippines and the Discovery of Philosophy
Albert entered the University of the Philippines believing he knew where his life was headed.

Like many children raised in families of physicians, he had long imagined himself following the path laid down by previous generations. Medicine seemed the natural destination. His parents had both graduated from the U.P. College of Medicine. His relatives occupied prominent places in academia, research, and healthcare. Becoming a physician felt less like a decision than the continuation of a family story already in progress.
Yet the University of the Philippines has a way of complicating certainty.

Albert initially enrolled in the Bachelor of Science in Public Health program at U.P. Manila, carrying with him the ambitions of a high-achieving student and the expectations that accompanied a distinguished family legacy. Academically, he performed well enough to earn recognition as an Entrance Scholar and later a College Scholar. Beneath the surface, however, he was beginning to encounter a problem that grades alone could not solve.
The subjects required by his chosen path failed to ignite his imagination.

Chemistry, in particular, proved to be a recurring adversary. More significantly, he found himself increasingly drawn toward questions that extended beyond laboratory work and scientific methodology. While many of his classmates were fascinated by formulas, pathways, and technical precision, Albert was preoccupied by ideas. He wanted to understand how institutions functioned, how societies organized themselves, why people believed what they believed, and how language itself shaped human understanding.
At first, these interests seemed peripheral to his education.
Eventually, they became central to it.

A series of academic detours — including a shift to Biology, a leave of absence, and an unsuccessful attempt to transfer into Psychology — left him searching for a new direction. The circumstances felt frustrating at the time. Looking back, they appear almost providential.

When the opportunity arose to transfer to the Philosophy program at U.P. Diliman, the decision was largely pragmatic. Philosophy happened to be one of the few programs available to him. He accepted the move without realizing that he was about to discover the discipline that would shape the rest of his intellectual life.
What he encountered at Diliman was not simply a new field of study but an entirely different way of thinking.

For the first time, education ceased to be primarily about mastering information. Instead, it became an exercise in examining assumptions, clarifying meanings, and exploring questions that resisted simple answers. Philosophy demanded a kind of intellectual honesty that Albert found both challenging and exhilarating. It encouraged skepticism without cynicism, inquiry without arrogance, and rigor without rigidity.
More importantly, it felt like home.

Courses in metaphysics, ethics, medieval philosophy, political philosophy, and philosophy of religion exposed him to ideas that would remain with him long after graduation. Under professors such as Agerico de Villa, Isidro Manuel Valero, and Dan Reynald Magat, he found mentors who challenged him to think more deeply and argue more carefully. Discussions about God, power, consciousness, morality, and existence stretched far beyond the boundaries of conventional classroom instruction.
Albert thrived.
The student who had struggled to find his place in earlier programs suddenly flourished. His grades soared, earning him University Scholar recognition twice and College Scholar honors once.

More importantly, he discovered a confidence rooted not in competition but in intellectual engagement. Philosophy rewarded precisely the qualities that came most naturally to him: curiosity, analysis, writing, and the relentless desire to understand how things fit together.

No thinker influenced him more profoundly than Bertrand Russell. Albert was particularly drawn to Russell's concept of logical atomism, the idea that complex realities become understandable only when broken down into their simplest components. The theory resonated deeply because it offered more than a philosophical framework; it provided a practical approach to life. Problems that appeared overwhelming could be understood by examining their constituent parts. Complexity could be reduced to clarity.
The principle would remain with him for decades.

He would later apply it to leadership, administration, legal reasoning, organizational management, and even personal adversity. Whenever confronted by complexity, his instinct was the same: break the problem apart, understand its elements, and rebuild it into something comprehensible. Philosophy also transformed his understanding of truth.

As a younger student, he had regarded truth as something to be discovered and possessed. His philosophical training led him toward a subtler view. Truth itself remained absolute, but human beings often struggled to grasp it completely. The greater challenge, therefore, was not discovering truth but clarifying meaning. Much of human conflict, he came to believe, arose not from disagreement over facts but from misunderstanding what words, ideas, and intentions actually meant.

This insight extended even to matters of faith. Far from weakening his religious convictions, philosophy deepened them by forcing him to confront difficult questions rather than avoid them. There were moments when his intellectual curiosity led him into spirited debates — even with priests delivering homilies on campus. Yet those encounters ultimately strengthened his belief that faith and inquiry need not be adversaries.
By the time Albert graduated from U.P. Diliman, he had undergone a transformation more profound than any change in academic program could explain.

He entered the university expecting to become a physician.
He left as a philosopher.

The distinction was not merely academic. Philosophy had given him a method for approaching life itself — a habit of questioning assumptions, seeking clarity amid confusion, and finding meaning beneath complexity. His graduation as Cum Laude, together with memberships in Phi Kappa Phi and Pi Gamma Mu, recognized his academic achievements. The deeper accomplishment, however, was the discovery of an intellectual compass that would guide him through every chapter that followed.

Ironically, the discipline he entered almost by accident became the foundation upon which much of his future would be built. Medicine, law, education, leadership, and public service would all come later. Yet each would bear the imprint of lessons first learned in the classrooms of U.P. Diliman.
For Albert, the University of the Philippines did more than provide an education.
It taught him how to think.
And in many ways, that proved far more important than teaching him what to think.
Medicine, the Family Dream, and the Road Not Taken
For as long as Albert could remember, medicine seemed less a career choice than an inheritance.

He had grown up in a world shaped by physicians. His father was a respected professor of microbiology and public health. His mother was an accomplished obstetrician-gynecologist, educator, and founding dean of a medical school. Uncles, cousins, mentors, and family friends populated hospitals, clinics, laboratories, and lecture halls.
Conversations at home often revolved around patients, research, medical education, and the evolving challenges of healthcare.
In such an environment, becoming a physician felt almost inevitable.

The dream took root early and remained remarkably persistent. Even as his academic interests expanded to include history, writing, philosophy, and law, medicine retained a powerful hold on his imagination. It represented not only professional prestige but continuity — a way of extending a family tradition that stretched across generations.

By the time he graduated Cum Laude from the University of the Philippines, the path appeared clear. He performed exceptionally well on the National Medical Admission Test and entered the U.P. College of Medicine carrying both the expectations of his family and the aspirations he had nurtured since childhood.
For a brief moment, it seemed that destiny and ambition had finally converged.
Yet the very experience that was supposed to confirm his calling gradually forced him to question it.

The difficulty was not intellectual. Albert possessed the discipline required to survive medical school and the academic record to prove it. What troubled him was something more subtle and, in many ways, more consequential. The subjects that fascinated many of his classmates left him strangely unmoved. While he admired the rigor of the basic sciences and respected the precision they demanded, he found himself increasingly drawn toward broader questions of ethics, institutions, human behavior, and meaning — questions that had first captivated him in philosophy.
The realization was unsettling.

For years, medicine had occupied a central place in his vision of the future. To question that dream felt almost like questioning a part of himself. Yet the further he progressed, the more apparent it became that admiration for a profession is not the same thing as a vocation.
Medicine was teaching him an unexpected lesson: one can respect a path deeply without being destined to follow it.

Compounding his uncertainty were the institutional tensions then affecting the medical school. Academic politics, faculty divisions, and conflicts beyond the control of students created an environment that made an already difficult transition even more challenging. Albert once again found himself confronting circumstances that seemed frustratingly familiar — a reminder that achievement is often shaped not only by talent and effort but also by forces outside one's control.

As the months passed, a difficult truth emerged. The qualities that had allowed him to flourish in philosophy — his fascination with ideas, language, argumentation, ethics, and public affairs — continued to assert themselves. While medicine focused on diagnosis and treatment, his instincts repeatedly gravitated toward analysis, interpretation, and inquiry. He was less interested in memorizing pathways than in understanding systems, less drawn to the mechanics of disease than to the ideas and institutions that shaped human behavior.

Looking back, the signs had been present for years. His success as a writer, his fascination with government and social science, his attraction to philosophy, and his instinctive tendency to question assumptions all pointed toward a different destination.
Recognizing that destination, however, required letting go of a dream.
That was not easy.

Abandoned ambitions often leave behind a sense of unfinished business, particularly when they involve family expectations and childhood aspirations. Yet Albert eventually came to understand that life's purpose is not to fulfill every dream we once imagined for ourselves. It is to discover where our gifts can be most fully expressed.
Medicine remained an important part of that discovery.

Although he would not become a physician, the experience profoundly influenced him. It taught him discipline under pressure, the importance of time management, and the responsibility that accompanies professional training. More importantly, it forced him to distinguish between what he admired and what he was genuinely called to do.

In hindsight, the road not taken proved every bit as important as the one he ultimately followed. For it was within the halls of medical school that Albert first confronted a question that would shape the rest of his life: whether success meant fulfilling the expectations of others or having the courage to follow one's own intellectual and professional instincts.

The answer would eventually lead him toward the law, where another set of challenges — and some of his greatest disappointments — awaited. Yet the decision to leave medicine behind was not a retreat from a dream. It was the beginning of a deeper understanding of himself.
Sometimes the most important discoveries are not about what we can become.
They are about recognizing who we already are.
Law, Failure, and the Long Road to Resilience
If philosophy taught Albert how to think, the law taught him how to endure.

The transition from medicine to law seemed natural enough. Philosophy had sharpened his ability to analyze ideas, challenge assumptions, and construct arguments, while law offered an arena where those skills could be applied to real world disputes and institutions. More importantly, it appealed to a fascination that had been quietly developing since childhood: a curiosity about rules, systems, and the often-complicated relationship between legality and justice.

Before committing himself to the legal profession, Albert briefly stood at a crossroads. He took both the National Medical Admission Test and the U.P. Law Aptitude Examination, leaving open the possibility of either path. While medicine remained the family tradition, the law increasingly captured his imagination. He was drawn to the elegance of legal reasoning and the way a carefully constructed argument could shape outcomes, influence policy, or alter the course of a dispute.

His first stop was the Ateneo School of Law, where he entered a class that would eventually produce prominent figures in government, business, and the legal profession. The environment was intellectually exhilarating and relentlessly competitive. Albert quickly immersed himself in student life, serving as class representative and joining the Fraternal Order of Utopia, whose ranks included many of the country's most distinguished jurists and public servants.

Yet law school demanded a different kind of discipline than anything he had previously encountered. Philosophy rewarded reflection; law rewarded preparation. Every class required mastery of volumes of assigned readings, familiarity with judicial decisions, and the ability to respond instantly under pressure. Success depended not only on understanding concepts but on remembering details, distinguishing precedents, and applying rules with precision.

The adjustment proved difficult. A combination of circumstances — including disruptions caused by flooding, classroom tensions, and the burdens of student leadership — eventually led to his departure after only a semester. For many aspiring lawyers, such an experience might have marked the end of the journey. For Albert, it became the first of several detours.

He enrolled at San Beda College of Law, attracted by its reputation for rigor and discipline. There he encountered an environment every bit as demanding as its reputation suggested. Once again, however, circumstances intervened, and another transfer followed. Eventually, he found a home at the University of Perpetual Help Rizal College of Law, where he completed his Bachelor of Laws degree in 2003.
By then, Albert had already learned a lesson that would recur throughout his life: progress is rarely linear. The path to a goal often bears little resemblance to the path one originally envisioned.
The diploma, however, was only one milestone. Like every law graduate, he now faced the challenge that looms over the profession — the Bar Examination.
For Albert, the Bar would become less an examination than a prolonged test of character.

He failed.
Then he failed again.
And again.
Five times in all.

What made the experience particularly painful was how close success seemed to be. His overall averages were consistently passing, yet each examination contained a single subject in which his score fell below the required threshold. The failures were never overwhelming; they were agonizingly narrow. Each result suggested that the dream remained within reach while simultaneously denying him the opportunity to grasp it.

The emotional toll was profound. Every attempt demanded months of preparation, sacrifice, and hope. Every unfavorable result reopened the same wound. There were periods of depression, moments of self-doubt, and times when continuing seemed irrational. Following one examination, the disappointment became severe enough to require hospitalization.
The experience forced Albert to confront a question that many high achievers eventually face: who are you when the goal you have pursued for years remains unattained?
For someone whose life had been marked by academic distinction, the question was deeply unsettling. Yet it was also transformative.

Throughout those difficult years, he drew strength from several sources. Family provided encouragement. Mentors offered perspective. Faith supplied a measure of peace that success alone could never provide. Among those who influenced him most was Court of Appeals Justice Artemon Luna, who never allowed him to define himself solely by examination results and consistently reminded him that professional setbacks need not diminish personal worth.

Gradually, Albert began to understand that the Bar Examination was teaching him lessons no classroom ever could. Failure stripped away illusions. It demanded humility. It revealed the limits of talent and the necessity of perseverance. Most importantly, it taught him that resilience is not the absence of disappointment but the decision to continue despite it.

Years later, when speaking about leadership, adversity, or personal growth, he often returned to a line from Rocky Balboa that had become something of a personal creed: "Every champion was once a challenger who refused to quit." The quotation resonated because it captured the essence of his experience.
His legal journey was not a story of effortless success but of persistence in the face of repeated disappointment.

Ironically, the profession that never fully opened its doors to him helped shape his character more profoundly than many of his accomplishments. The law sharpened his analytical mind, strengthened his appreciation for institutions, and reinforced his belief that precision matters. But its greatest gift was resilience.

The dream of joining the Philippine Bar remains alive, sustained in part by changes in the rules governing admission to the profession. Whether that dream is eventually realized is almost beside the point. The larger significance lies in what the journey revealed: that character is forged not in moments of triumph but in the willingness to continue after defeat.

In the years that followed, Albert would channel that hard-earned resilience into other arenas — education, administration, civic leadership, and service. The courtroom would not become the primary stage of his life. Yet the lessons he carried from law school and the Bar would accompany him everywhere, shaping not only the leader he became but the mentor he would eventually be to others facing struggles of their own.
The Educator and Institution Builder

Had Albert become a physician, he might have spent his life treating patients. Had he become a lawyer, he might have built a career in courtrooms and corporate boardrooms. Instead, the profession that would ultimately define much of his life was one he never consciously set out to pursue.
He became an educator.
The outcome was, in retrospect, almost inevitable.

Education ran deeply through his family's history. His grandfather had been a school superintendent. His father had spent decades in academia as a professor and administrator. His mother would become one of the country's respected medical educators and the founding dean of a medical school. Long before Albert entered a classroom as a teacher, he had been surrounded by people who believed that knowledge carried an obligation to be shared.

His entry into the University of Perpetual Help System in the late 1990s appeared modest enough. Initially serving as Executive Assistant to his mother, who was then building a new medical school from the ground up, Albert found himself immersed in the practical realities of institution-building. New schools do not emerge fully formed. They require policies, procedures, admissions systems, accreditation standards, and countless administrative decisions that often go unnoticed once an institution is established.
For Albert, however, those details were fascinating.

He enjoyed creating order from complexity. Whether interviewing prospective students, drafting policies, or helping shape academic regulations, he discovered a satisfaction that had little to do with prestige and everything to do with construction. He was helping build something that would outlast him.

The work also revealed an ability that would become increasingly important throughout his career: he understood systems. While some people focus on individual tasks, Albert instinctively looked at how the pieces fit together. He wanted to know not only what worked but why it worked, and how it could work better.
Teaching entered his life almost by accident.

When a faculty member handling History of Medicine departed unexpectedly, Albert was asked to step in. The assign ment seemed temporary, a practical solution to an immediate need. Instead, it became one of the most consequential turns in his professional life.

Standing before a classroom, he discovered that teaching appealed to the same instincts that had drawn him to philosophy years earlier. Both required curiosity. Both required the ability to connect ideas. Most importantly, both required helping others see relationships they had not previously noticed.

His courses in History of Medicine and Bioethics proved particularly well suited to his background. They occupied the intersection of medicine, philosophy, and law — the very disciplines that had shaped his own intellectual journey. Rather than simply delivering information, he encouraged students to grapple with questions that resisted easy answers. Ethical dilemmas, professional responsibilities, and the human dimensions of medical practice often became the heart of his classes.
In the process, Albert came to appreciate something that many educators eventually learn: teaching is not fundamentally about transferring knowledge. It is about shaping perspective.
Students rarely remember every lecture. They seldom retain every fact. What often remains are ways of thinking, habits of inquiry, and lessons that reveal their significance years later.
That realization gradually transformed his understanding of success.

As a student, he had measured achievement through grades, rankings, and honors. As an educator, he began measuring it differently. Success was no longer defined by personal accomplishment but by the accomplishments of others. A former student succeeding in medicine, education, or public service often felt more rewarding than any individual recognition he received himself.

Meanwhile, his responsibilities within the university continued to expand. Roles as College Secretary and later University Registrar placed him at the center of academic administration. To many outsiders, registrars appear to be custodians of records and transcripts.

Albert understood the position differently. The Registrar's Office served as the institutional memory of a university, safeguarding academic integrity while ensuring that students, faculty, and administrators could function effectively within a coherent system.
The challenge suited him.

His legal training sharpened his attention to detail. His administrative experience strengthened his ability to manage competing interests. His philosophical background encouraged him to search for underlying principles rather than merely address immediate problems.

Under his watch, processes became more efficient, records more accessible, and services more responsive. Yet what mattered most to him was not efficiency for its own sake. It was the conviction that institutions exist to serve people. Systems should make lives easier, not more complicated. Policies should facilitate learning, not obstruct it.

Over time, Albert realized that his greatest contributions often occurred far from public attention. Students rarely noticed the countless administrative decisions that made their education possible. Graduates seldom reflected on the systems that ensured their records were accurate and accessible. Yet these invisible structures formed the foundation upon which educational institutions rested.
Perhaps that is why he increasingly viewed himself not merely as a teacher or administrator but as a builder.

A builder of systems.
A builder of opportunities.
A builder of institutions.
Most importantly, a builder of people.

For all the degrees he earned and the positions he held, the most enduring legacy of his educational career would not be found in titles or accomplishments. It would be found in the thousands of students whose lives intersected with his own and who, in ways both large and small, carried forward the lessons of a man who never stopped believing that education remains the most powerful investment one generation can make in the next.
Service, Leadership, and the Art of Building People
For much of his early life, Albert's achievements were largely individual.

Success meant earning the highest grade, winning a competition, completing a degree, or overcoming a personal challenge. Whether in the classroom, law school, or graduate studies, the battles were usually his alone. Preparation, discipline, and perseverance determined the outcome, and the rewards were measured accordingly.
Over time, however, he began to realize that the most meaningful accomplishments in life rarely belong to a single person.

Schools are built collectively. Organizations thrive collectively. Communities improve collectively. Even the most accomplished individuals are, in many ways, the products of mentors, colleagues, institutions, and opportunities that helped shape them. The realization would gradually transform his understanding of leadership.
Rotary provided the first significant lesson.

When Albert joined the Rotary Club of Manila in 2005, he was drawn initially by its reputation. As the first Rotary club in Asia, its membership included many of the country's most distinguished businessmen, professionals, and public servants. To a newcomer, the organization seemed an impressive gathering of accomplished individuals.
What took longer to appreciate was that Rotary's true identity had little to do with status and everything to do with service. \

The more involved he became, the more he recognized that the organization's greatest strength lay not in the prominence of its members but in their willingness to place their talents in service of causes larger than themselves. Projects such as the Pasig River Floating Barrier initiative demonstrated how collective action could achieve results that no individual, regardless of influence or resources, could accomplish alone.

For a man who had spent much of his life pursuing personal excellence, the experience was quietly transformative. Rotary challenged him to think beyond achievement and toward impact. It introduced him to a form of leadership measured not by recognition but by contribution.
If Rotary taught him the value of service, JCI taught him the mechanics of leadership.

By the time Albert joined JCI Makati in 2011, he was already an experienced educator and administrator. Yet JCI offered something different. It functioned less as a civic organization than as a laboratory where leadership could be practiced, tested, and refined. Projects became classrooms. Volunteers became teammates. Challenges became opportunities for growth.

His first initiative, a dental mission called Ngiting May Ningning, was modest compared to the larger programs he would later encounter. Yet it reinforced an insight that remained with him for years: leadership is not conferred by title; it emerges through action.

As he became more active within the organization, Albert found himself increasingly fascinated by a question that had followed him throughout his life: what separates effective leaders from ineffective ones? The answer, he concluded, had surprisingly little to do with authority. The strongest leaders he encountered were not necessarily the most charismatic, the most visible, or even the most accomplished. They were the ones who developed other people.

The lesson became particularly clear through projects such as Give Jobs on Christmas Day, a large-scale employment initiative that demonstrated the multiplier effect of leadership. Its success did not depend on a single individual. It depended on teams, partnerships, and the ability to align many people behind a common purpose. The project reinforced Albert's growing conviction that leadership is fundamentally an act of empowerment.

This belief would eventually shape his approach to nearly every organization he served. Whether mentoring students, managing academic systems, drafting policies, or leading civic initiatives, he increasingly viewed leadership not as the exercise of authority but as the cultivation of potential.

The shift represented a significant departure from the competitive mindset of his youth. As a student, he had often measured success by how well he performed relative to others. As a leader, he came to judge success by how well others performed because of him.
That distinction may be the most important leadership lesson he learned.

The educator in him naturally gravitated toward developing people. The administrator sought to build systems that outlasted individuals. The Rotarian and Jaycee understood that organizations endure only when new leaders are continually prepared to take their place.

In time, Albert came to see leadership as a form of stewardship. Positions were temporary. Titles eventually passed to others. What remained were the institutions strengthened, the opportunities created, and the people encouraged to exceed their own expectations.

Looking back, he often reflects that the most satisfying moments of his career did not involve awards, appointments, or public recognition. They involved seeing former students become successful professionals, watching young leaders mature into capable executives, and witnessing organizations continue to flourish long after his direct involvement had ended.
Those moments confirmed a belief that had slowly emerged through decades of teaching, administration, service, and leadership.

Achievement is important.
Contribution is more important.
And the highest form of contribution is helping others discover what they are capable of becoming.
The Lifelong Student

One of the more revealing characteristics of Albert is that, despite spending much of his professional life as a teacher, administrator, and mentor, he has never stopped thinking of himself as a student.

For many people, education is a stage of life. It begins in childhood, culminates in a diploma, and eventually yields to the demands of career and family. Albert never saw it that way. Having grown up in a household where learning was treated almost as a family vocation, he came to regard education not as a destination but as a continuing process of discovery.

This instinct had followed him since his days at the University of the Philippines. What attracted him to Philosophy was not simply the subject matter but the realization that every answer inevitably led to another question. The discipline taught him that certainty is often overrated and that intellectual growth depends less on possessing answers than on maintaining curiosity. Long after he left U.P., that habit of inquiry remained intact.

It helps explain why, after earning degrees in philosophy and law and establishing himself in educational administration, Albert continued returning to the classroom — not as a lecturer this time, but as a student. The impulse was never driven solely by credentials or career advancement.
Rather, it reflected a genuine fascination with ideas and an enduring belief that there was always more to learn.

That belief eventually led him back to philosophy through doctoral studies in Metaphysics. The choice surprised some of his colleagues, but it made perfect sense to those who knew him well. Metaphysics dealt with questions that had captivated him since his undergraduate years: the nature of reality, the relationship between the material and spiritual worlds, and the mysteries of human existence that resist easy explanation. His dissertation, Soulmates: An Omnipresent Perspective, explored one such question, examining whether certain human relationships transcend a single lifetime and form part of a larger spiritual continuum. Whatever one may think of the conclusion, the project reflected a mind still drawn to questions that could not be answered by formulas, statutes, or laboratory tests.

The same intellectual restlessness later carried him halfway around the world — at least academically — to Boston University. When he learned of its Executive Master of Laws program in International Business Law, he saw an opportunity not merely to earn another degree but to experience a different legal tradition. Supported by his grand aunt, Dean Cristina Parel, whose faith in education had influenced him since childhood, Albert immersed himself in a curriculum that exposed him to international transactions, global commerce, arbitration, and corporate governance.

The experience broadened his perspective. American legal education differed markedly from the system he had known in the Philippines. It emphasized concepts as much as codal provisions, practical application as much as doctrine. More importantly, it reinforced a lesson he had been learning throughout his life: education's greatest gift is not information but perspective. Facts can be memorized. Perspectives reshape the way one sees the world.

Looking back, Albert often reflects that many of the most important lessons of his life came from places no syllabus could anticipate. They emerged from failures that forced self examination, mentors who offered guidance at critical moments, organizations that tested his leadership, and experiences that challenged long-held assumptions. The classroom provided foundations, but life supplied the deeper education.

Perhaps this is why he remains skeptical of the notion that learning ever truly ends. Degrees may signify completion of a program, but they do not signify completion of growth. The world changes too rapidly, human knowledge expands too quickly, and life's questions remain too complex for anyone to claim final mastery.

For Albert, curiosity has become a form of humility. It is an acknowledgment that no matter how much one has accomplished, there is always another idea to explore, another perspective to consider, another lesson waiting to be learned. It is also the thread that connects the many chapters of his life — from philosophy to medicine, from law to education, from leadership to service.

After all, beneath the professor, administrator, entrepreneur, Rotarian, and Jaycee remains the same young man who once discovered in the halls of U.P. that the most rewarding questions are often the ones that cannot be answered completely.
And in that sense, Albert's greatest degree may be the one he continues to pursue every day: the education of a lifetime.
The Legacy of Becoming

As Albert looks back on the path he has traveled, he does not see a life that unfolded according to a master plan. The story is far messier than that. It is filled with ambitions that were redirected, opportunities that slipped away, unexpected turns that altered the course of events, and setbacks that, at the time, felt impossible to understand.

Yet with the benefit of hindsight, a pattern begins to emerge. The disappointments that once appeared to be dead ends often became gateways to something else. The roads not taken proved just as formative as the ones he ultimately followed.

The aspiring physician discovered that his gifts lay beyond medicine. The law graduate who never crossed the final threshold of the Bar found himself shaping institutions, mentoring students, and influencing lives in ways no courtroom could have anticipated. The young scholar who once measured success through rankings and medals gradually came to understand that achievement, while gratifying, is ultimately transient. What endures is the impact one has on other people.

This realization transformed his understanding of leadership. In his younger years, leadership appeared inseparable from accomplishment. Over time, however, he came to see that the most effective leaders are rarely those who accumulate the greatest number of titles. They are the individuals who leave behind stronger organizations, more capable successors, and opportunities that outlive their own tenure. Whether as an educator, administrator, Rotarian, Jaycee, or entrepreneur, Albert increasingly judged success not by personal recognition but by the extent to which others were empowered to flourish.

It is perhaps no coincidence that this philosophy echoes the values that shaped him from the beginning. The examples set by his parents, grandparents, mentors, and teachers taught him that education is more than the acquisition of knowledge. It is the cultivation of character. It is the preparation of one generation to serve the next. In many ways, Albert's life can be understood as a continuation of that inheritance. The institutions changed, the professions evolved, and the challenges differed, but the underlying commitment remained remarkably constant: to learn, to serve, and to leave things better than he found them.

His unfinished dream of becoming a member of the Philippine Bar remains part of that story. Yet whether or not that goal is ultimately realized seems less important than it once did. The dream endures because it reflects something essential about his character. Albert has never measured life solely by outcomes. He has measured it by effort, perseverance, and the willingness to continue despite disappointment. The journey itself has become as meaningful as the destination.

When asked what legacy he hopes to leave behind, he answers with characteristic humility: that he gave more than his best despite the constraints he encountered along the way. It is an answer that captures the essence of his life. For beneath the degrees, awards, leadership positions, and professional accomplishments stands a man who repeatedly chose perseverance over surrender, service over self-interest, and growth over complacency.

Perhaps that is why one phrase continues to resonate throughout his story: Trust the process. What began as a lesson in leadership gradually evolved into a philosophy of life. It reflects the conviction that progress is often invisible while it is occurring, that setbacks can become preparation, and that meaning frequently reveals itself only in retrospect. The phrase acknowledges life's uncertainties without surrendering to them, insisting instead that patience, faith, and perseverance possess a quiet power of their own.

In the end, Albert Singson Alday's story is not simply the story of a scholar, educator, administrator, entrepreneur, Rotarian, or Jaycee. It is the story of a man who never stopped learning, never stopped striving, and never stopped believing that each challenge carried within it the possibility of growth. His legacy lies not in any single accomplishment but in the example of a life lived with curiosity, resilience, and purpose — a life defined not by arrival, but by the continual act of becoming.

Avelino Avantura Jr. The Breaking of a New RCM Dawn  IN the northern hemisphere from where I write to you, dear RCMers, this time of the year provides impressive sunrises quite early in the day. To the early risers pandiculating from slumber, and even to those who are headed home after partying throughout the night, the breaking of dawn comes with serenity and suffused light, the peace and quiet punctuated only by the chirping of the morning birds. Pregnant with possibilities, the new day leisurely unfolds, the sun taking its time before fully unveiling itself above the horizon, and the world seemingly pauses a moment in contemplation of the promise of a fresh start, a clean slate, a new beginning. A new day unfolds for the Rotary Club of Manila and the world of Rotary as the year of creating a lasting impact begins. In a time-honored ritual of passage, President Raoul C. Creencia, confident that the Club's accomplishments in his year in office have brought it on a higher plane, hands the bell and the gavel to his successor, President Reginald T. Yu, whose task it shall be to bring the first Rotary Club in Asia to even greater heights. This new day is for both of them to cherish, albeit with eyes cast on opposite directions, as one looks back to a year gilt with the gold of victory, and the other looks forward in anticipation of what is possible. This unfolding day also belongs to each Manila Rotarian as another chapter is written in the Club's history. For 107 years, the Club has built a legacy of leadership, service, and vocational excellence, and this legacy is bequeathed year after year to its new custodians, none other than the Board of Directors and Executive Officers, the existing membership, and the new inductees into the Club. Together we will write this new chapter, and it is up to all of us if it will be a stirring panegyric or an evanescent murmur. I have every confidence that it will be the former as our President leads us on a path Towards a Unified Rotary Nation. resident Reggie's ascent to the highest position the Club has in its power to bestow to any member has left a gaping hole in the editorial board of our beloved Balita. Because nature abhors a vacuum, it sucked the most lightweight particle available to fill that hole. And so the unenviable task of following in President Reggie's footsteps as Editor-in-Chief fell on this lap. It was accepted with great humility and the recognition that, first, it takes a village to publish a club bulletin, and second, we have been given the sacred trust of preserving the institutional memory of the Club through the written word. It is a trust that I will sedulously honor and serve every week. "Morning has broken," sang Cat Stevens, to which Nina Simone responds, "I'm feeling good." Feel good, my dear Brothers in RCM; the sun is up and we are off to a great start. Nigerian takes office as president of Rotary International  EVANSTON, Ill., USA (29 June 2026) — Olayinka Hakeem Babalola, a member of the Rotary Club of Trans Amadi, Nigeria, will take office as president of Rotary International on 1 July 2026, becoming the second African to lead the global membership organization. During his one-year term, Babalola will focus on strengthening Rotary’s contribution to peacebuilding and supporting sustainable, community- led solutions that address local and global challenges and improve lives. “Rotary gives people the opportunity not only to make a difference in their communities, but also to grow through meaningful relationships, collaboration, and a deeper appreciation of different perspectives,” said Babalola. “At a time when many societies face division and uncertainty, I believe Rotary has an important role to play in building understanding, advancing peace, and creating opportunities for communities to thrive. As president, I look forward to highlighting and strengthening that impact around the world.” Babalola brings to the role decades of experience advancing community development, peacebuilding, and public health initiatives across Africa. He has been actively involved with Rotary’s Peace Center at Makerere University in Uganda – the organization’s first on the continent. As head of Rotary’s 45,000 clubs worldwide, Babalola will lead Rotary’s top priority of ending polio. Together with its Global Polio Eradication Initiative partners, Rotary has reduced polio cases by 99.9 percent and contributed more than US$3 billion and countless volunteer hours to protect over 3 billion children from this paralyzing disease. He has also been deeply engaged in Rotary’s polio eradication efforts, serving on the End Polio Now Countdown to History Campaign Committee and advising the Nigeria National PolioPlus Committee. Rotary members throughout the world develop and implement sustainable, community-driven projects that fight disease, promote peace, provide clean water, support education, save mothers and children, grow local economies and protect the environment. More than US$5.5 billion has been awarded through The Rotary Foundation – Rotary’s charitable arm that helps clubs work together to perform meaningful, impactful service – to support these initiatives over the last 100 years. About Olayinka Hakeem Babalola Babalola holds a degree in engineering and spent more than 30 years in the oil and gas sector, including senior leadership roles at Shell PLC. He founded the Riviera Technical Services Ltd., an oil and gas infrastructure delivery firm, as well as Lead and Change Consulting, an executive coaching and organizational performance consultancy. Babalola is a member of the Nigerian Society of Engineers, the Institute of Safety Professionals, and the Association of Change Management Practitioners. He also belongs to the Jericho Business Club, a civic organization in Ibadan that contributes to national policy dialogue. Babalola became involved with Rotary in 1984 through Rotaract — Rotary’s program for young professionals and students — and joined the Rotary Club of Trans Amadi in 1994. He has since held a number of leadership roles within the organization and currently serves as a trustee of ShelterBox UK, Rotary’s official project partner for disaster relief. He and his wife, Preba, support The Rotary Foundation through a named endowment and are members of the Arch Klumph Society, which recognizes Rotary’s highest level of philanthropic giving. His Rotary honors include the Africa Centennial Heroes Award, the Service Above Self Award, the Regional Service Award for a Polio-Free World, and The Rotary Foundation Citation for Meritorious Service. articles.title: The Breaking of a New RCM Dawn

body.text: IN the northern hemisphere from where I write to you, dear RCMers, this time of the year provides impressive sunrises quite early in the day. To the early risers pandiculating from slumber, and even to those who are headed home after partying throughout the night, the breaking of dawn comes with serenity and suffused light, the peace and quiet punctuated only by the chirping of the morning birds.

Pregnant with possibilities, the new day leisurely unfolds, the sun taking its time before fully unveiling itself above the horizon, and the world seemingly pauses a moment in contemplation of the promise of a fresh start, a clean slate, a new beginning.
A new day unfolds for the Rotary Club of Manila and the world of Rotary as the year of creating a lasting impact begins.

In a time-honored ritual of passage, President Raoul C. Creencia, confident that the Club's accomplishments in his year in office have brought it on a higher plane, hands the bell and the gavel to his successor, President Reginald T. Yu, whose task it shall be to bring the first Rotary Club in Asia to even greater heights. This new day is for both of them to cherish, albeit with eyes cast on opposite directions, as one looks back to a year gilt with the gold of victory, and the other looks forward in anticipation of what is possible.

This unfolding day also belongs to each Manila Rotarian as another chapter is written in the Club's history. For 107 years, the Club has built a legacy of leadership, service, and vocational excellence, and this legacy is bequeathed year after year to its new custodians, none other than the Board of Directors and Executive Officers, the existing membership, and the new inductees into the Club. Together we will write this new chapter, and it is up to all of us if it will be a stirring panegyric or an evanescent murmur. I have every confidence that it will be the former as our President leads us on a path Towards a Unified Rotary Nation.

resident Reggie's ascent to the highest position the Club has in its power to bestow to any member has left a gaping hole in the editorial board of our beloved Balita. Because nature abhors a vacuum, it sucked the most lightweight particle available to fill that hole. And so the unenviable task of following in President Reggie's footsteps as Editor-in-Chief fell on this lap. It was accepted with great humility and the recognition that, first, it takes a village to publish a club bulletin, and second, we have been given the sacred trust of preserving the institutional memory of the Club through the written word. It is a trust that I will sedulously honor and serve every week.
"Morning has broken," sang Cat Stevens, to which Nina Simone responds, "I'm feeling good."
Feel good, my dear Brothers in RCM; the sun is up and we are off to a great start.
