articles.title: Nigerian takes office as president of Rotary International
articles.dek: Second African to lead the global membership organization will focus on peacebuilding and lasting community impact

body.text: EVANSTON, Ill., USA (29 June 2026) — Olayinka Hakeem Babalola, a member of the Rotary Club of Trans Amadi, Nigeria, will take office as president of Rotary International on 1 July 2026, becoming the second African to lead the global membership organization.

During his one-year term, Babalola will focus on strengthening Rotary’s contribution to peacebuilding and supporting sustainable, community- led solutions that address local and global challenges and improve lives.

“Rotary gives people the opportunity not only to make a difference in their communities, but also to grow through meaningful relationships, collaboration, and a deeper appreciation of different perspectives,” said Babalola. “At a time when many societies face division and uncertainty, I believe Rotary has an important role to play in building understanding, advancing peace, and creating opportunities for communities to thrive. As president, I look forward to highlighting and strengthening that impact around the world.”

Babalola brings to the role decades of experience advancing community development, peacebuilding, and public health initiatives across Africa. He has been actively involved with Rotary’s Peace Center at Makerere University in Uganda – the organization’s first on the continent.

As head of Rotary’s 45,000 clubs worldwide, Babalola will lead Rotary’s top priority of ending polio. Together with its Global Polio Eradication Initiative partners, Rotary has reduced polio cases by 99.9 percent and contributed more than US$3 billion and countless volunteer hours to protect over 3 billion children from this paralyzing disease. He has also been deeply engaged in Rotary’s polio eradication efforts, serving on the End Polio Now Countdown to History Campaign Committee and advising the Nigeria National PolioPlus Committee.

Rotary members throughout the world develop and implement sustainable, community-driven projects that fight disease, promote peace, provide clean water, support education, save mothers and children, grow local economies and protect the environment. More than US$5.5 billion has been awarded through The Rotary Foundation – Rotary’s charitable arm that helps clubs work together to perform meaningful, impactful service – to support these initiatives over the last 100 years.
About Olayinka Hakeem Babalola

Babalola holds a degree in engineering and spent more than 30 years in the oil and gas sector, including senior leadership roles at Shell PLC. He founded the Riviera Technical Services Ltd., an oil and gas infrastructure delivery firm, as well as Lead and Change Consulting, an executive coaching and organizational performance consultancy.

Babalola is a member of the Nigerian Society of Engineers, the Institute of Safety Professionals, and the Association of Change Management Practitioners. He also belongs to the Jericho Business Club, a civic organization in Ibadan that contributes to national policy dialogue. Babalola became involved with Rotary in 1984 through Rotaract — Rotary’s program for young professionals and students — and joined the Rotary Club of Trans Amadi in 1994. He has since held a number of leadership roles within the organization and currently serves as a trustee of ShelterBox UK, Rotary’s official project partner for disaster relief.

He and his wife, Preba, support The Rotary Foundation through a named endowment and are members of the Arch Klumph Society, which recognizes Rotary’s highest level of philanthropic giving. His Rotary honors include the Africa Centennial Heroes Award, the Service Above Self Award, the Regional Service Award for a Polio-Free World, and The Rotary Foundation Citation for Meritorious Service.

Healthy children build healthy communities, and healthy communities build a brighter future for all. Editorial: Disruption, Anyone?  DISRUPTION as a business strategy was first propounded by Professor Clayton Christensen of Harvard Business School. He taught disruptive innovation as a powerful tool for small companies with fewer resources to challenge established or incumbent businesses by addressing an underserved need. In his theory, Christensen identified three approaches to business innovation, namely: sustaining innovation which happens when an established company creates improved versions of its products to sell for a higher profit; low-end disruption, in which a company targets a segment on an established company’s market base and forces the latter to focus on its upmarket clientele; and new-market disruption, in which a company claims a new segment of an existing market by providing a solution to a need that was previously unfulfilled, unsatisfactorily fulfilled, or fulfilled at great cost. The third approach is the most disruptive. As the upstart improves and expands its range of products or services, the incumbent’s products or services become obsolete. Think of what Netflix, Spotify, and Zoom have done in their respective niches, while locally we can name Angkas, BYD, and Lalamove as some of those who are pursuing disruptive innovation in their fields. As often happens, strategies born in the boardroom find their way into the political sphere - the market being the voter base and the public persona or campaign platform of a politico as the product being sold. In the Philippines where there are no real distinguishable identifiers between and among political parties, disruption is perhaps the fastest and most effective way an upstart can challenge long-entrenched incumbents. By targeting underserved segments, whether the disservice is real or perceived, a “new- market”politico’s chances of garnering votes are increased. Hence one sees campaign slogans, jingles, and speeches targeting students, retirees, the poor, women, LBGTQI+, PWD’s, commuters, laborers, and the great unwashed, and promising them everything that they need that the incumbent apparently ignores or sweeps under a rug, if the challenger is to be believed. It is always interesting to watch when a disruptive challenger succeeds, takes office, and finds his expectations rudely meeting political reality. In the crucible of the plenary debates, hallway negotiations, and committee hearings for those in the legislative, or in budget deliberations, resource allocation, and filling administrative positions for those in the executive, the disruptor’s mettle is tested and his or her brand is either burnished or blemished. Disruption is inherently based on fostering conflict: Brand X is better than Brand Y, Candidate A is more responsive than Candidate B. This is why, like Marmite, disruptors are an acquired taste. Preferring the status quo to remain undisturbed, many may look on the disruptor as the fly in an otherwise sanitized and reliably familiar ointment. The sense of conflict enlarges the higher the position sought becomes or the more entrenched the incumbent is. How the disruptor absorbs, addresses and thrives in this high-pressure environment defines how he or she changes the system or is changed by the system. It is thus not entirely unusual to see disruptors becoming pariah in the company of peers, or being forced to compromise to the point of becoming more “trapo” than the incumbent they unseated. One thing is certain about disruptive innovation in business: only those companies that actually deliver for the underserved segment survives and thrives, while the rest wither and fall by the wayside. This becomes less certain in politics, especially when disruptors can themselves easily turn into traditional politicians, or if the disruptor is actually part of an entrenched clan. The litmus test is whether the needs of the underserved have been met or they are left searching for another promising upstart willing to joust against the constantly turning political windmills. Mayhaps Rotarians should paraphrase our Four-Way Test when meeting a political disruptor and ask: Is he true? Is he fair to all concerned? Does his disruption result to good governance and better public services? Is his disruption beneficial to the public he proposes to serve? Every child we immunize is another life protected, another family given peace of mind, and another step toward a healthier community. These are the moments that remind us why Rotary serves — not only to meet today's needs, but to invest in tomorrow's generation.
Healthy children build healthy communities, and healthy communities build a brighter future for all.

DISRUPTION as a business strategy was first propounded by Professor Clayton Christensen of Harvard Business School. He taught disruptive innovation as a powerful tool for small companies with fewer resources to challenge established or incumbent businesses by addressing an underserved need.

In his theory, Christensen identified three approaches to business innovation, namely: sustaining innovation which happens when an established company creates improved versions of its products to sell for a higher profit; low-end disruption, in which a company targets a segment on an established company’s market base and forces the latter to focus on its upmarket clientele; and new-market disruption, in which a company claims a new segment of an existing market by providing a solution to a need that was previously unfulfilled, unsatisfactorily fulfilled, or fulfilled at great cost.

The third approach is the most disruptive. As the upstart improves and expands its range of products or services, the incumbent’s products or services become obsolete. Think of what Netflix, Spotify, and Zoom have done in their respective niches, while locally we can name Angkas, BYD, and Lalamove as some of those who are pursuing disruptive innovation in their fields.

As often happens, strategies born in the boardroom find their way into the political sphere - the market being the voter base and the public persona or campaign platform of a politico as the product being sold. In the Philippines where there are no real distinguishable identifiers between and among political parties, disruption is perhaps the fastest and most effective way an upstart can challenge long-entrenched incumbents. By targeting underserved segments, whether the disservice is real or perceived, a “new- market”politico’s chances of garnering votes are increased. Hence one sees campaign slogans, jingles, and speeches targeting students, retirees, the poor, women, LBGTQI+, PWD’s, commuters, laborers, and the great unwashed, and promising them everything that they need that the incumbent apparently ignores or sweeps under a rug, if the challenger is to be believed.

It is always interesting to watch when a disruptive challenger succeeds, takes office, and finds his expectations rudely meeting political reality. In the crucible of the plenary debates, hallway negotiations, and committee hearings for those in the legislative, or in budget deliberations, resource allocation, and filling administrative positions for those in the executive, the disruptor’s mettle is tested and his or her brand is either burnished or blemished.

Disruption is inherently based on fostering conflict: Brand X is better than Brand Y, Candidate A is more responsive than Candidate B. This is why, like Marmite, disruptors are an acquired taste. Preferring the status quo to remain undisturbed, many may look on the disruptor as the fly in an otherwise sanitized and reliably familiar ointment.

The sense of conflict enlarges the higher the position sought becomes or the more entrenched the incumbent is. How the disruptor absorbs, addresses and thrives in this high-pressure environment defines how he or she changes the system or is changed by the system. It is thus not entirely unusual to see disruptors becoming pariah in the company of peers, or being forced to compromise to the point of becoming more “trapo” than the incumbent they unseated.

One thing is certain about disruptive innovation in business: only those companies that actually deliver for the underserved segment survives and thrives, while the rest wither and fall by the wayside. This becomes less certain in politics, especially when disruptors can themselves easily turn into traditional politicians, or if the disruptor is actually part of an entrenched clan. The litmus test is whether the needs of the underserved have been met or they are left searching for another promising upstart willing to joust against the constantly turning political windmills.

Mayhaps Rotarians should paraphrase our Four-Way Test when meeting a political disruptor and ask: Is he true? Is he fair to all concerned? Does his disruption result to good governance and better public services? Is his disruption beneficial to the public he proposes to serve?

articles.title: Rotary Club of Manila and PAFJO-TMJ Sign Memorandum of Understanding

body.text: The Rotary Club of Manila, as Funding Partner, and the Philippine Association of Functional Jaw Orthopedics-TMJ- Orofacial Pain, Inc., as Executory Partner, signed a Memorandum of Understanding last July 5, 2026 at the Lanson Place, Mall of Asia, Pasay City.

The MOU formalized the Handog Makeover para sa Maayos na Kabuhayan Program, a community service initiative that provides comprehensive dental rehabilitation to deserving beneficiaries to improve their oral health, confidence, employability, and quality of life. This happened during the 25th Anniversary and 25th Handover and Induction Ceremonies of the Philippine Association of Functional Jaw Orthopedics-TMJ-Orofacial Pain, Inc. Signing on behalf of the club were President Reggie Yu and DDPIC/Club Secretary Albert S. Alday in the presence of DGN Hermie Esguerra.

guest: Dr. Raymund E. Narag, Guest of Honor and Speaker
search_text: Guest of Honor & Speaker: Dr. Raymund E. Narag: From Prison Cell to Prison Reformer  THERE are scholars who study the criminal justice system. There are policymakers who attempt to improve it. And then there are those whose understanding was shaped not merely by books or classrooms, but by life itself. Dr. Raymund E. Narag belongs to this extraordinary and exceedingly rare group. Today, he is internationally recognized as one of the foremost Filipino authorities on corrections, prison reform, parole and probation, criminal justice administration, and human- rights-based correctional management. Governments, international organizations, universities, and justice institutions around the world seek his expertise. Yet his remarkable journey toward becoming one of the country's leading criminologists began in perhaps the least likely of places: a prison cell. As a young University of the Philippines student, Dr. Narag's life changed dramatically when he was wrongfully implicated in a fraternity-related killing in 1994. Although he was eventually acquitted, he spent seven years in detention awaiting justice. Those years exposed him to the harsh realities of Philippine incarceration, including overcrowded cells, inhumane living conditions, prolonged court delays, disease, violence, and the daily struggle for dignity among persons deprived of liberty. It was an experience that forever altered the course of his life. Most people would have emerged from such an ordeal consumed by bitterness. Dr. Narag emerged with purpose. Upon regaining his freedom, he resolved to devote his life to transforming the very system that had once failed him. Those seven years behind bars became not a prison for his future, but the foundation upon which he built an extraordinary career dedicated to justice. His life stands as a remarkable testament to resilience, demonstrating how profound personal adversity can be transformed into a lifelong mission of public service. His academic journey reflects that same determination. After graduating cum laude from the University of the Philippines Diliman, he pursued graduate studies at Michigan State University, earning both his Master's and Doctor of Philosophy in Criminal Justice as a Fulbright Scholar. Today, he serves as Graduate Program Director and Associate Professor at the School of Justice and Public Safety of Southern Illinois University Carbondale, where he teaches criminology, corrections, juvenile justice, comparative criminal justice, criminological theory, and research methods. Beyond the classroom, he mentors graduate students from around the world who will one day shape justice systems in their own countries. Yet to describe Dr. Narag simply as an academic would be to tell only half of his story. Unlike many scholars, he never forgot what it felt like to stand on the other side of the justice system. His research has consistently focused on the most urgent and complex issues confronting criminal justice, not because they are academically fashionable, but because he has personally witnessed their human consequences. His work spans prison overcrowding, prolonged pretrial detention, inmate classification, prison governance, juvenile justice, restorative justice, parole and probation, violent extremist offender management, and the development of correctional systems that protect public safety while preserving human dignity. His scholarship has produced landmark books, including Freedom and Death Inside the City Jail, Behind Bars at the New Bilibid Prison: A Call for Integrated Reforms, and Decongesting Philippine Jails. These works have become essential references for policymakers, correctional administrators, and scholars seeking evidence-based approaches to prison reform. His research has likewise appeared in leading international journals and books published by some of the world's most respected academic presses, firmly establishing his reputation as one of the leading voices in comparative criminology and corrections. Yet his research rarely ends with publication. Instead, it becomes policy. Over the years, Dr. Narag has served as consultant and adviser to the Philippine Supreme Court, the Department of Justice, the Bureau of Corrections, the Philippine Commission on Human Rights, the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, the United Nations Development Programme, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the Asian Development Bank, and numerous other institutions committed to strengthening justice systems around the world. His studies have directly influenced initiatives on jail decongestion, modernization of the parole and probation system, court case management, prison health, inmate risk assessment, human-rights-based prison administration, and correctional rehabilitation. Through international research grants and collaborative reform projects, he has translated rigorous scholarship into practical solutions that have improved the administration of justice for thousands of Filipinos. His influence extends even further. Dr. Narag has become one of the country's foremost educators of criminal justice practitioners. Over the years, he has personally trained thousands of jail wardens, correctional officers, parole and probation officers, judges, prosecutors, lawyers, volunteers, and policymakers through seminars, workshops, and capacity-building programs conducted throughout the Philippines. His work has helped professionalize correctional management while promoting evidence- based policies grounded in accountability, rehabilitation, and respect for human rights. His contributions have earned him numerous honors and distinctions, including the Judge William Holmes Cook Fellowship, the Living Hero Award from the J. Amado Araneta Foundation, the Outstanding Citizen of Quezon City Award, the Dangal ng Lahing Cagayano Award, and several academic and leadership recognitions from Michigan State University and other institutions. Yet awards alone cannot capture the significance of his life's work. What truly distinguishes Dr. Narag is the unique perspective from which he speaks. He understands incarceration not merely as a subject of academic inquiry but as a lived experience. He appreciates the importance of law enforcement, public safety, and accountability, while also recognizing the devastating human cost of delayed justice, overcrowded detention facilities, and ineffective correctional systems. Few experts possess both the empirical rigor of a world-class scholar and the moral authority of someone who has personally endured the very system he now strives to improve. His journey reminds us that justice is not measured solely by convictions or punishments. It is measured by how faithfully a society upholds the rule of law, protects the innocent, treats the accused fairly, rehabilitates offenders, and preserves the dignity of every human person. In an era when conversations about crime are often dominated by emotion, politics, or ideology, Dr. Raymund E. Narag offers something increasingly rare: a voice grounded in lived experience, rigorous scholarship, empirical evidence, and unwavering compassion. His life is more than an inspiring story of personal redemption. It is a powerful reminder that our deepest wounds can become our greatest calling, and that even from the confines of a prison cell can emerge a visionary whose work would one day help reshape the future of criminal justice in the Philippines and beyond. “Congress-Meow" Headlines RCM's First Weekly Membership Meeting  THE First Weekly Membership Meeting of the Rotary Club of Manila for Rotary Year 2026–2027 marked far more than the beginning of another Rotary calendar. It represented the first opportunity for Club President Reginald Yu to translate his vision of "Rotary T.U.R.N. — Toward a Unified Rotary Nation" into meaningful action. Coming just one week after the Club's historic 107th Anniversary and Induction Ceremonies, the meeting drew an encouraging turnout of more than one hundred Rotarians and guests. The strong attendance reflected the members' enthusiasm to reconnect, engage in meaningful dialogue, and actively participate in the life of the world's first Rotary club in Asia. The afternoon commenced with the traditions that have distinguished the Rotary Club of Manila for more than a century — the invocation, the singing of the Philippine National Anthem, the Club Hymn, the recitation of the Four- Way Test, and the recognition of visiting Rotarians and guests. While officers may change from year to year, these enduring traditions continue to remind members that Rotary's values remain constant. One of the most heartwarming portions of the meeting was the recognition of the Club's birthday celebrants, followed by the President's Time, during which President Reggie welcomed everyone to a new Rotary year and expressed his gratitude for the overwhelming support extended during the historic induction ceremonies. He then invited Induction Chairman Past District Governor Alexander Cureg to present a brief report on the successful culmination of the 107th Anniversary and Induction Ceremonies. The report was complemented by a professionally produced audio-visual presentation that allowed members to relive many of the memorable moments from that historic evening. A particularly moving highlight of the afternoon was the recognition of Past Internal Auditor Dr. Jaime "Jimmy" Laya, who achieved the extraordinary milestone of Fifty Years of Rotary Service. In his acceptance remarks, Dr. Laya reflected on the priceless friendships that Rotary had given him throughout five decades of service. He fondly recalled fellow Rotarians who stood beside him during some of the most challenging periods of his distinguished career in public service and spoke warmly of Rotary's unique ability to cultivate lifelong fellowship built on trust and shared ideals. He also reaffirmed Rotary's enduring commitment to serving the poorest of the poor through meaningful community service. Concluding his remarks, Dr. Laya expressed the heartfelt wish that every Rotarian present would one day receive the same Fifty-Year Service Award — a sentiment that resonated deeply throughout the ballroom and served as an inspiring reminder of Rotary's enduring legacy of commitment. The centerpiece of the afternoon was the address of Guest-of-Honor and Speaker, Former Congressman Francisco "Kiko" Barzaga. Few contemporary public figures have generated as much discussion as the former legislator. Elected to Congress at only twenty-seven years of age, he became one of the youngest members of the House of Representatives and among the earliest representatives of Generation Z to serve in the national legislature. In 2025, however, the House of Representatives overwhelmingly adopted the recommendation of its Committee on Ethics and Privileges to expel him for disorderly behavior and conduct unbecoming of a Member. Among the cited violations were unauthorized live social media broadcasts inside the session hall, repeated interruptions during important budget deliberations, sarcastic remarks directed at House leadership, and actions deemed disruptive to legislative proceedings. Yet despite the controversy, Congressman Barzaga demonstrated that his convictions remain unchanged. During both his formal address and subsequent conversations with members, it became evident that he continues to view those events through the lens of principle rather than political consequence. He likened his confron- tation with the House leadership to the biblical story of David and Goliath, explaining that he knowingly accepted the personal cost of standing up for what he believed was right. As he poignantly remarked: "I fought against the Speaker knowing the consequences to myself and my family. A soldier does not go to war believing he will return home safely; he fights for his country no matter the cost." Whether one agrees with his methods or not, there is little doubt about the depth of his conviction. Rotary does not exist to endorse political positions, nor does it seek ideological conformity. Instead, it provides a forum where differing viewpoints may be expressed respectfully, examined thoughtfully, and discussed with civility. One of Rotary's greatest strengths has always been its ability to bring together people of diverse perspectives in an atmosphere of friendship, mutual respect, and constructive dialogue. In his formal address, Congressman Barzaga underscored the indispensable role of non-government organizations in nation-building. Drawing upon his experience in public service, he observed that government — both local and national — often relies upon civic organizations to help address societal needs that public institutions alone cannot fully meet. He described philanthropy, particularly as exemplified by Rotary, as one of the highest expressions of moral responsibility, emphasizing that those who have been blessed with greater resources likewise bear a greater obligation to uplift those with less, especially during periods of economic uncertainty. The Open Forum that followed became one of the liveliest and most engaging portions of the afternoon. While members naturally raised questions concerning governance, leadership, and current national issues, one particularly memorable exchange revolved around a subject that has become inseparable from Congressman Barzaga's public identity — his affection for cats. Known by many on social media as "Congress-Meow," Congressman Barzaga explained that his advocacy for animal welfare extends well beyond the online world. His love for feline companions has become a defining aspect of both his personal life and public service. He spoke passionately about rescuing abandoned cats, promoting responsible pet ownership, and encouraging stronger animal welfare legislation. It offered members a refreshing glimpse into the more personal side of a public figure often viewed only through political headlines. One of the most meaningful moments of the day, however, unfolded after the meeting had officially concluded. Long after most members and guests had departed, Congressman Barzaga graciously accepted President Reggie's invitation to stay for a late lunch while waiting for his next appointment — a Taekwondo training session later that afternoon. Away from the podium, microphones, and cameras, the conversation became candid, relaxed, and remarkably introspective. They spoke at length about his journey in public service, his reflections on recent political developments, and his thoughts regarding his future plans. Naturally, the discussion also touched upon the ongoing impeachment proceedings that continue to dominate national discourse. While much of that conversation remains appropriately private, it provided an opportunity to understand the individual behind the headlines through direct and honest dialogue rather than through public commentary alone. The conversation eventually shifted to subjects far removed from politics — his lifelong passion for Taekwondo, his unwavering commitment to animal welfare, and the personal values that continue to guide his decisions. Like many conversations among Rotarians, the exchange was less about agreement than about understanding. That unexpected lunch served as a quiet reminder of one of Rotary's most enduring lessons: behind every public office, every headline, and every controversy is a fellow human being whose story is often far more complex and nuanced than public perception alone can reveal. For President Reggie, the First Weekly Membership Meeting could not have provided a more fitting beginning to Rotary Year 2026–2027. The afternoon embodied the very qualities that have defined the Rotary Club of Manila for more than a century — meaningful fellowship, recognition of exemplary service, respectful dialogue, and the willingness to engage even the most challenging and controversial issues with civility, open-mindedness, and mutual respect. The Club honored fifty years of faithful Rotary service through Dr. Jimmy Laya, welcomed a guest speaker whose life and career have sparked vigorous national discussion, encouraged thoughtful questions rather than unquestioning agreement, and demonstrated that genuine fellowship often continues long after the formal meeting has ended. If the First Weekly Membership Meeting is any indication of the year ahead, the Rotary Club of Manila is well positioned to continue building bridges, fostering meaningful conversations, strengthening friendships, and creating opportunities for service that transcend differences. Together, the Club moves forward in the spirit of the Rotary International theme, "Create Lasting Impact," while advancing President Yu's own vision of "Rotary T.U.R.N. — Toward a Unified Rotary Nation." Editorial: Just Deserts  ONE of my strongest motivations for leading a law- abiding life was the quality, or lack of it, of prison food. When I was preparing for the priesthood many pounds and locks of hair ago, my seminary classmates and I used to regularly visit Lex, the ominously named provincial jail of Bulacan, as part of our apostolate. We interacted with the detainees, talked a little about Jesus and a lot about themselves and their loved ones, and spent the rest of the visit playing basketball with them. We believed that our visit allowed them to have a casual conversation with someone from outside the prison walls so that they would feel like ordinary human beings instead of numbers on a list and wards under supervision by the State. One afternoon, as we were preparing to leave, a delivery of the ingredients for that evening’s dinner was taking place. I noticed one big plastic bag of pechay/pak choi, but instead of the green leafy parts of it, only the tougher white stems, most of them still with some roots protruding, were in the bag. They were obviously the discarded parts, perhaps from a big restaurant’s kitchen, and ‘donated’ to the jail. Naively, I asked the one receiving the ingredients what he intended to do with them and his curt reply was “Lulutuin siempre; buti nga at may gulay kami ngayon.” (We will cook them of course; we’re fortunate that we have veggies for tonight.) The question of what to do with those who violate norms, inflict harm, and cause damages has been central to the development of moral philosophy and criminal justice. What just deserts should offenders get for their transgressions against individuals or society itself has defined various approaches to penology from the earliest days of human civilization. Surviving legal codes from Mesopotamia such as those from Ur- Nammu and Hammurabi outlined various crimes and their corresponding punishments. Book 18 of Homer's Iliad, in describing the design of Achilles' armor, gave glimpses of penal practices in ancient Greece. The epic Mahabharata and the legal code Manusmriti provided insights into the social and moral norms of ancient Indian culture. There are basically four approaches to crime and punishment in current penology. First is retributive justice which focuses on exacting punishments that are proportional to the criminals' actions. Lex talionis, or "an eye for an eye" ensures fairness through strict proportionality. Chopping off an arm for thievery or capital punishment for murder are fine examples of the retributive approach. Second is restorative justice, which focuses on repairing the harm caused by crime through restitution. By emphasizing accountability and rebuilding relationships between offenders and victims, future harm is prevented and the community is protected. The payment of blood money to the family of a homicide victim is one example of restorative justice. The third approach is the theory of deterrence. By intimating what punishments are reserved for criminal behavior, society is giving would-be offenders pause, allowing them to weigh the consequences of their actions before they actually commit them. It must be noted, however, that deterrence requires effective policing and a high probability of arrest and conviction for it to work. The fourth approach is rehabilitation, which presupposes an individual's capacity to change as a result of interventions that address the root causes of criminal behavior. Rehabilitation prevents future crimes by helping offenders become useful members of society through education, work training, counseling and religious guidance. It takes into account societal factors such as drug dependency or poverty as causes of criminality and introduces programs that address those specific issues. As is often the case, a state may use any or a combination of these approaches in preventing criminality. A common denominator among the four is incapacitation by which society seeks to protect itself by removing the offender from the rest of the population and restricting his or her freedom. This is achieved through various modes such as house arrest, imprisonment, and, in extreme cases, execution. However, the jury is still out debating the effectiveness of incapacitation, particularly imprisonment, in controlling criminality. In many cases, those imprisoned and placed in close proximity day in and day out with hardened criminals may end up upgrading their criminal enterprise instead of getting rehabilitated. Outside the prison's walls, other offenders can easily take the place of those imprisoned, taking advantage of the vacancy afforded by the former's incarceration. Conditions in any Philippine prison should be enough of a deterrence for committing crimes. Inadequate ventilation, gross overcrowding, lack of potable water, poor food quality, poor sanitations, and lack of access to medical care are just some of the observations reported by entities such as the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime and the International Committee of the Red Cross. One UNODC report cited Manila City Jail prisoners having to sleep on their sides and on the concrete floor in neat rows of maybe 200 from one end of a dormitory to the other just to accommodate everyone, as the jail is overcrowded by whopping 168 per cent. A 2024 report ranked the Philippines alongside the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Haiti and Uganda in terms of prison congestion. Susmaryosep, as the late great Max Soliven would say. In 2023, the Philippines joined over 50 other states in the Group of Friends of the Nelson Mandela Rules which aims to promote humane conditions of imprisonment through the practical application of the United Nations Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners. By doing so, the Philippines has committed to undertaking prison and penal reform such as by resolving cases quickly to reduce the number of pre-trial detainees, offering better health and education facilities, preventing inhumane treatments in enforcing discipline, and improving record- keeping to aide early release of those who qualify. The way we treat persons deprived of liberty says a lot about the soul of our nation. It also has practical implications on our efforts to make our communities safer, as what happens to people during their imprisonment and following their release will affect the rise or fall of criminality. The road to judicial and penal reforms is long and hard and it behooves all of us to do what we can to hasten the journey and assist those who traverse that path. Because we Rotarians are People of Action. And because Together, We Transform.

Among the cited violations were unauthorized live social media broadcasts inside the session hall, repeated interruptions during important budget deliberations, sarcastic remarks directed at House leadership, and actions deemed disruptive to legislative proceedings.
Yet despite the controversy, Congressman Barzaga demonstrated that his convictions remain unchanged.

During both his formal address and subsequent conversations with members, it became evident that he continues to view those events through the lens of principle rather than political consequence. He likened his confron- tation with the House leadership to the biblical story of David and Goliath, explaining that he knowingly accepted the personal cost of standing up for what he believed was right.
As he poignantly remarked:
"I fought against the Speaker knowing the consequences to myself and my family. A soldier does not go to war believing he will return home safely; he fights for his country no matter the cost."
Whether one agrees with his methods or not, there is little doubt about the depth of his conviction.

Rotary does not exist to endorse political positions, nor does it seek ideological conformity. Instead, it provides a forum where differing viewpoints may be expressed respectfully, examined thoughtfully, and discussed with civility. One of Rotary's greatest strengths has always been its ability to bring together people of diverse perspectives in an atmosphere of friendship, mutual respect, and constructive dialogue.

In his formal address, Congressman Barzaga underscored the indispensable role of non-government organizations in nation-building. Drawing upon his experience in public service, he observed that government — both local and national — often relies upon civic organizations to help address societal needs that public institutions alone cannot fully meet.

He described philanthropy, particularly as exemplified by Rotary, as one of the highest expressions of moral responsibility, emphasizing that those who have been blessed with greater resources likewise bear a greater obligation to uplift those with less, especially during periods of economic uncertainty.
The Open Forum that followed became one of the liveliest and most engaging portions of the afternoon.

While members naturally raised questions concerning governance, leadership, and current national issues, one particularly memorable exchange revolved around a subject that has become inseparable from Congressman Barzaga's public identity — his affection for cats.

Known by many on social media as "Congress-Meow," Congressman Barzaga explained that his advocacy for animal welfare extends well beyond the online world. His love for feline companions has become a defining aspect of both his personal life and public service. He spoke passionately about rescuing abandoned cats, promoting responsible pet ownership, and encouraging stronger animal welfare legislation. It offered members a refreshing glimpse into the more personal side of a public figure often viewed only through political headlines.
One of the most meaningful moments of the day, however, unfolded after the meeting had officially concluded.

Long after most members and guests had departed, Congressman Barzaga graciously accepted President Reggie's invitation to stay for a late lunch while waiting for his next appointment — a Taekwondo training session later that afternoon. Away from the podium, microphones, and cameras, the conversation became candid, relaxed, and remarkably introspective.

They spoke at length about his journey in public service, his reflections on recent political developments, and his thoughts regarding his future plans. Naturally, the discussion also touched upon the ongoing impeachment proceedings that continue to dominate national discourse. While much of that conversation remains appropriately private, it provided an opportunity to understand the individual behind the headlines through direct and honest dialogue rather than through public commentary alone.

The conversation eventually shifted to subjects far removed from politics — his lifelong passion for Taekwondo, his unwavering commitment to animal welfare, and the personal values that continue to guide his decisions. Like many conversations among Rotarians, the exchange was less about agreement than about understanding.

That unexpected lunch served as a quiet reminder of one of Rotary's most enduring lessons: behind every public office, every headline, and every controversy is a fellow human being whose story is often far more complex and nuanced than public perception alone can reveal.
For President Reggie, the First Weekly Membership Meeting could not have provided a more fitting beginning to Rotary Year 2026–2027.

The afternoon embodied the very qualities that have defined the Rotary Club of Manila for more than a century — meaningful fellowship, recognition of exemplary service, respectful dialogue, and the willingness to engage even the most challenging and controversial issues with civility, open-mindedness, and mutual respect.

The Club honored fifty years of faithful Rotary service through Dr. Jimmy Laya, welcomed a guest speaker whose life and career have sparked vigorous national discussion, encouraged thoughtful questions rather than unquestioning agreement, and demonstrated that genuine fellowship often continues long after the formal meeting has ended.

If the First Weekly Membership Meeting is any indication of the year ahead, the Rotary Club of Manila is well positioned to continue building bridges, fostering meaningful conversations, strengthening friendships, and creating opportunities for service that transcend differences.

Together, the Club moves forward in the spirit of the Rotary International theme, "Create Lasting Impact," while advancing President Yu's own vision of "Rotary T.U.R.N. — Toward a Unified Rotary Nation."

ONE of my strongest motivations for leading a law- abiding life was the quality, or lack of it, of prison food. When I was preparing for the priesthood many pounds and locks of hair ago, my seminary classmates and I used to regularly visit Lex, the ominously named provincial jail of Bulacan, as part of our apostolate. We interacted with the detainees, talked a little about Jesus and a lot about themselves and their loved ones, and spent the rest of the visit playing basketball with them. We believed that our visit allowed them to have a casual conversation with someone from outside the prison walls so that they would feel like ordinary human beings instead of numbers on a list and wards under supervision by the State.

One afternoon, as we were preparing to leave, a delivery of the ingredients for that evening’s dinner was taking place. I noticed one big plastic bag of pechay/pak choi, but instead of the green leafy parts of it, only the tougher white stems, most of them still with some roots protruding, were in the bag. They were obviously the discarded parts, perhaps from a big restaurant’s kitchen, and ‘donated’ to the jail.

Naively, I asked the one receiving the ingredients what he intended to do with them and his curt reply was “Lulutuin siempre; buti nga at may gulay kami ngayon.” (We will cook them of course; we’re fortunate that we have veggies for tonight.)

The question of what to do with those who violate norms, inflict harm, and cause damages has been central to the development of moral philosophy and criminal justice. What just deserts should offenders get for their transgressions against individuals or society itself has defined various approaches to penology from the earliest days of human civilization. Surviving legal codes from Mesopotamia such as those from Ur- Nammu and Hammurabi outlined various crimes and their corresponding punishments. Book 18 of Homer's Iliad, in describing the design of Achilles' armor, gave glimpses of penal practices in ancient Greece. The epic Mahabharata and the legal code Manusmriti provided insights into the social and moral norms of ancient Indian culture.

There are basically four approaches to crime and punishment in current penology. First is retributive justice which focuses on exacting punishments that are proportional to the criminals' actions. Lex talionis, or "an eye for an eye" ensures fairness through strict proportionality. Chopping off an arm for thievery or capital punishment for murder are fine examples of the retributive approach.

Second is restorative justice, which focuses on repairing the harm caused by crime through restitution. By emphasizing accountability and rebuilding relationships between offenders and victims, future harm is prevented and the community is protected. The payment of blood money to the family of a homicide victim is one example of restorative justice.

The third approach is the theory of deterrence. By intimating what punishments are reserved for criminal behavior, society is giving would-be offenders pause, allowing them to weigh the consequences of their actions before they actually commit them. It must be noted, however, that deterrence requires effective policing and a high probability of arrest and conviction for it to work.

The fourth approach is rehabilitation, which presupposes an individual's capacity to change as a result of interventions that address the root causes of criminal behavior. Rehabilitation prevents future crimes by helping offenders become useful members of society through education, work training, counseling and religious guidance. It takes into account societal factors such as drug dependency or poverty as causes of criminality and introduces programs that address those specific issues.

As is often the case, a state may use any or a combination of these approaches in preventing criminality. A common denominator among the four is incapacitation by which society seeks to protect itself by removing the offender from the rest of the population and restricting his or her freedom. This is achieved through various modes such as house arrest, imprisonment, and, in extreme cases, execution. However, the jury is still out debating the effectiveness of incapacitation, particularly imprisonment, in controlling criminality. In many cases, those imprisoned and placed in close proximity day in and day out with hardened criminals may end up upgrading their criminal enterprise instead of getting rehabilitated. Outside the prison's walls, other offenders can easily take the place of those imprisoned, taking advantage of the vacancy afforded by the former's incarceration.

Conditions in any Philippine prison should be enough of a deterrence for committing crimes. Inadequate ventilation, gross overcrowding, lack of potable water, poor food quality, poor sanitations, and lack of access to medical care are just some of the observations reported by entities such as the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime and the International Committee of the Red Cross. One UNODC report cited Manila City Jail prisoners having to sleep on their sides and on the concrete floor in neat rows of maybe 200 from one end of a dormitory to the other just to accommodate everyone, as the jail is overcrowded by whopping 168 per cent. A 2024 report ranked the Philippines alongside the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Haiti and Uganda in terms of prison congestion. Susmaryosep, as the late great Max Soliven would say.

In 2023, the Philippines joined over 50 other states in the Group of Friends of the Nelson Mandela Rules which aims to promote humane conditions of imprisonment through the practical application of the United Nations Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners. By doing so, the Philippines has committed to undertaking prison and penal reform such as by resolving cases quickly to reduce the number of pre-trial detainees, offering better health and education facilities, preventing inhumane treatments in enforcing discipline, and improving record- keeping to aide early release of those who qualify.

The way we treat persons deprived of liberty says a lot about the soul of our nation. It also has practical implications on our efforts to make our communities safer, as what happens to people during their imprisonment and following their release will affect the rise or fall of criminality. The road to judicial and penal reforms is long and hard and it behooves all of us to do what we can to hasten the journey and assist those who traverse that path. Because we Rotarians are People of Action. And because Together, We Transform.

search_text: Editorial: Truth and Justice  WE expect to hear big words from today’s Guest of Honor and Speaker, and rightly so. Truth and justice are two of the strongest foundations of the moral and social order in any human civilization, and the National Bureau of Investigation’s mission statement itself avows that it will “provide quality investigative and forensic services to the people through advanced methods and equipment in the pursuit of truth and justice.” This writer is thus inspired to reflect about truth and justice, especially in light of the events unfolding in the Philippines that use these two as crutches for another ideal called accountability. Truth is distinct from fact although they are cousins once removed. Facts are verifiable, measurable, concrete, and unchanging realities not founded on subjective belief. That it did or did not rain this afternoon is a fact, no matter whether one slept through it. Truth, however, requires a subject consciousness to assert it. And it can change over time, such that before Copernicus and Galileo, it was true that the Earth was the center of the universe, and thereafter, it became the Sun. Nonetheless, human consciousness does not dwell singly on facts. The fact that water boils at 100 degrees Celsius achieves its best expression when a cook is able to serve hard-boiled, soft- boiled, and poached eggs as required. Truth therefore provides the “why” to the “what” of facts and, as human consciousness gains a deeper understanding, be it from experience or education, truth becomes the framework for the assignment of meaning and a rendering of reality. The problem with truth is that one’s truth may be different from another’s. Friedrich Nietzche, in his work Thus Spoke Zarathustra, wrote: “By many ways and modes I have come unto my truth… This – is my way – where is yours?” Are we thus consigned to relativism, with each individual asserting his or her own truth, unassailable by virtue of its utter subjectivity? In this writer’s humble opinion, Swiss theologian Hans Urs von Balthazar provides the best description of truth when he wrote that truth is symphonic. Each and every ‘truth’ put forward by anyone is akin to an instrument of a symphonic orchestra, not one instrument able to claim it is better than the others because each one has its part in the symphony. The orchestra itself may at times seem cacophonous, such as when the musicians tune up before the conductor takes his podium. But once he taps his baton and conducts, the composer’s design and the raison d’être for the inclusion of each instrument become undeniably clear. In the same manner, the plurality of cultures, multiplicity of worldviews, broad range of backgrounds, and variance in philosophies make for many truths, such that the totality of them would be difficult for one person to grasp. However, by actively listening and openly interacting with this plurality, one may get to appreciate a huge part of The Truth while humbly accepting that it is bigger than one person can handle. Justice is a bit more straightforward. Aristotle defines it as ensuring “a fair mean” – a sense of proportionate fairness that treats equals equally and unequals unequally – both in an individual’s conduct and in society’s socio-political arrangements. Our seminary professor, himself a theologian from the Dominican Order, used me and my classmate who was much slimmer than me to illustrate this. “Equality,” he said, “is giving Senen and Rodolfo equal lengths of leather, say 30 inches, for a belt. Senen will find the belt too short and Rodolfo will say it’s too long. Justice is giving each of them, unequal as they are, unequal lengths of leather.” It can also get complicated, however. Affirmative action in the United States, for instance, is supposed to dispense justice by favoring African Americans, Latinos and other minority groups in, say, university admissions, for the purpose of correcting perceived racial imbalance in the student body and deep inequality in society. But in two affirmative action cases brought before it, the US Supreme Court contradicted itself. In the Regents of the University of California v. Bakke, decided in 1978, the Court ruled that rigid racial quotas violate the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment and Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. The ruling allowed a white student with the right qualifications to be admitted to the medical school despite racial quotas. In Grutter v. Bollinger (2003) the Court ruled that the University of Michigan Law School could consider race as a factor in admissions and denied a white student’s appeal to be admitted because giving underrepresented minority groups more is a compelling state interest. It was a case of ensuring, as the cliché goes, that those who have less in life should have more in law. Was there justice in either case? Whatever criticisms may be labeled against state policies and legal instruments for failing to encompass the totality and multiplicity of truths, and whatever failings there may be in the dispensation of justice in our country, it remains clear as day that we need both to ensure moral and societal order. I hope our GOHAS will give our members a clearer insight into truth and justice as he sees them, and that he, in turn, will gain from what I expect to be a very lively Q&A session after his remarks. Matibag currently serves as the Director of the National Bureau of Investigation, appointed by President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. on 20 February 2026. He previously served as Acting Cabinet Secretary from March 2022 to June 2022. Prior to this, he was the President and Chief Executive Officer of the National Transmission Commission from January 2017 to March 2022. He also served as General Manager of the Manila International Airport Authority from October 2008 to 2010, in addition to holding various positions in both the government and private sectors. Director Matibag is the husband of Congresswoman Ma. Rene Ann Lourdes G. Matibag, Representative of the 1st District of Laguna, which includes the City of San Pedro. He earned his Bachelor of Arts, major in Philosophy, from the University of Santo Tomas; his Juris Doctor from the Ateneo de Manila University School of Law; and his Master of Laws, major in Corporate and Finance Law, from Wayne State University in Michigan, USA. He passed the Philippine Bar Examinations in 1996. Rotary Club of Manila Hears Powerful Call for Criminal Justice Reform at Second Weekly Membership Meeting President Reginald THE Rotary Club of Manila (RCM), the first Rotary Club in Asia, held its Second Weekly Membership Meeting for Rotary Year 2026–2027 on July 16 at the Fairmont Hotel Makati, featuring internationally recognized criminologist and criminal justice reform advocate Dr. Raymund E. Narag as Guest of Honor and Speaker. The meeting centered on the theme of hope, redemption, and meaningful reform of the Philippine criminal justice system, while reaffirming the Club's commitment to becoming a platform for ideas that inspire service and nation- building. The meeting was called to order by President Reginald T. Yu, who welcomed members and guests to another well-attended weekly gathering under the Club's new theme, "Rotary T.U.R.N. – Toward a Unified Rotary Nation." Director John Nico P. Valencia led the invocation, followed by the playing of the Philippine National Anthem through the Club's newly produced Lupang Hinirang video, the singing of the Rotary Club of Manila Hymn by the RCM World-Famous Music Chorale, the recitation of the Four- Way Test led by STAR Rotarian Winston Ginez, the introduction of visiting Rotarians and guests by Rotarian Ingill Ra, and the Welcome Song rendered by the Chorale. President's Time During the President's Time, President Reggie expressed his appreciation to the members for another strong turnout at the Club's weekly meeting, following the overwhelming attendance recorded during the Rotary Year's opening program. He announced the Club's first fellowship of the Rotary year, to be held on July 23 at the Fairmont Hotel, with the Board generously waiving the usual fellowship assessment to encourage wider participation and strengthen camaraderie among members. He also encouraged directors, officers, and members to enroll in the upcoming Rotary Learning Institute, emphasizing that it remains one of Rotary's most effective leadership development programs and has helped shape many of the organization's outstanding leaders. President Yu likewise revisited the Club's new presidential theme, Rotary T.U.R.N. – Toward a Unified Rotary Nation, emphasizing that Rotary's greatest impact is achieved when members work together in unity despite differences in background, profession, or perspective. One of the highlights of the President's Time was the presentation of a Certificate of Appreciation to Director Carlos G. "Charlie" Serapio in recognition of his invaluable contribution to the Club's historic 107th Induction Ceremonies through his sponsorship of the internationally acclaimed STA Concert Choir, whose performance elevated the solemnity and grandeur of the occasion. Introducing a Distinguished Scholar and Reformer Director Michael Jaey C. Albaña introduced the Guest of Honor and Speaker, Dr. Raymund E. Narag, highlighting his remarkable journey from adversity to becoming one of the world's foremost Filipino scholars in criminology and corrections. Dr. Narag currently serves as Associate Professor and Graduate Program Director of the School of Justice and Public Safety at Southern Illinois University Carbondale. A Fulbright Scholar, he earned both his master's and doctorate degrees from Michigan State University after graduating cum laude from the University of the Philippines Diliman. His research spans correctional administration, prison governance, jail decongestion, inmate rehabilitation, judicial reform, parole and probation, and comparative criminal justice. He has authored numerous books, technical reports, and internationally published studies that have influenced correctional policies in the Philippines and abroad. A Story of Hope, Redemption, and Purpose Speaking on the theme "Engaged Scholarship and the Story of Hope and Redemption," Dr. Narag captivated the audience with a deeply personal account of how he transformed one of the darkest chapters of his life into a lifelong mission of reform and public service. He recounted how, as a promising University of the Philippines student, he was wrongfully accused of murder arising from a fraternity-related incident in 1995. Despite maintaining his innocence, he spent six years, nine months, and four days in detention before finally being acquitted. Rather than allowing imprisonment to define him, he resolved to use the experience to better understand the country's correctional system and to help improve it for generations to come. Inside Quezon City Jail, Dr. Narag organized literacy classes, established one of the country's earliest inmate paralegal programs, promoted educational initiatives through UP Pahinungod, and became actively involved in inmate self-governance. These experiences provided him with an unprecedented understanding of prison life, correctional administration, and the realities faced by persons deprived of liberty. Upon his release, he immediately documented his experiences in the landmark book "Freedom and Death Inside the City Jail," which later became an important reference for judicial and correctional reforms. His advocacy extended beyond writing as he helped develop the Simplified Inmate Records System, the precursor of today's digital inmate management system within the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology, and proposed practical reforms that improved inmate documentation, sentence monitoring, and jail administration. His remarkable journey eventually earned him a Fulbright Scholarship, followed by graduate studies and a doctorate in criminal justice in the United States. Today, he has become one of the leading Filipino experts on correctional management, prison reform, and evidence-based criminal justice policy, while continuing to return regularly to the Philippines to assist government agencies in developing humane, efficient, and data-driven correctional systems. Focus of the Speaker's Message: Reform Through Compassion, Research, and Evidence At the heart of Dr. Narag's address was a compelling message that criminal justice reform must be anchored not only on punishment, but also on fairness, rehabilitation, human dignity, and evidence-based policymaking. Drawing from both lived experience and decades of academic research, he emphasized that prolonged pretrial detention, jail congestion, outdated management systems, and delayed judicial processes inflict unnecessary suffering not only on detainees but also on their families and society as a whole. He argued that meaningful reform requires better case management, modern digital information systems, improved inmate classification, expanded legal assistance, strengthened rehabilitation programs, and greater coordination among law enforcement, prosecutors, courts, correctional institutions, and community organizations. Most importantly, Dr. Narag challenged his audience to recognize that every individual deserves an opportunity for redemption. He reminded Rotarians that behind every inmate is a human story, and behind every successful reform is a community willing to extend compassion without compromising justice. His message resonated deeply with the Rotary ideals of Service Above Self, encouraging members to view criminal justice reform not merely as a legal issue, but as a humanitarian concern that demands leadership, innovation, and collective action. A Meaningful Open Forum The presentation was followed by an engaging open forum, where members actively participated by sharing their own experiences and raising questions on prison management, judicial reforms, alternatives to incarceration, inmate rehabilitation, and policy recommendations. Past Director Dean Amading Valdez fondly recounted his early association with Dr. Narag through the University of the Philippines Office of Legal Aid, where he first witnessed the young scholar's dedication to justice and public service. Other members likewise shared insights and reflections, resulting in a thoughtful exchange between practitioners, academics, and civic leaders. Fellowship and Shared Commitment The meeting also provided members and guests ample opportunity for fellowship before and after the program. Rotarians welcomed guests from various sectors, including members of Dr. Narag's advocacy network and representatives from public service offices, reflecting the Club's continuing role as a venue where government, academe, civil society, and business leaders engage in meaningful dialogue. As the meeting concluded, members expressed appreciation for one of the most inspiring and substantive presentations of the Rotary year. Dr. Narag's extraordinary journey — from wrongful imprisonment to internationally respected scholar and reform advocate — served as a powerful reminder that adversity can become purpose, knowledge can inspire reform, and hope can transform lives. President Reggie formally adjourned the meeting after the presentation of the Certificate of Appreciation to Dr. Narag, thanking him for sharing not only his scholarship but also his deeply personal testimony of resilience, redemption, and unwavering commitment to improving the Philippine justice system. Meeting of the Council of Past Presidents  Present at the meeting were (standing, from left, in the photo above) Consultant Anna Kun Toledo, District Governor Nominee Hermie Esguerra, Secretary Albert Alday, Past District Governor Alex Cureg, and Executive Secretary Lhea Lozano; (seated, from left) Past President Ebot Tan, Jujut Enriquez, President Reggie Yu, Past President Archit Bartolome, Past District Governor Jackie Rodriguez, Past District Governor Rudy Bediones, and Centennial President Susing Pineda.

His research spans correctional administration, prison governance, jail decongestion, inmate rehabilitation, judicial reform, parole and probation, and comparative criminal justice. He has authored numerous books, technical reports, and internationally published studies that have influenced correctional policies in the Philippines and abroad.
A Story of Hope, Redemption, and Purpose

Speaking on the theme "Engaged Scholarship and the Story of Hope and Redemption," Dr. Narag captivated the audience with a deeply personal account of how he transformed one of the darkest chapters of his life into a lifelong mission of reform and public service.

He recounted how, as a promising University of the Philippines student, he was wrongfully accused of murder arising from a fraternity-related incident in 1995. Despite maintaining his innocence, he spent six years, nine months, and four days in detention before finally being acquitted. Rather than allowing imprisonment to define him, he resolved to use the experience to better understand the country's correctional system and to help improve it for generations to come.

Inside Quezon City Jail, Dr. Narag organized literacy classes, established one of the country's earliest inmate paralegal programs, promoted educational initiatives through UP Pahinungod, and became actively involved in inmate self-governance. These experiences provided him with an unprecedented understanding of prison life, correctional administration, and the realities faced by persons deprived of liberty.

Upon his release, he immediately documented his experiences in the landmark book "Freedom and Death Inside the City Jail," which later became an important reference for judicial and correctional reforms. His advocacy extended beyond writing as he helped develop the Simplified Inmate Records System, the precursor of today's digital inmate management system within the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology, and proposed practical reforms that improved inmate documentation, sentence monitoring, and jail administration.

His remarkable journey eventually earned him a Fulbright Scholarship, followed by graduate studies and a doctorate in criminal justice in the United States. Today, he has become one of the leading Filipino experts on correctional management, prison reform, and evidence-based criminal justice policy, while continuing to return regularly to the Philippines to assist government agencies in developing humane, efficient, and data-driven correctional systems.
Focus of the Speaker's Message: Reform Through Compassion, Research, and Evidence

At the heart of Dr. Narag's address was a compelling message that criminal justice reform must be anchored not only on punishment, but also on fairness, rehabilitation, human dignity, and evidence-based policymaking. Drawing from both lived experience and decades of academic research, he emphasized that prolonged pretrial detention, jail congestion, outdated management systems, and delayed judicial processes inflict unnecessary suffering not only on detainees but also on their families and society as a whole.

He argued that meaningful reform requires better case management, modern digital information systems, improved inmate classification, expanded legal assistance, strengthened rehabilitation programs, and greater coordination among law enforcement, prosecutors, courts, correctional institutions, and community organizations.

Most importantly, Dr. Narag challenged his audience to recognize that every individual deserves an opportunity for redemption. He reminded Rotarians that behind every inmate is a human story, and behind every successful reform is a community willing to extend compassion without compromising justice.

His message resonated deeply with the Rotary ideals of Service Above Self, encouraging members to view criminal justice reform not merely as a legal issue, but as a humanitarian concern that demands leadership, innovation, and collective action.
A Meaningful Open Forum

The presentation was followed by an engaging open forum, where members actively participated by sharing their own experiences and raising questions on prison management, judicial reforms, alternatives to incarceration, inmate rehabilitation, and policy recommendations.

Past Director Dean Amading Valdez fondly recounted his early association with Dr. Narag through the University of the Philippines Office of Legal Aid, where he first witnessed the young scholar's dedication to justice and public service. Other members likewise shared insights and reflections, resulting in a thoughtful exchange between practitioners, academics, and civic leaders.
Fellowship and Shared Commitment

The meeting also provided members and guests ample opportunity for fellowship before and after the program. Rotarians welcomed guests from various sectors, including members of Dr. Narag's advocacy network and representatives from public service offices, reflecting the Club's continuing role as a venue where government, academe, civil society, and business leaders engage in meaningful dialogue.

As the meeting concluded, members expressed appreciation for one of the most inspiring and substantive presentations of the Rotary year. Dr. Narag's extraordinary journey — from wrongful imprisonment to internationally respected scholar and reform advocate — served as a powerful reminder that adversity can become purpose, knowledge can inspire reform, and hope can transform lives.

President Reggie formally adjourned the meeting after the presentation of the Certificate of Appreciation to Dr. Narag, thanking him for sharing not only his scholarship but also his deeply personal testimony of resilience, redemption, and unwavering commitment to improving the Philippine justice system.

Yu AT a time when public discourse is increasingly shaped by political polarization and instant opinion, National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) Director Atty. Melvin Alvarez Matibag delivered a compelling reminder that the rule of law must always be anchored on evidence, due process, and institutional integrity during the Rotary Club of Manila's Third Weekly Membership Meeting on July 23, 2026. Held at the Sheraton Manila Hotel, the gathering brought together Rotarians, civic leaders, and guests for an afternoon that extended beyond a discussion of the country's most pressing legal issues. Instead, it became a thoughtful conversation on leadership, accountability, and the enduring principles that underpin public service. Director Matibag's appearance came just one day after he had completed two grueling days of testimony before the Senate as a key witness in the ongoing impeachment proceedings. Having spent nearly eleven hours under intense questioning while continuing to oversee the country's premier investigative agency, many would have expected him to take a well-deserved respite. Instead, he honored his commitment to address the Rotary Club of Manila. Although visibly fatigued, the NBI chief immediately struck a personal note by sharing that the invitation held special significance. A former member of two Rotary clubs, Matibag revealed that addressing the Rotary Club of Manila had long been one of his aspirations. He described the club as the first Rotary club in Asia, the largest in the Philippines, and "the most prestigious Rotary club in the country." Despite no longer being an active member, he remarked that he had always remained "a Rotarian by heart and by mind." His remarks resonated strongly with the audience, affirming Rotary's century long legacy of cultivating leadership founded on service and ethical responsibility. He acknowledged that he assumed leadership of the Bureau at a time when nearly every major investigation was viewed through a political lens. In such an environment, he explained, investigative institutions face constant pressure from both public sentiment and political interests. Their credibility, however, depends precisely on their ability to remain independent of both. "The duty of investigators," he emphasized, "is not to validate public narratives but to establish facts through evidence, observe due process, and uphold the rule of law." Whether the subject of an investigation is popular or controversial, influential or unknown, he stressed that evidence — not personalities — must determine the outcome. The philosophy found a receptive audience among Rotarians, whose Four Way Test similarly emphasizes truth, fairness, goodwill, and integrity as guiding principles in both professional and civic life. Unsurprisingly, members also sought Director Matibag's perspective on the highly publicized impeachment proceedings that have dominated national attention. While careful not to discuss confidential matters, he explained that impeachment differs fundamentally from criminal prosecution because it examines whether public officials have remained faithful to the constitutional oath of office. Public accountability, he noted, should never be measured by opinion surveys or political popularity, but by fidelity to constitutional duty. The discussion later shifted to ongoing investigations into the alleged misuse of government flood control funds. Director Matibag assured attendees that the Bureau continues to pursue both so-called "ghost projects," where infrastructure exists only on paper, and "zombie projects," where completed public works allegedly used grossly substandard materials despite receiving full government funding. Such investigations, he explained, demand patience, meticulous documentation, and extensive evidence gathering before cases can withstand judicial scrutiny. Effective law enforcement, he observed, is often painstaking rather than dramatic. Another highlight of the forum was Director Matibag's discussion of the Bureau's intensified campaign against human trafficking and online sexual abuse and exploitation of children. Dispelling popular misconceptions fueled by television dramas, he explained that successful anti trafficking operations require weeks or even months of surveillance, intelligence gathering, confidential informants, documentary analysis, and close coordination with local government units and social workers before arrests are made. He likewise cited the Bureau's sustained efforts against agricultural smuggling and other forms of organized crime, noting that hundreds of successful operations had already been conducted during the first six months of his administration. Director Matibag also addressed the Bureau's investigation into the Ateneo de Manila University case, explaining that investigators ultimately recommended charges supported by the available evidence rather than those most demanded by public opinion. The case, he said, demonstrated that investigators must consistently follow where the facts lead, even when doing so may not satisfy prevailing public expectations. His goal, he said, is to leave behind an organization that will continue serving the Filipino people long after his tenure has ended — a philosophy that many participants regarded as a hallmark of enduring leadership. He described Rotarians as individuals who willingly step beyond their comfort zones to improve the lives of others and pledged the National Bureau of Investigation's readiness to partner with the Rotary Club of Manila in initiatives that promote peace, justice, public safety, and nation building. The commitment was warmly received by members, underscoring the important role that civic organizations and public institutions can play when united by common values of integrity, service, and accountability. More than a discussion of ongoing investigations or current events, the forum ultimately offered a broader reflection on the qualities required to lead institutions entrusted with public confidence. In an era marked by speculation and political division, Director Matibag's message remained clear: credibility is earned through discipline, unwavering fidelity to the truth, and a steadfast commitment to principle above popularity. RCM After Hours: An Evening that Reignited Rotary Fellowship  THE Rotary Club of Manila demonstrated that fellowship remains the heart and soul of Rotary as it successfully launched RCM After Hours, its first "assessment-free" Monthly Fellowship in nearly five years, on Thursday, July 23, 2026, at the elegant 11th Floor Social Lounge of Fairmont Makati.
