Held immediately after the Club's Third Weekly Membership Meeting, RCM After Hours officially opened at 3:00 p.m. What few anticipated, however, was that members would be enjoying one another's company until nearly 8:00 p.m., reluctant to call an end to an afternoon that rekindled friendships and revived the fellowship that has long distinguished Asia's First Rotary Club. The turnout was nothing short of remarkable. A total of 86 participants filled the Social Lounge, including an unprecedented 78 Rotary Club of Manila members, three Rotaractors from the Rotaract Club of Manila, and several invited guests. The impressive attendance made it one of the largest fellowship gatherings the Club has hosted in many years and reflected the growing enthusiasm among members to reconnect beyond the formal setting of weekly membership meetings. One of the most appreciated aspects of the afternoon was that every member attended free of charge. For the first time in approximately five years, the Club leadership deliberately waived all fellowship assessments, believing that removing financial barriers would encourage greater participation and allow members to simply relax, reconnect, and enjoy one another's company. The decision proved to be an overwhelming success, with many members expressing their appreciation for an initiative that placed fellowship ahead of formality and hospitality ahead of assessments. The atmosphere throughout the afternoon was warm, lively, and unmistakably Rotarian. Old friends reunited after long absences. Newer members found themselves sharing tables with Past Presidents and veteran Rotarians. Conversations flowed effortlessly across generations of membership, reminding everyone that while Rotary is renowned for its service projects, it is fellowship that sustains the organization year after year. Overflowing refreshments, an endless selection of drinks, and a generous spread of hors d'oeuvres ensured that no one left wanting, while the relaxed ambiance encouraged members to linger long after the formal meeting had concluded. The energy reached another level when Jan May de Vera and her acoustic band began performing. Their engaging repertoire quickly transformed the gathering into an impromptu sing-along, with members enthusiastically belting out timeless favorites, taking turns at the microphone, and even filling the dance floor as the afternoon gave way to evening. Among those entertaining fellow Rotarians with spirited musical performances were Immediate Past President Raoul Creencia, Director Mike Albaña, Past Director Rod Valencia, Rotarian Joanna Valencia, Director Mike Roxas, Past Director Pepo Nuñez, and Past Director Amading Valdez, whose enthusiasm proved infectious and kept the room alive with music, laughter, and applause. The fellowship likewise highlighted Rotary's commitment to nurturing future leaders, as members of the Rotaract Club of Manila joined senior Rotarians in an afternoon of conversation, music, and fellowship, strengthening the bonds between generations of leaders committed to the ideal of Service Above Self. Behind the tremendous success of the inaugural RCM After Hours was a dedicated team of Rotarians who worked tirelessly to transform an idea into one of the Club's most memorable fellowship events in recent years. Special recognition is due to the Fellowship Committee, led by Director Nico Valencia and Chairman Atty. Cris Tamesis, together with Vice President Karlo Castro, Past Director Pepo Nuñez, and Director Mike Albaña, whose careful planning, attention to detail, and commitment to creating an atmosphere of genuine warmth and hospitality ensured that every member felt welcomed and every guest left with lasting memories. Their collective efforts exemplified Rotary's enduring principle that the best fellowship is thoughtfully planned but effortlessly enjoyed. As the evening progressed, one observation became increasingly evident. Members simply did not want to go home. The overwhelmingly positive feedback that followed reflected a common sentiment throughout the Club: RCM After Hours should become a permanent monthly tradition. Many described it as one of the most enjoyable fellowship gatherings in years —a refreshing reminder of what had been missing and a welcome return to the camaraderie that has long been a hallmark of the Rotary Club of Manila. While Rotary is widely recognized for its impactful service projects and meaningful weekly programs, its enduring strength has always rested upon the friendships that unite its members. Service may bring Rotarians together, but fellowship is what keeps them together. The overwhelming success of the inaugural RCM After Hours demonstrated that meaningful fellowship remains as relevant today as it was when the Rotary Club of Manila was founded more than 107 years ago. Beyond the music, food, and festivities, the gathering rekindled old friendships, forged new ones, welcomed back familiar faces, and reminded everyone that the Club's greatest asset has never been its history alone, but the remarkable people who continue to write it. If this memorable afternoon and evening served as any indication, RCM After Hours has already become much more than a monthly social gathering. It is the revival of a cherished Rotary tradition. A celebration of friendship. A renewal of camaraderie. And a living expression of this Rotary year's guiding vision: Rotary T.U.R.N. — Toward a Unified Rotary Nation. For five unforgettable hours at the Fairmont Makati, that vision was not merely spoken about. It was joyfully lived. RCManila Foundation Inc.’s First ExeCom Meeting  THE first ExeCom Meeting under the leadership of Chair Raoul Creencia and President Mike Roxas was held on July 20, 2026, from 12:00 noon to 2:00 p.m., at the MOORE Roxas Tabamo & Co. office, Multina tional Bancorporation Centre, Makati City. Also in attendance were Secretary Anton Mauricio, Board Legal Adviser Chris Tamesis, and Assistant Treasurer Dean Cid. Golf Chair Rami Chahwan participated remotely via Zoom. Editorial: Joke? No!  ANYBODY who had been to Malcolm Hall in UP Diliman would have been confronted with the words, etched in stone, of Oliver Wendell Holmes, Jr., then Associate Justice of the Supreme Judicial Court of the State of Massachusetts. In his 1886 oration before an alumni homecoming of Harvard Law School, delivered as part of the larger celebration marking the 250th anniversary of Harvard University, Mr. Justice Holmes said: "So I say the business of a law school is not sufficiently described when you merely say that it is to teach law, or to make lawyers. It is to teach law in the grand manner, and to make great lawyers." Indeed, the business of a law school is not to teach content for students to memorize by rote but rather to teach students how to think - critically, analytically, bi-directionally, strategically - with the letter of the law and the spirit of it as gleaned from jurisprudence as their abundant resource. Mr. Justice Holmes continued: “The aim of a law school should be, the aim of the Harvard Law School has been, not to make men smart, but to make them wise in their calling - to start them on a road which will lead them to the abode of the masters.” The Rotary Club of Manila’s roster is replete with fine examples of men who were taught law in the grand manner, whether at Malcolm Hall or at other temples consecrated to the honing of the finest legal minds. And I have complete confidence that each one of them will attest that their experience in law school, what they have gone through to reach graduation, was no joke. In fact, Philippine law schools are known to have high attrition rates, some even seeing a reduction of up to 30% of the class size come graduation. Passing the bar is no cakewalk either. Data will show that generally, over 50% of bar takers would fail. Recent years’ passing rates illustrate this, to wit: 2025: 48.98%; 2024: 37.84%; 2023: 36.77%; 2022: 43.47%. In the 2012 Bar Exams, only 17.76% of the takers passed. Recent developments in the country have thrust lawyers into the limelight. In deliberating on the propriety of selecting an impeachment presiding officer, certain senators mentioned having or not having a law degree and passing the bar as important considerations. At the impeachment court, a counsel for the respondent, in cross-examining a prosecution witness, himself a lawyer, mentioned the impeached official as having passed the bar on first try and perhaps getting a higher grade than the others present in the chamber. RCM’s GOHAS for this meeting received a multitude of reactions, both favorable and unfavorable depending on which side of the political spectrum one is lodged, over his mastery of legal procedures, calm composure, and respectful demeanor as he sparred with both the defense and some senator-judges on the motion to subpoena bank, tax and AMLC records. Do these descriptors - graduating from a famed school of law, passing and topping the bar, mastery of legal procedures, oral eloquence, succinct writing prowess - make a lawyer great? Should a lawyer who graduated from an unheralded college and barely passed the bar exams but regularly got his clients redress for grievances be seen as less than another who is from contrasting circumstances? Would the magnitude of the acceptance fee and per hour billing be a fair measure of being a great lawyer? What actually makes a lawyer great? To answer this question, perhaps one should reflect on the role of law in human society. It can be asseverated that law is not only vital in preserving peace and order in society through its dispute-resolution mechanisms but, more importantly, provides the stable foundation and enabling environment wherein individual rights and collective necessities are managed, resources are justly allocated, and space for the fair pursuit of happiness is created. The rule of law defines what one is entitled to, how he or she can acquire it, what guarantees he or she has to enjoy it, and what consequence awaits anyone who illicitly upsets this well-arranged applecart. Thus, a great lawyer is one who uses his mastery of the nuances of law and jurisprudence to assist in maintaining this harmonious balance in society, provide relief to anyone unfairly wronged within this milieu, and contribute, through well-penned arguments or scholarly research, to the continuing development and evolution of legal theory and practice. By way of an example, there was once a great lawyer who achieved fame as the only Filipino, thus far, to top both the certified public accountant (CPA) board exams and the bar. In fact, this lawyer was one of probably only a handful of those allowed by the Supreme Court of the Philippines to take the bar exams without graduating with a degree in law, which is a feat unto itself. His intellectual prowess is indubitable, having graduated valedictorian in high school and summa cum laude in college. And his mastery of laws and legal procedures served him in good stead as he began his many years of outstanding private legal practice. But this lawyer’s greatness was not because of these accolades. This lawyer’s greatness, attested to by conferment of the Order of Lakandula among other honors, rests on his use of these intellectual and material blessings to speak truth to power by investigating massive government corruption even to the point of losing his job; resigning from a political party he nurtured or from a human rights portfolio he loved as soon as staying became inconsistent with his moral principles; coming to the aid of those whose human rights were impinged by martial law by establishing and leading the Philippines' first pro bono legal service group; championing human rights whether on the streets of Manila or at regional conferences in Asia; publishing sound legal commentaries on the burning issues of the day; and by putting the free and enabled Filipino first in all his advocacies. “Even if we have to wade through blood and fire, we will be free. We will develop. We will build our own societies. We will sing our own songs,” he said. He was Jose Wright Diokno accountant, lawyer, Secretary of Justice, Senator of the Republic, founder and chair of the Free Legal Assistance Group (FLAG), chair of the Civil Liberties Union, secretary general of the Regional Council on Human Rights in Asia, chair of the Presidential Committee on Human Rights, head of the first Philippine government panel that conducted peace negotiations with the National Democratic Front, loving husband to Carmen Icasiano Diokno and devoted father to ten children. Will the apple fall far from the tree? Our GOHAS today, Jose Manuel Tadeo “Chel” Icasiano Diokno, a member of the 20th Congress representing the Akbayan partylist in the House of Representatives, is a respected human rights lawyer, educator and public servant. He earned a Bachelor of Arts in philosophy from the University of the Philippines-Diliman and graduated magna cum laude with a juris doctor degree from the Northern Illinois University. He passed the Illinois bar exam in 1987 and the Philippine bar exam in 1988. He is the founding dean of the De La Salle College of Law, now known as the Tañada-Diokno School of Law, where he emphasized ethics, public service and social justice in legal education. Like his father, Chel served as FLAG chairman and also held advisory roles in government, serving under presidents Corazon Aquino and Fidel Ramos as part of the Presidential Committee on Human Rights, the same committee that his father chaired. From 2017 to 2019, he served as presidential adviser on human rights to the Integrated Bar of the Philippines. Since 2022, he has chaired the Bantayog ng mga Bayani Foundation. He was a private prosecutor during the impeachment trial of former president Joseph Estrada; he is now a member of the House prosecution panel in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte. He is married to the former Divina Aromin, with whom he has six children. Will the spring rise higher than its source? Let’s watch and see.

body.text: THE Rotary Club of Manila demonstrated that fellowship remains the heart and soul of Rotary as it successfully launched RCM After Hours, its first "assessment-free" Monthly Fellowship in nearly five years, on Thursday, July 23, 2026, at the elegant 11th Floor Social Lounge of Fairmont Makati. What began as a simple post-meeting gathering quickly evolved into one of the most vibrant and well attended fellowship events in recent Club memory, reaffirming that genuine camaraderie remains one of Rotary's greatest strengths.

Held immediately after the Club's Third Weekly Membership Meeting, RCM After Hours officially opened at 3:00 p.m. What few anticipated, however, was that members would be enjoying one another's company until nearly 8:00 p.m., reluctant to call an end to an afternoon that rekindled friendships and revived the fellowship that has long distinguished Asia's First Rotary Club.
The turnout was nothing short of remarkable.

A total of 86 participants filled the Social Lounge, including an unprecedented 78 Rotary Club of Manila members, three Rotaractors from the Rotaract Club of Manila, and several invited guests. The impressive attendance made it one of the largest fellowship gatherings the Club has hosted in many years and reflected the growing enthusiasm among members to reconnect beyond the formal setting of weekly membership meetings.
One of the most appreciated aspects of the afternoon was that every member attended free of charge.

For the first time in approximately five years, the Club leadership deliberately waived all fellowship assessments, believing that removing financial barriers would encourage greater participation and allow members to simply relax, reconnect, and enjoy one another's company. The decision proved to be an overwhelming success, with many members expressing their appreciation for an initiative that placed fellowship ahead of formality and hospitality ahead of assessments.
The atmosphere throughout the afternoon was warm, lively, and unmistakably Rotarian.

Old friends reunited after long absences. Newer members found themselves sharing tables with Past Presidents and veteran Rotarians. Conversations flowed effortlessly across generations of membership, reminding everyone that while Rotary is renowned for its service projects, it is fellowship that sustains the organization year after year.

Overflowing refreshments, an endless selection of drinks, and a generous spread of hors d'oeuvres ensured that no one left wanting, while the relaxed ambiance encouraged members to linger long after the formal meeting had concluded.
The energy reached another level when Jan May de Vera and her acoustic band began performing.

Their engaging repertoire quickly transformed the gathering into an impromptu sing-along, with members enthusiastically belting out timeless favorites, taking turns at the microphone, and even filling the dance floor as the afternoon gave way to evening.

Among those entertaining fellow Rotarians with spirited musical performances were Immediate Past President Raoul Creencia, Director Mike Albaña, Past Director Rod Valencia, Rotarian Joanna Valencia, Director Mike Roxas, Past Director Pepo Nuñez, and Past Director Amading Valdez, whose enthusiasm proved infectious and kept the room alive with music, laughter, and applause.

The fellowship likewise highlighted Rotary's commitment to nurturing future leaders, as members of the Rotaract Club of Manila joined senior Rotarians in an afternoon of conversation, music, and fellowship, strengthening the bonds between generations of leaders committed to the ideal of Service Above Self.

Behind the tremendous success of the inaugural RCM After Hours was a dedicated team of Rotarians who worked tirelessly to transform an idea into one of the Club's most memorable fellowship events in recent years.

Special recognition is due to the Fellowship Committee, led by Director Nico Valencia and Chairman Atty. Cris Tamesis, together with Vice President Karlo Castro, Past Director Pepo Nuñez, and Director Mike Albaña, whose careful planning, attention to detail, and commitment to creating an atmosphere of genuine warmth and hospitality ensured that every member felt welcomed and every guest left with lasting memories. Their collective efforts exemplified Rotary's enduring principle that the best fellowship is thoughtfully planned but effortlessly enjoyed.
As the evening progressed, one observation became increasingly evident.
Members simply did not want to go home.

The overwhelmingly positive feedback that followed reflected a common sentiment throughout the Club: RCM After Hours should become a permanent monthly tradition. Many described it as one of the most enjoyable fellowship gatherings in years —a refreshing reminder of what had been missing and a welcome return to the camaraderie that has long been a hallmark of the Rotary Club of Manila.

While Rotary is widely recognized for its impactful service projects and meaningful weekly programs, its enduring strength has always rested upon the friendships that unite its members. Service may bring Rotarians together, but fellowship is what keeps them together.

The overwhelming success of the inaugural RCM After Hours demonstrated that meaningful fellowship remains as relevant today as it was when the Rotary Club of Manila was founded more than 107 years ago.

Beyond the music, food, and festivities, the gathering rekindled old friendships, forged new ones, welcomed back familiar faces, and reminded everyone that the Club's greatest asset has never been its history alone, but the remarkable people who continue to write it.
If this memorable afternoon and evening served as any indication, RCM After Hours has already become much more than a monthly social gathering. It is the revival of a cherished Rotary tradition.
A celebration of friendship. A renewal of camaraderie. And a living expression of this Rotary year's guiding vision:
Rotary T.U.R.N. — Toward a Unified Rotary Nation.
For five unforgettable hours at the Fairmont Makati, that vision was not merely spoken about.
It was joyfully lived.

body.text: THE first ExeCom Meeting under the leadership of Chair Raoul Creencia and President Mike Roxas was held on July 20, 2026, from 12:00 noon to 2:00 p.m., at the MOORE Roxas Tabamo & Co. office, Multina tional Bancorporation Centre, Makati City.
Also in attendance were Secretary Anton Mauricio, Board Legal Adviser Chris Tamesis, and Assistant Treasurer Dean Cid. Golf Chair Rami Chahwan participated remotely via Zoom.

ANYBODY who had been to Malcolm Hall in UP Diliman would have been confronted with the words, etched in stone, of Oliver Wendell Holmes, Jr., then Associate Justice of the Supreme Judicial Court of the State of Massachusetts. In his 1886 oration before an alumni homecoming of Harvard Law School, delivered as part of the larger celebration marking the 250th anniversary of Harvard University, Mr. Justice Holmes said: "So I say the business of a law school is not sufficiently described when you merely say that it is to teach law, or to make lawyers. It is to teach law in the grand manner, and to make great lawyers."

Indeed, the business of a law school is not to teach content for students to memorize by rote but rather to teach students how to think - critically, analytically, bi-directionally, strategically - with the letter of the law and the spirit of it as gleaned from jurisprudence as their abundant resource. Mr. Justice Holmes continued: “The aim of a law school should be, the aim of the Harvard Law School has been, not to make men smart, but to make them wise in their calling - to start them on a road which will lead them to the abode of the masters.”

The Rotary Club of Manila’s roster is replete with fine examples of men who were taught law in the grand manner, whether at Malcolm Hall or at other temples consecrated to the honing of the finest legal minds. And I have complete confidence that each one of them will attest that their experience in law school, what they have gone through to reach graduation, was no joke. In fact, Philippine law schools are known to have high attrition rates, some even seeing a reduction of up to 30% of the class size come graduation.

Passing the bar is no cakewalk either. Data will show that generally, over 50% of bar takers would fail. Recent years’ passing rates illustrate this, to wit: 2025: 48.98%; 2024: 37.84%; 2023: 36.77%; 2022: 43.47%. In the 2012 Bar Exams, only 17.76% of the takers passed.

Recent developments in the country have thrust lawyers into the limelight. In deliberating on the propriety of selecting an impeachment presiding officer, certain senators mentioned having or not having a law degree and passing the bar as important considerations. At the impeachment court, a counsel for the respondent, in cross-examining a prosecution witness, himself a lawyer, mentioned the impeached official as having passed the bar on first try and perhaps getting a higher grade than the others present in the chamber. RCM’s GOHAS for this meeting received a multitude of reactions, both favorable and unfavorable depending on which side of the political spectrum one is lodged, over his mastery of legal procedures, calm composure, and respectful demeanor as he sparred with both the defense and some senator-judges on the motion to subpoena bank, tax and AMLC records.

Do these descriptors - graduating from a famed school of law, passing and topping the bar, mastery of legal procedures, oral eloquence, succinct writing prowess - make a lawyer great? Should a lawyer who graduated from an unheralded college and barely passed the bar exams but regularly got his clients redress for grievances be seen as less than another who is from contrasting circumstances? Would the magnitude of the acceptance fee and per hour billing be a fair measure of being a great lawyer? What actually makes a lawyer great?

To answer this question, perhaps one should reflect on the role of law in human society. It can be asseverated that law is not only vital in preserving peace and order in society through its dispute-resolution mechanisms but, more importantly, provides the stable foundation and enabling environment wherein individual rights and collective necessities are managed, resources are justly allocated, and space for the fair pursuit of happiness is created. The rule of law defines what one is entitled to, how he or she can acquire it, what guarantees he or she has to enjoy it, and what consequence awaits anyone who illicitly upsets this well-arranged applecart.

Thus, a great lawyer is one who uses his mastery of the nuances of law and jurisprudence to assist in maintaining this harmonious balance in society, provide relief to anyone unfairly wronged within this milieu, and contribute, through well-penned arguments or scholarly research, to the continuing development and evolution of legal theory and practice.

By way of an example, there was once a great lawyer who achieved fame as the only Filipino, thus far, to top both the certified public accountant (CPA) board exams and the bar. In fact, this lawyer was one of probably only a handful of those allowed by the Supreme Court of the Philippines to take the bar exams without graduating with a degree in law, which is a feat unto itself. His intellectual prowess is indubitable, having graduated valedictorian in high school and summa cum laude in college. And his mastery of laws and legal procedures served him in good stead as he began his many years of outstanding private legal practice. But this lawyer’s greatness was not because of these accolades.

This lawyer’s greatness, attested to by conferment of the Order of Lakandula among other honors, rests on his use of these intellectual and material blessings to speak truth to power by investigating massive government corruption even to the point of losing his job; resigning from a political party he nurtured or from a human rights portfolio he loved as soon as staying became inconsistent with his moral principles; coming to the aid of those whose human rights were impinged by martial law by establishing and leading the Philippines' first pro bono legal service group; championing human rights whether on the streets of Manila or at regional conferences in Asia; publishing sound legal commentaries on the burning issues of the day; and by putting the free and enabled Filipino first in all his advocacies. “Even if we have to wade through blood and fire, we will be free. We will develop. We will build our own societies. We will sing our own songs,” he said.

He was Jose Wright Diokno accountant, lawyer, Secretary of Justice, Senator of the Republic, founder and chair of the Free Legal Assistance Group (FLAG), chair of the Civil Liberties Union, secretary general of the Regional Council on Human Rights in Asia, chair of the Presidential Committee on Human Rights, head of the first Philippine government panel that conducted peace negotiations with the National Democratic Front, loving husband to Carmen Icasiano Diokno and devoted father to ten children.

Will the apple fall far from the tree? Our GOHAS today, Jose Manuel Tadeo “Chel” Icasiano Diokno, a member of the 20th Congress representing the Akbayan partylist in the House of Representatives, is a respected human rights lawyer, educator and public servant. He earned a Bachelor of Arts in philosophy from the University of the Philippines-Diliman and graduated magna cum laude with a juris doctor degree from the Northern Illinois University. He passed the Illinois bar exam in 1987 and the Philippine bar exam in 1988. He is the founding dean of the De La Salle College of Law, now known as the Tañada-Diokno School of Law, where he emphasized ethics, public service and social justice in legal education.

Like his father, Chel served as FLAG chairman and also held advisory roles in government, serving under presidents Corazon Aquino and Fidel Ramos as part of the Presidential Committee on Human Rights, the same committee that his father chaired. From 2017 to 2019, he served as presidential adviser on human rights to the Integrated Bar of the Philippines. Since 2022, he has chaired the Bantayog ng mga Bayani Foundation. He was a private prosecutor during the impeachment trial of former president Joseph Estrada; he is now a member of the House prosecution panel in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte. He is married to the former Divina Aromin, with whom he has six children.
Will the spring rise higher than its source? Let’s watch and see.

Guest of Honor and Speaker: Senator Ana Theresia "Risa" N. Hontiveros  SENATOR RISA HONTIVEROS
Senator of the Republic of the Philippines
Defender of Women, Children, and Vulnerable Sectors
Champion of Good Governance, Health, and Education SENATOR Risa Hontiveros is known for her tireless work in promoting public health, women's rights, and the welfare of the Filipino family. She is a multi awarded public servant, community organizer, and journalist elected to the Senate in 2016. In her first term, she successfully championed landmark laws, including the historic Expanded Maternity Leave Law that gives working moms 105 days of paid maternity leave, and the Philippine-Mental Health Law, the country's first ever national policy to care for Filipinos' mental health. As a longtime health advocate, she pushed for the passage of the Universal Healthcare Law and the Expanded Anti-hospital Deposit Law to ensure the Filipino family’s well-being before profit, and to make health more accessible to all. Even amidst the pandemic, Senator Risa pushed for free dialysis for senior citizens and for the timely release of benefits and salaries for health workers. As Chairperson of the Senate Committee on Women, Senator Hontiveros also authored the Safe Streets and Public Spaces Law or the Bawal Bastos Law that protects all Filipinos, particularly women, from gender-based harassment in the streets, public transportation, schools, and the workplace. During the biggest public health crisis of our time, she also pushed for the Maternity Benefit for Women in the Informal Economy Act, to help ease the multiple burdens of women exacerbated by the pandemic. Senator Hontiveros worked on expanding the Solo Parents' Act to further help single moms and dads in providing for their families. The Senator is also pushing for an increase on the monthly pension of senior citizens through the Lingap Para Kayo Lolo at Lola Bill. Even before becoming a legislator, in 2005, she was one of 27 Filipinas who earned a nomination to the prestigious Nobel Peace Prize for her work in the peace movement. Senator Hontiveros is a loving and hands-on solo mother to 4 children Kiko, Issa, Helena and Sinta. When Power Meets Accountability President Reginal T. Yu THE Rotary Club of Manila placed one of the country’s most consequential constitutional issues at the center of its civic forum on August 20, 2026, as Atty. Amando Virgil D. Ligutan, Private Prosecutor of the House Prosecution Panel in the impeachment proceedings against Vice President Sara Duterte, addressed the Club’s 7th Weekly Membership Meeting of Rotary Year 2026–2027 at Makati Shangri-La, Manila. With RCM Director Atty. Teodoro Alejandro Y. Kalaw IV serving as moderator, the gathering moved beyond the personalities and political divisions surrounding the impeachment and into a broader examination of accountability, public trust, equality before the law, and the resilience of Philippine democratic institutions. Ligutan opened his address by acknowledging the Rotary Club of Manila as an institution whose members have, for generations, helped shape the country’s civic, economic, and moral landscape. An invitation to speak before Rotary, he said, demanded more than the delivery of prepared remarks; it required an accounting of one’s principles, beliefs, and convictions. He then described the Philippines as being at an important crossroads, confronting profound questions about governance, accountability, and the durability of democracy. According to Ligutan, these questions transcend partisan politics because they test whether institutions are strong enough to withstand scrutiny, whether leaders are willing to accept oversight, and whether democratic systems remain capable of correcting themselves. “Accountability is not politics even when politics tries to make it look that way,” he said, describing it instead as a democratic necessity and impeachment as one of the constitutional mechanisms through which it is enforced. Ligutan stressed that impeachment should neither be treated as spectacle nor as an instrument for merely targeting political opponents. Rather, he described it as a serious constitutional inquiry into the conduct of officials occupying the highest levels of government. At its core, he said, impeachment asks a solemn question: Are the country’s highest officials still worthy of the public trust? A Call That Changed the Course of His Career Beyond the constitutional arguments, Ligutan gave RCM members a personal account of how he became involved in the impeachment proceedings. He recalled receiving a telephone call from a priest sometime in December 2024 asking whether he would help file an impeachment complaint against Vice President Duterte. Ligutan said he did not hesitate. He subsequently represented a group of priests, nuns, civic leaders, and lawyers seeking accountability from the Vice President. When the first impeachment proceeding was dismissed, Ligutan said the setback gave him time to reflect more deeply on the gravity of his responsibility and the reasons behind his decision to pursue the case. Months later, the group approached him again. “Attorney, will you lawyer for us once more?” he recalled being asked. Again, his answer was yes. For Ligutan, accountability could not be optional, seasonal, or dependent upon convenience. It demanded persistence and sacrifice, particularly when those being subjected to scrutiny occupied positions of considerable power. He argued that the impeachment therefore represented more than a trial of Vice President Duterte. It was also a test of the country’s systems, democratic norms, expectations of leadership, and collective commitment to truth. Even the senator-judges who would sit in judgment, Ligutan argued, faced their own institutional test: whether they would permit transparency, withstand political pressures, and remain faithful to both the letter and spirit of the Constitution. A Dream Born During the Estrada Impeachment One of the most personal moments of Ligutan’s address came when he traced his interest in accountability to another defining chapter in Philippine political history. As a young college student, Ligutan watched the impeachment trial of former President Joseph Estrada unfold on national television. He remembered watching the prosecutors walk out and the senators vote 11–10 against opening the controversial second envelope. While millions of Filipinos watched the same historic events, the proceedings left a particular impression on the young Ligutan. “Someday, I want to be there,” he remembered thinking. “Someday, I want to stand in that arena. Someday, I want to help hold power accountable.” At the time, Ligutan said he had neither political connections nor powerful patrons. He instead pursued the long route of study, legal practice, litigation and teaching, building his professional life “brick by brick, case by case, student by student.” Years later, when the House of Representatives asked him to serve as one of the private prosecutors in the impeachment proceedings against Vice President Duterte, the ambition first formed while watching the Estrada trial had come full circle. The account offered RCM members a glimpse into how an event witnessed by a young student decades ago would eventually influence the direction of his professional life — until he was no longer watching an impeachment from outside the arena but participating in another chapter of the country’s constitutional history. Justice for the Powerful and the Powerless The moral center of Ligutan’s address emerged from a story far removed from the halls of political power. He recalled reading a news report about a public school teacher who was convicted and ordered imprisoned for 11 years for stealing ₱5,000. The case prompted him to ask what justice demands when those accused are powerful and the amounts involved are exponentially greater. “If the law can be this unforgiving, this absolute toward a teacher who stole ₱5,000,” he asked, what should happen when the accused is powerful and the sums involved reach hundreds of millions of pesos? For Ligutan, equality before the law meant that justice could not become harsh toward the powerless while becoming timid in the presence of power. “The true test of justice is not how it treats the powerless, but how it confronts the powerful,” he said. He distilled the principle further: “The law must be big enough to protect the small, and strong enough to confront the big.” From there, Ligutan widened the discussion beyond the impeachment itself. Who guards those entrusted with guarding the country’s institutions? Who protects the public coffers? Who ensures that confidential funds remain confidential for legitimate reasons rather than becoming mechanisms for concealing wrongdoing? And who ensures that accountability does not stop with ordinary government employees, barangay treasurers, or school teachers but extends to the highest offices of the land? Ligutan also rejected the idea that pursuing one major controversy should require ignoring another. Referring to allegations involving flood-control projects alongside controversies over confidential funds, he argued that government should pursue wrongdoing wherever evidence leads. His message was clear: accountability loses its moral credibility when its application depends upon the political identity of the person involved. The People Are Not Mere Spectators Ligutan further argued that the significance of the impeachment extends far beyond the Vice President. Its consequences, he said, touch the “architecture” of Philippine democracy, the credibility of institutions, and the future direction of governance. A nation incapable of holding its leaders accountable, he warned, cannot move forward. But responsibility, he emphasized, does not rest solely upon prosecutors, defense lawyers, legislators, or senator judges. The Filipino people also have a role. Every document, witness, video, audit report, and piece of evidence presented in the proceedings should challenge citizens to think critically rather than simply choose a political camp, he said. Citizens should neither assume that every accusation establishes guilt nor automatically dismiss accusations as persecution. Instead, Ligutan urged the public to weigh the evidence and demand substantive answers, describing this responsibility as part of the people’s right to determine the kind of society they wish to live in and eventually leave to their children. For the Rotary Club of Manila, the discussion resonated naturally with the principles of the Four-Way Test, particularly its first two questions: Is it the truth? Is it fair to all concerned? The Four-Way Test offers no verdict on an impeachment proceeding. But its emphasis on truth and fairness provides a useful civic discipline: facts must be examined, evidence must be weighed, and standards should remain consistent regardless of the personalities or political affiliations involved. The Danger of ‘Moral Favoritism’ Near the end of his address, Ligutan turned to what he described as a quieter danger confronting Philippine society: “moral favoritism.” He questioned whether wrongdoing should ever become acceptable simply because people happen to admire or support the individual accused of committing it. Such selective morality, he suggested, risks weakening the very standards citizens expect government to uphold. The larger question, he said, was whether the country would regress or “turn the page” and move forward. For Ligutan, the impeachment was therefore not merely a legal contest between prosecution and defense. He framed it as a struggle over accountability and equality before the law, over progress rather than regression, and ultimately as “a fight for the soul of the nation.” RCM as a Forum for Consequential Conversations The presence of Ligutan at the RCM podium also underscored the Club’s continuing role as a civic forum where difficult national issues may be discussed without requiring institutional endorsement of a speaker’s position. The Rotary Club of Manila is not a political party, and hosting a prosecutor, public official, opposition figure, advocate, or critic does not in itself signify the Club’s adoption of that individual’s views. Rather, such meetings provide members an opportunity to hear consequential arguments firsthand, subject them to questions, and arrive at their own informed conclusions. That tradition was evident during the open forum that followed Ligutan’s address, with the official program providing for an exchange between the guest speaker and members before the presentation of the Club’s Certificate of Appreciation and adjournment. For more than a century, the Rotary Club of Manila has brought presidents, legislators, jurists, diplomats, business leaders, academics, reformers, artists and advocates before its membership. They have not always agreed with one another, nor have RCM members necessarily agreed with every position expressed from its podium. The enduring value of the forum lies precisely in that independence. On August 20, the Club heard from a lawyer directly involved in one of the most consequential constitutional controversies of the day. Behind the private prosecutor, however, was also the story of a college student who had once watched another impeachment trial through a television screen and quietly imagined that he might someday enter that arena himself. Decades later, he did. And inside Makati Shangri-La that Thursday afternoon, the discussion ultimately transcended the fate of any one public official. It returned instead to a principle that applies equally to government, civic institutions, business and individual citizenship: When power meets accountability, the true test is whether the same principles still apply regardless of who holds that power. Transformative Medical Mission 2026 PD Henry Go With Rotarian Nunnatus Jr. Cortez, President of the Rotary Club of Makati East, and our fellow RCMer, Rami Chahwan, during the Transformative Medical Mission 2026, held on August 22, 2026, at Lyceum University Laguna. Co-hosted by the Rotary Club of Manila, several other Rotary clubs and civic organizations, and the Chahwan family, the medical mission brought together doctors, nurses, medical professionals, Rotarians, volunteers, and community partners in a shared commitment to serve. I participated in this meaningful mission, representing the Rotary Club of Manila as Chair of its Rotary Community Corps. Approximately 1,200 patients benefited from a wide range of free medical services, including chest X rays and sputum examinations, dental services, blood extraction and laboratory tests, cardiovascular and heart health screening, women’s health and wellness services, endoscopy and colonoscopy, minor surgery, and surgical procedures for hernia and cleft lip. Beyond the numbers and the range of medical services, what made the day truly meaningful was seeing people come together to make healthcare accessible to those who may otherwise have difficulty obtaining it. Every consultation, examination, procedure, and act of assistance represented more than medical care. It was an expression of compassion— of giving people not only treatment, but also the reassurance that they are cared for and not forgotten. As Rotarians, we often speak of “Service Above Self.” On this day, that principle came alive through the generosity of the medical professionals who shared their expertise, the volunteers who gave their time, the organizations that provided support, and everyone who helped make the mission possible. Editorial: The Lonely Fight  ONE of the most beloved musicals both onstage and on-screen is The Sound of Music, which won five Tony Awards and five Oscars, including Best Musical and Best Picture. Its songs and storyline have since become a staple in many a school production, such that many viewers gloss over the social messages embedded in it. Set amid the harsh realities of impending war and the emergence of a fascist, repressive regime, it offers a lens onto realities of that point in history as seen through the life of a relatable family. The protagonists chose to sacrifice status, comfort, security, and potentially their own lives, to stand up for what they believed was right, despite urging from close friends to comply, ignore, and look out for oneself - a position taken by so many from that milieu. Recent developments in the Philippines also reveal harsh realities: the aftermath of a bloody drug war, a political landscape dominated by dynasties, natural disasters that transform communities into lakes and neighborhoods into raging rivers, public funds allegedly finding their way from infrastructure projects into suitcases if the stories are to be believed, and an infectious indifference to a bullying neighbor's encroachment upon the nation's patrimony. Meanwhile, solo parents raise families with little institutional support. LGBTQIA+ Filipinos still have no national law shielding them from discrimination. The elderly, already deemed uninsurable, do not get much from what was supposed to be universal healthcare. Filipino pupils and students, Jose Rizal's fair hope for the Motherland, rank among the lowest in the region, if not the world, when it comes to basic competencies such as reading and comprehension. Into this landscape steps Senator Ana Theresia Navarro Hontiveros Baraquel, Risa Hontiveros to most Filipinos, a figure whose career has been defined less by political comfort than by persistence in uncomfortable rooms. Incidentally, she performed in Repertory Philippines' '80s production of The Sound of Music alongside Leah Salonga, siblings Menchu and Raymond Lauchengco, and Monique Wilson. Hontiveros's legislative record is not built on speeches alone. She served as a young Akbayan party-list representative in the House from 2004 to 2010, and is now in her second term in the Senate - a term that currently includes a role as Senator-Judge in the impeachment trial of the Vice President. She focused early on health and social justice groundwork for a Senate career that would later produce the Expanded Maternity Leave Law (RA 11210) and the Expanded Solo Parents Welfare Act (RA 11861), a measure she authored after becoming a solo parent to four children herself following her husband's death in 2005. It is rare for a law to be so plainly autobiographical; rarer still for that law to pass. The Safe Spaces Act (RA 11313), which protects Filipinos - especially women from gender-based harassment in public spaces, the Anti-Online Sexual Abuse or Exploitation of Children Law (RA 11930), which boosts government efforts to end online abuse and exploitation of Filipino children, and the Mental Health Law (RA 11036), which provides the first legal framework for mental health care in the country, are the fruits of her advocacy on behalf of the vulnerable. Her most stubborn fight, however, remains unfinished. For years she has authored and re-filed the SOGIESC Equality Bill, seeking basic protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity. The measure has repeatedly stalled, blocked by those who favored a vaguer alternative and referred back to committee. What distinguishes Hontiveros from many of her colleagues is not simply what she has proposed, but the isolation in which she has often had to propose it. During her first term as a senator, she was a vocal critic - one of very few - of the Duterte administration and its war on drugs. After the 2022 elections swept in a Senate dominated by the Uniteam, she emerged as the lone opposition candidate to win a seat — a distinction that sounds like an honor but functions, in practice, as a burden. Without a reliable bloc, her leverage comes almost entirely from committee work, procedural persistence, and public pressure rather than vote-counting. That isolation has abated with developments after the 2025 mid-term elections and the leadership changes in the Senate. She is now a member of the majority, chairperson of three major committees, and a more audible fiscalizer both on the Senate floor and at the hearings of the powerful Commission on Appointments. However, the fight rages on, whether over press freedom, the West Philippine Sea, or dismissive remarks about her lack of a law degree. Being the last woman standing has its costs: red tagging, condescension, even death threats, and the simple exhaustion of relitigating the same fights year after year with little or no reinforcement. That track record — legislative substance paired with unwavering persistence — is precisely what her supporters now cite as she weighs a 2028 presidential run. The "Risa Na" movement, launched by Akbayan and allied groups, argues that her record of advocacy and integrity makes her a natural standard-bearer for a campaign still searching for a single, winnable candidate. The obstacles, though, are real and worth stating plainly. Early polling has been unkind: surveys through mid-2026 place her well behind frontrunner Vice President Sara Duterte, sometimes by margins as wide as 60 to 21 percent in head-to-head matchups. She has also trailed other opposition figures like Leni Robredo and Bam Aquino in multi candidate surveys. Critics — including allies of the Dutertes — have dismissed her confrontational Senate style as calculated positioning for exactly this moment, rather than principle. And the lay of the land remains unclear, with no consensus yet on whether Hontiveros, rather than someone else, should be the opposition's unifying figure. Whether her allies’ efforts translate into a viable campaign remains to be seen. What is not in question is the labor that precedes it: that of a legislator who has spent over two decades converting personal and political conviction into law, often as the only person in the room willing to do so. Whether Philippine voters reward that exertion with the presidency, or whether the numbers simply prove too steep to overcome, remains one of the more consequential open questions of the 2028 race. SENATOR Risa Hontiveros is known for her tireless work in promoting public health, women's rights, and the welfare of the Filipino family. She is a multi awarded public servant, community organizer, and journalist elected to the Senate in 2016.

In her first term, she successfully championed landmark laws, including the historic Expanded Maternity Leave Law that gives working moms 105 days of paid maternity leave, and the Philippine-Mental Health Law, the country's first ever national policy to care for Filipinos' mental health.

As a longtime health advocate, she pushed for the passage of the Universal Healthcare Law and the Expanded Anti-hospital Deposit Law to ensure the Filipino family’s well-being before profit, and to make health more accessible to all.
Even amidst the pandemic, Senator Risa pushed for free dialysis for senior citizens and for the timely release of benefits and salaries for health workers.

As Chairperson of the Senate Committee on Women, Senator Hontiveros also authored the Safe Streets and Public Spaces Law or the Bawal Bastos Law that protects all Filipinos, particularly women, from gender-based harassment in the streets, public transportation, schools, and the workplace. During the biggest public health crisis of our time, she also pushed for the Maternity Benefit for Women in the Informal Economy Act, to help ease the multiple burdens of women exacerbated by the pandemic.

Senator Hontiveros worked on expanding the Solo Parents' Act to further help single moms and dads in providing for their families. The Senator is also pushing for an increase on the monthly pension of senior citizens through the Lingap Para Kayo Lolo at Lola Bill.
Even before becoming a legislator, in 2005, she was one of 27 Filipinas who earned a nomination to the prestigious Nobel Peace Prize for her work in the peace movement.
Senator Hontiveros is a loving and hands-on solo mother to 4 children Kiko, Issa, Helena and Sinta.

THE Rotary Club of Manila placed one of the country’s most consequential constitutional issues at the center of its civic forum on August 20, 2026, as Atty. Amando Virgil D. Ligutan, Private Prosecutor of the House Prosecution Panel in the impeachment proceedings against Vice President Sara Duterte, addressed the Club’s 7th Weekly Membership Meeting of Rotary Year 2026–2027 at Makati Shangri-La, Manila.

With RCM Director Atty. Teodoro Alejandro Y. Kalaw IV serving as moderator, the gathering moved beyond the personalities and political divisions surrounding the impeachment and into a broader examination of accountability, public trust, equality before the law, and the resilience of Philippine democratic institutions.

Ligutan opened his address by acknowledging the Rotary Club of Manila as an institution whose members have, for generations, helped shape the country’s civic, economic, and moral landscape. An invitation to speak before Rotary, he said, demanded more than the delivery of prepared remarks; it required an accounting of one’s principles, beliefs, and convictions.
He then described the Philippines as being at an important crossroads, confronting profound questions about governance, accountability, and the durability of democracy.

According to Ligutan, these questions transcend partisan politics because they test whether institutions are strong enough to withstand scrutiny, whether leaders are willing to accept oversight, and whether democratic systems remain capable of correcting themselves.

“Accountability is not politics even when politics tries to make it look that way,” he said, describing it instead as a democratic necessity and impeachment as one of the constitutional mechanisms through which it is enforced.

Ligutan stressed that impeachment should neither be treated as spectacle nor as an instrument for merely targeting political opponents. Rather, he described it as a serious constitutional inquiry into the conduct of officials occupying the highest levels of government.
At its core, he said, impeachment asks a solemn question: Are the country’s highest officials still worthy of the public trust?
A Call That Changed the Course of His Career
Beyond the constitutional arguments, Ligutan gave RCM members a personal account of how he became involved in the impeachment proceedings.
He recalled receiving a telephone call from a priest sometime in December 2024 asking whether he would help file an impeachment complaint against Vice President Duterte.
Ligutan said he did not hesitate.

He subsequently represented a group of priests, nuns, civic leaders, and lawyers seeking accountability from the Vice President. When the first impeachment proceeding was dismissed, Ligutan said the setback gave him time to reflect more deeply on the gravity of his responsibility and the reasons behind his decision to pursue the case.
Months later, the group approached him again.
“Attorney, will you lawyer for us once more?” he recalled being asked.
Again, his answer was yes.

For Ligutan, accountability could not be optional, seasonal, or dependent upon convenience. It demanded persistence and sacrifice, particularly when those being subjected to scrutiny occupied positions of considerable power.

He argued that the impeachment therefore represented more than a trial of Vice President Duterte. It was also a test of the country’s systems, democratic norms, expectations of leadership, and collective commitment to truth.

Even the senator-judges who would sit in judgment, Ligutan argued, faced their own institutional test: whether they would permit transparency, withstand political pressures, and remain faithful to both the letter and spirit of the Constitution.
A Dream Born During the Estrada Impeachment
One of the most personal moments of Ligutan’s address came when he traced his interest in accountability to another defining chapter in Philippine political history.

As a young college student, Ligutan watched the impeachment trial of former President Joseph Estrada unfold on national television. He remembered watching the prosecutors walk out and the senators vote 11–10 against opening the controversial second envelope.
While millions of Filipinos watched the same historic events, the proceedings left a particular impression on the young Ligutan. “Someday, I want to be there,” he remembered thinking.
“Someday, I want to stand in that arena. Someday, I want to help hold power accountable.”

At the time, Ligutan said he had neither political connections nor powerful patrons. He instead pursued the long route of study, legal practice, litigation and teaching, building his professional life “brick by brick, case by case, student by student.”

Years later, when the House of Representatives asked him to serve as one of the private prosecutors in the impeachment proceedings against Vice President Duterte, the ambition first formed while watching the Estrada trial had come full circle.

The account offered RCM members a glimpse into how an event witnessed by a young student decades ago would eventually influence the direction of his professional life — until he was no longer watching an impeachment from outside the arena but participating in another chapter of the country’s constitutional history.
Justice for the Powerful and the Powerless

The moral center of Ligutan’s address emerged from a story far removed from the halls of political power. He recalled reading a news report about a public school teacher who was convicted and ordered imprisoned for 11 years for stealing ₱5,000.
The case prompted him to ask what justice demands when those accused are powerful and the amounts involved are exponentially greater.

“If the law can be this unforgiving, this absolute toward a teacher who stole ₱5,000,” he asked, what should happen when the accused is powerful and the sums involved reach hundreds of millions of pesos?
For Ligutan, equality before the law meant that justice could not become harsh toward the powerless while becoming timid in the presence of power.
“The true test of justice is not how it treats the powerless, but how it confronts the powerful,” he said.
He distilled the principle further: “The law must be big enough to protect the small, and strong enough to confront the big.”
From there, Ligutan widened the discussion beyond the impeachment itself.

Who guards those entrusted with guarding the country’s institutions? Who protects the public coffers? Who ensures that confidential funds remain confidential for legitimate reasons rather than becoming mechanisms for concealing wrongdoing? And who ensures that accountability does not stop with ordinary government employees, barangay treasurers, or school teachers but extends to the highest offices of the land?

Ligutan also rejected the idea that pursuing one major controversy should require ignoring another. Referring to allegations involving flood-control projects alongside controversies over confidential funds, he argued that government should pursue wrongdoing wherever evidence leads.
His message was clear: accountability loses its moral credibility when its application depends upon the political identity of the person involved.
The People Are Not Mere Spectators
Ligutan further argued that the significance of the impeachment extends far beyond the Vice President.

Its consequences, he said, touch the “architecture” of Philippine democracy, the credibility of institutions, and the future direction of governance. A nation incapable of holding its leaders accountable, he warned, cannot move forward.
But responsibility, he emphasized, does not rest solely upon prosecutors, defense lawyers, legislators, or senator judges.
The Filipino people also have a role.

Every document, witness, video, audit report, and piece of evidence presented in the proceedings should challenge citizens to think critically rather than simply choose a political camp, he said. Citizens should neither assume that every accusation establishes guilt nor automatically dismiss accusations as persecution.

Instead, Ligutan urged the public to weigh the evidence and demand substantive answers, describing this responsibility as part of the people’s right to determine the kind of society they wish to live in and eventually leave to their children.
For the Rotary Club of Manila, the discussion resonated naturally with the principles of the Four-Way Test, particularly its first two questions: Is it the truth? Is it fair to all concerned?

The Four-Way Test offers no verdict on an impeachment proceeding. But its emphasis on truth and fairness provides a useful civic discipline: facts must be examined, evidence must be weighed, and standards should remain consistent regardless of the personalities or political affiliations involved.
The Danger of ‘Moral Favoritism’
Near the end of his address, Ligutan turned to what he described as a quieter danger confronting Philippine society: “moral favoritism.”

He questioned whether wrongdoing should ever become acceptable simply because people happen to admire or support the individual accused of committing it. Such selective morality, he suggested, risks weakening the very standards citizens expect government to uphold.
The larger question, he said, was whether the country would regress or “turn the page” and move forward.

For Ligutan, the impeachment was therefore not merely a legal contest between prosecution and defense. He framed it as a struggle over accountability and equality before the law, over progress rather than regression, and ultimately as “a fight for the soul of the nation.”
RCM as a Forum for Consequential Conversations

The presence of Ligutan at the RCM podium also underscored the Club’s continuing role as a civic forum where difficult national issues may be discussed without requiring institutional endorsement of a speaker’s position.

The Rotary Club of Manila is not a political party, and hosting a prosecutor, public official, opposition figure, advocate, or critic does not in itself signify the Club’s adoption of that individual’s views. Rather, such meetings provide members an opportunity to hear consequential arguments firsthand, subject them to questions, and arrive at their own informed conclusions.

That tradition was evident during the open forum that followed Ligutan’s address, with the official program providing for an exchange between the guest speaker and members before the presentation of the Club’s Certificate of Appreciation and adjournment.

For more than a century, the Rotary Club of Manila has brought presidents, legislators, jurists, diplomats, business leaders, academics, reformers, artists and advocates before its membership. They have not always agreed with one another, nor have RCM members necessarily agreed with every position expressed from its podium.

The enduring value of the forum lies precisely in that independence. On August 20, the Club heard from a lawyer directly involved in one of the most consequential constitutional controversies of the day. Behind the private prosecutor, however, was also the story of a college student who had once watched another impeachment trial through a television screen and quietly imagined that he might someday enter that arena himself.
Decades later, he did.

And inside Makati Shangri-La that Thursday afternoon, the discussion ultimately transcended the fate of any one public official. It returned instead to a principle that applies equally to government, civic institutions, business and individual citizenship:
When power meets accountability, the true test is whether the same principles still apply regardless of who holds that power.

With Rotarian Nunnatus Jr. Cortez, President of the Rotary Club of Makati East, and our fellow RCMer, Rami Chahwan, during the Transformative Medical Mission 2026, held on August 22, 2026, at Lyceum University Laguna.

Co-hosted by the Rotary Club of Manila, several other Rotary clubs and civic organizations, and the Chahwan family, the medical mission brought together doctors, nurses, medical professionals, Rotarians, volunteers, and community partners in a shared commitment to serve.
I participated in this meaningful mission, representing the Rotary Club of Manila as Chair of its Rotary Community Corps.

Approximately 1,200 patients benefited from a wide range of free medical services, including chest X rays and sputum examinations, dental services, blood extraction and laboratory tests, cardiovascular and heart health screening, women’s health and wellness services, endoscopy and colonoscopy, minor surgery, and surgical procedures for hernia and cleft lip.

Beyond the numbers and the range of medical services, what made the day truly meaningful was seeing people come together to make healthcare accessible to those who may otherwise have difficulty obtaining it.

Every consultation, examination, procedure, and act of assistance represented more than medical care. It was an expression of compassion— of giving people not only treatment, but also the reassurance that they are cared for and not forgotten.

As Rotarians, we often speak of “Service Above Self.” On this day, that principle came alive through the generosity of the medical professionals who shared their expertise, the volunteers who gave their time, the organizations that provided support, and everyone who helped make the mission possible.

ONE of the most beloved musicals both onstage and on-screen is The Sound of Music, which won five Tony Awards and five Oscars, including Best Musical and Best Picture. Its songs and storyline have since become a staple in many a school production, such that many viewers gloss over the social messages embedded in it. Set amid the harsh realities of impending war and the emergence of a fascist, repressive regime, it offers a lens onto realities of that point in history as seen through the life of a relatable family.

The protagonists chose to sacrifice status, comfort, security, and potentially their own lives, to stand up for what they believed was right, despite urging from close friends to comply, ignore, and look out for oneself - a position taken by so many from that milieu.

Recent developments in the Philippines also reveal harsh realities: the aftermath of a bloody drug war, a political landscape dominated by dynasties, natural disasters that transform communities into lakes and neighborhoods into raging rivers, public funds allegedly finding their way from infrastructure projects into suitcases if the stories are to be believed, and an infectious indifference to a bullying neighbor's encroachment upon the nation's patrimony.

Meanwhile, solo parents raise families with little institutional support. LGBTQIA+ Filipinos still have no national law shielding them from discrimination. The elderly, already deemed uninsurable, do not get much from what was supposed to be universal healthcare. Filipino pupils and students, Jose Rizal's fair hope for the Motherland, rank among the lowest in the region, if not the world, when it comes to basic competencies such as reading and comprehension.

Into this landscape steps Senator Ana Theresia Navarro Hontiveros Baraquel, Risa Hontiveros to most Filipinos, a figure whose career has been defined less by political comfort than by persistence in uncomfortable rooms. Incidentally, she performed in Repertory Philippines' '80s production of The Sound of Music alongside Leah Salonga, siblings Menchu and Raymond Lauchengco, and Monique Wilson.

Hontiveros's legislative record is not built on speeches alone. She served as a young Akbayan party-list representative in the House from 2004 to 2010, and is now in her second term in the Senate - a term that currently includes a role as Senator-Judge in the impeachment trial of the Vice President. She focused early on health and social justice groundwork for a Senate career that would later produce the Expanded Maternity Leave Law (RA 11210) and the Expanded Solo Parents Welfare Act (RA 11861), a measure she authored after becoming a solo parent to four children herself following her husband's death in 2005. It is rare for a law to be so plainly autobiographical; rarer still for that law to pass.

The Safe Spaces Act (RA 11313), which protects Filipinos - especially women from gender-based harassment in public spaces, the Anti-Online Sexual Abuse or Exploitation of Children Law (RA 11930), which boosts government efforts to end online abuse and exploitation of Filipino children, and the Mental Health Law (RA 11036), which provides the first legal framework for mental health care in the country, are the fruits of her advocacy on behalf of the vulnerable. Her most stubborn fight, however, remains unfinished. For years she has authored and re-filed the SOGIESC Equality Bill, seeking basic protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity. The measure has repeatedly stalled, blocked by those who favored a vaguer alternative and referred back to committee.

What distinguishes Hontiveros from many of her colleagues is not simply what she has proposed, but the isolation in which she has often had to propose it. During her first term as a senator, she was a vocal critic - one of very few - of the Duterte administration and its war on drugs. After the 2022 elections swept in a Senate dominated by the Uniteam, she emerged as the lone opposition candidate to win a seat — a distinction that sounds like an honor but functions, in practice, as a burden. Without a reliable bloc, her leverage comes almost entirely from committee work, procedural persistence, and public pressure rather than vote-counting.

That isolation has abated with developments after the 2025 mid-term elections and the leadership changes in the Senate. She is now a member of the majority, chairperson of three major committees, and a more audible fiscalizer both on the Senate floor and at the hearings of the powerful Commission on Appointments.

However, the fight rages on, whether over press freedom, the West Philippine Sea, or dismissive remarks about her lack of a law degree. Being the last woman standing has its costs: red tagging, condescension, even death threats, and the simple exhaustion of relitigating the same fights year after year with little or no reinforcement.

That track record — legislative substance paired with unwavering persistence — is precisely what her supporters now cite as she weighs a 2028 presidential run. The "Risa Na" movement, launched by Akbayan and allied groups, argues that her record of advocacy and integrity makes her a natural standard-bearer for a campaign still searching for a single, winnable candidate.

The obstacles, though, are real and worth stating plainly. Early polling has been unkind: surveys through mid-2026 place her well behind frontrunner Vice President Sara Duterte, sometimes by margins as wide as 60 to 21 percent in head-to-head matchups. She has also trailed other opposition figures like Leni Robredo and Bam Aquino in multi candidate surveys. Critics — including allies of the Dutertes — have dismissed her confrontational Senate style as calculated positioning for exactly this moment, rather than principle. And the lay of the land remains unclear, with no consensus yet on whether Hontiveros, rather than someone else, should be the opposition's unifying figure.

Whether her allies’ efforts translate into a viable campaign remains to be seen. What is not in question is the labor that precedes it: that of a legislator who has spent over two decades converting personal and political conviction into law, often as the only person in the room willing to do so. Whether Philippine voters reward that exertion with the presidency, or whether the numbers simply prove too steep to overcome, remains one of the more consequential open questions of the 2028 race.
